name: 45-Degree Back Extension with Barbell
description: A weighted hyperextension exercise performed in the 45-degree back extension machine with a barbell held behind the head or at the chest. Adding barbell weight significantly increases the posterior chain loading, developing the glutes, hamstrings, and erector spinae simultaneously.

execution.starting_position: Position yourself in the 45-degree hyperextension bench with the pad across the hips. Hold a barbell plate at chest or a barbell behind the neck.
execution.setup_instructions: Set the hyperextension bench correctly. Load a barbell held at chest height or position a plate at the chest.
steps: Step 1: Lower the torso forward into full hip flexion, maintaining a neutral spine.
Step 2: Drive the hips into the pad and extend the torso upward using glute and hamstring strength.
Step 3: Extend to a neutral spine position at the top — do not hyperextend the lumbar.
Step 4: Lower back down under control.
execution.breathing_instructions: Inhale on the descent. Exhale on the extension.
common_mistakes: Hyperextending the lumbar spine at the top
Using momentum to swing the torso up
safety_considerations: Stop the ascent at a neutral spine position, not beyond it
execution.range_of_motion_guidance: Full hip flexion at the bottom. Neutral spine at the top — not hyperextended.
coaching_cues: Drive through the hips, not the lower back
Stop when the body is in a straight line

name: 90-90 Hip Stretch
description: The 90-90 hip stretch is a seated floor position in which both hips are bent to 90 degrees in different planes — one leg in external rotation in front and one in internal rotation behind. This position simultaneously loads the internal rotators of the front hip and the external rotators of the rear hip, making it one of the most comprehensive hip mobility exercises available. It addresses the full hip rotation spectrum in a single position.

execution.starting_position: Sit on the floor. Place the front leg with shin parallel to the front of the mat, knee and hip at 90 degrees. Place the rear leg to the side with the shin parallel to the side of the mat, also at 90 degrees.
execution.setup_instructions: Use a mat. Beginners may need a folded blanket under the front hip if it rises significantly off the floor.
steps: Step 1: Sit on the floor and position both legs in the 90-90 configuration.
Step 2: Sit tall with the spine upright. Both hips should ideally be in contact with the floor, though the rear hip will be elevated for many beginners.
Step 3: To stretch the front hip (internal rotation side): hinge the torso forward over the front shin, maintaining a long spine.
Step 4: To stretch the rear hip (external rotation side): lean toward the rear leg's shin.
Step 5: Hold each direction 30–90 seconds, then switch sides.
execution.breathing_instructions: Breathe deeply. Each exhale allows the hips to relax further toward the floor.
common_mistakes: One hip lifting excessively off the floor, which reduces the hip joint stretch
Collapsing the torso sideways rather than maintaining spine length
Moving too quickly between positions
safety_considerations: If knee discomfort occurs, adjust the degree of hip rotation or avoid if symptomatic
Do not force either hip to the floor — work at the available range
execution.range_of_motion_guidance: The goal is for both hip bones to eventually touch the floor. This may take weeks to months of consistent practice.
execution.tempo_recommendations: Hold 30–90 seconds per position per side. 2–3 rounds.
coaching_cues: Sit tall first — then lean
Press both hip bones toward the floor
Breathe wide into the hip that is working

name: Ab Wheel Rollout
description: The ab wheel rollout is an anti-extension core exercise in which the lifter rolls an ab wheel forward from a kneeling position and then uses core tension to pull it back. It is one of the most effective exercises for training the transverse abdominis and rectus abdominis under significant load, as the lever arm created by the extended arms is very long.

execution.starting_position: Kneel on the floor holding the ab wheel with both hands. Place the wheel directly in front of your knees. Core braced, back flat.
execution.setup_instructions: Beginners should use a limited range of motion (rolling forward 1–2 feet) before progressing to a full rollout. A mat under the knees is recommended.
steps: Roll the wheel forward, extending the arms and hips while maintaining a rigid spine.
Go as far as your core can maintain a neutral spine — do not let the lower back sag.
Pull the wheel back toward the knees using core contraction and lats.
execution.breathing_instructions: Exhale during the rollout. Inhale on the return or hold breath with a brace.
common_mistakes: Allowing the lower back to sag and hyperextend during the rollout
Starting at too long a range before the core is strong enough
safety_considerations: Lower back pain may result if the core is not strong enough — start with partial rollouts
execution.range_of_motion_guidance: Roll out until the body is as extended as can be controlled, then return.
coaching_cues: Brace like you are about to take a punch before each rep
Do not let your hips sag — your body is a rigid board from knees to shoulders

name: Ab Wheel Rollout from Feet
description: The standing ab wheel rollout, the most advanced variation of the rollout performed with straight legs from a standing position. The lifter rolls out to nearly horizontal then returns without touching the floor. This demands extraordinary anti-extension core strength.

execution.starting_position: Set up for Ab Wheel Rollout from Feet in proper position.
execution.setup_instructions: Prepare body and equipment for Ab Wheel Rollout from Feet.
steps: Step 1: Stand upright holding ab wheel at hips. Feet shoulder-width apart.
Step 2: Bend forward and roll wheel out in a controlled arc.
Step 3: Lower body nearly to horizontal position while maintaining rigid core.
Step 4: Pull wheel back using core and hip flexors to return to standing.
execution.breathing_instructions: Breathe steadily; never hold breath during static holds.
common_mistakes: Hyperextending lower back at bottom
Attempting without kneeling version mastery
safety_considerations: Build prerequisite strength before attempting advanced variations.
Stop if joint pain occurs.
execution.range_of_motion_guidance: Full range of motion with control at all times.
coaching_cues: Keep spine neutral throughout
Master kneeling rollouts before standing

name: Ab Wheel Rollout with Pause
description: An ab wheel rollout with a deliberate pause at the extended position before returning. The pause eliminates the elastic energy stored in the return and forces the core muscles to restart the return from a maximally stretched position. This significantly increases the training effect.

execution.starting_position: Set up for Ab Wheel Rollout with Pause in proper position.
execution.setup_instructions: Prepare body and equipment for Ab Wheel Rollout with Pause.
steps: Step 1: Begin kneeling with ab wheel. Roll out to nearly full extension.
Step 2: Hold the extended position for 3-5 seconds.
Step 3: Without bouncing, engage core to pull wheel back to knees.
Step 4: Complete reps with pause on each extension.
execution.breathing_instructions: Breathe steadily; never hold breath during static holds.
common_mistakes: Bouncing from the extended position
Hyperextending lower back at pause
safety_considerations: Build prerequisite strength before attempting advanced variations.
Stop if joint pain occurs.
execution.range_of_motion_guidance: Full range of motion with control at all times.
coaching_cues: The pause reveals your true rollout capacity
Spine neutral at the pause

name: Ab Wheel Rollout Single-Leg Extension
description: An ab wheel rollout with one leg extended straight while the other knee stays on the ground. The asymmetrical leg position creates a rotational challenge in addition to the standard anti-extension demand. This bridges the gap between kneeling and standing rollouts.

execution.starting_position: Set up for Ab Wheel Rollout Single-Leg Extension in proper position.
execution.setup_instructions: Prepare body and equipment for Ab Wheel Rollout Single-Leg Extension.
steps: Step 1: Kneel with one knee down and opposite leg extended back.
Step 2: Roll ab wheel forward while keeping extended leg straight.
Step 3: Roll to near-full extension maintaining rigid body.
Step 4: Pull back to start using core.
execution.breathing_instructions: Breathe steadily; never hold breath during static holds.
common_mistakes: Rotating toward the extended leg
Lower back sagging
safety_considerations: Build prerequisite strength before attempting advanced variations.
Stop if joint pain occurs.
execution.range_of_motion_guidance: Full range of motion with control at all times.
coaching_cues: Fight rotation throughout
More difficult than bilateral kneeling version

name: Air Bike Sprint — Assault / Echo Bike
description: The air bike (Assault, Echo, or Airdyne style) uses a large fan wheel that creates resistance proportional to pedalling speed — the harder you work, the more resistance is generated, making it impossible to outpace the machine. The dual-action design engages both the lower body (pedalling) and upper body (pushing and pulling the moving handlebars) simultaneously, recruiting the quadriceps, gluteus maximus, anterior and posterior deltoids, and pectorals in every stroke. Sprint intervals on the air bike are considered among the most demanding conditioning tools in existence and produce maximal cardiovascular stress in very short durations.

execution.starting_position: Adjust the seat so the knees are slightly bent at the bottom of the pedal stroke. Grip both moving handles. Sit upright with the core braced.
execution.setup_instructions: Set any desired calorie or time targets on the monitor. Clip in or use the flat pedal cages. The machine requires no resistance setting — it self-regulates based on output.
steps: Step 1: Warm up for 2–3 minutes at a moderate pace, alternating between legs-only and arms-only before combining both.
Step 2: Sprint at absolute maximum effort — push and pull the handles hard while pedalling as fast as possible. Duration: 10–20 seconds.
Step 3: Rest completely or pedal very slowly for 40–60 seconds.
Step 4: Repeat 6–10 rounds.
Step 5: Cool down for 3–5 minutes at an easy pace.
execution.breathing_instructions: During maximal sprints, breathe as powerfully as possible. Do not hold the breath. During rest, focus on slowing heart rate with controlled diaphragmatic breathing.
common_mistakes: Sprinting for too long — 10–20 seconds is usually the ceiling for truly maximal output on an air bike
Using arms only or legs only rather than combining both for maximum calorie and cardiovascular output
Not resting long enough between efforts, which prevents true maximal intensity on subsequent bouts
safety_considerations: The fan blades spin at high speed — keep fingers and clothing away from the fan housing
The air bike can be extremely demanding on the cardiovascular system — beginners should start with moderate efforts before attempting all-out sprints
execution.range_of_motion_guidance: Full push-and-pull through the handlebar range of motion. Full pedal stroke through the bottom of the arc.
execution.tempo_recommendations: Protocol 1 (maximal): 10 seconds max effort / 50 seconds rest × 10. Protocol 2 (Tabata-style): 20 seconds hard / 10 seconds rest × 8. Protocol 3: 30 calories as fast as possible / rest 2 minutes × 5.
coaching_cues: Push AND pull the handles — both phases generate power
Drive the elbows back hard — think of a sprint arm swing
Keep the core tight to transfer power from legs to arms

name: Alternate Leg Bound
description: Alternate leg bounding is an advanced plyometric drill in which the athlete performs exaggerated, explosive strides — alternating single-leg push-offs and landings across the ground with maximum stride length and height. Each stride resembles a running step taken with maximum power output. It develops unilateral explosive hip extension, stride power, and the stretch-shortening cycle in the hip extensors and plantarflexors, with strong carryover to sprinting acceleration.

execution.starting_position: Begin in a standing position. Transition to movement immediately at the start of the drill.
execution.setup_instructions: Use a flat, non-slip surface with 30–50 meters of clear running space.
steps: Step 1: Begin with a short run-up to initiate momentum.
Step 2: Drive off the right foot explosively, extending fully through the hip, knee, and ankle.
Step 3: Drive the left knee high and forward while the right arm mirrors with an aggressive drive.
Step 4: Land on the left foot and immediately drive off again with equal force.
Step 5: Continue alternating for the prescribed distance, maximizing each stride's length and height.
execution.breathing_instructions: Breathe rhythmically throughout the drill.
common_mistakes: Shuffling rather than bounding — each stride must be a true explosive effort
Insufficient knee lift of the swing leg
Weak arm drive — the arms contribute significantly to stride power
safety_considerations: High demand on the Achilles tendon and hamstrings. Not appropriate in the early season or after lower limb injury.
Progress from single-leg hops before adding alternate leg bounds.
execution.range_of_motion_guidance: Maximum stride length and height. Full hip and knee extension at each takeoff.
execution.tempo_recommendations: Performed for 20–40 meter sets. Maximum effort on each stride.
coaching_cues: Drive the knee up and push the ground away
Swing the arms hard — opposite arm to leg
Cover ground — big, powerful strides

name: Alternating Dumbbell Flat Bench Press
description: The Alternating Dumbbell Press is performed on a flat bench with one arm pressing while the other holds the dumbbell in a fixed position near the chest. The asymmetrical loading creates a significant anti-rotation demand on the core and obliques while one side presses. This variation also allows greater focus on each arm independently and can reveal strength imbalances between sides.

execution.starting_position: Lie on a flat bench holding a dumbbell in each hand at chest level with a neutral or pronated grip.
execution.setup_instructions: Start with both dumbbells at chest level. Begin with the non-dominant arm pressing first to identify any strength asymmetry.
steps: Step 1: Press one dumbbell up to lockout while keeping the other stationary at chest level.
Step 2: Lower the pressing arm back to the chest.
Step 3: Press the other arm while the first holds at chest level.
Step 4: Continue alternating for the prescribed reps per side.
execution.breathing_instructions: Exhale as each arm presses. Inhale as it returns to the chest.
common_mistakes: Letting the resting arm drift away from the body
Rotating the torso toward the pressing arm
safety_considerations: Keep the non-pressing arm safely resting at chest — do not let it fall to the side
Start with a lighter load than your standard dumbbell press
execution.range_of_motion_guidance: Full extension of pressing arm. Non-pressing arm held at 90 degrees of elbow flexion at chest level.
coaching_cues: Fight the rotation — your torso stays still
The resting arm is working too — keep it controlled

name: Alternating Dumbbell Shoulder Press
description: The alternating dumbbell shoulder press involves pressing one dumbbell overhead while the other remains at shoulder height, then alternating. The alternating pattern keeps one shoulder under constant work while the other rests briefly, extending the time under tension for each shoulder and creating an anti-lateral-flexion demand from the alternating load. It bridges the benefits of unilateral and bilateral pressing by maintaining both shoulder positions throughout the set.

execution.starting_position: Sit or stand with a dumbbell in each hand at shoulder height, palms facing forward or inward. Both dumbbells begin in the press-ready position.
execution.setup_instructions: Can be performed seated or standing. When standing, the core demand is higher. Count a rep as one press on each side.
steps: Step 1: Begin with both dumbbells at shoulder height.
Step 2: Press the right dumbbell overhead while keeping the left at shoulder height.
Step 3: As the right descends, begin pressing the left overhead.
Step 4: Continue alternating in a smooth, see-saw rhythm.
Step 5: One rep = one press per side.
execution.breathing_instructions: Breathe naturally with the alternating rhythm — typically exhale on each press.
common_mistakes: Leaning toward the pressing side — maintain an upright posture
Letting the resting arm drop below shoulder height between presses
safety_considerations: If the torso sways significantly, reduce the load
execution.range_of_motion_guidance: Shoulder height to full overhead lockout per arm.
coaching_cues: See-saw rhythm — smooth alternation
Stay upright — no lean
Full lockout each arm

name: Alternating Incline Dumbbell Press
description: The Alternating Incline Dumbbell Press is performed on an incline bench (30-45 degrees), targeting the clavicular head of the pectoralis major, with one arm pressing while the other holds the dumbbell in a fixed position near the upper chest. This anti-rotation, unilateral loading approach builds upper chest strength alongside core stability.

execution.starting_position: Set bench to 30-45 degrees. Hold a dumbbell in each hand at upper chest level. Both elbows bent at approximately 90 degrees.
execution.setup_instructions: Adjust bench angle. Set up the same as an alternating flat dumbbell press but on the incline.
steps: Step 1: Press one dumbbell upward from upper chest to full lockout.
Step 2: Return that arm to the starting position.
Step 3: Press the other arm while holding the first at chest level.
Step 4: Alternate for all prescribed reps.
execution.breathing_instructions: Exhale as each arm presses. Inhale as it returns.
common_mistakes: Steep angle (>45°) turning the movement into a shoulder press
Torso rotation toward the pressing arm
safety_considerations: Keep the stationary dumbbell secure — do not let it drift
Use a lighter load than bilateral incline press
execution.range_of_motion_guidance: Full extension per arm. Stationary arm at 90 degrees of elbow flexion.
coaching_cues: Hips and shoulders stay square to the ceiling
The resting arm is under constant isometric load — treat it seriously

name: Anderson Front Squat
description: A front squat performed from a dead stop with the barbell resting on safety pins inside a power rack, starting from the bottom position. Eliminating the stretch reflex removes elastic energy contribution and forces the lifter to generate strength from a fully stopped position, targeting the sticking point of the squat.

execution.starting_position: Set safety pins inside a power rack at a height corresponding to the bottom of your front squat. Bar rests on the pins. Duck under and take the front rack position.
execution.setup_instructions: Set safety pins at the correct height for your squat depth. Load the bar on the pins, then position yourself under it in the front rack before beginning each rep.
steps: Step 1: Position yourself under the bar in the front rack with elbows high.
Step 2: Brace your core hard from a complete dead-stop position.
Step 3: Drive through your legs to lift the bar off the pins and ascend to full lockout.
Step 4: Lower the bar back to the pins with control. Reset and repeat.
execution.breathing_instructions: Inhale and brace fully before each individual rep. Exhale at lockout.
common_mistakes: Rushing the start — ensure a full brace before each lift off the pins
Dropping the elbows and losing the front rack during the lift
safety_considerations: Use significantly less weight than your regular front squat — no stretch reflex means much less force production
execution.range_of_motion_guidance: Full extension at lockout. Bottom position is predetermined by pin height.
coaching_cues: Dead stop means dead stop
Elbows stay high through the entire lift

name: Barbell Anderson Squat / Bottom-Up Squat
description: The Anderson squat begins at the bottom of the squat position with the bar resting on safety pins inside a power rack. Because there is no eccentric loading or stretch reflex, the lifter must generate force from a dead stop, making it an excellent tool for building strength in the most difficult portion of the squat. It is named after the legendary powerlifter Paul Anderson.

execution.starting_position: Set the safety pins inside the power rack at your bottom squat position (hip crease at or below knee level). Crouch under the bar and position it on your upper traps or rear delts, feet in your normal squat stance.
execution.setup_instructions: Set pins at the depth you want to work from. Load a conservative weight initially. Duck under the bar in the bottom position.
steps: Step 1: Position yourself under the bar at the bottom, brace the core hard, and take a deep breath.
Step 2: Drive through the entire foot explosively from a dead stop, pushing the knees outward.
Step 3: Extend the hips and knees together, rising to full lockout.
Step 4: Lower yourself slowly back to the pins. Rest 1-2 seconds between each rep to eliminate the stretch reflex.
execution.breathing_instructions: Brace fully before each individual rep. Exhale at the top.
common_mistakes: Using the bounce off the pins instead of a true dead stop
Insufficient bracing before the drive
Pins set too high, reducing the training stimulus
safety_considerations: The power rack safeties must be set at a height that allows full depth
Start with significantly less weight than your regular squat maximum
execution.range_of_motion_guidance: Concentric only — no eccentric loading. Set pins at or below parallel.
execution.tempo_recommendations: Explosive concentric from dead stop. Slow controlled return to pins.
coaching_cues: Tight before you drive
Floor through your feet
Eliminate any bounce off the pins

name: Ankle Dorsiflexion — Band Traction Seated
description: A seated variation of the banded ankle dorsiflexion mobilization, performed with the ankle in a neutral position while the band provides posterior traction on the talus. The exerciser actively pumps the ankle through dorsiflexion and plantarflexion against the traction, which helps improve joint glide by reducing compression in the tibiotalar joint. This technique is based on joint mobilization principles and is used in ankle stiffness, ankle sprain rehabilitation, and before squatting sessions to improve dorsiflexion range.

execution.starting_position: Sit on the floor with one leg extended. Loop a stiff band around the front of the ankle, anchored to a fixed point directly behind the foot. The foot is in a neutral position with the band pulling horizontally (posteriorly).
execution.setup_instructions: Anchor the band behind the ankle at floor level. The band should pull the talus backward as you dorsiflex.
steps: Step 1: Sit with the leg extended and the band creating posterior traction on the ankle.
Step 2: Actively pump the ankle: dorsiflex (pull toes toward shin) then plantarflex (point toes) in continuous alternating motion.
Step 3: Perform 20-30 pumps with the band providing continuous traction throughout.
Step 4: Rest and repeat, or move to the wall version for weight-bearing loading.
execution.breathing_instructions: Breathe continuously and rhythmically throughout the pumping motion.
common_mistakes: Using a band that is too light to provide meaningful traction
Anchoring the band too high, creating a diagonal rather than horizontal pull
Moving too slowly — the pumping motion should be continuous and rhythmic, not held
safety_considerations: The sensation should be of joint opening and mobilization, not pain
If discomfort increases during the pumping motion, stop and assess with a physiotherapist
execution.range_of_motion_guidance: Full ankle dorsiflexion to full plantarflexion on each pump. The band traction is maintained throughout.
execution.tempo_recommendations: 1 pump per second. 20-30 pumps per set.
coaching_cues: Feel the band pulling the ankle backward as you pull the toes toward the shin — this is the joint glide happening
Keep the pumps rhythmic and continuous — do not pause between dorsiflexion and plantarflexion
The knee stays straight for gastrocnemius involvement; slightly bent for more soleus and joint-focused mobilization

name: Ankle Dorsiflexion Stretch
description: The ankle dorsiflexion stretch is a targeted mobility drill that improves the range of motion of the ankle into dorsiflexion — the movement of bringing the top of the foot toward the shin. Restricted dorsiflexion is one of the most common mobility limitations in athletes and gym-goers, contributing to limitations in squatting depth, running mechanics, and landing biomechanics. The knee-to-wall version provides a reliable, measurable way to assess and progressively improve dorsiflexion range.

execution.starting_position: Stand facing a wall with one foot approximately 10 cm from the base of the wall.
execution.setup_instructions: No equipment needed. Use a wall, rack, or any stable vertical surface. A tape measure or ruler can be used to track progress over time.
steps: Step 1: Place one foot 5–15 cm from the base of the wall with toes pointing straight at the wall.
Step 2: Keeping the heel flat on the floor, drive the knee toward the wall, aiming to touch the wall with the knee.
Step 3: Keep the knee tracking over the second toe — do not let it cave inward.
Step 4: If the knee touches the wall with the heel flat, move the foot further back and repeat.
Step 5: Find the maximum distance where the heel can remain flat while the knee touches the wall. Hold 5–10 seconds at that position.
Step 6: Perform 10–15 repetitions or hold for 30–60 seconds per side.
execution.breathing_instructions: Breathe normally throughout. On each exhale, gently drive the knee a little further toward the wall.
common_mistakes: Lifting the heel — this defeats the purpose of the stretch
Letting the knee cave inward medially — always keep the knee tracking over the second toe
Moving too fast — this is a mobility drill, not a ballistic movement
safety_considerations: If sharp pain occurs in the ankle joint (not muscle tightness), stop and consult a clinician
This drill is safe for most populations and is frequently prescribed in physical therapy
execution.range_of_motion_guidance: Track the foot-to-wall distance where you can maintain heel contact. A common benchmark is 10 cm or more. Progress by gradually increasing this distance over weeks.
execution.tempo_recommendations: 10–15 reps × 3 sets per side, or hold 30–60 seconds × 2–3 rounds.
coaching_cues: Heel stays glued to the floor the entire time
Drive the knee straight forward over the toes
Feel the stretch in the calf, not pain in the joint

name: Ankle Dorsiflexion Stretch — Wall with Band
description: A joint mobilization technique that combines a standard wall-supported ankle dorsiflexion stretch with a resistance band providing posterior traction on the talus (ankle bone). The band is looped around the ankle just above the malleolus, anchored behind the foot, and pulls the talus posteriorly as the exerciser drives the knee forward over the toes. This joint distraction improves the glide of the talus in the mortise and addresses the bony restriction component of limited dorsiflexion range, making it more effective than soft tissue stretching alone for many individuals.

execution.starting_position: Loop a stiff resistance band around the front of the ankle, just above the ankle bones. Anchor the other end of the band to a fixed point behind the foot at floor level (such as the base of a squat rack). Stand in a split stance with the banded foot forward, toes approximately 10-15 cm from a wall.
execution.setup_instructions: Anchor the band behind the ankle so it pulls posteriorly (backward) as you shift your weight forward. Use a stiff, non-stretch band for best traction effect.
steps: Step 1: Position the band around the ankle and anchor behind. Place the toes 10-15 cm from a wall.
Step 2: Drive the front knee forward toward the wall, keeping the heel flat on the floor.
Step 3: Touch the knee to the wall and hold for 2-3 seconds, feeling the dorsiflexion range with the traction assist.
Step 4: Return the knee to the starting position. Repeat, gradually moving the foot further from the wall as range improves.
execution.breathing_instructions: Exhale as you push the knee toward the wall. Breathe in the hold position.
common_mistakes: Allowing the heel to lift — the heel must stay flat for the full stretch to occur
Using a band that is too light to create meaningful joint distraction
Not anchoring the band low enough — the band must pull posteriorly at ankle level, not diagonally
safety_considerations: Avoid if you have acute ankle sprain (soft tissue must be assessed first before mobilization)
The sensation should be joint opening, not pain — if pain increases, stop
execution.range_of_motion_guidance: Drive the knee as far forward as the band and ankle allow while the heel stays flat.
execution.tempo_recommendations: 2-3s hold at end range per repetition. Perform 10-15 reps.
coaching_cues: Push the knee forward in line with the second toe — not inward or outward
Feel the band pulling the ankle backward as the knee drives forward
If the knee easily touches the wall, move the foot further away to increase the challenge

name: Arch Hold
description: The arch hold is a prone isometric exercise where the athlete lies face-down and simultaneously lifts the arms, chest, and legs off the floor, forming an arched shape. It is the antagonist to the hollow hold and develops the posterior chain, particularly the erector spinae and gluteus maximus, under sustained isometric tension. Regular training of the arch hold contributes to spinal extensor endurance and scapular stability.

execution.starting_position: Lie face-down (prone) on the floor with arms extended overhead, palms facing down, and legs straight.
execution.setup_instructions: No equipment needed. Use a mat for comfort on a hard floor.
steps: Step 1: Lie prone with arms extended overhead and legs together.
Step 2: Squeeze the glutes firmly and engage the lower back muscles.
Step 3: Simultaneously lift both arms and both legs off the floor, raising as high as comfortable without straining the neck.
Step 4: Hold the arched position with the neck in a neutral position — do not hyperextend the neck upward.
Step 5: Hold for the prescribed duration, then lower with control.
execution.breathing_instructions: Breathe shallowly through the nose during the hold. Exhale slowly as you lower.
common_mistakes: Hyperextending the neck by looking up excessively
Allowing the knees to bend during the hold
Failing to squeeze the glutes, leaving most of the work to the lower back alone
Holding the breath
safety_considerations: Keep the neck neutral — the gaze should be toward the floor, not the ceiling.
Avoid if experiencing acute lumbar hyperextension pain.
execution.range_of_motion_guidance: Lift arms and legs as high as can be maintained with a neutral neck and engaged glutes. Do not force range at the expense of form.
execution.tempo_recommendations: Hold for 20–60 seconds per set. Practice in conjunction with hollow holds to develop balanced spinal strength.
coaching_cues: Squeeze your glutes like you are holding a coin
Long arms, long legs — reach in opposite directions
Keep your eyes on the floor

name: Archer Pull-Up
description: The archer pull-up is an advanced calisthenics progression toward the one-arm pull-up. The lifter pulls up while simultaneously extending one arm out to the side straight, so the working arm performs most of the pulling while the extended arm assists with balance and grip. This creates a large strength imbalance that develops unilateral pulling strength without fully committing to a one-arm pull-up.

execution.starting_position: Hang from a pull-up bar with a wide overhand grip, arms fully extended.
execution.setup_instructions: Use a wide pull-up bar or gymnastic rings set wide enough to allow one arm to extend laterally. Ensure the bar or anchor point can support your full weight.
steps: Step 1: Begin in a dead hang with both hands gripping the bar wide.
Step 2: Initiate a pull-up toward one side, bending that elbow and pulling the chest toward the working hand.
Step 3: Simultaneously extend the opposite arm straight out to the side, keeping it relatively straight but with a slight soft elbow.
Step 4: At the top, the chin should be near or above the working hand, with the other arm extended.
Step 5: Lower under control back to a dead hang, then repeat on the opposite side.
execution.breathing_instructions: Exhale as you pull up. Inhale on the descent.
common_mistakes: Not extending the assisting arm fully, which makes it too similar to a standard pull-up
Kipping or using momentum rather than strict pulling strength
Not controlling the descent, which skips the eccentric stimulus
safety_considerations: This is an advanced exercise — only attempt after achieving 10+ strict pull-ups with ease
Ensure grip is secure before each rep
execution.range_of_motion_guidance: Full dead hang at the bottom to chin above working hand at the top.
coaching_cues: Think of it as a one-arm pull-up with a training wheel on the other side
The extended arm should feel like it is barely helping
Keep the core tight to prevent swinging

name: Archer Push-Up
description: The archer push-up is an advanced unilateral push-up variation where the body shifts laterally over one working arm while the opposite arm extends to the side for balance. This concentrates the pressing load onto a single side of the pectoralis major and triceps, serving as a progression toward the one-arm push-up.

execution.starting_position: Start in a wide push-up position with hands placed much wider than shoulder-width apart. Fingers point outward at a slight angle. Body is in a straight plank line.
execution.setup_instructions: Ensure adequate space on each side. Hands should be significantly wider than a standard push-up.
steps: Step 1: Begin in a wide push-up position with hands significantly wider than shoulder-width.
Step 2: Shift your bodyweight laterally over your right hand, bending the right elbow to lower your chest toward the right hand.
Step 3: As you lower to the right, the left arm extends straight with a slight bend, acting as a support and balance arm.
Step 4: Press through the right palm to return to the start, then shift to the left side. Alternate each repetition.
execution.breathing_instructions: Inhale as you lower to one side; exhale as you press back to center.
common_mistakes: Rotating the hips as the body shifts — keep the pelvis square
Bending the extended arm excessively, which reduces unilateral loading
safety_considerations: Build prerequisite strength with standard and wide push-ups before attempting this variation
Stop if you feel shoulder joint pain — this movement demands significant shoulder stability
execution.range_of_motion_guidance: Lower until the chest is at hand level on the working side, then press back to the top.
coaching_cues: Shift your center of mass directly over the working arm
Keep hips level — no rotation as you move side to side

name: Arnold Press
description: The Arnold press is a dumbbell shoulder exercise that incorporates a pronation-to-supination rotation of the forearm during the pressing motion. By starting with palms facing the body and rotating to a forward-facing position at the top, all three heads of the deltoid are engaged across a fuller range of motion than a standard overhead press.

execution.starting_position: Sit on a bench holding dumbbells at shoulder height with palms facing your body (supinated) and elbows pointing forward in front of the chest.
execution.setup_instructions: Start with dumbbells in front of the face at chin height with palms facing you, elbows low and in front.
steps: As you press the dumbbells upward, simultaneously rotate the forearms outward so palms face forward by the time the arms are overhead.
Press to full extension.
On the descent, reverse the rotation, returning to the starting position with palms facing the body.
execution.breathing_instructions: Exhale on the press and rotation. Inhale on the return.
common_mistakes: Rushing the rotation and doing it separately from the press instead of simultaneously
Using too heavy a weight that prevents controlled rotation
safety_considerations: The rotational component adds shoulder complexity — reduce weight compared to a standard press
execution.range_of_motion_guidance: Full overhead extension at the top, elbows forward and palms facing body at the bottom.
coaching_cues: Let the rotation happen naturally as you press — think of opening a jar as you push up
Full rotation at the top — thumbs should be pointing backward at lockout

name: Arnold Press with 2-Second Hold at Top
description: The Arnold press with 2-second hold at the top pauses in the fully overhead, fully pronated lockout position before descending, training the ability to stabilize and generate force from the locked-out shoulder position. The pause increases time under tension through the overhead range, challenges the upper trapezius and serratus anterior in their most shortened position, and builds confidence and strength in the full overhead lockout.

execution.starting_position: Seated with dumbbells at shoulder height, palms facing the body, elbows forward — standard Arnold press starting position.
execution.setup_instructions: Moderate weight — the lockout hold requires sustained overhead stability.
steps: Step 1: Press the dumbbells overhead while rotating the wrists to pronated.
Step 2: At full lockout, hold for 2 full seconds.
Step 3: During the hold, actively press through the traps — shrug slightly into the hold.
Step 4: Lower under control, reversing the rotation.
Step 5: Return to the starting position and repeat.
execution.breathing_instructions: Exhale pressing. Hold breath briefly at lockout. Exhale during descent.
common_mistakes: Not maintaining active overhead pressing tension during the hold — stay engaged
Using too heavy a weight — the hold becomes impossible
safety_considerations: Ensure elbows are locked before the hold — no hyperextension, just full extension
Avoid if shoulder impingement occurs at overhead lockout
execution.range_of_motion_guidance: Full supinated start to overhead pronated lockout with 2s hold.
coaching_cues: Press up through the hold — stay active
Squeeze the traps at the lockout
2 full seconds at the top — not a quick bounce

name: Arnold Press with Midpoint Pause
description: The Arnold press with midpoint pause pauses for 2-3 seconds at the halfway point of the rotation — when the palms face out to the sides and the elbows are at shoulder height — before continuing the press to lockout. The midpoint pause occurs at the most demanding position in the movement, maximizing deltoid recruitment at the transition from the anterior to lateral head activation pattern and training strength specifically through that challenging mid-range.

execution.starting_position: Seated with dumbbells in Arnold press starting position — palms facing body, elbows forward.
execution.setup_instructions: Reduce load by 20-30% compared to standard Arnold press to accommodate the mid-range pause.
steps: Step 1: Begin pressing and rotating the wrists outward.
Step 2: At the midpoint — palms facing out, elbows at shoulder height — stop and hold for 2-3 seconds.
Step 3: Hold strictly — no relaxing, no sinking.
Step 4: Continue pressing to full lockout, completing the rotation to pronated.
Step 5: Return under control, pausing again at the midpoint on the way down if desired.
execution.breathing_instructions: Exhale pressing to midpoint. Hold during pause. Exhale completing the press.
common_mistakes: Dropping the elbows below shoulder height during the pause
Not holding for full 2-3 seconds — the pause is the key variable
safety_considerations: Reduce load relative to standard Arnold press
High demand on the shoulder joints at the midpoint — moderate loads only
execution.range_of_motion_guidance: Full range from supinated start to overhead lockout with 2-3s midpoint hold.
coaching_cues: Stop when palms face outward — that is the midpoint
Hold it — no sinking through the pause
Drive overhead after the hold

name: Assisted One-Arm Pull-Up
description: The assisted one-arm pull-up uses a band or the free hand lightly touching the working arm's wrist to reduce the load while training the full range of motion required for a strict one-arm pull-up. It develops the extreme lat, biceps, and forearm strength needed for one of the most demanding upper-body pulling movements in calisthenics.

execution.starting_position: Grip the bar with one hand in the center. The free hand can lightly grip the working wrist or a looped band is placed under the working knee/foot. Begin in a dead hang.
execution.setup_instructions: Method 1: Loop a thin band around the bar and place one foot in it — provides variable resistance assistance. Method 2: Lightly touch the working arm's wrist with the fingertips of the free hand. Use only minimal assistance.
steps: Step 1: Begin hanging from one arm, opposite hand providing minimal assistance.
Step 2: Depress and retract the working shoulder blade.
Step 3: Pull the chest toward the bar by driving the working elbow down.
Step 4: Continue until the chin clears the bar.
Step 5: Lower under control — the eccentric is as valuable as the concentric.
execution.breathing_instructions: Exhale aggressively on the pull. Inhale on the controlled descent.
common_mistakes: Applying too much assistance — use the minimum needed to complete clean reps
Skipping negatives — the eccentric is essential for strength development
safety_considerations: Prerequisites: 15+ unassisted pull-ups. Progress extremely slowly.
High risk of elbow tendinopathy if volume is excessive — limit to 3-5 reps per side per session
execution.range_of_motion_guidance: Full dead hang to chin above bar.
coaching_cues: Use only a fingertip's worth of assistance
Own every inch of the descent
Keep the free arm close — do not reach across the body

name: Assisted Pull-Up Machine
description: The assisted pull-up machine uses a counter-weighted platform that the exerciser kneels or stands on, reducing the effective bodyweight being lifted. It allows beginners or those building toward an unassisted pull-up to train the full pulling movement pattern with correct form. The machine's assistance decreases as strength improves, providing a progressive path toward bodyweight pull-ups.

execution.starting_position: Set the desired assistance weight on the machine. Kneel or stand on the counter-weighted platform. Grip the overhead handles at shoulder width with an overhand grip.
execution.setup_instructions: Select a heavier assistance weight to make the exercise easier (more weight counter-balances more of your body weight). Adjust the platform height.
steps: Step 1: Kneel on the platform and grip the handles with an overhand shoulder-width grip.
Step 2: Begin with arms fully extended and scapulae elevated.
Step 3: Depress the scapulae and initiate the pull by driving the elbows toward the floor.
Step 4: Continue pulling until the chin clears the handles or chest approaches the bar.
Step 5: Lower under full control until arms are extended and repeat.
execution.breathing_instructions: Exhale on the way up, inhale on the way down.
common_mistakes: Using too much assistance weight, reducing training stimulus
Letting the platform crash down uncontrolled on each rep
Not fully extending the arms at the bottom
safety_considerations: Step off the platform carefully when dismounting — the platform will drop if you step off while weight is selected
Progressively reduce assistance over time to build toward unassisted pull-ups
execution.range_of_motion_guidance: Full arm extension at the bottom, chin above handle level at the top.
coaching_cues: Pull elbows down and back
Think about putting your shoulder blades in your back pockets
Full extension at the bottom every rep

name: Atlas Stone Lift and Load
description: The Atlas stone is a spherical concrete or stone implement used in strongman competition. The lift-and-load movement requires the athlete to roll the stone onto their thighs, hug it into the chest and abdomen, then extend the hips explosively to load it onto a platform or over a bar at a specified height. The Atlas stone imposes compressive loading on the spine and demands maximal effort from the entire posterior chain, biceps, and core in a movement pattern unlike any barbell exercise. It is an expert-level lift with significant injury risk if executed without proper technique and adequate preparation.

execution.starting_position: The stone is on the floor. Straddle the stone with feet wider than hip-width. Squat down, reaching around the stone with both arms in a 'bear hug' grip. The chest and abdomen make contact with the stone.
execution.setup_instructions: Apply tacky (a sticky compound used in strongman) to the forearms for grip on competition-style stones. Set the loading platform or bar height before beginning. Have a spotter/judge present for all heavy attempts.
steps: Step 1: Straddle the stone, squat deeply, and wrap both arms around it. Lock the hands together or grasp opposing wrists beneath the stone.
Step 2: Extend the hips and knees to drive the stone upward while pulling it into the lap and abdomen. The stone sits on the upper thighs at the lap position.
Step 3: Re-grip the stone — shift the hands higher up the stone's surface as it comes into the lap. This is the re-grip or 'lapping' phase.
Step 4: Drive the hips forward explosively, extending fully. Simultaneously pull the stone up the body and roll it over the platform edge or loading pin.
Step 5: Once the stone is on the platform, step back and release. Do not follow the stone over the platform.
execution.breathing_instructions: Brace maximally with a Valsalva manoeuvre (held breath) at the initial pull from the floor. Breathe again at the lap position before the final load.
common_mistakes: Not getting the chest and abs fully against the stone — the stone must be hugged in tight, not held with the hands alone
Attempting to muscle the stone up with the arms rather than using hip extension as the primary power source
Failing to re-grip (lap) the stone at the thighs before the final load — trying to load it in one continuous motion usually fails on heavy stones
safety_considerations: Never attempt a heavy Atlas stone without first training with lighter stones to develop technique and tendon strength in the forearms
The biceps tendon is at risk on heavy stones if the arms are not properly positioned — keep the elbows out and under the stone, not reaching over the top
Wear appropriate protective clothing — the stone will abrade bare skin
Always have a handler/spotter present for competition-weight attempts
Warm up the lower back, hips, and biceps extensively before heavy stone work
execution.range_of_motion_guidance: Full hip extension at the final load phase. The stone travels from the floor to above the platform height — typically 1.0–1.5 metres.
execution.tempo_recommendations: Competition: maximum reps in 60 seconds. Training: 1–3 reps per set × 3–5 sets. Rest 3–5 minutes between sets.
coaching_cues: Hug the stone — do not grab it
Lap it first, then load it
The power comes from the hips — pop them through

name: Atlas Stone Over Bar
description: The classic strongman atlas stone event where competitors load a heavy spherical stone over a tall bar or onto a platform. The stone must be lapped (rested on the thighs), then elevated over the target height. This tests raw pulling, pushing, and grip strength in a unique athletic pattern.

execution.starting_position: Set up for Atlas Stone Over Bar in proper strongman position.
execution.setup_instructions: Prepare all equipment and body position for Atlas Stone Over Bar.
steps: Step 1: Stand over stone with feet wide. Reach down and grip sides of stone.
Step 2: Pull stone up to lap position resting on thighs.
Step 3: Adjust grip higher on stone and drive hips forward explosively.
Step 4: Continue driving stone up and over the bar or platform target.
execution.breathing_instructions: Brace core maximally before every lift. Breathe between reps if needed.
common_mistakes: Not using the lap position
Pulling with arms instead of legs
safety_considerations: Use collars on all loaded barbells.
Ensure clear path for carries.
Have spotters for overhead movements.
execution.range_of_motion_guidance: Full range of motion specific to the implement being used.
coaching_cues: Lap the stone first, then elevate
Drive hips through aggressively

name: Axle Bar Deadlift
description: The axle bar deadlift uses a straight steel bar with a diameter of approximately 50 mm (2 inches) compared to the standard 28–32 mm Olympic barbell, which increases grip demand dramatically due to the larger circumference that the hand must span. The movement pattern is identical to a conventional barbell deadlift in terms of posterior chain loading, but the grip becomes the primary limiting factor at heavy loads, making it an effective training tool for grip strength development. It is a contested lift in strongman competition alongside the standard deadlift.

execution.starting_position: Stand with feet hip-width apart, toes pointing forward or slightly out. The axle bar rests at mid-shin. Grip the bar with a double-overhand grip (straps are permitted in training but not all competitions). Push hips back, chest up, neutral spine.
execution.setup_instructions: Note that the axle bar typically does not rotate like an Olympic barbell — the entire bar spins with the hands, which further increases grip demand. Load using bumper plates or standard plates with appropriate diameter.
steps: Step 1: Stand with feet hip-width, bar over mid-foot. Hinge the hips back and reach for the bar with a double-overhand grip, hands just outside the legs.
Step 2: Take slack out of the bar by pulling the lats back and down. Brace the core with a full breath (Valsalva).
Step 3: Initiate the pull by pushing the floor away with both feet. Keep the bar against the shins and thighs throughout the ascent.
Step 4: Extend the hips and knees simultaneously, maintaining a neutral spine. The bar passes the knees and the hips drive forward to lockout.
Step 5: At lockout, stand fully upright with hips extended and shoulders back. Lower the bar under control or drop from lockout (competition style).
execution.breathing_instructions: Take a full breath into the belly and brace hard before the pull begins. Hold the brace throughout the rep. Exhale at lockout.
common_mistakes: Attempting a grip-intensive axle deadlift without first developing adequate double-overhand grip strength on a standard barbell
Opening the fingers during the pull due to grip fatigue — this causes the bar to roll and dramatically increases drop risk
Rounding the lower back due to the grip failing before the posterior chain
safety_considerations: The bar may slip without warning on heavy loads due to the large diameter — have crash mats or bumper plates and be prepared to drop the bar
Build to heavy axle deadlift weights gradually — the grip demand exceeds that of a standard barbell at the same absolute weight
execution.range_of_motion_guidance: Full hip extension at lockout. The bar travels from the floor to the hip crease in a straight vertical path.
execution.tempo_recommendations: Strength: 1–3 reps × 5–6 sets. Grip conditioning: 5 reps × 4 sets at a moderate load. Rest 3–5 minutes for heavy sets.
coaching_cues: Squeeze the bar like you are trying to crush it
Push the floor away — do not think about pulling the bar up
Keep the bar dragging up the shins and thighs

name: B-Stance Landmine Squat
description: A landmine squat performed with a staggered B-stance where the lead leg does the majority of the work and the rear foot provides only balance support. The landmine anchors the bar at an angle, guiding the movement and allowing a more upright torso with less lower back stress than a traditional squat.

execution.starting_position: Hold the sleeve of a landmine barbell with both hands at chest height. Stand in a B-stance with the working foot forward and the rear foot's toes touching the floor behind for balance only.
execution.setup_instructions: Secure a barbell in a landmine base or wedge it into a corner. Load the sleeve. Stand facing the landmine anchor and grasp the loaded end.
steps: Step 1: Brace the core and push the hips back slightly.
Step 2: Lower into a squat on the lead leg, letting the rear foot remain as a balance point only.
Step 3: Descend until the front thigh is at or near parallel.
Step 4: Drive through the front heel to return to standing.
execution.breathing_instructions: Inhale and brace on the descent. Exhale on the ascent.
common_mistakes: Shifting too much load to the rear foot — the rear foot is for balance only
Allowing the front knee to cave inward
safety_considerations: Start with a light load to learn the balance requirements of the B-stance position
execution.range_of_motion_guidance: Lead leg thigh reaches parallel or below. Full extension at the top.
coaching_cues: Lead leg does the work
Rear toes touch for balance only

name: B-Stance / Kickstand Romanian Deadlift
description: The B-stance Romanian deadlift uses a staggered foot position where the front foot does the work and the rear foot rests on its toes for balance only. It functions as an effectively unilateral RDL while providing slightly more stability than a true single-leg version. The lead leg's hamstrings and glute are the primary movers, making it excellent for addressing limb asymmetries and training hamstrings with greater unilateral stimulus.

execution.starting_position: Stand holding dumbbells. Stagger your feet so one foot is about half a step ahead. The rear foot rests on its toes only — it is a kickstand for balance, not for weight-bearing.
execution.setup_instructions: Hold dumbbells in front of the thighs. Distribute almost all weight to the front leg before beginning.
steps: Step 1: Hinge at the hip of the front leg, pushing the hip back as the torso lowers.
Step 2: Lower the dumbbells along the front leg, feeling a deep stretch in the front leg's hamstring.
Step 3: Descend until the torso is roughly parallel to the floor or as far as hamstring flexibility allows.
Step 4: Drive through the front heel and squeeze the front glute to return to the standing position.
execution.breathing_instructions: Inhale and brace before the hinge. Exhale at the top.
common_mistakes: Rear foot bearing weight, reducing the unilateral stimulus
Lower back rounding at the bottom
Hip rotating outward on the working side
safety_considerations: Keep the spine neutral throughout — do not round the lower back to gain extra depth
execution.range_of_motion_guidance: Descend as far as hamstring flexibility allows without spinal flexion.
coaching_cues: Rear foot is just a kickstand
Push the hip back
Squeeze the glute to stand up

name: Back Lever Hold
description: A gymnastic hold where the athlete suspends horizontally below a bar or rings facing downward. The body forms a rigid plank with the back facing up and arms gripping overhead. This movement requires significant shoulder flexibility and total body tension.

execution.starting_position: Set up for Back Lever Hold in proper position.
execution.setup_instructions: Prepare body and equipment for Back Lever Hold.
steps: Step 1: Mount rings above in a skin-the-cat starting position.
Step 2: Lower body backward through rings to horizontal facing down.
Step 3: Maintain rigid body with arms straight and palms facing up.
Step 4: Hold position then carefully return by pulling back through rings.
execution.breathing_instructions: Breathe steadily; never hold breath during static holds.
common_mistakes: Bending at hips
Insufficient shoulder flexibility before attempting
safety_considerations: Build prerequisite strength before attempting advanced variations.
Stop if joint pain occurs.
execution.range_of_motion_guidance: Full range of motion with control at all times.
coaching_cues: Squeeze everything tight
Palms face up for shoulder safety

name: Back Lever Pullouts
description: Dynamic back lever training where the athlete moves from an inverted hang into the back lever position and returns. The pullout (exit from back lever upward) builds the posterior chain in the unique back lever pulling pattern. This is essential progression work for gymnastic ring strength.

execution.starting_position: Set up for Back Lever Pullouts in proper position.
execution.setup_instructions: Prepare body and equipment for Back Lever Pullouts.
steps: Step 1: From inverted hang on rings, lower backward into back lever position.
Step 2: Hold back lever briefly at horizontal.
Step 3: Pull up and back through rings to return to inverted hang.
Step 4: Control the transitions in both directions.
execution.breathing_instructions: Breathe steadily; never hold breath during static holds.
common_mistakes: Losing body tension during transition
Excessive shoulder stress
safety_considerations: Build prerequisite strength before attempting advanced variations.
Stop if joint pain occurs.
execution.range_of_motion_guidance: Full range of motion with control at all times.
coaching_cues: Build thorough shoulder flexibility first
Control both directions equally

name: Backward Sled Drag
description: A sled drag performed walking backward, pulling a weighted sled behind using handles or a rope. The backward walking pattern isolates the quadriceps in a unique terminal extension pattern that is excellent for knee rehabilitation and sports performance. This is very low impact for the joints.

execution.starting_position: Set up for Backward Sled Drag in proper strongman position.
execution.setup_instructions: Prepare all equipment and body position for Backward Sled Drag.
steps: Step 1: Attach straps or handles to loaded sled. Face away from sled.
Step 2: Walk backward with controlled steps, keeping tension on straps.
Step 3: Extend knees fully on each step for maximum quad recruitment.
Step 4: Continue for target distance, checking over shoulder periodically.
execution.breathing_instructions: Brace core maximally before every lift. Breathe between reps if needed.
common_mistakes: Shuffling without full knee extension
Leaning too far forward
safety_considerations: Use collars on all loaded barbells.
Ensure clear path for carries.
Have spotters for overhead movements.
execution.range_of_motion_guidance: Full range of motion specific to the implement being used.
coaching_cues: Full knee extension on each step
Drive through heel backward

name: Band-Assisted Pull-Up
description: The band-assisted pull-up uses a looped resistance band anchored around the bar and under the knees or feet to provide upward assistance throughout the range of motion. The band offloads the most bodyweight at the bottom — where the pull-up is mechanically hardest — allowing trainees to build pulling strength progressively before performing unassisted pull-ups.

execution.starting_position: Loop a resistance band over the pull-up bar. Place both knees (or one foot) in the bottom of the loop. Grip the bar shoulder-width with an overhand grip. Arms fully extended.
execution.setup_instructions: Choose a band thickness based on the amount of assistance needed — heavier individuals or beginners use a thicker band. Ensure the band is secure around the bar before loading it with body weight.
steps: Step 1: Hang from the bar with the band supporting the knees or feet, arms fully extended.
Step 2: Depress and retract the shoulder blades to initiate the movement.
Step 3: Pull the chest toward the bar by driving the elbows down and back.
Step 4: Continue pulling until the chin clears the bar.
Step 5: Lower under control to the dead-hang start position.
execution.breathing_instructions: Exhale on the way up, inhale on the way down.
common_mistakes: Using a band so thick that it removes all challenge — progress to thinner bands over time
Kipping or swinging rather than using controlled pulling strength
Not reaching full arm extension at the bottom of each rep
safety_considerations: Step into and out of the band carefully — do not let it snap back
Inspect the band for cracks or tears before each session
execution.range_of_motion_guidance: Full dead hang at the bottom to chin above the bar at the top.
coaching_cues: Lead with the chest, not the chin
Drive the elbows toward your hip pockets
Control the descent — do not drop

name: Banded Clamshell
description: The banded clamshell is a rehabilitation exercise for the hip abductors and external rotators, particularly gluteus medius and the deep external rotators. Performed side-lying with a resistance band loop above the knees, it isolates hip external rotation while the pelvis remains stable. It is widely prescribed for patellofemoral pain, IT band syndrome, and hip weakness contributing to knee valgus during functional movements.

execution.starting_position: Lie on one side with hips stacked, knees bent to approximately 45 degrees, and a resistance band loop positioned just above the knees.
execution.setup_instructions: Use a light-to-medium resistance band loop. The feet remain together and stacked throughout the movement.
steps: Step 1: Lie on your side with hips and knees bent to 45 degrees, feet stacked.
Step 2: Place the resistance band loop above both knees.
Step 3: Keeping feet together, rotate the top knee upward toward the ceiling like a clamshell opening.
Step 4: Rotate as high as the hip allows without the pelvis rocking backward.
Step 5: Slowly lower the knee back to the starting position with control.
Step 6: Complete all reps on one side, then switch.
execution.breathing_instructions: Exhale as the knee lifts. Inhale as it returns.
common_mistakes: Rolling the pelvis backward as the knee rises — the pelvis must stay completely still
Using momentum instead of a controlled, slow movement
Choosing too heavy a band, which forces compensation through pelvis rotation
safety_considerations: This exercise is generally appropriate for all rehabilitation populations
If hip pain occurs, reduce range of motion and consult a clinician
execution.range_of_motion_guidance: The knee should rise as far as the hip external rotators allow without pelvic rotation — typically 30–45 degrees from the starting position.
execution.tempo_recommendations: 2-second lift, 1-second hold at top, 2-second lower. 2–3 sets of 15–20 reps.
coaching_cues: Keep your pelvis completely still — do not let it rock back
Think about rotating the thigh, not lifting the knee
Slow and controlled wins over heavy and sloppy

name: Band Face Pull with External Rotation Lockout
description: The band face pull with external rotation lockout adds an end-range external rotation hold to a standard face pull, training the infraspinatus and teres minor through their full available range and at peak contraction. The resistance band provides accommodating resistance — lighter at the start (less stretched) and progressively heavier as the band stretches at end range — which matches the strength curve of the external rotators, applying peak load at peak contraction.

execution.starting_position: Anchor a resistance band at face height. Grip the band with both hands using an overhand grip, thumbs pointing outward. Step back until there is tension in the band with arms extended.
execution.setup_instructions: Light to moderate band resistance. This is primarily a rotator cuff and upper back exercise.
steps: Step 1: Begin with arms extended, band under tension.
Step 2: Pull the band toward the face, leading with the elbows flaring outward and upward to shoulder height.
Step 3: As the hands reach the face, externally rotate the shoulders — thumbs point behind you, hands above elbows.
Step 4: Hold the lockout position (full external rotation) for 2-3 seconds.
Step 5: Reverse to the starting position under control.
execution.breathing_instructions: Exhale pulling and rotating. Inhale returning.
common_mistakes: Skipping the external rotation — just pulling to the face without the ER misses the key benefit
Elbows dropping below shoulder height during the pull
safety_considerations: Light band resistance — this is a posture and rotator cuff health exercise
High volume is safe and appropriate for warm-up sets (20-30 reps)
execution.range_of_motion_guidance: Full band extension to full external rotation lockout at face height.
coaching_cues: Pull to your nose — not your chin or forehead
Thumbs behind you at the lockout
Hold it — 2-3 seconds of external rotation

name: Band Overhead Scapular Retraction
description: The band overhead scapular retraction holds a resistance band overhead with arms extended and retracts the shoulder blades toward each other without lowering the arms, training the lower trapezius and rhomboids through the overhead position. It reinforces proper scapular mechanics in the overhead range — essential for safe overhead pressing and injury prevention in athletes who frequently work above shoulder height.

execution.starting_position: Hold a resistance band with both hands wider than shoulder width. Raise arms overhead — band taut across the front. Arms stay extended throughout.
execution.setup_instructions: Use a light band — the focus is on scapular mechanics, not load. Stand tall with a neutral spine.
steps: Step 1: Begin with arms extended overhead, band taut.
Step 2: Without lowering the arms, retract the shoulder blades — squeezing them together.
Step 3: Hold the retracted position for 2 seconds.
Step 4: Protract back to the starting position.
Step 5: Repeat.
execution.breathing_instructions: Exhale on retraction. Inhale protracting.
common_mistakes: Lowering the arms to assist retraction — arms must stay overhead
Moving at the elbows rather than the shoulder blades
safety_considerations: Appropriate for all levels as a warm-up or shoulder health tool
Avoid overhead exercises if shoulder impingement is symptomatic
execution.range_of_motion_guidance: Full scapular protraction to full retraction, arms overhead throughout.
coaching_cues: Arms stay up — blades do the work
Think 'squeeze the pencil between your shoulder blades'
Full protraction before each retraction

name: Band Pull-Apart
description: The band pull-apart is a simple but highly effective prehabilitation exercise for the posterior shoulder and upper back. Holding a resistance band at arm's length, the exerciser pulls the band apart horizontally until it touches the chest, training the posterior deltoid, rhomboids, and middle trapezius. It is widely used as a warm-up drill, corrective exercise, and high-rep accessory movement for shoulder health.

execution.starting_position: Stand upright holding a resistance band at both ends with both arms extended straight in front of the body at approximately shoulder height. Palms face the floor. Hands are slightly wider than shoulder-width.
execution.setup_instructions: Choose a resistance band light enough to maintain good form for high reps. Choke up on a heavier band to increase resistance, or use a lighter band for more range.
steps: Step 1: Hold the band with both hands at shoulder height, arms extended in front.
Step 2: Keeping the arms straight (slight elbow bend allowed), exhale and pull the band apart by moving both hands outward and back.
Step 3: Continue until the band touches the chest, squeezing the rear delts and rhomboids at peak contraction.
Step 4: Inhale and slowly return the hands to the starting extended position.
execution.breathing_instructions: Exhale as you pull apart; inhale as you return.
common_mistakes: Bending the elbows heavily during the pull, which reduces the targeted muscles' load
Internally rotating the shoulders — keep thumbs slightly elevated (external rotation)
safety_considerations: Select band resistance you can control — do not let the band snap back
execution.range_of_motion_guidance: Pull until the band touches or nearly touches the sternum; return to fully extended arms.
coaching_cues: Lead with your elbows behind you as you pull the band apart
Think about bending the band around your chest — not just pulling the ends apart

name: Band Pull-Apart (Underhand Grip)
description: The underhand (supinated) grip band pull-apart shifts emphasis from the overhand version toward the lower trapezius and posterior deltoid, while also incorporating greater biceps tendon stress and external rotation. The supinated grip forces the humeral head into a more externally rotated position throughout the movement, which can be both a corrective exercise cue for those with internally rotated posture and a tool for targeting slightly different scapular retractor fibers than the standard overhand pull-apart.

execution.starting_position: Hold a resistance band with an underhand (supinated) grip, hands shoulder-width apart, arms extended in front at shoulder height. Palms face the ceiling.
execution.setup_instructions: Use a light resistance band. The supinated grip is the defining feature — ensure palms face up throughout the movement.
steps: Step 1: Hold the band underhand at shoulder height, arms extended.
Step 2: Pull the band apart by moving the arms outward and backward.
Step 3: Continue until the band touches the chest, maintaining the supinated grip.
Step 4: Squeeze the scapulae together and hold for a moment.
Step 5: Return under control to the starting position.
execution.breathing_instructions: Exhale as you pull apart, inhale as you return.
common_mistakes: Letting the grip rotate to neutral or pronated during the pull
Using a band that is too heavy, causing the elbows to bend excessively
safety_considerations: Ensure the band is in good condition before use — worn bands can snap
execution.range_of_motion_guidance: Band starts at shoulder height with arms forward, pulled to chest-contact at the rear.
coaching_cues: Palms face up the whole time
Pull through the rear deltoid
Feel the scapulae squeeze at the end

name: Band-Resisted Dumbbell Bench Press
description: A flat bench press variation where resistance bands are looped around the dumbbells and anchored under the bench legs, adding accommodating resistance that increases load through the lockout portion of the lift. This creates an ascending resistance curve that matches the strength curve of the pectoralis major and triceps, maximizing tension at the top where free weights become lighter.

execution.starting_position: Lie on a flat bench. Loop a resistance band around each dumbbell and anchor the other end securely under the bench legs. Hold dumbbells at chest level, elbows at 45–75 degrees.
execution.setup_instructions: Use light-to-medium bands — the dumbbell weight plus band tension at lockout should be your working load. Secure bands under bench legs before lying down. Test band security before full sets.
steps: Step 1: Lie on the bench with dumbbells at chest level. Feel the bands pulling the dumbbells downward with added force.
Step 2: Press dumbbells up and together toward the ceiling. Notice the resistance increases as you approach lockout.
Step 3: Fully extend arms at the top — this is where peak band tension occurs.
Step 4: Lower under full control. The band assistance on the way down helps deload the bottom position. Repeat.
execution.breathing_instructions: Inhale at the bottom, exhale forcefully through the press.
common_mistakes: Using bands that are too heavy, overwhelming the dumbbell weight
Inadequate band anchor — bands must be stable throughout the set
Pressing without committing to full lockout, missing the high-tension zone
safety_considerations: Verify band anchors are secure before each set
Start with lighter bands to understand the resistance curve before adding more tension
Have a spotter when using significant band tension
execution.range_of_motion_guidance: Full range from chest to full lockout. The lockout is intentional — this is where the bands provide maximum training stimulus.
coaching_cues: Press hard all the way to lockout — the bands are testing you there
Control the negative — the bands will try to pull the dumbbells down faster than free weights would

name: Band-Resisted Push-Up
description: A push-up variation where a resistance band is looped across the upper back and secured under both hands, adding accommodating resistance that increases toward the top of the press. Because band resistance is proportional to stretch, the lockout position receives the most resistance, training the pectorals and triceps through a fuller strength curve than bodyweight alone provides.

execution.starting_position: Loop a resistance band around your upper back at shoulder blade level. Grasp each end of the band under the corresponding hand in a standard push-up position. Hands are shoulder-width apart.
execution.setup_instructions: Choose a band tension that makes the last 2–3 reps of each set challenging. The band should have moderate tension even at the bottom position.
steps: Step 1: Begin in a high plank with the band looped across your upper back and held under palms. Body is straight from head to heels.
Step 2: Lower your chest to the floor, keeping elbows at a 45-degree angle from the torso. Band tension decreases at the bottom.
Step 3: Press powerfully back up — band tension increases as you rise toward lockout.
Step 4: Fully extend the arms at the top, feeling maximum band resistance. Repeat.
execution.breathing_instructions: Inhale on the descent, exhale on the press upward.
common_mistakes: Band sliding up to the neck during the set — reposition before starting
Choosing a band so heavy it compromises depth
Sagging at the hips, reducing core engagement
safety_considerations: Ensure band is securely positioned across the upper back before beginning
If band slips toward neck during the set, stop and reposition
execution.range_of_motion_guidance: Full range from chest to floor to full arm extension. Accommodating resistance rewards full lockout.
coaching_cues: Accelerate through the top — the band gets harder, so push harder
Keep wrists stacked under elbows throughout

name: Band Teardrop Lateral Raise
description: The band teardrop lateral raise traces a teardrop-shaped arc — raising the arms out to the side, then bringing them together overhead before returning. The combined abduction and overhead phase trains the medial deltoid through its full range of abduction while the overhead convergence challenges the upper trapezius and serratus anterior. The continuous band tension through the arc provides loading at positions that dumbbells cannot match.

execution.starting_position: Stand with both feet on a resistance band loop. Hold each side of the band with the corresponding hand. Bands hang beside the thighs.
execution.setup_instructions: Adjust foot position on the band to control tension. Light to moderate band tension for high quality reps.
steps: Step 1: Begin with arms at sides, hands on the band.
Step 2: Raise both arms out to the sides in a standard lateral raise to shoulder height.
Step 3: Continue the arc, bringing the hands together overhead.
Step 4: Lower the hands back overhead to the sides, then return to the starting position.
Step 5: One rep = out, up, together, down, in.
execution.breathing_instructions: Exhale on the raise. Inhale returning.
common_mistakes: Breaking the arc — the motion should be smooth and continuous
Insufficient tension — the band should be taut at the starting position
safety_considerations: Light loads only — high-rep focused exercise for deltoid pump and mobility
Avoid if shoulder impingement is present
execution.range_of_motion_guidance: Full arc from sides to overhead and back.
coaching_cues: Draw a teardrop shape with both hands
Lead with the elbows, not the hands
Pinkies up throughout the raise

name: Band Triceps Pushdown
description: A resistance band version of the cable pushdown that can be performed anywhere. The band's accommodating resistance makes the exercise hardest at full extension where the triceps are strongest. This makes bands excellent for pumping and finishing sets.

execution.starting_position: Set up for Band Triceps Pushdown in the appropriate position.
execution.setup_instructions: Prepare equipment and body position for Band Triceps Pushdown.
steps: Step 1: Secure band overhead at a fixed point. Grasp band ends at chest level.
Step 2: Keep elbows pinned at sides throughout the movement.
Step 3: Push hands down by extending elbows to full lockout.
Step 4: Return slowly allowing band to pull hands back to start.
execution.breathing_instructions: Exhale during the exertion phase, inhale during the return.
common_mistakes: Letting elbows drift forward
Using body weight to assist
safety_considerations: Keep joints aligned throughout the movement.
Use controlled weight appropriate for skill level.
execution.range_of_motion_guidance: Move through full range of motion without compromising joint integrity.
coaching_cues: Squeeze hard at full extension
Control the band on the way up

name: Banded Resistance Barbell Bench Press
description: The Banded Bench Press attaches resistance bands to the barbell and anchors them below the bench, creating accommodating resistance that increases as the bar approaches lockout. The bands also create an overspeed eccentric on the way down, demanding greater eccentric control. This tool trains explosive pressing intent and lockout strength simultaneously.

execution.starting_position: Loop bands around the barbell sleeves and anchor them under the bench feet or to the base of a power rack. Lie on the bench and grip the bar as for a standard bench press.
execution.setup_instructions: Secure bands symmetrically on both sides with equal tension. Reduce barbell plate load to account for band tension at lockout. The total load at lockout equals barbell weight plus band tension.
steps: Step 1: Unrack the bar; feel the band tension pulling the bar downward.
Step 2: Lower under full control — the bands create an overspeed eccentric pull.
Step 3: Touch the chest and immediately press with maximal intent.
Step 4: Drive to lockout against the increasing band resistance.
execution.breathing_instructions: Inhale and brace before the eccentric. Exhale through lockout.
common_mistakes: Using bands that are too heavy, turning the eccentric into an uncontrollable drop
Overloading the barbell — total load at lockout should not exceed your true max
safety_considerations: Bands can slip if not anchored correctly — double-check anchor points
Always use a power rack with safety bars
execution.range_of_motion_guidance: Full ROM — chest to lockout. Same as standard bench press.
coaching_cues: Fight the bands down and explode up
Press as fast as possible — your intent drives the adaptation

name: Banded Good Morning
description: A good morning exercise performed with a resistance band looped over the neck and under the feet, providing accommodating resistance that increases as the athlete stands. The band version allows training the hip hinge pattern with minimal equipment and is excellent for warming up the posterior chain or higher-rep conditioning work.
