execution.starting_position: Stand with a resistance band loop under both feet and looped over the upper back or neck. Stand tall with knees soft.
execution.setup_instructions: Step both feet onto the center of a resistance band loop. Loop the top over the back of the neck like a barbell.
steps: Step 1: Keep the knees slightly bent and the spine neutral.
Step 2: Hinge at the hips and push the hips back, allowing the torso to lower forward.
Step 3: Lower until a strong hamstring stretch is felt or the torso is roughly parallel to the floor.
Step 4: Drive the hips forward to return to standing, squeezing the glutes at the top.
execution.breathing_instructions: Inhale on the hinge. Exhale on the drive to standing.
common_mistakes: Rounding the lower back during the hinge
Bending the knees excessively, turning it into a squat
safety_considerations: Keep the knees soft but fixed — the bend should not change during the movement
execution.range_of_motion_guidance: Hinge until a strong hamstring stretch is felt. Full hip extension at the top.
coaching_cues: Push the hips back
Squeeze the glutes at the top

name: Banded Hip Thrust
description: A hip thrust exercise performed with a resistance band loop placed across the hips instead of a barbell. The band provides increasing resistance toward the top of the movement where the glutes are most capable of producing force, making it a highly effective tool for glute activation and home training.

execution.starting_position: Sit with your upper back against a flat bench. Place a resistance band loop across your hips, anchored under both feet. Feet flat on the floor.
execution.setup_instructions: Sit on the floor with upper back on a bench. Thread a resistance band loop under both feet and over the hips.
steps: Step 1: Drive through both heels to thrust the hips upward.
Step 2: Extend the hips fully at the top, squeezing the glutes hard.
Step 3: Hold for a moment at the top.
Step 4: Lower the hips back toward the floor under control.
execution.breathing_instructions: Exhale on the drive up. Inhale on the descent.
common_mistakes: Hyperextending the lumbar spine at the top
Not fully extending the hips at the top
safety_considerations: Chin stays tucked — do not hyperextend the neck at lockout
execution.range_of_motion_guidance: Full hip extension at the top — body forms a straight line from knees to shoulders.
coaching_cues: Full extension at the top
Squeeze and hold the glutes

name: Banded Pull-Apart
description: A simple but highly effective rear deltoid, rhomboid, and rotator cuff exercise performed by pulling a resistance band apart horizontally at chest height. The pull-apart is frequently used as a warm-up, postural corrective exercise, and high-volume accessory for upper back and shoulder health.

execution.starting_position: Stand tall holding a resistance band with both hands at chest height, arms extended forward, hands shoulder-width apart.
execution.setup_instructions: Select a light to medium resistance band. Hold it with palms facing down or facing each other.
steps: Step 1: Keep the arms relatively straight (elbows soft, not locked).
Step 2: Pull the band apart by moving both hands outward and backward.
Step 3: Continue until the band touches or nearly touches the chest, squeezing the rear delts and rhomboids.
Step 4: Return slowly to the starting position.
execution.breathing_instructions: Exhale on the pull apart. Inhale on the return.
common_mistakes: Using a band that is too heavy, causing the arms to bend excessively
Moving through too fast without feeling the rear delt contraction
safety_considerations: This exercise should be performed for higher reps (15-25) with a light band for best results
execution.range_of_motion_guidance: Full extension of the band behind the chest at the back position.
coaching_cues: Arms stay relatively straight
Squeeze the shoulder blades together at the end

name: Banded Squat Walk
description: The banded squat walk is a dynamic hip abduction exercise performed in a partial squat position while stepping laterally against the resistance of a loop band placed above the knees or around the ankles. Maintaining a squat while stepping sideways forces the gluteus medius to both stabilize the pelvis and drive abduction, making it an effective warm-up and accessory exercise for lower body training.

execution.starting_position: Place a loop resistance band above the knees (easier) or around the ankles (harder). Stand with feet shoulder-width apart and descend into a partial squat — roughly quarter to half squat depth.
execution.setup_instructions: Choose band tension based on ability. Heavier bands around the knees provide more resistance; lighter bands around the ankles increase range.
steps: Step 1: Place the band above knees or around ankles. Assume a partial squat with feet shoulder-width apart, chest up, core braced.
Step 2: Step one foot laterally to widen the stance beyond shoulder width, maintaining the squat depth.
Step 3: Bring the trailing foot to follow, returning to shoulder-width stance — still in squat.
Step 4: Continue walking in the same direction for the prescribed distance or steps.
Step 5: Repeat in the opposite direction.
execution.breathing_instructions: Breathe rhythmically throughout — exhale with each step.
common_mistakes: Standing up out of the squat between steps — maintain depth throughout
Letting the knees cave inward — push knees out against the band
Taking too large a step, which compromises squat position
safety_considerations: Low risk exercise; common as a warm-up before squats and deadlifts
Avoid if the band causes knee pain — use a lighter band or adjust position
execution.range_of_motion_guidance: Steps of 30–45 cm per stride. Stay in a consistent partial squat throughout.
execution.tempo_recommendations: Controlled step pace — roughly 1 step per second.
coaching_cues: Stay low — don't pop up between steps
Push knees out — fight the band
Keep toes forward — don't let feet turn out excessively

name: Barbell 21s
description: A barbell curl protocol using 21 total repetitions split into three segments: 7 reps from the bottom to the midpoint, 7 reps from the midpoint to the top, and 7 full-range reps. Each segment targets a different portion of the strength curve and produces significant metabolic stress in the biceps.

execution.starting_position: Stand holding a barbell with an underhand grip, arms fully extended.
execution.setup_instructions: Select a weight approximately 60-70% of your normal curl working weight. Stand tall with the bar hanging in front.
steps: Step 1 (reps 1-7): Curl from full extension to the midpoint only (forearms parallel to floor). Lower back down and repeat 7 times.
Step 2 (reps 8-14): Start from the midpoint and curl to full contraction at the top. Lower back to midpoint and repeat 7 times.
Step 3 (reps 15-21): Perform 7 full-range curls from full extension to full contraction.
execution.breathing_instructions: Breathe rhythmically throughout each segment. Exhale on the curl, inhale on the lower.
common_mistakes: Using too heavy a weight — the third segment of full reps becomes impossible
Resting between segments
safety_considerations: All 21 reps are performed without putting the bar down
execution.range_of_motion_guidance: Partial ranges in segments 1 and 2, full range in segment 3.
coaching_cues: No rest between segments
Feel the pump build through each set

name: Barbell Bench Press
description: The barbell bench press is a foundational horizontal pushing movement performed lying on a flat bench. It is one of the most effective exercises for developing overall chest mass, anterior deltoid strength, and triceps power. The fixed barbell path and bilateral loading allow for maximum load and progressive overload potential.

execution.starting_position: Lie supine on a flat bench with eyes directly under the bar. Place feet flat on the floor. Grip the bar slightly wider than shoulder width with an overhand grip. Unrack the bar and hold it directly over the chest with arms fully extended.
execution.setup_instructions: Set the barbell in a rack at a height you can unrack with arms nearly extended. Lie back so your eyes are under the bar. Arch your upper back naturally and retract your shoulder blades. Grip the bar with thumbs wrapped around it. Feet should be flat or on toes depending on preference.
steps: Take a deep breath and brace your core and upper back firmly.
Unrack the bar by pressing it out of the hooks and locking it over your chest with straight arms.
Lower the bar under control in a slight arc toward your lower chest or upper abdomen — roughly at the nipple line.
Touch the bar to your chest lightly without bouncing or losing tension.
Drive the bar back up along the same arc, pressing it toward your upper chest and exhaling forcefully at the top.
Re-rack the bar by guiding it back into the hooks after completing all reps.
execution.breathing_instructions: Inhale and brace before lowering the bar. Hold or take a controlled breath during the descent. Exhale forcefully as you press the bar back to the starting position.
common_mistakes: Allowing the wrists to bend excessively backward — keep wrists stacked over the forearms
Flaring the elbows to 90 degrees — tuck slightly at 45–75 degrees to protect the shoulder
Bouncing the bar off the chest to generate momentum
Losing upper back tightness by allowing shoulder blades to protract during the press
Raising the hips off the bench during the concentric phase
safety_considerations: Always use a spotter or safety catches when training near maximal loads
Warm up rotator cuff muscles before heavy pressing
Do not use a thumbless (suicide) grip — wrap the thumbs fully around the bar
execution.range_of_motion_guidance: Lower the bar until it touches the chest. Press to full elbow extension without locking out aggressively. A full range of motion maximizes pectoral stretch and development.
execution.tempo_recommendations: 2-1-1-0: 2 seconds eccentric descent, 1 second pause at chest, 1 second concentric press, 0 second pause at top. For strength, reduce eccentric to 1 second.
coaching_cues: Squeeze oranges in your armpits — retract and depress the shoulder blades
Drive your feet into the floor to create a stable base
Think about bending the bar like a horseshoe as you press

name: Barbell Curl
description: The barbell curl is the foundational barbell biceps exercise, performed by curling a straight barbell from the thighs to the shoulders in a supinated grip. It allows maximal loading of the biceps brachii and brachialis and is one of the most effective exercises for overall biceps mass and strength development.

execution.starting_position: Stand with feet shoulder-width apart holding a barbell at hip height with a supinated grip slightly wider than shoulder width. Elbows tucked against the sides of the torso.
execution.setup_instructions: Use a straight barbell or EZ-curl bar. Keep the elbows pinned to the sides throughout the movement to isolate the biceps.
steps: Curl the barbell upward by flexing the elbows, keeping upper arms stationary.
Continue until the barbell is at shoulder height and the biceps are fully contracted.
Lower the barbell under control back to the starting position with full elbow extension.
execution.breathing_instructions: Exhale on the curl, inhale on the descent.
common_mistakes: Swinging the torso to generate momentum — keep the back straight
Allowing the elbows to drift forward, reducing biceps tension
Stopping short of full extension at the bottom
safety_considerations: If wrist discomfort occurs, switch to an EZ-curl bar
execution.range_of_motion_guidance: Full extension at the bottom, full flexion with biceps contracted at top.
coaching_cues: Keep your elbows glued to your sides — only your forearms should move
Squeeze hard at the top of each rep

name: Barbell Dead Hang
description: The barbell dead hang involves gripping a loaded barbell in the rack or on the floor from a standing position and holding it for time. Unlike a pull-up bar hang, the arms remain straight and the body stands, loading the grip and forearm flexors isometrically with heavy weights. It directly trains the grip strength needed for deadlifts and other heavy pulling movements. It is typically performed with deadlift-level loads at the end of a training session.

execution.starting_position: Load a barbell at hip height in a rack. Stand and grasp the bar with a double overhand grip, shoulder-width.
execution.setup_instructions: Set the bar at deadlift height. Use loads at or above your deadlift working weight for grip training specificity.
steps: Step 1: Grip the barbell with a double overhand grip.
Step 2: Lift the bar off the pins or take it from the floor.
Step 3: Hold it in a standing position with arms fully extended for the prescribed duration.
Step 4: Set the bar down when grip is about to fail.
execution.breathing_instructions: Breathe freely throughout the hold.
common_mistakes: Using straps (negates the grip training purpose)
Holding past the point of technique breakdown
safety_considerations: Ensure the bar is secured and the hold is performed over a rubber-matted platform
execution.range_of_motion_guidance: Static hold — no movement.
coaching_cues: Grip hard throughout
Shoulders packed down
Control when you set it down

name: Barbell Finger Curls
description: An isolated forearm exercise performed by holding a barbell with an overhand grip and allowing the bar to roll down to the fingertips before curling the fingers and wrists back up. This exercise strengthens the finger flexors, forearm flexors, and grip in a unique fingertip-to-wrist range.

execution.starting_position: Sit at the end of a bench with forearms resting on the thighs. Hold a barbell with an underhand (supinated) grip, hands close together.
execution.setup_instructions: Sit with forearms resting on the thighs, wrists just past the knees. Hold a relatively light barbell with an underhand grip.
steps: Step 1: Open the fingers and allow the bar to roll down toward the fingertips.
Step 2: Curl the fingers closed to grip the bar again.
Step 3: Flex the wrist to curl the bar upward fully.
Step 4: Lower the bar back to the fingertips and repeat.
execution.breathing_instructions: Breathe steadily throughout — this is a low-load forearm exercise.
common_mistakes: Using too heavy a load, which prevents the bar from rolling to the fingertips
Moving the forearms off the thighs
safety_considerations: Keep the forearms firmly rested on the thighs throughout
execution.range_of_motion_guidance: Full extension (bar at fingertips) to full wrist flexion.
coaching_cues: Let the bar roll down to the fingertips
Curl the fingers first, then the wrist

name: Barbell Front Raise
description: The barbell front raise targets the anterior deltoid by raising a barbell from the thighs to shoulder height in front of the body. The bilateral nature and pronated grip load both anterior deltoids simultaneously and provide a simple progressive overload path compared to dumbbell variations. It is a straightforward anterior deltoid isolation exercise suitable for adding volume to shoulder training.

execution.starting_position: Stand upright holding a barbell with a pronated (overhand) grip at approximately shoulder width. The bar hangs at thigh level with arms nearly straight.
execution.setup_instructions: Use a relatively light load. The anterior deltoid is already heavily stressed from pressing — treat this as supplemental volume work.
steps: Step 1: Hold the bar at thigh level with an overhand grip.
Step 2: Keeping the arms nearly straight (slight elbow bend), raise the bar in front of the body.
Step 3: Raise until the bar is at shoulder height or slightly above.
Step 4: Pause at the top briefly.
Step 5: Lower under full control to the thighs.
execution.breathing_instructions: Exhale as you raise, inhale as you lower.
common_mistakes: Using body momentum by leaning back or rocking
Raising too high — above shoulder level recruits the traps excessively
Bending the elbows too much, turning it into a curl-raise hybrid
safety_considerations: Keep the lower back neutral — do not hyperextend as the bar rises
execution.range_of_motion_guidance: Thigh level to shoulder height (90 degrees).
coaching_cues: Arms like a robot — controlled arc
No lean back
Stop at shoulder height

name: Barbell Glute Bridge
description: The barbell glute bridge is performed lying on the floor with a barbell placed across the hips, driving the hips upward from the floor to full extension. Unlike the barbell hip thrust, the upper back remains flat on the floor rather than elevated on a bench, reducing the range of motion but requiring no bench. It is an effective and accessible glute exercise that provides high levels of gluteus maximus activation at the end-range hip extension position.

execution.starting_position: Lie on your back with knees bent and feet flat on the floor, hip-width apart. Place the barbell across your hips, with a pad or towel for comfort.
execution.setup_instructions: Roll the barbell over the legs to position it across the hip crease. Use a barbell pad or folded towel to reduce discomfort on the anterior hip bones.
steps: Step 1: Lie on your back, bar across the hips, feet hip-width, knees at approximately 90°. Hold the bar lightly at each side.
Step 2: Drive through both feet to push the hips upward toward the ceiling.
Step 3: Squeeze the glutes forcefully at the top until the hips, knees, and shoulders form a straight line.
Step 4: Hold the peak contraction for one second.
Step 5: Lower the hips to the floor in a controlled manner.
execution.breathing_instructions: Exhale as you drive the hips up. Inhale as you lower.
common_mistakes: Hyperextending the lower back at the top — the top position should be a neutral spine plank, not an arched back
Feet placed too far away, shifting load to the hamstrings rather than glutes
Not squeezing the glutes at the top
safety_considerations: Use a barbell pad — the hip crease is a sensitive area under load
Ensure the barbell is stable before beginning
execution.range_of_motion_guidance: Hips descend to the floor at the bottom. Full hip extension at the top — body forms a straight line from knees to shoulders.
coaching_cues: Drive through the heels — not the toes
Tuck the pelvis slightly at the top — don't arch the lower back
Squeeze the glutes hard — hold the top for a beat

name: Barbell Hip Thrust
description: The barbell hip thrust is a loaded hip extension exercise in which the upper back is braced against a bench and a barbell rests across the hips. It places the gluteus maximus under maximal tension at full hip extension and is widely considered the most effective exercise for direct glute development and hip extension strength.

execution.starting_position: Sit on the floor with your upper back against the long side of a flat bench. Roll a barbell over your thighs to rest across the crease of your hips. Place a barbell pad if needed for comfort. Feet flat on the floor at shoulder width.
execution.setup_instructions: Position the bench perpendicular to a wall or stabilize it. Ensure the barbell is centered and resting across the hip crease, not the lower abdomen.
steps: Drive through both heels and squeeze the glutes to thrust the hips upward.
At the top, the torso from knees to shoulders should be parallel to the floor.
Squeeze the glutes hard at the top for one second.
Lower the hips under control back toward the floor.
execution.breathing_instructions: Exhale on the hip thrust. Inhale on the descent.
common_mistakes: Arching the lower back at the top — tuck the chin and think about driving the ribs down
Pushing through the toes instead of the heels
Inadequate hip extension at the top — do not stop short
safety_considerations: Use a barbell pad to protect the hip bones and reduce discomfort
Ensure the bench is stable and cannot slip
execution.range_of_motion_guidance: Hips descend to just above the floor at the bottom, full horizontal lockout at the top.
coaching_cues: Drive your hips toward the ceiling, not toward the wall
Squeeze your glutes like you are holding a coin between them at the top

name: Barbell Hip Thrust with Pause
description: A barbell hip thrust performed with a deliberate pause at the top of each repetition. The pause eliminates elastic energy and forces the glutes to sustain maximum contraction isometrically, increasing time under tension and maximizing glute activation at peak hip extension.

execution.starting_position: Sit with your upper back against a flat bench, bar resting across your hips. Feet flat on the floor, knees bent approximately 90 degrees.
execution.setup_instructions: Roll the barbell over your legs and position it across your hip crease. Use a pad for comfort. Set up with the upper back on the bench edge.
steps: Step 1: Drive through both heels to thrust the hips upward.
Step 2: Extend the hips fully at the top, squeezing the glutes maximally.
Step 3: Hold the top position for 2 to 3 seconds while maintaining maximum glute contraction.
Step 4: Lower the hips back toward the floor under control and repeat.
execution.breathing_instructions: Exhale on the drive up and during the hold. Inhale on the way down.
common_mistakes: Hyperextending the lumbar spine at the top instead of using glute strength
Releasing the glute squeeze during the pause
safety_considerations: Keep the chin tucked — do not hyperextend the neck at the top
execution.range_of_motion_guidance: Full hip extension at the top — body forms a straight line from knees to shoulders. Hold this position.
coaching_cues: Squeeze the glutes hard at the top
Hold and breathe — do not relax

name: Forward Walking Lunges — Barbell
description: Barbell walking lunges are a compound unilateral exercise performed with a barbell across the upper traps. The lifter steps forward continuously, alternating legs for a set distance or rep count. The barbell adds significantly more load than dumbbells and challenges core stability and balance throughout the movement. The alternating nature trains dynamic single-leg strength and hip flexor flexibility.

execution.starting_position: Unrack the barbell from a power rack and position it across the upper traps (similar to a high-bar squat). Stand with feet hip-width apart at the edge of an open space.
execution.setup_instructions: Set the barbell at an appropriate weight — significantly less than a barbell squat. Ensure you have enough open floor space for the number of lunges planned.
steps: Step 1: Step one foot forward into a lunge stance, bending both knees simultaneously.
Step 2: Lower the rear knee to near the floor while keeping the front shin nearly vertical.
Step 3: Drive through the front heel to bring the rear foot forward past the front foot, completing one step.
Step 4: Immediately step the new leading foot forward and repeat on the opposite side.
execution.breathing_instructions: Breathe rhythmically — exhale on each drive up.
common_mistakes: Step length too short, causing the front shin to angle too far forward
Leaning the torso to one side under barbell load
Rear knee crashing to the floor
safety_considerations: Requires open floor space — ensure the path is clear
High demand on balance with a barbell — develop with dumbbells first
execution.range_of_motion_guidance: Rear knee to approximately 1-2 inches from the floor each step.
coaching_cues: Long step, vertical front shin
Rear knee drops, don't crash it
Stand tall with the barbell

name: Barbell Overhead Press
description: The barbell overhead press is a standing vertical pushing exercise in which a barbell is pressed from the front rack position to full overhead extension. It is the primary free-weight exercise for developing shoulder mass and pressing strength, and also trains the triceps and upper trapezius as significant synergists.

execution.starting_position: Stand with feet hip-width apart. Hold the barbell in a front rack position at the upper chest with hands slightly wider than shoulder width. Elbows just in front of the bar, wrists straight.
execution.setup_instructions: Unrack the barbell from a squat rack set at upper chest height. Brace the core and squeeze the glutes before pressing to stabilize the spine.
steps: Take a breath and brace the core hard.
Press the bar straight up and slightly back as it passes the face, sliding the head back slightly to allow bar clearance.
Lock the bar out directly overhead with arms fully extended and biceps close to the ears.
Lower the bar under control back to the front rack position.
execution.breathing_instructions: Inhale and brace before each press. Exhale at lockout.
common_mistakes: Pressing the bar forward instead of straight up and over the center of mass
Excessive lumbar hyperextension — maintain a braced, neutral lumbar curve
Not locking the bar out overhead fully
safety_considerations: If shoulder mobility limits an overhead lockout, work on thoracic extension and shoulder flexibility
Use a squat rack to unrack safely — do not clean from the floor for pressing sets
execution.range_of_motion_guidance: Full lockout overhead, bar returns to clavicle/upper chest level at the bottom.
coaching_cues: Press your head through your arms as the bar passes your face
Squeeze your glutes and abs hard — make your whole body a rigid pillar

name: Barbell Preacher Curl
description: The barbell preacher curl uses a preacher bench to brace the upper arms on an angled pad, eliminating any chance of swinging and fixing the elbow position. The braced arm position pre-loads the biceps in a lengthened state and forces strict elbow flexion. The preacher position emphasizes the lower portion of the bicep and the brachialis. It was popularized by Larry Scott, the first Mr. Olympia.

execution.starting_position: Sit at a preacher bench. Rest the upper arms on the slanted pad. Hold a barbell with a supinated grip, arms nearly fully extended.
execution.setup_instructions: Adjust the seat height so the top of the pad is at armpit level. Grip the bar at shoulder width.
steps: Step 1: Begin with the elbows nearly fully extended, feeling the stretch.
Step 2: Curl the barbell upward, bending the elbows until maximum flexion is reached.
Step 3: Hold briefly at the peak.
Step 4: Lower slowly, resisting the weight all the way down — do not drop.
execution.breathing_instructions: Exhale on the curl, inhale on the return.
common_mistakes: Dropping the bar at the bottom — control the full eccentric
Locking out the elbows fully at the bottom (high injury risk)
Flaring the elbows off the pad
safety_considerations: Never lock out fully with heavy weight — stop just short of full extension to protect the elbow joint
The bicep tendon is at risk with heavy dropped eccentrics
execution.range_of_motion_guidance: Stop just short of full elbow extension at the bottom; curl to full flexion at the top.
coaching_cues: Arms stay on the pad
Control the bottom — don't drop it
Stop just before lockout

name: Barbell Pullover
description: The barbell pullover is a classic strength and hypertrophy exercise that challenges the chest and lats through a sweeping arc from above the chest to behind the head. The barbell allows for heavier loading than a dumbbell version and provides a bilateral symmetrical grip, making it a staple for developing chest thickness and upper-body flexibility.

execution.starting_position: Lie along or across a flat bench with upper back and shoulders supported. Grip the barbell with an overhand, shoulder-width grip, holding it above the chest with arms extended.
execution.setup_instructions: Have a training partner hand you the bar, or lift it from the floor into position before lying back. Use a close grip to minimize stress on the shoulder at the extended position.
steps: Step 1: Lie on the bench holding the bar above the chest with arms nearly straight.
Step 2: Keeping the arms straight, slowly arc the bar backward over and behind the head.
Step 3: Lower until a full chest and lat stretch is felt, typically when the bar is below head level.
Step 4: Drive the bar back over the face in a reverse arc, squeezing the chest.
Step 5: Return to the starting position above the chest.
execution.breathing_instructions: Inhale deeply during the descent to assist ribcage expansion. Exhale forcefully as the bar arcs back overhead.
common_mistakes: Using too wide a grip, increasing shoulder impingement risk
Loading too heavily for the shoulder's stretched position to handle
Losing control during the descent
safety_considerations: This exercise is contraindicated with shoulder impingement or rotator cuff issues
Have a spotter assist with handing off and re-racking the bar
Start with an empty bar or light load to establish the arc pattern
execution.range_of_motion_guidance: Lower the bar behind the head to a point of deep stretch without discomfort. Full extension of arms is the goal, but slight elbow bend is acceptable for joint safety.
coaching_cues: Let the chest open wide on the way down
Think about moving the bar in an arc, not a straight line
Exhale powerfully on the way back up

name: Barbell Romanian Deadlift
description: The barbell Romanian deadlift is a hip-hinge exercise that primarily targets the hamstrings and gluteus maximus through a loaded eccentric stretch. Unlike the conventional deadlift, the barbell does not touch the floor between reps — the movement focuses on stretching the hamstrings under load by hinging at the hips with a slight knee bend and a neutral spine.

execution.starting_position: Stand with feet hip-width apart holding a barbell at hip level with an overhand grip. Maintain a neutral spine with the chest up and shoulders back.
execution.setup_instructions: Begin with the barbell held at the thighs after lifting it to standing. Engage the lats and brace the core before each rep.
steps: Initiate the movement by pushing the hips backward while maintaining a slight bend in the knees.
Lower the barbell along the front of the legs, keeping it close to the body.
Descend until you feel a strong stretch in the hamstrings — typically mid-shin level for most.
Drive the hips forward to return to the standing position, squeezing the glutes at the top.
execution.breathing_instructions: Inhale and brace before the descent. Exhale as you drive the hips forward on the ascent.
common_mistakes: Rounding the lower back — the movement is a hip hinge, not a spine flex
Bending the knees excessively, turning it into a deadlift
Lowering the barbell too far — only go as low as the hamstrings allow without spinal flexion
safety_considerations: If you feel the stretch in the lower back rather than the hamstrings, reduce range and focus on the hip hinge pattern
Use lifting straps for heavy sets to prevent grip from being the limiting factor
execution.range_of_motion_guidance: Lower until a strong hamstring stretch is felt. Typically between knee and mid-shin depending on individual hamstring flexibility.
coaching_cues: Push your hips back to a wall behind you
Keep the bar dragging up your legs on the way up — you should feel it on your shins

name: Barbell Row
description: The barbell row is a horizontal pulling exercise performed in a hinged position with a barbell. It trains the latissimus dorsi, rhomboids, and middle trapezius as primary movers and places significant isometric demand on the erector spinae and hamstrings to maintain the hip-hinge position. It is one of the most effective exercises for overall back thickness and strength.

execution.starting_position: Stand with feet shoulder-width apart over the barbell. Hinge forward at the hips until your torso is roughly parallel to the floor, with a slight knee bend. Grip the bar just outside shoulder width with an overhand or underhand grip.
execution.setup_instructions: Set up like the start of a deadlift but with a more pronounced hip hinge to get the torso near-parallel to the floor. Maintain a neutral spine. Brace the core and engage the lats before each rep.
steps: With a neutral spine and braced core, row the barbell toward your lower rib cage.
Lead with the elbows and squeeze the shoulder blades together at the top of the movement.
Lower the bar under control back toward the floor, maintaining the hinge position throughout.
execution.breathing_instructions: Exhale as you row the bar up. Inhale as you lower it.
common_mistakes: Allowing the lower back to round under load
Using body English and hip drive to jerk the bar up instead of pulling with the back
Pulling the bar to the waist rather than the lower ribs, reducing lat involvement
safety_considerations: Never compromise spinal position for more weight
If unable to maintain a hip-hinge position, reduce load
execution.range_of_motion_guidance: Full extension of the arms at the bottom, bar touches or nearly touches the lower ribs at the top.
coaching_cues: Row the bar into your hip pockets
Keep your chest up and your spine long throughout every rep

name: Barbell Shrug
description: The barbell shrug is an isolation exercise for the upper trapezius, performed by elevating the shoulders while holding a heavy barbell at arm's length. It is the primary direct exercise for developing upper trap thickness and neck size, and is commonly used by strength athletes to improve grip strength and upper back robustness.

execution.starting_position: Stand upright holding a barbell at arm's length in front of the thighs with a pronated or mixed grip. Feet shoulder-width apart, spine neutral.
execution.setup_instructions: Set up like a deadlift start position but keep the bar at thigh height. Use lifting straps for heavy sets to prevent grip from being the limiting factor.
steps: Elevate the shoulders straight upward as high as possible, contracting the upper trapezius.
Hold the top position for one second.
Lower the shoulders back down in a controlled manner to full depression.
execution.breathing_instructions: Exhale as you shrug up. Inhale as you lower.
common_mistakes: Rolling the shoulders forward or backward — shrug straight up
Using body swing or bend to generate momentum
Not achieving full range of motion in both directions
safety_considerations: Avoid heavy shrugs if you have neck or cervical spine issues
execution.range_of_motion_guidance: Full elevation of the shoulders at the top, full depression at the bottom.
coaching_cues: Shrug straight up — not forward, not back, just up
Try to touch your ears with your shoulders at the top

name: Barbell Snatch
description: The barbell snatch is one of the two Olympic weightlifting competition lifts, in which the athlete lifts the barbell from the floor to a locked-out overhead position in a single continuous movement, catching it in an overhead squat. The lift demands exceptional full-body power production, bar speed, coordination, shoulder mobility, and hip flexibility. It is among the most technically complex and physically demanding exercises in strength sports and develops explosive power, coordination, and total body strength simultaneously.

execution.starting_position: Stand with the barbell over the mid-foot. Take a wide snatch grip (outside the knees), feet hip-width apart. Bar is touching the shins, hips above knees, shoulders above the bar, back flat.
execution.setup_instructions: Use bumper plates and a lifting platform. The snatch grip width is determined by holding the bar in the hip crease with arms extended — the bar should contact the hip crease on extension. Warm up thoroughly.
steps: Step 1: Set the starting position — bar over mid-foot, wide grip, flat back, hips between shoulders and knees.
Step 2: First pull (floor to knee): drive legs into the floor to separate the bar from the ground, keeping the back angle constant and bar close to the body.
Step 3: Second pull (knee to hip): as the bar passes the knee, accelerate the legs further and open the hip powerfully while keeping the bar close to the thigh.

Step 4: Third pull (extension and turnover): at full hip extension, shrug the traps and pull the elbows high and outside. As the bar travels upward, pull yourself under the bar and rotate the hands into the overhead position.
Step 5: Catch in an overhead squat, stand to full extension, and lower the bar with control.
execution.breathing_instructions: Take a deep breath and brace before the lift. Hold the brace through the second pull. Exhale at the top after securing the catch.
common_mistakes: Early arm bend (pulling with the arms before the hip extension)
Bar drifting away from the body during the first pull
Insufficient hip extension before the turnover
Catching with soft elbows overhead
safety_considerations: Requires extensive technical coaching before loading significantly.
Always use bumper plates and a lifting platform for safe drops.
Never train to failure — drop the bar if the catch is compromised.
execution.range_of_motion_guidance: The bar travels from floor to fully locked overhead in an overhead squat catch. Full hip extension at the second pull is essential.
execution.tempo_recommendations: Explosive — the entire lift should be completed in under 2 seconds once initiated. There is no tempo prescription; maximum bar speed is the goal.
coaching_cues: Lats on — keep the bar close
Hips through — open explosively at the top
Punch up and pull under

name: Barbell Back Squat
description: The barbell back squat is the foundational lower body compound movement, in which a barbell rests on the upper back while the lifter descends into a full squat and returns to standing. It is unparalleled for developing quadriceps, glute, and hamstring strength and size, and also demands significant erector spinae and core stability.

execution.starting_position: Stand with feet shoulder-width apart or slightly wider, toes pointing outward 15–30 degrees. The barbell rests on the upper traps (high-bar) or rear delts (low-bar). Unrack from a rack with arms firmly bracing the bar.
execution.setup_instructions: Set the safety bars just below your squat depth in the rack. Position the bar on your upper back and grip firmly. Take a step back with both feet into your squat stance.
steps: Take a deep breath and brace the core hard with an intra-abdominal pressure brace.
Initiate the descent by pushing the knees outward in the direction of the toes while hinging the hips back and down.
Descend until the hips are at or below the top of the knees (parallel or deeper).
Drive through the whole foot — especially the mid-foot and heel — to stand back up.
Lock out the hips and knees fully at the top without hyperextending.
execution.breathing_instructions: Breathe in and brace before descent. Hold the brace through the bottom. Exhale at the top.
common_mistakes: Knees caving inward (valgus collapse) — cue knees out
Excessive forward lean from poor ankle mobility or bar position
Rounding the lower back at the bottom of the squat
Not reaching parallel depth
safety_considerations: Always use safety bars in a rack when squatting without a spotter
Learn the goblet squat and bodyweight squat before loading a barbell
execution.range_of_motion_guidance: Hip crease below the top of the knee at minimum (parallel). Greater depth is generally better for glute and hamstring development when mobility allows.
coaching_cues: Spread the floor with your feet — push out with knees
Big chest — keep the torso as upright as your bar position allows
Drive through the floor, not just the toes

name: Step-Up with Barbell
description: The barbell step-up is a unilateral lower body exercise performed with a barbell across the traps, stepping onto a box or bench. The added load of the barbell dramatically increases the difficulty compared to dumbbell step-ups and challenges the quadriceps, glutes, and hip extensors of the working leg. The box height determines the range of motion and muscle emphasis.

execution.starting_position: Unrack the barbell and position it across the upper traps. Stand facing a sturdy box or bench at knee height.
execution.setup_instructions: Use a box height that creates approximately 90 degrees of knee flexion when the foot is on top. Load conservatively.
steps: Step 1: Place the working foot fully on the box, ensuring the entire foot is on the surface.
Step 2: Drive through the working heel to extend the leg and lift the body onto the box.
Step 3: Stand fully upright on the box, bringing the trail foot up to touch the box surface (not pushing off with it).
Step 4: Lower the trail foot back to the floor in a controlled manner and repeat.
execution.breathing_instructions: Exhale on the step up, inhale on the controlled descent.
common_mistakes: Pushing off the floor foot, reducing working leg demand
Box too low — insufficient ROM
Leaning heavily with the torso
safety_considerations: Ensure the box is completely stable and can safely support the loaded barbell weight
Develop with dumbbell step-ups before using a barbell
execution.range_of_motion_guidance: Full extension at the top of the box. Full descent to both feet on the floor.
coaching_cues: Drive through the heel on the box
Floor foot is a passenger
Stand tall at the top

name: Battle Rope Waves with Lateral Shuffle
description: A dynamic battle rope conditioning drill in which the exerciser performs alternating rope waves while simultaneously shuffling laterally (side to side). The lateral shuffle adds lower body agility, hip abductor, and hip adductor demands to the standard battle rope work, making this a true full-body conditioning exercise. Used in sports conditioning, metabolic circuit training, and functional fitness programming.

execution.starting_position: Hold one end of a battle rope in each hand. Begin in an athletic stance (slight squat, knees soft) and start alternating arm waves.
execution.setup_instructions: Ensure adequate side-to-side space (3-5 meters). The rope must be long enough to allow lateral movement while maintaining wave mechanics.
steps: Step 1: Begin alternating arm waves from the starting position.
Step 2: While maintaining the rope waves, shuffle laterally to the right for 3-5 steps.
Step 3: Without stopping the waves, shuffle back to the left for 3-5 steps.
Step 4: Continue alternating directions for the prescribed interval.
execution.breathing_instructions: Breathe continuously and rhythmically. The demand is high — do not hold the breath.
common_mistakes: Stopping the waves to shuffle — the waves must continue during the lateral movement
Crossing the feet during the shuffle — use a true lateral shuffle pattern (no crossover)
Standing upright during the shuffle — stay in the athletic squat stance
safety_considerations: Ensure the floor is clear of obstacles in the shuffle path
If the rope cannot maintain wave mechanics during the shuffle, reduce the shuffle speed
execution.range_of_motion_guidance: Shuffle distance depends on rope length. Maintain wave quality throughout the entire shuffle distance.
execution.tempo_recommendations: 30-60 second work intervals. Shuffle speed dictated by wave quality — not so fast that waves collapse.
coaching_cues: Keep the waves going during the shuffle — that is the whole challenge
Stay in the athletic position — bent knees, chest up
Quick feet during the shuffle, but do not sacrifice wave quality for speed

name: Battle Rope Waves in Squat Position
description: Battle rope alternating waves performed from a sustained squat position, combining the cardiovascular and upper body demand of battle ropes with isometric quad and glute loading from the squat hold. The sustained squat depth during the wave sequence dramatically increases lower body time-under-tension while training the upper body explosively. This is a metabolic conditioning exercise that develops work capacity, leg endurance, and arm power simultaneously.

execution.starting_position: Hold one end of a battle rope in each hand. Descend to a squat position (60-90 degrees of knee flexion) and maintain this position throughout the exercise.
execution.setup_instructions: Ensure the battle rope anchor is secure. The rope must be long enough to allow the squat position while still creating waves toward the anchor.
steps: Step 1: Descend into the squat position and hold. Keep the chest up and back flat.
Step 2: Begin alternating arm waves — drive the right hand down then up, then the left, creating alternating waves toward the anchor.
Step 3: Maintain the squat depth throughout the entire wave sequence.
Step 4: Continue for the prescribed duration, then stand to rest.
execution.breathing_instructions: Breathe continuously and rhythmically throughout — do not hold the breath. The metabolic demand is high.
common_mistakes: Rising out of the squat as fatigue sets in — the squat hold is the primary loading stimulus
Slowing the wave speed during the set — maintain wave intensity throughout
Using a squat depth that is too deep to hold for the entire set duration — choose a sustainable depth
safety_considerations: Choose a squat depth you can hold for the full prescribed duration — shallow is fine initially
If knee pain occurs during the squat hold, reduce depth or rest
execution.range_of_motion_guidance: Squat depth that can be sustained for the full set. Waves should be full — rope touching the floor between waves.
execution.tempo_recommendations: 30-60 second work intervals. Alternate arms as fast as possible while maintaining squat depth.
coaching_cues: Stay down — the whole point of the squat position is the sustained lower body load
Drive the waves fast — the battle rope conditioning benefit comes from wave speed
Chest up in the squat — maintain a proud posture

name: Battle Ropes
description: Battle ropes are a conditioning exercise in which the athlete alternates or simultaneously waves heavy ropes anchored at one end, sustaining powerful arm and shoulder drive patterns for a timed interval. The continuous undulating motion of the ropes requires sustained explosive upper body work while the lower body is maintained in a stable athletic stance, creating high metabolic demand. Battle rope training is used for upper body power endurance, cardiovascular conditioning, and grip strength.

execution.starting_position: Stand facing the anchor point with feet shoulder-width apart in an athletic squat stance, one rope end in each hand. Slight hip hinge, slight knee bend.
execution.setup_instructions: Anchor a heavy rope (38–50mm diameter) at a fixed point. Stand at a distance that keeps the rope slightly slack. Maintain a consistent athletic stance throughout.
steps: Step 1: Hold one rope end in each hand with an overhand grip.
Step 2: Begin alternating waves: drive the right arm up and immediately bring it down while driving the left arm up.
Step 3: Keep the waves large and continuous — the rope should form visible undulations moving toward the anchor.
Step 4: Maintain an athletic stance throughout — do not let the torso collapse or the knees straighten.
Step 5: Continue for the prescribed duration at maximum sustainable effort.
execution.breathing_instructions: Breathe continuously at a rhythm matching the work rate. Do not hold breath.
common_mistakes: Standing up too tall — the athletic stance with hips back keeps the core engaged
Letting the waves die — maintain large, powerful waves throughout
Only moving from the elbows — the motion should initiate from the shoulders
safety_considerations: High demand on the shoulders and forearms — adequate warm-up required.
Build interval duration progressively — do not start at full intensity with long intervals.
execution.range_of_motion_guidance: Large amplitude waves — full shoulder range. Rope must reach the anchor on each wave.
execution.tempo_recommendations: Typically performed for 20–40 second intervals with equal rest. 5–8 rounds.
coaching_cues: Athletic stance — stay low
Big waves — full range
Drive from the shoulder — not just the elbow

name: Bear Crawl
description: The bear crawl is a locomotion-based functional exercise in which the athlete moves forward on hands and feet with the knees hovering a few centimeters above the floor, maintaining a flat back and neutral spine throughout the movement. It trains contralateral limb coordination, shoulder and hip stability under load, and deep core anti-extension strength. The bear crawl is widely used in athletic performance preparation, rehabilitation, and functional movement screen corrective programming.

execution.starting_position: Begin on hands and knees (quadruped) with the knees lifted to hover approximately 2–5 cm above the floor. Wrists under shoulders, knees under hips.
execution.setup_instructions: No equipment required. Adequate floor space needed for crawling distance.
steps: Step 1: Begin in the hovering quadruped position with knees 2–5 cm off the floor.
Step 2: Move the right hand and left foot forward simultaneously, maintaining a flat back.
Step 3: Follow with the left hand and right foot (contralateral pattern).
Step 4: Keep the hips level — do not let them rise or rotate as you move.
Step 5: Continue crawling forward for the prescribed distance while maintaining form throughout.
execution.breathing_instructions: Breathe continuously throughout. Do not hold breath.
common_mistakes: Letting the hips rise — the torso and hips should remain at a consistent, level height
Moving ipsilateral limbs (same-side hand and foot) — the pattern must be contralateral
Dropping the knees to the floor between steps
safety_considerations: Wrist discomfort is common for those with limited wrist extension — use fist position or push-up handles if needed.
Start with slow, deliberate movement before increasing pace.
execution.range_of_motion_guidance: Consistent knee hover. Full forward reach on each hand step.
execution.tempo_recommendations: Typically 10–20 meters per set. Slow for quality, faster for conditioning.
coaching_cues: Hips level — no rotation
Opposite arm and leg together
Knees hover — don't touch

name: Behind-Back Cable Shrug
description: The behind-back cable shrug uses a low cable pulley with the lifter standing facing away, the cable passing behind the body and grasped with arms behind the torso. This positioning places the trapezius under tension through a unique posterior angle that is difficult to replicate with any other equipment, and it allows the upper traps to work without the anterior deltoids assisting as occurs in front-loaded shrugs.

execution.starting_position: Stand facing away from a low cable pulley. Reach behind and grasp a straight bar or rope attached to the cable. Stand upright with arms behind the torso.
execution.setup_instructions: Set the cable to the lowest position. Use a straight bar attachment that can be held comfortably behind the body. Moderate weight to begin — the position is unfamiliar.
steps: Step 1: Stand upright with cable grasped behind the lower body.
Step 2: Shrug the shoulders straight upward — no rolling, no forward rounding.
Step 3: Elevate as high as possible.
Step 4: Hold 1 second at peak elevation.
Step 5: Lower under control.
execution.breathing_instructions: Exhale on the shrug. Inhale on the lowering.
common_mistakes: Rolling the shoulders — shrug straight up, not in a circular motion
Leaning forward — maintain upright posture throughout
safety_considerations: The behind-back position places the shoulder in internal rotation — keep loads moderate
Avoid if you experience shoulder or bicipital tendon pain
execution.range_of_motion_guidance: Full shoulder depression to full elevation.
coaching_cues: Straight up — not forward or backward
Ears to shoulders
Hold the squeeze at the top

name: Behind-the-Back Barbell Wrist Curl
description: The behind-the-back wrist curl is performed standing with a barbell held behind the body in a pronated grip. The wrists curl upward against the barbell's weight, targeting the wrist flexors from an extended arm angle. This standing position can allow heavier loading than the seated version, and the neutral standing position eliminates upper arm fatigue from supporting the forearms.

execution.starting_position: Stand upright holding a barbell behind the body, hands in a pronated grip (overhand), bar resting at the level of the glutes.
execution.setup_instructions: Can grip from a rack at hip height behind the body, or take from a standard deadlift position.
steps: Step 1: Begin with the bar resting behind the thighs, wrists in slight extension.
Step 2: Curl the wrists upward by flexing the wrist joint, raising the back of the hands.
Step 3: Hold briefly at the top of wrist flexion.
Step 4: Lower the wrists back to the starting position.
execution.breathing_instructions: Exhale on the curl, inhale on the return.
common_mistakes: Arms swinging forward — keep the bar behind the body
Flexing the elbows instead of just the wrists
safety_considerations: Use a grip that is comfortable — the behind-back position can stress the wrists
execution.range_of_motion_guidance: Full wrist extension to full flexion.
coaching_cues: Bar stays behind the body
Only the wrists move
Squeeze the forearms at the top

name: Behind-the-Back Barbell Shrug
description: The behind-the-back barbell shrug places the bar behind the body against the glutes, shifting the line of force to target the mid and upper trapezius with the shoulders in a slightly retracted position. This altered angle can reduce the anterior shoulder dominance common with front-loaded shrug variations and improve the peak contraction quality of the upper traps. It is typically performed from a power rack or Smith machine for safety.

execution.starting_position: Stand with the barbell behind the body, gripped with a pronated (overhand) grip at approximately hip width. The bar rests against the upper glutes. Stand upright.
execution.setup_instructions: Best performed from a power rack with the bar set at hip height, or using a Smith machine. The range of motion is slightly more limited than a front shrug.
steps: Step 1: Unrack the bar behind the body. Stand tall with arms straight.
Step 2: Elevate the shoulders as high as possible, drawing them directly upward.
Step 3: Hold the peak contraction for one second.
Step 4: Lower the shoulders under full control to the starting position.
Step 5: Allow the shoulders to depress fully before the next rep.
execution.breathing_instructions: Exhale on the shrug upward, inhale on the descent.
common_mistakes: Rolling the shoulders forward or backward — the motion is straight up and straight down
Using excessive load, which prevents full elevation
Failing to lower completely between reps, limiting the total range of motion
safety_considerations: The bar can scrape the lower back if gripped too wide — use a hip-width grip
Avoid this exercise if there is any lower back or glute pain from the bar contact
execution.range_of_motion_guidance: Full shoulder elevation at the top, full depression at the bottom.
coaching_cues: Shrug straight up — not forward or backward
Touch your ears with your shoulders
Full drop between every rep

name: Behind-the-Neck Press
description: The behind-the-neck press is an overhead barbell press where the bar is lowered behind the head to the base of the skull rather than in front of the face. This variation places the shoulder joint in a more horizontally abducted position, which some lifters use to target the lateral and posterior deltoids differently. It carries significant shoulder impingement risk for many individuals and requires excellent shoulder mobility and health.

execution.starting_position: Sit on a bench inside a rack with a barbell racked behind the head at approximately ear height. Grip the bar slightly wider than shoulder-width. The bar begins at the base of the skull/upper traps.
execution.setup_instructions: Set the safety pins at a height that catches the bar at the base of the skull if you fail. Requires excellent shoulder external rotation and thoracic mobility. Do not attempt without a spotter.
steps: Step 1: Sit under the bar in a rack, gripping it slightly wider than shoulder-width. Unrack the bar to rest on the upper traps behind the neck.
Step 2: Brace the core and keep the torso upright.
Step 3: Exhale and press the bar straight overhead to full arm extension.
Step 4: Inhale and lower the bar back to the base of the skull in a controlled manner.
execution.breathing_instructions: Exhale on the press; inhale on the return.
common_mistakes: Letting the neck jut forward during the movement
Lowering the bar too quickly which stresses the rotator cuff
safety_considerations: Not recommended for those with shoulder impingement, rotator cuff injuries, or limited external rotation mobility
Always use a spotter and set safety pins
If neck or shoulder pain occurs, switch to front overhead press
execution.range_of_motion_guidance: Lower to the base of the skull — not down to the traps — and press to full overhead extension.
coaching_cues: Keep the elbows tracking directly under the bar throughout the movement
Press the bar in a vertical line — not forward

name: Behind-the-Neck Lat Pulldown
description: The behind-the-neck lat pulldown pulls the bar down behind the head to touch the base of the neck. While it creates a different angle of lat engagement and places greater emphasis on the rear deltoid and rhomboids, this exercise places the shoulder joint in an impingement-prone position and is contraindicated for individuals with shoulder or cervical spine issues. It should only be performed by experienced trainees with demonstrated shoulder mobility.

execution.starting_position: Sit at a lat pulldown machine with a wide-grip bar attachment. Grip the bar with an overhand grip 4-6 inches wider than shoulder width. Lean the torso slightly forward and tuck the chin to the chest.
execution.setup_instructions: Secure thighs under the pads. Set an appropriate weight. Tuck the chin before each repetition.
steps: Step 1: Grip the bar wide with an overhand grip.
Step 2: Tuck the chin firmly to the chest before initiating the movement.
Step 3: Pull the bar downward and behind the head, aiming to touch the base of the neck.
Step 4: Squeeze the shoulder blades together at the bottom position.
Step 5: Return the bar under control to full arm extension.
execution.breathing_instructions: Exhale on the pull, inhale on the return.
common_mistakes: Not tucking the chin, risking impact with the cervical vertebrae
Using excessive weight, forcing poor positioning
Pulling too aggressively with shoulder impingement concerns
safety_considerations: Not recommended for individuals with shoulder impingement, rotator cuff issues, or cervical spine problems
Always tuck the chin before each repetition
Many coaches recommend the standard front pulldown as a safer alternative with comparable lat activation
execution.range_of_motion_guidance: Full arm extension at top to bar touching the base of the neck at the bottom.
coaching_cues: Chin tucked before every rep
Bar to the base of the skull, not lower
Retract shoulder blades at the bottom

name: Belt Squat Machine
description: The belt squat attaches a loaded belt around the lifter's hips rather than placing a barbell on the back or in the hands. The lifter stands elevated on two platforms or a dedicated machine, allowing the weight to hang between the legs. Because the spine is completely unloaded, the belt squat is ideal for athletes with lower back injuries who still want to train the legs with heavy compound squatting movements.

execution.starting_position: Attach the loaded dip belt or use a dedicated belt squat machine. Stand on the elevated platforms with the weight hanging between the legs. Feet shoulder-width, toes turned out slightly.
execution.setup_instructions: Attach plates to the belt and stand on two sturdy boxes or the dedicated machine platforms, allowing room for the weight to hang freely between them.
steps: Step 1: Stand tall and brace the core lightly — no spinal loading is required.
Step 2: Bend the knees and hips to squat down, allowing the weight to hang and descend freely.
Step 3: Descend to depth, maintaining an upright torso.
Step 4: Drive through the feet to extend back to standing.
execution.breathing_instructions: Breathe naturally — spinal loading is minimal so heavy bracing is less critical.
common_mistakes: Leaning too far forward despite the absence of spinal loading
Insufficient depth
Belt shifting during the movement
safety_considerations: Ensure the platforms are stable and wide enough
Verify the belt attachment is secure before each set
execution.range_of_motion_guidance: Full depth — hip crease below knee. The belt position encourages upright posture.
coaching_cues: Stand tall
Weight hangs — don't pull it
Full depth every rep

name: Bench Dips Single-Leg with Plate
description: Bench dips performed with one leg raised while a weight plate sits on the thigh, adding resistance without bilateral loading. The single-leg variation adds core stabilization demands. This is an accessible way to progressively overload bench dips.

execution.starting_position: Set up for Bench Dips Single-Leg with Plate in the appropriate position.
execution.setup_instructions: Prepare equipment and body position for Bench Dips Single-Leg with Plate.
steps: Step 1: Sit on bench edge with hands behind hips. Place plate on one thigh.
Step 2: Slide hips off bench and raise the weighted leg slightly.
Step 3: Lower body by bending elbows, maintaining balance.
Step 4: Press back to full extension using tricep strength.
execution.breathing_instructions: Exhale during the exertion phase, inhale during the return.
common_mistakes: Using leg to push up
Leaning forward too much
safety_considerations: Keep joints aligned throughout the movement.
Use controlled weight appropriate for skill level.
execution.range_of_motion_guidance: Move through full range of motion without compromising joint integrity.
coaching_cues: Hips stay close to bench edge
Keep weighted leg parallel to floor

name: Bench Dips on Swiss Ball with Weighted Vest
description: Bench dips with feet on a Swiss ball while wearing a weighted vest for maximum difficulty. The vest distributes weight evenly while the ball adds instability, demanding substantial tricep strength and core control. This is an advanced progression of standard bench dips.

execution.starting_position: Set up for Bench Dips on Swiss Ball with Weighted Vest in the appropriate position.
execution.setup_instructions: Prepare equipment and body position for Bench Dips on Swiss Ball with Weighted Vest.
steps: Step 1: Wear weighted vest. Set hands on bench, feet on Swiss ball.
Step 2: Slide hips off bench maintaining balance on ball.
Step 3: Lower body by bending elbows to full depth.
Step 4: Press back to full extension, stabilizing ball with legs.
execution.breathing_instructions: Exhale during the exertion phase, inhale during the return.
common_mistakes: Letting ball roll uncontrolled
Leaning torso forward
safety_considerations: Keep joints aligned throughout the movement.
Use controlled weight appropriate for skill level.
execution.range_of_motion_guidance: Move through full range of motion without compromising joint integrity.
coaching_cues: Engage core throughout
Control ball with isometric leg tension

name: Bent-Over Row with Snatch Grip
description: The snatch-grip bent-over row uses an extra-wide grip (wider than the standard clean-grip row) that places the shoulder blades at maximum abduction at the bottom of the movement, allowing greater scapular excursion and therefore a fuller contraction of the middle and lower trapezius on each rep. The wide grip also reduces elbow flexion range, shifting more emphasis to the rhomboids and trapezius relative to the biceps.

execution.starting_position: Stand with feet hip-width apart. Grip the barbell in a snatch-width grip (roughly 1.5 times shoulder width, or use the bar's snatch-grip markings). Hinge to 45-70 degrees, arms extended.
execution.setup_instructions: The snatch grip on most bars places the hands just inside or at the outer knurling rings. Use straps if grip limits training volume.
steps: Step 1: Begin hinged with the wide-grip barbell hanging.
Step 2: Row the bar toward the lower abdomen, driving the elbows out wide.
Step 3: At peak, hold 1 second with shoulder blades fully retracted.
Step 4: Lower under control — feel the shoulder blades protract fully at the bottom.
Step 5: Repeat.
execution.breathing_instructions: Exhale on the row. Inhale returning.
common_mistakes: Elbows tracking close to the body — the wide grip requires wide elbow tracking
Using a narrower grip than true snatch width — the wide grip is what differentiates this variation
safety_considerations: The snatch grip puts the wrists in greater extension — assess wrist mobility before loading
Moderate loads; this is a technique and upper-back variation, not a max-load lift
execution.range_of_motion_guidance: Full scapular protraction at bottom to full retraction at top.
coaching_cues: Wide grip, wide elbows
Think 'shoulder blades apart at the bottom, together at the top'
Upright chest at peak — do not round

name: Bicycle Crunch
description: The bicycle crunch combines trunk flexion with rotation and simultaneous leg movement, training the rectus abdominis and obliques in a dynamic, integrated pattern. The alternating elbow-to-knee motion engages the obliques more than a standard crunch and creates significant rotational core demand.

execution.starting_position: Lie on your back with hands lightly behind the head, shoulders off the floor, knees bent at 90 degrees.
execution.setup_instructions: Keep both shoulders off the floor throughout. The rotation comes from the torso, not from pulling the neck.
steps: Extend one leg straight while simultaneously rotating the opposite elbow toward the bent knee.
Alternate sides in a smooth, controlled cycling motion.
Keep the lower back pressed into the floor throughout.
execution.breathing_instructions: Exhale with each rotation. Try to maintain a rhythm.
common_mistakes: Pulling the neck with the hands
Rushing through reps with poor form — go slow for greater activation
Lifting the lower back off the floor
safety_considerations: If neck discomfort is significant, reduce range or regress to basic crunches
execution.range_of_motion_guidance: Full elbow-to-knee contact or as close as possible on each side. Fully extended opposite leg.
execution.tempo_recommendations: Controlled — 1 second per rep each side
coaching_cues: Rotate from the ribcage, not from the neck
Keep both shoulders off the floor — do not rock side to side

name: Bird Dog
description: The bird dog is a quadruped core stability exercise in which the athlete extends the opposite arm and leg simultaneously while maintaining a neutral spine and level pelvis. It directly trains the erector spinae, multifidus, and gluteus maximus in their stabilization roles while challenging the core to resist lateral and rotational forces. Widely used in rehabilitation and athletic training for its effectiveness in developing lumbar stability and spinal health without compressive loading.

execution.starting_position: Begin on all fours (quadruped position) with hands directly under the shoulders and knees directly under the hips. Spine is neutral — not arched or rounded.
execution.setup_instructions: Use a mat for knee comfort. Set the neutral spine position before each repetition.
steps: Step 1: Begin in quadruped with neutral spine.
Step 2: Brace the core gently — think about stiffening the entire trunk.
Step 3: Simultaneously extend the right arm forward (thumb up) and the left leg back until both are parallel to the floor.
Step 4: Hold the extended position for 1–2 seconds. The pelvis should remain level — do not rotate or hike the hip.
Step 5: Return with control and repeat on the opposite side.
execution.breathing_instructions: Exhale as you extend arm and leg. Inhale as you return.
common_mistakes: Rotating the pelvis and hiking the hip on the extending-leg side
Hyperextending the lower back during the leg extension
Rushing the movement — the value comes from slow, controlled execution
safety_considerations: Appropriate for most populations. Modify by reducing lever arm (extend arm only or leg only) if full coordination is challenging.
Keep the neck neutral — do not look up.
execution.range_of_motion_guidance: Arm and leg should reach full extension, parallel to the floor, without any spinal rotation or hip hiking.
execution.tempo_recommendations: 2–3 second hold at extension, controlled return. 3-1-2 tempo.
coaching_cues: Long from fingertips to heel — reach in opposite directions
The pelvis stays flat like a table — do not spill the imaginary glass of water on your back
Engage your glute — squeeze the extended leg's buttock

name: Bird-Dog Row on Bench
description: A bird-dog performed on a flat bench holding a dumbbell, combining the spinal stability demands of the bird-dog with a rowing motion. The bench elevates the hands and allows the working arm to row while the opposite leg extends. This integrates core stability with pulling strength.

execution.starting_position: Set up for Bird-Dog Row on Bench in proper position.
execution.setup_instructions: Prepare body and equipment for Bird-Dog Row on Bench.
steps: Step 1: Kneel on bench with one hand holding dumbbell below.
Step 2: Extend opposite leg behind, maintaining level pelvis.
Step 3: Row dumbbell to ribs while keeping hips and shoulders square.
Step 4: Lower dumbbell and return leg, then repeat.
execution.breathing_instructions: Breathe steadily; never hold breath during static holds.
common_mistakes: Rotating hips to assist the row
Dropping the extended leg
safety_considerations: Build prerequisite strength before attempting advanced variations.
Stop if joint pain occurs.
execution.range_of_motion_guidance: Full range of motion with control at all times.
coaching_cues: No rotation allowed
Imagine a glass of water on your lower back

name: Bird-Dog on Stability Ball with Dumbbell
description: A bird-dog performed with knees on a stability ball while holding a dumbbell in the extended arm. The unstable surface dramatically increases the stabilization demand throughout the spine and hip. This version builds core endurance and proprioception for unstable surface training.

execution.starting_position: Set up for Bird-Dog on Stability Ball with Dumbbell in proper position.
execution.setup_instructions: Prepare body and equipment for Bird-Dog on Stability Ball with Dumbbell.
steps: Step 1: Place knees on stability ball, hands on floor in tabletop position.
Step 2: Hold dumbbell in one hand. Stabilize on ball.
Step 3: Extend arm with dumbbell forward and opposite leg back simultaneously.
Step 4: Return and repeat without letting ball shift excessively.
execution.breathing_instructions: Breathe steadily; never hold breath during static holds.
common_mistakes: Ball rolling uncontrolled
Rotating hips during extension
safety_considerations: Build prerequisite strength before attempting advanced variations.
Stop if joint pain occurs.
execution.range_of_motion_guidance: Full range of motion with control at all times.
coaching_cues: Ball movements reveal instability
Start without dumbbell to build skill

name: Block Clean and Jerk
description: A strongman variant of the Olympic clean and jerk performed with a heavy implement starting from blocks or a platform at knee height. The elevated start reduces the range of pull and allows greater loads. This builds explosive hip extension for transferring power from the floor.

execution.starting_position: Set up for Block Clean and Jerk in proper strongman position.
execution.setup_instructions: Prepare all equipment and body position for Block Clean and Jerk.
steps: Step 1: Set blocks to knee height with heavy barbell loaded.
Step 2: Perform clean pull from blocks, driving hips explosively.
Step 3: Catch bar in front rack position with elbows high.
Step 4: Dip and drive to jerk bar overhead to lockout.
execution.breathing_instructions: Brace core maximally before every lift. Breathe between reps if needed.
common_mistakes: Slow bar speed at the hip
Soft elbows in front rack
safety_considerations: Use collars on all loaded barbells.
Ensure clear path for carries.
Have spotters for overhead movements.
execution.range_of_motion_guidance: Full range of motion specific to the implement being used.
coaching_cues: Explode through the hip at blocks
Fast elbows in the catch

name: Block Pull
description: The block pull is similar to the rack pull but with the barbell resting on blocks or bumper plates rather than rack pins. This setup allows the bar to remain free-floating, more closely replicating full deadlift mechanics, while reducing the range of motion to overload a specific portion of the pull. Block pulls are commonly used in Olympic weightlifting and powerlifting to build strength in a specific phase of the deadlift without the bar being in a mechanically fixed position.

execution.starting_position: Stack bumper plates or wooden blocks to the desired height (typically mid-shin to below-knee). Rest a loaded barbell on the blocks. Stand behind the bar as you would for a conventional deadlift.
execution.setup_instructions: Stack rubber bumper plates or wooden pulling blocks to the target height. Ensure the stacking surface is stable and will not tip. Load the barbell on top.
steps: Step 1: Set up with feet hip-width apart, the bar over mid-foot. Grip the bar with a double overhand or mixed grip.
Step 2: Hinge to the bar, set the back with a neutral spine, and brace the core.
Step 3: Push the floor away and pull the bar in a straight vertical line.
Step 4: Lock out the hips fully at the top by driving the hips through.
Step 5: Lower the bar under control to the blocks, reset, and repeat.
execution.breathing_instructions: Inhale and brace before each rep. Exhale at lockout.
common_mistakes: Letting the bar drift forward away from the body
Not resetting posture and brace between reps — each rep should be treated as a new lift
Hyperextending the lower back at lockout
safety_considerations: Ensure the block or plate stack is completely stable before loading
Block height should be chosen based on the specific sticking point being targeted
execution.range_of_motion_guidance: From block height to full lockout. The partial ROM is intentional for overload purposes.
execution.tempo_recommendations: Controlled pull, locked top position (1–2s), controlled 2s lowering to blocks.
coaching_cues: Drive the floor away with both feet equally
Bar stays in contact with the thighs all the way up
Hips and shoulders rise at the same rate

name: 2-Board Close-Grip Board Press
description: A powerlifting accessory exercise using a 2-board on the chest to limit range of motion. The close grip emphasizes the triceps while the boards train lockout strength. This builds tricep power for the sticking point in a standard bench press.

execution.starting_position: Set up for 2-Board Close-Grip Board Press in the appropriate position.
execution.setup_instructions: Prepare equipment and body position for 2-Board Close-Grip Board Press.
steps: Step 1: Place 2-board on chest held by training partner. Set up close grip on bar.
Step 2: Unrack bar and lower to board with control.
Step 3: Press bar back to lockout emphasizing tricep drive.
Step 4: Repeat for target reps then rerack with spotter.
execution.breathing_instructions: Exhale during the exertion phase, inhale during the return.
common_mistakes: Letting elbows flare wide
Bouncing off boards
safety_considerations: Keep joints aligned throughout the movement.
Use controlled weight appropriate for skill level.
execution.range_of_motion_guidance: Move through full range of motion without compromising joint integrity.
coaching_cues: Drive elbows toward feet at lockout
Tight wrist alignment

name: Bodyweight Skullcrusher (Smith Machine)
description: A bodyweight triceps exercise performed under a fixed barbell in a Smith machine. The lifter positions their body at an angle and lowers their head toward the bar using elbow flexion, then presses back up. The fixed bar provides stability while body angle controls difficulty.

execution.starting_position: Set up for Bodyweight Skullcrusher (Smith Machine) in the appropriate position.
execution.setup_instructions: Prepare equipment and body position for Bodyweight Skullcrusher (Smith Machine).
steps: Step 1: Set Smith bar at hip height. Grip bar slightly narrower than shoulder width.
Step 2: Walk feet back so body is at an angle with arms extended.
Step 3: Keeping elbows stationary, lower head toward bar by bending elbows.
Step 4: Press back to start through triceps extension.
execution.breathing_instructions: Exhale during the exertion phase, inhale during the return.
common_mistakes: Flaring elbows outward
Moving hips instead of using elbows
safety_considerations: Keep joints aligned throughout the movement.
Use controlled weight appropriate for skill level.
execution.range_of_motion_guidance: Move through full range of motion without compromising joint integrity.
coaching_cues: Keep elbows pointing forward
Control the descent

name: BOSU Squat — Eyes Closed
description: A bodyweight squat performed on the dome of a BOSU ball (dome side up) with the eyes closed. The unstable dome surface creates multi-directional instability, and removing the visual input further challenges the proprioceptive and vestibular systems to control the squat movement. This is a high-level proprioceptive challenge used in late-stage ankle, knee, and ACL rehabilitation when functional dynamic balance under load with no visual input is being restored.

execution.starting_position: Stand on the dome of the BOSU ball, feet hip-width apart, centered. Find balance with eyes open first. Have a wall or partner nearby.
execution.setup_instructions: Master BOSU squats with eyes open before attempting eyes closed. ALWAYS have a safety surface or person nearby. Never attempt on an elevated surface.
steps: Step 1: Step onto the BOSU dome and find balance with eyes open.
Step 2: Once stable, slowly close the eyes.
Step 3: Perform a controlled squat to approximately 60-70 degrees of knee flexion with eyes closed, focusing on proprioceptive feedback from the feet and ankles.
Step 4: Return to standing. Open the eyes between repetitions if needed.
execution.breathing_instructions: Breathe normally throughout. Calm rhythmic breathing aids balance and reduces anxiety.
common_mistakes: Attempting eyes-closed before mastering eyes-open BOSU squats
Squatting too deeply too soon — the balance challenge increases dramatically with depth
Tensing the whole body to manage instability — allow the ankle and hip to respond naturally
safety_considerations: ALWAYS have a safety surface within reach — a wall, rack, or partner
If dizziness or significant loss of balance occurs, open the eyes immediately and step off the BOSU
This is for late-stage rehabilitation only — not for anyone with acute balance deficits or vertigo
execution.range_of_motion_guidance: 60-70 degrees of knee flexion is appropriate — do not go to full depth with eyes closed on a BOSU initially.
execution.tempo_recommendations: 3s eccentric, 1s pause at bottom, 2s concentric return.
coaching_cues: Feel the dome through your feet — let the ankle and hip respond to the wobble
Breathe slowly — calm breathing reduces instability
Close the eyes slowly — do not snap them shut

name: Box Jump
description: The box jump is a foundational plyometric exercise in which the athlete jumps from the floor onto an elevated box or platform, training explosive lower body power through rapid force production in the quadriceps, glutes, and calves.
