The landing should be controlled and soft — absorbing the impact through the entire lower limb — to protect the joints and train the deceleration pattern. Box jumps are widely used in sport conditioning, athletic development, and high-intensity interval training.

execution.starting_position: Stand facing a sturdy box or platform at a comfortable height (begin at 30–50 cm). Feet shoulder-width apart.
execution.setup_instructions: Use a sturdy, non-slip plyo box. Begin with a height that allows full foot landing on the box. Never use a surface that can tip or slip.
steps: Step 1: Stand facing the box, feet shoulder-width apart.
Step 2: Dip into a quarter squat, swinging the arms back.
Step 3: Explosively extend the hips, knees, and ankles while driving the arms forward and upward.
Step 4: Bring the knees toward the chest to clear the height, landing softly on the box with both feet flat — hips slightly hinged, knees over toes.
Step 5: Stand to full extension on the box, then step (or jump) down and reset.
execution.breathing_instructions: Exhale sharply at takeoff. Inhale on the descent or reset phase.
common_mistakes: Landing with straight legs and stiff joints — this increases impact forces significantly
Landing only on the toes without full foot contact
Jumping down rather than stepping down (increases eccentric load unnecessarily)
safety_considerations: Step down rather than jump down unless specifically training depth jumps.
Never jump onto an unstable surface.
Shin scrapes are common when failing a rep — be prepared to bail forward.
execution.range_of_motion_guidance: Full takeoff extension. Land in a controlled partial squat position on the box.
execution.tempo_recommendations: Maximum explosive effort on each jump. Rest fully between sets — plyometrics require high CNS output per rep.
coaching_cues: Hips back and down in the dip — then explode up
Land soft — quiet feet
Full extension at takeoff

name: Box Squat
description: The box squat involves sitting back onto a box or bench at the bottom of a squat movement before returning to standing. By sitting back to the box, the movement emphasizes hip-hinge mechanics and posterior chain engagement more than a standard back squat. The brief pause on the box eliminates momentum from the stretch-shortening reflex and teaches controlled descent with hip-dominant mechanics.

execution.starting_position: Position a sturdy box or bench of appropriate height (parallel or just below parallel) behind you. Set up as for a back squat with the bar on the upper traps.
execution.setup_instructions: Choose a box height that positions your hips at or below parallel when seated. Stand close enough to the box that you will sit back onto it at the bottom without having to search for it.
steps: Step 1: Unrack the bar and position yourself directly in front of the box. Feet wider than shoulder-width is common. Brace the core.
Step 2: Initiate the descent by sitting the hips back aggressively — more so than a standard back squat — while pushing the knees outward.
Step 3: Sit fully onto the box in a controlled manner. Pause completely, maintaining core tension and an upright spine.
Step 4: Drive forcefully through the entire foot — particularly the heel and midfoot — to stand back up. Do not lean forward excessively off the box.
Step 5: Exhale at the top and reset.
execution.breathing_instructions: Inhale and brace before descent. Hold through the pause and ascent. Exhale at the top.
common_mistakes: Rocking forward on the box to build momentum instead of pausing with tension
Using a box that is too high, which prevents reaching proper depth
Placing feet too close together, reducing hip-back mechanics
safety_considerations: Ensure the box is stable and can support the weight of the lifter plus barbell
Do not use a wheeled box or any unstable surface
execution.range_of_motion_guidance: Hips should reach the box when thighs are parallel to or below the floor.
execution.tempo_recommendations: 3-2-X-0 (controlled descent, 2s pause on box, explosive concentric)
coaching_cues: Sit back — don't just sit down
Stay tight on the box — don't relax
Push the floor away, not forward

name: Broad Jump
description: The broad jump is a horizontal plyometric exercise in which the athlete uses an explosive two-legged takeoff to cover maximum horizontal distance. Unlike the vertical box jump, the broad jump trains the ability to project force at an angle, which closely mirrors the acceleration mechanics of sprinting and many field sport movements. It is used as both a training exercise and a standard assessment of lower body explosive power in sport science settings.

execution.starting_position: Stand with feet shoulder-width apart behind a takeoff line. Arms extended down at the sides.
execution.setup_instructions: Use a flat, non-slip surface with enough landing space. Mark the takeoff point.
steps: Step 1: Stand at the takeoff line, feet shoulder-width apart.
Step 2: Swing the arms back and sink into a quarter to half squat simultaneously.
Step 3: Drive the arms forward and upward explosively while extending the hips, knees, and ankles to project the body forward and slightly upward.
Step 4: Extend the legs forward during flight to maximize distance.
Step 5: Land with both feet simultaneously, absorbing the impact by bending the hips, knees, and ankles. Maintain balance on landing.
execution.breathing_instructions: Exhale sharply at takeoff. Breathe freely during rest.
common_mistakes: Taking off at too steep an angle (too vertical) — optimal projection is approximately 45 degrees
Not fully extending at takeoff — a partial extension leaves horizontal power on the table
Landing with stiff legs — this increases injury risk
safety_considerations: Ensure the landing zone is clear and has adequate floor space.
Avoid on slippery surfaces.
execution.range_of_motion_guidance: Full extension at takeoff. Legs reach forward during flight. Soft, two-foot landing.
execution.tempo_recommendations: Maximum effort on each rep. 3–5 reps per set, full rest between sets.
coaching_cues: Reach with the arms — swing them hard forward
Extend fully at takeoff — hips, knees, ankles
Reach the feet forward in flight

name: Bulgarian Split Squat
description: The Bulgarian split squat is a unilateral lower body exercise in which the rear foot is elevated on a bench while the front foot bears most of the load. It provides deep quadriceps and glute stimulation with a significant hip flexor stretch on the rear leg. It is considered one of the most challenging and effective single-leg movements for hypertrophy.

execution.starting_position: Stand about two feet in front of a bench. Place the top of the rear foot on the bench. Front foot should be far enough forward that the shin remains near-vertical at the bottom of the movement.
execution.setup_instructions: Test the front foot position before adding load. If the front knee tracks excessively over the toes, step the front foot further forward.
steps: Lower the body by bending the front knee, keeping the torso upright.
Descend until the rear knee is just above the floor.
Drive through the front heel to return to the starting position.
execution.breathing_instructions: Inhale on descent, exhale on the drive up.
common_mistakes: Front foot too close to the bench — causes excessive forward knee travel
Torso leaning excessively forward
Knee caving inward on the front leg
safety_considerations: If balance is an issue, hold onto a fixed surface with one hand initially
Hip flexor on the rear leg will be stretched aggressively — ease into depth
execution.range_of_motion_guidance: Rear knee nearly touching the floor at the bottom. Full extension of front leg at top.
coaching_cues: Drop straight down — do not lean forward
Front shin stays close to vertical throughout the descent

name: Burpee
description: The burpee is a full-body plyometric conditioning exercise that cycles through a squat, plank, push-up, squat, and vertical jump in a continuous sequence. It places simultaneous demands on the upper body, lower body, and core while elevating cardiovascular demand significantly, making it one of the highest-intensity bodyweight exercises. The burpee is widely used in metabolic conditioning, military fitness testing, and interval training protocols.

execution.starting_position: Stand upright with feet hip-width apart.
execution.setup_instructions: No equipment required. Adequate floor space needed.
steps: Step 1: From standing, squat down and place both hands on the floor.
Step 2: Jump or step both feet back to arrive in a push-up plank position.
Step 3: Perform one push-up — lower the chest to the floor and press back up.
Step 4: Jump or step both feet forward to return to a squat position.
Step 5: Explosively jump up with arms overhead, fully extending the body.
Step 6: Land softly and immediately repeat the sequence.
execution.breathing_instructions: Breathe continuously throughout. Exhale on the push-up press and on the jump.
common_mistakes: Skipping the push-up — reduces the upper body demand
Not fully extending on the jump at the top
Landing with rigid legs — absorb through the knees and hips
safety_considerations: High cardiovascular and musculoskeletal demand — progress gradually in volume.
Not appropriate immediately post lower extremity injury.
execution.range_of_motion_guidance: Full push-up range. Full hip and knee extension on the jump.
execution.tempo_recommendations: Performed for time (20–60 second intervals) or for reps (5–15). Pace sustainable throughout.
coaching_cues: Hips high in the plank
Full push-up — chest touches
Jump tall at the top

name: Burpee Box Jump
description: The burpee box jump combines the full-body conditioning demand of a burpee with the explosive vertical jump mechanics of a box jump, requiring the athlete to perform a burpee on the floor in front of a plyo box and then immediately jump onto the box. It is one of the most metabolically demanding plyometric exercises, training both the aerobic and anaerobic energy systems while developing lower body explosive power under fatigued conditions — closely mimicking the demands of competitive functional fitness.

execution.starting_position: Stand facing a plyo box at a distance of roughly one step away.
execution.setup_instructions: Use a sturdy plyo box of appropriate height (20–24 inches for most athletes). Ensure the box does not slide.
steps: Step 1: Perform a full burpee — squat down, kick feet back to plank, do a push-up, return feet to squat.
Step 2: From the squat position, explosively jump forward and upward onto the plyo box.
Step 3: Land on the box with both feet, absorbing through the hips and knees.
Step 4: Stand tall on the box, then step down (not jump down) to the starting position.
Step 5: Immediately begin the next burpee.
execution.breathing_instructions: Breathe continuously. Exhale on the push-up press and on the box jump.
common_mistakes: Jumping down from the box — step down to protect the Achilles and knees on fatigued landings
Rushing the burpee so the push-up is sloppy
Undershooting the box jump when fatigued — reduce box height before reducing effort
safety_considerations: Very high demand — only for well-conditioned athletes with established burpee and box jump proficiency.
Always step down from the box, never jump down when fatigued.
execution.range_of_motion_guidance: Full push-up depth. Full extension on box jump. Full standing on the box.
execution.tempo_recommendations: Performed for reps (5–10) or time (20–40 second efforts). Full recovery between sets.
coaching_cues: Burpee first — box jump second
Step down — never jump down
Hips fully open at the top of the jump

name: Cable Anti-Rotation Lift and Chop
description: A combined cable movement pairing a low-to-high lift with a high-to-low chop through the frontal plane. The anti-rotation demand comes from resisting the cable's rotational pull throughout the full arc. This integrates oblique and transverse abdominis function in sport-specific patterns.

execution.starting_position: Set up for Cable Anti-Rotation Lift and Chop in proper position.
execution.setup_instructions: Prepare body and equipment for Cable Anti-Rotation Lift and Chop.
steps: Step 1: Stand sideways to low cable. Grip handle with both hands at hip level.
Step 2: Rotate and lift cable diagonally across body to high opposite position.
Step 3: Reverse the motion, chopping back down to starting position.
Step 4: Complete reps on one side then switch.
execution.breathing_instructions: Breathe steadily; never hold breath during static holds.
common_mistakes: Using momentum instead of muscular control
Excessive spinal flexion
safety_considerations: Build prerequisite strength before attempting advanced variations.
Stop if joint pain occurs.
execution.range_of_motion_guidance: Full range of motion with control at all times.
coaching_cues: Move from your core, not your arms
Full rotation with stable base

name: Flat Cable Bench Flye
description: The flat cable bench flye uses a flat bench positioned between two low cable pulleys to deliver constant tension throughout the chest fly arc. Unlike dumbbells that lose tension at peak contraction, cables maintain resistance from stretch to squeeze, making this an effective hypertrophy exercise.

execution.starting_position: Place a flat bench in the center of a dual cable machine. Set both pulleys to their lowest position. Lie on the bench and hold one D-handle in each hand, arms extended upward with palms facing each other.
execution.setup_instructions: Attach D-handles to the low cable pulleys on each side. Set the bench horizontally in the center so both cables run at equal angles.
steps: Step 1: Lie flat on the bench, holding both handles with arms extended and a slight elbow bend.
Step 2: Lower both arms out to the sides in a wide arc, allowing a full stretch across the chest.
Step 3: Drive both handles upward and together, squeezing the chest as the hands meet above the sternum.
Step 4: Slowly reverse the motion back to the starting position with control.
Step 5: Maintain a consistent elbow angle throughout the arc.
execution.breathing_instructions: Exhale as you bring the cables together. Inhale as you lower the arms out to the sides.
common_mistakes: Bending elbows too much, turning it into a press
Letting the arms drop too fast on the descent
Arching the lower back excessively
safety_considerations: Keep the shoulder blades retracted and down on the bench
Do not go lower than a comfortable shoulder stretch
Use a weight that allows full range of motion
execution.range_of_motion_guidance: Lower until a comfortable chest stretch is felt. Bring hands together at the top without touching; focus on squeezing the chest rather than completing hand contact.
coaching_cues: Keep elbows slightly bent like you're hugging a barrel
Squeeze hard at the top
Feel the stretch in the chest at the bottom

name: Cable Crossover
description: The cable crossover uses dual high-pulley cables to train the pectoral muscles in horizontal adduction and slight downward adduction. Unlike dumbbells, cables maintain constant tension throughout the full range of motion, including at the peak contraction point, making it effective for building chest definition and size.

execution.starting_position: Stand between two cable stacks with the pulleys set at the highest position. Hold one handle in each hand, stagger your stance for balance, and lean slightly forward at the hips. Arms should be extended out to the sides with a slight elbow bend.
execution.setup_instructions: Set both cable pulleys to the highest position. Attach single handles. Stand centered between the two cable columns.
steps: With a fixed elbow bend, bring both handles downward and inward in an arc toward the center of your body.
Allow the hands to cross slightly at the bottom center for a full pectoral contraction.
Squeeze the chest hard at the peak, then slowly return to the start position.
execution.breathing_instructions: Exhale as you bring the handles together. Inhale as you return to start.
common_mistakes: Standing too upright — a slight forward lean ensures the cable angle targets the chest
Allowing the elbows to bend excessively during the movement
Releasing tension too quickly during the return phase
safety_considerations: Control the return phase — do not let the cables pull the arms back aggressively
Ensure cable attachments are secured before use
execution.range_of_motion_guidance: Open arms out to the sides until a strong chest stretch is felt. Cross hands slightly at the bottom for maximum contraction.
coaching_cues: Squeeze your pecs like you are trying to crack a walnut between them
Keep a proud chest throughout — do not let the shoulders roll forward

name: Kneeling Cable Crossover
description: A cable crossover performed in a kneeling position rather than standing. Kneeling eliminates the ability to use leg drive or hip momentum, ensuring the work is isolated to the chest and shoulders. It also changes the cable angle relative to the torso, shifting the tension vector to better align with horizontal chest fiber recruitment.

execution.starting_position: Kneel centered between two cable stacks with both pulleys set to high or shoulder height relative to the kneeling position. Hold one handle in each hand with arms extended to the sides.
execution.setup_instructions: Set pulleys to approximately shoulder height when kneeling. Kneel on a mat for comfort. Have handles already attached before kneeling.
steps: Step 1: Kneel upright between the stacks. Arms extended out to the sides with a slight elbow bend, cables taught.
Step 2: Bring both handles together in front of the chest in a sweeping arc — the crossover motion.
Step 3: At the midpoint, hands cross slightly (crossover) and squeeze the chest.
Step 4: Return under control, letting the handles sweep back to the starting position. Alternate which hand crosses on top.
execution.breathing_instructions: Exhale on the crossover contraction, inhale on the return.
common_mistakes: Leaning forward excessively from the hips — stay upright
Bending elbows too much and turning it into a press
Cables pulling the arms too far back past the torso plane
safety_considerations: Kneel on a padded surface for comfort
Keep the core braced to prevent excessive anterior pelvic tilt while kneeling
execution.range_of_motion_guidance: Full sweep from arms extended sideways to full crossover in front. Avoid letting cables pull arms behind the torso plane.
execution.tempo_recommendations: 2-1-2-1 (2s sweep in, 1s cross squeeze, 2s return, 1s reset)
coaching_cues: Lead with the elbows, not the hands — this keeps the chest driving the motion
Stay tall through the knees — do not lean forward

name: Seated Bench Cable Crossover
description: A cable crossover performed while seated on a flat bench placed centrally between two cable stacks. The seated position eliminates leg drive and postural compensation, ensuring the movement is driven entirely by the pectoralis major and anterior deltoid. The bench also anchors the torso, allowing the arms to sweep fully without the torso swaying, which can improve mind-muscle connection and consistency.

execution.starting_position: Place a flat bench centered between two cable stacks. Set both pulleys to shoulder height when seated. Sit on the bench, hold one handle in each hand with arms extended to the sides.
execution.setup_instructions: Position the bench so the seat is at the exact midpoint between the two stacks. Adjust pulley height to shoulder level in the seated position. Sit tall with the spine neutral.
steps: Step 1: Sit tall on the bench, arms extended to the sides at shoulder height, slight elbow bend.
Step 2: Bring both handles together in front of the chest in a sweeping arc.
Step 3: At the midpoint, hands cross slightly (crossover) and squeeze hard.
Step 4: Return under control, letting handles sweep back to the sides. Alternate which hand crosses on top each rep.
execution.breathing_instructions: Exhale on the crossover, inhale on the return.
common_mistakes: Leaning forward during the movement — maintain an upright seated position throughout
Bending elbows too much — keep the slight, fixed bend throughout the arc
Bench placed off-center, creating uneven cable tension
safety_considerations: Ensure the bench is stable and not at risk of tipping
Keep the spine neutral — avoid rounding forward during the crossover
execution.range_of_motion_guidance: Full sweep from arms extended to full crossover. The seated position and bench anchor point define the natural range.
coaching_cues: Sit tall — imagine a string pulling you up from the crown of your head
Sweep from the chest — think of hugging a barrel

name: Cable Crunch
description: The cable crunch is a weighted abdominal flexion exercise performed kneeling in front of a high cable pulley. The cable provides resistance throughout the full range of motion and allows progressive overload on the rectus abdominis, making it one of the most effective exercises for building abdominal strength and thickness.

execution.starting_position: Kneel in front of a high cable pulley with a rope attachment held at the sides of the head. Hips should start in a relatively upright position.
execution.setup_instructions: Set the pulley high. Grip the rope and hold it at the sides of the head — not at the neck. Kneel far enough back that the cable angle is comfortable.
steps: Curl the torso downward and forward by flexing the spine, pulling the ribcage toward the pelvis.
Crunch down until maximum abdominal contraction is achieved.
Slowly return to the starting position, maintaining tension on the cable.
execution.breathing_instructions: Exhale forcefully as you crunch down. Inhale on the return.
common_mistakes: Pulling with the arms instead of flexing the spine
Not focusing on spinal flexion — the hip hinge is not the goal
Standing up too much between reps, losing the working position
safety_considerations: Ensure the cable attachment is secure before kneeling
execution.range_of_motion_guidance: Full spinal flexion at the bottom — the head comes toward the floor. Return to a tall kneeling position.
coaching_cues: Think about curling your sternum toward your bellybutton
The movement is a spine curl — not a hip hinge

name: Cable Curl
description: The cable curl uses a low-pulley cable to maintain constant tension on the biceps throughout the full range of motion, including at the bottom where free weights lose tension. This makes it particularly effective as a finishing biceps exercise and is commonly performed with a straight bar or rope attachment.

execution.starting_position: Stand facing a low pulley cable machine holding a straight bar or EZ-bar attachment. Arms extended downward, elbows at the sides.
execution.setup_instructions: Set the pulley to the lowest position. Step back slightly so there is tension on the cable at full arm extension.
steps: Curl the bar upward by flexing the elbows, keeping upper arms stationary.
Raise until full contraction, then lower under control back to the starting position.
execution.breathing_instructions: Exhale on the curl, inhale on the descent.
common_mistakes: Allowing the elbows to drift forward
Using body swing
execution.range_of_motion_guidance: Full extension at the bottom, full contraction at the top.
coaching_cues: Feel the constant tension throughout the full range
Keep upper arms pinned to sides

name: Cable Triceps Extension (High Anchor)
description: A cable extension with the cable anchored very high, creating a nearly vertical downward pull. This angle creates unique loading through the triceps that complements standard horizontal pushdowns. The high anchor position can be achieved with a rope or straight bar.

execution.starting_position: Set up for Cable Triceps Extension (High Anchor) in the appropriate position.
execution.setup_instructions: Prepare equipment and body position for Cable Triceps Extension (High Anchor).
steps: Step 1: Position very high cable attachment, stand directly below it.
Step 2: Grip attachment overhead with elbows at sides.
Step 3: Push attachment down by extending elbows against nearly vertical cable.
Step 4: Return slowly as cable pulls back to starting position.
execution.breathing_instructions: Exhale during the exertion phase, inhale during the return.
common_mistakes: Standing too far from anchor point
Moving elbows away from sides
safety_considerations: Keep joints aligned throughout the movement.
Use controlled weight appropriate for skill level.
execution.range_of_motion_guidance: Move through full range of motion without compromising joint integrity.
coaching_cues: Stand directly below anchor for vertical resistance
Full extension at bottom

name: Cable Triceps Extension (Low Pulley)
description: A triceps pushdown or extension variation using a low pulley, requiring the arms to push downward at an angle. The low cable angle creates a different line of pull than high cables, emphasizing the triceps from the stretch position throughout the movement.

execution.starting_position: Set up for Cable Triceps Extension (Low Pulley) in the appropriate position.
execution.setup_instructions: Prepare equipment and body position for Cable Triceps Extension (Low Pulley).
steps: Step 1: Attach handle to low cable. Stand close facing the pulley.
Step 2: Bend forward at hips and grip handle at chest level.
Step 3: Push handle down and back by extending elbows.
Step 4: Return to bent start position with control.
execution.breathing_instructions: Exhale during the exertion phase, inhale during the return.
common_mistakes: Using body swing to assist
Starting with elbows too high
safety_considerations: Keep joints aligned throughout the movement.
Use controlled weight appropriate for skill level.
execution.range_of_motion_guidance: Move through full range of motion without compromising joint integrity.
coaching_cues: Hinge at hips, brace core
Feel the tension from the lower pull angle

name: Cable External Rotation at 90 Degrees
description: Cable external rotation at 90 degrees is performed with the shoulder abducted to 90 degrees and the elbow bent to 90 degrees, rotating the forearm from pointing downward to pointing upward. This position replicates the late-cocking phase of throwing motions and directly trains the infraspinatus and teres minor — the primary external rotators of the shoulder — in a functionally relevant position that is critical for overhead athlete shoulder health.

execution.starting_position: Set a cable pulley at approximately waist or chest height. Stand side-on with the working shoulder abducted to 90 degrees and elbow bent to 90 degrees. Grip the cable handle — forearm pointing toward the floor.
execution.setup_instructions: Set the cable height so the forearm is horizontal when the shoulder is abducted. Use very light weight — the rotator cuff is a small and injury-prone muscle group.
steps: Step 1: Position the working arm at 90-90 (shoulder at 90 degrees abduction, elbow at 90 degrees).
Step 2: Keeping the elbow fixed at shoulder height, rotate the forearm upward.
Step 3: Continue until the forearm is pointing toward the ceiling or as far as comfortable.
Step 4: Hold 1 second.
Step 5: Rotate back slowly to the starting position (forearm toward floor).
execution.breathing_instructions: Exhale rotating up. Inhale rotating down.
common_mistakes: Elbow dropping below shoulder level during the rotation
Using too heavy a load — this is a small muscle isolation exercise
safety_considerations: Very light loads only — rotator cuff overloading is a common cause of impingement
Stop immediately if sharp pain occurs in the shoulder
execution.range_of_motion_guidance: Forearm from pointing down to pointing up — approximately 180 degrees of forearm arc.
coaching_cues: Elbow stays at shoulder height — it is the fixed point
Rotate the forearm only — the upper arm does not move
Light weight, high quality

name: Cable External Rotation (High Pulley)
description: Cable external rotation from a high pulley trains the infraspinatus and teres minor with the shoulder in an elevated (flexed) starting position, pulling the cable from overhead and externally rotating the shoulder against the resistance. This overhead starting position is used in overhead sport rehabilitation protocols where the rotator cuff must be strengthened at angles of elevated humeral position.

execution.starting_position: Set a cable pulley to the highest position. Grip the handle and position the working arm at approximately 120-150 degrees of flexion (angled overhead). Elbow bent to 90 degrees.
execution.setup_instructions: Stand at a distance that keeps the cable taut in the starting position. Use very light weight.
steps: Step 1: Begin with arm elevated forward-overhead, elbow bent to 90 degrees, forearm roughly parallel to floor.
Step 2: Externally rotate the shoulder — forearm moves upward and backward.
Step 3: Continue rotation as far as comfortable.
Step 4: Return to starting position.
Step 5: Complete all reps then switch sides.
execution.breathing_instructions: Exhale rotating out. Inhale returning.
common_mistakes: Dropping the entire arm rather than rotating at the shoulder
Moving too fast — this is a slow, controlled rehabilitation exercise
safety_considerations: Very light loads — rotator cuff rehabilitation exercise
If pain occurs at any elevation level, reduce range or stop
execution.range_of_motion_guidance: Available pain-free range of external rotation with arm elevated.
coaching_cues: Elbow stays fixed — only the forearm moves
Smooth rotation — no jerky movement
Light weight, high precision

name: Cable EZ-Bar Curl
description: The cable EZ-bar curl attaches an EZ-curl bar to a low cable pulley and performs a bilateral curl. The cable maintains constant tension throughout the full arc — unlike free weight EZ-bar curls which go slack at the bottom — while the EZ-bar's angled grip reduces wrist stress. This combination provides constant tension with wrist-friendly positioning, making it a highly effective and comfortable hypertrophy exercise.

execution.starting_position: Attach an EZ-bar to the low cable pulley. Stand facing the cable machine. Grasp the EZ-bar with a semi-supinated grip. Arms extended toward the pulley.
execution.setup_instructions: Clip the EZ-bar to the low pulley carabiner. Stand one step back from the stack.
steps: Step 1: Begin with arms extended, EZ-bar at thigh level, cable taut.
Step 2: Curl the bar upward by flexing the elbows, maintaining semi-supinated grip.
Step 3: Curl to maximum elbow flexion.
Step 4: Return slowly to the starting position.
execution.breathing_instructions: Exhale on the curl, inhale on the return.
common_mistakes: Swinging the torso
Elbows drifting forward
Moving too fast
safety_considerations: Ensure the EZ-bar attachment is secure before beginning
execution.range_of_motion_guidance: Full extension to full flexion with constant cable tension throughout.
coaching_cues: Feel the tension at the bottom
Elbows stay at the sides
Squeeze at the peak

name: Cable Fly
description: The cable fly is a pectoral isolation exercise using a dual-pulley cable machine with the cables set at mid-height (chest level). Unlike dumbbell flyes, cable tension remains constant throughout the full arc, maintaining meaningful resistance at both the stretched and contracted positions. This makes it highly effective for pectoralis major hypertrophy.

execution.starting_position: Stand in the center of a dual-pulley cable machine with the pulleys set at chest height. Grasp the handles, stagger one foot slightly forward for balance, and lean the torso forward slightly. Arms are open wide with a slight bend at the elbow.
execution.setup_instructions: Set both cable pulleys to chest or mid-torso height. Attach single-handle attachments. Select a moderate weight that allows full range of motion.
steps: Step 1: Stand between the two cable stacks, grasp the handles, and step forward to create tension. Stagger stance slightly; hinge torso forward slightly.
Step 2: Begin with arms wide, elbows slightly bent, feeling a stretch across the chest.
Step 3: Exhale and arc both arms together in front of your body, squeezing the chest at the point of peak contraction.
Step 4: Inhale and slowly return the arms to the wide starting position, controlling the eccentric stretch.
execution.breathing_instructions: Exhale as you bring the cables together; inhale as you open the arms back to the start.
common_mistakes: Fully straightening the elbows, which shifts load to the shoulder joint
Using momentum by swinging the torso rather than controlling with the pecs
safety_considerations: Maintain a slight, fixed bend in the elbows throughout — the arm angle should not change during the arc
Do not let the weight stack slam down at the end of the eccentric
execution.range_of_motion_guidance: Open arms as wide as comfortable without shoulder discomfort; squeeze hard at the midline at the top of the rep.
execution.tempo_recommendations: 2-1-2-0 (2 seconds open, 1 second squeeze, 2 seconds close)
coaching_cues: Imagine hugging a large tree — maintain that arm shape throughout
Lead with your pecs, not your hands

name: Cable Front Raise
description: The cable front raise is a shoulder isolation exercise using a low-pulley cable machine. The cable provides constant tension throughout the raising arc, unlike dumbbells which lose tension at the top of the movement. This makes it effective for targeting the anterior deltoid through the full range of motion, particularly at the top where the shoulder is at greatest challenge.

execution.starting_position: Stand facing away from a low-pulley cable machine, holding the handle(s) with an overhand grip at hip level. Stand upright with a slight forward lean and core braced.
execution.setup_instructions: Attach a straight bar or rope or single handle to the low pulley. Stand with enough distance from the machine so the cable is taut at the bottom starting position.
steps: Step 1: Stand facing away from the cable machine, holding the handle at thigh level with an overhand grip.
Step 2: Keep the elbow slightly bent and the wrist neutral.
Step 3: Exhale and raise the arm(s) forward and up to approximately shoulder height or slightly above.
Step 4: Pause briefly, then inhale and slowly lower back to the starting position.
execution.breathing_instructions: Exhale as you raise the arm; inhale on the controlled lowering.
common_mistakes: Swinging the torso to generate momentum — keep the torso still
Raising past shoulder height into impingement territory for those with existing shoulder issues
safety_considerations: Stop the movement at or just above shoulder height unless mobility allows pain-free overhead reach
execution.range_of_motion_guidance: Raise from hip level to just above shoulder height.
coaching_cues: Raise with a slight elbow bend — do not swing a stiff arm
Lead with the thumb side of the hand

name: Cable Hammer Curl
description: The cable hammer curl is a biceps and brachialis exercise using a cable machine with a rope attachment, performed with a neutral (palms-facing) grip. The neutral grip activates the brachioradialis to a greater degree than a supinated grip and maintains constant cable tension throughout the arc, unlike dumbbells. This variation effectively builds the outer arm thickness and brachialis definition.

execution.starting_position: Attach a rope to the low pulley of a cable machine. Stand facing the machine, holding each end of the rope with a neutral grip (palms facing each other). Arms extended toward the cable.
execution.setup_instructions: Attach a rope to the low pulley. Stand close enough to the machine that the rope is taut at full arm extension with the hands near the thighs.
steps: Step 1: Hold the rope ends with a neutral grip, arms fully extended toward the low pulley.
Step 2: Brace the core and keep the upper arms stationary at the sides.
Step 3: Exhale and curl the rope upward by bending the elbows, keeping the neutral grip throughout.
Step 4: Curl to full contraction, then inhale and lower back to full extension.
execution.breathing_instructions: Exhale on the curl; inhale on the return.
common_mistakes: Letting the elbows drift forward — keep the upper arms pinned at the sides
Supinating the wrists at the top — maintain neutral grip
safety_considerations: Keep the wrists neutral and in line with the forearm — avoid wrist flexion or extension
execution.range_of_motion_guidance: Full extension at the bottom; full curl at the top.
coaching_cues: Keep the pinkies up and grip the ends of the rope firmly
Elbows stay at your sides — they are the pivot point

name: Standing Cable Hip Abduction
description: A glute medius isolation exercise performed standing, using a cable ankle attachment to provide resistance as the leg is abducted outward to the side. The cable provides consistent resistance throughout the range of motion and allows for progressive overload of the hip abductors.

execution.starting_position: Attach an ankle cuff to the low pulley and around the working ankle. Stand sideways to the machine, holding the frame for support.
execution.setup_instructions: Attach the ankle cuff to the cable low pulley. Stand perpendicular to the machine with the working leg furthest from the pulley.
steps: Step 1: Keep the torso upright and stable throughout.
Step 2: Abduct the working leg outward to the side, keeping the leg relatively straight.
Step 3: Raise the leg as high as hip mobility allows while keeping the torso stationary.
Step 4: Return the leg to the starting position in a controlled manner.
execution.breathing_instructions: Exhale as the leg lifts. Inhale on the return.
common_mistakes: Leaning the torso away to assist the leg lift
Using momentum to swing the leg
safety_considerations: Keep the torso upright and still — the movement should be isolated to the hip joint
execution.range_of_motion_guidance: Abduct the leg as high as mobility allows without trunk lateral flexion.
coaching_cues: Torso stays tall
Lift from the hip, not the waist

name: Cable Standing Hip Extension / Donkey Kickback
description: The cable standing hip extension uses a low cable pulley with an ankle cuff to provide resistance against hip extension. The lifter stands facing the cable stack and extends one leg backward, squeezing the glute at the peak of the movement. Unlike machine glute kickbacks, the cable maintains constant resistance throughout the full range of motion. It is a popular isolation exercise for targeting the gluteus maximus.

execution.starting_position: Attach an ankle cuff to the low cable pulley. Stand facing the cable machine, holding the frame for balance. Ankle cuff on the working leg.
execution.setup_instructions: Set a light to moderate weight. Attach the cuff securely. Stand close to the machine with the working ankle directly over the pulley.
steps: Step 1: Keep the torso upright or with a slight forward lean, bracing the core.
Step 2: Keeping the knee nearly straight, extend the working leg backward.
Step 3: Squeeze the glute hard at the peak of the extension.
Step 4: Return the leg forward in a controlled manner, maintaining cable tension.
execution.breathing_instructions: Exhale on the extension, inhale on the return.
common_mistakes: Hyperextending the lower back instead of using glute force
Swinging the leg with momentum rather than deliberate contraction
Leaning forward excessively
safety_considerations: Keep the lower back neutral — avoid arching to extend further
Use a moderate weight that allows full glute control
execution.range_of_motion_guidance: Extend as far as the glute can control without lower back compensation.
coaching_cues: Squeeze the glute at the top
Stand tall — don't arch
No swinging

name: Cable Internal Rotation at 90 Degrees
description: Cable internal rotation at 90 degrees abduction trains the subscapularis — the primary internal rotator and the largest rotator cuff muscle — with the shoulder abducted to 90 degrees. This angle tests internal rotation strength in the most functionally loaded position for overhead athletes, and weak internal rotation at 90 degrees is associated with increased injury risk in throwers.

execution.starting_position: Set a cable pulley above shoulder height. Stand side-on with the working shoulder abducted to 90 degrees, elbow bent to 90 degrees, forearm pointing toward the ceiling. Grip the cable handle.
execution.setup_instructions: The cable should pull from above when the forearm is in the starting overhead position. Use light weight.
steps: Step 1: Begin with the shoulder at 90 degrees abduction, forearm pointing to ceiling, elbow at 90 degrees.
Step 2: Keeping the elbow fixed at shoulder height, rotate the forearm downward.
Step 3: Continue until the forearm is pointing toward the floor.
Step 4: Hold 1 second.
Step 5: Rotate back to the starting position.
execution.breathing_instructions: Exhale rotating down. Inhale returning.
common_mistakes: Elbow dropping below shoulder level
Upper arm adducting (moving toward the body) instead of only the forearm rotating
safety_considerations: Very light loads — subscapularis isolation is performed with low resistance
Stop if sharp anterior shoulder pain occurs
execution.range_of_motion_guidance: Forearm from ceiling to floor — approximately 180 degrees.
coaching_cues: Elbow is the pivot point — it does not move
Forearm rotates down — not the entire arm
Light and controlled

name: Cable Internal Rotation (Low Pulley)
description: Cable internal rotation from a low pulley trains the subscapularis — the primary internal rotator and largest rotator cuff muscle — with the shoulder adducted at the side and elbow bent to 90 degrees. This is the most commonly prescribed rotator cuff strengthening exercise in rehabilitation settings and is performed with extremely light loads for high repetitions.

execution.starting_position: Stand with one side facing the cable machine. Set the pulley at waist height. Elbow of the working arm bent to 90 degrees, upper arm held against the side, forearm pointing away from the cable.
execution.setup_instructions: Place a rolled towel between the working-side elbow and the torso to maintain consistent positioning. Use very light weight.
steps: Step 1: Begin with elbow at 90 degrees, forearm pointing away from the cable.
Step 2: Keeping the upper arm fixed against the side, rotate the forearm inward (toward the abdomen).
Step 3: Continue until the forearm is parallel to the floor pointing toward the abdomen.
Step 4: Hold 1 second.
Step 5: Return to starting position.
execution.breathing_instructions: Exhale rotating in. Inhale returning.
common_mistakes: Upper arm moving away from the torso — it must stay fixed
Using too much load — subscapularis work requires light resistance
safety_considerations: Light load only — 2-5 kg is typical for this exercise
Appropriate for everyone as a shoulder health exercise
execution.range_of_motion_guidance: Forearm from pointing away from cable to pointing across the abdomen.
coaching_cues: Upper arm stays glued to the side
Rotate only the forearm
Towel under elbow helps maintain position

name: Cable Iron Cross
description: The cable iron cross is a chest isolation exercise that mimics the gymnastic iron cross position. Standing between two high cable pulleys, the athlete holds a handle in each hand with arms extended to the sides at shoulder height, then pulls both cables downward and inward to meet at the midline. The constant cable tension provides consistent pectoral loading through the entire arc of motion.

execution.starting_position: Stand centered between two high cable pulleys set at shoulder height or above. Grip a single handle in each hand with arms extended straight out to the sides, forming a T-shape. Step slightly forward to put tension on the cables.
execution.setup_instructions: Set both pulleys to the highest position on a functional trainer. Attach single-grip handles to each cable. Select equal weight on both sides.
steps: Step 1: Stand tall with arms extended out to the sides at shoulder height, slight forward lean from the hips.
Step 2: Keeping arms as straight as possible (elbows almost locked, very slight bend), pull both handles downward and inward in a large arc.
Step 3: Bring hands together at hip or lower-chest level, squeezing the pectorals at peak contraction.
Step 4: Slowly return to the start position, resisting the cable pull and feeling the chest stretch.
execution.breathing_instructions: Exhale as hands come together toward the midline. Inhale as you return to the starting position.
common_mistakes: Bending the elbows and turning the movement into a cable crossover
Using momentum by swinging the torso
Setting cables too heavy, compromising straight-arm position
safety_considerations: Keep weight light — this movement has poor mechanical leverage with straight arms
Avoid if experiencing shoulder impingement or rotator cuff issues
execution.range_of_motion_guidance: Full extension of arms to the sides with a wide arc downward to the midline. The straighter the arms, the greater the pectoral demand.
coaching_cues: Keep the elbows almost locked — this is not a crossover
Think of the hands moving in a wide circle rather than a straight line

name: Cable Kickback
description: The cable kickback is a glute isolation exercise in which an ankle cuff attached to a low cable pulley is used to extend the hip against continuous resistance. Standing on one leg and extending the other hip backward against the cable provides isolated gluteus maximus stimulation through the hip extension range of motion. The cable provides consistent tension throughout the movement, unlike bodyweight hip extension variations.

execution.starting_position: Attach an ankle cuff to the low pulley of a cable machine. Attach the cuff to one ankle. Face the cable machine, holding the frame for support, with the working leg slightly bent.
execution.setup_instructions: Set the pulley at the lowest position. Attach the ankle cuff to the working leg. Stand close enough to the machine that the cable is taut at the starting position.
steps: Step 1: Face the cable machine, holding the frame with both hands. Stand on the non-working leg with a soft knee.
Step 2: With the working leg slightly bent, extend the hip backward — kick the leg rearward while contracting the glute.
Step 3: Extend until the hip is fully extended or the cable limits further range.
Step 4: Hold the peak contraction briefly with the glute fully squeezed.
Step 5: Return the leg to the starting position under control. Complete all reps then switch.
execution.breathing_instructions: Exhale as you extend. Inhale as you return.
common_mistakes: Swinging the leg — the movement should be controlled, not momentum-driven
Hyperextending the lower back to increase the range, compensating for limited glute activation
Using too much weight, which causes the hip to flex during the movement
safety_considerations: Keep the core braced to protect the lower back from excessive extension
Avoid if the cuff irritates the ankle — use an alternative setup
execution.range_of_motion_guidance: Hip extends from neutral to maximum extension without lumbar hyperextension.
coaching_cues: Squeeze the glute — make the glute do the work
Don't arch the lower back — the motion comes from the hip
Control the return — don't let the cable snap the leg forward

name: Cable Lateral Raise
description: The cable lateral raise is a unilateral shoulder isolation exercise using a low cable pulley. Unlike the dumbbell version, the cable maintains constant tension throughout the full range of motion, including at the bottom where gravity removes load on a dumbbell. This makes it particularly effective for sustained lateral deltoid stimulation.

execution.starting_position: Stand beside a low cable pulley with the cable attachment in the hand farthest from the machine. The cable passes in front of your body. Hold a natural stance with the arm hanging at the side.
execution.setup_instructions: Set the pulley to the lowest position. Attach a single handle. Stand far enough from the stack to feel tension at the bottom of the movement.
steps: With a slight elbow bend, raise the arm out to the side away from the cable machine.
Raise until the upper arm is parallel to the floor.
Lower under control, maintaining tension on the cable throughout.
execution.breathing_instructions: Exhale on the raise, inhale on the return.
common_mistakes: Standing too close to the machine, losing the constant tension benefit
Raising the arm too high above parallel
safety_considerations: Keep the working shoulder's path controlled — avoid shrugging the trap to lift the arm
execution.range_of_motion_guidance: Full bottom position with arm at side, raise to parallel at top.
coaching_cues: Lead with the elbow, not the wrist
Squeeze the lateral delt at the top of each rep

name: Cable Lateral Raise (Cable Behind Glutes)
description: The cable lateral raise with the cable passing behind the glutes positions the cable at the low-back or glute level before the lift, changing the angle of resistance throughout the raise. This positioning maintains lateral deltoid tension through the bottom portion of the movement — where dumbbell raises have minimal tension — making it mechanically advantageous for complete medial deltoid loading across the full range.

execution.starting_position: Stand side-on to a low cable pulley. Reach behind the body and grasp the cable handle with the far hand, so the cable passes behind the glutes. Stand tall.
execution.setup_instructions: The cable should run behind the lower back and under the opposite arm's side. Grip the handle with the arm that is furthest from the cable stack.
steps: Step 1: Begin with the cable behind the glutes, arm at the side.
Step 2: Raise the working arm out to the side and upward to shoulder height.
Step 3: The cable will pull from behind — this unique angle provides early-range tension.
Step 4: Lower under control.
Step 5: Complete all reps then turn and repeat on the other side.
execution.breathing_instructions: Exhale raising. Inhale lowering.
common_mistakes: Not actually passing the cable behind the glutes — the cable must run behind the body
Excessive lean toward the cable — maintain upright posture
safety_considerations: Light loads — this is a finisher or detail exercise, not a strength builder
Ensure cable attachment does not catch on clothing
execution.range_of_motion_guidance: Arm at side to shoulder height.
coaching_cues: Cable runs behind your back — not to the side
Lead with the elbow, not the hand
Feel the tension from the very bottom of the movement

name: Cable Low Flye to Press
description: A combination movement that begins as a low-to-high cable flye targeting the upper pectoralis major, then transitions into a press motion at the top of the arc to fully extend the arms and further load the chest. This two-phase movement recruits both the isolation benefits of the flye and the loading capacity of the press in a single continuous rep.

execution.starting_position: Stand between two low cable pulleys. Hold one handle in each hand, cables running from low pulleys below hip level. Stand tall with a slight forward lean, arms extended down and to the sides.
execution.setup_instructions: Set both pulleys to the lowest position. Attach single D-handles. Stand centered between the two stacks.
steps: Step 1: Begin with arms extended downward and outward, cables taught from the low pulleys.
Step 2: Sweep both arms upward and inward in a wide arc — the flye phase — keeping elbows slightly bent.
Step 3: As the hands meet in front of the chest, transition to a press: bend the elbows and bring the handles toward the chest.
Step 4: Press the handles forward and together to full arm extension.
Step 5: Reverse the motion: unpress back to handle-at-chest, then open out and down in the flye return. Repeat.
execution.breathing_instructions: Exhale through the flye and press phases combined. Inhale on the return.
common_mistakes: Transitioning to the press too early before the hands meet
Excessive forward lean that reduces the cable's tension angle effectiveness
Straightening elbows completely during the flye — maintain a soft bend
safety_considerations: Use moderate weight — the transition from flye to press can stress the shoulder if too heavy
Keep core braced throughout to stabilize the torso
execution.range_of_motion_guidance: Full sweep from low-to-high, then full press extension. The combo requires deliberate transition at the midpoint.
coaching_cues: Flye first, then press — two distinct phases per rep
Lead with the chest, not the arms, on the upward sweep

name: Cable Overhead Tricep Extension
description: The cable overhead tricep extension is performed with a cable machine set to the high position and the rope pulled overhead, then the elbows bent to lower the attachment behind the head. With the shoulder in flexion, the long head of the triceps is placed under maximum stretch, making this variation particularly effective for developing the long head bulk that gives the arm its thickness from the rear view.

execution.starting_position: Attach a rope to the high pulley. Grip the rope ends, turn to face away from the machine, and hold the rope behind the head with elbows bent and pointing toward the ceiling. Stand in a split stance for stability.
execution.setup_instructions: Set the cable pulley to the highest position. Attach a rope. Grip ends, face away from the cable stack, and position rope behind the neck/head before starting.
steps: Step 1: Face away from the high pulley, holding the rope ends behind the head with elbows pointing up.
Step 2: Begin with elbows fully bent, feeling the long head of the triceps stretched.
Step 3: Exhale and extend the elbows overhead, pushing the rope ends apart slightly as you extend.
Step 4: Fully extend the arms, hold for a moment, then inhale and return to the bent position.
execution.breathing_instructions: Exhale on extension; inhale on the return.
common_mistakes: Letting the elbows flare wide — keep them pointing relatively forward/upward
Using the shoulders to lift rather than extending the elbows
safety_considerations: If discomfort is felt at the shoulder during the stretch position, reduce range of motion
Keep the core braced to avoid lower back arching during the overhead position
execution.range_of_motion_guidance: Full elbow bend (deep stretch of long head) to full elbow extension overhead.
coaching_cues: Elbows point to the ceiling — not outward
Feel the deep stretch in the back of the arm at the bottom before pressing up

name: Cable Pullover
description: The cable pullover is a lat isolation exercise performed with a high-pulley cable attachment. The lifter stands or kneels and pulls the cable down and back in a sweeping arc, keeping the arms straight throughout. Because tension from the cable remains constant across the full range of motion, this movement provides superior lat stretch at the top compared to dumbbell variations.

execution.starting_position: Stand facing a high-pulley cable machine. Attach a straight bar or rope. Grip the attachment with both hands using a pronated grip and step back so the cable pulls your arms overhead. Hinge slightly at the hips with a soft bend in the knees.
execution.setup_instructions: Set the cable pulley to its highest position. Attach a straight bar or tricep rope. Select an appropriate weight and step far enough from the machine to feel stretch in the lats with arms raised overhead.
steps: Step 1: Begin with arms extended overhead and elbows slightly soft, feeling a full stretch in the lats.
Step 2: Keeping the arms straight, initiate the movement by depressing the scapulae and driving the elbows toward the hips.
Step 3: Pull the cable down in a wide arc until the hands are roughly at hip level and the lats are fully contracted.
Step 4: Pause briefly at the bottom, squeezing the lats.
Step 5: Slowly return to the starting position under control, allowing the lats to fully lengthen at the top.
execution.breathing_instructions: Exhale as you pull the cable downward and the lats contract. Inhale as you return to the starting position.
common_mistakes: Bending the elbows and turning it into a pulldown — keep arms straight throughout
Using momentum or body sway to initiate the movement
Not allowing a full stretch at the top position
safety_considerations: Avoid hyperextending the lumbar spine by maintaining a neutral spine and slight hip hinge
Use a weight that allows full range of motion without compensatory movement
execution.range_of_motion_guidance: Arms should travel from fully overhead to hip level, achieving a full lat stretch at the top and full contraction at the bottom.
execution.tempo_recommendations: 2-0-2-1 (2s pull down, no pause, 2s return, 1s stretch at top)
coaching_cues: Think 'elbows to hips' rather than 'hands down'
Imagine you are trying to bend the bar over your thighs
Keep your ribcage down — do not flare at the top

name: Cable Tricep Pushdown V-Bar
description: The V-bar (or triangle bar) pushdown attachment on a high cable creates a pronated grip angle that emphasizes the lateral and medial heads of the tricep. The rigid V-bar allows the lifter to generate maximum downward force with both hands simultaneously without any cable or rope instability. Many lifters find the V-bar pushdown allows the most weight of any pushdown variation, making it effective for strength and hypertrophy.

execution.starting_position: Attach a V-bar to a high cable pulley. Stand facing the cable, grip the V-bar with a pronated grip, elbows at the sides, bar at chest level.
execution.setup_instructions: Set the high cable pulley. The V-bar hangs in a pronated (overhand) position when gripped.
steps: Step 1: Begin with the elbows at the sides and the V-bar at chest/upper abdomen level.
Step 2: Push the V-bar straight down by extending the elbows.
Step 3: Push until the elbows are fully extended.
Step 4: Return with control to the starting position.
execution.breathing_instructions: Exhale on the pushdown, inhale on the return.
common_mistakes: Flaring the elbows away from the body
Leaning over the bar to use body weight
Not fully extending the elbows at the bottom
safety_considerations: Keep the elbows pinned to the sides throughout
execution.range_of_motion_guidance: Upper arm vertical, full elbow extension at the bottom.
coaching_cues: Elbows stay at the sides
Straighten the arms fully
Squeeze the triceps at the bottom

name: Cable Rear Delt Fly
description: The cable rear delt fly targets the posterior deltoid and upper back musculature by pulling a cable across the body in a horizontal abduction pattern. Using cables maintains tension throughout the full range of motion. This exercise is essential for shoulder health and postural balance, counteracting the forward shoulder position often caused by excessive pressing work.

execution.starting_position: Stand between two cable stacks set at face height with handles crossed (right hand to left cable, left hand to right cable). Hold handles with palms facing down. Lean forward slightly at the hip or stand upright.
execution.setup_instructions: Set both cable pulleys to face or upper-chest height. Cross the cables and grasp handles so each arm crosses to the opposite stack at the start.
steps: Step 1: Cross-grip the cable handles (right to left pulley, left to right pulley) with arms crossed in front at face height.
Step 2: Begin with arms extended slightly in front and crossed, feeling tension in the cables.
Step 3: Exhale and pull the handles outward and back in a wide arc, extending the arms to either side.
Step 4: Squeeze the rear delts and rhomboids at the peak, then inhale and slowly return to the crossed start position.
execution.breathing_instructions: Exhale as you pull outward; inhale on the return.
common_mistakes: Bending the elbows heavily during the movement, turning it into a row
Using body momentum by rocking — keep the torso still
safety_considerations: Keep a consistent, slight elbow bend — do not lock out the arms
execution.range_of_motion_guidance: Pull until the arms are fully spread to either side with the rear delts maximally contracted.
coaching_cues: Lead with your elbows behind you, not with your hands outward
Feel the squeeze behind your shoulder at the end of each rep

name: Cable Rope Hammer Curl
description: A hammer curl performed with a rope attachment on a low cable pulley. The cable provides constant tension throughout the movement and the neutral grip (palms facing each other) targets the brachialis and brachioradialis to a greater degree than a supinated curl, building arm thickness and elbow flexor strength.

execution.starting_position: Stand facing a low cable pulley, holding a rope attachment with a neutral grip (palms facing each other).
execution.setup_instructions: Attach a rope to the low cable pulley. Stand back enough for the cable to be taut with arms extended.
steps: Step 1: Keeping the upper arms stationary at your sides, curl the rope upward.
Step 2: Pull the ends of the rope apart slightly at the top of the movement.
Step 3: Lower back to full arm extension in a controlled manner.
Step 4: Repeat without letting the upper arms swing forward.
execution.breathing_instructions: Exhale on the curl. Inhale on the return.
common_mistakes: Swinging the upper arms to generate momentum
Not fully extending at the bottom
safety_considerations: Keep the upper arms pinned to the sides throughout
execution.range_of_motion_guidance: Full extension at the bottom. Full flexion at the top.
coaching_cues: Split the rope at the top
Upper arms stay still

name: Cable Rope Pushdown
description: The cable rope pushdown is a cable isolation exercise for the triceps using a rope attachment on a high pulley. At the bottom of the movement, the rope ends are spread apart, which supinates the wrists slightly and creates a wider range of motion compared to a bar attachment. This spreading action produces a more complete contraction of all three triceps heads, particularly the lateral head, making it a popular finisher exercise.

execution.starting_position: Attach a rope to the high pulley. Grip one end in each hand with a neutral grip, thumbs up. Stand facing the cable stack with the elbows bent at 90 degrees and tucked to the sides.
execution.setup_instructions: Set the cable to the highest position. Attach a rope handle. Grip the knots at each end of the rope. Stand close enough that the cable is taut at the starting position.
steps: Step 1: Grip the rope ends, elbows bent at approximately 90 degrees and pinned at the sides.
Step 2: Keep the upper arms stationary throughout — only the forearms move.
Step 3: Exhale and press the rope downward by extending the elbows. As the arms approach full extension, spread the rope ends outward and slightly apart.
Step 4: Hold the peak contraction with the arms fully extended and the rope spread, then inhale and return to the starting position.
execution.breathing_instructions: Exhale on the pushdown; inhale on the return.
common_mistakes: Not spreading the rope at the bottom, which reduces the range of contraction
Letting the elbows drift forward away from the sides during the movement
safety_considerations: Keep wrists neutral throughout — do not flex or hyperextend them under load
execution.range_of_motion_guidance: Full extension with rope spread at the bottom; elbows at 90 degrees at the top.
coaching_cues: Spread the rope ends at the bottom like you are trying to touch each hip
Elbows stay pinned to your sides — they are the fulcrum, not the driver

name: Cable Shrug
description: The cable shrug is a trapezius isolation exercise using a low-pulley cable, which provides constant tension throughout the range of motion unlike a barbell or dumbbell shrug. The cable angle also allows a slight forward lean that can increase the stretch on the upper trapezius at the bottom of the movement, potentially improving hypertrophy stimulus.

execution.starting_position: Stand facing a low-pulley cable machine. Attach a straight bar or rope. Grasp the attachment and step back so the cable pulls the arms slightly forward with arms hanging at the sides.
execution.setup_instructions: Attach a straight bar to the low pulley. Stand close enough to maintain slight cable tension at the bottom of the shrug. Use a shoulder-width overhand grip.
steps: Step 1: Begin standing with arms extended at the sides, allowing the upper traps to stretch slightly downward with the cable pulling forward.
Step 2: Elevate the shoulders straight up toward the ears without bending the elbows.
Step 3: Hold the top position for 1–2 seconds, fully contracting the upper trapezius.
Step 4: Lower the shoulders slowly back to the starting position, allowing a full stretch.
Step 5: Repeat without rolling the shoulders or rotating through the movement.
execution.breathing_instructions: Exhale as you shrug up. Inhale as you lower.
common_mistakes: Rolling the shoulders forward or backward — shrug strictly vertically
Bending the elbows to assist the movement
Using a quick bouncing motion without achieving a full contraction at the top
safety_considerations: Avoid excessive loading that causes cervical spine compression
Do not roll the shoulders — this adds no benefit and may stress the AC joint
execution.range_of_motion_guidance: Full depression of shoulders at the bottom to maximum elevation at the top.
coaching_cues: Try to touch your shoulders to your ears
Keep the arms straight — elbows locked
Move only the shoulders — nothing else moves

name: Cable Woodchopper High Speed
description: A high-velocity cable woodchopper aimed at training rotational power for sport. The explosive rotation from high to low develops the same energy transfer pattern used in throwing, swinging, and striking sports. The speed demands coordination and reactive core stability.

execution.starting_position: Set up for Cable Woodchopper High Speed in proper position.
execution.setup_instructions: Prepare body and equipment for Cable Woodchopper High Speed.
steps: Step 1: Set cable high on pulley. Stand sideways with arms extended to cable.
Step 2: Rotate explosively, pulling cable diagonally downward across body.
Step 3: Finish at low opposite position, following through fully.
Step 4: Return slowly and repeat, using power for each chopping rep.
execution.breathing_instructions: Breathe steadily; never hold breath during static holds.
common_mistakes: Using arms instead of rotating from hips
No follow-through
safety_considerations: Build prerequisite strength before attempting advanced variations.
Stop if joint pain occurs.
execution.range_of_motion_guidance: Full range of motion with control at all times.
coaching_cues: Power comes from hip rotation, not arms
Pivot trailing foot for full rotation

name: High-to-Low Cable Woodchopper
alternative_names: Diagonal Cable Chop High to Low
description: The high-to-low cable woodchopper trains diagonal trunk rotation in a downward arc, emphasizing the external oblique on the pulling side and the contralateral internal oblique. The diagonal movement pattern closely replicates the biomechanics of a downward striking action used in chopping, overhead throwing follow-through, and many racquet-sport movements. The continuous cable tension challenges both the rotational prime movers and the hip stabilizers throughout a large three-dimensional arc.

execution.starting_position: Set the cable pulley to its highest position. Stand side-on to the machine, grasping the handle with both hands above and outside the shoulder closest to the stack.
execution.setup_instructions: Attach a rope or single handle to the high pulley. Stand far enough away that the cable is loaded at the start.
steps: Step 1: Begin with arms extended upward toward the cable, torso rotated toward the stack.
Step 2: Pull the handle diagonally downward and across the body in a chopping arc, rotating the torso away from the cable.
Step 3: Finish with the handle outside the far hip, knees slightly bent and weight shifted.
Step 4: Resist the cable and return in a controlled arc to the start position.
Step 5: Complete all reps then switch sides.
execution.breathing_instructions: Exhale forcefully on the downward chop. Inhale on the controlled return upward.
common_mistakes: Bending the elbows — the movement should originate from the trunk, not the arms
Squatting down instead of rotating — the squat component should be minimal
safety_considerations: Keep the spine neutral throughout — avoid lateral spinal flexion
execution.range_of_motion_guidance: Full diagonal arc from high outside one shoulder to low outside the opposite hip.
coaching_cues: Imagine swinging an axe — the power comes from the whole trunk
Keep the arms long

name: Standing Cable Horizontal Woodchopper
description: The standing cable horizontal woodchopper trains transverse-plane rotation of the trunk by pulling a cable handle from one side of the body to the other at chest height, challenging the obliques, transverse abdominis, and hip rotators in a movement pattern directly applicable to throwing, striking, and swinging sports. The cable provides consistent tension throughout the rotation in both directions — unlike medicine ball throws — allowing controlled loading at all points in the arc.

execution.starting_position: Stand side-on to a cable machine set at chest height. Grasp the handle with both hands, arms extended, feet shoulder-width apart.
execution.setup_instructions: Set the cable pulley to chest height. Stand far enough from the machine that the cable is taut at the start.
steps: Step 1: Begin with the handle in front of the shoulder closest to the cable stack, arms extended.
Step 2: Rotate the trunk away from the cable stack, pulling the handle horizontally across the body.
Step 3: Rotate until the handle is in front of the far shoulder, keeping arms straight throughout.
Step 4: Resist the cable and return to the starting position in a controlled manner.
Step 5: Complete all reps on one side before switching.
execution.breathing_instructions: Exhale as the handle crosses the body. Inhale on the return.
common_mistakes: Bending the elbows and turning a rotation exercise into an arm pull
Rotating from the hips only without engaging the trunk rotators
safety_considerations: Keep the spine neutral — do not laterally flex toward the cable
execution.range_of_motion_guidance: Shoulder-to-shoulder rotation arc. Keep the spine tall throughout.
coaching_cues: Keep the arms straight — this is a torso rotation
Drive with the far hip to initiate the rotation

name: Low-to-High Cable Woodchopper
alternative_names: Diagonal Cable Chop Low to High
description: The low-to-high cable woodchopper trains diagonal trunk rotation in an upward arc from a low starting position, heavily emphasizing the internal oblique on the leading side and contralateral external oblique. This movement pattern mirrors upward striking, throwing from low positions, and the drive phase of many sport actions. The low starting position also engages the hip extensors to initiate the movement, adding a functional lower-body component to the rotational chain.

execution.starting_position: Set the cable pulley to its lowest position. Stand side-on to the machine. Squat and rotate toward the stack to grip the handle with both hands near the outside of the lower knee.
execution.setup_instructions: Attach a rope or single handle to the low pulley. Stand far enough away that there is tension on the cable at the starting position.
steps: Step 1: Begin in a rotated, partially squatted position with the handle near the low outside knee.
Step 2: Drive upward and rotate the trunk away from the cable stack, extending the hips and knees simultaneously.
Step 3: Pull the handle in a diagonal upward arc, finishing with arms extended above and outside the far shoulder.
Step 4: Resist the cable and return in a controlled arc to the starting low position.
Step 5: Complete all reps then switch sides.
execution.breathing_instructions: Exhale as the handle rises. Inhale on the controlled return.
common_mistakes: Using only the arms — the drive should come from extending the hip and rotating the torso
Starting too upright — the low-loading position is essential for the full exercise stimulus
safety_considerations: Avoid if hip or lumbar rotation is limited — the combined hip and spinal movement requires adequate mobility
execution.range_of_motion_guidance: Full diagonal arc from low outside the near knee to high outside the far shoulder.
coaching_cues: Extend the hip to start the upward drive
Finish tall with the arms extended high

name: Wall Calf Stretch
description: The wall calf stretch uses a wall for support and targets the gastrocnemius with the knee straight and the soleus with the knee bent. With the knee straight, the gastrocnemius — which crosses the knee — is placed on maximal tension as the heel is pressed toward the floor and the foot dorsiflexed. The bent-knee version specifically isolates the soleus, which does not cross the knee joint.

execution.starting_position: Stand facing a wall at arm's length. Place both hands on the wall for support.
execution.setup_instructions: Stand near a solid wall. No equipment needed.
steps: Step 1: Place both hands on the wall and step one foot back approximately 60–90 cm.
Step 2: Keep the rear knee straight and press the rear heel firmly into the floor.
Step 3: Lean gently into the wall by bending the front knee, dorsiflexing the rear ankle.
Step 4: Hold until a stretch is felt in the calf of the rear leg — 30–60 seconds.
Step 5: To target the soleus, slightly bend the rear knee while keeping the heel down. Hold again.
execution.breathing_instructions: Breathe naturally and steadily throughout the hold.
common_mistakes: Lifting the heel of the rear foot off the floor, which eliminates the stretch
Rotating the rear foot outward rather than keeping it straight
Not stepping back far enough to feel the stretch
safety_considerations: Avoid this stretch during acute Achilles tendon injury — consult a clinician first
Ensure the wall can support body weight without slipping
execution.range_of_motion_guidance: Lean into the wall until a noticeable but comfortable calf stretch is felt. The rear heel must remain on the floor.
execution.tempo_recommendations: 30–60 seconds straight-leg for gastrocnemius, 30–60 seconds bent-knee for soleus. 2–3 rounds.
coaching_cues: Press the heel through the floor — the stretch comes from the floor pushing back
Keep the rear foot pointing straight ahead
Bend the rear knee slightly to shift the stretch from the gastrocnemius to the soleus

name: Cambered Bar Bench Press
description: The Cambered Bar Bench Press uses a specialty bar with the bar sleeves suspended below the main grip section by a curved or cambered frame. When pressing, the bar hangs several inches below the grip, allowing the elbows to drop lower than the bench surface and providing a greater pectoral stretch at the bottom of the movement than is achievable with a standard straight barbell.

execution.starting_position: Load the cambered bar on the rack. The swinging pendulum effect means the bar is inherently unstable. Grip firmly and establish upper back contact with the bench before unracking.
execution.setup_instructions: Set the rack hooks to accommodate the cambered bar's height. Due to the bar drop, hooks will need to be set higher than for a standard bench press. Test the swing of the bar before loading heavily.
steps: Step 1: Unrack and control the pendulum sway of the bar.
Step 2: Lower under control — the elbows drop below the bench level, creating deep pectoral stretch.
Step 3: Press up from the deep stretched position.
Step 4: Reach full lockout, controlling bar sway throughout.
execution.breathing_instructions: Deep breath and brace before lowering. Hold through the deep stretch position. Exhale on press.
common_mistakes: Panicking at the instability and rushing through the bottom position
Not adjusting rack height to account for the dropped sleeve position
safety_considerations: The swinging of the loaded sleeves creates unpredictable movement — reduce load significantly from your standard bench max
Use a power rack with spotter arms
execution.range_of_motion_guidance: Deeper than a standard bench press. Allow elbows to descend fully below the bench surface.
coaching_cues: Fight the swing — stay tight
Feel the deep pec stretch at the bottom before pressing

name: Cambered Bar Deep Squat
description: A barbell squat variation using a cambered (arched or bowed) bar. The cambered bar hangs the weight below the axis of the bar, lowering the center of mass and creating greater stability demands as the suspended weight shifts during the squat. The bar's shape also allows the torso to remain more upright compared to a straight bar squat, reducing lower back stress while maintaining high quadriceps and glute demand. This is used by powerlifters and strength athletes as a variation squat to develop stability and work around shoulder limitations.

execution.starting_position: Position the cambered bar across the upper back (high or low bar position) in a power rack. The bow of the bar hangs below the loaded sleeves. Step out and assume a standard squat stance.
execution.setup_instructions: Cambered bars require a power rack with standard J-hooks. The bar must sit stably on the hooks before unracking. Never set up without a rack.
steps: Step 1: Unrack the cambered bar and step out to your squat stance.
Step 2: Descend to depth (below parallel or as deep as mobility allows), managing the increased stability demand from the suspended load.
Step 3: Drive through the floor to return to the standing position.
Step 4: Re-rack after completing the set.
execution.breathing_instructions: Inhale and brace before descent. Exhale at the top or in a controlled Valsalva throughout.
common_mistakes: Using too much weight without first adapting to the cambered bar's stability demands
Allowing the suspended load to swing anteriorly during descent
Collapsing the knees inward during the ascent
safety_considerations: The suspended load shifts the balance challenge — reduce weight compared to straight bar squat and build progressively
Use safeties in the rack at all times
Learn the barbell squat and standard specialty bar variations before the cambered bar
execution.range_of_motion_guidance: Below parallel (hip crease below knee) is the standard target. Full depth if mobility allows.
execution.tempo_recommendations: 3s eccentric, 1s pause at bottom optional, 2s concentric ascent
coaching_cues: The bar hangs lower — feel the difference in balance point compared to a standard bar
Keep the chest up — the cambered bar encourages a more upright torso
Control the descent — the swinging load amplifies any forward lean

name: Captain's Chair Knee Raise
description: The captain's chair knee raise is performed on a vertical knee-raise station where the athlete supports their body weight on forearm pads and raises the knees toward the chest. The bent-knee position reduces the lever arm compared to a straight-leg raise, making this more accessible and placing greater relative demand on the rectus abdominis through hip flexion rather than purely the hip flexors. It is a highly effective mid-section exercise that also challenges the shoulder girdle isometrically as it supports the bodyweight.
