execution.starting_position: Mount the captain's chair station by gripping the handles and resting forearms on the pads. The back rests against the back pad. Legs hang straight below.
execution.setup_instructions: Adjust the pad height if the station allows, so the forearms rest comfortably with shoulders away from the ears.
steps: Step 1: Begin hanging with legs straight. Engage the core before initiating the movement.
Step 2: Bend the knees and draw them upward toward the chest, curling the pelvis slightly forward (posterior pelvic tilt) at the top.
Step 3: Hold the top position for 1 second, squeezing the abs.
Step 4: Slowly lower the knees back to the hanging position, resisting gravity throughout.
Step 5: Repeat without swinging.
execution.breathing_instructions: Exhale as the knees rise. Inhale as they lower.
common_mistakes: Swinging the legs up with momentum rather than using slow, controlled ab contraction
Not curling the pelvis at the top, which limits rectus abdominis involvement
safety_considerations: Avoid if shoulder or elbow pain is present — the forearm support places demand on the shoulder girdle
execution.range_of_motion_guidance: Knees travel from straight hanging to above hip level — ideally with the thighs at or above horizontal.
coaching_cues: Curl the pelvis under at the top
No swinging — control the descent

name: Captain's Chair Knee Raise with Isometric Hold
description: A captain's chair knee raise where the knees are held at the top position isometrically before lowering. The isometric hold at peak hip flexion intensifies the hip flexor and lower abdominal challenge. This targets the lower rectus abdominis more effectively than standard raises.

execution.starting_position: Set up for Captain's Chair Knee Raise with Isometric Hold in proper position.
execution.setup_instructions: Prepare body and equipment for Captain's Chair Knee Raise with Isometric Hold.
steps: Step 1: Position in captain's chair with forearms on pads.
Step 2: Raise knees to chest with hip flexion.
Step 3: Hold top position for 3-5 seconds with maximum compression.
Step 4: Lower slowly back to hanging position.
execution.breathing_instructions: Breathe steadily; never hold breath during static holds.
common_mistakes: Using momentum to swing up
Dropping fast from the hold
safety_considerations: Build prerequisite strength before attempting advanced variations.
Stop if joint pain occurs.
execution.range_of_motion_guidance: Full range of motion with control at all times.
coaching_cues: Compress hard at the top hold
Control the lower

name: Captain's Chair Leg Raise
alternative_names: Hanging Straight Leg Raise on Captain's Chair
description: The captain's chair straight-leg raise extends the legs fully during the raise, dramatically increasing the lever arm compared to a knee raise and imposing a significantly greater demand on both the rectus abdominis and hip flexors. The long-lever position requires the athlete to control a larger moment of force and recruit more of the lower rectus abdominis to posteriorly tilt the pelvis at the top of the movement. It is a more advanced progression from the knee raise on the same station.

execution.starting_position: Mount the captain's chair with forearms on the pads and back against the pad. Legs hang straight below the body.
execution.setup_instructions: Ensure the shoulder pads are positioned to allow the arms to support bodyweight without shrugging the shoulders excessively.
steps: Step 1: Begin with legs hanging straight. Engage the core.
Step 2: Keeping the legs straight (or with a very slight bend at the knees), raise both legs upward until the thighs are at or above horizontal.
Step 3: At the top, curl the pelvis slightly forward (posterior tilt) to maximally engage the lower abs.
Step 4: Lower the legs slowly and with full control back to the hanging position.
Step 5: Avoid swinging — maintain tension throughout the entire set.
execution.breathing_instructions: Exhale as legs rise. Inhale on the controlled descent.
common_mistakes: Swinging the legs with momentum rather than controlling the full range
Only raising legs to 45° and missing the upper rectus abdominis contribution from posterior pelvic tilt at the top
safety_considerations: Avoid if hip flexor tightness causes anterior pelvic tilt to worsen — use knee raises instead
execution.range_of_motion_guidance: Legs from full hang to horizontal or above. Posterior pelvic tilt at the top is essential for full ab engagement.
execution.tempo_recommendations: 3-1-3-0. Fully controlled. No kipping or swinging.
coaching_cues: Keep legs straight and squeeze the quads
Curl the tailbone up at the top
Resist gravity on the way down

name: Cat-Cow
description: Cat-cow is a dynamic spinal mobilization exercise performed on hands and knees that alternates between full spinal flexion (cat) and full spinal extension (cow). Moving through the full range of sagittal plane spinal motion warms up the intervertebral joints and muscles, promotes synovial fluid circulation, and is widely used as a preparatory movement before training or as morning mobility work. It is suitable for virtually all populations.

execution.starting_position: Begin in a tabletop position on hands and knees. Wrists directly under shoulders, knees directly under hips. Spine neutral.
execution.setup_instructions: Use a mat for comfort on the knees and wrists.
steps: Step 1: Begin in a neutral tabletop with spine parallel to the floor.
Step 2: CAT — Exhale and round the spine toward the ceiling, tucking the tailbone under and dropping the head. Hold 2 seconds.
Step 3: Return slowly through neutral.
Step 4: COW — Inhale and allow the spine to extend, letting the belly drop toward the floor while lifting the head and tailbone. Hold 2 seconds.
Step 5: Return to neutral. Repeat the cycle 10–15 times.
execution.breathing_instructions: Exhale into the cat (flexion) position. Inhale into the cow (extension) position. Let the breath drive the movement.
common_mistakes: Only moving in the lumbar spine — try to distribute the motion through the thoracic and cervical spine as well
Moving too quickly — this is a slow, mindful mobilization
Not reaching full range in both directions
safety_considerations: If wrist discomfort occurs, make fists to reduce wrist extension load
Those with severe spinal pathology should consult a clinician before performing flexion-based movements
execution.range_of_motion_guidance: Aim for full spinal flexion in cat and full extension in cow. Move through as much range as is comfortable.
coaching_cues: Start from the tailbone — curl the pelvis first, then move segment by segment up the spine
In cow, imagine filling your belly with air as you drop it toward the floor
In cat, press the floor away with your hands to maximize the spinal flexion

name: Chain-Loaded Barbell Bench Press
description: The Chain-Loaded Bench Press attaches heavy chains to each end of the barbell so that more chain links rest on the floor at the bottom of the movement (reducing effective load) and more links are suspended off the floor at lockout (increasing effective load). This accommodating resistance technique matches the natural strength curve of the press — lighter where you are weakest at the bottom, heavier where you are strongest at the top.

execution.starting_position: Attach chains to each sleeve of the barbell using a small pilot chain looped over the sleeve. Chains should partially deload to the floor at the bottom of the rep. Lie on the bench and grip normally.
execution.setup_instructions: Loop a pilot chain over each barbell sleeve. Attach the main chains so that roughly half the chain length rests on the floor at the bottom of the movement. Adjust to ensure full chain suspension at lockout.
steps: Step 1: Unrack the bar and begin the descent.
Step 2: Lower the bar to touch the chest as more chain piles onto the floor, reducing load.
Step 3: Press the bar upward; as it rises, more chain lifts off the floor, increasing load.
Step 4: Drive to full lockout where the full chain weight is suspended.
execution.breathing_instructions: Inhale and brace before the eccentric. Exhale through the sticking point on the concentric.
common_mistakes: Chains too short so they never deload at the bottom
Chains too long so they never fully lift off the floor at lockout
safety_considerations: Account for chain weight when calculating barbell load — reduce plate weight accordingly
Use a power rack with safety bars
execution.range_of_motion_guidance: Full ROM from chest-touch to lockout, same as standard bench press.
execution.tempo_recommendations: 3-0-X-0 (explosive concentric to maximize accommodating resistance benefit)
coaching_cues: Press as fast as you can — speed overcomes the increasing chain weight
Stay tight; the swinging chains create additional stabilization demands

name: Chained Decline Dumbbell Press
description: A decline dumbbell press with chains attached to the dumbbells and draped on the floor. The decline angle targets the sternal and lower pectoral fibers while the chains provide accommodating resistance — increasing load as the dumbbells rise and chain links lift off the floor. At full lockout, the maximal chain load challenges the peak contraction where free weights typically feel easiest.

execution.starting_position: Lie on a decline bench (15–30 degrees) with feet secured. Attach chains to dumbbells so they drape to the floor from the bottom position. Hold dumbbells at chest level.
execution.setup_instructions: Secure chains to dumbbell handles with carabiners. Adjust chain length so they begin lifting off the floor in the mid-to-upper range of the press. Reduce dumbbell weight to account for the chain addition.
steps: Step 1: Begin at the bottom position with elbows at chest level. Chains drape to the floor.
Step 2: Press the dumbbells upward. Chain links progressively lift as the dumbbells rise.
Step 3: At full lockout, all chains are suspended and the peak load occurs.
Step 4: Lower under control. Chains re-contact the floor, deloading the bottom. Repeat.
execution.breathing_instructions: Inhale at the bottom, exhale forcefully through the press.
common_mistakes: Chains that don't engage — means they are too long for the decline setup
Underestimating the total load — count dumbbell plus chain weight when programming
Feet unsecured — always secure feet on the decline
safety_considerations: Secure feet firmly on the decline bench
Secure chain attachments before beginning
Use significantly less dumbbell weight than normal to account for chain addition
execution.range_of_motion_guidance: Full range from lower chest to lockout. Chain loading is highest at the top.
coaching_cues: Press hard all the way through — the chains reward explosive effort at the top
Feel the bottom deload as the chains hit the floor — that tells you the range of engagement

name: Chained Incline Dumbbell Press
description: An incline dumbbell press with chains attached to the dumbbells and draped on the floor. As the dumbbells rise, more chain links lift off the floor, progressively increasing the load through the top range of motion. This accommodating resistance technique challenges the pectoralis major clavicular fibers through the top portion where free weights typically become easier due to mechanical advantage.

execution.starting_position: Set the incline bench to 30–45 degrees. Attach chains to the dumbbell handles so they drape to the floor when held at the bottom position. Lie on the bench with the loaded dumbbells at chest level.
execution.setup_instructions: Chains can be attached with carabiners or looped through the dumbbell plate holes. The chain should begin lifting off the floor when the arms reach roughly the midpoint of the press.
steps: Step 1: Begin at the bottom position with elbows at chest level. Chains drape to the floor.
Step 2: Press the dumbbells upward. As they rise, chain links progressively lift off the floor, increasing the load.
Step 3: At full lockout, all chains are suspended and the peak load occurs.
Step 4: Lower under control. As dumbbells descend, chains re-contact the floor, deloading the bottom. Repeat.
execution.breathing_instructions: Inhale at the bottom, exhale forcefully through the press.
common_mistakes: Chains that never lift off the floor — means chains are too long or dumbbells don't travel high enough
Using dumbbell weight that is too heavy before accounting for chain load
Chains not secured and sliding off mid-set
safety_considerations: Secure chain attachments before beginning
Reduce dumbbell weight below normal incline press weight to account for chain addition
Have a training partner observe chain behavior during the first set
execution.range_of_motion_guidance: Full range, bottom to lockout. Chain loading is greatest at the top.
coaching_cues: Press hard all the way to lockout — the chains test you there
The bottom feels light, the top feels heavy — that's the point

name: Cheat Curl
description: A barbell curl variation that uses a slight body swing to initiate the movement, allowing the lifter to use heavier loads than a strict curl. The overloaded eccentric phase provides a strong hypertrophy stimulus for the biceps as the weight is lowered under control, making cheat curls a classic bodybuilding technique.

execution.starting_position: Stand holding a barbell with an underhand grip, arms extended down. Feet shoulder-width apart.
execution.setup_instructions: Pick up a barbell heavier than you would use for strict curls. Stand with feet shoulder-width apart and core engaged.
steps: Step 1: Use a slight hip and knee dip to initiate momentum and swing the bar upward.
Step 2: Continue the curl motion, bringing the bar to the chest.
Step 3: Lower the bar very slowly and under strict control over 3 to 4 seconds.
Step 4: At the bottom, use the next swing to begin the following rep.
execution.breathing_instructions: Exhale during the curl. Inhale slowly during the controlled eccentric descent.
common_mistakes: Excessive body English that turns the movement into a full-body swing
Not controlling the eccentric — the eccentric is the purpose of the exercise
safety_considerations: The weight should be heavier than a strict curl but not so heavy that form completely breaks down
Do not use this technique as a crutch — it is a deliberate advanced technique
execution.range_of_motion_guidance: Full range of curl at the top. Fully extend at the bottom before the next rep.
coaching_cues: Use the momentum to get it up
Take your time on the way down

name: Chest Dip
description: The chest dip is a compound bodyweight or weighted pushing exercise performed on parallel bars with a forward torso lean. By inclining the torso forward, the lower and outer pectoral muscles are emphasized over the triceps, making it an effective mass-building exercise for the lower chest.

execution.starting_position: Support yourself on parallel dip bars with arms extended. Lean your torso forward at approximately 30 degrees by crossing your feet behind and allowing your hips to tilt forward.
execution.setup_instructions: Set dip bar width to slightly wider than shoulder width. The forward lean is what distinguishes a chest dip from a tricep dip — without it, the triceps dominate.
steps: With the forward lean maintained, lower yourself by bending the elbows, allowing them to flare slightly outward.
Descend until shoulders are at the same height as the elbows or slightly below.
Press back up to the starting position, maintaining the forward lean throughout.
execution.breathing_instructions: Inhale on descent. Exhale on the press up.
common_mistakes: Maintaining an upright torso, shifting emphasis to the triceps instead of the chest
Dipping below the shoulder level of safe range, stressing the anterior shoulder capsule
Allowing the elbows to flare excessively wide
safety_considerations: Stop the descent when shoulders begin to feel uncomfortable — this varies by individual
Individuals with shoulder impingement or anterior shoulder pain should approach with caution
execution.range_of_motion_guidance: Upper arms reach parallel or slightly below parallel to the floor at the bottom.
coaching_cues: Lean forward — the more you lean, the more chest you use
Think about pushing the bars behind you rather than pressing straight down

name: Doorway Chest Stretch
description: The doorway chest stretch uses a door frame to passively stretch the pectoral muscles and anterior deltoids into horizontal abduction, which is the antagonist movement to pushing and pressing. Regular stretching of the anterior chest is associated with improved shoulder posture, reduced risk of rounded shoulders, and better overhead shoulder mobility. The arm position can be adjusted to target the clavicular or sternal head of the pectoralis major.

execution.starting_position: Stand in an open doorway. Raise both arms to form a 90-degree angle at the elbow with forearms resting on the door frame.
execution.setup_instructions: Find a doorway wide enough to place forearms on each side of the frame. No equipment needed.
steps: Step 1: Stand in the center of a doorway with one foot slightly forward for stability.
Step 2: Place both forearms on the door frame at approximately shoulder height (elbows at 90 degrees).
Step 3: Lean gently forward through the doorway, allowing the chest to open and shoulders to rotate back.
Step 4: When a stretch is felt across the chest and front of the shoulders, hold the position.
Step 5: Hold 30–60 seconds. Raise forearms slightly higher to stretch the clavicular head, lower to target the sternal head.
execution.breathing_instructions: Breathe normally and slowly. Each exhale allows the chest to open slightly more.
common_mistakes: Leaning forward excessively with the lower back arching rather than the chest opening
Placing the arms too high, which shifts the stretch to the shoulder rather than the pec
Holding the breath and creating tension in the shoulders and neck
safety_considerations: If shoulder pain is experienced — especially at the front of the shoulder — reduce the range of forward lean
Those with anterior shoulder instability should use caution with this stretch
execution.range_of_motion_guidance: Lean forward until a comfortable pectoral stretch is felt. No need to overreach.
execution.tempo_recommendations: Hold 30–60 seconds. 2–3 rounds at different arm heights.
coaching_cues: Lead the chest through the door, not the head
Squeeze the shoulder blades together gently during the stretch
Breathe wide — expand the chest on each inhale

name: Chest-Supported Landmine T-Bar Row
description: The chest-supported landmine T-bar row combines the unique angled force vector of a landmine setup with the strict torso support of an incline bench. The chest pad eliminates lower back involvement entirely, directing all effort to the lats and upper back while the landmine angle provides a natural arc that accommodates shoulder mechanics better than many cable or barbell row variations.

execution.starting_position: Position an incline bench (30-45 degrees) over the loaded end of a landmine barbell. Lie prone on the bench with the chest supported. Reach down and grasp the barbell end with both hands (or a V-handle attachment).
execution.setup_instructions: Adjust bench position so that arms can reach full extension at the bottom. A V-grip handle over the bar sleeve makes bilateral gripping easier.
steps: Step 1: Lie prone on the incline bench, chest supported, arms extended holding the bar end.
Step 2: Depress and retract both shoulder blades simultaneously.
Step 3: Row the bar toward the chest by driving elbows back.
Step 4: At the top, hold 1 second.
Step 5: Lower under control to full arm extension.
execution.breathing_instructions: Exhale on the row. Inhale on the descent.
common_mistakes: Head craning forward — keep neck neutral against the bench pad
Insufficient lat engagement — focus on depressing scaps before the pull
safety_considerations: Ensure the bench is stable and won't slide on the floor
Secure the barbell in a landmine unit or corner before loading
execution.range_of_motion_guidance: Full arm extension to elbows behind torso line.
coaching_cues: Lead with the elbows, not the hands
Chest stays in contact with the bench throughout
Squeeze the blades together at the top

name: Chest-Supported Dumbbell Row
description: The chest-supported dumbbell row eliminates lower back involvement by bracing the chest on an inclined bench, allowing complete isolation of the upper back musculature. Because the spine is supported, there is no temptation to extend the torso to generate momentum, making this one of the most reliable exercises for targeting the rhomboids, middle trapezius, and rear deltoids independently.

execution.starting_position: Set an adjustable bench to a 30–45 degree incline. Lie prone (face down) on the bench with the chest and stomach resting on the pad. Let both arms hang straight down toward the floor, each holding a dumbbell with a neutral or pronated grip.
execution.setup_instructions: Set the bench incline to approximately 30–45 degrees. Choose dumbbells lighter than you would use for a standard dumbbell row since there is no lower back contribution. Position feet flat on the floor or on the bench footrest for stability.
steps: Step 1: Begin with arms hanging directly below the shoulders, fully extended.
Step 2: Retract the scapulae and row both dumbbells simultaneously toward the lower ribcage.
Step 3: Drive the elbows up and back, keeping them close to or slightly outside the torso.
Step 4: At the top, squeeze the shoulder blades together firmly.
Step 5: Slowly lower the dumbbells back to the starting position, fully extending the arms and protracting the scapulae.
execution.breathing_instructions: Exhale as you row the dumbbells up. Inhale as you lower them.
common_mistakes: Lifting the chest off the pad — this negates the purpose of the chest support
Using a grip that internally rotates the shoulder (overgripping with excessive wrist flexion)
Insufficient range of motion by not fully protracting and retracting the scapulae
safety_considerations: Ensure the bench is stable on the floor before loading it with your body weight and dumbbells
Avoid craning the neck — keep the head in a neutral position aligned with the spine
execution.range_of_motion_guidance: Full hang at the bottom with scapular protraction to maximum retraction at the top. This movement has a relatively short ROM — prioritize muscle contraction quality.
coaching_cues: Squeeze a pencil between your shoulder blades at the top
Row to your hip pockets, not your armpits
Keep the chest pinned to the pad throughout

name: Chest-Supported Row (Alternating Arms)
description: The alternating chest-supported row performs each arm separately on an incline bench, allowing the non-working arm to hold at peak contraction while the other arm descends and returns. This creates a unique combination of isometric and dynamic loading within a single set, increasing total upper back time under tension while maintaining strict torso support.

execution.starting_position: Lie prone on an incline bench set to 30-45 degrees. Hold a dumbbell in each hand, arms hanging down.
execution.setup_instructions: Set the incline bench so that the chest is fully supported throughout the movement. Use a weight that allows clean alternating reps.
steps: Step 1: Row both dumbbells to the top position simultaneously to start.
Step 2: Hold the left dumbbell at peak contraction.
Step 3: Lower the right dumbbell to full extension while holding the left.
Step 4: Row the right dumbbell back to the top.
Step 5: Hold right at top; lower left; repeat the alternating pattern.
execution.breathing_instructions: Breathe continuously — do not hold breath for the entire set.
common_mistakes: Not actually holding at peak — both arms should not move simultaneously
Losing scapular retraction during the hold phase
safety_considerations: The chest-supported position eliminates lower back stress — suitable for lower back pain sufferers
Keep the head in a neutral position — do not crane the neck
execution.range_of_motion_guidance: Full arm extension to elbows behind torso on each arm.
coaching_cues: One arm holds while the other works
Keep both shoulder blades retracted throughout
Full stretch on every descent

name: Chest-Supported T-Bar Row Machine
description: The chest-supported T-bar row uses a dedicated machine with an angled pad that supports the chest, eliminating lower back involvement entirely. The bilateral T-bar handle allows both hands to row simultaneously at a neutral or pronated grip position. Because the chest is supported, trainees can focus entirely on maximizing back muscle contraction without compensatory trunk extension, making it an excellent hypertrophy tool for the mid and upper back.

execution.starting_position: Load the T-bar machine with appropriate weight. Step onto the footrests and lean the chest into the angled support pad. Grip the handles and let the arms hang extended.
execution.setup_instructions: Adjust the chest pad height so the arms can fully extend without the weight touching the floor. Ensure the chest stays in contact with the pad throughout.
steps: Step 1: Position the chest on the support pad, feet on the footrests, arms extended holding the handles.
Step 2: Retract the scapulae and initiate the row.
Step 3: Pull the handles toward the lower chest, driving the elbows straight back.
Step 4: Squeeze the entire upper back at peak contraction.
Step 5: Lower the weight under control until arms are fully extended.
execution.breathing_instructions: Exhale on the row, inhale on the descent.
common_mistakes: Lifting the chest off the pad, negating the support
Not retracting the scapulae — just bending the elbows without moving the shoulder blades
Using too heavy a weight, reducing ROM
safety_considerations: Ensure the chest pad is at a comfortable height — too low or high causes neck strain
Dismount carefully after each set
execution.range_of_motion_guidance: Full arm extension at the bottom to handles touching or near the lower chest at the top.
coaching_cues: Let the shoulder blades spread at the bottom
Row the elbows straight back
Chest stays on the pad

name: Child's Pose
description: Child's pose is a resting yoga posture that places the spine in a supported flexed position and gently stretches the latissimus dorsi, thoracic extensors, and hip flexors simultaneously. The extended arm variation provides a substantial lat stretch while the kneeling position creates mild hip flexor lengthening. It is used widely as a recovery position, a breathing exercise, and a preparatory or finishing movement in mobility routines.

execution.starting_position: Kneel on the floor with knees wide and toes touching. Sit the hips back toward the heels.
execution.setup_instructions: Use a mat for comfort. If the hips do not reach the heels, place a folded blanket between the thighs and calves.
steps: Step 1: Kneel on the floor with knees wider than hip-width and toes together.
Step 2: Sit the hips back toward the heels.
Step 3: Extend both arms forward on the floor as far as possible, lowering the chest toward the floor.
Step 4: Rest the forehead on the floor or a cushion.
Step 5: Hold 60–120 seconds, breathing deeply into the back body.
execution.breathing_instructions: Breathe deeply. On each inhale, feel the ribcage expand sideways and upward. On each exhale, allow the body to sink more completely into the position.
common_mistakes: Keeping the knees together, which limits hip comfort — wider knees are more accommodating for most people
Not allowing the arms to extend fully overhead, limiting the lat stretch
Tensing the neck — allow the head to rest completely
safety_considerations: If knee discomfort is present, place padding under the knees or avoid if severe
Those with ankle mobility limitations may need a rolled towel under the ankles
execution.range_of_motion_guidance: Extend the arms as far forward as comfortable and allow the forehead to rest on the floor.
coaching_cues: Let gravity do the work — just breathe and release
Walk your fingers further away from your body on each exhale
Allow the shoulder blades to spread apart

name: Chin-Up
description: The chin-up is a vertical pulling bodyweight exercise performed with a supinated (underhand) grip. The supinated grip places the biceps in a mechanically advantageous position, increasing their contribution compared to the pull-up. The chin-up is often considered slightly easier for beginners and provides excellent simultaneous stimulation of the lats and biceps.

execution.starting_position: Hang from a bar with a supinated (palms facing you) grip at shoulder width or slightly narrower. Arms fully extended, core lightly engaged.
execution.setup_instructions: Grip the bar underhand at shoulder width. The narrower grip and supinated wrist position is what distinguishes this from a pull-up.
steps: Initiate the movement by depressing the shoulder blades.
Pull yourself up by driving the elbows down and toward your sides.
Continue until your chin is above the bar.
Lower under control until arms are fully extended.
execution.breathing_instructions: Exhale on the pull, inhale on the descent.
common_mistakes: Using excessive momentum
Not reaching full extension at the bottom
safety_considerations: Avoid if experiencing acute biceps tendon pain
Fully extend at the bottom of each rep
execution.range_of_motion_guidance: Full dead hang at bottom, chin above bar at top.
coaching_cues: Pull the bar toward your chest rather than your chin toward the bar
Maintain proud posture — do not let the shoulders creep toward the ears

name: Circus Dumbbell Clean and Press
description: A strongman event using an oversized dumbbell that must be cleaned to shoulder and pressed overhead. The huge size makes gripping and balancing the implement uniquely challenging. Athletes typically use a combination of a swing, lap, and shoulder technique to get the dumbbell overhead.

execution.starting_position: Set up for Circus Dumbbell Clean and Press in proper strongman position.
execution.setup_instructions: Prepare all equipment and body position for Circus Dumbbell Clean and Press.
steps: Step 1: Position over circus dumbbell. Swing handle and use momentum to pull to lap.
Step 2: Shoulder the dumbbell from lap position resting on forearm.
Step 3: Dip slightly and drive dumbbell overhead using leg drive.
Step 4: Lock out arm fully overhead before lowering.
execution.breathing_instructions: Brace core maximally before every lift. Breathe between reps if needed.
common_mistakes: Trying to strict press without leg drive
Poor grip on oversized handle
safety_considerations: Use collars on all loaded barbells.
Ensure clear path for carries.
Have spotters for overhead movements.
execution.range_of_motion_guidance: Full range of motion specific to the implement being used.
coaching_cues: Use aggressive leg drive
Find the balanced center of the implement

name: Clamshell
description: The clamshell is a side-lying hip external rotation exercise in which the feet remain stacked and together while the top knee is raised toward the ceiling, mimicking the opening of a clamshell. It isolates the gluteus medius with a focus on external rotation and abduction, making it one of the most prescribed exercises in physical therapy for hip, knee, and lower back rehabilitation. A resistance band above the knees increases the load.

execution.starting_position: Lie on one side with hips stacked, knees bent to approximately 45°, and feet together. The head rests on the lower arm.
execution.setup_instructions: No equipment needed for bodyweight. Place a mini loop band just above the knees for added resistance.
steps: Step 1: Lie on your side with hips stacked and knees bent at 45°. Keep the feet together throughout.
Step 2: Keeping the feet together, raise the top knee toward the ceiling by externally rotating the hip.
Step 3: Open until the top knee is as high as possible without letting the pelvis roll backward.
Step 4: Hold the peak position, then lower the knee back to the start under control.
Step 5: Complete all reps on one side then switch.
execution.breathing_instructions: Exhale as you open the knee. Inhale as you close.
common_mistakes: Rolling the pelvis backward to increase range — the hip should rotate, not the spine
Raising the knee so high that the pelvis tilts — control the range
Using momentum instead of a slow, controlled movement
safety_considerations: Very low-risk exercise suitable for all fitness levels
Often prescribed in rehabilitation for IT band syndrome, patellofemoral pain, and hip pain
execution.range_of_motion_guidance: Open the knee as far as possible without pelvic roll. Quality of rotation matters more than range.
coaching_cues: Open like a clamshell — feet stay touching
Don't let the pelvis roll back — keep the hips stacked
Squeeze the glute at the top

name: Clamshell with Resistance Band
description: The banded clamshell is a foundational hip abductor strengthening exercise performed side-lying. A resistance band placed above the knees increases the challenge compared to bodyweight alone. By rotating the top knee upward while keeping the feet together and pelvis stable, the gluteus medius and hip external rotators are isolated. This exercise is essential for knee and hip rehabilitation, correcting valgus collapse, and preventing IT band issues.

execution.starting_position: Lie on your side with hips stacked, knees bent to approximately 45 degrees and feet together. Place a resistance band just above both knees. Rest your head on your lower arm.
execution.setup_instructions: Choose a band resistance that allows 15-20 quality reps with control. The band should not cause the pelvis to rotate during the movement.
steps: Step 1: Brace the core lightly and ensure the pelvis remains stacked and still throughout.
Step 2: Keeping the feet together and the lower leg on the floor, rotate the top knee upward toward the ceiling like a clamshell opening.
Step 3: Raise the top knee as high as possible without the pelvis tilting backward.
Step 4: Slowly lower the knee back to the starting position under control. Complete all reps then switch sides.
execution.breathing_instructions: Exhale as you open the knee upward. Inhale as you return to the starting position.
common_mistakes: Rolling the pelvis backward to gain extra range — this removes glute med work
Letting the top foot lift off the bottom foot
Using too heavy a band and compensating with the hip flexors
safety_considerations: Consult a physiotherapist if you have hip labral pathology
Keep the movement slow and controlled
execution.range_of_motion_guidance: Open to approximately 45-60 degrees of hip external rotation without pelvic rotation. Focus on quality, not range.
execution.tempo_recommendations: 2-1-2-1 (2s up, 1s hold at top, 2s down, 1s pause at bottom)
coaching_cues: Keep your pelvis still — do not let it roll back
Think about leading with the outer hip, not the knee
Control the return — do not let the band snap it down

name: Clamshell with Band — Top Leg Straight Raise
description: An advanced clamshell progression that extends the top of the clamshell motion into a straight-leg hip abduction. After rotating the bent top knee as high as possible (clamshell), the exerciser straightens the knee and raises the now-extended leg further in abduction before returning. The resistance band increases the challenge throughout both phases. This combination targets the gluteus medius through its full hip abduction arc while simultaneously engaging the hip external rotators in the clamshell phase.

execution.starting_position: Lie on one side with hips stacked and knees bent to approximately 60-90 degrees. Place a resistance band loop just above both knees.
execution.setup_instructions: Choose a band resistance that allows the clamshell phase at full range before the leg extension. The pelvis must not rotate at any point.
steps: Step 1: Begin the clamshell — rotate the top knee upward against the band as far as hip external rotation allows without the pelvis rotating.
Step 2: At the top of the clamshell, straighten the top knee to extend the leg.
Step 3: With the leg now fully extended, raise it slightly further in abduction against the band.
Step 4: Lower the extended leg to the starting position, bend the knee, and return to the folded starting position. That is one repetition.
execution.breathing_instructions: Exhale as you open the clamshell. Continue exhaling through the extension and abduction. Inhale on the return.
common_mistakes: Rotating the pelvis backward during the clamshell phase to gain extra range
Straightening the leg without first reaching the top of the clamshell range
Using a band that is too heavy, preventing full range in either phase
safety_considerations: If knee pain occurs during the leg extension phase, stop and assess
Keep the pelvis stable — place a hand on the top hip to monitor for rotation
execution.range_of_motion_guidance: Full clamshell range before extension; abduction phase is a small additional lift after the leg straightens.
execution.tempo_recommendations: 2s clamshell open, 1s extend leg, 1s additional abduction, 3s full return.
coaching_cues: Complete the clamshell before extending the leg — the hip must be fully rotated first
Keep the foot of the extended leg in a neutral position, not rotated
Feel the outer hip burning — that is the target

name: Clap / Plyometric Push-Up
description: The clap push-up is a plyometric variation in which the pressing phase is explosive enough to launch the hands off the floor, allowing a clap before landing. This develops upper-body power, rate-of-force development, and reactive strength in the chest, triceps, and anterior deltoids through a true stretch-shortening cycle.

execution.starting_position: Begin in a standard push-up position with hands shoulder-width apart and body in a straight line.
execution.setup_instructions: Perform on a firm, flat surface that provides enough friction for a safe hand landing. Ensure there is adequate floor space.
steps: Step 1: Lower into the bottom of a push-up under control.
Step 2: At the bottom, explosively press the floor away with maximum force.
Step 3: Drive the torso upward fast enough for the hands to leave the floor.
Step 4: Clap the hands together while airborne.
Step 5: Land with hands in the original position, absorbing impact by bending the elbows immediately into the next rep.
execution.breathing_instructions: Inhale on the way down. Exhale explosively on the press.
common_mistakes: Not lowering enough before the explosive press, reducing power output
Landing stiff-wristed, risking wrist injury
Attempting this exercise without sufficient standard push-up strength
safety_considerations: Master push-ups with a minimum of 20 consecutive reps before attempting plyometric variation
Land with bent elbows to absorb impact
Perform on a padded or non-slip surface
Do not perform to failure — stop well before form breaks
execution.range_of_motion_guidance: Full depth on the descent. The press must be explosive enough to generate meaningful air time.
coaching_cues: Push the floor through the Earth
Land soft — absorb with the elbows
Quality over quantity — explosive intent every rep

name: Clean and Jerk
description: The clean and jerk is the second of the two Olympic weightlifting competition lifts, consisting of two distinct phases: the clean, which brings the bar from the floor to the front rack position on the shoulders, and the jerk, which drives the bar from the shoulders to a fully locked overhead position. It is typically the stronger of the two Olympic lifts and demands whole-body explosive power, precise technique, and excellent mobility throughout the shoulders, hips, and ankles.

execution.starting_position: Bar over mid-foot, shoulder-width clean grip (narrower than snatch), flat back, shoulders slightly in front of the bar.
execution.setup_instructions: Use bumper plates and a lifting platform. The jerk requires sufficient shoulder mobility to achieve a stable overhead catch. Warm up shoulders, hips, and ankles thoroughly.
steps: Step 1 (Clean): First pull — drive legs into the floor, keeping back angle constant and bar close.
Step 2 (Clean): Second pull — extend hips explosively as the bar passes the hip. Shrug and pull elbows high.
Step 3 (Clean): Pull under the bar and receive it in the front rack position (elbows high, bar on shoulders) in a front squat. Stand to full extension.
Step 4 (Jerk): From the front rack, take a controlled dip — bend the knees 10–15 cm, keeping the torso upright.
Step 5 (Jerk): Drive upward explosively with the legs, then drop under the bar into a split or push position with arms locked overhead. Stand to full extension.
execution.breathing_instructions: Brace before the clean. Reset and re-brace in the front rack before the jerk. Exhale after the overhead lock-out.
common_mistakes: Early arm bend during the clean pull
Insufficient hip extension before the second pull
Dipping forward during the jerk dip, shifting the bar off the ideal catch position
Soft elbows in the overhead catch
safety_considerations: Requires extensive technical coaching. Never compromise the catch to avoid dropping the bar.
Use bumper plates and be prepared to bail safely.
Wrist mobility is essential for the front rack — develop it before loading the clean.
execution.range_of_motion_guidance: Full hip extension on the second pull. Full overhead lockout with stable shoulder and spine in the jerk.
execution.tempo_recommendations: Maximum explosive intent throughout. The clean is typically under 2 seconds; there is a deliberate pause in the front rack before the jerk.
coaching_cues: High elbows in the rack — bar on the shoulders, not the hands
Dip straight down — not forward
Lock out the elbows fast in the catch

name: Clean Pull
description: The clean pull is a pulling accessory exercise for the clean in which the athlete performs the full pulling mechanics of the clean — first pull, second pull, and shrug — without catching the bar in the front rack. It allows heavier loads than the clean to be used to overload the pulling musculature and reinforce pulling mechanics. The clean pull is essential for developing the hip drive strength and bar path needed in the full clean.

execution.starting_position: Bar over mid-foot, shoulder-width clean grip, flat back, hips above knees, shoulders above bar.
execution.setup_instructions: Same starting position as the clean. Use lifting straps if grip is limiting pulling load.
steps: Step 1: Set up in clean starting position.
Step 2: First pull — drive the floor away, keeping the bar close and back angle constant.
Step 3: Second pull — extend hips explosively as the bar passes the hip crease.
Step 4: Shrug the traps aggressively at full extension.
Step 5: Allow the bar to continue upward from the shrug momentum, then lower with control — do not catch.
execution.breathing_instructions: Brace before initiating. Hold through the pull. Exhale as the bar descends.
common_mistakes: Bending the arms before the shrug (early arm pull)
Not achieving full hip extension before the shrug
Letting the bar drift away from the body
safety_considerations: Lower the bar with control to avoid excessive stress on the lower back.
Use lifting straps to allow full focus on pulling mechanics without grip limitation.
execution.range_of_motion_guidance: Full hip extension and triple extension (ankle, knee, hip) at the top of the pull.
execution.tempo_recommendations: Explosive pull. Controlled lower. Can be loaded 10–20% above clean maximum.
coaching_cues: Full extension before the shrug
Bar close — brush the thighs
Shrug tall — rise onto the toes at the top

name: Close-Grip Bench Press
description: The close-grip bench press is a barbell pressing variation using a narrower grip (shoulder-width or slightly inside), which reduces pectoral involvement and shifts the primary load to the triceps. It allows heavy triceps training with more load than isolation exercises and is a staple accessory for pressing strength development.

execution.starting_position: Lie on a flat bench. Grip the barbell at shoulder width or slightly inside with an overhand grip. Unrack and hold with arms extended over the mid-chest.
execution.setup_instructions: Do not go excessively narrow — shoulder-width grip is sufficient. Going too narrow increases wrist stress without benefiting tricep isolation.
steps: Lower the bar to the lower chest keeping elbows tucked close to the torso.
Touch the chest and immediately press back to full arm extension.
Re-rack after the final rep.
execution.breathing_instructions: Inhale on descent, exhale on the press.
common_mistakes: Gripping too narrow — inside shoulder width increases wrist discomfort
Flaring the elbows wide, negating the tricep emphasis
safety_considerations: Use a spotter or rack safety catches
Keep thumbs wrapped around the bar
execution.range_of_motion_guidance: Full extension at top, bar touches lower chest at bottom.
coaching_cues: Keep elbows close to the body — tuck them in toward the ribs
Press the bar in a straight line upward

name: 3-Board Close-Grip Board Press
description: A powerlifting accessory exercise with a 3-board to train the top portion of the bench press range. Close grip focuses effort on the triceps at near-lockout angles. Useful for overloading the triceps with weights above max bench capability.

execution.starting_position: Set up for 3-Board Close-Grip Board Press in the appropriate position.
execution.setup_instructions: Prepare equipment and body position for 3-Board Close-Grip Board Press.
steps: Step 1: Position 3-board on chest held by training partner. Use close grip on bar.
Step 2: Lower bar to board surface with controlled descent.
Step 3: Drive bar back to lockout focusing on tricep extension.
Step 4: Complete reps then rerack with assistance.
execution.breathing_instructions: Exhale during the exertion phase, inhale during the return.
common_mistakes: Letting elbows drift
Using momentum from boards
safety_considerations: Keep joints aligned throughout the movement.
Use controlled weight appropriate for skill level.
execution.range_of_motion_guidance: Move through full range of motion without compromising joint integrity.
coaching_cues: Treat boards as a pause point, not a bounce
Full lockout every rep

name: Close-Grip EZ-Bar Curl
description: The close-grip EZ-bar curl uses the inner grip position on an EZ-curl bar, which externally rotates the shoulders and shifts greater emphasis to the long head of the biceps. The long head contributes to the peak height of the bicep. The EZ-bar's angled grip reduces wrist strain compared to a straight close-grip barbell curl, making it more comfortable for high-volume training.

execution.starting_position: Stand holding an EZ-bar with hands on the inner (narrow) grip position, arms extended.
execution.setup_instructions: Use the inner grip knurling of the EZ-bar. Stand with feet hip-width, brace the core.
steps: Step 1: Curl the EZ-bar upward by flexing the elbows.
Step 2: Keep the upper arms stationary at the sides.
Step 3: Curl to full elbow flexion.
Step 4: Lower slowly to the starting position.
execution.breathing_instructions: Exhale on the curl, inhale on the return.
common_mistakes: Swinging the torso
Elbows drifting forward
Locking out too aggressively
safety_considerations: EZ-bar reduces wrist stress — preferred over close-grip straight bar for comfort
execution.range_of_motion_guidance: Full extension to full flexion.
coaching_cues: Long head focus — feel the stretch at the bottom
Elbows stay at the sides
Squeeze at the top

name: Close-Grip Incline Barbell Bench Press
description: An incline bench press with a narrow, shoulder-width grip that dramatically increases triceps long head involvement while still loading the clavicular pectoralis major. The incline angle lengthens the triceps long head, which crosses the shoulder joint, creating a potent position for triceps development. This variation is prized for simultaneously developing upper chest and triceps in a single heavy compound movement.

execution.starting_position: Lie on an incline bench (30–45 degrees). Grip the barbell at shoulder-width — this is narrow enough to be a close grip relative to a standard bench press grip. Unrack and hold above the upper chest.
execution.setup_instructions: Set incline to 30–45 degrees. The close grip should be shoulder-width, not inside-shoulder-width. Inside shoulder-width stresses the wrists excessively.
steps: Step 1: Unrack with a close grip, bar above the upper chest.
Step 2: Lower the bar toward the upper chest with elbows tracking relatively close to the body.
Step 3: Touch the upper chest gently and press immediately back to lockout.
Step 4: At lockout, the triceps are under significant tension — squeeze through full extension.
execution.breathing_instructions: Inhale before descent, exhale through the press.
common_mistakes: Grip too narrow — inside shoulder-width stresses wrists and reduces stability
Elbows flaring excessively — keep them roughly 45 degrees from the torso
Not pressing to full lockout — the triceps benefit requires complete extension
safety_considerations: Use a spotter for heavier loads
Avoid grip inside shoulder-width due to wrist discomfort risk
The incline creates a longer moment arm on the shoulder — do not use ego weight
execution.range_of_motion_guidance: Full range from upper chest to complete elbow lockout.
coaching_cues: Tuck the elbows — the close grip is not a reason to flare
Drive through the lockout — the triceps long head works hardest in the extended position

name: Close-Grip Lat Pulldown
description: The close-grip lat pulldown uses a V-bar or narrow handle attachment that positions the elbows close to the torso during the pull. This grip allows a greater range of elbow travel and places substantial load on the biceps alongside the lats, making it a preferred variation for lifters seeking combined lat and biceps development or for those transitioning toward chin-up proficiency.

execution.starting_position: Sit at a lat pulldown machine and attach a V-bar or close-grip handle. Adjust the thigh pad to secure the legs. Grasp the handle with a neutral grip and extend the arms fully overhead, allowing the lats to stretch.
execution.setup_instructions: Attach a V-bar or close-grip handle to the lat pulldown machine pulley. Set an appropriate weight. Secure thighs under the pad.
steps: Step 1: Begin seated with arms fully extended overhead, lats on stretch.
Step 2: Depress the shoulder blades and initiate the pull by driving the elbows down toward the hips.
Step 3: Pull the bar toward the upper chest, bringing the elbows close to the sides of the torso.
Step 4: At the bottom, squeeze the lats and hold briefly.
Step 5: Return slowly to full arm extension, maintaining scapular control.
execution.breathing_instructions: Exhale as you pull the bar down. Inhale as you return to the starting position.
common_mistakes: Leaning back excessively, which turns the movement into a partial row
Pulling the bar behind the head, which stresses the cervical spine
Using momentum by rocking the torso
safety_considerations: Never pull behind the head — always pull to the front of the chest
Maintain a neutral or slightly arched lumbar spine throughout
execution.range_of_motion_guidance: Full extension at the top to the bar reaching the upper chest at the bottom.
coaching_cues: Lead with the elbows, not the hands
Think 'elbows to ribs' and they will naturally come to the right position
Let your chest rise slightly to meet the bar at the bottom

name: Close-Grip Neutral T-Bar Row
description: The close-grip neutral T-bar row uses a parallel/neutral grip with hands close together, allowing the elbows to track tightly alongside the torso for maximum lat engagement. The neutral wrist position is comfortable for most trainees and reduces forearm fatigue, allowing greater lat-focused loading than pronated or supinated alternatives.

execution.starting_position: Straddle the T-bar machine. Grip the V-handle or close neutral-grip attachment. Hinge to 45-60 degrees, arms extended.
execution.setup_instructions: Set chest pad to allow full arm extension at the bottom. Keep feet straddling the bar, slightly wider than hip width.
steps: Step 1: Begin hinged with arms fully extended holding the V-handle.
Step 2: Drive elbows back alongside the torso.
Step 3: Row until elbows are past the torso level.
Step 4: Hold 1 second at the top.
Step 5: Lower under control to full extension.
execution.breathing_instructions: Exhale on the row. Inhale descending.
common_mistakes: Elbows flaring wide — keep them tucked for lat emphasis
Excessive torso bounce — control the torso angle throughout
safety_considerations: Maintain neutral lumbar spine — do not hyperextend at the top
Use straps if grip limits lat training volume
execution.range_of_motion_guidance: Full arm extension to elbows past torso level.
coaching_cues: Elbows hugging the ribs on the way up
Lead with the elbows, not the hands
Feel the lats at the bottom stretch

name: Close-Grip Push-Up
description: The close-grip push-up is a push-up variation where the hands are placed directly beneath the shoulders or slightly closer together than a standard push-up. The reduced hand spacing shifts the mechanical advantage toward the triceps brachii while maintaining significant pectoral involvement. It is easier than the diamond push-up but more tricep-focused than the standard push-up.

execution.starting_position: Begin in a plank position with hands placed directly beneath or slightly inside the shoulders. Fingers point forward. Body forms a straight line from head to heels.
execution.setup_instructions: No equipment required. Use a mat for wrist comfort if needed.
steps: Step 1: Position hands shoulder-width or slightly narrower, directly under or slightly inside the shoulders.
Step 2: Hold a rigid plank body position with core engaged.
Step 3: Inhale and lower the chest toward the hands by bending the elbows, which track close to the sides of the torso.
Step 4: Pause at the bottom, then exhale and press back to the top.
execution.breathing_instructions: Inhale on the descent; exhale on the press.
common_mistakes: Flaring the elbows wide, which shifts the exercise back to a standard push-up
Letting hips sag or rise
safety_considerations: If wrist discomfort occurs, use push-up handles or rotate hands slightly outward
execution.range_of_motion_guidance: Full range from near chest-to-floor to full arm extension.
coaching_cues: Keep the elbows tracking along the sides of the torso like train tracks
Think 'elbows in' on the descent

name: Close-Grip Push-Up with Hand Deficit
description: A close-grip push-up with hands on elevated platforms, allowing the chest to descend below hand level for greater range of motion. The deficit increases the stretch on the triceps and chest at the bottom position, increasing overall training effect.

execution.starting_position: Set up for Close-Grip Push-Up with Hand Deficit in the appropriate position.
execution.setup_instructions: Prepare equipment and body position for Close-Grip Push-Up with Hand Deficit.
steps: Step 1: Place hands close together on two equal platforms. Extend body to push-up position.
Step 2: Lower chest below hands taking advantage of full depth.
Step 3: Hold briefly at bottom to eliminate elastic rebound.
Step 4: Press back to full extension.
execution.breathing_instructions: Exhale during the exertion phase, inhale during the return.
common_mistakes: Hands too close causing wrist pain
Piking hips to avoid depth
safety_considerations: Keep joints aligned throughout the movement.
Use controlled weight appropriate for skill level.
execution.range_of_motion_guidance: Move through full range of motion without compromising joint integrity.
coaching_cues: Hands inside shoulder width
Get full depth at the bottom

name: Close-Grip Push-Up with Pause (Chain Weighted)
description: A close-grip push-up performed with chains draped over the back for added resistance, combined with a pause at the bottom for increased time under tension. The pause eliminates elastic energy storage and demands pure tricep and chest strength to initiate the push.

execution.starting_position: Set up for Close-Grip Push-Up with Pause (Chain Weighted) in the appropriate position.
execution.setup_instructions: Prepare equipment and body position for Close-Grip Push-Up with Pause (Chain Weighted).
steps: Step 1: Drape chains over upper back. Set up close-grip push-up position.
Step 2: Lower body to floor maintaining close hand position.
Step 3: Hold chest position for 2-3 seconds at bottom.
Step 4: Press explosively back to top position.
execution.breathing_instructions: Exhale during the exertion phase, inhale during the return.
common_mistakes: Losing chain placement mid-set
Lifting hips during pause
safety_considerations: Keep joints aligned throughout the movement.
Use controlled weight appropriate for skill level.
execution.range_of_motion_guidance: Move through full range of motion without compromising joint integrity.
coaching_cues: Full pause with no bouncing
Chains should stay across shoulder blades

name: Cobra Push-Up
description: The cobra push-up begins in a downward-dog position and dips the body forward in a sweeping arc until the chest is near the floor, then extends the spine into a cobra-like backbend. This movement trains the chest at the bottom of the arc while also opening the thoracic spine, shoulders, and hip flexors through a full-body coordinated motion.

execution.starting_position: Begin in a downward-facing dog position: hips high, arms and legs straight, forming an inverted V with the body.
execution.setup_instructions: No equipment needed. Clear enough floor space for a full-body extended position.
steps: Step 1: Start in a downward-dog position with hips elevated.
Step 2: Bend the elbows and dip the head and chest forward and down toward the floor in a sweeping arc.
Step 3: As the chest passes between the hands, begin extending the elbows and driving the hips toward the floor.
Step 4: Fully extend the arms and open the chest upward into a cobra or upward-dog back extension.
Step 5: Reverse the motion or return to the downward-dog position to complete one rep.
execution.breathing_instructions: Exhale as you dip forward and down. Inhale as you extend up into the cobra position.
common_mistakes: Skipping the arc and just doing an up-down movement
Letting the hips touch the floor during the dip phase
Not opening the chest fully at the top
safety_considerations: Avoid if you have lumbar spine issues — the cobra extension loads the low back
Warm up wrists and shoulders before performing
Progress from a modified version if thoracic mobility is limited
execution.range_of_motion_guidance: The dip phase brings the chest close to the floor between the hands. The cobra phase extends fully overhead without letting the hips touch down.
coaching_cues: Dive down through the arms, not straight into the floor
Open the chest to the sky at the top
Think about drawing a 'U' shape with your body

name: Concentration Curl
description: The concentration curl is a seated, single-arm curl performed with the elbow braced against the inner thigh, completely eliminating swinging and momentum. This isolation technique concentrates all the load directly on the biceps brachii, particularly the short head, and allows strong peak contraction at the top of the movement. It is one of the most effective exercises for isolating the biceps muscle.

execution.starting_position: Sit on the edge of a flat bench, feet flat on the floor, spread wider than hip-width. Hold a dumbbell in one hand and brace the back of the upper arm against the inner thigh on the same side. Arm is extended downward.
execution.setup_instructions: Sit with feet wide apart. Use a dumbbell light enough to perform with strict form. The key is brace the elbow against the inner thigh.
steps: Step 1: Sit on the bench, feet wide. Hold a dumbbell in one hand, upper arm pressed firmly against the inner thigh.
Step 2: Begin with the arm fully extended toward the floor, palm facing up.
Step 3: Exhale and curl the dumbbell upward by bending the elbow, keeping the upper arm stationary against the thigh.
Step 4: Curl until the forearm is roughly vertical; hold the peak contraction for 1 second, then inhale and lower slowly.
execution.breathing_instructions: Exhale on the curl up; inhale on the controlled descent.
common_mistakes: Letting the elbow drift away from the thigh, which removes the isolation
Swinging the torso to assist the curl at the bottom
safety_considerations: Full extension at the bottom ensures maximum bicep stretch — do not limit ROM
execution.range_of_motion_guidance: Full extension at the bottom to full curl at the top — the forearm stops near vertical.
coaching_cues: Pin the elbow to the inner thigh and do not let it move
Think about bringing your pinky to your shoulder at the top to maximize short head contraction

name: Converging Plate-Loaded Chest Press
description: The Converging Plate-Loaded Chest Press uses an independent-arm machine where each handle moves in a converging arc (the arms come together as they extend forward), mimicking the natural adduction component of the pectoral contraction. The plate-loaded design allows greater load than selectorized machines and the converging motion provides superior pectoral peak contraction.

execution.starting_position: Load the machine with weight plates. Sit with back against the pad and grip the handles at chest level.
execution.setup_instructions: Adjust the seat height so handles align with the mid-chest. Load plates evenly on each side. Use the starting pin to bring handles to the starting position if provided.
steps: Step 1: Grip both handles and press forward, allowing the arms to naturally converge toward the midline.
Step 2: Fully extend the arms and squeeze the chest as the handles come together.
Step 3: Return under control, allowing the arms to diverge back to the starting position.
Step 4: Repeat without letting the weight stack touch at the bottom.
execution.breathing_instructions: Exhale as you press and handles converge. Inhale as you return.
common_mistakes: Letting the weight stack slam at the bottom
Not squeezing the chest at peak contraction when arms converge
safety_considerations: Load plates evenly — imbalanced loading creates asymmetric movement
Use the starting pin to control the entry and exit safely under heavy loads
execution.range_of_motion_guidance: Full arm extension and convergence at front; return to full stretch of pectorals at back.
coaching_cues: Let the arms come together at the top — squeeze the pecs hard
Control the return — feel the stretch

name: Copenhagen Adduction
description: The Copenhagen adduction exercise is a high-load hip adductor strengthening exercise performed in a side-plank position with the top foot supported on a bench or partner. The bottom leg performs adduction to lift the body or hold isometrically. It produces very high adductor longus forces compared to other adductor exercises, making it effective for groin injury prevention and rehabilitation of adductor strains. Research has demonstrated its effectiveness in reducing groin injury rates in football players.

execution.starting_position: Lie on one side on the floor. Support the upper body on the forearm. Rest the top foot on a bench or box at hip height. The bottom leg is free below the bench.
execution.setup_instructions: Use a bench or plyo box at hip height. Begin with the isometric hold version before progressing to the dynamic version.
steps: Step 1: Lie on your side with forearm on the floor. Rest the top foot on a bench at hip height.
Step 2: The bottom leg hangs freely below the bench level.
Step 3: Lift the bottom leg up to meet the top leg, using the inner thigh (adductors) of the bottom leg.
Step 4: Hold the lifted position for 2 seconds.
Step 5: Lower the bottom leg slowly with control. Complete reps on one side, then switch.
execution.breathing_instructions: Exhale as the bottom leg lifts. Inhale on the return.
common_mistakes: Using momentum or hip flexion rather than pure adduction
Not controlling the eccentric — the lowering phase is where the injury-prevention benefit occurs
Bench set too high, which reduces the adductor load
safety_considerations: High load exercise — begin with isometric holds before the dynamic version
In acute adductor strain, start very conservatively and progress by clinical guidance
execution.range_of_motion_guidance: Lift the bottom leg from hanging below the bench to meeting the top leg. The key is the eccentric control on the way down.
execution.tempo_recommendations: 2-second lift, 2-second hold, 3-second lower. 8–12 reps × 2–3 sets per side.
coaching_cues: Focus on the slow, controlled lowering — that is the key training stimulus
Do not let the bottom leg just drop
Think about squeezing the inner thighs together

name: Copenhagen Plank
description: The Copenhagen plank is an advanced side plank variation in which the top leg is supported on a bench or box while the bottom leg hangs or is adducted upward. It is one of the most effective exercises for training the hip adductors under a high-force isometric demand while simultaneously loading the lateral core. Research has demonstrated its effectiveness in both adductor strengthening and groin injury prevention in sports athletes.

execution.starting_position: Position a flat bench alongside you. Rest the top ankle or shin on the bench edge in a side plank position with the forearm on the floor. The bottom leg hangs beneath the bench.
execution.setup_instructions: Set a bench at a height that challenges the adductors — typically 40–50 cm. The top leg should be supported at the ankle for maximum leverage.
steps: Step 1: Set up with the top ankle or shin on the bench, bottom forearm on the floor, and body in a straight side-plank line.
Step 2: Drive the top leg down into the bench and simultaneously lift the hips off the floor to form a straight plank line.
Step 3: The bottom leg can either hang (supported hold) or be lifted to meet the top leg (dynamic version).
Step 4: Hold the position with hips fully extended and body in a straight line.
Step 5: Lower with control. Perform equal sets on each side.
execution.breathing_instructions: Breathe shallowly and continuously during the hold.
common_mistakes: Allowing the hips to drop, reducing adductor tension
Rotating the torso forward or backward
Using the ankle — placing the foot on the bench instead of the ankle/shin reduces adductor leverage
safety_considerations: Groin soreness in the days following initial training is normal — progress load conservatively.
If experiencing groin pain, regress to a short-lever Copenhagen plank with the knee on the bench.
execution.range_of_motion_guidance: Full isometric hold with hips elevated and body straight. Progress from short-lever (knee on bench) to long-lever (ankle on bench).
execution.tempo_recommendations: Hold for 10–30 seconds. Progress duration before adding dynamic repetitions.
coaching_cues: Drive the top leg into the bench
Keep your hips tall — no sagging
Straight line from shoulder to ankle

name: Copenhagen Plank with Hip Dip
description: A Copenhagen plank variation where the top hip is slowly lowered toward the floor and raised back up in a controlled arc. This adds a strength-endurance element to the isometric hold, targeting the adductors and lateral core through a range of motion rather than statically.

execution.starting_position: Set up for Copenhagen Plank with Hip Dip in proper position.
execution.setup_instructions: Prepare body and equipment for Copenhagen Plank with Hip Dip.
steps: Step 1: Set up Copenhagen plank with top foot on bench, bottom foot free.
Step 2: Raise body into full side plank position, bottom foot off floor.
Step 3: Slowly lower hip toward floor in a controlled arc.
Step 4: Drive hip back up to full plank height.
execution.breathing_instructions: Breathe steadily; never hold breath during static holds.
common_mistakes: Dropping hip uncontrolled
Letting shoulder collapse
safety_considerations: Build prerequisite strength before attempting advanced variations.
Stop if joint pain occurs.
execution.range_of_motion_guidance: Full range of motion with control at all times.
coaching_cues: Full controlled range of motion
Bottom foot can be used for balance assistance

name: Corner T-Bar Row
description: The corner T-bar row wedges one end of a standard barbell into a corner of a room rather than using a landmine unit, creating an improvised pivot point. The lifter straddles the bar and rows the loaded end with both hands using a V-handle or towel grip. It is functionally identical to a landmine T-bar row and allows heavy bilateral back training without specialized equipment.

execution.starting_position: Wedge the collar end of a barbell into a padded corner (use a folded mat to protect the wall). Load weight on the other end. Stand straddling the bar, hinge at the hips to 45 degrees, grasp the bar end with both hands or a V-handle.
execution.setup_instructions: Pad the corner generously to prevent wall damage. Keep feet hip to shoulder width apart, straddling the bar. A towel looped around the bar makes a bilateral grip possible without a handle attachment.
steps: Step 1: Hinge at the hips and grip the bar end.
Step 2: Depress and retract the shoulder blades.
Step 3: Row the bar end toward the sternum by driving elbows back.
Step 4: Squeeze at the top for 1 second.
Step 5: Lower under control to arm extension.
execution.breathing_instructions: Exhale on the row. Inhale on the descent.
common_mistakes: Rounding the lower back under heavy loads — brace harder
Letting the bar slip in the corner — ensure adequate padding and angle
safety_considerations: The corner must be solid and padded — a slipping bar can be dangerous
Keep a collar on the loaded end to prevent plates sliding off
execution.range_of_motion_guidance: Full arm extension to elbows behind torso.
coaching_cues: Drive the elbows high and back
Keep the bar path tight to the body
Maintain flat back throughout

name: Cossack Squat / Weighted Lateral Squat
description: The Cossack squat is a deep lateral squatting pattern where the lifter shifts their weight to one side, bending that knee deeply while keeping the opposite leg straight with the foot flat on the floor. It simultaneously trains hip flexion, knee flexion, and hip adductor flexibility on the extended leg, making it both a strength and mobility exercise. The movement can be loaded with a kettlebell or dumbbell held at the chest.

execution.starting_position: Stand with feet approximately 1.5-2 times shoulder-width apart, toes pointed forward or slightly outward. Hold a kettlebell or dumbbell at chest height if loading.
execution.setup_instructions: Begin with bodyweight to assess hip mobility. Add load only when you can reach depth with control.
steps: Step 1: Shift your weight to one side, bending that knee and hip while keeping the opposite leg straight.
Step 2: Continue descending until the bent knee is fully flexed and the hip is as low as comfortable.
Step 3: Keep the foot of the working leg fully flat on the floor. The straight leg's heel may rise slightly.
Step 4: Drive through the working heel to return to standing, then shift to the opposite side.
execution.breathing_instructions: Inhale as you descend, exhale as you drive back to standing.
common_mistakes: Heel of working leg lifting off the floor
Insufficient adductor flexibility causing the straight leg to bend
Rounding the lower back at the bottom
safety_considerations: High demand on hip and groin flexibility — warm up thoroughly
Do not force depth beyond your current flexibility
execution.range_of_motion_guidance: Work to the deepest depth where you can maintain a flat foot and straight opposite leg.
coaching_cues: Foot flat, heel down on working side
Sit into the hip
Keep the chest up

name: Barbell Cossack Squat
description: A barbell-loaded version of the cossack squat, a lateral squat pattern that trains unilateral quad and hip strength through a large range of lateral motion. The loaded version increases mechanical demand on the working leg's quad, adductor, and glute while also training hip mobility under load.

execution.starting_position: Position a barbell on your upper back as for a back squat. Stand with feet significantly wider than shoulder width.
execution.setup_instructions: Set up the barbell in a rack to the correct height for a back squat. Unrack and walk out to a wide stance.
steps: Step 1: Shift your weight to one side, bending that knee deeply while keeping the opposite leg straight.
Step 2: Lower yourself into a full lateral squat on the working side, keeping the working foot fully flat.
Step 3: The straight leg remains extended on the floor with the toes pointing up or slightly outward.
Step 4: Drive through the working leg heel to return to the center and repeat on the opposite side.
execution.breathing_instructions: Inhale on the descent. Exhale on the drive to center.
common_mistakes: Allowing the working heel to lift off the floor
Collapsing the torso forward excessively
safety_considerations: Ensure adequate hip mobility before loading — practice the bodyweight version first
Keep the bar securely on the upper back
execution.range_of_motion_guidance: Deep lateral squat with the working thigh well below parallel. Opposite leg extended.
coaching_cues: Foot stays flat on the working side
Sit into the hip of the working leg

name: Cossack Squat with Kettlebell Counterbalance
description: A cossack squat performed holding a kettlebell at chest height (goblet position) as a counterbalance. The forward weight of the kettlebell acts as a counterbalance, allowing a more upright torso and deeper squat depth than the unloaded version for many people. This makes the goblet cossack an effective teaching tool for those who lack the mobility to perform an upright unloaded cossack squat, while simultaneously providing a strength stimulus for the deep lateral squat pattern.

execution.starting_position: Hold a kettlebell at chest height in the goblet position (bell up, hands around the horns, elbows pointing down). Stand with feet 2-2.5 times shoulder-width, toes slightly out.
execution.setup_instructions: Choose a kettlebell that is light enough to hold comfortably at chest for the duration of the exercise. 8-16 kg is typical for most users.
steps: Step 1: Hold the kettlebell at chest height. Shift weight to the right and descend into the right cossack squat, keeping the kettlebell at chest level.
Step 2: At the bottom, the kettlebell helps keep the torso upright by acting as a counterbalance.
Step 3: Hold the bottom position for 3-5 seconds, feeling the deep adductor and glute stretch.
Step 4: Drive through the right foot to shift to the left side, descending into the left cossack. Alternate sides in a continuous flow.
execution.breathing_instructions: Exhale as you descend. Breathe at the bottom. Inhale as you transition through center.
common_mistakes: Letting the kettlebell drift too far forward (pressing it rather than holding it at chest)
Heel of the squatting leg lifting off the floor — the counterbalance should help prevent this
Moving too quickly without pausing at the bottom of each side
safety_considerations: If the goblet hold creates shoulder discomfort, switch to the unloaded cossack or the overhead plate version
Start with a lighter kettlebell to feel the counterbalance effect before increasing load
execution.range_of_motion_guidance: Full depth lateral squat with heel flat. The kettlebell counterbalance should allow greater depth than unloaded.
coaching_cues: Let the kettlebell pull you upright — do not fight it
Drive the squat heel into the floor
Feel deeper into the stretch at the bottom than you can in the unloaded version

name: Cossack Squat Mobility Flow
description: A dynamic hip and ankle mobility flow based on the Cossack squat pattern. The exerciser moves continuously from side to side in deep lateral squats, spending time at the bottom of each position to load the hip into adduction and the ankle into dorsiflexion. This flowing version covers more ground than a static stretch and trains hip mobility through its full adduction and external rotation range simultaneously, making it valuable for dancers, martial artists, and anyone addressing hip mobility deficits.

execution.starting_position: Stand with feet approximately 2-2.5 times shoulder-width apart and toes pointed slightly outward.
execution.setup_instructions: Wear flat-soled shoes or perform barefoot. Have a wall or pole available for balance assistance during learning.
steps: Step 1: Shift your weight to the right side and bend the right knee deeply, lowering your hips toward the floor on the right side.
Step 2: At the bottom of the right Cossack squat, the left leg is fully extended with the left foot flat or heel up.
Step 3: Hold the right bottom position for 3-5 seconds.
Step 4: Transition through the center by rising slightly, then shift weight to the left and descend into the left Cossack squat. Hold 3-5 seconds. Continue flowing side to side.
execution.breathing_instructions: Exhale as you descend into each side. Breathe deeply at the bottom position. Inhale as you transition through center.
common_mistakes: Lifting the heel of the squatting side — work on ankle dorsiflexion if this occurs
Leaning excessively forward with the torso
Rushing through the transition without pausing at the bottom of each side
safety_considerations: Avoid if you have acute hip labral tears or medial knee pain with deep adductor loading
Begin with a reduced depth and wider foot position if hip or ankle mobility is limited
execution.range_of_motion_guidance: Descend as deep as the hip and ankle allow while maintaining the heel on the floor.
execution.tempo_recommendations: 3-5s hold at each bottom position. Slow controlled transitions through center.
coaching_cues: Keep the squatting heel down — this is the primary mobility goal
Let the hip open at the bottom — feel the deep groin stretch
Transition slowly — the value is at the bottom, not in the movement

name: Cossack Squat with Overhead Plate
description: A loaded cossack squat performed with a weight plate held overhead. The overhead position shifts the center of mass upward and forward, demanding more thoracic extension, shoulder stability, and ankle dorsiflexion than the unloaded version. The combined demands of deep lateral hip mobility (cossack) with overhead stability create a full-body mobility and strength stimulus. Used in advanced mobility programming, weightlifting preparation, and functional strength development.

execution.starting_position: Stand with feet approximately 2-2.5 times shoulder-width apart, toes slightly out. Hold a weight plate (5-10 kg) overhead with arms fully extended.
execution.setup_instructions: Master the unloaded cossack squat before adding the overhead plate. Use a very light plate initially (5 kg or less) to feel the balance shift.
steps: Step 1: Begin standing with the plate overhead, arms extended, feet wide.
Step 2: Shift weight to the right, bending the right knee deeply into the cossack squat position while keeping the plate overhead.
Step 3: Keep the squat heel flat, chest up, and plate directly overhead (not in front).
