Step 4: Drive through the right foot to transition through center, then descend to the left side. Alternate sides in a flowing pattern.
execution.breathing_instructions: Exhale as you descend into the squat. Inhale as you rise through center.
common_mistakes: Letting the plate drift forward rather than staying directly overhead — this causes forward torso lean
Heel of the squatting side lifting — work on ankle mobility if this occurs
Using too heavy a plate before the movement pattern is solid
safety_considerations: Only add the overhead component after the unloaded cossack squat is mastered
Avoid if shoulder mobility prevents a true overhead lockout — the plate must be directly overhead, not in front
execution.range_of_motion_guidance: Full depth cossack squat with the heel flat and the plate locked overhead.
execution.tempo_recommendations: 3-5s hold at each bottom position. Slow controlled transitions.
coaching_cues: Keep the plate directly overhead — if it drifts forward, the torso will too
Drive the squat heel into the floor — heel down at all costs
Feel the stretch from the inner thigh to the outer shoulder on each side

name: Couch Stretch
alternative_names: Rear Foot Elevated Hip Flexor Stretch
description: The couch stretch is an aggressive hip flexor and quadriceps stretch performed with the rear foot elevated against a wall, couch, or rack, placing the hip into deep extension and the knee into deep flexion simultaneously. This creates maximal lengthening of the iliopsoas, rectus femoris, and other quad muscles and is considered one of the most effective stretches for hip flexor mobility. It is particularly valued for addressing the stiffness that develops from repeated squatting and from prolonged sitting.

execution.starting_position: Kneel near a wall or couch. Place the rear shin and foot against the wall so the ankle is against the baseboard and the knee is on the floor just in front of the wall.
execution.setup_instructions: Use a mat under the rear knee. Start close enough to the wall so the shin rests flat against it. Use a couch, wall, or rack upright as the foot support.
steps: Step 1: Place the rear shin flat against the wall, knee close to the base of the wall.
Step 2: Step the front foot forward into a lunge position with front foot flat on the floor.
Step 3: Squeeze the glute of the rear leg and tuck the pelvis posteriorly — this is the key technique point.
Step 4: Bring the torso upright as tolerated. The more upright the torso, the more intense the hip flexor stretch.
Step 5: Hold 60–120 seconds per side.
execution.breathing_instructions: Breathe deeply and steadily. The sensation should be intense but tolerable.
common_mistakes: Not squeezing the glute of the rear leg — this is essential for maximizing the iliopsoas stretch
Anterior pelvic tilt rather than posterior tilt, which decreases the stretch
Being too far from the wall so the shin angle is insufficient
safety_considerations: Knee discomfort under the rear knee is common — use padding
The intensity of this stretch can be very high — start with 20–30 seconds and build tolerance progressively
execution.range_of_motion_guidance: Work toward an upright torso with the rear shin fully against the wall. This is a very advanced position for many people.
coaching_cues: Squeeze the glute of the leg with the foot on the wall
Tuck the tailbone under — do not arch the lower back
Breathe through the tension

name: Crawling Pattern
description: The crawling pattern is a broad category of contralateral ground locomotion exercises performed close to the floor, including variations such as the leopard crawl, army crawl, and lateral crawl. All variations emphasize the same neurological contralateral coordination pattern as the bear crawl but with the torso positioned lower to the ground, further increasing the demands on shoulder stability, hip flexor engagement, and spinal control in a more mechanically challenging position.

execution.starting_position: Begin in a low plank or prone position depending on variation. For leopard crawl: in a low quadruped close to the floor.
execution.setup_instructions: No equipment required. Adequate clean floor space for crawling distance. Consider knee pads on hard surfaces.
steps: Step 1: Begin in the low quadruped position with the body close to the floor.
Step 2: Move contralaterally — right hand and left foot advance simultaneously.
Step 3: Keep the torso parallel to and close to the floor throughout.
Step 4: Continue forward for the prescribed distance, maintaining body position.
Step 5: Can also be performed laterally, backward, or in combination patterns.
execution.breathing_instructions: Breathe continuously. The low position can restrict breathing — keep breaths controlled.
common_mistakes: Rising too high — the body should stay low to the floor
Moving ipsilateral limbs — the contralateral pattern is essential
Letting the core sag and hips drop to the floor
safety_considerations: Floor hygiene is relevant for direct skin contact in army-crawl variants.
High hip flexor and shoulder demand — progress gradually.
execution.range_of_motion_guidance: Full forward reach on each step. Body remains consistently close to the floor.
execution.tempo_recommendations: 10–20 meters per set. Quality of movement over speed.
coaching_cues: Stay low — belly close to the floor
Opposite arm and leg
Breathe through the movement

name: Cross-Body Cable Tricep Extension
description: The cross-body cable extension uses a cable set at shoulder height on one side while the lifter stands facing away or perpendicular, extending the arm across the body in a diagonal path. The cross-body path creates a unique torque on the tricep and allows the elbow to travel through a wider arc than standard pushdowns. It is an excellent cable tricep variation for targeting the lateral and medial heads with constant tension.

execution.starting_position: Attach a single handle to a high cable on one side. Stand perpendicular to the cable or facing away from the cable on the same side. Grasp the handle with the near hand, elbow bent.
execution.setup_instructions: The arm extends diagonally across the body — the cable should pull from the side, not from above.
steps: Step 1: Begin with the elbow bent and the handle near the shoulder.
Step 2: Extend the elbow, pressing the handle diagonally across and downward.
Step 3: Hold at full extension for one second.
Step 4: Return with control to the bent position.
execution.breathing_instructions: Exhale on extension, inhale on return.
common_mistakes: Using the shoulder to push rather than tricep extension
Torso rotating
safety_considerations: Keep the shoulder stable — only the elbow joint moves
execution.range_of_motion_guidance: Full elbow flexion to full extension.
coaching_cues: Extension only — don't rotate
Squeeze at lockout
Upper arm stays still

name: Cross-Body Dual Cable Lat Pulldown
description: The cross-body dual cable pulldown uses both sides of a functional trainer simultaneously, with each hand pulling the opposite cable downward in a crossing motion. This arrangement places the lats under constant tension through a rotational arc and challenges the core's rotational stability. The crossed cable path provides a unique contraction angle not replicable with straight-down pulldown machines.

execution.starting_position: Set both pulleys on a dual cable machine to the highest position. Attach single handles to each. Stand in the center and reach up to grip the handles — right hand grips the left cable, left hand grips the right cable.
execution.setup_instructions: Set both sides to equal weight. Stand centered between the cable columns with arms crossed and extended overhead.
steps: Step 1: Stand between the cable columns holding crossed handles, arms fully extended overhead.
Step 2: Brace the core and maintain a slight forward lean.
Step 3: Simultaneously pull both handles downward and inward, drawing the elbows to the sides of the torso.
Step 4: At the bottom, hands finish near the hips with lats fully contracted.
Step 5: Slowly return both arms to the overhead crossed start position.
execution.breathing_instructions: Exhale on the pull, inhale on the return.
common_mistakes: Using momentum or rocking to initiate the pull
Not controlling the return phase, losing lat engagement
safety_considerations: Start with light weight to learn the coordination pattern
Ensure both cable sides are set to equal weights
execution.range_of_motion_guidance: Full overhead extension at the start to arms at sides with lats contracted at the finish.
coaching_cues: Pull elbows to your sides
Squeeze lats hard at the bottom
Control the return slowly

name: Cross-Body Dumbbell Triceps Extension
description: A unique triceps isolation movement where a dumbbell is lowered across the body to the opposite shoulder. This creates a distinctive stretch on the triceps long head from an oblique angle. The movement offers a different stimulus than standard overhead extensions.

execution.starting_position: Set up for Cross-Body Dumbbell Triceps Extension in the appropriate position.
execution.setup_instructions: Prepare equipment and body position for Cross-Body Dumbbell Triceps Extension.
steps: Step 1: Lie on bench holding one dumbbell with arm extended toward ceiling.
Step 2: Bend elbow to lower dumbbell across body toward opposite shoulder.
Step 3: Lower until forearm is parallel to floor or slight stretch is felt.
Step 4: Extend arm back to straight position above chest.
execution.breathing_instructions: Exhale during the exertion phase, inhale during the return.
common_mistakes: Moving shoulder joint instead of elbow
Excessive cross-body rotation
safety_considerations: Keep joints aligned throughout the movement.
Use controlled weight appropriate for skill level.
execution.range_of_motion_guidance: Move through full range of motion without compromising joint integrity.
coaching_cues: Pivot at elbow only
Feel the cross-body stretch at the bottom

name: Cross-Body Hammer Curl
description: The cross-body hammer curl is performed by curling the dumbbell across the body toward the opposite shoulder rather than straight up. This altered path places more emphasis on the brachialis and brachioradialis than a standard hammer curl and allows the elbow to flex through a slightly longer arc. The alternating arm action also provides a brief rest between reps, allowing slightly more weight or reps per set.

execution.starting_position: Stand upright holding a dumbbell in each hand, arms at sides, neutral grip (palms facing the body).
execution.setup_instructions: Choose a moderate weight. Stand with feet hip-width, slight core brace.
steps: Step 1: Begin curling one dumbbell but direct it diagonally across the body toward the opposite shoulder.
Step 2: Curl until the dumbbell is near the opposite shoulder, maintaining neutral grip.
Step 3: Lower slowly back to the starting position.
Step 4: Alternate arms, curling the other dumbbell across the body.
execution.breathing_instructions: Exhale on each curl, inhale on each return.
common_mistakes: Rotating the grip to supination — keep it neutral
Using momentum by swinging the torso
Pulling too high
safety_considerations: Keep the shoulder down and relaxed
execution.range_of_motion_guidance: Full extension to opposite shoulder height.
coaching_cues: Neutral grip throughout
Curl to the opposite shoulder
No swing

name: Cross-Body Shoulder Stretch
description: The cross-body shoulder stretch targets the posterior shoulder capsule, posterior deltoid, and teres minor by drawing the arm across the body in horizontal adduction. It is one of the most effective and accessible stretches for the posterior shoulder structures, commonly used to manage shoulder impingement risk factors and improve internal rotation mobility. The key technique point is keeping the shoulder depressed and not elevated during the stretch.

execution.starting_position: Stand or sit upright. Bring one arm across the body at approximately shoulder height.
execution.setup_instructions: No equipment needed. This stretch can be done standing, seated, or lying down.
steps: Step 1: Raise one arm to shoulder height and reach it across the body horizontally.
Step 2: Use the opposite hand or forearm to gently press the extended arm closer to the chest.
Step 3: Keep the shoulder of the working arm pressed down — do not let it shrug toward the ear.
Step 4: Hold until a stretch is felt in the back of the shoulder — 30–60 seconds.
Step 5: Release and switch sides.
execution.breathing_instructions: Breathe slowly throughout the hold.
common_mistakes: Shrugging the shoulder during the stretch — depress and pack the shoulder first
Pulling too aggressively with the assisting hand
Flexing the elbow — keep the arm relatively straight for maximum tension on the posterior shoulder
safety_considerations: If acute shoulder pain is present, avoid and consult a clinician
The stretch should be felt in the back of the shoulder — if felt in the front or as a sharp pain, adjust or stop
execution.range_of_motion_guidance: Draw the arm across the body until a comfortable stretch is felt in the posterior shoulder.
coaching_cues: Press the shoulder blade down before you apply any pressure with the other hand
Feel the stretch in the back of your shoulder, not the top
Breathe wide

name: Cross-Cable Rear Delt Row
description: The cross-cable rear delt row uses a cable crossover station with the cables set at upper chest height and crossed (right hand grips left cable, left hand grips right cable). The crossed configuration creates a unique pulling vector that emphasizes horizontal abduction with an adducted scapular endpoint, maximally loading the posterior deltoid and rhomboids through the full range of motion. The cable tension remains constant through the entire pull — unlike dumbbells, which lose tension at the beginning of the movement.

execution.starting_position: Stand in the center of a cable crossover machine. Set both pulleys to upper chest height. Cross the cables — grip the right cable handle with the left hand and the left cable handle with the right hand. Arms extended forward at chest height.
execution.setup_instructions: Moderate weight on each stack. Stand with feet staggered slightly for balance.
steps: Step 1: Begin with arms extended forward, cables crossed at chest height.
Step 2: Pull both handles outward and back simultaneously, leading with the elbows.
Step 3: Keep the elbows at shoulder height through the entire pull.
Step 4: At the end of the row, the hands are out to the sides and the rear delts are fully contracted.
Step 5: Hold 1 second. Return under control.
execution.breathing_instructions: Exhale pulling back. Inhale returning.
common_mistakes: Elbows dropping below shoulder level — keep them at shoulder height throughout
Using torso rotation to generate momentum
safety_considerations: Moderate load — the constant cable tension accumulates quickly
Keep the core braced to avoid torso rotation
execution.range_of_motion_guidance: Full extension (cables crossed at chest) to full horizontal abduction (hands at sides).
coaching_cues: Elbows at shoulder height — not dropping
Pull apart like you're opening a door wide
Squeeze the rear delts at the endpoint

name: Crunch
description: The crunch is a foundational abdominal exercise that trains the rectus abdominis through a short-range trunk flexion movement. Unlike the sit-up, the crunch limits the range of motion to protect the lumbar spine, keeping the lower back on the floor and moving only the upper back and shoulders off the ground.

execution.starting_position: Lie on your back with knees bent and feet flat on the floor. Place hands lightly behind the head or crossed on the chest.
execution.setup_instructions: Keep the lower back in contact with the floor throughout. The movement range is short — only the upper back and shoulders come off the floor.
steps: Breathe out and curl the shoulders and upper back off the floor toward the knees.
Hold the top position briefly, squeezing the abdominals.
Lower under control back to the starting position.
execution.breathing_instructions: Exhale as you crunch up. Inhale on the descent.
common_mistakes: Pulling the neck with the hands
Using momentum by bouncing the head up
Raising the lower back off the floor
safety_considerations: If neck pain occurs, cross arms on chest instead of placing hands behind the head
execution.range_of_motion_guidance: Upper back and shoulders come 2–4 inches off the floor. Lower back remains in contact with the floor.
coaching_cues: Think about bringing your ribcage toward your pelvis — not your head toward your knees
Keep your neck neutral — do not lead with the chin

name: Cuban Press
description: The Cuban press is a three-phase shoulder exercise that combines an upright row, external rotation, and an overhead press in a single movement. It trains the full rotator cuff through a functional arc, particularly emphasizing the external rotators and infraspinatus. Originally developed for overhead athletes requiring rotator cuff health and shoulder mobility, the Cuban press is used both as a corrective exercise and as a warm-up for heavy overhead pressing sessions.

execution.starting_position: Stand holding dumbbells (or a barbell) at thigh level with an overhand grip.
execution.setup_instructions: Use very light weights — this is a technique and health exercise, not a strength movement. 2.5-10 lbs per dumbbell is typical.
steps: Step 1: Begin with dumbbells at the thighs.
Step 2: Upright row phase: raise the elbows up and out to bring the weights to shoulder height with elbows at 90 degrees and upper arms parallel to the floor.
Step 3: External rotation phase: rotate the forearms upward until forearms are vertical (elbows still at 90 degrees, now pointing up).
Step 4: Press phase: press the dumbbells overhead to full lockout.
Step 5: Reverse the motion through each phase back to the starting position.
execution.breathing_instructions: Breathe naturally — this is typically used for warm-up or corrective purposes.
common_mistakes: Using too much weight, which corrupts the rotation technique
Skipping the controlled return through all three phases
Rushing through the exercise without pausing at each transition
safety_considerations: This exercise should feel comfortable — any shoulder pain is a signal to stop and assess
execution.range_of_motion_guidance: Full upright row height, full external rotation, full overhead lockout — three distinct positions.
execution.tempo_recommendations: Slow and deliberate through each phase — no specific tempo beyond controlled execution
coaching_cues: Three distinct movements — row, rotate, press
Light weight — quality of motion matters
Reverse every phase on the way down

name: Curtsy Lunge
description: The curtsy lunge steps the rear foot behind and across the midline of the body, creating an adducted hip position that increases the demand on the gluteus medius and tensor fasciae latae of the working (front) leg. The crossed foot position forces the hip of the front leg to work in an abducted position against additional resistance, making this a particularly effective exercise for lateral hip development and glute medius targeting.

execution.starting_position: Stand with feet together, hands on hips or holding dumbbells at the sides.
execution.setup_instructions: No equipment needed for bodyweight version. Dumbbells add load. Perform slowly and with control, especially as a beginner.
steps: Step 1: Take a large step backward and across the midline with one foot — as though performing a curtsy.
Step 2: Lower the rear knee toward the floor while keeping the front knee tracking over the front foot.
Step 3: The front knee should track slightly to the outside as the hip of the front leg works against the adducted position of the rear foot.
Step 4: Drive through the front heel to return to standing.
Step 5: Alternate sides each rep.
execution.breathing_instructions: Inhale as you lower. Exhale as you return to standing.
common_mistakes: Not crossing the rear foot far enough across the midline, which reduces the glute medius emphasis
Allowing the front knee to cave inward
Placing excessive bodyweight on the rear toes instead of using the front leg
safety_considerations: The crossed position can stress the knee ligaments if the knee tracks medially — ensure the front knee stays in line with or outside the foot
Reduce stride width if balance is compromised
execution.range_of_motion_guidance: Rear knee descends to just above the floor. Front shin remains mostly vertical.
coaching_cues: Cross behind as if stepping over a low rope
Keep the front knee over the pinky toe
Drive up through the front foot

name: Cyclist Squat — Heel-Elevated Narrow Stance
description: The cyclist squat uses a narrow stance with significant heel elevation, achieved by placing the heels on plates or a wedge. This combination of foot positioning and heel elevation allows the knees to travel far forward, maximizing quadriceps recruitment while minimizing hip and glute involvement. The name reflects its popularity among cyclists and those seeking maximal quadriceps isolation.

execution.starting_position: Stand with heels elevated 2-4 inches on weight plates or a squat wedge. Feet hip-width or narrower, toes pointing forward or slightly out. Hold a dumbbell or kettlebell at the chest for resistance, or use a barbell on the back.
execution.setup_instructions: Position two weight plates flat on the floor for heel elevation. Ensure they are stable and will not shift. Begin with bodyweight or light load.
steps: Step 1: Stand tall, brace the core, and allow the knees to track forward over the toes.
Step 2: Bend the knees and squat down, letting the knees travel well past the toes due to the heel elevation.
Step 3: Descend until thighs are parallel or below, maintaining an upright torso.
Step 4: Drive through the heels (which are elevated) to extend the knees and return to the starting position.
execution.breathing_instructions: Inhale at the top, exhale on the drive up.
common_mistakes: Heels not elevated enough to allow knee travel
Allowing the torso to lean excessively forward
Insufficient depth, reducing quad stretch
safety_considerations: High patellar tendon load — progress gradually if you have knee sensitivity
Ensure heel elevation surface is stable
execution.range_of_motion_guidance: Aim for thighs parallel or below. The heel elevation enables much greater depth for most people.
execution.tempo_recommendations: 3-1-1-0 (slow descent, brief pause at bottom, controlled ascent)
coaching_cues: Knees forward over the toes
Sit tall, don't lean
Feel the quad stretch at the bottom

name: Dead Bug
description: The dead bug is an anti-extension core stability exercise performed supine. By alternately extending opposite arm and leg while maintaining a stable spine, it challenges the deep core musculature to resist lumbar extension. It is widely used in rehabilitation and athletic training for spinal stability and motor control development.

execution.starting_position: Lie on your back with arms extended toward the ceiling and knees bent at 90 degrees (tabletop position). Lower back is pressed flat into the floor.
execution.setup_instructions: Press the entire lower back into the floor before starting. This position must be maintained throughout each rep.
steps: Simultaneously extend the right arm backward toward the floor and extend the left leg forward toward the floor.
Lower both limbs as far as possible while maintaining the lower back pressed flat against the floor.
Return to the starting position and repeat on the opposite side.
execution.breathing_instructions: Exhale as you extend the limbs. Inhale as you return.
common_mistakes: Allowing the lower back to lift off the floor during the limb extension
Moving too fast — control is the purpose of this exercise
Extending same-side arm and leg instead of opposite
safety_considerations: This is a low-risk exercise appropriate for most populations including those with lower back issues
execution.range_of_motion_guidance: Extend as far as possible while the lower back remains flat on the floor.
coaching_cues: Push your lower back into the floor like you are pressing it through the earth
Move slowly — control every inch of the limb extension

name: Dead Bug with Band (Feet and Hands)
description: A dead bug progression using a resistance band looped around both feet and held by both hands. This creates a constant challenge to maintain tension while performing the alternating extension pattern. The band provides feedback for maintaining anti-extension throughout the movement.

execution.starting_position: Set up for Dead Bug with Band (Feet and Hands) in proper position.
execution.setup_instructions: Prepare body and equipment for Dead Bug with Band (Feet and Hands).
steps: Step 1: Lie on back. Loop band around feet. Hold band ends in hands.
Step 2: Raise legs to 90 degrees maintaining band tension.
Step 3: Extend one arm and opposite leg while keeping tension on band.
Step 4: Return and alternate sides.
execution.breathing_instructions: Breathe steadily; never hold breath during static holds.
common_mistakes: Losing band tension during extension
Lower back rising
safety_considerations: Build prerequisite strength before attempting advanced variations.
Stop if joint pain occurs.
execution.range_of_motion_guidance: Full range of motion with control at all times.
coaching_cues: Keep band taut throughout
Press lower back to floor always

name: Dead Bug
description: The dead bug is a supine core stability exercise that challenges the ability to maintain a neutral lumbar spine while simultaneously moving the opposite arm and leg. The key training stimulus is anti-extension — resisting the tendency of the lower back to arch away from the floor as the limbs extend. It is a preferred core exercise in lumbar rehabilitation because it allows full core engagement without spinal loading, making it appropriate in early recovery stages.

execution.starting_position: Lie on the back with the lower back pressed flat against the floor. Arms point straight toward the ceiling. Hips and knees are both bent to 90 degrees (tabletop position).
execution.setup_instructions: No equipment required. Use a mat.
steps: Step 1: Lie supine with arms vertical, hips and knees at 90 degrees (table-top).
Step 2: Take a deep breath in. On the exhale, brace the core hard and press the lower back firmly into the floor.
Step 3: Simultaneously lower the right arm overhead (toward the floor behind the head) and extend the left leg toward the floor.
Step 4: Lower as far as the lower back can remain flat on the floor — stop if the low back begins to arch.
Step 5: Return both limbs to the starting position on the next exhale. Switch sides.
execution.breathing_instructions: Exhale forcefully to brace before each limb extension. Breathe in at the top.
common_mistakes: Letting the lower back arch off the floor — this is the main error; range must be reduced if it occurs
Moving too fast and using momentum rather than deliberate control
Neck tension from trying to hold the head up — rest the head on the floor
safety_considerations: Safe for most low back pain patients — often one of the first exercises reintroduced
If pain increases during the movement, stop and consult a clinician
execution.range_of_motion_guidance: Full extension of the working arm and leg to just above the floor — only go as far as lumbar neutrality can be maintained.
execution.tempo_recommendations: 3-second lowering, 1-second pause near floor, 2-second return. 8–12 reps each side × 2–3 sets.
coaching_cues: Flatten your back into the floor before each movement
Move like you are lowering in slow motion
If your back lifts off the floor, only go halfway

name: Dead Bug with Arm/Leg Extension
description: The dead bug with arm and leg extension is a rehabilitation-originated core stability exercise in which the athlete lies supine with the lower back pressed flat, then alternately extends the opposite arm and leg toward the floor while resisting spinal rotation and lumbar extension. Unlike crunches, this exercise trains the core in its primary stabilization function — resisting motion while the limbs create destabilizing forces — making it highly transferable to athletic performance and injury prevention.

execution.starting_position: Lie on your back with the lower back pressed firmly to the floor. Arms extended vertically above the chest, hips and knees at 90 degrees (tabletop position for the legs).
execution.setup_instructions: Use a mat. The key is to feel the lower back pressing into the floor and to maintain this contact throughout the entire movement.
steps: Step 1: Begin in the starting position with arms vertical and legs in tabletop.
Step 2: Take a deep breath and brace the core by pushing the lower back into the floor.
Step 3: Simultaneously lower the right arm overhead toward the floor and extend the left leg, lowering the heel toward the floor.
Step 4: Move slowly and do not let the lower back arch away from the floor.
Step 5: Return to the starting position with control, then repeat on the opposite side.
execution.breathing_instructions: Exhale forcefully before each rep to engage the core. Breathe continuously but maintain the brace throughout the limb extension.
common_mistakes: Allowing the lower back to arch away from the floor as the limbs extend
Moving too fast — this is a slow, deliberate stability exercise
Extending the leg at the knee rather than lowering the entire leg as a unit
safety_considerations: If the lower back arches, reduce leg extension (do not fully straighten the leg or only lower the leg partway).
Appropriate for most populations including post-partum and those with lower back pain, when performed correctly.
execution.range_of_motion_guidance: Full extension means the extended leg is nearly parallel to the floor and the arm reaches fully overhead. Reduce range if lower back contact is lost.
execution.tempo_recommendations: 3–4 seconds per limb extension, 2 seconds to return. Slow and deliberate.
coaching_cues: Flatten your back into the floor — no gaps
Move like you are in slow motion
Opposite arm and leg extend together

name: Dead Bug with Weighted Plate
description: A weighted dead bug variation where a plate is held overhead to increase core demand. The load increases anti-extension and anti-rotation requirements. This builds practical core stability for movements that require overhead strength and spinal control simultaneously.

execution.starting_position: Set up for Dead Bug with Weighted Plate in proper position.
execution.setup_instructions: Prepare body and equipment for Dead Bug with Weighted Plate.
steps: Step 1: Lie on back holding plate overhead with arms straight.
Step 2: Raise legs to 90 degrees at hips and knees.
Step 3: Extend one arm back and opposite leg down simultaneously.
Step 4: Return and repeat on opposite side while maintaining plate overhead.
execution.breathing_instructions: Breathe steadily; never hold breath during static holds.
common_mistakes: Lower back lifting off floor
Moving arm holding plate
safety_considerations: Build prerequisite strength before attempting advanced variations.
Stop if joint pain occurs.
execution.range_of_motion_guidance: Full range of motion with control at all times.
coaching_cues: Keep lower back pressed to floor
Plate stays over chest throughout

name: Dead-Stop Dumbbell Row
description: The dead-stop dumbbell row involves lowering the dumbbell to the floor and coming to a complete pause before initiating the next repetition, eliminating all stretch reflex and momentum. This technique demands greater muscle activation at the initiation of each rep and is effective for building raw pulling strength and preventing the common tendency to bounce reps.

execution.starting_position: Set up in a standard dumbbell row stance — one knee and hand on a bench, the dumbbell on the floor directly beneath the working shoulder.
execution.setup_instructions: Use a hex dumbbell or place round dumbbells on plates so they rest stably on the floor. Ensure the bench is stable.
steps: Step 1: Lower the dumbbell fully to the floor from the previous rep or from the starting position.
Step 2: Release grip pressure momentarily — the dumbbell is resting on the floor.
Step 3: Re-grip the dumbbell firmly.
Step 4: Drive the elbow up and back, rowing the dumbbell to the hip.
Step 5: Lower under control to the floor and repeat.
execution.breathing_instructions: Inhale during the pause on the floor. Exhale forcefully on the row.
common_mistakes: Not actually pausing — touching and immediately lifting does not count as dead-stop
Releasing spinal tension during the floor pause — maintain position throughout
safety_considerations: Keep the spine neutral during the pause — do not round or extend excessively
Ensure the floor surface is flat and stable under the dumbbell
execution.range_of_motion_guidance: Full dead stop on floor to elbow above torso level.
execution.tempo_recommendations: 1s pause-1-1-2 (pause on floor, quick initiation, 2s lower)
coaching_cues: Full stop on the floor — no bounce, no cheat
Re-grip with intent before each rep
Explode from the floor each time

name: Deadlift
description: The conventional deadlift is a fundamental hip-hinge movement in which a loaded barbell is lifted from the floor to a standing position. It is the most effective exercise for overall posterior chain development, training the erector spinae, gluteus maximus, and hamstrings as primary movers while also demanding significant contribution from the upper back and quadriceps.

execution.starting_position: Stand with feet hip-width apart, toes pointing slightly outward. Place the barbell over your mid-foot, about 1 inch from your shins. Hinge at the hips and bend the knees to grip the bar just outside your legs.
execution.setup_instructions: Set the barbell on the floor with appropriate weight. Take either a double overhand or mixed grip. Push the floor away rather than thinking about pulling the bar up.
steps: Take a deep breath, brace your core hard, and create tension through your lats by imagining you are bending the bar around your legs.
Drive your feet through the floor to initiate the lift, keeping the bar in contact with your shins as it rises.
As the bar passes the knees, drive your hips forward and stand tall, squeezing your glutes at the top.
Lower the bar under control by hinging at the hips first, then bending the knees once the bar passes them.
execution.breathing_instructions: Take a full breath before each rep. Hold through the lift and exhale at the top after locking out. Use a Valsalva maneuver for heavy sets.
common_mistakes: Allowing the bar to drift away from the body, increasing lower back lever arm
Rounding the lower back under load — maintain a neutral spine
Jerking the bar off the floor rather than applying steady tension first
Hyperextending the lower back at lockout
safety_considerations: Never attempt a heavy deadlift without properly warming up the posterior chain
If lower back pain is present, reduce weight and focus on movement quality
Learn the hip-hinge pattern with a kettlebell or trap bar before loading heavily
execution.range_of_motion_guidance: Full range: bar starts on the floor, full hip and knee extension at lockout. Do not hyperextend at the top.
coaching_cues: Push the floor away — do not think about pulling the bar up
Keep your chest up and lats engaged throughout the entire pull
Squeeze your glutes hard at the top of each rep

name: Decline Barbell Bench Press
description: The decline barbell bench press is performed on a bench declined at 15–30 degrees, shifting emphasis to the sternal (lower) head of the pectoralis major. The decline position also reduces the range of motion and allows some lifters to handle more load than the flat bench press.

execution.starting_position: Set the bench to a 15–30 degree decline. Hook your feet under the foot pad. Lie back and grip the bar slightly wider than shoulder width with an overhand grip. The bar should be over your lower chest when unracked.
execution.setup_instructions: Secure feet in the ankle pads before lying back. Position body so the bar aligns with the lower pectoral region when at chest level.
steps: Unrack the bar and hold it directly over the lower chest with arms extended.
Lower the bar under control to the lower chest, maintaining retracted shoulder blades.
Touch the lower chest lightly and press back up along the same arc.
execution.breathing_instructions: Inhale and brace before descent. Exhale on the press.
common_mistakes: Extreme decline angles (beyond 30 degrees) reduce pectoral stretch
Lowering the bar too high on the chest negates the decline-specific benefit
safety_considerations: Blood can rush to the head in the decline position — avoid very heavy singles if susceptible to this
Always use a spotter or safety catches
execution.range_of_motion_guidance: Lower bar to lower chest. Press to full extension. ROM will be shorter than flat or incline due to bench angle.
coaching_cues: Press the bar in a straight line — the decline angle handles the arc naturally
Keep your lower back in contact with the bench at all times

name: Decline Barbell Skullcrusher
description: A decline bench skullcrusher with a straight barbell. The decline angle increases the stretch on the triceps long head and allows heavier loading than flat variations. This is a staple mass-building exercise for advanced tricep development.

execution.starting_position: Set up for Decline Barbell Skullcrusher in the appropriate position.
execution.setup_instructions: Prepare equipment and body position for Decline Barbell Skullcrusher.
steps: Step 1: Set bench to decline angle. Lie with head lower end, unrack bar with shoulder-width grip.
Step 2: Lower bar toward forehead by bending elbows, keeping upper arms fixed.
Step 3: Lower until forearms break parallel, then reverse.
Step 4: Extend elbows to full lockout.
execution.breathing_instructions: Exhale during the exertion phase, inhale during the return.
common_mistakes: Letting elbows wander outward
Bouncing at bottom
safety_considerations: Keep joints aligned throughout the movement.
Use controlled weight appropriate for skill level.
execution.range_of_motion_guidance: Move through full range of motion without compromising joint integrity.
coaching_cues: Upper arms stay vertical
Squeeze triceps at top

name: Decline Bench Press 3-Second Pause
alternative_names: Decline Bench Press Pause at Bottom
description: A decline barbell bench press with a deliberate three-second pause at the chest. The pause eliminates the elastic energy stored in the pectoral musculature and connective tissues, requiring a true concentric contraction from a dead stop. This powerlifting-derived technique builds strength off the chest and develops the ability to generate force without momentum, which transfers directly to competition bench press and overall chest strength.

execution.starting_position: Lie on a decline bench (15–30 degrees) with feet secured. Grip the barbell at standard bench press width. Unrack and hold above the lower chest.
execution.setup_instructions: Reduce weight by 15–20% from your standard decline press weight. The 3-second pause creates significantly greater demand. Use collars. Spotter required.
steps: Step 1: Unrack and position the bar above the lower chest.
Step 2: Lower the bar to the lower chest with control — do not bounce.
Step 3: At chest contact, hold the bar motionless for a full 3-second count. Maintain tension throughout — bar stays on chest but all muscles remain actively engaged.
Step 4: At the end of the pause, press powerfully to full lockout without bouncing or using momentum.
execution.breathing_instructions: Inhale before descent, hold (Valsalva) through the pause and press, exhale at the top.
common_mistakes: Bouncing the bar off the chest instead of pausing — this defeats the technique entirely
Relaxing completely during the pause — maintain active tension even while stopped
Underestimating the weight reduction needed — the pause adds enormous difficulty
safety_considerations: Always use a spotter for paused pressing — muscular fatigue mid-set is abrupt and unpredictable
Secure feet firmly on the decline bench
Use safety pins if training without a spotter
execution.range_of_motion_guidance: Full range from lockout to chest contact. Bar must touch the chest during the pause — no floating.
coaching_cues: Press tight even during the pause — do not go limp at the bottom
The pause should feel uncomfortable — that discomfort is the training stimulus

name: Decline Bench Press with Midpoint Pause
description: A decline barbell bench press variation that includes a deliberate pause at the midpoint of the descent (halfway between the top and chest), rather than the traditional chest pause. This mid-range isometric hold eliminates the stretch reflex contribution and targets the lower pectoralis major at a point in the range where it must generate force without elastic energy assistance. This technique is particularly effective for building strength through the mid-range sticking point.

execution.starting_position: Lie on a decline bench with feet secured. Grip the barbell at standard bench press width. Unrack and hold above the lower chest with arms extended.
execution.setup_instructions: Use significantly less weight than a standard decline press — 20–30% less is typical. The mid-pause creates enormous isometric demand. Set the decline to 15–30 degrees.
steps: Step 1: Begin with arms fully extended above the lower chest.
Step 2: Lower the bar toward the chest. At the midpoint — elbows bent approximately 90 degrees — stop and hold the bar completely still for 2–3 seconds.
Step 3: After the hold, continue lowering to the chest.
Step 4: Press back to the starting position without pausing on the way up.
execution.breathing_instructions: Inhale before descent, hold breath during the pause (Valsalva), exhale through the press.
common_mistakes: Not holding the pause long enough — 2 seconds minimum is required for the technique to be effective
Using too much weight, unable to maintain the hold
Letting the bar drift or shoulders shift during the isometric hold
safety_considerations: Use a spotter — the mid-range hold is the most demanding part and fatigue may cause bar drop
Feet must be secured on the decline for this technically demanding variation
execution.range_of_motion_guidance: Full range: top to chest. The pause is in the middle of the descent, not at the top or bottom.
execution.tempo_recommendations: 1.5s to midpoint — 2-3s hold — 1.5s to chest — 2s press up
coaching_cues: Fight the urge to drop through the pause — the isometric is the entire point
Brace hard during the hold — think of trying to crush the bar

name: Decline Cable Flye
description: The decline cable flye isolates the lower and sternal portions of the pectoralis major using a cable machine set at a low pulley angle combined with a decline bench. By lying on a decline bench and pressing handles from a low cable angle, the arc of motion closely matches the lower fiber direction of the pectoralis major, creating targeted stretch and contraction.

execution.starting_position: Position a decline bench between two low cable pulleys. Lie on the bench with feet secured. Hold a cable handle in each hand, arms extended to sides at approximately chest level, with a slight bend in the elbows.
execution.setup_instructions: Set both pulleys to the lowest position. Attach single-grip handles. Position the decline bench so that the cables create a low-to-inward pull angle when you lie on it.
steps: Step 1: Lie on the decline bench with arms extended out to the sides, slight elbow bend, handles gripped with palms facing up.
Step 2: Drive both handles upward and inward in a wide arc, maintaining the same elbow angle.
Step 3: Bring handles together above your lower chest, squeezing the pectorals at peak contraction.
Step 4: Slowly lower the handles back to the starting position, feeling the stretch across the lower chest.
execution.breathing_instructions: Exhale as you bring the handles together. Inhale during the return phase.
common_mistakes: Bending the elbows too much and converting to a pressing motion
Allowing the arms to drop below the bench level, overstressing the shoulder
Using too much weight, compromising the arc of motion
safety_considerations: Keep elbows slightly bent and fixed — do not straighten or flex them during the rep
Secure feet firmly on the decline bench to prevent sliding
execution.range_of_motion_guidance: Open arms to full stretch at the bottom (cable level), close to full adduction at the top. Avoid hyperextension at shoulder.
coaching_cues: Pretend you are hugging a large tree
The elbows never change their angle — only the shoulder joint moves

name: Decline Cable Press
description: A cable chest press performed in a decline body position or with the cables set at a high angle to simulate a decline press vector. This arrangement maintains constant tension through the full pressing range of motion — unlike barbells or dumbbells that become lighter at lockout — while targeting the lower pectoralis major with a consistent force curve throughout the rep.

execution.starting_position: Set a decline bench inside a cable machine or face away from two high pulleys. On a decline bench: lie with head lower, cables running from behind and above. Hold handles at upper chest level, elbows bent.
execution.setup_instructions: Option 1: Use a cable machine with adjustable arms set to high position and lie on a decline bench below them. Option 2: Set a decline bench between two cable stacks with high pulleys. Attach single handles to each cable.
steps: Step 1: Lie on the decline bench, gripping cable handles at upper chest/shoulder level. Elbows bent at approximately 90 degrees.
Step 2: Press the handles forward and downward (following the decline press vector) toward the lower chest area.
Step 3: Extend arms fully, feeling the constant cable tension even at lockout.
Step 4: Return under control to the starting position with elbows back at 90 degrees. Repeat.
execution.breathing_instructions: Inhale to load the chest at the bottom, exhale during the press.
common_mistakes: Press direction going straight forward instead of slightly downward following the decline angle
Losing upper back contact with the bench during the press
Allowing cables to pull arms too far back behind the chest at the start
safety_considerations: Get a spotter or use a rack to position on the decline bench safely with cables attached
Secure feet firmly on the decline bench before initiating the press
execution.range_of_motion_guidance: Full elbow extension at the top. At the bottom, elbows align with or slightly below the torso plane.
coaching_cues: Press along the decline line — think down and forward, not straight out
Feel the cables pulling at the top — that constant tension is the advantage over free weights

name: Decline Close-Grip Bench Press
description: A compound triceps exercise combining the decline bench angle with a close grip. The decline reduces shoulder involvement and increases triceps work, while the close grip further isolates the triceps. This is an excellent mass builder for the entire triceps.

execution.starting_position: Set up for Decline Close-Grip Bench Press in the appropriate position.
execution.setup_instructions: Prepare equipment and body position for Decline Close-Grip Bench Press.
steps: Step 1: Set bench to decline. Secure legs. Grip bar shoulder-width or slightly inside.
Step 2: Unrack bar and lower to lower chest with elbows tucked.
Step 3: Keep elbows close to body throughout descent.
Step 4: Press bar back to lockout contracting triceps.
execution.breathing_instructions: Exhale during the exertion phase, inhale during the return.
common_mistakes: Gripping too narrow causing wrist strain
Letting elbows flare
safety_considerations: Keep joints aligned throughout the movement.
Use controlled weight appropriate for skill level.
execution.range_of_motion_guidance: Move through full range of motion without compromising joint integrity.
coaching_cues: Elbows track close to ribs
Full lockout each rep

name: Decline Dumbbell Skullcrusher
description: A decline bench variation of the skullcrusher performed with dumbbells. The decline angle shifts emphasis to the long head of the triceps and reduces elbow stress. Using dumbbells allows independent arm movement and a natural rotation of the wrists.

execution.starting_position: Set up for Decline Dumbbell Skullcrusher in the appropriate position.
execution.setup_instructions: Prepare equipment and body position for Decline Dumbbell Skullcrusher.
steps: Step 1: Set bench to decline. Lie with head lower, hold dumbbells at arm's length.
Step 2: Bend elbows to lower dumbbells toward temples, keeping upper arms fixed.
Step 3: Lower until forearms are past parallel to floor.
Step 4: Press back to full extension.
execution.breathing_instructions: Exhale during the exertion phase, inhale during the return.
common_mistakes: Letting upper arms drift
Using too much weight
safety_considerations: Keep joints aligned throughout the movement.
Use controlled weight appropriate for skill level.
execution.range_of_motion_guidance: Move through full range of motion without compromising joint integrity.
coaching_cues: Keep upper arms perpendicular to floor
Full extension without locking harshly

name: Decline Dumbbell Squeeze Press
description: A decline bench pressing variation where both dumbbells are pressed together throughout the entire movement, creating a constant adduction force that maximally activates the medial and sternal fibers of the pectoralis major. The decline angle combines with the continuous squeeze to target the lower chest with both pressing and adduction force simultaneously.

execution.starting_position: Lie on a decline bench with feet secured. Hold two dumbbells pressed firmly together above the lower chest with palms facing each other. Arms extended.
execution.setup_instructions: Set the bench to a 15–30 degree decline. Use hexagonal dumbbells as their flat sides make maintaining contact easier.
steps: Step 1: Begin with dumbbells pressed together above the lower chest, palms facing each other. Maintain active squeezing pressure throughout.
Step 2: Lower the dumbbells as a single unit toward the lower chest, keeping them in constant contact.
Step 3: Descend until the dumbbells are at chest level.
Step 4: Press the unit back up to the starting position, squeezing the dumbbells together the entire time.
execution.breathing_instructions: Inhale on descent, exhale on the press back up.
common_mistakes: Letting the dumbbells separate during the movement — the squeeze must be continuous
Using dumbbells too heavy to maintain the squeeze while pressing
Excessively flaring the elbows
safety_considerations: Secure feet firmly on the decline to avoid sliding
Get a spotter to hand you the dumbbells in position to avoid awkward setup
execution.range_of_motion_guidance: Full range from chest to full arm extension. The adduction force is maintained throughout.
execution.tempo_recommendations: 3-1-2-1 (3s descent, 1s pause, 2s press, 1s squeeze at top)
coaching_cues: Squeeze the dumbbells together as hard as possible the entire set
Press from the inside out — the squeeze generates the tension

name: Decline EZ-Bar Skull Crusher
description: The decline EZ-bar skull crusher uses a decline bench (typically -15 to -30 degrees) which moves the target area from the forehead downward, allowing the bar to travel further behind the head at the bottom of the movement. The decline angle places the medial and lateral heads under greater relative load compared to the flat version, and many lifters find the decline position more comfortable on the elbows. The extended range behind the head increases tricep stretch.

execution.starting_position: Set a bench to a slight decline. Secure feet. Lie back and have a spotter hand the EZ-bar to full extension above the lower chest/face.
execution.setup_instructions: Foot hooks are needed for the decline position. Keep the decline moderate (around 15 degrees).
steps: Step 1: Begin with EZ-bar above the chest/lower face at full elbow extension.
Step 2: Lower the bar by bending only the elbows, letting the bar travel toward and behind the head.
Step 3: Lower as far as comfortable without straining the elbows.
Step 4: Press back to the starting position by extending the elbows.
execution.breathing_instructions: Inhale on descent, exhale on press.
common_mistakes: Letting the bar travel too far behind the head with heavy loads
Upper arms moving — keep them fixed
safety_considerations: The decline position makes the bar harder to control if dropped — always use a spotter
execution.range_of_motion_guidance: Full extension to bar behind the top of the head.
coaching_cues: Upper arms fixed — perpendicular to bench
Let the bar go behind the head
Drive up through the triceps

name: Decline Machine Chest Press
description: The Decline Machine Chest Press performs a chest press movement at a downward angle, targeting the sternal and lower fibers of the pectoralis major. The machine provides a guided bar path, and the decline angle increases the mechanical emphasis on the lower chest region compared to flat or incline pressing variations.

execution.starting_position: Sit in the decline machine with the seat adjusted so handles are at lower chest level. Secure feet if the machine provides ankle support.
execution.setup_instructions: Adjust the seat height and handle depth. The machine should guide the press in a downward-angled path relative to the user's torso.
steps: Step 1: Grip the handles at lower chest level.
Step 2: Press forward and downward along the machine's guided path to full extension.
Step 3: Return under control to the starting position.
Step 4: Repeat for the prescribed reps.
execution.breathing_instructions: Exhale on the press. Inhale on the return.
common_mistakes: Seat height set incorrectly so the press does not target the lower chest
Rushing the eccentric phase
safety_considerations: Secure feet in the ankle holds if provided — especially important at a decline angle
Adjust weight incrementally — machine weight stacks feel different from free weights at decline angles
execution.range_of_motion_guidance: Full extension at the front; full return to deep stretch without discomfort.
coaching_cues: Press downward and outward to feel the lower chest working
Keep the shoulder blades retracted

name: Decline Plate-Loaded Reverse-Grip Press
description: A decline press using a plate-loaded chest press machine with the hands in a supinated (palms-up, reverse) grip. The reverse grip on the decline angle creates a unique pressing vector that shifts significant tension to the clavicular pectoralis major despite the decline body position, while also increasing biceps brachii involvement as a secondary mover. This unusual combination can overcome training plateaus and add variety to lower-chest training.

execution.starting_position: Sit in a plate-loaded chest press machine set to the decline angle setting. Grip the handles with palms facing upward (supinated grip) rather than the standard overhand grip. Feet secured. Machine loaded appropriately.
execution.setup_instructions: Only use this variation if the machine's handle design allows a comfortable supinated grip without wrist strain. Set the decline angle on the machine. Use less weight than standard grip pressing.
steps: Step 1: Sit in the machine with a supinated grip, handles loaded at chest level.
Step 2: Press the handles forward/out along the machine's guided arc, maintaining the supinated wrist position.
Step 3: Fully extend the arms to the end of the machine's range.
Step 4: Return under control, letting the weight stack descend fully before the next rep.
execution.breathing_instructions: Inhale before the press, exhale during the pressing movement.
common_mistakes: Wrist discomfort due to forcing a supinated grip on a machine not designed for it — stop if wrists hurt
Using the same weight as standard grip — the supinated position typically requires 10–20% less load
Rotating forearms mid-rep back to a neutral position
safety_considerations: If the machine handles do not support a comfortable supinated grip, do not force this variation
Start with light weight to assess wrist comfort in the reverse grip position
Secure feet or use the machine's foot support as decline orientation requires
execution.range_of_motion_guidance: Full range of the machine from fully loaded to full extension.
coaching_cues: Palms face up the entire time — the supinated grip is what makes this unique
Press from the chest, not the arms — the biceps stabilize but the pecs drive

name: Decline Push-Up
description: The decline push-up is performed with the feet elevated above the hands, creating a downward angle of the body. This positioning shifts the pressing stimulus toward the upper (clavicular) portion of the pectoralis major and anterior deltoid, while also increasing the total amount of body weight lifted compared to a standard push-up.

execution.starting_position: Place feet on a bench or elevated surface and hands on the floor slightly wider than shoulder-width. Body should form a straight angled line with hips higher than shoulders.
execution.setup_instructions: Choose a stable elevated surface for the feet. Higher elevation increases upper chest and anterior deltoid contribution and difficulty.
steps: Step 1: Place hands on the floor slightly wider than shoulder-width; rest feet on an elevated surface such as a bench.
Step 2: Extend arms fully and brace the core to create a straight line from head through hips to feet.
Step 3: Inhale and lower the chest toward the floor by bending the elbows, keeping them at roughly 45 degrees from the torso.
Step 4: Pause when the chest is close to the floor, then exhale and press back to the starting position.
execution.breathing_instructions: Inhale on the way down; exhale as you press up.
common_mistakes: Letting the hips sag — this reduces the pec load and stresses the lower back
Placing the bench too high before adequate shoulder stability is developed
safety_considerations: Avoid this variation if you experience shoulder impingement during the descent
Keep the neck neutral — do not let the chin jut forward
execution.range_of_motion_guidance: Lower until the chest nearly touches the floor, then press to full extension.
coaching_cues: Drive the floor away from you as you press
Keep your glutes squeezed to maintain a rigid body line

name: Decline Sit-Up
description: The decline sit-up is performed on a decline bench with the feet secured at the high end, increasing the range of motion and gravitational challenge compared to a flat-surface sit-up. The decline angle lengthens the rectus abdominis at the starting position, providing a greater stretch-to-contraction range that is not achievable on a flat surface. Hip flexors contribute significantly at the lower portion of the movement, while the rectus abdominis dominates during the final degrees of spinal flexion at the top.

execution.starting_position: Lie on the decline bench with feet secured under the ankle pads, knees bent. Cross arms over the chest or place fingertips behind the ears.
execution.setup_instructions: Set the bench to a moderate decline (20–40°). Ensure the ankle pads firmly hold the feet without causing ankle discomfort.
steps: Step 1: Begin lying fully extended on the bench. Engage the core.
Step 2: Curl the chin toward the chest, then lift the torso by sequentially contracting the abs and flexing the spine.
Step 3: Continue rising until the torso is fully upright or slightly past vertical.
Step 4: Lower slowly back to the starting position with control, allowing the spine to extend fully against the bench.
Step 5: Avoid jerking the neck or using momentum from the arms.
execution.breathing_instructions: Exhale on the way up. Inhale on the controlled descent.
common_mistakes: Pulling the neck with the hands behind the head — this compresses the cervical spine
Using a momentum bounce at the bottom rather than a controlled eccentric
safety_considerations: Those with lower-back issues should consult a clinician before performing decline sit-ups due to substantial lumbar loading
execution.range_of_motion_guidance: Full extension at the bottom to full upright (or slightly forward) at the top.
execution.tempo_recommendations: 2-1-2-0. Slow and controlled. No bouncing at the bottom.
coaching_cues: Lead with the chest, not the neck
Control the way down — don't drop

name: Deficit Barbell Bent-Over Row
description: The deficit barbell row is performed with the lifter standing on elevated plates or a platform, allowing the barbell to descend lower than floor level. This increased range of motion provides a greater lat stretch at the bottom of each repetition and may enhance muscle fiber recruitment through the extended pull. The exercise requires superior hamstring flexibility and hip hinge mechanics compared to a standard barbell row.

execution.starting_position: Stand on 2-4 bumper plates or a low platform (2-4 inches elevation). Position the barbell over the mid-foot. Hinge at the hips to approximately parallel with the floor.
execution.setup_instructions: Stack plates or use a wooden platform. Ensure the surface is stable and will not shift. The deficit increases the bottom ROM of each rep.
steps: Step 1: Stand on the elevated platform with the barbell hanging below the platform level.
Step 2: Hinge at the hips until the torso is near parallel, maintaining a neutral spine.
Step 3: Brace the core, retract the scapulae, and pull the bar toward the lower sternum.
Step 4: Squeeze rhomboids and lats at the top of the movement.
Step 5: Lower the bar past the platform edge under full control.
execution.breathing_instructions: Inhale and brace before each rep. Exhale through the pull.
common_mistakes: Using a platform so high that lumbar rounding occurs to reach the bar
Not controlling the eccentric, letting the bar drop past the platform level
Insufficient hamstring flexibility causing the hips to rise
safety_considerations: Requires good hamstring flexibility — do not force depth beyond what neutral spine allows
Use a stable, non-slip platform only
Reduce weight relative to your standard barbell row
execution.range_of_motion_guidance: Bar descends below platform level at the bottom, pulled to lower sternum at the top.
coaching_cues: Let the bar drop below the platform
Spine stays neutral even at the extended bottom position
Pull with the elbows, not the hands

name: Deficit Bulgarian Split Squat
description: The deficit Bulgarian split squat elevates the front foot on a plate or platform in addition to the rear foot being elevated on a bench. This creates a greater range of motion at the hip and knee of the working leg, increasing the stretch on the quadriceps and hip flexors at the bottom of the movement. It is an advanced variation that places significantly higher demands on flexibility and strength through a longer range of motion.

execution.starting_position: Place a weight plate or low platform under the front foot. Rear foot on a bench. Stand tall holding dumbbells. Ensure the front foot elevation is 1-3 inches high.
execution.setup_instructions: Set up a bench for the rear foot and a plate or step for the front foot. The front foot elevation increases depth, so position farther back than a standard Bulgarian split squat.
steps: Step 1: Brace and control the descent, bending the front knee and dropping the rear knee.
Step 2: Due to the front foot elevation, descend deeper than a standard RFESS.
Step 3: Reach the greatest depth you can with control — this is significantly deeper than a standard split squat.
Step 4: Drive through the front foot to return to standing.
execution.breathing_instructions: Inhale on the descent, exhale on the ascent.
common_mistakes: Collapsing into the bottom without control
Front knee caving inward
Excessive forward torso lean
safety_considerations: Requires significant hip flexor and quad flexibility — develop standard Bulgarian split squat first
Ensure front foot elevation is stable
execution.range_of_motion_guidance: Rear knee should travel well below the front foot level due to the deficit. Greater ROM than standard RFESS.
coaching_cues: Sink into the stretch
Control the bottom
Front knee tracks over second toe

name: Deficit Barbell Deadlift
description: The deficit deadlift is performed with the lifter standing on a raised platform (typically 1-4 inches), which lowers the starting position of the barbell relative to the hips. This requires greater knee flexion and hip hinge depth, increasing quadriceps engagement at the initiation of the pull. It is used to build strength off the floor and address weakness in the initial pull phase of the conventional deadlift.

execution.starting_position: Stand on a platform (bumper plates, wooden block, or dedicated riser) 1-4 inches high. The barbell sits on the floor below. Foot position is the same as conventional deadlift.
execution.setup_instructions: Ensure the platform is completely stable. The deficit increases the range of motion — reduce training load relative to your conventional deadlift maximum.
steps: Step 1: Stand on the platform, barbell over mid-foot below the platform level.
Step 2: Hinge at the hips and bend the knees more than in a conventional deadlift to reach the bar.
Step 3: Grip the bar, brace the core, and set the spine to neutral.
Step 4: Drive the floor away with the legs while keeping the back angle constant from the floor through knee height.
Step 5: Lock out hips and knees at the top. Return under control to the floor below the platform.
execution.breathing_instructions: Take a deep breath and brace (Valsalva) before each rep. Exhale at lockout or after the bar is secured on the floor.
common_mistakes: Using too large a deficit before having the flexibility to maintain a neutral spine
The hips shooting up at the start, turning it into a stiff-leg deadlift
Losing lat engagement, allowing the bar to drift forward
safety_considerations: Requires superior hamstring flexibility compared to a floor deadlift
Reduce weight relative to conventional deadlift maximum
Inspect the platform stability before each set
execution.range_of_motion_guidance: Bar starts below the platform level (greater depth than floor deadlift). Full hip and knee extension at lockout.
coaching_cues: More knee bend than a standard deadlift
Lat engagement — protect the bar path
Drive the floor away

name: Deficit Diamond Push-Up
description: A diamond push-up performed with hands elevated on plates or blocks to allow greater depth of chest descent. The deficit increases the range of motion and time under tension for the triceps and chest. This advanced variation builds significant tricep mass.

execution.starting_position: Set up for Deficit Diamond Push-Up in the appropriate position.
execution.setup_instructions: Prepare equipment and body position for Deficit Diamond Push-Up.
steps: Step 1: Place hands on two equal-height elevations with thumbs and forefingers touching in diamond shape.
Step 2: Assume push-up position with body rigid.
Step 3: Lower chest below hand level taking advantage of deficit.
Step 4: Press back up through triceps and chest to full extension.
execution.breathing_instructions: Exhale during the exertion phase, inhale during the return.
common_mistakes: Letting hips drop
Wide hand placement
safety_considerations: Keep joints aligned throughout the movement.
Use controlled weight appropriate for skill level.
execution.range_of_motion_guidance: Move through full range of motion without compromising joint integrity.
coaching_cues: Thumbs and index fingers form a diamond
Lower chest as far as range allows

name: Deficit Handstand Push-Up
description: The deficit handstand push-up places the hands on elevated surfaces (parallettes, blocks, or plates) to allow the head to descend below hand level, dramatically increasing the range of motion compared to a standard wall HSPU. The greater depth significantly increases the stretch placed on the anterior deltoid and upper pectoralis, and demands substantially more shoulder strength and stability through the extended range.

execution.starting_position: Place parallettes, yoga blocks, or stable elevated surfaces at appropriate hand positions. Kick to a handstand against a wall with hands on the elevated surface. Hands at shoulder width or slightly wider.
execution.setup_instructions: Elevation of 10-20 cm is a typical starting deficit. Ensure the elevated surfaces are stable and non-slip before loading.
steps: Step 1: Kick up to a handstand with hands on elevated surfaces.
Step 2: Lower the head below hand level — the degree of descent depends on the elevation height.
Step 3: Hold the bottom position briefly if training strength.
Step 4: Press back to full arm extension.
Step 5: Maintain rigid body position — no arch or piked hips.
execution.breathing_instructions: Inhale descending. Exhale pressing.
common_mistakes: Attempting too large a deficit before the standard HSPU is mastered
Instability in the elevated surface — safety first
safety_considerations: Prerequisites: 10+ clean wall HSPUs before adding a deficit
Start with a small deficit (5-10 cm) and progress gradually
execution.range_of_motion_guidance: Full arm extension to head below hand level.
coaching_cues: Let the head descend below the hands
Press all the way to full arm extension
Body stays straight — no hip pike

name: Deficit Inverted Row
description: The deficit inverted row elevates the feet above the bar height so the body is declined rather than horizontal, dramatically increasing the percentage of bodyweight lifted compared to standard inverted rows. It effectively bridges the gap between bodyweight rows and full pull-ups, loading the lats and upper back with near-vertical force angles from a horizontal plane.

execution.starting_position: Place feet on a bench, box, or elevated surface above the bar. Grip the bar with an overhand or neutral grip. Body hangs below bar level, arms extended.
execution.setup_instructions: The greater the foot elevation, the more vertical the angle and the harder the exercise. Start with feet at the same height as the bar and progress to elevated positions.
steps: Step 1: Begin hanging below the bar with feet elevated, arms fully extended.
Step 2: Depress and retract scapulae to initiate.
Step 3: Row the chest to the bar by driving elbows back.
Step 4: At the top, chest should contact or nearly contact the bar.
Step 5: Lower under control to full arm extension.
execution.breathing_instructions: Exhale on the row. Inhale descending.
common_mistakes: Hips dropping below the torso line
Using excessive shoulder elevation instead of lat drive
safety_considerations: Ensure the elevated surface for feet is stable and won't slide
Use a sturdy rack or bar rated for bodyweight suspension
execution.range_of_motion_guidance: Full arm extension to chest at bar level.
coaching_cues: The more you elevate the feet, the harder it gets
Body stays rigid — no hip drop
Lead with the chest

name: Deficit Push-Up
description: The deficit push-up is performed with the hands elevated on platforms, blocks, or dumbbells, allowing the chest to descend below the level of the hands for a deeper range of motion than a standard push-up. This extended stretch under load increases time under tension and pectoral recruitment, making it a more demanding bodyweight pressing variation.

execution.starting_position: Place hands on two elevated platforms (push-up handles, dumbbells, or sturdy blocks) slightly wider than shoulder width. Assume a push-up position with straight body alignment.
execution.setup_instructions: Set the platforms at an equal height between 4 and 6 inches. Ensure they are stable and will not slide on the surface.
steps: Step 1: Begin in a high plank position with hands on the platforms, body in a straight line.
Step 2: Lower the chest between and below the platforms by bending the elbows to roughly 45 degrees.
Step 3: Continue lowering until the chest is below the level of the hands, feeling a deep stretch.
Step 4: Press powerfully upward through the palms, extending the elbows fully at the top.
Step 5: Maintain a rigid plank body position from head to heels throughout.
execution.breathing_instructions: Inhale as you lower the chest toward the floor. Exhale forcefully as you push back up.
common_mistakes: Allowing the hips to sag downward on the descent
Not descending low enough to benefit from the deficit
Flaring the elbows to 90 degrees, increasing shoulder stress
safety_considerations: Ensure the platforms are on a non-slip surface
Only perform this variation if you can complete standard push-ups with solid form
Avoid if you have shoulder instability or rotator cuff issues
execution.range_of_motion_guidance: Descend until the chest drops 2–4 inches below the hand level for a meaningful deficit. Full elbow extension at the top.
coaching_cues: Chest drops below the hands — that's the whole point
Keep the body rigid from heels to crown
Press hard through the platforms on the way up

name: Depth Jump
description: The depth jump is an advanced plyometric exercise in which the athlete steps off an elevated box, contacts the ground, and immediately jumps as high as possible with minimal ground contact time. By utilizing the stretch-shortening cycle — the rapid eccentric loading followed by an immediate concentric contraction — the depth jump trains reactive strength and enhances the stretch reflex more effectively than standard box jumps. It places significant stress on the musculotendinous system and requires a solid strength foundation before use.

execution.starting_position: Stand on the edge of a plyo box at 30–75 cm height. Toes at the edge of the box.
execution.setup_instructions: Appropriate box height must be selected carefully — too high increases ground contact time and reduces reactive demand. 30–60 cm is typical for most athletes.
steps: Step 1: Stand at the edge of the box.
Step 2: Step (not jump) off the box — a step produces a more controlled landing stimulus than a jump.
Step 3: Upon ground contact, absorb the landing through the forefoot and ankle with a minimal knee bend.
Step 4: Immediately and explosively jump as high as possible — minimize ground contact time.
Step 5: Land softly from the subsequent jump, rest fully, and repeat.
execution.breathing_instructions: Exhale sharply on the takeoff jump. Breathe freely during rest between reps.
common_mistakes: Excessive knee bend on landing — the goal is a stiff, rapid absorption and re-expression
Pausing on the ground before jumping (this negates the stretch-shortening cycle benefit)
Using too high a drop height — this increases ground contact time, not reactive strength
safety_considerations: Requires a squat 1RM of at least 1.5x bodyweight before incorporating depth jumps at meaningful volumes.
High musculotendinous stress — not suitable for those with Achilles, patellar tendon, or knee pathology.
Total volume should be low — this is a CNS-intensive exercise.
execution.range_of_motion_guidance: Minimal ground contact and maximal jump height are the two key metrics.
execution.tempo_recommendations: Maximum explosive intent. Ground contact time of under 250ms is the goal for advanced athletes. 3–5 reps per set, full rest between sets.
coaching_cues: Touch and go — ground contact is lightning fast
Stiff ankle on landing — spring, not squat
Jump as high as possible on each rep

name: Diamond Push-Up
description: The diamond push-up is a push-up variation where the thumbs and index fingers touch to form a diamond or triangle shape beneath the chest. This narrow hand position dramatically increases triceps brachii activation while the pectoralis major acts as a secondary mover. It is one of the most effective bodyweight exercises for tricep development.

execution.starting_position: Begin in a standard push-up position, then bring both hands together under the sternum with the thumbs and forefingers touching to form a diamond shape. Arms should be fully extended.
execution.setup_instructions: No equipment needed. Find a flat, stable surface for the hands.
steps: Step 1: Position hands together on the floor below the chest with thumbs and index fingers touching to form a diamond shape.
Step 2: Extend arms fully; keep the body in a rigid plank from head to heels.
Step 3: Inhale and lower the chest toward the diamond by bending the elbows, which will move outward slightly to either side.
Step 4: Lower until the chest nearly touches the hands, pause briefly, then exhale and press back to the starting position.
execution.breathing_instructions: Inhale on the descent; exhale on the press.
common_mistakes: Flaring the elbows wide, which shifts load away from the triceps
Letting the hips drop or rise out of a neutral plank position
safety_considerations: If wrist discomfort occurs, slightly rotate hands outward a few degrees
Reduce range of motion if shoulder impingement is felt
execution.range_of_motion_guidance: Lower the chest to touch or nearly touch the hands, then press fully back to extension.
coaching_cues: Think 'elbows back' as you descend to maximize tricep engagement
Keep the torso rigid — imagine a straight rod from crown to heel

name: Diamond Push-Up (Feet Elevated)
description: A diamond push-up with feet raised on a bench or box to increase difficulty and shift loading toward the triceps. The elevated position changes the angle of force application and allows greater body weight to be recruited. This demands significant tricep strength.

execution.starting_position: Set up for Diamond Push-Up (Feet Elevated) in the appropriate position.
execution.setup_instructions: Prepare equipment and body position for Diamond Push-Up (Feet Elevated).
steps: Step 1: Place feet on bench. Position hands in diamond shape on floor.
Step 2: Maintain rigid body alignment from heels to shoulders.
Step 3: Lower chest toward hands while keeping elbows tracking over wrists.
Step 4: Press back to full arm extension.
execution.breathing_instructions: Exhale during the exertion phase, inhale during the return.
common_mistakes: Letting hips pike up
Wide hand placement
safety_considerations: Keep joints aligned throughout the movement.
Use controlled weight appropriate for skill level.
execution.range_of_motion_guidance: Move through full range of motion without compromising joint integrity.
coaching_cues: Diamond stays centered under sternum
Control the descent

name: Tricep Dip
description: The tricep dip is a bodyweight or weighted vertical pushing exercise using parallel bars. By maintaining an upright torso with minimal forward lean, the emphasis shifts to the triceps rather than the pectorals. It is an effective compound movement for triceps mass and elbow extension strength.

execution.starting_position: Support yourself on parallel bars with arms extended. Keep the torso upright with minimal forward lean. Feet may hang freely or cross behind.
execution.setup_instructions: Keeping the torso upright is what distinguishes a tricep dip from a chest dip. Avoid leaning more than 10 degrees forward.
steps: Lower yourself by bending the elbows, keeping the torso upright.
Descend until the upper arms are parallel to the floor.
Press back up to full arm extension.
