execution.breathing_instructions: Inhale on descent, exhale on the press.
common_mistakes: Excessive forward lean shifting emphasis to the chest
Dipping below shoulder-level if mobility is limited
safety_considerations: If shoulder discomfort occurs, limit depth and ensure the torso is upright
execution.range_of_motion_guidance: Descend to upper arms parallel to the floor. Full arm extension at the top.
coaching_cues: Stay upright — your torso is a flagpole
Lock out completely at the top — squeeze the triceps hard

name: Donkey Calf Raise
description: The donkey calf raise is performed with the torso bent forward at approximately 90° with the hips flexed, which places the gastrocnemius under a greater stretch at the hip than a standing calf raise. Because the gastrocnemius is a biarticular muscle crossing both the knee and hip, the hip-flexed position elongates it, increasing the range of motion and stretch on the gastrocnemius medial and lateral heads. It was popularized as a mass-building calf exercise and can be loaded by having a training partner sit on the hips.

execution.starting_position: Hinge at the hips and brace the hands on a bench, barbell, or wall at hip height. Keep the knees very slightly bent. Stand with the balls of the feet on a raised surface (step edge or plate).
execution.setup_instructions: Place the toes on a step edge or plate so the heels can drop below the platform for full stretch. Hinge the torso to 90° — this is essential for the elongated gastrocnemius position.
steps: Step 1: Position the toes on the edge of a raised surface. Hinge the torso forward 90° and hold onto a support.
Step 2: Lower the heels as far below the step as range of motion allows — full gastrocnemius stretch.
Step 3: Rise onto the toes as high as possible, fully plantar-flexing both ankles.
Step 4: Hold the peak contraction briefly with the calves fully contracted.
Step 5: Lower under control to the stretched position.
execution.breathing_instructions: Exhale as you rise onto the toes. Inhale as you lower.
common_mistakes: Performing with an upright torso, which removes the gastrocnemius pre-stretch benefit
Insufficient heel drop at the bottom — reduces the range of motion
Bouncing through the bottom position — slow the eccentric
safety_considerations: If a partner is adding load by sitting on the hips, communication is essential
Start with bodyweight to establish the movement pattern
execution.range_of_motion_guidance: Full heel drop below the platform at the bottom; maximum plantar-flexion at the top.
execution.tempo_recommendations: 2-1-3-0 — slow controlled descent (3s) to maximize gastrocnemius stretch
coaching_cues: Drop the heels all the way — don't cheat the stretch
Rise all the way onto the big toe
Hips bent 90° — don't stand up during the exercise

name: Donkey Kick
description: The donkey kick is performed on all fours, kicking one leg backward and upward with the knee bent at 90° to extend the hip. The all-fours position allows the gluteus maximus to work through hip extension with the torso stabilized, isolating the glute from most other muscles. It is a beginner-friendly and low-impact exercise commonly used in rehabilitation, general fitness, and glute activation protocols. Resistance bands or ankle weights can add load.

execution.starting_position: Begin on hands and knees (quadruped position) with wrists under shoulders and knees under hips. Spine neutral.
execution.setup_instructions: No equipment required. A resistance band looped around both legs just above the knee adds progressive resistance.
steps: Step 1: Begin on all fours with a neutral spine. Keep the core braced.
Step 2: Keeping the knee bent at 90°, raise one leg backward and upward by extending the hip.
Step 3: Drive the foot toward the ceiling until the thigh is parallel to the floor and the knee is fully extended at the hip (hip is extended, not hyperextended at the spine).
Step 4: Hold the peak position briefly and squeeze the glute.
Step 5: Lower the knee back to the starting position. Complete all reps, then switch legs.
execution.breathing_instructions: Exhale as you kick back. Inhale as you lower.
common_mistakes: Rotating the hip open toward the ceiling — keep the pelvis level and facing down
Extending the lower back to increase range — the hip should extend, not the spine
Letting the core sag — the spine stays neutral throughout
safety_considerations: Wrist discomfort can be reduced by making fists or using push-up handles
Very low risk exercise suitable for beginners and those in rehabilitation
execution.range_of_motion_guidance: Extend the hip until the thigh is parallel to the floor. No higher — additional range comes from lumbar extension, not hip extension.
coaching_cues: Kick back and up — not just back
Keep the hip facing down — no rotation
Brace the core — no spine sagging

name: Double-Under
description: The double-under is an advanced jump rope skill in which the rope passes under the feet twice in a single jump, requiring a higher jump and faster rope rotation than a standard single-under. It significantly elevates the cardiovascular demand over single-unders, while also training rope timing, wrist speed, and the explosive ankle and calf plantarflexion needed to achieve sufficient jump height. Double-unders are a standard exercise in competitive functional fitness.

execution.starting_position: Stand upright with the jump rope behind the heels, one handle in each hand.
execution.setup_instructions: Use a speed rope with handles appropriate for double-under rotation. The rope should be slightly shorter than used for single-unders.
steps: Step 1: Begin with a standard single-under rhythm to establish timing.
Step 2: On a chosen jump, explode upward more powerfully than a single-under to achieve greater jump height.
Step 3: Simultaneously accelerate wrist rotation to pass the rope under the feet twice before landing.
Step 4: Land softly on the balls of the feet with slightly bent knees.
Step 5: Return to the standard rhythm or continue consecutive double-unders.
execution.breathing_instructions: Breathe continuously. The higher metabolic demand requires efficient breathing rhythm.
common_mistakes: Piking the hips — kicking the heels back instead of jumping straight up
Moving the arms wide to slow the rope — wrists should do the work
Panicking and breaking rhythm — stay composed and consistent
safety_considerations: High Achilles and calf demand — do not progress volume too rapidly.
Master single-unders and consistent rhythm before attempting.
execution.range_of_motion_guidance: Enough jump height for the rope to pass twice — typically 10–15 cm off the floor.
execution.tempo_recommendations: Typically programmed in sets of 50–100 reps unbroken, or for time intervals.
coaching_cues: Jump straight — no piking
Flick the wrist fast — not the arms
Stay relaxed and trust the rhythm

name: Downward-Facing Dog
description: Downward-facing dog is a foundational yoga posture that simultaneously stretches the hamstrings, calves, and latissimus dorsi while building shoulder stability and core engagement. With the hips raised into an inverted V shape and heels pressed toward the floor, the entire posterior chain is loaded in a lengthened position. It is used extensively as a transitional movement in yoga, as a warm-up for athletic activities, and as a standalone mobility exercise.

execution.starting_position: Begin in a push-up or tabletop position with hands shoulder-width apart and feet hip-width apart.
execution.setup_instructions: Use a mat to prevent hand and foot slipping.
steps: Step 1: Begin from a tabletop on hands and knees or a push-up position.
Step 2: Press through the palms and lift the hips toward the ceiling, straightening the knees and forming an inverted V.
Step 3: Press the heels toward the floor. They need not touch — a stretch in the calves and hamstrings should be felt.
Step 4: Externally rotate the arms slightly so the elbow creases face forward.
Step 5: Hold 30–60 seconds, pressing firmly through the hands and reaching the hips high.
execution.breathing_instructions: Breathe slowly and deeply. Exhale and press the hips higher. Inhale and settle into the position.
common_mistakes: Rounding the upper back and collapsing the shoulder blades — press through the hands and spread them
Not pressing the heels toward the floor — work toward this even if the calves are tight
Bending the knees excessively, which reduces the hamstring and calf stretch
safety_considerations: Wrist discomfort is common — reduce by turning fingertips outward or using fists or push-up handles
Shoulder injuries: consult a clinician before including overhead loaded positions
execution.range_of_motion_guidance: The goal is a straight spine from hands to hips and heels as close to the floor as the posterior chain allows.
coaching_cues: Press the floor away with your hands
Reach the tailbone toward the ceiling
Press your heels toward the floor — imagine footprints on a mat

name: Barbell Drag Curl
description: The drag curl is a barbell curl variation where the bar is dragged upward along the torso rather than curled forward in a standard arc. By pulling the elbows back as the bar rises, the biceps are placed under a unique tension angle and the brachialis is recruited heavily. The dragging path also eliminates front deltoid assistance, making it a stricter bicep isolation exercise than the standard curl.

execution.starting_position: Stand upright holding a barbell at arm's length in a supinated grip. Bar rests at thigh level.
execution.setup_instructions: Use a straight barbell or EZ-bar. Grip shoulder-width. Stand tall.
steps: Step 1: Begin curling by pulling the elbows back and dragging the barbell upward along the torso.
Step 2: The bar should stay close to the body — almost touching — as it travels from thighs to upper abs.
Step 3: Continue until maximum elbow flexion is reached and the bar is near the upper chest.
Step 4: Lower the bar slowly back to the thighs along the same dragging path.
execution.breathing_instructions: Exhale on the curl, inhale on the return.
common_mistakes: Swinging the bar forward instead of dragging it up the body
Flaring the elbows outward
Leaning back for momentum
safety_considerations: Keep the lower back neutral — do not hyperextend to assist the curl
execution.range_of_motion_guidance: Thighs to upper chest, bar stays in contact or near contact with the torso throughout.
coaching_cues: Drag the bar up your shirt
Elbows pull back as the bar rises
No swing

name: Dragon Flag
description: The dragon flag is an expert-level isometric and dynamic core exercise popularized by Bruce Lee, performed supine on a bench. The athlete grips the bench behind the head, then raises the entire body from shoulders to feet in one rigid plank-like unit using only the upper back as the pivot point. The exercise demands extraordinary anterior chain strength throughout its full range of motion, particularly of the rectus abdominis, and serves as one of the most demanding bodyweight core exercises.

execution.starting_position: Lie on a flat bench with your head near one end. Reach back and grip the sides of the bench at head level with both hands.
execution.setup_instructions: Use a sturdy flat bench that is bolted or stable. The bench must be able to support the twisting forces generated during this exercise.
steps: Step 1: Lie supine on the bench, gripping the sides firmly behind your head.
Step 2: Press through the elbows and upper back to create a stable base.
Step 3: Brace the entire core and raise your legs, hips, and lower back off the bench until your body is vertical or near-vertical.
Step 4: Lower your body as a single rigid unit — do not let the hips break or the lower back sag.
Step 5: Control the descent to just above the bench, then raise again or hold the lowered position isometrically.
execution.breathing_instructions: Exhale sharply as you raise. Breathe shallowly and brace continuously during any isometric hold.
common_mistakes: Breaking at the hips — allowing the lower back to sag instead of maintaining a rigid plank
Attempting the exercise without adequate core strength prerequisites
Using momentum to swing the legs rather than controlling the movement
safety_considerations: This is an expert exercise. Train hollow holds, L-sits, and hanging leg raises to mastery before attempting.
Never allow the lower back to hyperextend under load — lower the legs only as far as core rigidity can be maintained.
Use a stable, anchored bench.
execution.range_of_motion_guidance: The body raises from horizontal to near-vertical. Control is more important than range — lower only as far as a rigid plank position can be maintained.
execution.tempo_recommendations: 3–5 second eccentric (lowering), 1 second pause at bottom, explosive concentric. Can also be performed as a static hold at various angles.
coaching_cues: One rigid line from shoulders to toes
Never let your hips break — plank the whole way
Fight gravity with your whole body

name: Dragon Flag Leg Lowering
description: A dragon flag variation where the legs are slowly lowered from vertical to horizontal in a controlled descent, emphasizing the eccentric phase. This eccentric-focused approach builds anterior chain strength for full dragon flags. The slow lower is significantly harder than the raise.

execution.starting_position: Set up for Dragon Flag Leg Lowering in proper position.
execution.setup_instructions: Prepare body and equipment for Dragon Flag Leg Lowering.
steps: Step 1: Lie on bench and grip behind head. Press shoulders into bench.
Step 2: Raise legs and hips to vertical position.
Step 3: Lower body slowly in rigid plank taking 5+ seconds to reach horizontal.
Step 4: When horizontal, use hands to reset to vertical.
execution.breathing_instructions: Breathe steadily; never hold breath during static holds.
common_mistakes: Hinging at hips to cheat
Lowering too quickly
safety_considerations: Build prerequisite strength before attempting advanced variations.
Stop if joint pain occurs.
execution.range_of_motion_guidance: Full range of motion with control at all times.
coaching_cues: Rigid plank from shoulder to toes
5-10 second lowering for maximum effect

name: Dual Cable Front Raise
description: The dual cable front raise uses a cable behind the body from two low pulleys — one handle in each hand — raising both arms simultaneously to shoulder or eye level. The cables provide constant tension throughout the full range of motion, unlike dumbbells which unload near the top, making this variation superior for hypertrophy through the anterior deltoid and upper chest.

execution.starting_position: Stand between two low cable pulleys with one handle in each hand. Face away from the cable stack. Arms at sides, cables running from behind.
execution.setup_instructions: Set both pulleys to the lowest position. Adjust cable weights equally. Stand close to the cable stack initially to gauge tension.
steps: Step 1: Begin with arms at sides, cables taut running from behind.
Step 2: Raise both arms simultaneously forward and upward to shoulder height.
Step 3: Maintain slight elbow bend throughout — not fully locked, not deeply bent.
Step 4: Hold 1 second at shoulder height.
Step 5: Lower under control.
execution.breathing_instructions: Exhale on the raise. Inhale lowering.
common_mistakes: Raising above shoulder height — this recruits traps and reduces anterior delt emphasis
Using momentum from the torso — strict movement only
safety_considerations: Light loads recommended — anterior deltoid isolation exercises have high leverage disadvantage
Avoid if experiencing shoulder impingement
execution.range_of_motion_guidance: Arms at sides to shoulder height.
coaching_cues: Thumbs slightly up at the peak
No torso lean — strict upright posture
Lead with the pinkies as the arms rise

name: Dual Kettlebell Press
description: The dual kettlebell overhead press is performed with two kettlebells racked in the front-rack position, pressing both simultaneously overhead. The racked position places the kettlebells against the forearms with the bells resting on the shoulder girdle, which requires unique shoulder positioning and upper body tension compared to dumbbell pressing. The simultaneous bilateral load demands greater core bracing against the compressed, weighted rack position.

execution.starting_position: Clean two kettlebells to the front-rack position: bells resting on the forearms and upper arms, elbows pointing slightly forward and down. Feet hip-width apart, core braced.
execution.setup_instructions: Learning the kettlebell front-rack position is prerequisite — it differs substantially from a barbell rack. Practice with lighter kettlebells first.
steps: Step 1: Clean both kettlebells to the front-rack position.
Step 2: Brace the core and set the feet.
Step 3: Press both kettlebells overhead simultaneously, keeping them in a vertical path.
Step 4: At lockout, arms fully extended with the bells directly above the shoulders.
Step 5: Lower both under control to the front-rack position.
execution.breathing_instructions: Exhale on the press, inhale on the descent.
common_mistakes: Flaring the elbows wide in the rack — elbows should point forward and down, not to the sides
Pressing one side before the other — the press should be simultaneous
safety_considerations: Learn the front-rack position before adding heavy loads
execution.range_of_motion_guidance: Front-rack position to full overhead lockout.
coaching_cues: Rack them tight — bells on the forearms
Press together
Lockout fully at the top

name: Dual Landmine Standing Chest Press
description: The dual landmine standing chest press uses two barbells anchored side by side to perform a bilateral pressing motion that mimics the arc of a dumbbell press with the stability benefits of a fixed load path. Standing during the press increases core and hip engagement, making it both a chest and full-body stability exercise.

execution.starting_position: Set up two landmine attachments side by side. Hold the free end of each barbell at chest height, standing with feet shoulder-width apart.
execution.setup_instructions: Anchor two barbells in adjacent landmine sleeves. Load equal weight on each. Stand close enough to hold both bar ends at chest height simultaneously without awkward angles.
steps: Step 1: Hold both bar ends at chest height with palms facing inward.
Step 2: Press both bars forward and slightly upward simultaneously, extending the arms.
Step 3: At full extension, attempt to squeeze the hands toward each other to increase pectoral contraction.
Step 4: Slowly lower both bars back to the chest in a controlled arc.
Step 5: Maintain a neutral spine and braced core throughout all reps.
execution.breathing_instructions: Exhale as you press forward. Inhale as you lower the bars back to the chest.
common_mistakes: Allowing the elbows to flare far out to the sides
Using momentum or leg drive to help each rep
Letting the lower back arch excessively
safety_considerations: Ensure both landmine sleeves are secure and the barbells are equally loaded
Start with the bars unloaded to learn the motion
Have a spotter available when using heavier loads
execution.range_of_motion_guidance: Press until both arms are fully extended. Lower until hands return to chest level, keeping the bar ends together as much as possible.
coaching_cues: Press the bars in converging arcs
Squeeze the chest at the top
Keep the belly tight and ribs down

name: Duck Walk
description: A loaded locomotion exercise performed in a deep squat position, walking forward with short steps while maintaining a consistent low position. The duck walk builds quad endurance, glute strength, and challenges hip mobility over a large range of motion under sustained muscular tension.

execution.starting_position: Hold a dumbbell at chest height in a goblet position or at both sides. Descend into a deep squat position with feet shoulder-width apart.
execution.setup_instructions: Select a moderate weight. Clear a straight path of at least 10 to 15 meters. Begin in a deep squat.
steps: Step 1: Lower into a deep squat, keeping your chest up and feet flat on the floor.
Step 2: Take small deliberate steps forward while maintaining the low squat position throughout.
Step 3: Keep knees tracking over your toes with each step.
Step 4: Continue for the prescribed distance or duration, then stand to rest.
execution.breathing_instructions: Breathe rhythmically throughout. Short breaths are normal due to trunk compression.
common_mistakes: Allowing the hips to rise during the walk, reducing the squat depth
Letting the heels come off the floor
safety_considerations: Avoid if you have significant patellar tendinopathy or acute knee injuries
Start with bodyweight before adding load
execution.range_of_motion_guidance: Maintain thighs at or below parallel throughout the entire walk.
coaching_cues: Stay low throughout
Knees track over toes on every step

name: Duck Walk with Chains
description: A heavy squat walk performed with a loaded barbell in the low-bar or Zercher position, moving in a waddling gait pattern. Adding chains provides accommodating resistance. This develops leg drive and hip stability under constant load while moving forward.

execution.starting_position: Set up for Duck Walk with Chains in proper strongman position.
execution.setup_instructions: Prepare all equipment and body position for Duck Walk with Chains.
steps: Step 1: Load barbell with chains attached. Set bar in low-bar or Zercher position.
Step 2: Descend to below parallel squat position.
Step 3: Walk forward in waddle pattern maintaining squat depth.
Step 4: Continue for target distance before standing and racking.
execution.breathing_instructions: Brace core maximally before every lift. Breathe between reps if needed.
common_mistakes: Rising out of squat position during walk
Narrow stance limiting mobility
safety_considerations: Use collars on all loaded barbells.
Ensure clear path for carries.
Have spotters for overhead movements.
execution.range_of_motion_guidance: Full range of motion specific to the implement being used.
coaching_cues: Stay deep throughout
Wide stance allows forward movement

name: Dumbbell Around-The-Worlds
description: Dumbbell around-the-worlds move two dumbbells in a wide circular arc from the thighs, out to the sides at shoulder level, and over the chest to meet above the sternum. This continuous circular movement engages the pectorals across multiple angles and enhances shoulder mobility while delivering a unique stretch-to-contraction stimulus.

execution.starting_position: Lie on a flat bench holding a light dumbbell in each hand, arms at the sides of the body near the hips, palms facing up.
execution.setup_instructions: Use a very light dumbbell — far lighter than you would for a dumbbell fly. Lie flat with arms alongside the body.
steps: Step 1: Begin with the dumbbells at the sides of your hips, palms facing upward.
Step 2: Sweep both arms out to the sides in a wide arc, keeping them close to the bench surface.
Step 3: Continue the arc upward and inward until the dumbbells meet above the chest, palms now facing each other.
Step 4: Reverse the motion, parting the hands and sweeping them back down in the same arc to the hips.
Step 5: Perform the full circle smoothly and slowly, feeling the chest engage throughout.
execution.breathing_instructions: Breathe naturally throughout. Exhale as the hands come together above the chest.
common_mistakes: Using dumbbells that are too heavy, compromising the arc
Rushing through the movement instead of feeling each position
Bending the elbows significantly
safety_considerations: Keep weights very light — this is a mobility and isolation exercise, not a loading exercise
Avoid this exercise if you have shoulder impingement
Perform slowly and with full control
execution.range_of_motion_guidance: The circle should be as wide as comfortably possible at the bottom and converge tightly at the top. Feel a stretch at the sides and a contraction at the top.
coaching_cues: Draw big circles on the ceiling with the dumbbells
Light weight, feel everything
Squeeze the chest as hands meet

name: Dumbbell Bench Press
description: The dumbbell bench press is a horizontal pushing exercise performed on a flat bench using independent dumbbells. The free movement of each arm allows a greater range of motion than the barbell version and helps identify and correct left-right strength imbalances. It is excellent for developing pectoral size and symmetry.

execution.starting_position: Sit on the edge of a flat bench holding a dumbbell on each knee. Use your knees to kick the dumbbells up as you lie back. Hold the dumbbells at chest level with palms facing forward and elbows bent at roughly 75 degrees.
execution.setup_instructions: Choose an appropriate weight. Sit at the end of the bench, place dumbbells on thighs, then use leg drive to bring them into position as you lie back. Keep shoulder blades retracted and depressed throughout.
steps: Brace your core and press both dumbbells simultaneously upward and slightly inward until arms are nearly fully extended.
Lower the dumbbells under control, allowing elbows to drop slightly below the level of the bench for a full chest stretch.
Pause briefly at the bottom without losing shoulder blade position.
Press back up, bringing the dumbbells slightly together at the top to maximize pectoral contraction.
execution.breathing_instructions: Inhale as you lower the dumbbells. Exhale as you press them back to the starting position.
common_mistakes: Allowing dumbbells to drift too wide, stressing the shoulder capsule
Losing scapular retraction at the bottom of the movement
Using an excessively wide elbow flare
safety_considerations: Drop the dumbbells to the sides if you fail a rep — do not attempt to sit up with heavy dumbbells above your head
Use a spotter who can support your wrists when training near maximum effort
execution.range_of_motion_guidance: Lower dumbbells until your upper arms are slightly below parallel to the floor. Press to near full extension without fully locking out.
coaching_cues: Bring the dumbbells together at the top to feel the chest contract
Keep your shoulder blades pinched together throughout the entire set

name: Dumbbell Curl
description: The dumbbell curl trains the biceps brachii and brachialis using independent dumbbells, allowing the wrist to supinate freely through the range of motion which maximizes biceps activation. It can be performed with both arms simultaneously or alternating, and the independent loading helps identify and correct biceps strength imbalances.

execution.starting_position: Stand or sit holding a dumbbell in each hand at the sides with a neutral or supinated grip, elbows against the sides.
execution.setup_instructions: Can be performed seated or standing. Seated reduces the temptation to use body swing.
steps: Curl one dumbbell (or both) upward, rotating the wrist to full supination as the dumbbell rises.
Fully contract the bicep at the top.
Lower under control, rotating back to neutral if alternating.
Repeat on the other side if alternating.
execution.breathing_instructions: Exhale on the curl, inhale on the descent.
common_mistakes: Using body swing to lift the dumbbell
Not fully supinating the forearm during the curl
safety_considerations: If using alternating technique, maintain a neutral wrist at the bottom
execution.range_of_motion_guidance: Full extension at the bottom with full supination at the top.
coaching_cues: Turn the pinky toward the ceiling at the top to maximize supination
Keep the elbow pinned — it should not drive forward

name: Dumbbell Deadlift
description: The dumbbell deadlift replicates the conventional deadlift pattern using two dumbbells instead of a barbell. Each dumbbell hangs at the sides of the thighs, allowing for a more neutral wrist position and a slightly narrower stance. It is an excellent entry point for learning the deadlift pattern, training at home without a barbell, or adding variety to posterior-chain programming.

execution.starting_position: Place two dumbbells on the floor at the sides of the feet. Stand with feet hip-width apart, toes pointing forward. Hinge at the hips and bend the knees to grip the dumbbells with palms facing the thighs.
execution.setup_instructions: Because each dumbbell is narrower than a barbell plate, you can stand in a narrower stance and the weight travels through a fuller range of motion if standing on a slight elevation.
steps: Step 1: Grip both dumbbells, ensuring a neutral spine and chest up.
Step 2: Brace the core and maintain lat engagement throughout.
Step 3: Drive through the floor, extending the hips and knees simultaneously.
Step 4: At lockout, stand fully erect with hips forward and shoulders back.
Step 5: Hinge back to lower the dumbbells under full control to the floor.
execution.breathing_instructions: Brace before each rep. Exhale as you stand up.
common_mistakes: Rounding the lower back at the start position
Letting the dumbbells drift forward away from the body
Not achieving full hip extension at lockout
safety_considerations: If using large-diameter dumbbells, the range of motion will be limited — use a step or platform to restore full ROM
Ensure a neutral spine before initiating the pull
execution.range_of_motion_guidance: Floor to full lockout. Full hip and knee extension at the top.
coaching_cues: Keep dumbbells close — drag them up the legs
Drive the floor away
Hips and shoulders rise together

name: Dumbbell Fly
description: The dumbbell fly is a chest isolation exercise that trains the pectorals in a horizontal adduction arc. Unlike pressing movements, the fly provides maximal pectoral stretch at the bottom position with minimal triceps involvement, making it effective for targeting chest development and improving chest flexibility.

execution.starting_position: Lie on a flat bench holding a dumbbell in each hand. Press the dumbbells to the starting position above the chest with palms facing each other and a slight bend in the elbows.
execution.setup_instructions: Use a weight that allows controlled movement — this is an isolation exercise. Maintain a fixed, slight elbow bend throughout the movement; do not let the elbow angle change.
steps: With a fixed elbow bend, open your arms out to the sides in an arc, lowering the dumbbells toward the level of the bench.
Lower until you feel a strong stretch in the chest — upper arms roughly parallel to the floor.
Reverse the arc, bringing the dumbbells back together above the chest as if hugging a barrel.
Squeeze the chest at the top of the movement before the next rep.
execution.breathing_instructions: Inhale as you open the arms outward. Exhale as you bring the dumbbells back together.
common_mistakes: Bending the elbows too much, turning it into a press
Lowering the dumbbells too far, stressing the anterior capsule of the shoulder
Using too much weight, which forces a pressing motion
safety_considerations: Keep a consistent bend in the elbows to protect the elbow joint from hyperextension under load
If you feel anterior shoulder pain, reduce range of motion
execution.range_of_motion_guidance: Lower until upper arms are parallel to the floor or the stretch becomes uncomfortable. Do not force a greater range than your shoulder mobility allows.
coaching_cues: Think about hugging a giant tree trunk
Maintain the same elbow bend from start to finish — do not let elbows straighten or bend more

name: Dumbbell Front-to-Lateral Raise Complex
description: The dumbbell front-to-lateral raise complex combines a front raise and a lateral raise into one continuous repetition, training the anterior and lateral deltoid within a single set without putting the dumbbells down. The combined movement increases total time under tension for the deltoids per set and trains the transition between the two deltoid heads' force production, making it a time-efficient way to address both anterior and lateral deltoid development. The front raise phase begins each rep; the lateral raise completes it.

execution.starting_position: Stand with dumbbells at the sides. Arms straight, slight elbow bend.
execution.setup_instructions: Use lighter than standard front raise weight since both heads are trained in one rep. The cumulative fatigue is high.
steps: Step 1: Begin with dumbbells at the sides.
Step 2: Raise both dumbbells forward (front raise) to shoulder height, palms down.
Step 3: At the top of the front raise, without pausing, sweep both arms outward to the sides (lateral raise position) — arms now horizontal, perpendicular to the torso.
Step 4: Lower both arms from the lateral position back to the sides.
Step 5: That is one repetition. Repeat from the front raise.
execution.breathing_instructions: Exhale through the front raise and lateral transition. Inhale lowering.
common_mistakes: Pausing between the front and lateral portion — the complex should flow continuously
Raising too high — shoulder height is the target for both raises
safety_considerations: Very light dumbbells — the continuous nature of the complex creates sustained deltoid demand
Avoid swinging or using momentum
execution.range_of_motion_guidance: Sides to shoulder height (front), then sweep to shoulder height (lateral), then lower.
coaching_cues: Front raise first — then sweep to the sides
No pause at the transition
Own the lower — 2 seconds down from the lateral

name: Dumbbell Halo
description: The dumbbell halo circles a dumbbell around the head in a continuous halo motion, training the shoulder complex and upper back through rotational ranges that standard linear exercises do not reach. It mobilizes the glenohumeral joint and trains the stabilizing rotator cuff and serratus anterior through dynamic control — commonly used as a shoulder warm-up or finisher.

execution.starting_position: Stand with feet shoulder-width apart. Hold a light dumbbell vertically with both hands cupping one end (the other end pointing up). Hold at chest level.
execution.setup_instructions: Use a light dumbbell (5-10 kg). Heavier loads significantly increase the difficulty and risk of losing control.
steps: Step 1: Begin with the dumbbell at chest level.
Step 2: Circle the dumbbell around the head — moving it to one side, overhead, behind the head, and back to the starting side.
Step 3: Complete a full revolution to constitute one rep.
Step 4: Alternate direction every rep or perform sets in one direction.
execution.breathing_instructions: Breathe continuously throughout the circular motion.
common_mistakes: Using too heavy a dumbbell — control and range are more important than load
Moving only the arms while the torso sways — keep the core stable
safety_considerations: Ensure a firm grip — a dumbbell dropped behind the head is dangerous
Avoid if experiencing any neck or shoulder pain during the motion
execution.range_of_motion_guidance: Full circular path around the head — do not reduce the circle.
execution.tempo_recommendations: Slow and controlled, 3-4 seconds per revolution
coaching_cues: Keep the dumbbell close to the head throughout the circle
Core stays braced — only the arms move
Smooth, continuous motion

name: Dumbbell Hex Press
description: A chest press variation where two dumbbells are pressed together throughout the entire movement, maintaining constant medial pressure. This squeeze activates the pectoralis major's adduction function and significantly increases sternal head activation, making it a highly effective inner chest exercise.

execution.starting_position: Lie on a flat bench holding two dumbbells pressed together at chest height with the flat ends facing each other (hence hex).
execution.setup_instructions: Select two hex-sided dumbbells that can be pressed together stably. Lie on a flat bench and press them together.
steps: Step 1: Keep the dumbbells pressed together throughout — do not let them separate.
Step 2: Lower the dumbbells as a single unit to your chest, elbows tucked at about 45 degrees.
Step 3: Press back up to lockout while continuing to squeeze the dumbbells together.
Step 4: Maintain medial pressure throughout the entire set.
execution.breathing_instructions: Inhale on the descent. Exhale on the press.
common_mistakes: Letting the dumbbells separate, reducing the adduction stimulus
Flaring the elbows wide
safety_considerations: Use hex dumbbells or dumbbells with flat sides — round dumbbells will roll and may be unsafe
execution.range_of_motion_guidance: Lower until the dumbbells touch the chest. Full extension at the top.
coaching_cues: Squeeze the dumbbells together the whole time
Inner chest is working

name: Dumbbell Hip Thrust
description: The dumbbell hip thrust is a beginner-friendly alternative to the barbell hip thrust that allows the load to rest comfortably across the hips using one or two dumbbells. The upper back is supported on a bench, and the hips drive upward against the dumbbell's weight. It is easier to set up than the barbell version and allows precise load increments, making it ideal for beginners learning the hip thrust movement pattern.

execution.starting_position: Sit on the floor with the upper back against a flat bench. Place a dumbbell horizontally across the hip crease. Feet flat on the floor, shoulder-width apart.
execution.setup_instructions: Position the bench against a wall so it doesn't slide. Hold the dumbbell in place with both hands during the thrust.
steps: Step 1: Begin with hips low, dumbbell at the hip crease, upper back against the bench.
Step 2: Drive through both heels and squeeze the glutes to extend the hips.
Step 3: Push up until hips are fully extended, body forming a straight line from knees to shoulders.
Step 4: Lower the hips slowly back to the floor and repeat.
execution.breathing_instructions: Exhale on the hip drive up, inhale on the return.
common_mistakes: Hips not fully extending at the top
Dumbbell sliding off the hip crease
Feet too close or too far from the body
safety_considerations: Use a folded towel under the dumbbell for comfort on the hip bones if needed
execution.range_of_motion_guidance: Full hip extension at top without hyperextending the lower back.
coaching_cues: Drive through the heels
Full glute squeeze at the top
Chin stays tucked — don't look at the ceiling

name: Dumbbell Overhead Press
description: The dumbbell overhead press trains the deltoids and triceps in an overhead pressing pattern using independent dumbbells, which allows each arm to move freely and reduces the risk of one side compensating for the other. It can be performed seated or standing, with the seated variation providing lumbar support.

execution.starting_position: Sit on a bench with back support (or stand) holding a dumbbell in each hand at shoulder height. Palms face forward, elbows at approximately 90 degrees and slightly in front of the torso.
execution.setup_instructions: If seated, set the bench back to 90 degrees for spinal support. Use knee-kick technique to bring heavy dumbbells into position.
steps: Press both dumbbells upward and slightly inward until arms are fully extended overhead.
At the top, the dumbbells can touch lightly without clashing.
Lower the dumbbells under control back to shoulder height with elbows at 90 degrees.
execution.breathing_instructions: Exhale on the press. Inhale on the descent.
common_mistakes: Pressing with palms facing each other (neutral grip) reduces anterior delt involvement
Allowing the elbows to flare excessively wide behind the torso
safety_considerations: Avoid if shoulder impingement is present — neutral grip or reduced range may help
Use knee-kick technique to avoid shoulder injury when loading heavy dumbbells
execution.range_of_motion_guidance: Full extension overhead, return to 90-degree elbow angle at the bottom.
coaching_cues: Press up and in slightly — finish with biceps close to your ears
Keep your ribcage down — do not flare it to fake overhead mobility

name: Dumbbell Straight-Arm Pullover
description: The dumbbell straight-arm pullover is a classic exercise that places a deep stretch on the chest and lats as the arms arc behind the head. When performed with a focus on the chest and ribs flaring, it stimulates the sternal head of the pectoralis major and the serratus anterior in a range of motion not achievable with most pressing movements.

execution.starting_position: Lie across a flat bench with only your upper back and shoulders supported. Hold a single dumbbell by one end with both hands, arms extended above the chest.
execution.setup_instructions: Position yourself perpendicular or along the bench so your upper back is supported. Hips may hang lower than the bench. Grasp the dumbbell with both hands overlapping around the top weight plate.
steps: Step 1: Begin with arms extended above your chest, slight bend at the elbows.
Step 2: Slowly lower the dumbbell in an arc behind your head, keeping the arms as straight as possible.
Step 3: Lower until a stretch is felt through the chest and lats, typically when the arms are parallel to the floor or slightly below.
Step 4: Squeeze the chest and arc the dumbbell back over the face to the starting position.
Step 5: Focus on a smooth, controlled arc — not a pulldown.
execution.breathing_instructions: Inhale as you lower the dumbbell behind your head. Exhale as you return it to the starting position.
common_mistakes: Bending the elbows too much, turning it into a triceps extension
Going too heavy and losing control at the bottom
Dropping the hips during the movement
safety_considerations: Avoid this exercise with any shoulder impingement or injury
Use a moderate weight — excessive load stresses the glenohumeral joint
Keep the core engaged to prevent lower back arching
execution.range_of_motion_guidance: Lower the dumbbell until a comfortable chest and lat stretch is achieved. Never force the arms past a point of shoulder discomfort.
coaching_cues: Breathe deeply as you lower — let the ribcage expand
Feel the stretch from armpit to armpit
Drive the dumbbell back with the chest, not the arms

name: Dumbbell Romanian Deadlift
description: The dumbbell Romanian deadlift trains the hamstrings and glutes in the same hip-hinge pattern as the barbell version but with independent dumbbells that allow each limb to move freely. The dumbbells can be held in front of the thighs or to the sides, and the movement is a good introduction to the hip-hinge pattern before progressing to a barbell.

execution.starting_position: Stand with feet hip-width apart holding a dumbbell in each hand in front of the thighs. Spine neutral, chest up.
execution.setup_instructions: Hold the dumbbells with palms facing the thighs. Engage lats and brace before each rep.
steps: Push the hips backward while maintaining a slight knee bend.
Lower the dumbbells along the front of the legs, keeping the spine neutral.
Descend until a hamstring stretch is felt, then drive the hips forward to return to standing.
execution.breathing_instructions: Inhale on descent, exhale on the hip drive upward.
common_mistakes: Rounding the lower back
Bending the knees too much
safety_considerations: Focus on the hip hinge pattern before adding significant load
execution.range_of_motion_guidance: Lower until a hamstring stretch is felt — typically around knee to mid-shin level.
coaching_cues: Push your hips back as if closing a car door with your glutes
Keep the dumbbells close to your legs — drag them down the thighs

name: Single-Arm Dumbbell Row
description: The single-arm dumbbell row is a unilateral horizontal pulling exercise. With one hand and knee braced on a bench, the lifter rows a dumbbell toward the hip with the working arm. The unilateral setup allows a greater range of motion than bilateral rows and helps correct strength imbalances between sides.

execution.starting_position: Place one hand and the same-side knee on a flat bench, forming a stable support. Hold a dumbbell in the opposite hand with arm hanging straight down toward the floor. Keep the spine neutral and parallel to the floor.
execution.setup_instructions: Position the supporting hand and knee so the torso is flat. The foot of the working side should be flat on the floor beside the bench.
steps: With the core braced and spine neutral, row the dumbbell toward your hip by driving the elbow toward the ceiling.
At the top, squeeze the shoulder blade toward the spine and hold briefly.
Lower the dumbbell under control to the starting position with full arm extension.
execution.breathing_instructions: Exhale on the row, inhale on the descent.
common_mistakes: Rotating the torso aggressively to gain momentum
Pulling the dumbbell toward the shoulder instead of the hip
Not fully extending the arm at the bottom
safety_considerations: Ensure the supporting knee and hand are firmly planted to avoid lower back strain
execution.range_of_motion_guidance: Full arm extension at the bottom, upper arm at or above parallel at the top.
coaching_cues: Drive your elbow toward the ceiling, not your hand
Think about putting the dumbbell in your back pocket

name: Dumbbell Shrug
description: The dumbbell shrug is a trapezius isolation exercise where dumbbells are held at the sides and the shoulders are elevated (shrugged) upward toward the ears. The upper trapezius is the primary mover responsible for scapular elevation. Dumbbells allow a natural path of motion and can be rotated during the shrug for a variation that also engages the mid-trapezius.

execution.starting_position: Stand upright holding a dumbbell in each hand at the sides, arms fully extended. Feet shoulder-width apart. Shoulders are in a neutral, depressed position.
execution.setup_instructions: Select appropriately heavy dumbbells. Stand tall with good posture before beginning.
steps: Step 1: Hold dumbbells at the sides with arms fully extended. Stand tall, shoulders neutral.
Step 2: Exhale and elevate both shoulders straight upward toward the ears as high as possible.
Step 3: Hold the peak shrug for 1 second.
Step 4: Inhale and lower the shoulders back to the starting neutral position.
execution.breathing_instructions: Exhale on the shrug upward; inhale on the return.
common_mistakes: Rolling the shoulders forward or backward — shrug straight up, not in a circle
Using heavy weight that reduces range of motion — prioritize full elevation
safety_considerations: Keep the neck long — do not let the head jut forward as the shoulders rise
execution.range_of_motion_guidance: Elevate fully to the ears; return to fully depressed and neutral position.
coaching_cues: Shrug straight up — not forward, not back, not in a circle
Feel the traps 'peaking' at the top of each rep

name: Dumbbell Side Bend
description: The dumbbell side bend trains lateral flexion of the spine against a unilateral resistance load, primarily targeting the obliques and quadratus lumborum on the working side while the contralateral side resists gravitational pull isometrically. The exercise is commonly performed with a single dumbbell in one hand, allowing a full lateral range of motion. It is important to perform the exercise bilaterally to avoid asymmetrical development.

execution.starting_position: Stand upright holding a dumbbell in one hand at the side, feet shoulder-width apart, free hand placed lightly behind the head or on the hip.
execution.setup_instructions: Choose a moderate weight — excessive load encourages compensation through the hips rather than pure lateral spinal flexion.
steps: Step 1: Stand tall with the dumbbell at the side, spine neutral.
Step 2: Laterally flex the spine toward the dumbbell side, lowering the weight along the outer thigh.
Step 3: Return to upright by contracting the opposite-side obliques.
Step 4: Optionally continue past neutral to the opposite side for a full range of motion bend.
Step 5: Complete all reps then switch the dumbbell to the other hand.
execution.breathing_instructions: Inhale at neutral. Exhale as returning to upright.
common_mistakes: Bending forward or backward instead of purely laterally
Rotating the torso — the movement should be in the frontal plane only
safety_considerations: Use controlled movement — avoid lateral flexion under load with momentum
execution.range_of_motion_guidance: Full comfortable lateral flexion range on each side. Quality of movement over depth.
coaching_cues: Slide the dumbbell down the leg — no rotation
Think of your spine as a hinge opening sideways

name: Dumbbell Windmill
description: A windmill movement performed with a dumbbell held overhead in one hand. The hips shift laterally while the torso hinges sideways, lowering the free hand toward the floor. This develops lateral hip mobility, oblique strength, and shoulder stability simultaneously.

execution.starting_position: Set up for Dumbbell Windmill in proper position.
execution.setup_instructions: Prepare body and equipment for Dumbbell Windmill.
steps: Step 1: Hold dumbbell overhead in one hand, feet wider than shoulder-width.
Step 2: Rotate toes of lower foot 45 degrees outward.
Step 3: Shift hips toward the weighted side, hinging torso sideways.
Step 4: Lower free hand down leg toward floor while keeping overhead arm straight.
execution.breathing_instructions: Breathe steadily; never hold breath during static holds.
common_mistakes: Rotating torso forward instead of lateral hinge
Losing overhead arm position
safety_considerations: Build prerequisite strength before attempting advanced variations.
Stop if joint pain occurs.
execution.range_of_motion_guidance: Full range of motion with control at all times.
coaching_cues: Hinge sideways, not forward
Eyes track the dumbbell overhead

name: Earthquake Bar Bench Press
description: The earthquake bar (or bamboo bar) bench press uses a highly flexible bar with plates or kettlebells hanging from bands at each end. The hanging load swings and oscillates continuously throughout the lift, creating unpredictable oscillating kinetic energy (OKE) that the nervous system and stabilizing muscles must dampen. This dramatically increases rotator cuff and periscapular muscle activation compared to a standard barbell press with the same weight. It is used by powerlifters, Olympic athletes, and rehabilitation specialists for shoulder stability development.

execution.starting_position: Lie on a flat bench with the earthquake bar racked above. The hanging kettlebells or plates should be allowed to swing freely from the band attachments. Unrack the bar and allow it to settle before beginning the first repetition.
execution.setup_instructions: Earthquake bars are specialty equipment. Bands must be attached to the ends of the bar and kettlebells or small plates hang from the bands. Use significantly less load than your standard bench press — the instability demands more from the stabilizers than the prime movers.
steps: Step 1: Unrack the bar and allow the oscillations to settle partially. Keep the arms rigid.
Step 2: Lower the bar slowly to the chest, managing the oscillating load throughout the descent.
Step 3: Press the bar back to the starting position, maintaining control of the oscillating kettlebells throughout.
Step 4: Rerack carefully, ensuring the hanging load is controlled before racking.
execution.breathing_instructions: Inhale and brace during the descent. Exhale during the press.
common_mistakes: Using too much weight — the earthquake bar exercise is primarily a stability and motor control challenge
Trying to stop the oscillation completely — focus on managing it, not eliminating it
Pressing too fast, which amplifies oscillation and reduces control
safety_considerations: This is advanced equipment — learn the standard barbell bench press first
Have a spotter who understands the oscillating nature of the load
Start with kettlebells of 8-12 kg each, regardless of your standard bench press strength
execution.range_of_motion_guidance: Full range: bar to chest, full extension at the top.
execution.tempo_recommendations: 3s eccentric, 1s pause at chest, 2s press. Slow tempo reduces oscillation amplitude.
coaching_cues: Think of dampening the oscillation, not stopping it
Keep the shoulder blades retracted and depressed throughout the entire set
Slow is better — faster pressing creates more instability than you can manage initially

name: Cable External Rotation
description: The cable external rotation targets the external rotators of the shoulder — primarily the infraspinatus and teres minor — using a cable machine at elbow height. The cable maintains continuous tension through the full arc of motion unlike rubber bands or manual resistance, providing a consistent training stimulus to the rotator cuff throughout the range. It is a cornerstone exercise for rotator cuff health, shoulder injury prevention, and rehabilitation.

execution.starting_position: Stand beside a cable machine with the pulley set at elbow height. Grip the handle with the inside hand. The upper arm is at the side, elbow bent to 90 degrees, forearm pointing toward the cable machine.
execution.setup_instructions: Keep a small towel or folded pad tucked between the elbow and the torso to maintain the upper arm position throughout the movement.
steps: Step 1: Stand with the cable at elbow height, grip the handle with the inside hand.
Step 2: Bend the elbow to 90 degrees, upper arm at the side.
Step 3: Rotate the forearm outward (away from the body) while keeping the upper arm stationary.
Step 4: Rotate until the forearm is pointing forward or slightly past neutral.
Step 5: Return under full control to the starting position.
execution.breathing_instructions: Breathe naturally throughout — this is a low-load exercise.
common_mistakes: Allowing the elbow to lift away from the side — the upper arm must remain still
Using too heavy a weight, which causes shoulder shrugging or body rotation
safety_considerations: Very light loads only — this is a targeted rotator cuff exercise, not a strength movement
execution.range_of_motion_guidance: From internal rotation (forearm toward cable) to external rotation (forearm pointing forward or beyond neutral).
coaching_cues: Elbow stays glued to your side
Rotate from the shoulder only
Light and controlled — rotator cuff work

name: Side-Lying External Rotation
description: The side-lying dumbbell external rotation is a classic rotator cuff exercise performed lying on one side, rotating a dumbbell upward from a position of internal rotation to external rotation with the elbow bent to 90 degrees. The gravity-resisted motion precisely isolates the infraspinatus and teres minor throughout the full range, as the body position eliminates most compensatory movements. It is widely prescribed for rotator cuff rehabilitation and shoulder health maintenance.

execution.starting_position: Lie on one side with the bottom arm supporting the head. Hold a light dumbbell in the top hand with the elbow bent to 90 degrees and the forearm pointing toward the floor (internally rotated position).
execution.setup_instructions: Use extremely light dumbbells — 2.5-5 lbs is typically sufficient. A small rolled towel under the elbow can help maintain proper positioning.
steps: Step 1: Lie on your side, top elbow bent at 90 degrees, forearm pointing to the floor.
Step 2: Keep the elbow against the side of the torso throughout.
Step 3: Rotate the forearm upward toward the ceiling (external rotation).
Step 4: Rotate as far as comfortable — typically until the forearm is perpendicular to the floor or slightly past.
Step 5: Lower slowly back to the starting position.
execution.breathing_instructions: Breathe naturally throughout — this is a low-load exercise.
common_mistakes: Using too heavy a dumbbell — technique breaks down immediately
Letting the elbow drift away from the body during rotation
safety_considerations: If there is any pain in the shoulder, stop immediately and consult a healthcare professional
execution.range_of_motion_guidance: From internal rotation (forearm toward floor) to external rotation (forearm toward ceiling, up to 90 degrees of rotation).
coaching_cues: Elbow stays at your side — only the forearm moves
Rotate up slowly
This is rehab work — quality over load

name: EZ-Bar Curl
description: The EZ-bar curl is a barbell curl variation using the angled cambered EZ-curl bar, which places the wrists in a semi-supinated position that reduces ulnar deviation stress compared to a straight bar. This grip positioning strongly activates the brachialis alongside the biceps brachii, and is often considered more joint-friendly for lifters who experience wrist or elbow discomfort with straight-bar curls.

execution.starting_position: Stand upright holding the EZ-bar using the inner angled grip, wrists in a semi-supinated (angled) position. Arms fully extended, bar at hip level.
execution.setup_instructions: Load the EZ-curl bar with appropriate weight. Grip the inner angled portion of the bar with both hands for the standard semi-supinated grip. Stand with feet shoulder-width apart.
steps: Step 1: Hold the EZ-bar at arm's length with the inner angled grip. Stand tall with the core braced.
Step 2: Keep the elbows pinned at the sides — they should not travel forward.
Step 3: Exhale and curl the bar upward in an arc until it reaches approximately shoulder level and the biceps are fully contracted.
Step 4: Inhale and lower the bar in a controlled arc back to the starting position.
execution.breathing_instructions: Exhale on the curl up; inhale on the controlled lowering.
common_mistakes: Letting the elbows travel forward significantly as the bar rises, which recruits the anterior deltoid
Swinging the torso to generate momentum — the movement should be strict
safety_considerations: If wrist discomfort occurs with the inner grip, try the outer angled grip
Avoid hyperextending the elbows at the bottom of each rep
execution.range_of_motion_guidance: Full extension at the bottom; curl to full bicep contraction at the top.
coaching_cues: Elbows stay at your sides — curl the weight, do not swing it
Squeeze at the top before lowering slowly

name: EZ Bar Preacher Curl 21s
description: A preacher curl 21s protocol using an EZ bar on a preacher bench. The preacher bench eliminates cheating by fixing the upper arm against the pad, and the 21s protocol applies partial and full-range stress to maximize bicep time under tension.

execution.starting_position: Sit at a preacher bench with the upper arms firmly against the angled pad. Grip an EZ bar with an underhand grip.
execution.setup_instructions: Set up the preacher bench. Load a light EZ bar. Position upper arms on the pad.
steps: Step 1 (reps 1-7): Curl from full extension to the halfway point (forearms parallel to floor). Return and repeat 7 times.
Step 2 (reps 8-14): Start from the halfway point and curl to full contraction. Return to halfway and repeat 7 times.
Step 3 (reps 15-21): Perform 7 full-range reps from full extension to full contraction.
execution.breathing_instructions: Exhale on each curl, inhale on each lowering.
common_mistakes: Lifting the upper arms off the pad to assist the movement
Using too heavy a weight
safety_considerations: Upper arms must remain on the pad throughout — the pad is the stabilizer
execution.range_of_motion_guidance: Full extension (arms straight) in segment 1. Full contraction in segment 2 and 3.
coaching_cues: Upper arms stay on the pad
Feel the bottom stretch in segment 1

name: Face Pull
description: The face pull is a cable pulling exercise targeting the rear deltoids, infraspinatus, teres minor, and middle trapezius. It trains the muscles responsible for shoulder external rotation and horizontal abduction, which are often underdeveloped relative to pressing muscles. Regular face pulls support shoulder health and posture.

execution.starting_position: Set a rope attachment on a high cable pulley at face height. Stand back far enough that the cable is taut at arm's length. Hold one end of the rope in each hand with a neutral grip.
execution.setup_instructions: Use a rope attachment for maximum external rotation. Keep the elbows elevated — at or above shoulder height throughout the pull.
steps: With elbows elevated, pull the rope toward your face, separating your hands as you pull.
Externally rotate the shoulders at the peak so your hands end up beside your ears or behind your head.
Squeeze the rear delts and rotator cuff muscles hard at the peak contraction.
Return the rope to the starting position with control.
execution.breathing_instructions: Exhale as you pull toward your face. Inhale on the return.
common_mistakes: Letting the elbows drop below shoulder height, shifting the movement toward a row
Using excessive weight that compromises elbow position
Not externally rotating at the end of the movement
safety_considerations: This exercise is typically used as a corrective and accessory movement — do not load it heavily
Focus on quality of movement over load
execution.range_of_motion_guidance: Pull until hands are beside the ears with elbows flared and upper arms horizontal.
coaching_cues: Lead with your elbows — keep them up
Think about putting your thumbs behind your ears at the peak

name: Face Pull with External Rotation
description: A cable face pull variation where the hands are pulled to face level and then actively rotated outward at the end of the movement. The external rotation component powerfully targets the infraspinatus, teres minor, and rear deltoids, making this one of the most effective exercises for shoulder health, posture correction, and rotator cuff strengthening.

execution.starting_position: Stand facing a high cable pulley with a rope attachment at face height. Grip both ends of the rope with palms facing inward.
execution.setup_instructions: Attach a rope to the high cable pulley set at upper chest or face height. Stand back enough to create tension with arms extended.
steps: Step 1: Pull the rope toward your face, allowing the elbows to flare out to the sides.
Step 2: As the rope reaches face level, rotate the hands outward so the knuckles point toward the ceiling.
Step 3: Hold the peak contraction briefly, squeezing the rear delts and rotator cuff.
Step 4: Return to the starting position under control.
execution.breathing_instructions: Exhale during the pull and rotation. Inhale on the return.
common_mistakes: Pulling too heavy and using momentum
Skipping the external rotation component at the end
safety_considerations: Use a light weight to ensure full range and proper activation
This exercise is excellent for shoulder health — program it regularly
execution.range_of_motion_guidance: Full extension at the start. Rope pulled to face level with hands rotated outward at the end.
coaching_cues: Pull to the face, then rotate the hands out
Light weight, full range

name: Band Face Pull
description: The band face pull is a rehabilitation exercise for the posterior deltoid, infraspinatus, and middle trapezius, performed by pulling a resistance band toward the face with elbows flared high. It directly counteracts the internal rotation and forward shoulder posture associated with heavy pressing and prolonged sitting. It is used in rotator cuff rehabilitation, shoulder impingement treatment, and general shoulder health maintenance.

execution.starting_position: Anchor the resistance band loop at face height or slightly above. Grip the band with both hands using a neutral or overhand grip, arms extended in front at shoulder height.
execution.setup_instructions: Anchor the band at a door frame, rack, or any stable point at face height. Stand far enough back to have tension in the band with arms extended.
steps: Step 1: Hold the band with both hands at shoulder width, arms extended toward the anchor.
Step 2: Pull the band toward the face, leading with the elbows flared outward and upward.
Step 3: As the hands approach the face, externally rotate the shoulders so the hands splay outward and the elbows point to the sides.
Step 4: Hold briefly at full contraction — elbows should be at or above shoulder height and hands near the temples.
Step 5: Slowly extend the arms back to the start under control.
execution.breathing_instructions: Exhale as you pull toward the face. Inhale on the return.
common_mistakes: Keeping the elbows low — elbows must flare high to recruit the posterior rotator cuff
Pulling toward the neck or chest instead of the face
Excessive torso lean or momentum from the lower body
safety_considerations: Use a light band for rehabilitation — this is a high-rep, low-load exercise
If impingement symptoms occur with elbows high, temporarily reduce elbow height
execution.range_of_motion_guidance: Full extension of the arms at the start, full retraction with elbows flared and hands near face at the end.
coaching_cues: Lead with the elbows — pull them back and apart
Think about showing your armpits at the top
Squeeze the shoulder blades together at the end of each rep

name: Face Pull with External Rotation
description: The face pull with external rotation is an enhanced variation of the standard face pull that adds an external rotation of the shoulder at the end of the pulling motion. By pulling the rope to the face level and then rotating the forearms upward and back, it simultaneously trains the posterior deltoid, rotator cuff external rotators, and middle trapezius, making it one of the most comprehensive exercises for shoulder health and long-term pressing longevity.

execution.starting_position: Attach a rope to a high-pulley cable machine at face height. Grip the rope with both hands, palms facing each other. Stand back enough to create tension with arms extended toward the cable.
execution.setup_instructions: Set the cable pulley to approximately eye or forehead level. Attach a rope attachment. Use a light to moderate weight — form matters more than load here.
steps: Step 1: Grip the rope with both hands. Step back so the cable is under tension. Elbows slightly bent at the start.
Step 2: Pull the rope toward the face by driving the elbows out and back, aiming to pull the hands to either side of the face.
Step 3: At the end of the pull, externally rotate the shoulders by pulling the forearms and hands upward and back — the forearms should now point toward the ceiling.
Step 4: Pause at the top, squeezing the rear delts and infraspinatus, then return slowly to the start.
execution.breathing_instructions: Exhale as you pull and rotate; inhale on the return.
common_mistakes: Skipping the external rotation component at the end of the pull
Using too heavy a weight, which causes the torso to rock backward
safety_considerations: Keep the cable at face height — not overhead — to protect the shoulder
Light weight is recommended; heavy loads undermine the form
execution.range_of_motion_guidance: Pull until the hands reach the sides of the face; then rotate forearms fully upward.
coaching_cues: Pull to your ears, not your chin
Finish with forearms pointing to the ceiling — that is the external rotation you want

name: Farmer's Carry
description: The farmer's carry is a full-body loaded carry exercise in which the athlete holds heavy weights in both hands at their sides and walks for a prescribed distance or duration. It develops grip strength, trapezius endurance, anti-lateral flexion core strength, and cardiovascular capacity simultaneously. The exercise mimics the movement pattern of carrying heavy objects in daily life and strongly transfers to general physical preparedness and work capacity.

execution.starting_position: Stand tall with a dumbbell, kettlebell, or trap bar handle in each hand, arms at your sides. Feet shoulder-width apart.
execution.setup_instructions: Select weights that allow a walking pace while maintaining posture. Begin with a clear path of at least 20–30 meters.
steps: Step 1: Pick up the implements with a firm grip, one in each hand.
Step 2: Stand tall: chest up, shoulders back and down, core braced.
Step 3: Walk forward at a controlled pace with short, deliberate steps.
Step 4: Maintain an upright torso throughout — do not lean to either side.
Step 5: Set the weights down with control at the end of the prescribed distance.
execution.breathing_instructions: Breathe continuously with a moderate brace. Avoid holding the breath for the entire carry duration.
common_mistakes: Shrugging the shoulders excessively — the traps are loaded but the shoulders should be retracted and depressed, not elevated
Leaning to one side due to unbalanced loads
Taking overly long strides that cause trunk rotation
safety_considerations: Ensure the floor is clear of obstacles.
Pick up and set down the implements with a hip-hinge pattern — not a rounded back.
execution.range_of_motion_guidance: Walk 20–50 meters per set, or for 30–60 seconds. Load and distance are primary variables.
execution.tempo_recommendations: Moderate walking pace. Focus on posture and grip endurance.
coaching_cues: Stand tall — imagine a string pulling the crown of your head to the ceiling
Pack your shoulders back and down
Crush the handles

name: Farmer's Walk / Farmer's Carry
description: The farmer's walk involves gripping a heavy implement in each hand — typically farmer's walk handles, dumbbells, or kettlebells — and walking a prescribed distance under that loaded bilateral carry. It simultaneously trains grip strength, trapezius endurance, core anti-lateral flexion stability, and cardiovascular capacity, making it one of the most efficient total-body strength and conditioning exercises available. The bilateral loaded carry pattern has direct functional carryover to any task requiring the transport of heavy objects.

execution.starting_position: The implements are placed on the floor on either side of the body. Stand between them in an athletic stance. Hinge at the hips and grip one implement in each hand.
execution.setup_instructions: Choose a weight that allows an upright walking posture — if the torso is visibly leaning laterally, the weight is too heavy. For farmer's walk handles (competition equipment), load plates evenly on both sides.
steps: Step 1: Deadlift both implements from the floor simultaneously. Stand tall with the implements hanging at the sides.
Step 2: Brace the core, retract the shoulder blades, and begin walking with controlled, quick steps.
Step 3: Maintain an upright torso throughout the walk. Resist lateral lean from the weight.
Step 4: Keep the gaze forward and walk at a brisk pace for the target distance.
Step 5: At the end of the distance, slow down, then hinge at the hips to lower the implements to the floor safely.
execution.breathing_instructions: Breathe short and regularly throughout the carry. Do not hold the breath for extended durations — take controlled breaths every 2–3 steps.
common_mistakes: Letting the shoulders round forward and down, which loses trap tension and can strain the shoulder girdle
Walking with long, slow strides — shorter, quicker steps are more stable and efficient
Looking down, which causes spinal flexion and balance disruption
safety_considerations: If the grip fails during the walk, let the implements drop to the sides — do not attempt to catch them awkwardly
Clear the walking path before beginning — trip hazards are especially dangerous under heavy bilateral loading
execution.range_of_motion_guidance: Walk 20–50 metres per set for training. Competition distances vary (15–25 metres for single lengths). Grip the implement firmly throughout.
execution.tempo_recommendations: Strength carry: 20–30m × 4–6 sets at heavy load. Conditioning carry: 40–60m at moderate load × 4–6 sets. Rest 90–120 seconds between sets.
coaching_cues: Stand tall — imagine a rod through the spine
Quick feet, not big strides
Crush the handles and retract the shoulder blades

name: Farmers Walk with Axle Bar and Hanging Plates
description: A farmers walk using an axle bar (thick bar) with plates hung from chains rather than loaded directly on the bar. The hanging plates oscillate during the walk, creating a dynamic stability challenge not present with standard farmers walk implements. This builds extraordinary grip and core strength.

execution.starting_position: Set up for Farmers Walk with Axle Bar and Hanging Plates in proper strongman position.
execution.setup_instructions: Prepare all equipment and body position for Farmers Walk with Axle Bar and Hanging Plates.
steps: Step 1: Set up axle bar with plates hanging from chains at appropriate height.
Step 2: Grip bar with both hands using double overhand grip.
Step 3: Deadlift bar and walk with control, managing plate oscillation.
Step 4: Set down carefully as oscillating plates make lowering challenging.
execution.breathing_instructions: Brace core maximally before every lift. Breathe between reps if needed.
common_mistakes: Walking too fast increasing oscillation
Soft grip on thick axle
safety_considerations: Use collars on all loaded barbells.
Ensure clear path for carries.
Have spotters for overhead movements.
execution.range_of_motion_guidance: Full range of motion specific to the implement being used.
coaching_cues: Smooth controlled steps minimize swing
Crush grip on axle throughout

name: Farmer's Walk on Heels
description: A farmer's carry variation performed entirely on the heels, with the forefoot elevated off the floor throughout the walk. This unusual position forces sustained contraction of the tibialis anterior and ankle dorsiflexors while simultaneously loading the grip and core through the weighted carry. Used in tibialis anterior rehabilitation, shin splint prevention, anterior compartment strengthening, and foot drop recovery programs. The loaded walking component adds cardiovascular and grip demand to the tibialis training.

execution.starting_position: Pick up a dumbbell or kettlebell in each hand. Rise onto the heels by pulling the toes and forefoot up into dorsiflexion, lifting the forefoot entirely off the floor.
execution.setup_instructions: Begin unloaded to practice the heel-walking gait before adding implements. Choose a weight that allows heel-only contact for the entire carry distance.
steps: Step 1: Pick up the implements and immediately dorsiflex the ankles to raise the forefoot.
Step 2: Walk forward entirely on the heels, with the toes and forefoot elevated throughout.
Step 3: Keep the shoulders packed, core braced, and gaze forward.
Step 4: Walk the prescribed distance, then lower the forefeet back to the floor safely before setting the weights down.
execution.breathing_instructions: Breathe rhythmically throughout. The effort is sustained — do not hold your breath.
common_mistakes: Allowing the forefoot to contact the floor during the walk — the dorsiflexion must be sustained the entire distance
Using too heavy a weight that makes maintaining the heel-only position impossible
Leaning backward excessively to shift weight onto the heels
safety_considerations: This exercise requires good ankle dorsiflexion range — assess range before loading
Avoid on slippery surfaces
For foot drop rehabilitation, begin without weights and shorter distances
execution.range_of_motion_guidance: Maximum dorsiflexion sustained throughout the carry. No forefoot contact.
execution.tempo_recommendations: Walk at approximately 1 step per second. Focus on maintaining dorsiflexion over speed.
coaching_cues: Pull the toes up hard and keep them up — the forefoot never touches the floor
Walk tall — do not lean back excessively to put weight on the heels
Feel the outer shin burning — that is the tibialis anterior at work

name: Farmer's Walk on Toes — Calf and Grip
description: A farmer's carry variation performed on the balls of the feet (tiptoe), combining loaded carry with continuous calf raise demands. Walking with heavy weights while staying elevated on the toes dramatically increases the sustained contraction demand on the gastrocnemius and soleus, while also loading the forearms and core. This exercise builds functional calf endurance, ankle stability, and grip strength simultaneously.

execution.starting_position: Stand with a dumbbell or kettlebell in each hand at your sides. Rise onto the balls of both feet, maintaining the elevated position throughout the exercise.
execution.setup_instructions: Choose a weight that allows you to maintain tiptoe position for the full distance. Clear a straight path of at least 10-15 meters.
steps: Step 1: Pick up the implements and rise onto the balls of the feet, maintaining a tall posture.
Step 2: Walk forward in controlled steps while remaining elevated on the toes.
Step 3: Keep the shoulders packed, core braced, and gaze forward throughout.
Step 4: Walk the prescribed distance, set the weights down safely, and rest before repeating.
execution.breathing_instructions: Breathe rhythmically throughout. Do not hold your breath during the carry.
common_mistakes: Heel striking during the walk — heels must stay elevated the entire distance
Leaning forward excessively with the torso
Using too heavy a weight that forces heel contact
safety_considerations: Reduce weight or distance if ankle stability is compromised
Avoid on slippery surfaces
Consult a physiotherapist if used for Achilles tendinopathy rehabilitation — load must be appropriate
execution.range_of_motion_guidance: Maintain maximum plantarflexion (full tiptoe) throughout the entire distance.
execution.tempo_recommendations: Walk at a controlled pace — approximately 1 step per second
coaching_cues: Stay up on the balls of the feet — heels never touch the floor
Pack the shoulders — do not let them rise toward the ears
Brace the core as if bracing for a punch

name: Fat Bar Bent-Over Row
description: A barbell bent-over row performed with a thick-diameter bar (fat bar or axle bar, typically 2-inch diameter versus the standard 1-inch). The increased diameter forces the hands to remain in a more neutral, open grip position and dramatically increases the demand on the forearm flexors and grip musculature to maintain hold of the bar throughout the row. The back and lat mechanics are identical to a standard bent-over row, but the grip limitation often becomes the performance-limiting factor. Used in grip-strength development programs, strongman training, and as a plateau-breaking variation for intermediate lifters.

execution.starting_position: Load a fat bar or axle bar and position it on the floor or in a rack at a pulling height. Hinge at the hips to 45-70 degrees torso inclination with the bar hanging at arm's length.
execution.setup_instructions: No straps — the entire point of the fat bar variation is grip development. Expect to use less weight than a standard barbell row. The thicker bar requires a more open hand position.
steps: Step 1: Grip the fat bar with an overhand or underhand grip, hands just outside hip width. Hinge to the rowing position with a neutral spine.
Step 2: Row the bar toward the lower sternum or navel by driving the elbows back and squeezing the shoulder blades.
Step 3: Hold at the top of the row for 1 second, feeling the lats and mid-back contract.
Step 4: Lower the bar under control to full arm extension. Maintain a firm grip throughout.
execution.breathing_instructions: Brace the core and inhale before initiating the row. Exhale forcefully at the top. Inhale as you lower the bar.
common_mistakes: Using straps — this negates the purpose of the fat bar
Gripping with just the fingers instead of the full hand — wrap the whole hand around the bar
Rounding the lower back due to the grip failing — reduce weight before this occurs
safety_considerations: The grip will fatigue faster than the back — stop the set when grip fails rather than compromising spinal position
Ensure the bar has consistent knurling or texture to maintain grip safety
