execution.range_of_motion_guidance: Full elbow extension at the bottom. Bar touches or nearly touches the torso at the top.
execution.tempo_recommendations: 1s pull, 1s hold at top, 3s controlled eccentric.
coaching_cues: Squeeze the bar as hard as possible — the fat diameter requires maximum grip tension
Lead with the elbows, not the hands
Think chest to the bar, not bar to the chest — keep the torso still

name: Feet-Elevated Dumbbell Flye
description: A dumbbell flye performed with the feet elevated on a bench to place the body in a slight decline position, shifting the stretch and contraction emphasis toward the lower and sternal fibers of the pectoralis major. The decline angle changes the direction of force relative to the lower chest muscle fibers, providing targeted isolation of the lower pectoral region.

execution.starting_position: Lie on a flat bench with feet elevated on a box or second bench. Hold a dumbbell in each hand above the chest, arms extended with a slight elbow bend, palms facing each other.
execution.setup_instructions: Set up a flat bench with a box or second flat bench of similar height for feet. Select dumbbells appropriate for a flye movement (lighter than pressing weight).
steps: Step 1: Begin with arms extended above the lower chest, dumbbells nearly touching, palms facing each other.
Step 2: Lower dumbbells out to the sides in a wide arc, maintaining the fixed elbow bend. Feel a deep stretch in the lower chest.
Step 3: Reverse the arc, driving the dumbbells back together above the chest.
Step 4: Squeeze the pectorals at the top and repeat.
execution.breathing_instructions: Inhale as you lower the dumbbells to the sides. Exhale as you bring them back together.
common_mistakes: Letting the elbows bend excessively, turning it into a press
Lowering too fast with heavy dumbbells, risking shoulder strain
Feet slipping off the elevated surface during the set
safety_considerations: Keep elbows slightly bent and fixed — do not straighten them
Use a conservative weight until the shoulder feels stable in this decline angle
execution.range_of_motion_guidance: Open to full stretch where shoulder allows, closing fully at top with dumbbells almost touching.
coaching_cues: Bend in the elbows stays exactly the same the whole way
Think of your arms as the arms of a clock sweeping from 10 and 2 to 12

name: Feet-Elevated Ring Push-Up
description: A challenging combination of ring instability and decline body angle that shifts the loading emphasis toward the upper and clavicular portions of the pectoralis major. With feet elevated on a bench and hands in gymnastic rings, the athlete must simultaneously stabilize the unstable rings and generate pressing force, creating significant demands on the chest, anterior deltoid, and scapular stabilizers.

execution.starting_position: Set rings at approximately knee height. Place feet on a sturdy bench behind you, hands in rings below your shoulders. Body forms a decline plank position with arms extended.
execution.setup_instructions: Secure rings at a consistent height. The elevation of the feet relative to hand height determines the degree of decline. Set rings close together (shoulder width) for more chest emphasis.
steps: Step 1: Begin in the top position with arms extended, body forming a straight inclined plank from feet (elevated) to hands (rings below).
Step 2: Lower your chest toward the rings, allowing elbows to flare slightly while keeping rings stable.
Step 3: Descend until chest is level with or just below the rings.
Step 4: Press powerfully back to the starting position, squeezing the chest at the top.
execution.breathing_instructions: Inhale on descent, exhale on the press upward.
common_mistakes: Letting the rings wobble uncontrollably — build ring stability before adding feet elevation
Pike hips to reduce difficulty, breaking the straight line
Flaring elbows excessively causing shoulder impingement
safety_considerations: Establish proficiency with flat ring push-ups before elevating feet
Ensure the bench is stable and will not slide when feet are placed on it
execution.range_of_motion_guidance: Full range from arms extended to chest at ring level. Turn rings out slightly at top position (rings turn out or RTO) to increase pectoral contraction.
execution.tempo_recommendations: 3-1-1-1 (3s descent, 1s pause at bottom, 1s press, 1s RTO hold)
coaching_cues: Turn the rings out at the top — externally rotate wrists
Keep the body in one rigid plank — no sagging or piking

name: Figure-Four Stretch
description: The figure-four stretch is a supine alternative to pigeon pose that stretches the hip external rotators and gluteus maximus without the knee torque risk. Lying on the back with one ankle crossed over the opposite knee creates a 'figure four' shape, and pressing the thigh away provides a gentle but effective stretch for the piriformis and deep hip rotators. It is suitable for a wide population including those with knee sensitivity.

execution.starting_position: Lie on your back with knees bent and feet flat on the floor.
execution.setup_instructions: Use a mat for comfort. No equipment needed.
steps: Step 1: Lie on your back with knees bent, feet flat on the floor.
Step 2: Cross the left ankle over the right knee, creating a figure-four shape with the legs.
Step 3: Flex the left foot to protect the knee joint.
Step 4: Reach through or around the legs and grasp the right thigh, drawing it toward the chest.
Step 5: Hold 30–90 seconds, then switch sides.
execution.breathing_instructions: Breathe slowly throughout. Each exhale allows greater relaxation into the stretch.
common_mistakes: Dropping the foot — keep the top ankle flexed to protect the knee
Pulling the bottom leg too aggressively — a gentle pull is sufficient
Holding the breath, which creates tension and reduces stretch effectiveness
safety_considerations: Flex the foot of the crossed leg to maintain a neutral ankle and reduce knee stress
If the stretch is felt in the knee rather than the hip, adjust ankle position
execution.range_of_motion_guidance: Draw the bottom thigh toward the chest until a stretch is felt in the outer hip of the crossed leg.
coaching_cues: Push the crossed knee away from your chest to deepen the stretch
Keep your foot flexed — this protects your knee
Let gravity help you — relax into the floor

name: Fire Hydrant
description: The fire hydrant is performed on all fours by raising one bent knee out to the side, training hip abduction while the torso is stabilized on the hands and opposite knee. The movement targets the gluteus medius and tensor fasciae latae — muscles critical for pelvic stability, lateral movement, and injury prevention. The name comes from the resemblance to a dog approaching a fire hydrant.

execution.starting_position: Begin on hands and knees with wrists under shoulders and knees under hips. Spine is neutral.
execution.setup_instructions: Bodyweight is sufficient. A mini resistance band around the thighs just above the knees adds progressive load.
steps: Step 1: Begin on all fours, core braced, spine neutral.
Step 2: Keeping the knee bent at 90°, raise one knee out to the side — abducting the hip — until the thigh is parallel to the floor.
Step 3: Hold the peak position with the hip fully abducted.
Step 4: Lower the knee back to the starting position under control.
Step 5: Complete all reps then switch sides.
execution.breathing_instructions: Exhale as you raise the knee. Inhale as you lower.
common_mistakes: Rotating the whole pelvis to raise the knee higher — the movement should come from the hip only
Only partially abducting — aim for the thigh to reach parallel to the floor
Letting the core sag during the movement
safety_considerations: Very low risk exercise
Wrist discomfort can be reduced with fists or push-up handles
execution.range_of_motion_guidance: Raise the knee until the thigh reaches parallel to the floor. The pelvis should not rotate.
coaching_cues: Open the hip like a book — not by rotating the pelvis
Keep the spine still — only the hip moves
Control the return — don't let the knee drop

name: Floor Barbell Skullcrusher
description: Skullcrushers performed lying on the floor instead of a bench. The floor limits the range of motion at the bottom, reducing shoulder stress while still providing excellent triceps training. The floor version is accessible and forgiving for those with shoulder limitations.

execution.starting_position: Set up for Floor Barbell Skullcrusher in the appropriate position.
execution.setup_instructions: Prepare equipment and body position for Floor Barbell Skullcrusher.
steps: Step 1: Lie on floor with barbell held at arm's length above chest.
Step 2: Bend elbows to lower bar toward forehead, keeping upper arms vertical.
Step 3: Lower until triceps contact or nearly contact floor.
Step 4: Extend elbows back to starting position.
execution.breathing_instructions: Exhale during the exertion phase, inhale during the return.
common_mistakes: Lowering too fast
Moving upper arms
safety_considerations: Keep joints aligned throughout the movement.
Use controlled weight appropriate for skill level.
execution.range_of_motion_guidance: Move through full range of motion without compromising joint integrity.
coaching_cues: Keep upper arms perfectly still
Touch and go from floor

name: Floor Dumbbell Flye with Glute Bridge Hold
description: A floor dumbbell flye performed while holding a glute bridge position throughout the set. The supine floor position provides a natural range-of-motion stop for the arms, protecting the shoulder, while the sustained hip bridge simultaneously activates the glutes and posterior chain. This exercise trains chest isolation alongside isometric hip extension, making it a time-efficient movement with significant glute and core co-activation.

execution.starting_position: Lie on the floor with knees bent and feet flat. Perform a glute bridge and hold the hips elevated. Hold one dumbbell in each hand above the chest with arms extended, palms facing each other.
execution.setup_instructions: No equipment needed beyond two dumbbells. The bridge should be established and stable before the flye begins. Use flye-appropriate weight — lighter than pressing weight.
steps: Step 1: Perform a glute bridge: lift and hold the hips so body forms a line from knees to shoulders.
Step 2: With arms extended above the chest, open them out to the sides in a wide arc — the flye.
Step 3: Lower until the upper arms contact the floor. Hold the bridge throughout.
Step 4: Bring the arms back together above the chest, squeezing the pectorals at the top.
Step 5: Repeat for all reps, maintaining the bridge hold throughout the set.
execution.breathing_instructions: Inhale as the arms open, exhale as they close. Breathe steadily through the bridge hold.
common_mistakes: Hips dropping during the flye — the bridge hold is as important as the flye
Bending elbows excessively during the arc
Using too heavy a weight, losing control at the bottom
safety_considerations: If unable to maintain both the bridge and the flye with good form, reduce dumbbell weight
Use a mat for lower back and hip comfort during the bridge
execution.range_of_motion_guidance: Open to floor contact on the arms. The floor stop protects the shoulder naturally.
coaching_cues: Squeeze the glutes to keep the hips up — they must not drop during the fly
Maintain the same elbow bend throughout — do not let the arms straighten completely

name: Floor Dumbbell Flye to Press
description: A combination chest exercise performed on the floor that begins as a dumbbell flye and transitions into a press on each repetition. The floor limits elbow travel below shoulder level, reducing shoulder stress while still providing significant chest stretch. The flye-to-press combo increases time under tension and trains both adduction and horizontal pushing in a single movement.

execution.starting_position: Lie on the floor with knees bent, feet flat. Hold a dumbbell in each hand, arms extended above the chest with palms facing each other.
execution.setup_instructions: Select a weight appropriate for a flye — lighter than pressing weight. The floor prevents excessive arm travel below the torso.
steps: Step 1: Begin with arms extended above the chest, dumbbells nearly touching, palms facing each other.
Step 2: Open the arms out wide in a flye arc, lowering until the upper arms contact or near the floor.
Step 3: At the bottom of the flye, bend the elbows and bring the dumbbells to chest level (now in press position).
Step 4: Press the dumbbells back up to the starting position.
Step 5: That is one rep: flye open → elbows bend → press up. Repeat.
execution.breathing_instructions: Inhale on the flye open, exhale on the press back up.
common_mistakes: Opening too fast and slamming arms into the floor
Using too heavy a weight for the flye portion — leads to poor form on the arc
Skipping the elbow bend at the bottom — this is what distinguishes the combo from a pure flye
safety_considerations: The floor stops elbow travel and protects the shoulder naturally — do not force past the floor stop
Keep elbows slightly bent throughout the flye arc
execution.range_of_motion_guidance: Open to floor contact on the flye. Press to full arm extension. Floor contact provides natural range of motion limit.
execution.tempo_recommendations: 2-1-1-1 (2s flye open, 1s bend elbows, 1s press, 1s reset)
coaching_cues: Flye first, then press — the two phases are distinct within each rep
Soft elbows on the flye — do not lock the arms straight

name: Floor Dumbbell Tate Press
description: The Tate press performed lying on the floor, limiting range of motion at the bottom. The floor eliminates the possibility of excessive shoulder lowering, making this a safer variation. The triceps work intensely through the available range.

execution.starting_position: Set up for Floor Dumbbell Tate Press in the appropriate position.
execution.setup_instructions: Prepare equipment and body position for Floor Dumbbell Tate Press.
steps: Step 1: Lie on floor holding dumbbells with elbows flared to sides.
Step 2: Lower dumbbells in arc toward chest keeping elbows wide.
Step 3: Lightly touch or stop just above chest at floor.
Step 4: Press back to straight arms through tricep contraction.
execution.breathing_instructions: Exhale during the exertion phase, inhale during the return.
common_mistakes: Closing elbows inward
Excessive wrist bend
safety_considerations: Keep joints aligned throughout the movement.
Use controlled weight appropriate for skill level.
execution.range_of_motion_guidance: Move through full range of motion without compromising joint integrity.
coaching_cues: Elbows stay flared perpendicular to torso
Full lockout at top

name: Floor Press
description: The floor press is a horizontal pressing exercise performed lying on the floor rather than on a bench. The floor limits the range of motion by stopping the elbows at the floor's surface, eliminating the deep pectoral stretch of the bench press and placing the emphasis on the lockout portion of the press. This makes it an excellent accessory lift for building triceps strength and training through joint-friendly range of motion.

execution.starting_position: Lie on the floor with knees bent and feet flat. Hold a barbell or dumbbells above the chest with arms extended. The barbell should be unracked from safeties or handed off by a partner.
execution.setup_instructions: Set the barbell in a rack or on safeties at a low height before lying under it, or have a partner hand it off after you are in position on the floor.
steps: Step 1: Lie on the floor with knees bent, feet flat. Unrack or accept the barbell above your chest.
Step 2: Inhale and lower the bar by bending the elbows until both upper arms rest on the floor.
Step 3: Pause momentarily with the upper arms resting on the floor — do not bounce.
Step 4: Exhale and press the bar back to the top with triceps emphasis.
execution.breathing_instructions: Inhale on the descent; exhale on the press.
common_mistakes: Bouncing the elbows off the floor, which uses momentum rather than muscle
Flaring the elbows wide, which reduces tricep activation
safety_considerations: Without a rack, you need a training partner to hand off and receive the bar
Keep the lower back flat against the floor — avoid arching
execution.range_of_motion_guidance: Lower until the upper arms touch the floor gently; press to full extension.
execution.tempo_recommendations: 2-1-2-0 (pause 1 second on the floor before pressing)
coaching_cues: Pause dead-stop before pressing — eliminate all momentum
Drive the bar up and slightly back toward the head during extension

name: Floor Press Close-Grip with Chains
description: A close-grip floor press with chain accommodating resistance added to the barbell. Chains reduce weight at the bottom and add resistance at lockout, training the triceps hardest where they are strongest. This is a powerlifting accessory for lockout strength.

execution.starting_position: Set up for Floor Press Close-Grip with Chains in the appropriate position.
execution.setup_instructions: Prepare equipment and body position for Floor Press Close-Grip with Chains.
steps: Step 1: Set up chains hanging from barbell ends. Lie on floor with close grip.
Step 2: Lower bar to floor level as triceps contact ground, elbows tucked.
Step 3: Pause briefly then press bar up as chains lift and add weight.
Step 4: Lock out hard at top with full tricep extension.
execution.breathing_instructions: Exhale during the exertion phase, inhale during the return.
common_mistakes: Bouncing from floor
Letting elbows drift at lockout
safety_considerations: Keep joints aligned throughout the movement.
Use controlled weight appropriate for skill level.
execution.range_of_motion_guidance: Move through full range of motion without compromising joint integrity.
coaching_cues: Chains should touch floor at the bottom
Accelerate through the sticking point

name: Floor Skullcrusher Neutral Grip
description: Skullcrushers performed on the floor with dumbbells in a neutral grip (palms facing each other). The neutral grip reduces elbow stress compared to pronated variations and allows natural forearm rotation. The floor limits depth for added safety.

execution.starting_position: Set up for Floor Skullcrusher Neutral Grip in the appropriate position.
execution.setup_instructions: Prepare equipment and body position for Floor Skullcrusher Neutral Grip.
steps: Step 1: Lie on floor with dumbbells held at arm's length above chest, palms facing each other.
Step 2: Bend elbows to lower dumbbells toward temples keeping upper arms vertical.
Step 3: Lower until triceps contact floor or end of range.
Step 4: Extend elbows back to starting position.
execution.breathing_instructions: Exhale during the exertion phase, inhale during the return.
common_mistakes: Rotating wrists out of neutral position
Letting upper arms drift
safety_considerations: Keep joints aligned throughout the movement.
Use controlled weight appropriate for skill level.
execution.range_of_motion_guidance: Move through full range of motion without compromising joint integrity.
coaching_cues: Maintain neutral wrist throughout
Upper arms stay perpendicular to floor

name: Flutter Kick
description: Flutter kicks are a supine endurance core exercise borrowed from swimming training in which the athlete alternately raises and lowers each leg in a small, rapid, continuous motion while keeping both legs straight and the lower back pressed to the floor. The exercise trains the hip flexors and rectus abdominis under sustained anti-extension loading across a large number of repetitions, making it a popular conditioning finisher and military fitness staple.

execution.starting_position: Lie flat on your back with arms at your sides or under the lower back for support. Legs extended, heels slightly off the floor.
execution.setup_instructions: Use a mat for comfort. Place hands under the lumbar curve if lower back arching is an issue.
steps: Step 1: Lie supine with legs straight. Press the lower back into the floor.
Step 2: Raise both feet approximately 15–30 cm off the floor.
Step 3: Rapidly alternate kicking each leg up and down in small amplitude oscillations, like swimming freestyle.
Step 4: Keep the lower back pressed to the floor throughout — if it arches, raise leg height.
Step 5: Continue for the prescribed duration or rep count.
execution.breathing_instructions: Breathe continuously in a relaxed rhythm throughout the set. Do not hold the breath.
common_mistakes: Allowing the lower back to arch away from the floor
Using too large an amplitude — small, rapid kicks are correct
Relaxing the leg muscles and letting the knees bend
safety_considerations: If the lower back arches despite effort, raise leg height or place hands under the lower back as a proprioceptive cue.
Not suitable during acute lower back pain flare-ups.
execution.range_of_motion_guidance: Legs move through a small arc of approximately 20–30 cm. The focus is speed and endurance, not amplitude.
execution.tempo_recommendations: Performed for time (20–60 seconds) or count (20–50 kicks per leg). Moderate to high speed.
coaching_cues: Press your back into the floor — there should be no gap
Quick, small kicks — not big swings
Point your toes and squeeze your quads

name: Forearm Roller
description: The forearm roller is a forearm conditioning exercise that uses a weighted cylinder attached to a rope or cord, which is wound up and then unwound by alternating wrist flexion and extension. It simultaneously trains both the wrist flexors and wrist extensors through the full range of motion against continuous resistance. Because of the extended time under tension, it produces significant forearm hypertrophy and grip endurance improvements that are difficult to replicate with other exercises.

execution.starting_position: Hold the roller handle with both hands using an overhand grip, arms extended straight out in front at shoulder height. The weight hangs from the rope beneath the roller.
execution.setup_instructions: A forearm roller is a short bar or cylinder with a rope through its center attached to a weight plate. Begin with a very light plate (2.5–5 kg) as the sustained tension is significantly more challenging than it appears.
steps: Step 1: Hold the roller at arm's length in front of the body at shoulder height. Weight hangs beneath on the rope.
Step 2: Alternate wrist flexion on each hand to wind the rope upward, lifting the weight toward the bar.
Step 3: Continue winding until the weight reaches the bar (rope fully wound).
Step 4: Reverse the direction, alternating wrist extension on each hand to lower the weight back to the starting position in a controlled manner.
execution.breathing_instructions: Breathe continuously — do not hold the breath. Use short rhythmic breaths throughout the extended set.
common_mistakes: Starting with too much weight — the sustained isometric hold fatigues the shoulders and forearms very quickly
Letting the arms drop below shoulder height partway through the set, reducing forearm engagement
safety_considerations: Keep the arms at shoulder height throughout — if they drop significantly, the set is over
Stop if sharp elbow or wrist pain is felt
execution.range_of_motion_guidance: Wind fully upward until the weight touches the bar; unwind fully downward until the rope is extended.
execution.tempo_recommendations: Continuous alternating motion — no specific tempo; controlled throughout
coaching_cues: Arms stay straight out — your shoulders will burn too, and that is part of the work
Wind all the way up and all the way down — no shortcuts

name: Freestanding Handstand Push-Up
description: The freestanding handstand push-up performs the full handstand press without any wall support, requiring simultaneous balance, pressing strength, and proprioceptive control. The absence of wall support forces the entire posterior and anterior shoulder girdle to continuously stabilize the handstand position while generating vertical pressing force — the gold standard of shoulder pressing in calisthenics.

execution.starting_position: Kick up to a freestanding handstand on the floor. Find balance before initiating the descent.
execution.setup_instructions: Develop a 60-second freestanding handstand hold before attempting pressing reps. Practice near a wall initially in case of loss of balance.
steps: Step 1: Establish a stable freestanding handstand.
Step 2: Slowly lower the head toward the floor while maintaining balance.
Step 3: Touch or nearly touch the top of the head to the floor.
Step 4: Press back to full arm extension, managing balance with finger pressure.
Step 5: Stabilize at the top before attempting the next rep.
execution.breathing_instructions: Inhale descending. Exhale pressing.
common_mistakes: Attempting freestanding reps without adequate handstand balance — build the hold first
Lowering too fast — the descent must be controlled to maintain balance
safety_considerations: Practice in an open area with a mat
Learn forward and sideways bail-out techniques before attempting
execution.range_of_motion_guidance: Full arm extension to head lightly touching floor.
coaching_cues: Press your fingertips into the floor to steer balance
Look between your hands
Stay hollow — no arch

name: Frog Pump
description: The frog pump is a floor glute bridge variation performed with the soles of the feet pressed together and knees flared outward, resembling a frog's legs. The externally rotated hip position places the hip flexors and adductors in a lengthened state, reducing their contribution and allowing the gluteus maximus to work in a shortened range with high activation. It is often used for glute activation and high-rep pump work at the end of a training session.

execution.starting_position: Lie on your back with the soles of the feet pressed together and knees fallen outward (externally rotated), forming a diamond shape with the legs. Feet close to the hips.
execution.setup_instructions: No equipment required. A dumbbell or weight plate can be rested on the hips for added resistance.
steps: Step 1: Lie on your back with soles of feet pressed together, knees flared outward. Feet 20–30 cm from the hips.
Step 2: Drive the hips upward by squeezing the glutes.
Step 3: Extend until the hips are fully extended and the body forms a straight line from shoulders to knees.
Step 4: Squeeze the glutes hard at the top for 1–2 seconds.
Step 5: Lower the hips back to the floor under control.
execution.breathing_instructions: Exhale as you drive the hips up. Inhale as you lower.
common_mistakes: Not fully extending the hips at the top — push all the way up
Letting the lower back arch excessively — posterior pelvic tilt at the top
Allowing the feet to separate — keep the soles pressed together
safety_considerations: Very low-risk exercise
Hip discomfort in the externally rotated position may indicate hip flexibility limitations — do not force the range
execution.range_of_motion_guidance: Full hip extension at the top. Hips to floor at the bottom.
coaching_cues: Squeeze the glutes — not the lower back
Push hips fully up — don't stop short
Keep feet pressed together throughout

name: Front Foot Elevated Reverse Lunge
description: The front-foot elevated reverse lunge places the working foot on a slight elevation (a plate or low step), increasing the range of motion as the rear knee descends below the level of the front foot. This creates greater hip flexion and quad stretch on the working leg while also increasing glute recruitment. It bridges the gap between a standard reverse lunge and the Bulgarian split squat in terms of difficulty and range of motion.

execution.starting_position: Stand on a weight plate or low step (1-3 inches high) with the working foot. Hold dumbbells at the sides if loading.
execution.setup_instructions: Place a single weight plate flat on the floor. Stand on it with both feet, then step one foot back off the plate to perform the reverse lunge.
steps: Step 1: Stand on the elevation with the working foot. Step one foot back into a reverse lunge stance.
Step 2: Lower the rear knee directly down toward the floor, allowing it to descend below the level of the elevated front foot.
Step 3: The front foot knee bends deeply as the rear knee approaches the floor.
Step 4: Drive through the front foot to return to the starting position. Alternate legs each rep.
execution.breathing_instructions: Inhale on the descent, exhale on the drive.
common_mistakes: Front foot rolling off the edge of the elevation
Rear knee touching and resting on the floor
Torso leaning excessively forward
safety_considerations: Ensure the elevation surface is stable and non-slip
Master the standard reverse lunge before adding a deficit
execution.range_of_motion_guidance: Rear knee should travel to or near the floor below the front foot level.
coaching_cues: Front foot stays centered on the elevation
Rear knee drops straight down
Drive up through the front heel

name: Front Lever Hold
description: A gymnastic straight-body hold where the athlete suspends horizontally below a bar with arms straight overhead. The entire posterior chain and core must work isometrically to maintain the rigid plank position parallel to the floor. Mastery requires months of progressive training.

execution.starting_position: Set up for Front Lever Hold in proper position.
execution.setup_instructions: Prepare body and equipment for Front Lever Hold.
steps: Step 1: Hang from bar with overhand grip. Tuck body and slowly extend hips.
Step 2: Engage lats to pull bar toward hips while extending body horizontal.
Step 3: Hold rigid plank position parallel to floor with arms straight.
Step 4: Lower with control rather than dropping.
execution.breathing_instructions: Breathe steadily; never hold breath during static holds.
common_mistakes: Allowing hips to drop
Bending arms
safety_considerations: Build prerequisite strength before attempting advanced variations.
Stop if joint pain occurs.
execution.range_of_motion_guidance: Full range of motion with control at all times.
coaching_cues: Pull bar into hips with straight arms
Body makes perfectly flat plank

name: Front Lever Raises
description: A dynamic front lever exercise where the athlete raises the body from a vertical hang to the front lever position. This eccentric-concentric approach builds front lever strength faster than static holds alone. The raise phase develops the pulling muscles through the full arc.

execution.starting_position: Set up for Front Lever Raises in proper position.
execution.setup_instructions: Prepare body and equipment for Front Lever Raises.
steps: Step 1: Hang from bar with straight arms and tuck body.
Step 2: Engage lats and pull body to horizontal front lever position.
Step 3: Hold briefly at horizontal then lower back to vertical with control.
Step 4: Repeat for reps, maintaining rigidity throughout.
execution.breathing_instructions: Breathe steadily; never hold breath during static holds.
common_mistakes: Using momentum to swing up
Breaking rigid body position
safety_considerations: Build prerequisite strength before attempting advanced variations.
Stop if joint pain occurs.
execution.range_of_motion_guidance: Full range of motion with control at all times.
coaching_cues: Pull bar into hips as you raise
Full front lever mastery before raises

name: Front-Rack Bulgarian Split Squat
description: A Bulgarian split squat performed with the barbell in the front rack position, resting on the front deltoids. This variation promotes a more upright torso than the back rack version and increases upper back and core stability requirements while heavily loading the working quadriceps and glutes.

execution.starting_position: Position a barbell in the front rack (resting on the clavicles and anterior deltoids). Stand in a split stance with the rear foot elevated on a bench.
execution.setup_instructions: Set the barbell in a rack to shoulder height. Take the front rack position and walk back to position the rear foot on a bench.
steps: Step 1: Brace your core hard and keep elbows high to maintain the front rack position.
Step 2: Lower the rear knee toward the floor by bending both knees.
Step 3: Descend until the front thigh is at or below parallel, keeping the torso upright.
Step 4: Drive through the front heel to return to the starting position.
execution.breathing_instructions: Inhale and brace before the descent. Exhale on the ascent.
common_mistakes: Dropping the elbows, causing the bar to roll forward off the shoulders
Allowing the front knee to collapse inward
safety_considerations: Front rack requires adequate wrist and shoulder mobility — do not force the position if mobility is limited
execution.range_of_motion_guidance: Rear knee approaches the floor. Front thigh at or below parallel.
coaching_cues: Elbows stay high throughout
Drive the front knee out over the pinky toe

name: Front Raise
description: The front raise is a shoulder isolation exercise targeting the anterior (front) head of the deltoid through shoulder flexion. It can be performed with dumbbells, a barbell, or a plate. It is typically used as an accessory exercise to complement compound overhead pressing movements.

execution.starting_position: Stand with feet shoulder-width apart. Hold a dumbbell in each hand in front of the thighs with palms facing back (pronated) or neutral.
execution.setup_instructions: Use light to moderate weight. The anterior deltoid is frequently overtrained from pressing movements, so this is primarily a finishing or accessory exercise.
steps: With a slight elbow bend, raise both dumbbells in front of you to approximately shoulder height.
Pause briefly at the top, then lower under control to the starting position.
execution.breathing_instructions: Exhale on the raise, inhale on the descent.
common_mistakes: Swinging the torso to generate momentum
Raising the dumbbells above shoulder height unnecessarily
safety_considerations: The anterior deltoid is typically already well-trained from pressing movements — program conservatively to avoid overuse
execution.range_of_motion_guidance: Raise to shoulder height. Going higher primarily increases trap involvement.
coaching_cues: Keep your torso still — only your arms should move
Maintain a slight elbow bend throughout — do not lock out

name: Front Squat
description: The front squat places the barbell across the front deltoids and clavicles, requiring a markedly more upright torso than the back squat. This positioning shifts loading emphasis toward the quadriceps and demands significant thoracic extension and wrist mobility. It is a staple of Olympic weightlifting and an effective tool for quad-dominant lower body development.

execution.starting_position: Stand inside the rack with the bar set at collarbone height. Step under the bar and push your elbows forward and up until they are parallel to the floor, allowing the bar to rest across your front deltoids and clavicles. Your fingertips can rest on the bar with a loose grip or cross your arms in a clean grip. Stand tall, brace your core, and unrack the bar.
execution.setup_instructions: Set the barbell on the rack at collarbone height. Use either a clean grip (elbows high, bar resting on fingertips) or a crossed-arm grip. Position feet shoulder-width apart with toes turned slightly outward.
steps: Step 1: Unrack the bar and take two steps back. Stand with feet shoulder-width apart, toes pointed 15–30° outward, elbows driven high.
Step 2: Take a deep breath into your abdomen and brace your core firmly as though bracing for a punch.
Step 3: Initiate the descent by pushing your knees out in line with your toes while simultaneously sitting your hips back and down. Keep the elbows high throughout.
Step 4: Descend until your thighs are at least parallel to the floor or deeper if mobility allows. The torso should remain nearly vertical.
Step 5: Drive through the full foot to extend your knees and hips back to the starting position. Exhale at the top.
execution.breathing_instructions: Inhale and brace before descent. Hold breath through the sticking point. Exhale at the top of the rep.
common_mistakes: Dropping the elbows during descent, causing the bar to roll forward off the shoulders
Allowing the knees to cave inward (valgus collapse) during the ascent
Rising onto the toes due to insufficient ankle dorsiflexion
Excessive forward lean from poor thoracic mobility
safety_considerations: Develop adequate wrist and thoracic mobility before loading heavily
Use safety bars in a rack in case of a failed rep — the bar can be dropped forward safely with bumper plates
Heel elevation (small plates or wedges) can compensate for limited ankle dorsiflexion while mobility is being developed
execution.range_of_motion_guidance: Aim to reach at least parallel (thighs horizontal) or deeper if mobility allows without lumbar rounding.
execution.tempo_recommendations: 3-1-1-0 (3 seconds down, 1 second pause at bottom, 1 second up, no pause at top)
coaching_cues: Elbows up — if they drop, the bar rolls off
Sit between your knees, not behind them
Knees track over the pinky toe

name: Full Planche Push-Up
description: A push-up performed while maintaining the full planche position throughout the range of motion. The body remains parallel to the floor while the arms bend and extend to lower and raise the body. This is among the most difficult bodyweight pushing movements in existence.

execution.starting_position: Set up for Full Planche Push-Up in proper position.
execution.setup_instructions: Prepare body and equipment for Full Planche Push-Up.
steps: Step 1: Establish full planche hold with body horizontal, arms straight.
Step 2: Bend elbows to lower body toward floor maintaining horizontal position.
Step 3: Lower until elbows reach 90 degrees or body nearly touches floor.
Step 4: Press back to straight arms maintaining planche throughout.
execution.breathing_instructions: Breathe steadily; never hold breath during static holds.
common_mistakes: Dropping hips during the push
Attempting before achieving static planche
safety_considerations: Build prerequisite strength before attempting advanced variations.
Stop if joint pain occurs.
execution.range_of_motion_guidance: Full range of motion with control at all times.
coaching_cues: Full planche must be mastered first
Body stays horizontal throughout

name: Glute-Ham Developer GHD Leg Curl
description: The glute-ham developer leg curl is performed on a GHD machine where the feet are secured in the foot plates and the thigh pads support the lower thighs. The lifter performs knee flexion to bring the torso upright from a prone extended position, working the hamstrings both as a knee flexor and hip extensor simultaneously. This makes the GHD curl unique in its ability to train the hamstrings through both their functions in one movement.

execution.starting_position: Set the GHD machine so the thigh pads rest just above the knees. Secure the feet in the foot plates. Begin with the body extended downward, hands at chest for safety.
execution.setup_instructions: Adjust the GHD foot plate and thigh pad distance for your height. Begin with a controlled eccentric to test the difficulty before attempting full reps.
steps: Step 1: Begin in the extended position (torso roughly parallel to the floor or angled below horizontal).
Step 2: Drive the toes into the foot plate and curl the hamstrings to flex the knees.
Step 3: Use the hamstrings to curl the torso upright until the body is fully erect.
Step 4: Lower slowly back to the starting position by extending the knees under control.
execution.breathing_instructions: Exhale on the curl up, inhale on the controlled descent.
common_mistakes: Using the lower back (hip extension) to compensate for weak hamstrings
Dropping too fast on the eccentric
Insufficient foot plate pressure
safety_considerations: Extremely demanding — master the Nordic hamstring curl before progressing here
Use hands to assist if needed in early training
execution.range_of_motion_guidance: Full extension at the start (body near horizontal), full flexion with torso erect at the top.
coaching_cues: Drive the toes into the plate
Hamstrings pull you up — not your back
Control the descent

name: Glute Bridge
description: The glute bridge is a bodyweight or lightly loaded hip extension exercise performed flat on the floor. It is an accessible entry-level glute activation exercise that trains the glutes through hip extension and is frequently used in warm-ups, rehabilitation, and beginner training programs before progressing to the barbell hip thrust.

execution.starting_position: Lie on your back with knees bent at approximately 90 degrees and feet flat on the floor hip-width apart. Arms at the sides.
execution.setup_instructions: No equipment needed. Can be performed anywhere. Place feet close enough that heels are under or slightly behind the knees.
steps: Press through the heels and squeeze the glutes to lift the hips toward the ceiling.
At the top, the body from knees to shoulders forms a straight line.
Hold the top position and squeeze the glutes firmly for one to two seconds.
Lower the hips under control back toward the floor.
execution.breathing_instructions: Exhale on the hip drive up. Inhale on the descent.
common_mistakes: Thrusting with the lower back rather than squeezing the glutes
Feet too far from the body — this reduces glute activation
safety_considerations: Safe for most populations including beginners and those in rehabilitation
execution.range_of_motion_guidance: Full hip extension at the top, hips nearly touching the floor at the bottom.
coaching_cues: Squeeze your glutes — do not just raise your hips
Imagine you are trying to push your hips through the ceiling

name: Glute Bridge March
description: An isometric and dynamic glute challenge performed by holding a glute bridge position while alternately lifting each foot off the floor in a marching pattern. The alternating leg lift forces the planted glute and core to resist pelvic rotation and maintain a stable bridge, increasing unilateral demand without additional load.

execution.starting_position: Lie on your back with knees bent, feet flat on the floor hip-width apart. Drive the hips up into a glute bridge position.
execution.setup_instructions: No equipment needed. Optionally place a resistance band loop just above the knees for additional challenge.
steps: Step 1: Lift the hips into a glute bridge and hold the position, squeezing both glutes.
Step 2: Keeping the hips level, lift one foot off the floor and bring the knee toward the chest.
Step 3: Hold for a moment, then return the foot to the floor.
Step 4: Repeat on the opposite side while maintaining the bridge position.
execution.breathing_instructions: Breathe steadily throughout. Do not hold your breath.
common_mistakes: Allowing the hips to drop or rotate when lifting each foot
Pushing through the lower back rather than the glutes
safety_considerations: Ensure the hips stay level — place a dumbbell on the hips as a feedback tool if needed
execution.range_of_motion_guidance: Hips fully extended throughout. Each knee lifts to approximately 90 degrees.
coaching_cues: Keep the hips level
Squeeze both glutes even when one leg is marching

name: Glute-Focused 45-Degree Hyperextension
description: A hyperextension machine exercise performed with a rounded lower back and posterior pelvic tilt to isolate the glutes rather than the erector spinae. By flexing the spine slightly and driving the hips into extension, the glutes become the primary mover rather than the back extensors.

execution.starting_position: Position yourself in the 45-degree hyperextension machine with the pad below the hip crease, not across the hips. Begin with the torso hanging forward.
execution.setup_instructions: Set the hyperextension bench pad below the hip crease so the hips can fully flex. Optionally hold a plate at chest for load.
steps: Step 1: Allow the torso to drop forward so the hips are fully flexed.
Step 2: Drive the hips up by squeezing the glutes, keeping the lower back slightly rounded.
Step 3: Extend the hips fully at the top — the goal is hip extension, not lumbar extension.
Step 4: Lower back to the starting position with control.
execution.breathing_instructions: Exhale on the drive up. Inhale on the lower.
common_mistakes: Hyperextending the lumbar spine at the top instead of stopping at hip extension
Using momentum to swing up
safety_considerations: The lower back should be slightly rounded to shift the emphasis to the glutes away from the erectors
execution.range_of_motion_guidance: Full hip flexion at the bottom. Full hip extension at the top — stop before lumbar hyperextension.
coaching_cues: Squeeze the glutes, not the back
Drive the hips up, not the chest up

name: Side-Lying Hip Abduction
description: Side-lying hip abduction is a classic rehabilitation exercise for the gluteus medius and tensor fasciae latae. Performed lying on the side with the top leg raised directly upward in the frontal plane, it provides direct strengthening of the hip abductors without requiring upright balance or complex movement patterns. It is prescribed for IT band syndrome, patellofemoral pain, hip weakness, low back pain, and as a foundational glute exercise for all populations.

execution.starting_position: Lie on one side with the body in a straight line. The bottom arm extends under the head. The top leg is straight and stacked on the bottom leg.
execution.setup_instructions: No equipment required. A resistance band loop above the knees may be added for progressive resistance.
steps: Step 1: Lie on one side with hips stacked and both legs straight.
Step 2: Turn the top foot slightly toward the floor (internal rotation) to target the posterior fibers of the gluteus medius.
Step 3: Raise the top leg toward the ceiling, keeping it in line with the torso (not in front of it).
Step 4: Raise to approximately 30–45 degrees — not so high that the pelvis rotates.
Step 5: Slowly lower the leg back to the starting position with control. Do not let it rest on the bottom leg between reps.
execution.breathing_instructions: Exhale as the leg lifts. Inhale as it lowers.
common_mistakes: Letting the top hip roll forward — the pelvis must stay stacked
Raising the leg too far, which recruits the hip flexors and reduces glute med isolation
Pointing the top toe toward the ceiling (external rotation) — slight internal rotation targets the posterior glute med
safety_considerations: Safe for all rehabilitation populations including post-partum and elderly
If lateral hip pain occurs with the band, try without band first
execution.range_of_motion_guidance: Raise the leg 30–45 degrees from the floor. Keep the movement in the frontal plane.
execution.tempo_recommendations: 2-second lift, 1-second hold, 2-second lower. 15–20 reps × 2–3 sets per side.
coaching_cues: Lead with the heel — think about reaching the heel up to the ceiling
Keep the hip stacked and do not let it roll backward
Slight internal rotation of the foot targets the best part of the glute med

name: Goblet Squat
description: The goblet squat is a beginner-friendly squat variation in which a single kettlebell or dumbbell is held at chest height with both hands. The front-loaded weight counterbalances the lifter and encourages a more upright torso, making it an excellent teaching tool for squat mechanics and a valuable accessory exercise for quad development.

execution.starting_position: Stand with feet shoulder-width apart, toes flared outward. Hold a kettlebell or dumbbell vertically at chest height with both hands, elbows pointing down.
execution.setup_instructions: No special setup needed. Hold the weight close to the chest. The front loading naturally encourages a more upright torso.
steps: Push the knees out in line with the toes as you descend.
Lower until hips are at or below knee level.
Drive through the whole foot to return to standing.
execution.breathing_instructions: Inhale on descent, exhale on the ascent.
common_mistakes: Letting the weight pull the torso forward — keep it close to the chest
Knees caving inward
safety_considerations: An excellent movement for anyone learning to squat before progressing to a barbell
execution.range_of_motion_guidance: Full depth, hips at or below knee level.
coaching_cues: Sit between your legs, not on top of them
Keep the weight close to your chest — do not let it drift forward

name: Goblet Squat with Pause
description: The goblet squat with pause combines the upright-torso goblet squat position with a deliberate hold at the bottom. The pause eliminates the stretch-shortening reflex, forcing the quadriceps, glutes, and core to generate force from a dead stop. It is particularly effective for building squat positional strength in beginners and for improving hip mobility by using the pause position to open the hips.

execution.starting_position: Hold a dumbbell or kettlebell vertically at chest height with both hands cupping the top of the weight. Feet shoulder-width apart, toes pointed slightly out.
execution.setup_instructions: Same as the goblet squat setup. The weight held at the chest acts as a counterbalance, promoting a more upright torso.
steps: Step 1: Hold the weight at chest height. Core braced. Push the knees out over the toes.
Step 2: Descend to full depth — hips below knees if possible.
Step 3: Hold the bottom position for 2–5 seconds. Use the elbows to gently push the knees outward at the bottom. Breathe steadily.
Step 4: Drive through the entire foot to return to standing.
Step 5: Exhale at the top.
execution.breathing_instructions: Inhale before descent, breathe steadily through the pause, exhale on the ascent.
common_mistakes: Heels rising at the bottom — caused by insufficient ankle dorsiflexion
Lumbar rounding at depth — reduce weight or elevate heels slightly
Relaxing the knees inward during the pause
safety_considerations: If heels rise, place a small plate under them to elevate until ankle mobility improves
Start with a light dumbbell
execution.range_of_motion_guidance: Full depth. The pause is at the deepest achievable position with neutral spine.
coaching_cues: Elbows push knees apart at the bottom
Stay tight in the pause — don't sit and relax
Drive up with your legs, not by leaning forward

name: Good Morning
description: The good morning is a barbell hip-hinge exercise in which the bar rests on the upper traps as in a back squat, but the movement involves bowing forward at the hips while maintaining a relatively straight knee, stretching the hamstrings under a significant load. It is a potent posterior chain developer and also conditions the erector spinae under substantial spinal loading. Proper technique is essential as errors under heavy load significantly increase injury risk.

execution.starting_position: Position the barbell on the upper traps as in a back squat. Stand with feet hip to shoulder-width apart and knees soft (slight bend).
execution.setup_instructions: Begin with a very light load — this exercise has enormous moment arm leverage on the lower back. Build load conservatively over many sessions.
steps: Step 1: Stand with the bar on upper traps, core braced, knees soft. Foot width is hip to shoulder-width.
Step 2: Initiate the movement by pushing the hips backward — not by bending at the waist. Maintain a neutral spine throughout.
Step 3: Continue hinging until the torso approaches horizontal (or until hamstring flexibility limits further range without lumbar rounding).
Step 4: Reverse the movement by contracting the hamstrings and glutes to drive the hips forward and return the torso to vertical.
Step 5: Exhale at the top.
execution.breathing_instructions: Inhale and brace before the hip hinge. Hold through the descent. Exhale as you return to vertical.
common_mistakes: Rounding the lower back — this significantly increases disc injury risk under a loaded barbell
Bending the knees excessively, turning it into a squat
Using more load than hamstring flexibility allows, forcing lumbar flexion
safety_considerations: This exercise places high compressive and shear load on the lumbar spine — do not load it heavily without established hip hinge mechanics
If you feel any sharp pain in the lower back, stop immediately
Master the Romanian deadlift before attempting the good morning with significant load
execution.range_of_motion_guidance: Hinge until hamstrings limit further range without lumbar rounding. Quality of position is more important than depth.
coaching_cues: Push the hips back, don't bow at the waist
Chest tall, spine long throughout
Feel the hamstrings stretch — stop before the lower back rounds

name: Seated Good Morning
description: The seated good morning is performed seated on a bench with a barbell across the upper back, then hinging the torso forward over the thighs. Because the seated position eliminates the hip hinge that characterizes the standing version, this variation more directly loads the erector spinae by forcing the spinal extensors to resist and control trunk flexion without the hip contribution, making it a highly specific lower back strengthening exercise.

execution.starting_position: Sit on a bench with feet flat on the floor, wider than hip-width for stability. Rest a lightly loaded barbell across the upper traps in the same position as a low-bar squat. Sit upright with a neutral spine.
execution.setup_instructions: Use a lightly loaded barbell — this exercise is not suitable for heavy loads. Sit near the front of a flat bench. Have the bar in a rack and unrack it in a seated position, or have a spotter assist.
steps: Step 1: Begin seated with the barbell on the upper back and spine neutral.
Step 2: Brace the core and begin to slowly hinge the torso forward over the thighs.
Step 3: Lower as far as flexibility allows while maintaining a neutral or slightly extended spine — avoid rounding.
Step 4: Pause briefly at the bottom.
Step 5: Drive the torso back to vertical by contracting the erectors, not by pushing off the thighs.
execution.breathing_instructions: Inhale and brace before hinging forward. Exhale as you return to vertical.
common_mistakes: Using too much load — this is a technique and endurance exercise, not a maximum strength lift
Rounding the lower back at the bottom of the movement
Pushing off the knees with the hands to return to vertical
safety_considerations: This is an advanced exercise that places high demand on the erector spinae with no hip contribution to assist — do not load heavily
Those with lumbar disc issues should consult a professional before attempting
Always use a spotter or perform inside a rack
execution.range_of_motion_guidance: Torso should travel as far forward as the erectors can control under a neutral or slightly extended spine. For most people, 45–70 degrees of torso lean from vertical.
coaching_cues: Spine long — imagine balancing a glass of water on your back
Only go as far forward as you can keep your back flat
Return by squeezing the lower back and abs simultaneously

name: Good Morning Squat Hybrid
description: The good morning squat hybrid begins in a squat stance but hinges the torso deeply forward during the descent (resembling a good morning), then drives back to upright by extending both the hips and knees together. It simultaneously loads the erector spinae, glutes, and hamstrings through a range of motion that blends both exercises, increasing total posterior chain recruitment and training spinal erector endurance under axial load.

execution.starting_position: Barbell in a high-bar back squat position. Feet shoulder-width apart, toes slightly out.
execution.setup_instructions: Begin with a moderate load — this is a technique and endurance lift, not a max squat. Ensure the barbell is seated high on the traps.
steps: Step 1: Begin standing with barbell on the upper traps.
Step 2: Simultaneously hinge the hips back and descend into a squat, allowing the torso to lean forward significantly.
Step 3: At the bottom, the torso should be at 45 degrees or more of forward lean.
Step 4: Drive up by extending hips and knees simultaneously, restoring upright torso.
Step 5: Repeat.
execution.breathing_instructions: Inhale and brace before descent. Exhale on the drive to the top.
common_mistakes: Rounding the lower back at the bottom — the erector spinae must maintain spinal extension
Insufficient hip hinge — the torso should lean significantly more than a standard squat
safety_considerations: High demand on the spinal erectors — build up gradually and avoid with lower back injuries
Do not use a load that compromises neutral spine maintenance at the bottom
execution.range_of_motion_guidance: Full depth squat with significant forward torso lean to fully upright at the top.
coaching_cues: Let the chest fall toward the thighs on the way down
Drive the hips and chest up simultaneously on the way back
Spine stays long — not round

name: Gorilla Row — Alternating Kettlebell
description: The gorilla row is performed with two kettlebells on the floor in a hip-hinge position, alternating rows with each arm while the other holds the kettlebell stationary on the floor. The alternating action requires significant anti-rotation core stability, as the shifting load constantly challenges the obliques. The ground-based starting position adds a natural dead-stop at each repetition, eliminating momentum between reps.

execution.starting_position: Place two matching kettlebells on the floor, positioned shoulder-width apart. Stand between them and hinge at the hips to approximately parallel. Grip both kettlebells while maintaining a neutral spine.
execution.setup_instructions: Use matching kettlebells. The hip hinge position must be maintained throughout the entire set.
steps: Step 1: Hinge to roughly parallel, gripping both kettlebells on the floor.
Step 2: Brace the core hard against the anti-rotation demand.
Step 3: Row one kettlebell to the hip while the other stays on the floor.
Step 4: Return the rowed kettlebell to the floor under control.
Step 5: Immediately row the other side. Continue alternating.
execution.breathing_instructions: Exhale on each row, maintain bracing between alternating reps.
common_mistakes: Rotating the hips when switching arms — maintain square hips
Letting the stationary kettlebell move on the floor
Rising out of the hip hinge during the set
safety_considerations: The hip hinge must be maintained for the duration — fatigue causing the torso to rise places greater lumbar load
Ensure kettlebells will not tip — use flat-bottomed kettlebells on a flat surface
execution.range_of_motion_guidance: Kettlebell returns to floor between each rep, pulled to hip level at the top.
coaching_cues: Hips stay square — no rotating
Dead stop each rep on the floor
Brace your core like you're taking a punch

name: Guillotine Press
description: The guillotine press is a barbell bench press variation where the bar is lowered to the neck or upper chest rather than the mid-sternum. This higher bar contact point increases pectoralis major stretch and horizontal adduction range, shifting more of the load to the clavicular head and maximizing muscle fiber recruitment across the chest. Due to the extreme shoulder position, it carries higher injury risk and should be reserved for experienced lifters.

execution.starting_position: Lie on a flat bench under a barbell rack. Grip the bar wide (index fingers on the smooth ring or slightly outside). Position yourself so the bar tracks over the neck/clavicle area, not the mid-chest.
execution.setup_instructions: Use a spotter at all times. Use lighter weight than a standard bench press — the increased stretch significantly reduces the amount that can be safely lifted. Set safety bars.
steps: Step 1: Position on the bench so the bar will descend to the clavicle or upper chest. Grip wide with elbows flared.
Step 2: Unrack the bar and hold it above the clavicular area.
Step 3: Inhale and slowly lower the bar toward the neck/upper chest, allowing the elbows to flare to approximately 90 degrees.
Step 4: Touch the upper chest/clavicle lightly, then exhale and press back to the starting position.
execution.breathing_instructions: Inhale on the descent; exhale on the press.
common_mistakes: Using the same weight as a standard bench press — reduce load significantly
Lowering too quickly, which can injure the shoulder capsule
safety_considerations: Always use a spotter and set the safety bars
Not recommended for those with existing shoulder impingement, labrum issues, or AC joint problems
This exercise carries higher injury risk than standard bench press — build shoulder health first
execution.range_of_motion_guidance: Touch the upper chest or clavicle — do not bounce. Control the full descent.
coaching_cues: Let the elbows flare wide — this is intentional for this variation
Use lighter load than standard press and focus on the stretch

name: Hack Squat
description: The hack squat is a machine-based squat variation where the lifter stands on an angled platform and pushes a sled upward. The fixed back-pad support eliminates lower back involvement, allowing very heavy quadriceps loading. Foot position can be varied to emphasize different portions of the quads.

execution.starting_position: Stand on the platform with feet shoulder-width apart and the back and shoulders against the pads. Unhook the safety handles. Feet can be placed lower for more quad emphasis.
execution.setup_instructions: Load the machine with appropriate weight. Set the sled to a starting position you can safely unrack. Keep the back flat against the pad throughout.
steps: Release the safety handles and lower the sled by bending the knees.
Descend until knees reach approximately 90 degrees or deeper.
Press through the whole foot to extend the knees and push the sled back to the top position.
execution.breathing_instructions: Inhale on descent, exhale on the press.
common_mistakes: Heels lifting off the platform — place feet high enough on the platform
Locking the knees out aggressively at the top
safety_considerations: Always use the safety catches — do not unrack without them engaged first
Re-engage safety catches before stepping off the machine
execution.range_of_motion_guidance: 90-degree knee flexion at the bottom. Full extension (no hyperextension) at the top.
coaching_cues: Press through the whole foot — do not rise onto the toes
Keep the back welded to the pad throughout the entire set

name: Hammer Curl
description: The hammer curl is performed with a neutral (hammer) grip throughout the full range of motion. This grip maximizes brachioradialis involvement and also provides strong brachialis stimulation. The neutral grip reduces wrist stress and builds forearm thickness alongside biceps development.

execution.starting_position: Stand or sit holding dumbbells at the sides with a neutral grip (thumbs pointing up). Elbows against the sides of the torso.
execution.setup_instructions: Keep the neutral grip throughout — do not rotate the wrist during the curl.
steps: Curl the dumbbell upward while maintaining the neutral grip.
Raise until the dumbbell is at shoulder height.
Lower under control back to the starting position.
execution.breathing_instructions: Exhale on the curl, inhale on the descent.
common_mistakes: Rotating the wrist to supinate — this turns it into a regular dumbbell curl
Using body swing
safety_considerations: The neutral grip is typically easier on the wrist than a supinated curl
execution.range_of_motion_guidance: Full extension at bottom, shoulder height at top.
coaching_cues: Keep thumbs pointing up throughout — think of hammering a nail
Squeeze the forearm and brachialis at the top

name: Plate-Loaded Machine Row — High Row
description: The plate-loaded high row machine (such as the Hammer Strength High Row) features independent arms that allow each side to move through a natural arc, accommodating individual shoulder mechanics. The high row angle targets the upper lats, rhomboids, and rear deltoids more directly than a low or neutral row. The chest is supported, eliminating lower back involvement and allowing isolation of the upper back musculature.

execution.starting_position: Load the machine with weight plates. Sit facing the machine with the chest on the pad. Grip the handles at a neutral or pronated position with arms extended.
execution.setup_instructions: Adjust seat height so the handles are level with the upper chest or face when seated. Keep the chest on the pad throughout the movement.
steps: Step 1: Grip the handles with the arms extended, chest on the pad.
Step 2: Retract the scapulae and pull both handles toward the upper chest/face.
Step 3: Drive the elbows back and out, keeping them at approximately shoulder height.
Step 4: Squeeze hard at peak contraction.
Step 5: Return under control to full extension.
execution.breathing_instructions: Exhale on the pull, inhale on the return.
common_mistakes: Pulling the handles too low, shifting from a high row to a mid row pattern
Not fully extending at the bottom of each rep
safety_considerations: Adjust seat height carefully — improper positioning causes shoulder impingement
Do not use excessive weight that prevents full scapular retraction
execution.range_of_motion_guidance: Full arm extension at the start to handles near the upper chest at the finish.
coaching_cues: Elbows high and back
Chest on the pad
Think rear delt and rhomboids — not just lats

name: Plate-Loaded Machine Row — Low Row
description: The plate-loaded low row machine targets the lower lats and mid-back through a horizontal pulling path at approximately waist height. The low cable angle maximizes latissimus dorsi engagement compared to a high row configuration. The chest-supported position allows trainees to train to muscular failure safely without lower back fatigue limiting back muscle training.

execution.starting_position: Sit facing the machine with the chest on the pad. Set the seat so the handles are at approximately waist-to-lower-chest height. Grip the handles with arms fully extended.
execution.setup_instructions: Load the machine with appropriate weight. The low angle maximizes lat stretch at the start.
steps: Step 1: Sit with chest on the support pad, arms fully extended gripping the handles.
Step 2: Retract the scapulae and pull the handles toward the lower chest or abdomen.
Step 3: Keep the elbows close to the torso to maximize lat activation.
Step 4: Squeeze the lats at peak contraction.
Step 5: Return under control to full extension.
execution.breathing_instructions: Exhale on the row, inhale on the return.
common_mistakes: Flaring the elbows too wide, shifting to a rhomboid-dominant movement
Using too much weight, reducing range of motion
safety_considerations: Check chest pad height before loading heavy — improper fit causes shoulder discomfort
execution.range_of_motion_guidance: Full extension at the start to handles at lower ribcage level at the finish.
coaching_cues: Elbows stay close
Think about pulling the elbows to your pockets
Full stretch at the start of every rep

name: Standing Hamstring Stretch
description: The standing hamstring stretch targets all three hamstring muscles through hip flexion with the knees extended. Standing with feet flat on the floor and hinging forward at the hips places the hamstrings under lengthening tension. Keeping the spine relatively neutral during the stretch is preferred over spinal flexion to maximize the hamstring load and reduce lumbar stress.

execution.starting_position: Stand with feet hip-width apart and knees straight but not locked. Arms at sides.
execution.setup_instructions: No equipment needed. Stand on a flat, non-slip surface.
steps: Step 1: Stand tall with feet hip-width apart and knees extended.
Step 2: Hinge forward at the hips, keeping the spine long and chest forward rather than rounding the back.
Step 3: Lower the torso toward the floor, reaching the hands toward the feet or floor.
Step 4: When a moderate hamstring stretch is felt, stop and hold the position.
Step 5: Hold 30–90 seconds, then slowly return to standing by extending the hips.
execution.breathing_instructions: Breathe deeply and steadily. Each exhale allows the muscles to relax slightly, permitting a deeper position.
common_mistakes: Rounding the spine excessively rather than hinging from the hips, which shifts tension to the lumbar spine
Bouncing in the stretch (ballistic stretching), which can trigger the stretch reflex and reduce the stretch
Locking the knees in a hyperextended position — keep them straight but not hyperextended
safety_considerations: Those with hamstring tears or acute lower back pain should avoid or modify this stretch
Return to standing slowly to avoid a head rush
execution.range_of_motion_guidance: Hinge as far as the hamstrings allow while maintaining a relatively neutral spine. The hands do not need to reach the floor for an effective stretch.
coaching_cues: Hinge from the hips, not the lower back
Think of trying to touch the floor with a flat back rather than a rounded spine
Soften the knees very slightly if the stretch is too intense to control form

name: Wall Handstand Push-Up
description: The wall handstand push-up is a vertical pressing calisthenics movement performed inverted with the feet supported against a wall. It loads the anterior and medial deltoids, triceps, and upper trapezius with the full bodyweight through a vertical pressing plane, making it one of the most demanding shoulder exercises achievable with no equipment beyond a wall. The wall provides balance support, allowing focus on pressing strength.

execution.starting_position: Kick up to a handstand against a wall. Hands shoulder-width or slightly wider, fingers spread. Arms fully extended, body in a straight line.
execution.setup_instructions: Practice the kick-up and handstand hold before attempting pressing reps. Clear the area of obstacles. Use a gym mat for hand comfort.
steps: Step 1: Kick up to a handstand with feet resting against the wall.
Step 2: Lower the head toward the floor by bending the elbows out to the sides.
Step 3: Touch or nearly touch the top of the head to the floor.
Step 4: Press back to fully extended arms.
Step 5: Maintain a tight core throughout — avoid banana-arching.
execution.breathing_instructions: Inhale on the descent. Exhale on the press.
common_mistakes: Flaring the elbows wide — keep them at ~45 degrees for shoulder safety
Excessive lumbar arch — maintain a hollow or neutral body position
safety_considerations: Prerequisites: 20+ standard push-ups, comfortable headstand or partial handstand
Have a spotter for initial attempts
execution.range_of_motion_guidance: Full arm extension to head lightly touching the floor.
coaching_cues: Press the floor away with your hands
Core tight — no banana back
Elbows slightly forward, not straight out to the side

name: Hang Clean
description: The hang clean is a clean variation that begins from a hang position at the hip or knee rather than the floor, eliminating the first pull and focusing all training stimulus on the explosive second pull and front rack catch. It develops hip drive power and clean mechanics and is frequently used as a teaching progression, warm-up, or accessory movement. The hang clean tends to have a more horizontal bar path than the full clean and requires excellent hip snap timing.

execution.starting_position: Hold the bar at hip height with a shoulder-width clean grip. Hips hinged, back flat.
execution.setup_instructions: Begin from hip hang or knee hang position. The hip hang (bar at the hip crease) is the standard starting position.
steps: Step 1: Hold the bar in the hang position at hip height. Hips hinge back slightly with a flat back.
Step 2: Explosively drive the hips forward, extending fully.
Step 3: Shrug the traps and pull the elbows high and outside.
Step 4: Drop under the bar and rotate the elbows forward to receive in the front rack.
Step 5: Catch in a full or partial front squat, then stand to full extension.
execution.breathing_instructions: Brace before initiating. Exhale after standing from the catch.
common_mistakes: Not fully extending the hips before pulling under
Catching with the arms instead of using the shoulder shelf (front rack)
Bar drifting away from the body
safety_considerations: Develop front rack mobility before loading. Use bumper plates.
Start from the hip position before progressing to below the knee.
execution.range_of_motion_guidance: Full hip extension before catch. Catch in front rack with elbows high.
execution.tempo_recommendations: Explosive hip drive. Fast turnover. Controlled stand.
coaching_cues: Pop the hips — fast and violent
High elbows — bar on the shoulders
Drop under fast

name: Hang Power Clean
description: The hang power clean combines the starting position of the hang clean with the above-parallel catch of the power clean. The athlete begins from the hip or knee hang position and receives the bar above parallel, requiring both high bar speed from the hip drive and a quick partial drop under the bar. It is widely used in sport conditioning as a power development tool and requires less front rack mobility than the full clean.

execution.starting_position: Bar at hip height, shoulder-width clean grip, hips hinged, flat back.
execution.setup_instructions: Same setup as hang clean. Use bumper plates.
steps: Step 1: Hold bar at hip height in hang position.
Step 2: Drive hips forward explosively with full extension.
Step 3: Shrug and pull elbows high.
Step 4: Quickly rotate elbows under and catch in front rack above parallel (quarter squat).
Step 5: Stand fully and lower the bar to the hang or floor.
execution.breathing_instructions: Brace before pull. Exhale after standing from the catch.
common_mistakes: Catching below parallel
Using arm strength rather than hip drive
Collapsing the front rack on catch
safety_considerations: Use bumper plates. Practice the hip drive and high pull separately first.
execution.range_of_motion_guidance: Full hip extension. Above-parallel catch with locked elbows in front rack.
execution.tempo_recommendations: Explosive drive. Quick catch. Controlled stand.
coaching_cues: Hips fully open before elbows turn
Catch above parallel
High elbows in the rack

name: Hang Snatch
description: The hang snatch is a snatch variation in which the lift begins from a hang position — typically at the hip or knee — rather than from the floor. By eliminating the first pull from the floor, the hang snatch simplifies the lift and focuses training on the explosive second pull and catch mechanics. It is commonly used as a teaching tool, warm-up drill, or accessory exercise to reinforce hip drive and turnover speed.

execution.starting_position: Stand with the barbell held in a wide snatch grip at hip or knee height. Hips are hinged, back flat, weight balanced over mid-foot.
execution.setup_instructions: Begin from a hip hang (bar at hip crease) or knee hang (bar just above the knees). The hip hang is easier to learn.
steps: Step 1: Hold the bar at hip height with a wide snatch grip. Hinge the hips back slightly.
Step 2: Drive the hips forward explosively, extending fully through the hip and knee.
Step 3: Shrug the traps and guide the bar upward close to the body.
Step 4: Turn over the hands and pull yourself under the bar, locking out overhead.
Step 5: Catch in an overhead squat or above-parallel catch, then stand and lower.
execution.breathing_instructions: Brace before the pull. Exhale after the overhead catch is stabilized.
common_mistakes: Leaning back excessively instead of driving the hips through
Letting the bar swing away from the body
Not completing full hip extension before pulling under
safety_considerations: Use bumper plates. Train from the hip hang position first before progressing to knee hang.
Bail safely forward if the catch is missed.
execution.range_of_motion_guidance: Full hip extension before pulling under. Catch with locked overhead position.
execution.tempo_recommendations: Explosive. Build rhythm from hang to catch.
coaching_cues: Hips through — open explosively
Bar stays close — elbows high and outside
Fast hands — turnover is the key

name: Hanging Dragon Flag
description: A dragon flag variation where the body hangs from a pull-up bar, lowering the legs from vertical to horizontal while supporting only by the arms. This targets the entire anterior chain through an enormous range of motion. The hanging version adds lat and grip demands.

execution.starting_position: Set up for Hanging Dragon Flag in proper position.
execution.setup_instructions: Prepare body and equipment for Hanging Dragon Flag.
steps: Step 1: Hang from pull-up bar with straight arms. Raise legs to vertical.
Step 2: Lower legs slowly in a rigid plank from vertical toward horizontal.
Step 3: Maintain body rigidity without bending hips or knees.
Step 4: Lower to 10 degrees from horizontal then return to vertical.
execution.breathing_instructions: Breathe steadily; never hold breath during static holds.
common_mistakes: Hinging at hips to cheat
Dropping too fast
safety_considerations: Build prerequisite strength before attempting advanced variations.
Stop if joint pain occurs.
execution.range_of_motion_guidance: Full range of motion with control at all times.
coaching_cues: Body must remain perfectly rigid
5+ second lowering tempo

name: Hanging Knee Raise
description: The hanging knee raise is a beginner-to-intermediate hanging core exercise in which the athlete draws both knees toward the chest while hanging from a bar. By reducing the lever arm compared to straight-leg variations, it makes hip flexor and rectus abdominis training accessible to those building toward hanging leg raises and toes-to-bar. Proper posterior pelvic tilt during the top of the movement ensures abdominal engagement beyond mere hip flexion.

execution.starting_position: Hang from a pull-up bar with an overhand grip at shoulder-width. Arms fully extended, body still.
execution.setup_instructions: Use a secure overhead bar. Strive for a stable dead hang before initiating the movement.
steps: Step 1: Begin in a stable dead hang with arms fully extended.
Step 2: Brace the core and draw both knees upward toward the chest.
Step 3: At the top, tuck the pelvis posteriorly and compress the abs to ensure the rectus abdominis is loaded.
Step 4: Lower the knees with control back to the starting position.
Step 5: Avoid swinging at the bottom — pause briefly in dead hang before the next repetition.
execution.breathing_instructions: Exhale as the knees rise. Inhale on the controlled descent.
common_mistakes: Swinging the body to generate momentum rather than using core strength
Dropping the knees too fast — the eccentric phase should be controlled
Failing to posteriorly tilt the pelvis at the top, leaving the movement as pure hip flexion
safety_considerations: Grip strength limits many beginners — use chalk or straps if needed.
Avoid swinging as it places uneven load on the shoulder joints.
execution.range_of_motion_guidance: Knees should rise to at least hip height; ideally toward the chest for maximum abdominal involvement.
execution.tempo_recommendations: 2-0-2: 2 seconds concentric, 2 seconds eccentric. Eliminate momentum.
coaching_cues: Pull your knees into your belly
Round the lower back at the top — don't just lift legs
Pause at the bottom — no swinging

name: Hanging L-Sit Pull-Up
