description: A pull-up performed while maintaining an L-sit position with legs parallel to the floor. This requires the hip flexors and core to maintain the L-sit while the back and biceps perform the pull-up. The combined demand makes this one of the most challenging bodyweight pulling movements.

execution.starting_position: Set up for Hanging L-Sit Pull-Up in proper position.
execution.setup_instructions: Prepare body and equipment for Hanging L-Sit Pull-Up.
steps: Step 1: Hang from bar and raise legs to horizontal L-sit position.
Step 2: Maintaining leg position, pull up until chin clears bar.
Step 3: Lower with control while keeping legs horizontal.
Step 4: Complete all reps without letting legs drop.
execution.breathing_instructions: Breathe steadily; never hold breath during static holds.
common_mistakes: Letting legs drop during the pull
Using kip to assist
safety_considerations: Build prerequisite strength before attempting advanced variations.
Stop if joint pain occurs.
execution.range_of_motion_guidance: Full range of motion with control at all times.
coaching_cues: Legs must stay horizontal throughout
Master L-sit and strict pull-up separately first

name: Hanging V-Sit
description: A compression strength movement where the body hangs from a bar with legs raised to form a V-shape rather than a traditional L-sit angle. The V-shape requires superior hip flexor and core compression compared to a standard L-hang. This is a step toward more advanced compression skills.

execution.starting_position: Set up for Hanging V-Sit in proper position.
execution.setup_instructions: Prepare body and equipment for Hanging V-Sit.
steps: Step 1: Hang from bar with straight arm grip.
Step 2: Compress hips to raise legs above horizontal into V-shape.
Step 3: Keep legs straight and toes pointed throughout.
Step 4: Hold V position for target duration then lower slowly.
execution.breathing_instructions: Breathe steadily; never hold breath during static holds.
common_mistakes: Bending knees to cheat the angle
Swinging body
safety_considerations: Build prerequisite strength before attempting advanced variations.
Stop if joint pain occurs.
execution.range_of_motion_guidance: Full range of motion with control at all times.
coaching_cues: Legs must come above 90 degrees
Active shoulder engagement

name: Hanging Windshield Wiper Bent Knee with Pause
description: A windshield wiper variation with bent knees and a deliberate pause at each end range of rotation. The knee bend reduces the lever arm making this accessible before the straight-leg version, while the pause maximizes oblique time under tension at the most challenging point.

execution.starting_position: Set up for Hanging Windshield Wiper Bent Knee with Pause in proper position.
execution.setup_instructions: Prepare body and equipment for Hanging Windshield Wiper Bent Knee with Pause.
steps: Step 1: Hang from bar with knees bent at 90 degrees and legs raised to horizontal.
Step 2: Rotate bent legs to one side until thighs are nearly parallel to floor.
Step 3: Pause for 2 seconds at the endpoint.
Step 4: Return through center and rotate to opposite side, pausing again.
execution.breathing_instructions: Breathe steadily; never hold breath during static holds.
common_mistakes: Swinging to generate momentum
Not pausing at the endpoint
safety_considerations: Build prerequisite strength before attempting advanced variations.
Stop if joint pain occurs.
execution.range_of_motion_guidance: Full range of motion with control at all times.
coaching_cues: The pause is what makes it effective
Control the speed throughout

name: Hanging Windshield Wipers Weighted
description: Windshield wiper movements performed with ankle weights or a medicine ball held between the feet. The added weight dramatically increases the oblique and hip flexor demands. This advanced variation builds toward the elite level of rotational core strength needed for gymnastics.

execution.starting_position: Set up for Hanging Windshield Wipers Weighted in proper position.
execution.setup_instructions: Prepare body and equipment for Hanging Windshield Wipers Weighted.
steps: Step 1: Hang from bar with medicine ball squeezed between feet, legs at 90 degrees.
Step 2: Rotate legs to one side maintaining ball between feet.
Step 3: Pass through center and rotate to the opposite side.
Step 4: Control speed of rotation throughout.
execution.breathing_instructions: Breathe steadily; never hold breath during static holds.
common_mistakes: Dropping the ball
Using momentum rather than muscular control
safety_considerations: Build prerequisite strength before attempting advanced variations.
Stop if joint pain occurs.
execution.range_of_motion_guidance: Full range of motion with control at all times.
coaching_cues: Squeeze ball tightly throughout
Slower is harder

name: Hatfield Safety Squat Bar Squat
description: A squat performed with a safety squat bar while the hands brace against the upright posts of a power rack. The rack contact eliminates balance demands, allowing higher training intensities or deeper ranges of motion. The SSB's camber promotes an upright torso naturally, making this a useful tool for athletes with shoulder or wrist mobility restrictions.

execution.starting_position: Stand inside a power rack with the safety squat bar on your upper back. Grip the rack uprights at a comfortable height with both hands.
execution.setup_instructions: Set the SSB in the rack at the correct height. Load the bar. Stand inside the rack and grip the uprights before unracking.
steps: Step 1: Brace your core and unrack the bar, gripping the uprights lightly.
Step 2: Descend into a squat while keeping hands lightly on the rack uprights for balance — do not press off the rack to aid the ascent.
Step 3: Reach depth (at or below parallel) with an upright torso.
Step 4: Drive through the heels to return to standing.
execution.breathing_instructions: Inhale and brace before descent. Exhale during the ascent.
common_mistakes: Pressing hard off the rack uprights to cheat the ascent
Excessive forward lean due to overloading
safety_considerations: Use the uprights only for balance — pressing off them turns this into an assisted exercise rather than a true squat
execution.range_of_motion_guidance: Squat to at least parallel. The SSB's camber angle naturally encourages an upright torso.
coaching_cues: Sit between your heels
Use the rack for balance only, not assistance

name: Heavy Dumbbell Suitcase Row
description: The heavy dumbbell suitcase row is performed with the dumbbell at the side of the body (like carrying a suitcase) while bent over, rowing the weight upward in a path parallel to the torso rather than toward the hip. The unique line of pull challenges the mid and lower trapezius and rhomboids through a range often undertrained in standard dumbbell rows.

execution.starting_position: Stand with feet shoulder width apart. Hold a heavy dumbbell in one hand at the side, as if holding a suitcase. Hinge at the hips to 45-60 degrees, allowing the dumbbell to hang beside the working hip.
execution.setup_instructions: Use a heavy dumbbell — typically heavier than standard rows since the range of motion is shorter. The free hand can rest on the thigh for light support.
steps: Step 1: Begin hinged with the dumbbell hanging beside the hip.
Step 2: Row the dumbbell directly upward, keeping it close to the thigh and torso.
Step 3: Drive the elbow upward rather than backward — the motion is more vertical than horizontal.
Step 4: At the top, the elbow should be at torso height with the forearm vertical.
Step 5: Lower under control and repeat.
execution.breathing_instructions: Exhale rowing up. Inhale lowering.
common_mistakes: Pulling the dumbbell toward the chest rather than straight up alongside the body
Allowing the torso to rotate excessively — control anti-rotation
safety_considerations: Maintain neutral spine throughout — heavy loads demand braced core
Avoid if experiencing lower back pain until cleared
execution.range_of_motion_guidance: Dumbbell at full arm extension beside hip to elbow at torso height.
coaching_cues: Row straight up — not back, not forward
Keep the dumbbell close to the thigh throughout
Drive the elbow toward the ceiling

name: Heavy Sled Backward Drag
description: The backward sled drag involves attaching a harness or straps to a loaded sled and walking backward, pulling the sled along behind. The backward walking motion activates the hamstrings and quadriceps in an unusual anti-gravity pattern and places high demand on the knee extensors throughout the entire range, making it an excellent rehabilitation tool for knee health and an effective conditioning tool for the posterior chain. Unlike forward sled pushing, the backward drag emphasises the hamstrings and gluteus maximus and is particularly effective for VMO (vastus medialis oblique) strengthening.

execution.starting_position: Attach a pulling harness around the waist or hold the strap handles. Stand facing away from the loaded sled with the straps taut. Take an athletic stance.
execution.setup_instructions: Attach the sled harness securely. Ensure there is slack-free connection between the harness and the sled. The sled can also be dragged holding straps in both hands at hip height.
steps: Step 1: Face away from the sled with straps taut. Stand tall with a slight forward lean at the hips.
Step 2: Drive the rear foot into the ground and step backward, taking a full backward step.
Step 3: Continue walking backward with alternating steps, keeping tension in the straps throughout. Do not allow the straps to go slack.
Step 4: Maintain an upright posture and consistent pull tension. Look over the shoulder periodically to check the path.
Step 5: At the end of the distance, slow and stop. Turn and re-position for the next set.
execution.breathing_instructions: Breathe regularly throughout the drag. Short, rhythmic breathing with each backward step.
common_mistakes: Allowing the straps to go slack between steps — this loses the continuous tension that makes the exercise effective
Walking with very short shuffle steps — full backward strides produce more hip and hamstring demand
Looking down rather than forward/backward, which disrupts posture and balance
safety_considerations: Glance over the shoulder regularly to check for obstacles in the backward path
Use this exercise on a clear, flat surface
execution.range_of_motion_guidance: Walk 20–40 metres per set. Full stride length backward. Continuous strap tension.
execution.tempo_recommendations: Rehabilitation/prehab: light load, 30–40m × 4–6 sets with 60 seconds rest. Conditioning: moderate load, 20m × 6–8 sets with 60–90 seconds rest.
coaching_cues: Keep the straps taut at all times
Take big backward strides
Squeeze the glutes and hamstrings with every step

name: Heel-Elevated Goblet Squat
description: A goblet squat performed with the heels raised on a wedge or plates. Heel elevation reduces ankle dorsiflexion demands, allows greater squat depth, and shifts loading emphasis further toward the quadriceps — particularly the rectus femoris — while reducing hip flexor and lower back involvement.

execution.starting_position: Stand with heels raised on a 25lb plate or squat wedge, feet shoulder-width apart. Hold a dumbbell vertically at chest height with both hands cupping the top end.
execution.setup_instructions: Place a 25lb plate flat on the floor. Stand on it with just the heels. Hold a dumbbell at chest height.
steps: Step 1: Brace your core and keep the dumbbell tight to your chest throughout.
Step 2: Push your hips back and down, keeping the torso upright.
Step 3: Descend to full depth or until thighs are parallel to the floor.
Step 4: Drive through the entire foot to stand, squeezing the glutes at lockout.
execution.breathing_instructions: Inhale as you descend. Exhale on the way up.
common_mistakes: Letting the knees cave inward at the bottom
Leaning the torso excessively forward
safety_considerations: Ensure the plate or wedge is stable and will not slip before adding significant load
execution.range_of_motion_guidance: Aim for full depth (hips below knees). The heel elevation makes this more accessible for those with limited ankle mobility.
coaching_cues: Sit between your heels
Chest up, elbows down

name: Helms Cable Row
description: The Helms cable row (a variation associated with physique coach Eric Helms) positions the lifter on a high-incline bench facing a low cable pulley, with the torso supported at approximately 60-70 degrees. This angle creates a combined vertical and horizontal pull that maximally stretches the lats and teres major throughout the range of motion, and the chest support eliminates lower back involvement.

execution.starting_position: Set a bench at 60-70 degrees incline near a low cable pulley. Lie prone with chest on the pad, feet on the floor. Grab the cable handle (rope, V-handle, or bar) with arms extended toward the pulley.
execution.setup_instructions: Position the bench close enough to the cable stack that the arms are fully extended toward the pulley in the starting position.
steps: Step 1: Begin with arms fully extended, feeling a deep lat stretch.
Step 2: Row the cable toward the torso, driving elbows back.
Step 3: At peak contraction, hold 1 second.
Step 4: Return under control to full arm extension.
Step 5: Emphasize the stretch at the bottom — this differentiates the Helms row.
execution.breathing_instructions: Exhale on the row. Inhale returning to the stretch.
common_mistakes: Bench angle too low — the incline must be steep enough to allow full lat stretch
Insufficient cable distance — the bench must be positioned to achieve true full extension
safety_considerations: Adjust cable height and bench position carefully before loading
Keep the neck neutral — avoid craning while lying prone
execution.range_of_motion_guidance: Maximum lat stretch at full arm extension to full retraction at peak contraction.
coaching_cues: Let the weight pull you into a full stretch at the bottom
Think 'lat stretch to lat squeeze'
The bench angle is what makes this special — get it right

name: Helms Row
description: The Helms Row is performed with the chest supported on an incline bench set to 30-45 degrees, with a dumbbell in each hand hanging freely. The chest support eliminates lower back and hip contribution, allowing the back muscles to work in complete isolation. The incline angle also allows greater shoulder extension ROM compared to a flat bench row, increasing lat engagement at the bottom of each repetition.

execution.starting_position: Set an adjustable bench to 30-45 degrees of incline. Lie prone (chest-down) with the chest on the pad, feet on the floor. Hold a dumbbell in each hand, arms hanging straight down.
execution.setup_instructions: Adjust bench angle so the arms can fully extend downward without hitting the floor. Use a bench height that allows free arm movement.
steps: Step 1: Lie on the incline bench with chest fully supported, dumbbells hanging.
Step 2: Retract the scapulae slightly to begin the movement.
Step 3: Row both dumbbells toward the lower ribcage, driving the elbows upward and back.
Step 4: At the top, squeeze the rhomboids and mid-traps hard.
Step 5: Lower both dumbbells fully under control to the extended starting position.
execution.breathing_instructions: Exhale on the row, inhale on the descent.
common_mistakes: Lifting the chest off the pad, reintroducing lower back and hip involvement
Using too heavy a weight, causing the elbows to flare excessively
Not fully extending the arms at the bottom
safety_considerations: Keep the chest on the pad throughout — that is the defining feature of this exercise
Neck should remain in neutral — do not crane the head up
execution.range_of_motion_guidance: Full arm extension at the bottom to elbows above the torso level at the top.
coaching_cues: Chest stays on the pad
Squeeze your shoulder blades together at the top
Let the dumbbells hang fully at the bottom

name: Dumbbell Hex Press / Squeeze Press
description: The Hex Press (or Squeeze Press) is performed by holding two dumbbells pressed flat together and maintaining that pressing contact throughout the entire movement. The continuous inward squeezing force creates constant isometric adduction demand on the pectoral muscles throughout the press, providing a unique chest contraction stimulus that differs from standard dumbbell pressing.

execution.starting_position: Lie on a flat bench holding two dumbbells pressed flat against each other with a neutral grip (palms facing each other). Position the dumbbells above the chest.
execution.setup_instructions: Choose dumbbells with flat sides (hex dumbbells work best). Start light — the constant adduction effort is fatiguing. Lie back on the bench and press the dumbbells together before starting the movement.
steps: Step 1: Hold both dumbbells pressed firmly together with neutral grip above the chest.
Step 2: Lower them together toward the lower chest, maintaining constant inward pressing force.
Step 3: Touch the chest and press back up to the starting position.
Step 4: Squeeze the dumbbells together as hard as possible throughout — if they separate, you have lost the key stimulus.
execution.breathing_instructions: Inhale before lowering. Exhale as you press up.
common_mistakes: Letting the dumbbells separate, removing the adduction stimulus
Using too heavy a load, making it impossible to maintain the squeeze
safety_considerations: If dumbbells are round, they may roll apart — hex dumbbells are significantly safer for this exercise
Start with light weight and focus on maintaining contact
execution.range_of_motion_guidance: Lower to light chest contact; full extension at top.
coaching_cues: Pretend you are trying to crush both dumbbells into one
Squeeze harder at the top — peak chest contraction happens at lockout

name: High-Bar Barbell Back Squat
description: The high-bar barbell back squat places the barbell on the upper trapezius, just below the base of the neck. This position encourages a more upright torso throughout the movement, placing greater demand on the quadriceps compared to the low-bar variation. It is the squat style used in Olympic weightlifting as it closely mimics the receiving position of the clean and snatch.

execution.starting_position: Stand inside a power rack with the bar resting on the upper traps, below the base of the neck. Feet shoulder-width apart, toes turned out 15-25 degrees. Grip slightly wider than shoulders.
execution.setup_instructions: Set the rack hooks at upper-chest height. Position bar across upper traps, unrack with a controlled step back.
steps: Step 1: Brace the core fully and take a deep breath before beginning the descent.
Step 2: Break at the knees and hips simultaneously, keeping the torso relatively upright.
Step 3: Descend with knees tracking over the toes until the hip crease passes below the knee.
Step 4: Drive through the full foot and extend both the hips and knees to return to standing.
execution.breathing_instructions: Inhale and brace before descent. Exhale at the top of each rep.
common_mistakes: Excessive forward lean (more typical of low-bar)
Heels rising due to limited ankle dorsiflexion
Knees collapsing inward at the bottom
Losing upper back tension under the bar
safety_considerations: Set safety bars appropriately in the power rack
Develop adequate ankle dorsiflexion and hip mobility
Consider heel elevation with plates if ankle mobility is limited
execution.range_of_motion_guidance: Full depth requires hip crease below the top of the knee. The more upright torso allows greater depth for many lifters.
coaching_cues: Chest up throughout
Knees forward and out
Sit between the heels
Stand tall at the top

name: High Cable Rope Crunch
description: The high cable rope crunch uses a rope attachment on a high pulley to provide constant tension throughout the entire range of spinal flexion, unlike bodyweight crunches where tension drops as the crunch deepens. The athlete kneels facing the cable stack, holds the rope behind the head, and flexes the spine downward to bring the elbows toward the knees. This constant-tension loading makes it one of the most effective loaded abdominal exercises and allows progressive overload of the rectus abdominis in a way that bodyweight crunches cannot replicate.

execution.starting_position: Attach a rope to the high pulley. Kneel facing the cable machine, approximately 60–80 cm from the base of the stack. Hold the rope with both hands, thumbs pointed inward, and position the rope on either side of the head. The hips remain fixed throughout.
execution.setup_instructions: Set the cable height to the high pulley. Attach a rope handle. Kneel on a mat for comfort. Choose a weight that allows full range of motion with controlled eccentric.
steps: Step 1: Kneel facing the cable machine with rope held at the sides of the head. Hips remain stationary throughout — do not sit back.
Step 2: Flex the spine forward and downward, bringing the elbows toward the floor in front of the knees. Focus on rounding the spine, not simply hinging at the hips.
Step 3: Hold the contracted position for 1–2 seconds, feeling the maximal contraction of the rectus abdominis.
Step 4: Slowly return to the starting position, allowing a full stretch of the abs at the top. Do not allow the spine to hyperextend.
Step 5: Repeat for the prescribed number of repetitions.
execution.breathing_instructions: Exhale forcefully at the bottom of the crunch (fully contracted position). Inhale on the controlled return to the start.
common_mistakes: Hinging at the hips and sitting back rather than flexing the spine — this uses the hip flexors, not the abs
Using momentum by swinging forward rather than contracting the abs deliberately
Not allowing a full stretch at the top of the movement, limiting the range of motion
safety_considerations: Avoid neck strain by keeping the rope at the sides of the head, not behind it — the hands should not pull the head forward
execution.range_of_motion_guidance: Full spinal flexion from an extended position at the top to maximum forward flex at the bottom. Elbows should travel toward the floor.
execution.tempo_recommendations: 2-1-2-0 (2 seconds down, 1 second hold, 2 seconds up). Do not rush the eccentric.
coaching_cues: Round the spine — do not hinge at the hips
Imagine trying to bring your sternum to your pelvis
The hips do not move

name: High Cable Bicep Curl (Peak Curl)
description: The high cable peak curl is performed facing a high cable pulley, with the arm raised to shoulder height or above and the elbow flexed against the cable resistance. Because the cable pulls from behind and above, the bicep is under constant tension in the shortened position — unlike free weight curls which lose tension at the top. This makes it exceptional for training the bicep in its contracted peak position and is a classic bodybuilding pose and exercise.

execution.starting_position: Stand side-on to a high cable pulley. Grasp the single handle with the inside arm, arm extended toward the pulley at shoulder height.
execution.setup_instructions: Set the cable pulley at or slightly above shoulder height. Attach a single handle. Stand far enough from the stack to put tension on the cable at full extension.
steps: Step 1: Begin with the arm extended toward the cable at shoulder height.
Step 2: Curl the forearm toward the shoulder by flexing the elbow.
Step 3: Hold the peak contraction for one second, squeezing the bicep hard.
Step 4: Extend the arm slowly back to the starting position.
execution.breathing_instructions: Exhale on the curl, inhale on the return.
common_mistakes: Upper arm dropping down during the curl, losing the high-cable advantage
Using shoulder to assist
Rushing through the peak
safety_considerations: Keep the upper arm stable — only the forearm should move
execution.range_of_motion_guidance: Full elbow extension to maximum flexion.
coaching_cues: Upper arm stays high and still
Squeeze hard at the top
Feel the peak contraction

name: High Cable Rear Delt Fly
description: The high cable rear delt fly is performed with both cable pulleys set at above-head height, gripping the opposing handles and pulling them down and outward in a horizontal arc to the sides of the body. The high-to-low angle applies a unique line of force on the posterior deltoid and scapular retractors compared to low-cable or dumbbell variations, targeting the rear deltoid from a mechanically different angle and improving overall posterior shoulder development.

execution.starting_position: Stand between a cable crossover station with both pulleys set above head height. Reach across and grip the left pulley handle with the right hand, and right pulley with the left hand (cables cross). Arms extended upward.
execution.setup_instructions: Because cables cross, the motion pulls them apart and downward. Use very light weight — rear deltoids have limited absolute strength.
steps: Step 1: Cross-grip the cable handles above head height. Arms extended overhead.
Step 2: With arms remaining straight (slight elbow bend), pull the cables downward and outward.
Step 3: Continue the arc until arms are level with the shoulders and wide to the sides.
Step 4: Squeeze the rear delts at the bottom of the pull.
Step 5: Return under control to the starting overhead position.
execution.breathing_instructions: Exhale on the pull, inhale on the return.
common_mistakes: Bending the elbows too much — the arms should remain nearly straight throughout
Using too heavy a load, which recruits the traps and lats instead of the rear delts
safety_considerations: The cables cross above the head — ensure the cable crossover station height is appropriate before starting
execution.range_of_motion_guidance: From cables crossed overhead to arms wide at shoulder height.
coaching_cues: Straight arms — pull with the rear delts not the elbows
High to wide
Squeeze the back of the shoulder at the bottom

name: High Cable Triceps Extension — Kneeling Drop Set
description: A triceps overhead cable extension performed from the kneeling position facing away from a high pulley, executed as a drop set where the weight is immediately reduced after reaching failure and the exerciser continues the set. The kneeling position provides a stable base, the high cable angle stretches the long head of the triceps maximally, and the drop set structure maximizes time-under-tension and metabolic stress for triceps hypertrophy.

execution.starting_position: Kneel on the floor facing away from a high cable pulley. Hold a rope attachment behind the head with both hands, elbows pointing upward and slightly forward.
execution.setup_instructions: Set up two weight settings in advance for the drop: a heavier starting weight and a lighter follow-up. Some machines allow quick pin changes; otherwise have a training partner help reduce the weight.
steps: Step 1: Begin kneeling with the rope held behind the head. Extend the elbows to full lockout, pressing the rope forward and downward.
Step 2: Squeeze the triceps at full extension, then slowly return to the bent-elbow start.
Step 3: Continue until failure at the starting weight.
Step 4: Immediately reduce the weight (drop) and continue the set for additional reps to secondary failure.
execution.breathing_instructions: Exhale during the extension (press). Inhale during the return.
common_mistakes: Flaring the elbows wide — keep them in line with the head, not splayed out
Moving the upper arm during the extension — only the forearms should move
Allowing the torso to lean excessively forward to assist the press
safety_considerations: Ensure quick weight reduction is possible before beginning — plan the drop logistics first
Avoid excessive neck strain — the rope attachment should not press on the neck
execution.range_of_motion_guidance: Full elbow extension at the bottom. Full elbow flexion (rope behind head) at the top.
execution.tempo_recommendations: 2s extension, 1s lockout, 3s eccentric return. Full ROM on each rep of both the initial and drop set.
coaching_cues: Keep the elbows tight — do not let them flare during the press
Squeeze the triceps at lockout — the constant tension from the high cable makes this very effective
The drop set should be a smooth transition — have the lighter weight ready to go immediately

name: High Push-Up Position Plank
description: The high push-up position plank is a foundational isometric core stability exercise in which the body is held in a rigid, straight line from head to heel while supported on the hands and toes. Compared to the forearm plank, the extended-arm position places greater demand on the shoulder girdle stabilizers and serratus anterior, while the core musculature functions identically to maintain spinal stiffness. It is a prerequisite position for push-up and many other calisthenic progressions and should be mastered before advancing to dynamic variations.

execution.starting_position: Place the hands on the floor directly under the shoulders. Extend the legs behind, toes on the floor. The body forms a straight line from head to heel.
execution.setup_instructions: No equipment needed. Use a mat for wrist comfort on hard surfaces.
steps: Step 1: Position hands under shoulders, fingers spread for grip.
Step 2: Drive the floor away — imagine pushing the ground down. Protract the scapulae slightly.
Step 3: Squeeze the glutes and brace the core. Lock out the knees.
Step 4: Keep the body in a straight line — no hip hiking, sagging, or piking.
Step 5: Hold for the target duration, maintaining perfect alignment throughout.
execution.breathing_instructions: Breathe continuously with shallow breaths. Do not hold the breath.
common_mistakes: Hips piking up — this reduces core demand and places it on the shoulders
Hips sagging — this compresses the lumbar spine under load
safety_considerations: Avoid if wrist pain is present — substitute forearm plank
execution.range_of_motion_guidance: Isometric hold. Perfect alignment must be maintained for the full duration.
execution.tempo_recommendations: Hold for target time: beginners 20–30 s; intermediate 45–60 s; advanced 60–90 s+.
coaching_cues: Push the floor away
Squeeze the glutes — the whole posterior chain is a unit
Long spine — from crown to heel

name: High Pulley Straight-Arm Pull (Facing Away)
description: The facing-away high pulley straight-arm pull has the lifter facing away from the cable stack, gripping a high attachment and pulling it forward and downward with straight arms. Unlike the standard straight-arm pulldown (facing the cable), this variation loads the lats through a forward-to-down arc that challenges them in both the overhead stretched position and the contracted position differently, with greater emphasis on the lower lat fibers.

execution.starting_position: Stand facing away from a high cable pulley. Reach back overhead and grasp a rope or straight bar. Begin with arms extended overhead toward the pulley.
execution.setup_instructions: Set the pulley to the highest position. Stand close enough that the arms are reaching overhead at approximately the cable's exit angle.
steps: Step 1: Begin with arms extended overhead gripping the attachment.
Step 2: With straight arms, pull the attachment forward and downward in an arc.
Step 3: Continue until the arms are at approximately hip or thigh level.
Step 4: Hold 1 second at peak contraction.
Step 5: Return under control — arms travel back and overhead.
execution.breathing_instructions: Exhale on the pull. Inhale on the return overhead.
common_mistakes: Bending the elbows — arms must stay straight
Leaning forward excessively to extend range — keep the torso relatively upright
safety_considerations: The overhead starting position requires shoulder mobility — assess before loading
Moderate loads only — straight-arm exercises have high moment arm demands
execution.range_of_motion_guidance: Arms overhead to arms at hips, maintaining straight elbows throughout.
coaching_cues: Arms stay locked — think 'pull the earth down'
Feel the lat at the top stretch
Hips stay stationary throughout

name: High-to-Low Cable Fly
description: The high-to-low cable fly is performed with the cable pulleys set at the highest position, with the arms arcing downward and inward. This downward adduction path matches the line of pull of the sternal (lower) pectoralis major fibers, making this variation particularly effective for lower chest development. Constant cable tension provides loading through the full range of motion.

execution.starting_position: Set both cable pulleys to the highest position. Grasp the handles and step forward so the cables pull from above. Stand tall or stagger your stance slightly. Arms begin high and wide with a slight elbow bend.
execution.setup_instructions: Set both cable pulleys to the topmost position. Attach single-handle D-ring attachments. Stand between the stacks and step forward far enough to feel tension from above.
steps: Step 1: Set the pulleys to their highest setting. Grip the handles and step forward into the center.
Step 2: Raise arms out wide at shoulder height or above with a fixed, slight elbow bend.
Step 3: Exhale and arc both arms down and inward in a downward sweeping motion, meeting the handles in front of the lower torso.
Step 4: Squeeze the lower chest at the bottom of the arc, then inhale and slowly return to the high, wide position.
execution.breathing_instructions: Exhale as you arc downward and together; inhale as you return to the high, open position.
common_mistakes: Bending the elbows too much, converting the fly into a pushing movement
Leaning excessively forward to generate momentum
safety_considerations: Maintain a slight, consistent elbow bend — keep the shoulder in a safe range
Do not cross the hands aggressively past the midline if shoulder impingement is present
execution.range_of_motion_guidance: Open wide to feel the stretch at the top; bring hands to meet at or slightly below waist level for maximum lower pec contraction.
coaching_cues: Think of drawing a rainbow arc from high and wide to low and together
Squeeze the lower chest like you are trying to crack a walnut between your pecs at the bottom

name: Hip 90-90 with Reach and Thoracic Twist
description: A combined hip mobility and thoracic rotation exercise built on the 90-90 position. While seated in the 90-90 hip configuration, the exerciser rotates the thoracic spine toward the front leg while reaching the same-side arm forward and the opposite arm backward. This integrates thoracic rotation with hip external rotation mobility, training both simultaneously and improving the movement coupling required for many athletic and functional tasks.

execution.starting_position: Sit in the 90-90 position with the right leg externally rotated in front and the left leg internally rotated behind. Both shins on or close to the floor.
execution.setup_instructions: Hands can be lightly on the floor to begin. Remove hand support as ability improves.
steps: Step 1: Begin in the 90-90 position, seated upright.
Step 2: Rotate the torso toward the right (front) leg, reaching the right arm forward and the left arm back.
Step 3: Hold the rotated position for 2-3 seconds, feeling the combined hip and thoracic stretch.
Step 4: Return to center. Rotate to the opposite side, reaching the left arm forward and right arm back. Hold 2-3 seconds. Alternate sides.
execution.breathing_instructions: Exhale as you rotate and reach. Inhale as you return to center.
common_mistakes: Rotating through the lumbar rather than the thoracic spine — the rotation should come from the mid and upper back
Lifting the knees from the floor to assist the rotation — maintain the 90-90 hip configuration
Using a very limited range — the thoracic rotation should be substantial
safety_considerations: If lumbar pain occurs during the rotation, reduce the rotation range and focus on thoracic movement only
If hip pain is aggravated by the 90-90 position, check with a physiotherapist
execution.range_of_motion_guidance: Full thoracic rotation available from this hip position. The hip position is maintained; only the thorax rotates.
coaching_cues: Let the thoracic spine lead the rotation — not the hips
Reach long through both arms — the reach amplifies the thoracic rotation
Feel the hip of the front leg staying anchored while the upper body rotates

name: Hip 90/90 Rotation
description: The hip 90/90 rotation is an active mobility drill that trains the ability to transition the hips between internal and external rotation by moving both legs simultaneously from one 90-90 configuration to the opposite. Unlike the passive 90-90 stretch, this version is performed as a controlled active movement. It develops proprioceptive awareness of hip rotation and is used in hip rehabilitation, athletic movement prep, and general hip mobility programs.

execution.starting_position: Sit on the floor with both legs in a 90-90 configuration — front leg with the shin facing forward (external rotation), rear leg to the side with the shin facing back (internal rotation).
execution.setup_instructions: Use a mat. Hands can be placed on the floor beside the hips for support in early stages.
steps: Step 1: Begin in a 90-90 seated position.
Step 2: Internally rotate both hips simultaneously — the front knee drops inward and the rear knee drops toward the floor in front.
Step 3: Both legs pass through a brief neutral position in the middle.
Step 4: Continue rotating to arrive in the 90-90 position on the opposite side.
Step 5: Pause, then rotate back to the starting side. Each full trip counts as one rep.
execution.breathing_instructions: Breathe freely and steadily. Do not hold the breath.
common_mistakes: Using the hands heavily for support, which reduces core and hip engagement
Moving too quickly — this requires deliberate slow control at each stage
One hip excessively lagging behind the other
safety_considerations: If sharp hip or knee pain occurs, stop and consult a clinician
Avoid if currently experiencing acute hip labral symptoms without clinical clearance
execution.range_of_motion_guidance: Full transition from one 90-90 configuration to the other, with both hips as close to the floor as available range allows.
execution.tempo_recommendations: 3–4 seconds per transition, 5–10 reps each direction × 2–3 sets.
coaching_cues: Rotate both hips at the same time, not one then the other
Move as far through each transition as your hip allows
Gradually reduce your hand support as you gain confidence

name: Hip 90-90 Position Switch
description: The 90-90 hip switch is a floor-based hip mobility exercise in which both hips are bent to 90 degrees in a seated position — one leg in external rotation in front and one in internal rotation behind. The switch involves transitioning from one side to the other by lifting both knees and rotating the entire lower body to the opposite 90-90 configuration. This exercise challenges hip internal and external rotation range, adductor flexibility, and hip socket mobility through a continuous dynamic flow.

execution.starting_position: Sit on the floor with both knees bent to 90 degrees. The front leg is in external rotation (shin perpendicular to the body) and the back leg is in internal rotation (shin parallel to and alongside the body).
execution.setup_instructions: No equipment needed. A mat is recommended. Sit tall with an upright torso. Using hands on the floor for support is encouraged initially.
steps: Step 1: Begin in the 90-90 position with the right leg externally rotated in front and the left leg internally rotated behind.
Step 2: Lift both knees off the floor slightly and rotate them to the opposite side, so the left knee comes in front and the right goes behind.
Step 3: Lower both knees to the floor in the new 90-90 position (left front, right back). This is one switch.
Step 4: Hold the new position for 2-3 seconds, then switch back or continue to alternate.
execution.breathing_instructions: Exhale during the transition. Inhale and settle into each position.
common_mistakes: Collapsing the torso toward the front leg — maintain an upright position throughout
Forcing range by pushing the knees down with the hands — the range should come from the hip joint passively
Lifting both knees high and using momentum — aim for a controlled, low transition
safety_considerations: If sharp hip or knee pain occurs during the rotation, reduce range or stop and assess with a physiotherapist
Hip internal rotation restriction is common — work at the available range, not beyond it
execution.range_of_motion_guidance: Both shins to the floor in both 90-90 positions is the target. Work toward this progressively.
execution.tempo_recommendations: 2-3s hold in each position before switching. Transitions should be slow and controlled.
coaching_cues: Sit tall — do not lean over the front leg
Feel the outer hip of the front leg and the inner hip of the back leg stretching
The switch is a rotation — lead from the knees, not the feet

name: Hip 90-90 Position — Hands Free
description: The hip 90-90 hands-free variation requires the exerciser to maintain the 90-90 hip position (front leg externally rotated, back leg internally rotated, both knees at 90 degrees) without using the hands for support. This demands greater hip joint control, core stability, and hip mobility than the supported version. The challenge is to sit upright, balanced purely by the hip joint's ability to control the positions of both legs simultaneously. A key milestone in hip mobility rehabilitation.

execution.starting_position: Sit on the floor in the 90-90 position with the right leg externally rotated in front and the left leg internally rotated behind. Both knees are at 90 degrees.
execution.setup_instructions: Master the supported 90-90 position before attempting the hands-free version. Begin by lifting the hands just off the floor while maintaining balance.
steps: Step 1: Establish the 90-90 position with hands lightly on the floor for reference.
Step 2: Slowly lift both hands off the floor and raise them in front of the chest or cross them over the chest.
Step 3: Maintain the upright position with both shins as close to the floor as possible, without the hands.
Step 4: Hold for the prescribed duration, then place the hands back down. Switch sides and repeat.
execution.breathing_instructions: Deep breathing throughout. Each exhale can allow deeper settling into the position.
common_mistakes: Collapsing the torso toward the front leg as soon as the hands are lifted — the core must hold the upright position
Cheating by keeping the fingertips lightly touching the floor — hands should be fully lifted
Allowing the back knee to rise significantly off the floor — work on the hold even with the knee elevated if needed
safety_considerations: If the hip positions are acutely painful without hand support, return to the supported version
Rounded lower back is common — focus on sitting taller rather than trying to get the shins to the floor
execution.range_of_motion_guidance: Both shins as low as possible to the floor, held without hands. The torso must remain upright.
execution.tempo_recommendations: Hold for 20-60 seconds per side. Build to 60 seconds.
coaching_cues: Sit tall — imagine a string pulling the top of your head toward the ceiling
Breathe into the front hip — feel the external rotation holding without hands to assist
The shins not touching the floor is fine — the work is in the hold, not the contact

name: Hip Abduction Machine
description: The hip abduction machine provides seated, bilateral hip abduction against a weight stack, targeting the gluteus medius, gluteus minimus, and tensor fasciae latae. The seated position eliminates balance demands and allows the abductors to be loaded in isolation through a full controlled range of motion. It is a popular machine exercise for developing lateral hip width and stability.

execution.starting_position: Sit in the hip abduction machine with back against the pad, knees against the inner pads, and feet on the footrests. Adjust the pads to a comfortable starting position.
execution.setup_instructions: Adjust the seat and pad width to a comfortable range. Set weight stack to a load that allows full range motion with control.
steps: Step 1: Sit in the machine with back flat against the pad. Place knees against the inner surfaces of the pads.
Step 2: Push both knees apart — abducting the hips — against the pad resistance.
Step 3: Push until the pads reach the end of range or until maximum comfortable abduction.
Step 4: Hold the peak position briefly.
Step 5: Return the knees inward under control to the starting position.
execution.breathing_instructions: Exhale as you push the knees apart. Inhale as you bring them back.
common_mistakes: Using too much weight, which causes the torso to lean or the lower back to arch
Releasing the tension too quickly on the return — control the eccentric
Not adjusting the pad to a comfortable starting range
safety_considerations: Low risk when performed with appropriate weight
Avoid if the exercise causes hip or groin pain
execution.range_of_motion_guidance: Push the knees as far apart as the machine allows or until comfortable. Full excursion of the pads.
coaching_cues: Push through the outer knees — not just the thighs
Control the return — don't let the weight snap back
Keep the back flat against the pad

name: Hip Adduction Machine
description: The hip adduction machine is a seated machine exercise that works the inner thigh adductors by pressing the knees inward against pad resistance. The adductor magnus, adductor longus, adductor brevis, and gracilis are the primary movers. The machine isolates the adductors by removing the balance requirements of standing adduction exercises, and provides consistent resistance through the entire range of motion.

execution.starting_position: Sit in the hip adduction machine with back against the pad. Place legs on the outer sides of the pads with knees and ankles against the pad surfaces. Set pads to a wide starting position.
execution.setup_instructions: Adjust seat height and pad width for a comfortable starting stretch. Use a weight that allows full range of motion.
steps: Step 1: Sit in the machine with back flat, legs on outer sides of pads. Begin with pads in the wide starting position.
Step 2: Press both legs inward — adducting the hips — by squeezing the inner thighs.
Step 3: Press until the pads are as close together as the machine allows.
Step 4: Hold the peak contraction briefly.
Step 5: Return slowly to the wide starting position under control.
execution.breathing_instructions: Exhale as you press the legs together. Inhale as you open.
common_mistakes: Using momentum — slow, controlled movement throughout
Not controlling the eccentric — the opening phase should be slow
Rounding the lower back against the pad
safety_considerations: Avoid if the exercise causes groin strain — reduce range or weight
Start conservatively — the adductors can be strained if loaded aggressively without warm-up
execution.range_of_motion_guidance: Open to a comfortable stretch at the start. Close fully at the end.
coaching_cues: Squeeze the inner thighs — not the glutes
Control the opening — resist the pads on the way out
Keep the back flat — don't lean forward

name: Kneeling Hip Flexor Stretch
description: The kneeling hip flexor stretch targets the iliopsoas and rectus femoris through sustained hip extension of the rear leg in a kneeling lunge position. It is one of the most effective and widely used stretches for counteracting hip flexor tightness from prolonged sitting, which is associated with anterior pelvic tilt and lower back discomfort. The stretch should be felt in the front of the hip of the kneeling leg.

execution.starting_position: Kneel on one knee on the floor or a mat, with the other foot forward in a lunge position. The rear knee is on the ground, the front foot is flat. Torso upright.
execution.setup_instructions: Use a mat or folded towel under the kneeling knee for comfort. Place hands on the front knee or the front thigh for balance.
steps: Step 1: Begin in a kneeling lunge with the rear knee on the floor and front foot forward.
Step 2: Tuck the pelvis under by gently squeezing the glutes of the rear leg — this posteriorly tilts the pelvis and increases the stretch.
Step 3: Shift the hips forward gently until a stretch is felt in the front of the rear hip.
Step 4: Hold the position for 30–90 seconds, breathing normally.
Step 5: Release and switch sides.
execution.breathing_instructions: Breathe deeply and slowly throughout the hold. Each exhale can allow the hips to relax slightly further into the stretch.
common_mistakes: Anterior pelvic tilt during the stretch, which reduces tension on the iliopsoas — tuck the pelvis
Leaning the torso forward, which reduces hip extension and diminishes the stretch
Not holding long enough — brief holds provide minimal flexibility adaptation
safety_considerations: If the kneeling knee causes discomfort, place padding underneath
Do not force past the point of a moderate stretch sensation
execution.range_of_motion_guidance: Shift the hips forward until a moderate stretch is felt in the front of the rear hip. The front knee should not extend beyond the toes.
execution.tempo_recommendations: Hold 30–90 seconds per side. Perform 2–4 rounds.
coaching_cues: Squeeze the glute of the rear leg to deepen the stretch
Stand tall through the torso — do not collapse forward
Breathe into the front of your hip

name: Plate-Loaded Hip Thrust Machine
description: The plate-loaded hip thrust machine positions the lifter on a padded seat with a shoulder pad that presses downward, allowing the hips to extend against resistance without the need to load a barbell over the hips. This eliminates the setup discomfort of the barbell hip thrust and allows for quick load changes. The machine provides a stable environment for maximum glute loading through the full range of hip extension.

execution.starting_position: Sit in the machine with the upper back against the shoulder pad and feet flat on the foot platform. Hips are at the starting low position.
execution.setup_instructions: Adjust the foot platform so the knees are at 90 degrees at the top of the movement. Load the machine appropriately.
steps: Step 1: Begin with the hips low, back supported by the pad.
Step 2: Drive through the heels and squeeze the glutes to extend the hips upward.
Step 3: Push until the hips are fully extended, forming a straight line from knees to shoulders.
Step 4: Lower the hips under control back to the starting position.
execution.breathing_instructions: Exhale as you extend the hips, inhale on the return.
common_mistakes: Hyperextending the lower back at the top
Pushing through the toes instead of heels
Insufficient glute squeeze at lockout
safety_considerations: Keep chin tucked and do not crane the neck during the thrust
execution.range_of_motion_guidance: Full hip extension at top — do not go beyond neutral spine.
coaching_cues: Drive through the heels
Squeeze the glutes at the top
Chin tucked — look forward not up

name: Hollow Body Rock with Weight
description: A hollow body hold performed while holding a plate overhead, then rocking forward and back to add dynamic challenge. The weight increases the anti-extension demand while the rocking motion adds timing and coordination elements. This is a staple of gymnastics conditioning.

execution.starting_position: Set up for Hollow Body Rock with Weight in proper position.
execution.setup_instructions: Prepare body and equipment for Hollow Body Rock with Weight.
steps: Step 1: Lie on back holding plate overhead. Create hollow body by pressing back flat.
Step 2: Raise arms, head, and legs off floor into hollow position.
Step 3: Rock forward and back while maintaining hollow shape.
Step 4: Keep the same curve throughout the rocking motion.
execution.breathing_instructions: Breathe steadily; never hold breath during static holds.
common_mistakes: Losing hollow position on the rock
Lower back lifting off floor
safety_considerations: Build prerequisite strength before attempting advanced variations.
Stop if joint pain occurs.
execution.range_of_motion_guidance: Full range of motion with control at all times.
coaching_cues: Same shape throughout the entire rock
Press back flat to floor

name: Hollow Hold
description: The hollow hold is a foundational gymnastics isometric that trains the entire anterior chain in a compressed, coordinated position. The athlete lies supine, pressing the lower back into the floor, tucking the pelvis posteriorly, and raising the arms, shoulders, and legs off the floor while maintaining a curved, rigid body shape. It develops the rectus abdominis and transverse abdominis under sustained tension and serves as a prerequisite for many advanced calisthenics skills.

execution.starting_position: Lie flat on your back on the floor with your arms extended overhead and legs straight. Your entire back should be in contact with the floor.
execution.setup_instructions: No equipment needed. Find a flat, firm surface with enough length to extend your body fully.
steps: Step 1: Lie on your back with arms extended overhead and legs straight.
Step 2: Exhale fully and press your lower back firmly into the floor by posteriorly tilting the pelvis.
Step 3: Raise your arms, shoulders, and head off the floor while simultaneously lifting your legs to approximately 30–45 degrees.
Step 4: Point your toes, squeeze your thighs together, and hold the curved position for the prescribed duration.
Step 5: Breathe shallowly through the nose to maintain tension. Lower with control when done.
execution.breathing_instructions: Exhale deeply to initiate the brace, then breathe shallowly through the nose during the hold. Avoid taking large breaths that cause the lower back to lift.
common_mistakes: Allowing the lower back to arch away from the floor
Raising the legs too high, which reduces core challenge
Relaxing the shoulder and neck position midway through the hold
Holding the breath instead of breathing shallowly
safety_considerations: If the lower back cannot stay flat on the floor, raise the legs higher or bend the knees to reduce the lever arm.
Avoid if experiencing acute lower back pain.
execution.range_of_motion_guidance: The body should form a shallow concave curve from fingertips to toes. The lower back must remain in contact with the floor throughout.
execution.tempo_recommendations: Hold for 20–60 seconds. Progress duration before adding any weight or hollow body variations.
coaching_cues: Press your belly button to the floor
Make your body look like a banana
Think long and tight — squeeze everything

name: Human Flag
description: An iconic calisthenics feat where the body is held horizontally from a vertical pole. The bottom arm pushes while the top arm pulls, creating lateral force to hold the flag position. This requires tremendous lateral chain strength developed over years.

execution.starting_position: Set up for Human Flag in proper position.
execution.setup_instructions: Prepare body and equipment for Human Flag.
steps: Step 1: Grip vertical pole with one hand above the other, shoulder-width apart.
Step 2: Push with bottom arm and pull with top arm to lever body sideways.
Step 3: Extend body to fully horizontal position with feet together.
Step 4: Hold position with entire body rigid then lower with control.
execution.breathing_instructions: Breathe steadily; never hold breath during static holds.
common_mistakes: Bending at the hips
Attempting without adequate strength base
safety_considerations: Build prerequisite strength before attempting advanced variations.
Stop if joint pain occurs.
execution.range_of_motion_guidance: Full range of motion with control at all times.
coaching_cues: Top arm pulls, bottom arm pushes simultaneously
Build through progressions first

name: Human Flag Pull-Ups
description: An extreme variation where pull-ups are performed while maintaining the human flag position on a vertical pole. The body stays horizontal while the athlete performs elbow flexion and extension. This movement is accessible only to elite calisthenics athletes with established flag holds.

execution.starting_position: Set up for Human Flag Pull-Ups in proper position.
execution.setup_instructions: Prepare body and equipment for Human Flag Pull-Ups.
steps: Step 1: Establish full human flag hold on vertical pole.
Step 2: From flag position, bend both elbows to perform a pull-up laterally.
Step 3: Extend arms back to flag position.
Step 4: Maintain horizontal body throughout the movement.
execution.breathing_instructions: Breathe steadily; never hold breath during static holds.
common_mistakes: Dropping hips during the pull
Attempting without stable flag hold
safety_considerations: Build prerequisite strength before attempting advanced variations.
Stop if joint pain occurs.
execution.range_of_motion_guidance: Full range of motion with control at all times.
coaching_cues: Fully master the static flag before this
Lateral pull direction, not vertical

name: Husafell Stone Carry
description: A traditional Icelandic strongman event using a large fan-shaped stone carried as far as possible. The stone is cradled against the chest and stomach while walking, demanding exceptional grip endurance, core bracing, and mental fortitude. Modern versions use custom replica stones or sandbags.

execution.starting_position: Set up for Husafell Stone Carry in proper strongman position.
execution.setup_instructions: Prepare all equipment and body position for Husafell Stone Carry.
steps: Step 1: Position stone on the floor with flat side facing up.
Step 2: Bear hug stone with arms wrapping underneath and around.
Step 3: Deadlift stone up, cradling it against chest and abdomen.
Step 4: Walk forward maintaining stone against body for target distance.
execution.breathing_instructions: Brace core maximally before every lift. Breathe between reps if needed.
common_mistakes: Letting stone drift away from body
Bent-over carry position
safety_considerations: Use collars on all loaded barbells.
Ensure clear path for carries.
Have spotters for overhead movements.
execution.range_of_motion_guidance: Full range of motion specific to the implement being used.
coaching_cues: Keep stone as close to body as possible
Walk tall, not hunched

name: Husafell Stone Carry on Incline
description: A husafell stone carry performed on an inclined surface such as a ramp or steep hill. The incline dramatically increases the difficulty as the athlete must both carry the stone and fight against gravity on the slope. This variation is used in highland games and specialty strongman events.

execution.starting_position: Set up for Husafell Stone Carry on Incline in proper strongman position.
execution.setup_instructions: Prepare all equipment and body position for Husafell Stone Carry on Incline.
steps: Step 1: Deadlift husafell stone to bear hug position.
Step 2: Begin walking up incline with stone pressed against body.
Step 3: Take short controlled steps managing the increased effort demand.
Step 4: Reach top of incline and set stone down safely.
execution.breathing_instructions: Brace core maximally before every lift. Breathe between reps if needed.
common_mistakes: Taking too large steps on incline
Leaning stone away from body
safety_considerations: Use collars on all loaded barbells.
Ensure clear path for carries.
Have spotters for overhead movements.
execution.range_of_motion_guidance: Full range of motion specific to the implement being used.
coaching_cues: Shorter steps on incline
Stone stays against body throughout

name: Back Extension (45-Degree Hyperextension)
description: The 45-degree back extension is performed on a hyperextension bench and trains hip extension and spinal erector function simultaneously. The lifter flexes forward at the hip and spine under gravity then extends back to neutral or slightly beyond, challenging the erector spinae, gluteus maximus, and hamstrings through a moderate range of motion. This exercise is a primary developer of the posterior chain when performed with controlled technique.

execution.starting_position: Position yourself on the 45-degree hyperextension bench with the front of the thighs resting on the pads. Hook the ankles behind the foot supports. Cross arms over the chest or place hands behind the head. The body should form a straight line in the starting position.
execution.setup_instructions: Adjust the bench pad height so the hip crease is just above or at the top of the pad — this allows full range of hip flexion. Secure the ankles firmly.
steps: Step 1: Begin in the neutral starting position — body in a straight line from head to hips.
Step 2: Slowly lower the torso toward the floor by hinging at the hips, allowing the spine to flex slightly.
Step 3: Lower until a full stretch is felt in the glutes and hamstrings, or the torso is roughly perpendicular to the floor.
Step 4: Drive the hips into extension and raise the torso back to neutral by contracting the glutes and erectors.
Step 5: At the top, the body should return to a neutral straight line — do not hyperextend the lumbar spine aggressively.
execution.breathing_instructions: Inhale as you lower the torso. Exhale as you extend back to neutral.
common_mistakes: Hyperextending the lumbar spine aggressively at the top — stop at neutral or just slightly above
Rounding the upper back excessively at the bottom, which may stress the thoracic spine
Using momentum to swing up rather than controlled muscle contraction
safety_considerations: Avoid excessive spinal hyperextension at the top — this loads the facet joints unnecessarily
If using added weight, hold it at the chest rather than behind the head to reduce cervical strain
Those with existing lower back issues should consult a healthcare professional before performing this exercise
execution.range_of_motion_guidance: From torso perpendicular to the floor at the bottom to neutral body alignment at the top. Some lifters may extend slightly past neutral — avoid aggressive lumbar hyperextension.
coaching_cues: Squeeze the glutes at the top — this cues hip extension rather than lower back arching
Think of your body as a pendulum hinging at the hip
Stop when your body is straight — do not arch further

name: Inchworm
description: The inchworm is a dynamic warm-up and functional movement exercise in which the athlete bends forward to place the hands on the floor and walks the hands out to a push-up plank position, then walks the feet back toward the hands to return upright. It simultaneously provides a hamstring stretch during the foot-walk phase, shoulder and chest warm-up in the plank phase, and an optional push-up for further activation. The inchworm is a highly efficient all-in-one mobility and activation drill used globally as a warm-up.

execution.starting_position: Stand upright with feet hip-width apart.
execution.setup_instructions: No equipment required. Adequate floor space for the walk-out length.
steps: Step 1: Stand upright, then hinge forward at the hips and bend the knees slightly to place both hands on the floor.
Step 2: Walk the hands forward — step by step — until arriving in a full push-up plank position.
Step 3: Optional: perform one push-up in the plank position.
Step 4: Walk the feet toward the hands in small steps, keeping the legs as straight as hamstring flexibility allows.
Step 5: Arrive in a standing position and repeat for the prescribed number of reps.
execution.breathing_instructions: Exhale as you walk out. Inhale as you walk feet back in.
common_mistakes: Bending the knees excessively during the foot-walk phase — the hamstring stretch is the goal of that phase
Letting the hips sag in the plank position
Rushing — the inchworm is a quality movement, not a speed exercise
safety_considerations: Limited hamstring flexibility will cause excessive knee bend — this is fine initially, improve over time.
Wrist discomfort in the plank position — warm up wrists before.
execution.range_of_motion_guidance: Walk hands as far as a full plank. Walk feet as close to hands as hamstring flexibility allows with minimal knee bend.
execution.tempo_recommendations: 5–10 reps as a warm-up. Slow and deliberate.
coaching_cues: Long walk-out — full plank
Walk the feet in — feel the hamstring stretch
Hips level in the plank

name: Incline Barbell Bench Press
description: The incline barbell bench press is performed on a bench set to 30–45 degrees, shifting emphasis toward the clavicular (upper) head of the pectoralis major and the anterior deltoid. It is a staple exercise for developing the upper chest and creating a fuller, more complete pectoral appearance.

execution.starting_position: Set an adjustable bench to 30–45 degrees and position it inside a rack. Lie back with eyes under the bar, shoulder blades retracted, and feet flat on the floor. Grip the bar slightly wider than shoulder width.
execution.setup_instructions: Set bench to 30–45 degrees — higher angles increase anterior deltoid involvement at the expense of pectoral activation. Position the barbell in the rack so it unracks with arms nearly extended.
steps: Unrack the bar and position it directly over your upper chest with arms extended.
Lower the bar under control to your upper chest, keeping elbows at about 60–75 degrees from your torso.
Touch the bar lightly to your upper chest without losing upper back tension.
Press the bar back to the starting position, exhaling as you push.
execution.breathing_instructions: Inhale and brace before the descent. Exhale on the concentric press.
common_mistakes: Setting the bench too steep (above 45 degrees), turning the exercise into a shoulder press
Letting the bar drift down to the lower chest — keep it at the clavicular region
Losing upper back tightness as the weight gets heavy
safety_considerations: Use a spotter or set safety bars in the rack
A 30-degree incline is generally safer for the shoulder than 45 degrees
execution.range_of_motion_guidance: Lower the bar until it touches the upper chest. Press to full extension without hyperextending the elbows.
coaching_cues: Think about pressing the bar up and slightly back toward the rack
Keep the upper back welded to the bench throughout the set

name: Incline Bench Cable Flye — Drop Set
alternative_names: High Cable Incline Flye Drop Set
description: An incline cable flye performed on an adjustable bench set between two cable stacks, executed as a drop set. The incline position targets the clavicular (upper) portion of the pectoralis major, and the cable provides constant tension through the entire arc — unlike dumbbells which lose tension at the top. The drop set structure allows training past initial failure, maximizing upper chest hypertrophy stimulus. The cable's constant tension through the stretch (bottom) and squeeze (top) positions makes this a superior flye variation for complete fiber recruitment.

execution.starting_position: Set an adjustable bench to 30-45 degrees incline and position it between two cable stacks with the cables at the lowest setting. Lie on the incline bench and hold the low-cable D-handles with arms extended above the chest.
execution.setup_instructions: Set up two weight loads in advance for the drop: initial heavier load and lighter follow-up. Have a training partner ready to quickly change the weight stacks.
steps: Step 1: Begin with arms extended above the chest, handles together, cables from low pulleys.
Step 2: Lower the arms out to the sides in a wide arc, feeling the stretch in the upper chest at the bottom.
Step 3: Bring the arms back together in an arc, squeezing the chest at the top. Continue until failure.
Step 4: Immediately drop to the lighter weight and continue for additional reps to secondary failure.
execution.breathing_instructions: Inhale as the arms lower outward. Exhale as you bring them together.
common_mistakes: Excessively bending the elbows, converting the flye into a press — maintain a slight fixed elbow bend throughout
Allowing the cable to pull the arms too far back, causing shoulder stress at the bottom stretch position
Rushing the transition during the drop — ensure a safe, quick change
safety_considerations: The bottom stretch position with cable tension can stress the anterior shoulder — do not go beyond a comfortable stretch
Have the lighter weight ready before beginning the initial set
execution.range_of_motion_guidance: From cables together above chest to a wide arc where the hands are at approximately shoulder height with a full upper chest stretch.
execution.tempo_recommendations: 3s eccentric (open), 1s stretch, 2s press back together. Full ROM on all reps.
coaching_cues: Think of hugging a barrel — the arms maintain the same slight bend throughout the entire arc
Feel the upper chest stretch at the bottom — the cable maintains tension even here
Squeeze the hands toward each other at the top — not just touching, but pressing

name: Incline Bench Dumbbell Pullover
description: A dumbbell pullover performed with the torso on an incline bench, changing the arc of motion compared to a flat pullover. The incline alters which fibers of the pectoralis major and latissimus dorsi are under greatest stress throughout the movement. The serratus anterior and long head of the triceps also contribute significantly, making this a unique exercise that spans both chest and back training.

execution.starting_position: Lie on an incline bench set to 30–45 degrees. Hold one dumbbell with both hands (overlapping grip on the inner plate). Begin with the dumbbell above the chest, arms extended.
execution.setup_instructions: Set the incline to 30–45 degrees. The incline changes the arc compared to a flat pullover, shifting the muscle emphasis slightly. Lie fully on the bench with the head at the top.
steps: Step 1: Begin with arms extended above the chest, dumbbell held with both hands.
Step 2: Keeping elbows slightly bent, arc the dumbbell back over the head and toward the floor.
Step 3: Lower until the arms are roughly in line with the torso or slightly past — stop when tension diminishes.
Step 4: Bring the dumbbell back along the same arc to the starting position above the chest.
execution.breathing_instructions: Inhale on the way back (expansion), exhale on the return to start.
common_mistakes: Bending elbows too much, turning it into a triceps extension
Going too far back and losing control of the dumbbell
Using too heavy a dumbbell that compromises the arc control
safety_considerations: Avoid excessive range of motion — the shoulder is at risk of impingement if forced past comfortable range
Keep a firm grip on the dumbbell throughout; it can slip if the hands are sweaty
execution.range_of_motion_guidance: Arc back until arms approach parallel with torso or slightly past — stop at the first sign of shoulder discomfort.
coaching_cues: Lead with the elbows slightly — this keeps the chest in the movement
Think of the arc as a circle — the dumbbell traces a consistent path around your shoulder joint

name: Incline Bench Lateral Raise (Chest Down)
description: The incline bench lateral raise performed face-down (prone) on an incline bench trains the lateral deltoid with gravity acting directly on the arm through the full range of motion without any torso lean compensation. The prone position eliminates all momentum from torso swing, isolates the medial deltoid more completely than standing versions, and also trains the posterior deltoid through the horizontal abduction component of the exercise.

execution.starting_position: Lie face-down on an incline bench (30-45 degrees). Hold a dumbbell in each hand hanging below the bench. Arms relaxed, perpendicular to the floor.
execution.setup_instructions: Set the bench high enough that the arms can hang freely. Light weight only.
steps: Step 1: Begin hanging, arms perpendicular to floor.
Step 2: Raise both arms out laterally to shoulder height (horizontal).
Step 3: Hold 1 second.
Step 4: Lower under control back to hanging.
Step 5: Repeat.
execution.breathing_instructions: Exhale raising. Inhale lowering.
common_mistakes: Raising the arms too far beyond horizontal — shoulder height is the target
Using too heavy a load — the hanging start position is fully gravity-loaded
safety_considerations: Very light loads — the prone position with hanging arms creates substantial lever arm
Avoid if shoulder impingement is present
execution.range_of_motion_guidance: Full hang to arms horizontal at shoulder height.
coaching_cues: Lead with the elbows — slight bend
Pinkies up at the top
Own the descent — slow 3-second lower

name: Incline Cable Bench Flye
alternative_names: High Cable Flye on Incline Bench
description: The incline cable bench flye targets the clavicular head of the pectoralis major by combining the stretch-loaded arc of a cable fly with an inclined torso position. The constant tension from cables provides superior stimulus to the upper chest fibers compared to free-weight alternatives.

execution.starting_position: Set an adjustable bench to a 30-45 degree incline and position it between dual low cable pulleys. Lie back on the bench, holding one D-handle in each hand with arms extended above the upper chest.
execution.setup_instructions: Attach D-handles to the lowest pulley setting on both sides of a dual cable machine. Set the bench incline between 30 and 45 degrees and center it in the cable station.
steps: Step 1: Lie on the incline bench and grasp both handles, arms extended up and inward.
Step 2: Open the arms out to the sides in a wide arc, lowering until a stretch is felt across the upper chest.
Step 3: Squeeze the chest and drive both handles together, meeting above the upper pectorals.
Step 4: Pause briefly at the peak contraction before slowly reversing the motion.
Step 5: Maintain a fixed elbow angle and avoid letting the shoulder blades lift off the bench.
execution.breathing_instructions: Exhale as you bring the cables together. Inhale as you lower the arms out to the sides.
common_mistakes: Setting the cables too high, reducing target stretch on the clavicular head
Straightening the elbows fully under load
Letting the shoulders creep toward the ears
safety_considerations: Retract and depress the shoulder blades before beginning
Start with lighter weight to find comfortable range of motion
Stop if you feel pinching in the anterior shoulder
execution.range_of_motion_guidance: Lower arms until the elbows are roughly level with the bench, allowing a full upper chest stretch. Bring hands together above the upper chest for a strong peak contraction.
coaching_cues: Push through the outer arm, not the hands
Upper chest is the target — feel it stretch wide
Squeeze and hold for a beat at the top

name: Incline Cable Overhead Tricep Extension
description: The incline cable overhead extension is performed lying on an incline bench facing away from a low cable, with the arms raised overhead to extend the triceps against the cable's resistance. The incline provides back support and positions the arms at an angle that creates an extended stretch on the tricep long head throughout the movement. The cable maintains constant tension unlike free weight incline overhead extensions.

execution.starting_position: Set an incline bench in front of a low cable pulley, facing away. Lie back on the incline. Hold a rope or straight bar attached to the cable with arms overhead.
execution.setup_instructions: Place the bench close to the pulley so the cable runs overhead without interference. Incline at 45 degrees.
steps: Step 1: Begin with elbows bent, hands near the head, feeling the tricep stretch.
Step 2: Extend the elbows to straighten the arms overhead.
Step 3: Hold the locked-out position briefly.
Step 4: Return with control to the starting stretched position.
execution.breathing_instructions: Exhale on extension, inhale on return.
common_mistakes: Elbows flaring outward
Bench not positioned close enough to the cable (causes awkward pull angle)
safety_considerations: Ensure the bench is stable and the cable path is clear
execution.range_of_motion_guidance: Full elbow flexion with overhead stretch to full extension.
coaching_cues: Elbows point toward the ceiling
Stretch at the bottom — savor it
Extend fully and squeeze

name: Incline Cable Overhead Extension (Away from Stack)
description: An overhead extension on an incline bench positioned away from the cable stack. This angle provides a unique long-head stretch position. The cable maintains constant tension through the eccentric, which is valuable for tricep hypertrophy.

execution.starting_position: Set up for Incline Cable Overhead Extension (Away from Stack) in the appropriate position.
execution.setup_instructions: Prepare equipment and body position for Incline Cable Overhead Extension (Away from Stack).
steps: Step 1: Set incline bench facing away from low pulley. Lie back and hold cable handle overhead.
Step 2: Keep elbows pointing toward ceiling with upper arms by ears.
Step 3: Lower handle behind head until triceps are fully stretched.
Step 4: Extend elbows to full lockout overhead.
execution.breathing_instructions: Exhale during the exertion phase, inhale during the return.
common_mistakes: Letting elbows drop to sides
Arching excessively
safety_considerations: Keep joints aligned throughout the movement.
Use controlled weight appropriate for skill level.
execution.range_of_motion_guidance: Move through full range of motion without compromising joint integrity.
coaching_cues: Feel the stretch at the bottom
Drive elbows toward ceiling

name: Incline Dumbbell Curl
description: The incline dumbbell curl is performed lying on an incline bench set to approximately 45–60 degrees, with arms hanging behind the torso. This shoulder extension position places the long head of the biceps brachii under a greater stretch at the bottom of the movement, increasing its activation throughout the curl. The long head is particularly stimulated, contributing to the peak bicep appearance and the outer bicep fullness.

execution.starting_position: Set an adjustable bench to a 45–60 degree incline. Sit back against it with dumbbells in each hand, arms hanging straight down toward the floor. Palms face forward (supinated grip).
execution.setup_instructions: Adjust bench to between 45 and 60 degrees. Sit fully against the pad. The key is allowing the arms to hang behind the hip line for maximum bicep long head stretch.
steps: Step 1: Sit on the incline bench with arms hanging straight down behind the hips. Palms face forward.
Step 2: Begin from full arm extension — do not start with elbows bent.
Step 3: Exhale and curl both dumbbells upward simultaneously by flexing the elbows, keeping the upper arms stationary.
Step 4: Curl to full contraction, then inhale and lower slowly back to full arm extension.
execution.breathing_instructions: Exhale on the curl; inhale on the slow descent.
common_mistakes: Allowing the elbows to swing forward during the curl, reducing the long head stretch
Using too heavy a weight that shortens the range of motion
safety_considerations: The hanging arm position can stress the bicep tendon at the shoulder — start with lighter weight
Do not yank or jerk from the bottom position
execution.range_of_motion_guidance: Full hang at the bottom (arms fully extended); full curl at the top.
coaching_cues: Let the arms hang completely free behind you at the bottom — feel the long head stretching
Keep the elbows pinned back as you curl — do not let them drift forward

name: Incline Dumbbell Front Raise
