description: The incline dumbbell front raise is performed lying face-down on an incline bench set to 45-60 degrees, raising dumbbells from the hanging position to shoulder height in front of the body. The incline position eliminates torso momentum and places the anterior deltoid under a greater stretch at the start of the movement. This improved bottom-position stretch and strict form requirement make it more effective as a pure anterior deltoid isolation exercise than the standing version.

execution.starting_position: Set an adjustable bench to 45-60 degrees. Lie face-down on the bench with the chest on the pad. Hold dumbbells with an overhand or neutral grip, arms hanging below the bench.
execution.setup_instructions: Use lighter weight than standing front raises. The hanging position creates a pre-stretch on the anterior deltoid.
steps: Step 1: Lie face-down on the incline bench, dumbbells hanging below.
Step 2: Begin from the full hang (arms straight down) for a maximum anterior deltoid stretch.
Step 3: Raise both dumbbells forward and upward in an arc.
Step 4: Raise until the arms are parallel to the floor.
Step 5: Lower slowly under full control to the hanging position.
execution.breathing_instructions: Exhale on the raise, inhale on the descent.
common_mistakes: Not using the full hang at the bottom, missing the stretch
Raising the head to look forward, which strains the neck
safety_considerations: Keep the head in a neutral position resting on the bench pad
execution.range_of_motion_guidance: Full hanging position to shoulder height (parallel to the floor).
coaching_cues: Full hang between reps
Raise forward — not to the side
Slow and controlled — this is not a strength exercise

name: Incline Dumbbell Press
description: The incline dumbbell press targets the upper pectoralis major using independent dumbbells on an inclined bench. The unilateral loading allows each arm to move independently, promoting balanced development and enabling a greater range of motion at the bottom of the lift.

execution.starting_position: Set an adjustable bench to 30–45 degrees. Sit on the bench with a dumbbell on each knee, then use leg drive to bring them to chest level as you recline. Hold dumbbells with palms facing forward at the sides of your upper chest.
execution.setup_instructions: Adjust the bench angle before loading up. Use knee-kick technique to get heavy dumbbells into position safely. Retract and depress shoulder blades before pressing.
steps: Press both dumbbells upward and slightly inward until arms are nearly extended.
Lower under control until your upper arms are parallel to the floor or slightly below, feeling a stretch in the upper chest.
Pause briefly at the bottom, then press back up with controlled power.
execution.breathing_instructions: Inhale on the way down, exhale on the press.
common_mistakes: Letting the dumbbells drift too wide at the bottom, overstressing the front of the shoulder
Excessive bench angle reducing pec involvement
safety_considerations: Drop dumbbells to the sides rather than trying to sit up with them after a failed rep
Use a spotter when attempting heavy weights
execution.range_of_motion_guidance: Full range: upper arms slightly below parallel at the bottom, arms nearly extended at top.
coaching_cues: Press the dumbbells in an arc — not straight up
Feel the upper chest stretching at the bottom position

name: Incline Dumbbell Row
description: The incline dumbbell row is performed lying prone on an incline bench, allowing each arm to row freely from a fully extended position. The incline angle shifts emphasis toward the upper back and rear deltoids relative to flat or horizontal rows, while the bench support reduces lower back fatigue and allows higher quality reps later in a training session.

execution.starting_position: Set a bench to a low incline of approximately 30 degrees. Lie prone on the bench with the chest supported and feet on the floor. Hold a dumbbell in each hand with arms hanging below the bench.
execution.setup_instructions: Set the adjustable bench to a 30-degree incline. Use lighter dumbbells than you would use for a bent-over row since the range of motion is longer from this position.
steps: Step 1: Begin with arms hanging straight down, fully extended.
Step 2: Row both dumbbells simultaneously toward the waist by driving the elbows up and back.
Step 3: Retract the shoulder blades at the top of the movement.
Step 4: Lower the dumbbells slowly to full arm extension, allowing the shoulder blades to protract.
Step 5: Repeat without letting momentum take over.
execution.breathing_instructions: Exhale as you row up. Inhale as you lower the dumbbells.
common_mistakes: Setting the bench too steep, which changes the movement pattern significantly
Short repping at the bottom and not achieving full scapular protraction
Internally rotating the shoulders by rowing with palms facing backward
safety_considerations: Keep the head neutral — do not crane the neck upward
Ensure the bench is on a stable, non-slip surface
execution.range_of_motion_guidance: Maximize scapular protraction at the bottom and retraction at the top.
coaching_cues: Lead with the elbows, not the hands
Think of pulling your shoulder blades into your back pockets

name: Incline Dumbbell Shrug
description: The incline dumbbell shrug is performed face-down on an incline bench set to 45 degrees, with dumbbells hanging beneath the shoulders. The prone position pre-stretches the upper trapezius and eliminates postural cheating, ensuring pure scapular elevation. This setup isolates the upper trapezius more effectively than standing shrug variations, as the torso support removes lower body momentum and spinal compensation.

execution.starting_position: Set an adjustable bench to 45 degrees. Lie face-down with the chest on the pad, head slightly up, and arms hanging straight below the shoulders holding dumbbells.
execution.setup_instructions: Use lighter weight than standing shrugs. The prone position eliminates momentum and isolates the traps effectively at lower loads.
steps: Step 1: Lie prone on the incline bench with dumbbells hanging below.
Step 2: Begin from a fully depressed (hanging) scapular position to maximize stretch.
Step 3: Elevate the shoulders as high as possible, moving the scapulae straight upward.
Step 4: Pause at the top for 1-2 seconds for maximum contraction.
Step 5: Lower fully under control, allowing the scapulae to depress completely.
execution.breathing_instructions: Exhale on the shrug, inhale on the lowering phase.
common_mistakes: Not lowering fully between reps — the full hang is where the stretch occurs
Using too heavy a weight, which prevents full elevation
safety_considerations: Ensure the bench is stable before beginning
execution.range_of_motion_guidance: Full scapular depression at the bottom (deep hang), full elevation at the top.
coaching_cues: Full hang between every rep
Elevate straight up — no roll
Feel the trap squeeze at the top

name: Incline Dumbbell Tate Press
description: The Tate press performed on an incline bench, shifting the angle of triceps recruitment. The incline creates a greater stretch position for the long head of the triceps. This variation challenges coordination and targets the triceps from a fresh angle.

execution.starting_position: Set up for Incline Dumbbell Tate Press in the appropriate position.
execution.setup_instructions: Prepare equipment and body position for Incline Dumbbell Tate Press.
steps: Step 1: Set bench to 30-45 degree incline. Lie back holding dumbbells with elbows wide.
Step 2: Lower dumbbells in Tate arc toward upper chest with elbows flared.
Step 3: Lightly touch upper chest region at bottom of arc.
Step 4: Press back to straight arms through tricep drive.
execution.breathing_instructions: Exhale during the exertion phase, inhale during the return.
common_mistakes: Closing elbows during the press
Bench angle too steep
safety_considerations: Keep joints aligned throughout the movement.
Use controlled weight appropriate for skill level.
execution.range_of_motion_guidance: Move through full range of motion without compromising joint integrity.
coaching_cues: Elbows remain flared throughout
Adjust angle to feel long head stretch

name: Incline EZ-Bar Skull Crusher
description: The incline EZ-bar skull crusher is performed on an incline bench (typically 30-45 degrees), which shifts the angle of the arms relative to the torso. The incline position places even greater stretch on the tricep long head compared to flat skull crushers, as the shoulder angle changes the long head's initial length. This enhanced stretch stimulus at the bottom of the movement may improve hypertrophic adaptation in the long head.

execution.starting_position: Set an adjustable bench to 30-45 degrees. Lie back with the EZ-bar pressed to full extension above the face/forehead.
execution.setup_instructions: Have a spotter hand the bar off. The incline means the bar is above the face rather than above the chest.
steps: Step 1: Begin with EZ-bar extended above the face.
Step 2: Lower by bending only the elbows, bar traveling toward the forehead.
Step 3: Feel the stretch in the tricep long head at the bottom.
Step 4: Extend the elbows to press back to the starting position.
execution.breathing_instructions: Inhale on descent, exhale on press.
common_mistakes: Upper arms drifting on the incline
Using too heavy a load — the stretch position is more vulnerable
safety_considerations: The incline increases long head stretch — use lighter load than flat skull crushers until comfortable
execution.range_of_motion_guidance: Full extension to maximum elbow flexion with bar at forehead level.
coaching_cues: Feel the stretch at the bottom
Upper arms stay fixed
Squeeze at lockout

name: Incline Barbell Guillotine Press
description: The incline guillotine press is a barbell pressing variation performed on an incline bench where the bar is lowered toward the neck and upper chest rather than the mid-chest. This extreme stretch position maximally loads the clavicular head of the pectoralis major under a wide grip. Due to the high shoulder stress in this position, it is considered a high-risk exercise requiring significant shoulder health and experience.

execution.starting_position: Set an adjustable bench to a 30–45 degree incline and position it inside a power rack. Lie back and grip the barbell with a wide pronated grip, slightly wider than shoulder width.
execution.setup_instructions: Set the safety catches at an appropriate height. The bar path target is the neck and clavicle area, so ensure the spotter or safety pins are positioned accordingly.
steps: Step 1: Unrack the bar with arms extended, holding it above the upper chest and clavicle area.
Step 2: Lower the bar slowly toward the neck and upper chest (clavicle region), maintaining control throughout the descent.
Step 3: Touch or come very close to the clavicle/upper chest area without bouncing.
Step 4: Press the bar back to the starting position by driving through the chest and triceps.
execution.breathing_instructions: Inhale during the controlled descent to the neck. Exhale powerfully during the press upward.
common_mistakes: Using excessive weight — this is a stretch-focused exercise requiring relatively light loads
Lowering too fast, losing control at the bottom
Performing with shoulder impingement or prior shoulder injuries
safety_considerations: HIGH RISK: This exercise places the shoulder in an extreme externally rotated, horizontally abducted position under load — not recommended for beginners or those with shoulder pathology
Always use safety pins or a spotter
Start with an empty bar or very light weight to assess shoulder tolerance
If any shoulder pain is felt, stop immediately
execution.range_of_motion_guidance: Lower bar to clavicle or neck level only if shoulder health permits. Partial range may be appropriate for most trainees.
coaching_cues: Wide grip, elbows flared — this is intentional for upper pec targeting
Control the descent — do not drop the bar toward the neck

name: Incline Hammer Curl
description: The incline hammer curl is performed seated on an incline bench with the arms hanging behind the torso at the bottom, stretching the biceps and brachialis in the lengthened position before the curl. The neutral grip and incline angle together emphasize the brachialis and long head of the biceps. The pre-stretched starting position is associated with enhanced muscle growth stimulus.

execution.starting_position: Set an adjustable bench to 45-60 degrees. Sit with the back against the pad, dumbbells hanging at the sides in a neutral grip, arms fully extended behind the body line.
execution.setup_instructions: Set the bench to approximately 45 degrees. Use lighter weight than standing hammer curls due to the stretch position.
steps: Step 1: Begin with arms fully extended downward, neutral grip, feeling the stretch.
Step 2: Curl both dumbbells simultaneously upward, maintaining neutral grip.
Step 3: Curl until maximum elbow flexion.
Step 4: Lower slowly back to the hanging position.
execution.breathing_instructions: Exhale on the curl, inhale on the return.
common_mistakes: Swinging the torso off the bench
Rotating the grip during the curl
Rushing the eccentric and losing the stretch benefit
safety_considerations: The stretched position increases injury risk — use controlled weight
execution.range_of_motion_guidance: Full hang at the bottom to maximum elbow flexion.
coaching_cues: Feel the stretch at the bottom
Neutral grip all the way up
Slow on the way down

name: Incline Dumbbell Hex Press
description: The Incline Hex Press performs the dumbbell squeeze press on an incline bench, directing the adduction and pressing force toward the clavicular (upper) head of the pectoralis major. It combines the unique constant-squeeze stimulus of the hex press with the upper chest emphasis of an incline angle.

execution.starting_position: Set an adjustable bench to 30-45 degrees. Lie back and hold two hex dumbbells pressed firmly together with a neutral grip, positioned above the upper chest.
execution.setup_instructions: Set incline to 30-45 degrees. Use hex-sided dumbbells to prevent rolling. Press dumbbells together before each set.
steps: Step 1: Hold dumbbells squeezed together above the upper chest.
Step 2: Lower under control to the upper chest while maintaining inward squeeze.
Step 3: Press up and slightly back to the starting position.
Step 4: Squeeze hard throughout; do not let the dumbbells separate.
execution.breathing_instructions: Inhale before lowering. Exhale pressing up.
common_mistakes: Bench angle too steep (above 45°), shifting load to shoulders
Losing the squeeze through fatigue
safety_considerations: Use lighter dumbbells than your standard incline press — the squeeze adds significant demand
Hex or flat-sided dumbbells only
execution.range_of_motion_guidance: Light touch of upper chest at bottom; full extension at top.
coaching_cues: Squeeze the dumbbells together as if your life depends on it
The harder you squeeze, the more upper chest activation

name: Incline Dumbbell Tricep Kickback
description: The incline dumbbell kickback is performed face-down on an incline bench, with the chest resting on the pad and the arms hanging. The incline position allows gravity to fully load the tricep in the extended (kickback) position — where standard kickbacks rely on a horizontal upper arm for resistance. By using an incline, the peak contraction in the extended position is better maintained. The prone position also eliminates any torso rocking.

execution.starting_position: Set an incline bench to 30-45 degrees. Lie face-down with the chest on the pad. Hold a dumbbell in each hand, arms hanging down.
execution.setup_instructions: Use light dumbbells — the incline kickback is a strict isolation movement with limited leverage.
steps: Step 1: Begin with the arms hanging down, upper arms at the sides of the body.
Step 2: Extend the elbows rearward, kicking the dumbbells back behind the body.
Step 3: Hold at full extension for one second, squeezing the triceps.
Step 4: Return the dumbbells to the hanging position with control.
execution.breathing_instructions: Exhale on the kickback, inhale on the return.
common_mistakes: Swinging the dumbbells using shoulder movement
Not fully extending the elbows at the peak
Using too heavy a weight
safety_considerations: The prone position limits cheating — keep the chest on the bench
execution.range_of_motion_guidance: Full extension at the top — pause and squeeze.
coaching_cues: Upper arms pinned to sides
Kick back and squeeze hard
Return with control

name: Incline Lever Machine Alternating Press
description: A machine incline chest press performed in an alternating arm pattern rather than simultaneously. Each arm presses independently while the other holds the contracted or extended position. The alternating pattern creates greater focus on each side individually, allows detection of left-right strength imbalances, and increases the total time under tension per set compared to bilateral pressing.

execution.starting_position: Sit in an incline chest press machine. Grip both handles with an overhand grip. Adjust the seat height so the handles are at upper chest level. Begin with both arms in the loaded (retracted) position.
execution.setup_instructions: Set the seat height so the handles align with the upper chest/clavicle. Select a moderate weight appropriate for single-arm pressing (lighter than bilateral weight).
steps: Step 1: Begin with both arms loaded at the chest. Press the right arm to full extension.
Step 2: Hold the right arm extended. Begin pressing the left arm to full extension.
Step 3: Return the right arm to the loaded position as the left arm finishes its extension.
Step 4: Alternate: right press → left press → right return → left return. Each full alternating cycle is one rep.
execution.breathing_instructions: Exhale as each arm presses, inhale as it returns. Breathing rhythm may need to be adapted to the alternating cadence.
common_mistakes: Rotating the torso to assist the pressing arm — keep shoulders square
Resting at the loaded position rather than maintaining active tension
Pressing too fast to maintain control of the alternating pattern
safety_considerations: Machine provides a fixed path — ensure seat height is correct before beginning
If the machine does not allow true alternating independent arms, perform standard bilateral pressing instead
execution.range_of_motion_guidance: Full extension on each arm, fully loaded at the bottom. Each arm completes a full range per alternation.
coaching_cues: Press one side, hold the other — do not let the resting arm drop completely
Keep shoulders square — the alternating load tries to rotate you

name: Incline Machine Chest Press
description: The Incline Machine Chest Press uses a selectorized or plate-loaded machine set at an inclined angle to target the clavicular head of the pectoralis major. The machine guides the press path, reducing stabilization demands and allowing higher training volumes or isolation work at the end of a session when stabilizers are fatigued.

execution.starting_position: Adjust the seat height so the handles align with the upper chest. Sit back against the pad with feet flat on the floor.
execution.setup_instructions: Set the seat height on the incline machine so the pressing handles are at upper chest level. Adjust the starting position handle if present to bring the handles to the starting position.
steps: Step 1: Grip the handles at upper chest level.
Step 2: Press forward and upward along the machine's guided path to full arm extension.
Step 3: Squeeze the chest at the peak.
Step 4: Return under control to the starting position.
execution.breathing_instructions: Exhale as you press. Inhale as you return.
common_mistakes: Seat set too low, turning it into a flat press rather than incline
Releasing the weight stack at the bottom, losing continuous tension
safety_considerations: Adjust seat height for each user — do not assume it is set correctly
Control the weight on the return — do not let the stack drop
execution.range_of_motion_guidance: Full extension at top; return until chest is fully stretched without losing tension.
coaching_cues: Lead with the chest, not the shoulders
Squeeze at the top of every rep

name: Incline Push-Up
description: The incline push-up is a modified push-up performed with the hands on an elevated surface such as a bench, box, or step. Elevating the hands shifts the loading emphasis toward the lower (sternal) portion of the pectoralis major and reduces the total bodyweight lifted, making this an accessible entry point for beginners building pressing strength.

execution.starting_position: Place both hands on a bench or elevated surface slightly wider than shoulder-width apart. Walk your feet back until your body forms a straight diagonal line from head to heels, with arms fully extended.
execution.setup_instructions: Choose a surface height that matches your current strength level — higher elevation means easier. Ensure the surface is stable and will not slide.
steps: Step 1: Position hands on the elevated surface slightly wider than shoulder-width, fingers pointing forward.
Step 2: Walk feet back to form a straight plank line from head to heels. Brace the core.
Step 3: Inhale and lower the chest toward the surface by bending the elbows, keeping them at roughly 45 degrees from the torso.
Step 4: Pause when the chest is an inch from the surface, then exhale and press back to the starting position.
execution.breathing_instructions: Inhale as you lower toward the surface; exhale as you push back up.
common_mistakes: Allowing the hips to sag or pike — maintain a rigid plank throughout
Flaring the elbows out to 90 degrees, which stresses the shoulder joint
safety_considerations: Keep wrists stacked directly under the shoulders to minimize wrist stress
execution.range_of_motion_guidance: Lower until the chest nearly touches the surface, then press fully back to arm extension without locking the elbows aggressively.
coaching_cues: Keep your body as stiff as a board from head to heels
Think about spreading the floor apart with your hands as you press up

name: Incline Squeeze Press with Chains
description: An incline squeeze press — both dumbbells pressed together — with chains attached to each dumbbell for accommodating resistance. The continuous adduction squeeze targets the medial clavicular pectoral fibers, while the chains progressively load the lockout, maximizing tension through the top range where free weights typically feel easiest. This combination of technique and load variety creates an unusually high stimulus for the upper chest.

execution.starting_position: Lie on an incline bench (30–45 degrees). Attach chains to both dumbbells so they drape to the floor from the bottom of the press. Hold dumbbells pressed together at upper chest level, palms facing each other.
execution.setup_instructions: Use hex dumbbells for flat-face contact. Secure chains to handles. Reduce dumbbell weight below normal squeeze press weight due to chain addition. Chains should begin engaging near the mid-range of the press.
steps: Step 1: Begin with dumbbells pressed firmly together at the upper chest, chains draping to floor.
Step 2: Squeeze the dumbbells together and press them upward as a unit. Chains progressively engage as the dumbbells rise.
Step 3: At full lockout, all chains are suspended. Maintain the inward squeeze throughout.
Step 4: Lower under control, allowing chains to re-contact the floor, deloading the bottom. Repeat.
execution.breathing_instructions: Inhale at the bottom, exhale forcefully through the press.
common_mistakes: Letting the dumbbells separate — the squeeze must be constant throughout
Using too much dumbbell weight before adding chain load
Chains not engaging — means they are too long or not properly attached
safety_considerations: Secure chain attachments before beginning
Significantly reduce dumbbell weight relative to standard squeeze press
Have a spotter hand the dumbbells into position with chains attached
execution.range_of_motion_guidance: Full range from upper chest to lockout, squeeze maintained throughout.
coaching_cues: Squeeze the dumbbells together as hard as you can the entire set
Press hard to the top — the chains reward complete lockout

name: Incline Squeeze Press with Plate
description: An incline pressing variation where both palms press against opposite sides of a weight plate, maintaining continuous adduction force throughout the movement. The incline angle targets the clavicular pectoralis major while the sustained lateral squeeze on the plate creates constant isometric adduction that significantly increases medial pectoral fiber activation.

execution.starting_position: Lie on an incline bench (30–45 degrees). Hold a weight plate with both palms pressing inward against its flat sides. Begin with arms extended above the upper chest.
execution.setup_instructions: Select a weight plate appropriate for pressing — typically 10–25 kg. The plate should be held vertically with both palms on the faces. Lie on the incline bench.
steps: Step 1: Begin with the plate held above the upper chest, arms extended. Squeeze the plate hard inward with both palms.
Step 2: Lower the plate toward the upper chest, maintaining maximum inward pressure.
Step 3: Touch the upper chest gently with the plate and press back up.
Step 4: At the top, maintain the squeeze and repeat. The squeeze never stops.
execution.breathing_instructions: Inhale on descent, exhale on press.
common_mistakes: Relaxing the inward squeeze — the constant pressure is essential to the technique
Using a plate too heavy to hold with palm-to-face grip
Elbows flaring away — keep them pointing relatively forward due to the neutral grip
safety_considerations: Use a plate with smooth outer faces — textured plates can cause hand pain
Ensure a secure grip before pressing — the plate should feel firmly held between both palms
execution.range_of_motion_guidance: Full range from upper chest to lockout. Squeeze maintained throughout.
coaching_cues: Try to press your palms through the plate — the squeeze generates the chest tension
Think of crushing the plate: that internal force activates the medial pecs

name: Cable Internal Rotation
description: The cable internal rotation targets the subscapularis — the primary internal rotator of the shoulder — using a cable at elbow height. The subscapularis is often undertrained despite being the largest rotator cuff muscle, and weakness in internal rotation can contribute to shoulder impingement and dysfunction. The cable provides consistent resistance through the full range, making it superior to band-based alternatives for precise loading.

execution.starting_position: Stand beside a cable machine with the pulley set at elbow height. Grip the handle with the outside hand. Elbow bent to 90 degrees, forearm pointing toward the cable machine (externally rotated position).
execution.setup_instructions: Tuck a small towel between the elbow and the torso to keep the upper arm fixed. Keep loads very light — this is a corrective exercise.
steps: Step 1: Stand with the cable at elbow height, grip the handle with the outside hand.
Step 2: Elbow at 90 degrees, forearm pointing toward the cable.
Step 3: Rotate the forearm toward the body (internal rotation) while keeping the upper arm stationary.
Step 4: Rotate until the forearm points across the body.
Step 5: Return slowly under control to the starting position.
execution.breathing_instructions: Breathe naturally throughout.
common_mistakes: Allowing the elbow to move away from the side during rotation
Using weight that causes body rotation instead of isolated shoulder rotation
safety_considerations: Very light loads only — the subscapularis is targeted for health, not hypertrophy
execution.range_of_motion_guidance: From external rotation (forearm toward cable) to internal rotation (forearm across the body).
coaching_cues: Elbow stays anchored — only the forearm moves
Rotate from the shoulder joint
Think subscapularis — the front of the rotator cuff

name: Inverted Row on Rings with False Grip
description: The inverted row on rings with a false grip (wrist draped over the rings) is a horizontal pulling exercise that simultaneously trains rowing strength and the grip position required for ring muscle-ups. The unstable ring surface recruits additional stabilizer muscle activity compared to fixed-bar rows, while the false grip develops wrist and forearm strength essential for advanced ring skills.

execution.starting_position: Set rings at approximately waist-to-chest height. Take a false grip on each ring (wrist over the ring, not just fingers gripping the strap). Lean back so the body is at a 30-45 degree angle to the floor, arms extended.
execution.setup_instructions: Adjust ring height to control difficulty — lower = harder. The false grip feels uncomfortable initially; build wrist tolerance gradually.
steps: Step 1: Establish the false grip and lean back into the starting position with arms extended.
Step 2: Keeping the body in a rigid plank, row the chest toward the rings by driving elbows back.
Step 3: At the top, the hands should be at or near the chest with elbows behind the torso.
Step 4: Lower slowly under control back to the extended arm position.
Step 5: Maintain the false grip throughout the entire set.
execution.breathing_instructions: Exhale on the row up. Inhale on the descent.
common_mistakes: Releasing the false grip mid-set — the wrist should remain over the ring
Hips sagging — maintain a rigid plank body line
Pulling with the arms only — initiate with scapular retraction
safety_considerations: The false grip can cause wrist discomfort — build duration gradually
Avoid if you have wrist injuries or tendinopathies
execution.range_of_motion_guidance: Full arm extension to hands at chest level.
coaching_cues: Maintain the false grip — wrist over the ring at all times
Lead with the chest, not the chin
Body stays rigid like a plank — no hip hinge

name: Inverted Row with Feet on Swiss Ball
description: The inverted row with feet elevated on a Swiss ball combines horizontal pulling with continuous lower-body stability demand. The unstable foot surface requires constant hip extension and core engagement to prevent the ball from rolling, increasing total muscle recruitment compared to feet-on-floor versions while also training posterior chain co-activation.

execution.starting_position: Grip a fixed bar with both hands and walk the feet onto a Swiss ball. Extend hips to form a plank, arms extended toward the bar.
execution.setup_instructions: Ensure the bar is at an appropriate height relative to the ball — experiment to find the right position for the desired difficulty. Use a bar slightly narrower than shoulder width.
steps: Step 1: Establish the starting plank position with feet centered on the ball.
Step 2: Brace core and squeeze glutes to stabilize the ball.
Step 3: Row the chest to the bar, driving elbows back.
Step 4: At the top, hold 1 second while maintaining ball control.
Step 5: Lower under control to starting position.
execution.breathing_instructions: Exhale on the row. Inhale on the descent.
common_mistakes: Letting the hips drop as fatigue sets in
Feet sliding on the ball — press the calves firmly into the surface
Rushing the rep to avoid the balance challenge
safety_considerations: Ensure the ball is properly inflated and rated for body weight
Have the bar set low enough that a fall from the ball does not cause injury
execution.range_of_motion_guidance: Full arm extension to chest touching or near bar.
coaching_cues: Press your calves into the ball to control it
Hips stay high — do not let them drop
Full lockout on every descent

name: Iron Cross Hold
description: A rings gymnastic skill where the arms are held out to the sides at shoulder height while the body hangs vertically. The massive internal rotation force demands extraordinary pectoral and shoulder strength. This is considered one of the ultimate tests of upper body strength in gymnastics.

execution.starting_position: Set up for Iron Cross Hold in proper position.
execution.setup_instructions: Prepare body and equipment for Iron Cross Hold.
steps: Step 1: Mount rings with arms overhead. Lower body while spreading arms to the sides.
Step 2: Arms reach out at shoulder height with elbows slightly bent.
Step 3: Body hangs vertically below rings in rigid position.
Step 4: Hold position then slowly bring rings overhead to exit.
execution.breathing_instructions: Breathe steadily; never hold breath during static holds.
common_mistakes: Fully locked elbows causing injury
Attempting without prerequisites
safety_considerations: Build prerequisite strength before attempting advanced variations.
Stop if joint pain occurs.
execution.range_of_motion_guidance: Full range of motion with control at all times.
coaching_cues: Slight elbow bend for safety
Years of ring strength needed first

name: Jackknife Sit-Up — Swiss Ball
description: The Swiss ball jackknife sit-up combines simultaneous hip flexion and spinal flexion by having the athlete curl both the lower body (rolling the ball forward) and the upper body upward to meet in the middle in a folding or jackknife motion. The unstable surface of the Swiss ball challenges core stability throughout the movement, while the simultaneous recruitment of the upper and lower rectus abdominis creates a unique peak-contraction stimulus. The movement requires significant hip flexor and abdominal coordination.

execution.starting_position: Lie back on the Swiss ball with the ball under the lower to mid-back, feet flat on the floor. Arms can be extended back overhead or crossed at the chest.
execution.setup_instructions: Ensure the Swiss ball is adequately inflated and placed on a non-slip surface. Use a size appropriate to your height.
steps: Step 1: Begin draped over the ball, spine extended, arms overhead or at chest.
Step 2: Simultaneously curl the upper body upward (spinal flexion) while drawing the knees toward the chest by rolling the feet back.
Step 3: Both the upper and lower body converge at the top of the movement — the knees and chest meet over the top of the ball.
Step 4: Extend back out in a controlled manner, letting both the upper and lower body lower simultaneously.
Step 5: Return to full extension and repeat.
execution.breathing_instructions: Exhale on the jackknife. Inhale on the controlled extension.
common_mistakes: Only performing the upper-body crunch without bringing the knees up
Losing balance on the ball — start with feet slightly wider for stability
safety_considerations: Ensure the ball is on a non-slip surface and correctly sized
execution.range_of_motion_guidance: Full extension draped over the ball to full jackknife with knees and chest meeting.
execution.tempo_recommendations: 2-1-2-0. Fully controlled — the ball challenges coordination.
coaching_cues: Bring the knees and chest to meet each other
Control both directions equally

name: Jefferson Curl
description: The Jefferson curl is a slow, controlled weighted spinal flexion exercise in which the lifter intentionally rounds the spine segment by segment from the neck downward while holding a light load. It is used in strength sports and gymnastics for building spinal flexion strength and hamstring flexibility under load. This exercise is controversial and is generally restricted to experienced trainees with no history of spinal disc pathology.

execution.starting_position: Stand on a box or elevated surface with feet together and knees soft but mostly straight. Hold a very light dumbbell or kettlebell in both hands in front of the thighs.
execution.setup_instructions: Use a very light load — 5–15 kg is typically sufficient. Stand on a box so the hands can travel below foot level. Knees remain soft throughout.
steps: Step 1: Begin standing with the weight held in front. Take a breath.
Step 2: Tuck the chin to chest and begin to curl the spine downward, one vertebra at a time — start at the neck, then upper thoracic, mid thoracic, lumbar.
Step 3: Continue curling until the hands are as far toward the floor as possible, allowing a full spinal flexion stretch.
Step 4: Pause at the bottom, breathing naturally.
Step 5: Reverse the movement in the opposite order — start by uncurling the lumbar, then thoracic, then cervical, returning to standing upright.
execution.breathing_instructions: Breathe naturally throughout. Do not hold the breath during flexion.
common_mistakes: Using too much weight — this is a flexibility exercise, not a strength exercise
Performing with straight knees and tight hamstrings before adequate flexibility has been developed
Rushing through the movement rather than moving slowly segment by segment
safety_considerations: This exercise is contraindicated for anyone with herniated discs, spinal stenosis, spondylolisthesis, or any condition aggravated by spinal flexion
Only suitable for advanced trainees with a thorough understanding of spinal mechanics
Start without weight until movement quality is high, then add minimal load
Stop immediately if any sharp or radiating pain occurs
execution.range_of_motion_guidance: The goal is maximum spinal flexion through the full range, with the hands reaching as far below the feet as possible. Build this range gradually over months.
execution.tempo_recommendations: Very slow — 5–10 seconds to descend, 10–30 second hold at the bottom, 5–10 seconds to ascend.
coaching_cues: Melt from the top down — start from the neck, not the lower back
Think of your spine as a string of pearls uncurling one at a time
The weight is a guide, not resistance — it should be almost nothing

name: Jefferson Deadlift
description: A unique deadlift variation where the lifter straddles the barbell with one foot in front of and one foot behind the bar, then lifts with both hands gripping the bar between the legs. This asymmetrical loading pattern places uneven forces on the spine and hips, training rotational stability and offering an alternative for lifters who struggle with conventional or sumo deadlifts.

execution.starting_position: Stand straddling the barbell with one foot in front of the bar and one foot behind. Reach down and grip the bar with one hand on each side of the front foot.
execution.setup_instructions: Load a barbell on the floor. Stand directly over it, straddling it. Grip the bar with both hands in a staggered position.
steps: Step 1: Brace the core and grip the bar with one hand in front of the leading thigh and one behind.
Step 2: Drive through both feet to stand, lifting the bar between the legs.
Step 3: Lock out at the top with hips and knees fully extended.
Step 4: Lower the bar back to the floor under control.
execution.breathing_instructions: Inhale and brace before the pull. Exhale at the top.
common_mistakes: Rotating the torso excessively — the spine rotates slightly but should not collapse
Using too much weight before learning the movement
safety_considerations: This movement is naturally asymmetrical — alternate which foot leads each set for even development
execution.range_of_motion_guidance: Full extension at the top. Bar returned to the floor between reps.
coaching_cues: Drive through both feet equally
Alternate the lead foot each set

name: Jefferson Deadlift — Alternating Grips
description: The Jefferson deadlift is a unique straddle-stance deadlift where the barbell passes between the lifter's legs and the two hands grip the bar at different positions — one in front and one behind. This unconventional stance loads the spine asymmetrically in rotation while the hips and legs drive the bar upward. By alternating which hand is in front and which is behind across sets, the rotational loading is balanced. The Jefferson deadlift challenges hip adductor strength, core anti-rotation, and hip external rotation simultaneously.

execution.starting_position: Straddle the barbell with one foot in front and one foot behind, feet approximately shoulder-width apart in a lunge-like orientation. Bend down to grip the bar with one hand in front of the leading thigh and one hand behind the trailing thigh.
execution.setup_instructions: Begin with a light load to learn the unusual stance geometry. The bar should sit at the same height as a standard deadlift. Alternate which side is 'leading' every set.
steps: Step 1: Straddle the barbell with one foot forward and one back. Grip the bar with an overhand grip on both hands — one in front, one behind.
Step 2: Take a breath, brace the core, and begin the pull by driving both feet into the floor simultaneously.
Step 3: Rise to standing, keeping the bar close to the body (it will pass between the thighs).
Step 4: Lower the bar under control by hinging at the hips and bending the knees until the bar returns to the floor.
execution.breathing_instructions: Inhale and brace before the pull. Exhale at the top or during the descent.
common_mistakes: Setting up with too narrow a stance — the bar must pass between the thighs cleanly
Not alternating grip orientation across sets — this causes asymmetrical loading over time
Rounding the lower back as the bar rises through the thighs
safety_considerations: The Jefferson deadlift places rotational stress on the spine — start light and prioritize technique before loading
Keep the spine neutral throughout — no twisting of the torso to assist the lift
execution.range_of_motion_guidance: Full deadlift range — bar from floor to full hip extension at the top.
coaching_cues: Both feet drive into the floor equally — this is a squat-deadlift hybrid
Keep the bar between the thighs, not to one side
Switch your foot and grip orientation every set to balance the rotational load

name: JM Press
description: The JM press is a powerlifting-derived tricep exercise invented by JM Blakley that blends a close-grip bench press and a skull crusher. The bar is unracked and lowered to the neck area with the elbows moving forward (past the bar's path), then pressed back to lockout. The position combines elbow flexion and shoulder flexion, loading the triceps in a unique way that transfers directly to lockout strength in the bench press. It is primarily used by powerlifters for tricep mass and strength.

execution.starting_position: Lie on a flat bench, bar in a close-grip bench press position (hands slightly inside shoulder width). Bar pressed to full extension.
execution.setup_instructions: Have a spotter. Use a moderate load — lighter than your close-grip bench press. This is a technical movement requiring practice.
steps: Step 1: Lower the bar toward the neck, allowing the elbows to push forward and down simultaneously.
Step 2: The bar travels toward the throat or chin as the elbows drop below the bar path.
Step 3: The bar barely touches or floats just above the throat.
Step 4: Drive the bar back to the starting position by extending the elbows and pushing the arms back.
execution.breathing_instructions: Inhale on descent, exhale on press.
common_mistakes: Attempting heavy loads before mastering the technique
Letting the bar rest on the throat rather than controlling it
safety_considerations: This exercise involves the bar approaching the throat — always use a spotter
Master lighter loads before increasing weight
execution.range_of_motion_guidance: Bar to throat level at the bottom, full lockout at the top.
coaching_cues: Elbows forward on the descent
Think skull crusher + close-grip press hybrid
Spotter required

name: Decline Dumbbell JM Press
description: A decline bench JM press variation using dumbbells instead of a barbell. The decline angle increases tricep activation and allows natural wrist rotation. Each dumbbell moves independently, requiring more stabilization and potentially revealing asymmetries.

execution.starting_position: Set up for Decline Dumbbell JM Press in the appropriate position.
execution.setup_instructions: Prepare equipment and body position for Decline Dumbbell JM Press.
steps: Step 1: Lie on decline bench with dumbbells at arm's length above chest.
Step 2: Lower dumbbells toward throat with elbows flaring to 45 degrees.
Step 3: Lower until forearms are past parallel, feeling tricep stretch.
Step 4: Press dumbbells back overhead in a tricep-dominant path.
execution.breathing_instructions: Exhale during the exertion phase, inhale during the return.
common_mistakes: Lowering dumbbells to chest instead of throat
Excessive elbow flare
safety_considerations: Keep joints aligned throughout the movement.
Use controlled weight appropriate for skill level.
execution.range_of_motion_guidance: Move through full range of motion without compromising joint integrity.
coaching_cues: Throat is the target, not the chest
Control the arc path

name: JM Press EZ Bar (Strict Form)
description: The JM press performed with strict technique using an EZ curl bar. The angled EZ bar reduces wrist discomfort at the unusual elbow-flare position this exercise requires. Strict form emphasizes pure tricep strength without momentum or body English.

execution.starting_position: Set up for JM Press EZ Bar (Strict Form) in the appropriate position.
execution.setup_instructions: Prepare equipment and body position for JM Press EZ Bar (Strict Form).
steps: Step 1: Lie on bench with EZ bar at arm's length. Set grip slightly wider than close.
Step 2: Lower bar toward throat with elbows pointing at approximately 45 degrees.
Step 3: Lower under full control until forearms break horizontal.
Step 4: Drive bar back to lockout through tricep extension.
execution.breathing_instructions: Exhale during the exertion phase, inhale during the return.
common_mistakes: Lowering to chest instead of throat
Letting elbows drift wide
safety_considerations: Keep joints aligned throughout the movement.
Use controlled weight appropriate for skill level.
execution.range_of_motion_guidance: Move through full range of motion without compromising joint integrity.
coaching_cues: Throat is the target, not the chest
EZ bar reduces wrist angle stress

name: JM Press (Smith Machine)
description: The JM press performed in a Smith machine for added safety and stability. This hybrid movement between a close-grip bench press and a skullcrusher emphasizes triceps strength at the sticking point. The Smith allows solo heavy work without fear of bar path deviation.

execution.starting_position: Set up for JM Press (Smith Machine) in the appropriate position.
execution.setup_instructions: Prepare equipment and body position for JM Press (Smith Machine).
steps: Step 1: Set up under Smith bar as for close-grip bench. Lie on flat bench.
Step 2: Unhook bar with close grip. Keep elbows slightly outside shoulder width.
Step 3: Lower bar toward chin or throat with elbows flaring naturally.
Step 4: Press back up focusing on tricep lockout.
execution.breathing_instructions: Exhale during the exertion phase, inhale during the return.
common_mistakes: Letting elbows flare too wide
Lowering too deep causing shoulder strain
safety_considerations: Keep joints aligned throughout the movement.
Use controlled weight appropriate for skill level.
execution.range_of_motion_guidance: Move through full range of motion without compromising joint integrity.
coaching_cues: Bar path goes to throat, not chest
Drive elbows forward on press

name: Jump Lunge
description: The jump lunge is a plyometric exercise in which the lifter starts in a lunge position and explosively jumps into the air, switching the position of the feet mid-air to land in a lunge on the opposite leg. It trains explosive hip and knee extension power, cardiovascular conditioning, and single-leg landing mechanics. The continuous alternating nature makes it one of the most demanding bodyweight lower body exercises.

execution.starting_position: Begin in a lunge position with one foot forward and the rear knee just above the floor. Arms are bent at the sides or in running position.
execution.setup_instructions: Ensure adequate ceiling height and clear landing space. Master the stationary lunge before progressing to the jump lunge.
steps: Step 1: Start in the bottom of a lunge with one foot forward, back knee near the floor.
Step 2: Swing the arms explosively and drive through both feet to jump vertically off the ground.
Step 3: While airborne, switch the position of the legs so that the previously rear leg is now forward.
Step 4: Land softly by absorbing through the toes, then ball of foot, then heel — landing back in a lunge position.
Step 5: Immediately upon landing, absorb and spring back up into the next jump.
execution.breathing_instructions: Breathe rhythmically — exhale sharply at takeoff, inhale during flight, absorb on landing.
common_mistakes: Landing stiff-legged instead of absorbing through the hip and knee — high injury risk
Landing with the feet too close together, reducing stability
Using too shallow a lunge on landing, reducing the eccentric braking benefit
safety_considerations: Land softly — impact forces during plyometric landing can be 3–5 times bodyweight
Develop adequate single-leg strength before performing jump lunges
Avoid on hard surfaces — rubber flooring or grass is preferable
execution.range_of_motion_guidance: Lunge depth at both takeoff and landing should be near the bottom of a standard lunge.
execution.tempo_recommendations: Performed for time (20–60 seconds) or for reps with maximal effort on each jump
coaching_cues: Use your arms — they help drive the jump height
Land soft like a feather — quiet feet
Deep lunge on landing before you launch again

name: Plyometric Jump Lunge
description: The plyometric jump lunge combines a reverse lunge with a vertical jump, in which the athlete lunges down and then explosively jumps from the lunge position, landing softly back into the same lunge before repeating. Unlike the split jump, the athlete does not switch legs mid-air, making it a true unilateral explosive exercise per leg. It develops single-leg explosive power and lunge-pattern deceleration strength, and is an effective conditioning tool for lower body power endurance.

execution.starting_position: Stand upright with feet together. Step one foot back into a reverse lunge to begin.
execution.setup_instructions: No equipment required. Non-slip surface with adequate overhead clearance.
steps: Step 1: Step into a reverse lunge with the right foot back, lowering until both knees are near 90 degrees.
Step 2: Drive off the front (left) foot explosively, extending fully through the hip and knee to jump upward.
Step 3: Land softly back in the same lunge position and absorb through the front leg.
Step 4: Complete all reps on one leg before switching.
Step 5: Perform equal reps on each side.
execution.breathing_instructions: Exhale sharply at takeoff. Inhale as you descend into the lunge.
common_mistakes: Landing with the front knee caving inward
Insufficient depth — the rear knee should approach the floor
Using the rear leg to push off — the front leg does the work
safety_considerations: High demand on the front knee — ensure solid lunge mechanics before adding the jump.
Progress from walking lunges and reverse lunges before this variation.
execution.range_of_motion_guidance: Full lunge depth — rear knee approaching the floor. Full extension at takeoff.
execution.tempo_recommendations: 6–10 explosive reps per leg for power. Up to 15 for conditioning.
coaching_cues: Drive off the front foot — not the back
Land quiet and deep
Front knee over the toes at all times

name: Jump Rope
description: Jump rope is a rhythmic cardiovascular and plyometric exercise in which a rope is swung overhead in a continuous arc as the athlete hops over it with both feet on each revolution. It simultaneously trains cardiovascular fitness, ankle and calf elasticity, timing, coordination, and foot speed, making it one of the most efficient conditioning tools available. Single-under jump rope — one revolution per jump — is the standard entry point before progressing to double-unders.

execution.starting_position: Stand upright holding one handle of the jump rope in each hand, rope behind the heels.
execution.setup_instructions: Use a rope long enough that it reaches the armpits when both handles are held together underfoot. Adequate overhead and frontal clearance needed.
steps: Step 1: Hold one handle in each hand with elbows near the sides, rope behind the body.
Step 2: Swing the rope overhead using wrist rotation — not full arm swings.
Step 3: As the rope descends in front, hop off both feet with a small jump — just enough for the rope to pass underneath (2–3 cm clearance).
Step 4: Land softly on the balls of both feet with slightly bent knees.
Step 5: Continue the rhythm continuously for the prescribed duration or rep count.
execution.breathing_instructions: Breathe continuously at a rhythm matching your jump cadence.
common_mistakes: Jumping too high — wastes energy and slows rhythm
Swinging the arms instead of using wrist rotation
Landing on the heels — should land on the balls of the feet
safety_considerations: High repetitive calf and Achilles demand — increase volume gradually.
Ensure the floor surface is not too hard (concrete) for extended sessions.
execution.range_of_motion_guidance: Minimal hop height — just enough rope clearance. Soft ball-of-foot landing.
execution.tempo_recommendations: Typically performed for time: 1–5 minute continuous intervals. Or for rep counts in circuits.
coaching_cues: Wrist rotation — not arms
Small hops — stay light
Ball of foot landing — quiet and springy

name: Jump Rope — Steady State
description: Steady-state jump rope is a continuous rhythmic cardiovascular exercise that develops coordination, calf strength, and aerobic capacity simultaneously. The repetitive small-amplitude jumps demand rapid and repeated plantarflexion from the gastrocnemius and soleus, while the wrist rotation engages the forearms and the rhythm demands precise coordination between upper and lower body. Jump rope is one of the most calorie-dense and equipment-minimal forms of cardiovascular training available, burning approximately 10–16 calories per minute depending on pace and bodyweight.

execution.starting_position: Stand with feet together on a flat, non-slip surface. Hold the rope handles at hip width, with the rope hanging behind the heels. Stand tall with a slight bend in the knees.
execution.setup_instructions: Size the rope correctly: step on the middle of the rope and the handles should reach armpit height. Use a jump mat or sprung floor to reduce impact. Wear supportive footwear.
steps: Step 1: Hold one handle in each hand with the rope hanging behind. Swing the rope overhead and begin turning the wrists in small circles — the wrists, not the arms, drive the rotation.
Step 2: As the rope sweeps under the feet, jump just high enough to clear it — 1–2 inches off the ground.
Step 3: Land softly on the balls of the feet with knees slightly bent. Do not land flat-footed.
Step 4: Maintain a consistent rhythm. Keep the elbows close to the body and the rope motion driven by wrist rotation.
Step 5: Continue for the target duration, starting with 30–60 second bouts if new to jump rope.
execution.breathing_instructions: Breathe rhythmically throughout. Nasal breathing at moderate intensity helps regulate pace. At higher intensities, breathe through both nose and mouth.
common_mistakes: Using large arm swings to turn the rope instead of small wrist rotations — this wastes energy and disrupts rhythm
Jumping too high, which is exhausting and unnecessary
Landing heavily on the heels, increasing joint impact
safety_considerations: Jump on a forgiving surface — avoid concrete without a mat
Beginners should start with short intervals (30–60 seconds) to allow calf adaptation before longer steady-state sessions
execution.range_of_motion_guidance: Jump height should be just enough to clear the rope — 2–3 cm off the ground. Feet stay close together. Wrist circles are small and fast.
execution.tempo_recommendations: Beginner: 30 seconds on / 30 seconds off × 10. Intermediate steady-state: 5–10 minutes continuous. Advanced: 20–30 minutes continuous at 120–140 RPM.
coaching_cues: Turn with the wrists, not the arms
Stay on the balls of your feet
Think light — imagine the floor is hot

name: Keg Toss
description: A throwing event where a water-filled keg or weighted container is tossed backward over a crossbar. The athlete swings the keg between the legs and releases it overhead. This event tests explosive hip extension and shoulder power in a unique overhead throwing pattern.

execution.starting_position: Set up for Keg Toss in proper strongman position.
execution.setup_instructions: Prepare all equipment and body position for Keg Toss.
steps: Step 1: Stand with keg between feet, hinged at hips.
Step 2: Swing keg backward between legs for momentum.
Step 3: Drive hips explosively forward and swing keg up and overhead.
Step 4: Release keg at peak of arc aiming for target over crossbar.
execution.breathing_instructions: Brace core maximally before every lift. Breathe between reps if needed.
common_mistakes: Too short a swing before release
Releasing too early
safety_considerations: Use collars on all loaded barbells.
Ensure clear path for carries.
Have spotters for overhead movements.
execution.range_of_motion_guidance: Full range of motion specific to the implement being used.
coaching_cues: Full hip extension drives the toss
Release at peak of arc for height

name: Kettlebell American Swing (Overhead)
description: The kettlebell American swing extends the traditional Russian swing by swinging the kettlebell fully overhead to lockout, rather than stopping at shoulder height. This demands greater shoulder stability and hip power through a larger arc. The overhead finish requires the core and lats to stabilize forcefully at the top. It is popular in CrossFit and conditioning contexts, though it demands solid shoulder mobility and strength before attempting.

execution.starting_position: Stand with feet hip- to shoulder-width, kettlebell on the floor between feet. Hinge at the hips, grab the handle with both hands, tilt the bell back.
execution.setup_instructions: Confirm full shoulder flexion range before attempting. Use a lighter kettlebell than your Russian swing weight.
steps: Step 1: Hike the kettlebell back between the legs with a hip hinge.
Step 2: Drive the hips explosively forward, standing tall, and let the bell swing upward.
Step 3: Continue the arc overhead until the bell is fully above the head, arms locked, biceps near the ears.
Step 4: Control the descent, let the bell swing back between the legs, and repeat.
execution.breathing_instructions: Exhale sharply at hip extension, inhale on the downswing.
common_mistakes: Squatting instead of hinging
Pressing the kettlebell overhead with arm strength rather than hip drive
Lumbar hyperextension at lockout
safety_considerations: Requires overhead shoulder mobility — screen before prescribing
Do not attempt with shoulder impingement
execution.range_of_motion_guidance: Full hip hinge to full overhead lockout with straight arms.
coaching_cues: Power from the hips
Lock out overhead — squeeze everything
Control the downswing

name: Kettlebell Bottoms-Up Carry
description: The bottoms-up kettlebell carry holds the inverted kettlebell at chest/rack height (not overhead) while walking. The rack position (inverted bell at chest) demands significant forearm, wrist, and rotator cuff activation to prevent the bell from tipping, while the walk challenges anti-rotation and lateral core stability. This version is more accessible than the overhead variation and serves as a progressive step toward the bottoms-up overhead carry, also functioning as a standalone rotator cuff and grip strength exercise.

execution.starting_position: Hold a kettlebell in the bottoms-up position at chest height — handle pointing down, bell balanced on top of the fist at shoulder level. Elbow bent approximately 90 degrees.
execution.setup_instructions: Begin with a very light kettlebell. The rack version is easier than overhead, but still requires significant grip strength and rotator cuff activation.
steps: Step 1: Hold the inverted kettlebell at chest/rack height. Squeeze the handle.
Step 2: Walk a designated distance while maintaining the bottoms-up balance.
Step 3: Keep the elbow close to the body and the wrist straight.
Step 4: Maintain a vertical, unrotated torso.
Step 5: Lower and switch sides.
execution.breathing_instructions: Breathe freely. Brace the core throughout.
common_mistakes: Too heavy — the bell will tip; much lighter than expected is appropriate
Rotating the torso toward the loaded side
safety_considerations: Have a clear area in case the bell falls
Build grip endurance before increasing distance or load
execution.range_of_motion_guidance: Maintained bottoms-up rack position for the full walking distance.
coaching_cues: Squeeze the handle — continuous grip
Wrist stacked above elbow
Tall and vertical — no rotation

name: Kettlebell Bottoms-Up Press
description: The kettlebell bottoms-up press inverts the kettlebell so the bell faces upward above the handle, requiring intense grip and forearm engagement to keep the bell stabilized throughout the press. The unstable inverted position activates the rotator cuff and scapular stabilizers far more than conventional pressing, making it an exceptional shoulder health and stability exercise. The unilateral nature also develops anti-rotation core strength.

execution.starting_position: Hold a kettlebell by the handle with the bell inverted (pointing up), arm at shoulder height. The wrist must be straight and directly under the bell to maintain balance. Begin with a light kettlebell.
execution.setup_instructions: Start with 25-35% of normal press load. The balance demand changes the nature of the exercise entirely. This can be performed standing, seated, or kneeling.
steps: Step 1: Grip the kettlebell handle firmly with the bell balanced above.
Step 2: Bring the bell to shoulder height with elbow at 90 degrees.
Step 3: Press directly overhead, keeping the bell balanced at all times.
Step 4: At lockout, the arm is fully extended with the bell balanced above.
Step 5: Lower under full control to the starting position.
execution.breathing_instructions: Exhale on the press, inhale on the descent.
common_mistakes: Using too heavy a kettlebell — balance failure is the limiting factor initially
Flaring the elbow wide — keep it slightly forward in the press
Bracing insufficiently against the unilateral load
safety_considerations: Have a plan if the kettlebell falls — step away from it rather than catching it
Begin over a padded surface when learning
execution.range_of_motion_guidance: Shoulder height to full lockout overhead.
coaching_cues: Tight grip — the bell tells you when you're losing it
Press in a straight line
Keep your wrist stacked under the bell

name: Kettlebell Clean
description: The kettlebell clean is a single-arm ballistic exercise in which the kettlebell is swung from between the legs to a racked position at the shoulder using a hip hinge and arm pull. Unlike a barbell clean, the kettlebell is guided into the rack by the forearm rather than caught with the hands, requiring specific wrist positioning and elbow control. It trains hip hinge power transfer, shoulder girdle stability in the racked position, and the coordination of the lower and upper body in force transmission.

execution.starting_position: Stand with feet shoulder-width apart. Kettlebell on the floor between the feet, hinged forward to grip with one hand.
execution.setup_instructions: Choose a weight manageable for clean technique — wrist bruising usually means the bell is swinging out too wide before the catch.
steps: Step 1: Hinge at the hip to grip the kettlebell. Hike it back between the legs like a hike pass in American football.
Step 2: Explosively extend the hips and drive the kettlebell upward, pulling the elbow high as the bell rises.
Step 3: As the bell rises to shoulder height, rotate the hand and guide the bell into the racked position — bell resting on the forearm at the shoulder.
Step 4: Stand tall in the racked position. The bell should sit quietly without banging the forearm.
Step 5: Hinge back and let the bell descend in a controlled arc back between the legs for the next rep.
execution.breathing_instructions: Exhale sharply at hip extension. Inhale during the swing back.
common_mistakes: Letting the bell loop out wide — guide it in a tight arc close to the body
Catching the bell with a limp wrist — the forearm and wrist must be firm
Not fully extending the hips at the top of the drive
safety_considerations: Wrist bruising is a learning artifact of incorrect bell path, not a training adaptation — fix technique.
Start with lighter weight to learn the racking position.
execution.range_of_motion_guidance: Full hip extension at the top of the drive. Bell fully racked at shoulder.
execution.tempo_recommendations: 5–10 reps per arm per set. Fluid, rhythmic cadence.
coaching_cues: Hike hard — drive the hips
Pull the elbow high and tight
Guide the bell in — don't let it loop out

name: Kettlebell Curl
description: The kettlebell curl uses a kettlebell's offset center of mass, which hangs below the handle, creating a different lever and tension pattern than dumbbells. At the bottom of the curl, the hanging bell creates more tension than a dumbbell at the same arm position. The kettlebell can be held by the handle for a neutral-to-supinated curl or by the horns for a supinated grip curl, offering useful variation.

execution.starting_position: Stand upright holding one or two kettlebells by the handle. Arms extended at sides.
execution.setup_instructions: Hold by the handle for a neutral/supinated curl. Can hold by the horns for more supination.
steps: Step 1: Begin with arms extended, kettlebell(s) hanging.
Step 2: Curl the kettlebell(s) upward by flexing the elbows, supinating the grip as you curl.
Step 3: Curl until maximum elbow flexion.
Step 4: Lower with control.
execution.breathing_instructions: Exhale on the curl, inhale on the return.
common_mistakes: Letting the kettlebell swing outward
Using body sway
safety_considerations: The offset weight can torque the wrist — control the bell
execution.range_of_motion_guidance: Full extension to full flexion.
coaching_cues: Let the bell hang — control it
Supinate at the top
No swing

name: Kettlebell Halo
description: The kettlebell halo circles a kettlebell around the head held by the horns (handles), identical in movement to the dumbbell halo but with the unique loading distribution of the kettlebell's offset center of mass. The asymmetric weight creates a rotating moment that challenges the shoulder stabilizers differently on each half of the circle, making it a popular kettlebell shoulder warm-up and mobility drill.

execution.starting_position: Stand with feet shoulder-width apart. Hold a light kettlebell by the horns (handles) with both hands, bell facing up. Hold at chest level.
execution.setup_instructions: Use a light kettlebell (8-16 kg typically). The asymmetric load of the KB makes this more challenging than a dumbbell at the same weight.
steps: Step 1: Begin with kettlebell at chest level.
Step 2: Circle the kettlebell around the head, moving it to one side, then behind the head.
Step 3: Continue the circle to the other side and return to front.
Step 4: Complete desired reps in one direction, then reverse.
execution.breathing_instructions: Breathe continuously with the circular motion.
common_mistakes: Letting the bell flip over — maintain a stable grip on the horns throughout
Rushing through the motion — slow and deliberate
safety_considerations: Firm grip at all times — a dropped KB behind the head is dangerous
Start with a lighter bell than expected — the motion is awkward initially
execution.range_of_motion_guidance: Full circle around the head.
coaching_cues: Bell stays upright throughout the circle
Circle close to the head, not wide
Core braced — torso does not sway

name: Kettlebell Press
description: The kettlebell press is a unilateral overhead pressing exercise performed from the kettlebell rack position, pressing the bell directly overhead to full arm lockout. The offset center of mass of the kettlebell compared to a dumbbell requires greater forearm and wrist stability to control the bell path. As a strict press with no leg drive, it isolates the deltoid, triceps, and upper trapezius, while the unilateral nature demands significant anti-lateral flexion core engagement throughout.

execution.starting_position: Stand with feet shoulder-width apart. Kettlebell in the rack position on the right side — bell resting on the forearm, elbow close to the body, upper arm vertical.
execution.setup_instructions: Clean the kettlebell into the rack position to begin. Stand tall with the torso upright.
steps: Step 1: Begin in the racked position with the bell at shoulder height, elbow close to the torso.
Step 2: Press the kettlebell directly overhead by extending the elbow and driving the hand upward.
Step 3: Lock out the arm fully overhead — the bicep should be near the ear.
Step 4: Lower the bell under control back to the rack position.
Step 5: Complete all reps on one side before switching.
execution.breathing_instructions: Exhale on the press. Inhale on the return to rack.
common_mistakes: Side-bending away from the bell — maintain an upright torso
Not fully locking out the elbow at the top
Starting with the elbow flared out — it should be close to the body in the rack
safety_considerations: Shoulder impingement or instability should be assessed before heavy overhead pressing.
Ensure full lockout on each rep to protect the shoulder joint.
execution.range_of_motion_guidance: Full elbow lockout overhead. Full return to racked position.
execution.tempo_recommendations: 3–8 reps per side. Controlled tempo — 2 seconds up, pause at top, 2 seconds down.
coaching_cues: Press straight up — not forward
Lock out — bicep near the ear
Stay tall — no lean

name: Kettlebell Snatch
description: The kettlebell snatch is a single-arm ballistic exercise in which the kettlebell is swung from between the legs directly overhead in one continuous motion, arriving in a locked-out overhead position on the same side as the working hand. It is considered the king of kettlebell exercises, demanding explosive hip extension power, shoulder stability, overhead mobility, and the precise timing to guide the bell into a safe overhead position. The kettlebell snatch is used in competitive kettlebell sport as well as general athletic conditioning.

execution.starting_position: Stand with feet shoulder-width apart, kettlebell on the floor between the feet. Hinge to grip with one hand.
execution.setup_instructions: Master the kettlebell swing and clean before attempting the snatch. Choose a moderate weight.
steps: Step 1: Hike the kettlebell between the legs with a sharp hip hinge.
Step 2: Explosively extend the hips to drive the kettlebell upward in a tight arc close to the body.
Step 3: As the bell rises past the shoulder, punch the hand up and forward to rotate underneath the bell.
Step 4: Lock out the arm overhead, with the bell resting against the back of the forearm and the arm fully extended.
Step 5: Hold briefly, then hinge back and guide the bell down in a controlled descent back between the legs.
execution.breathing_instructions: Exhale sharply at hip drive. Inhale on the descent.
common_mistakes: Letting the bell loop away from the body — keep it tight on the way up
Punching late — if timed wrong, the bell flips over and bangs the wrist
Not locking out the elbow fully overhead
safety_considerations: Wrist impact during the punch-through phase is a common beginner hazard — use lighter weight until timing is established.
Shoulder instability contraindicates this exercise.
execution.range_of_motion_guidance: Full hip extension at drive. Full elbow lockout overhead. Full controlled descent.
execution.tempo_recommendations: 5–10 reps per arm. Used in timed sets (5–10 minutes) in kettlebell sport.
coaching_cues: Tight arc — bell stays close
Punch through at the top
Lock out — pause — then descend

name: Kettlebell Swing
description: The kettlebell swing is a ballistic hip-hinge exercise in which the kettlebell is swung from between the knees to chest height (Russian) or overhead (American) using explosive hip extension. Despite the apparent arm movement, the swing is fundamentally a posterior chain exercise — the glutes and hamstrings generate the force that propels the kettlebell, while the arms merely guide it. It develops explosive hip power, posterior chain endurance, and cardiovascular conditioning simultaneously.

execution.starting_position: Stand with feet slightly wider than shoulder-width with the kettlebell on the floor just in front. Hinge at the hip to grip the kettlebell with both hands, tilting it toward you.
execution.setup_instructions: Choose a kettlebell weight that allows explosive hip drive without compromising lumbar position. Beginners: 12–16 kg. Intermediate: 20–28 kg. The first swing begins from a hip hinge, not a squat.
steps: Step 1: Hike the kettlebell back between the legs like a hike pass in American football — hinging at the hip, loading the hamstrings.
Step 2: Explosively extend the hips forward — the glutes contract hard and the hips snap to full extension.
Step 3: The momentum of the hip drive propels the kettlebell forward and upward. The arms guide, not lift.
Step 4: At the top (chest height for Russian swing), the core is braced hard and the body is a straight line.
Step 5: Allow the kettlebell to arc back down, hinge at the hip again, guide the bell between the legs, and repeat.
execution.breathing_instructions: Exhale sharply as the hips snap forward. Inhale as the bell swings back. The breathing pattern reinforces core bracing at the apex.
common_mistakes: Squatting during the downswing instead of hinging — the knees should stay relatively extended as the hips hinge back
Using the arms to lift the bell — the arms should hang loose; the hip drive does the work
Hyperextending the lower back at the top — the top position should be tall and plank-like, not arched
safety_considerations: Learn the hip hinge pattern with a Romanian deadlift before attempting swings under load
Ensure adequate ceiling height (minimum 3 m) for overhead swings
Do not swing near other people — a released bell is a serious hazard
execution.range_of_motion_guidance: Full hip hinge at the bottom (hamstrings loaded) to full hip extension at the top (glutes fully contracted, body upright).
execution.tempo_recommendations: Ballistic — the swing is not tempo-controlled but should be fluid and controlled, not frantic
coaching_cues: Hike it back like a football hike
Hips, not arms — the bell floats because of your hip drive
Stand tall at the top — plank position, not arched

name: Kettlebell Windmill
description: A windmill performed with a kettlebell overhead, identical in pattern to the dumbbell version but using the kettlebell's unique center of gravity that demands greater shoulder stability. The offset weight of the kettlebell adds rotational challenge to the overhead arm.

execution.starting_position: Set up for Kettlebell Windmill in proper position.
execution.setup_instructions: Prepare body and equipment for Kettlebell Windmill.
steps: Step 1: Clean and press kettlebell overhead in one hand, feet wide.
Step 2: Turn lower foot 45 degrees outward. Begin lateral hip shift.
Step 3: Hinge torso sideways, lowering free hand down the inside of the thigh.
Step 4: Return to upright by reversing the hinge.
execution.breathing_instructions: Breathe steadily; never hold breath during static holds.
common_mistakes: Letting overhead elbow bend
Looking down instead of at kettlebell
safety_considerations: Build prerequisite strength before attempting advanced variations.
Stop if joint pain occurs.
execution.range_of_motion_guidance: Full range of motion with control at all times.
coaching_cues: Keep eyes on the kettlebell
Full hip shift before beginning the hinge

name: Kipping Muscle-Up
description: The kipping muscle-up uses a hip-generated swing to create upward momentum that assists the transition from hanging to support position above the bar. Commonly used in functional fitness competitions, it places high demand on the shoulder complex and core during the aggressive hip-kick phase and requires exceptional timing to coordinate the kip with the pulling transition.

execution.starting_position: Hang from the pull-up bar with a shoulder-width overhand grip. Begin a controlled kipping swing — arch and hollow alternately.
execution.setup_instructions: Master the kipping pull-up and the strict muscle-up independently before combining them. Use chalk for grip security.
steps: Step 1: Establish a controlled kipping swing by alternating between hollow and arch positions.
Step 2: At the peak of the front swing (hollow position), aggressively drive the hips upward.
Step 3: Simultaneously pull the bar down to hip level, riding the momentum upward.
Step 4: As the hips rise above bar level, transition by pressing the bar down and leaning forward.
Step 5: Lock out the elbows at the top of the dip position.
Step 6: Lower under control or redrop into the swing for the next repetition.
execution.breathing_instructions: Breathe rhythmically with the kipping swing cycle; hold breath through the transition.
common_mistakes: Initiating the pull before the hip kick is at peak — timing is critical
Insufficient hip drive producing insufficient upward momentum
Missing the false grip, making the transition impossible
safety_considerations: High shoulder shear forces during the kip — not suitable for shoulder injuries
Prerequisite: proficiency in strict pull-ups and dips is essential
execution.range_of_motion_guidance: Full dead hang through to lockout in dip support position.
execution.tempo_recommendations: Explosive and rhythmic; rep speed driven by kipping timing
coaching_cues: Hips drive up first, then the arms pull
Think 'jump the bar' with your hips
Link the kip to the pull — do not pause between them

name: Ab Wheel Rollout — Kneeling
description: The kneeling ab wheel rollout is a highly effective anti-extension core exercise in which the athlete rolls a wheel forward from a kneeling position while resisting lumbar hyperextension through maximal core bracing. The movement recruits the transverse abdominis, rectus abdominis, and latissimus dorsi isometrically and eccentrically in a coordinated chain, training the core's ability to resist spinal extension forces — a fundamental quality for athletic performance and injury prevention.

execution.starting_position: Kneel on the floor with knees hip-width apart. Grip the ab wheel handles and position the wheel directly under the shoulders.
execution.setup_instructions: Place a mat under the knees for comfort. Keep the hips at roughly a 90° angle to start.
steps: Step 1: Brace the core fully. Begin rolling the wheel forward slowly.
Step 2: Extend the arms overhead as the torso lowers toward the floor, maintaining a straight line from knees through hips to shoulders.
Step 3: Roll out as far as can be controlled without the lower back arching.
Step 4: Pull the wheel back toward the knees using the lats and abs simultaneously.
Step 5: Return to the starting position and repeat.
execution.breathing_instructions: Inhale and brace before rolling out. Exhale on the return.
