common_mistakes: Allowing the hips to drop and the lumbar spine to hyperextend during the rollout
Not engaging the lats on the pullback — leads to arm-only return
safety_considerations: Regress to a shorter range of motion if back pain occurs
execution.range_of_motion_guidance: Roll out until hips begin to drop — that is the individual limit. Build range gradually.
coaching_cues: Squeeze the abs like you're about to be punched
Pull the wheel back with your lats — elbows to hips

name: Kneeling Single-Arm Cable Chest Press
description: The Kneeling Single-Arm Cable Press is performed in a half-kneeling or tall-kneeling position, pressing one cable handle forward while the kneeling stance eliminates leg drive and demands significant hip flexor and core stability. The unilateral load creates anti-rotation demands on the torso, making this a functional press variation that builds pressing strength alongside core and hip stability.

execution.starting_position: Set a cable pulley to chest height. Kneel facing away from the machine (tall kneeling) or in a half-kneeling stance (one knee down, one foot forward). Hold one handle at chest level on the same side as the working arm.
execution.setup_instructions: Set cable to mid-chest height. Kneel on a mat for comfort. In a half-kneeling stance, the kneeling leg is on the same side as the cable for optimal stability.
steps: Step 1: Hold the cable handle at chest level, brace the core.
Step 2: Press forward until the arm is fully extended.
Step 3: Return under control to the starting position.
Step 4: Complete all reps on one side, then switch.
execution.breathing_instructions: Exhale on the press. Inhale on return.
common_mistakes: Rotating the torso toward the pressing arm
Leaning excessively forward or backward during the press
safety_considerations: Kneel on a padded mat
Start light until the stabilization pattern is established
execution.range_of_motion_guidance: Full arm extension; return to chest-level start.
coaching_cues: Hips stay neutral — don't let them shift
Squeeze the chest and think about pressing through the target, not just extending the arm

name: Kneeling Cable Crunch with Twist
description: A kneeling cable crunch that adds a rotational element at the bottom of each rep. The twist targets the obliques in addition to the rectus abdominis, making this a comprehensive anterior core exercise. Using a rope attachment facilitates the twisting motion.

execution.starting_position: Set up for Kneeling Cable Crunch with Twist in proper position.
execution.setup_instructions: Prepare body and equipment for Kneeling Cable Crunch with Twist.
steps: Step 1: Kneel facing cable machine, rope held behind head.
Step 2: Crunch down and simultaneously rotate one elbow toward opposite knee.
Step 3: Return to upright position with spinal extension.
Step 4: Alternate sides on each rep.
execution.breathing_instructions: Breathe steadily; never hold breath during static holds.
common_mistakes: Pulling with arms instead of crunching core
Insufficient rotation
safety_considerations: Build prerequisite strength before attempting advanced variations.
Stop if joint pain occurs.
execution.range_of_motion_guidance: Full range of motion with control at all times.
coaching_cues: Drive elbow to opposite knee
Exhale hard on the crunch

name: Kneeling Cable Lat Pulldown
description: The kneeling lat pulldown is performed with the lifter kneeling on the floor in front of a high-pulley cable rather than seated in a machine. The kneeling position eliminates the ability to use the thigh pad for stabilization and increases core anti-extension demand. It trains the lat through a fuller overhead range of motion and allows the torso to shift freely, making it a useful variation for developing overhead pulling strength.

execution.starting_position: Attach a straight bar or rope to a high-pulley cable. Kneel on both knees directly below or slightly in front of the cable stack, hips over knees.
execution.setup_instructions: Position the knees hip-width apart. Set an appropriate weight for the kneeling position, which will typically be lighter than a seated pulldown.
steps: Step 1: Kneel facing the cable stack with arms extended overhead gripping the attachment.
Step 2: Brace the core and maintain a neutral spine throughout.
Step 3: Initiate by depressing the scapulae and pulling the elbows down toward the floor.
Step 4: Pull until the bar or hands reach chin or upper chest level.
Step 5: Return under control to full overhead extension without losing spinal alignment.
execution.breathing_instructions: Exhale as you pull down, inhale as you return to the overhead position.
common_mistakes: Allowing the lower back to hyperextend as the cable pulls the torso forward
Using momentum by rocking the hips
Not fully extending the arms at the top
safety_considerations: Keep the core braced throughout to protect the lumbar spine under the overhead cable pull
Use a lighter weight than your seated pulldown to account for reduced stability
execution.range_of_motion_guidance: Arms fully extended overhead at the start, pulled to upper chest or chin level at the bottom.
coaching_cues: Don't let the cable pull you forward
Elbows to the floor
Squeeze the lats hard at the bottom

name: Kneeling Leg Curl
description: The kneeling leg curl is performed with the feet anchored and the knees on a padded surface, using the hamstrings to curl the body toward the heels from a kneeling position with the torso upright. Unlike the Nordic hamstring curl which is a full eccentric movement, the kneeling leg curl is a concentric-focused variation that develops hamstring strength closer to the shortened position and serves as a bridge exercise between machine curls and the Nordic curl.

execution.starting_position: Kneel on a padded surface with the feet anchored behind (use a partner, barbell, or machine). Start with the torso vertical over the knees.
execution.setup_instructions: Have a partner hold the ankles or wedge the heels under a barbell secured at floor height. Knee padding is essential.
steps: Step 1: Kneel upright with feet anchored and hips extended.
Step 2: Lower the torso forward a small amount, then use the hamstrings to pull the body back upright — the motion is a 'pull toward the heels' action.
Step 3: Hold the upright position briefly, then lower forward under control.
Step 4: Repeat for the prescribed reps, controlling both phases.
Step 5: Avoid falling too far forward — this transitions into a Nordic curl and should be progressed to separately.
execution.breathing_instructions: Exhale as you pull up. Inhale as you lower.
common_mistakes: Hinging at the hip (the motion should come from knee flexion, not hip hinging)
Swinging the torso rather than contracting the hamstrings
Moving through a range the hamstrings cannot control
safety_considerations: If unable to perform even a minimal controlled range, begin with machine leg curls to build hamstring strength first
Knee padding is essential to prevent bruising
execution.range_of_motion_guidance: Work in the range the hamstrings can actively control — typically 20–60° initially.
coaching_cues: Pull your heels toward your glutes — think of it like a standing leg curl
Keep the hips extended — don't fold forward at the hip
Own both directions — control the lowering too

name: Kneeling Single-Arm Lat Pulldown
description: The kneeling single-arm lat pulldown removes leg drive and hip momentum by placing the lifter in a tall kneeling position, while the unilateral arm action allows independent lat development. The kneeling position also engages the core and hip flexors for stability, and the single-arm pull allows the working-side shoulder to fully protract and retract throughout the range of motion.

execution.starting_position: Kneel upright facing a cable machine. Attach a single handle at the highest position. Grip with one hand, arm extended overhead.
execution.setup_instructions: Kneel on a mat or pad for comfort. Place the kneeling position far enough from the cable to allow full arm extension overhead.
steps: Step 1: Kneel tall — hips extended, torso upright.
Step 2: Reach the working arm fully overhead.
Step 3: Pull the handle down and toward the working-side hip by driving the elbow down.
Step 4: At peak, hold 1 second.
Step 5: Return to full overhead extension. Complete all reps then switch sides.
execution.breathing_instructions: Exhale on the pull. Inhale returning to full extension.
common_mistakes: Hips flexing (sitting back) during the pull — maintain upright kneeling
Leaning back to assist — stay tall and let the lat do the work
safety_considerations: Kneel on a padded surface to protect the knees
Do not load beyond what allows perfect upright posture
execution.range_of_motion_guidance: Full overhead extension to elbow at or below shoulder level.
coaching_cues: Hips tall — do not sit back
Drive the elbow to the hip
Full reach at the top of every rep

name: Korean Dips / Behind-the-Back Dips
description: Korean dips are a highly specialized calisthenics exercise in which the hands grip a bar behind the body with the palms facing backward, and the lifter dips downward in front of the bar. This unusual positioning places tremendous stretch on the chest and anterior shoulder, requires significant shoulder flexibility, and targets the lower pectoral fibers in a range of motion not achievable in standard dips.

execution.starting_position: Sit on a low parallel bar or sturdy surface, gripping the bar behind the hips with palms facing back and fingers pointing away. Slide the hips off the bar in front, body hanging in front of the bar.
execution.setup_instructions: This exercise requires significant shoulder extension and external rotation flexibility. Begin by practicing shoulder bridge stretches and passive hangs before attempting Korean dips.
steps: Step 1: Grip the bar behind the hips with palms facing backward, fingers forward.
Step 2: Extend the arms to lift the hips and hang the body in front of the bar.
Step 3: Slowly lower the body downward by bending the elbows, feeling the chest and shoulder stretch.
Step 4: Lower as far as shoulder flexibility comfortably allows.
Step 5: Press back up by extending the arms, returning to the starting position.
execution.breathing_instructions: Inhale as you lower. Exhale as you press back up.
common_mistakes: Attempting this exercise without adequate shoulder flexibility
Lowering past the point of safe shoulder range of motion
Gripping too wide, increasing shoulder impingement risk
safety_considerations: This exercise is contraindicated with shoulder impingement or anterior instability
Build shoulder extension flexibility over weeks before attempting
Start with a very limited range of motion and progress slowly
Have a spotter on standby in case of shoulder cramping
execution.range_of_motion_guidance: Lower only as far as shoulder flexibility allows without pain. Even a small range of motion provides training stimulus for this unique position.
coaching_cues: Warm up the shoulders extensively before this
Feel the chest open as you lower
Respect your flexibility — this is a long-term progression

name: Kroc Row
description: The Kroc Row is a heavy, high-repetition unilateral dumbbell row popularized by powerlifter Janae Marie Kroc. Unlike a strict dumbbell row, controlled body rotation is intentionally used on the concentric phase to allow heavier loading and more complete lat contraction, while the eccentric remains deliberate. The result is a unique combination of raw back strength and muscular endurance that bridges bodybuilding and strength sport.

execution.starting_position: Support one hand on a bench or rack. Hold a heavy dumbbell in the other hand, arm extended toward the floor. Stagger the feet for a stable base.
execution.setup_instructions: Select a heavier dumbbell than you would use for a strict row — the controlled cheat on the concentric allows for greater load. Use lifting straps to remove grip as the limiting factor.
steps: Step 1: Begin with the dumbbell hanging at arm's length, non-working hand on support.
Step 2: Initiate a controlled pull by driving the elbow upward and back.
Step 3: Allow the torso to rotate slightly toward the working side to maximize lat contraction at the top.
Step 4: At peak contraction, the elbow is well above the torso and the lat is fully shortened.
Step 5: Lower the dumbbell under strict control — the eccentric should be deliberate and slow.
execution.breathing_instructions: Exhale forcefully on the row, inhale on the descent.
common_mistakes: Using so much body swing that the row becomes a deadlift rather than a back exercise
Rushing the eccentric — the slow descent is critical to the exercise's effectiveness
Not using straps, allowing grip to limit the target muscle's training
safety_considerations: The controlled cheat on the concentric is intentional, but should not degrade into uncontrolled momentum
High rep sets with heavy weight create significant fatigue — use a spotter or rack for safety
execution.range_of_motion_guidance: Full arm extension at the bottom, elbow driven well above the torso at the top.
coaching_cues: Use the torso rotation to your advantage
Slow it down on the way down
Straps on — grip is not the target here

name: Kroc Row with Strict Pause
description: The Kroc row with pause applies the heavy-load, high-rep philosophy of the original Kroc row but adds a 1-2 second isometric hold at peak contraction. The pause prevents the ballistic bounce common in standard Kroc rows and ensures each rep has genuine muscular engagement, combining the high metabolic demand of Kroc rows with the quality control of paused training.

execution.starting_position: One knee and hand braced on a bench. Heavy dumbbell in working hand, arm extended.
execution.setup_instructions: Use a heavy dumbbell — Kroc rows are characterized by maximal loaded sets. The pause reduces the number of reps achievable vs. standard Kroc rows.
steps: Step 1: Row the heavy dumbbell explosively to the hip.
Step 2: At the top, hold for 1-2 seconds with elbow as high as possible.
Step 3: Lower under control — do not simply drop the weight.
Step 4: Repeat for maximum quality reps.
Step 5: Perform one set per side to near failure.
execution.breathing_instructions: Breathe continuously with the rhythm of the reps.
common_mistakes: Turning the pause into a pendulum swing — the weight must pause, not just slow
Using a weight so heavy that the torso rotates dramatically
safety_considerations: Straps are acceptable for Kroc rows as grip is not the training target
High-rep heavy sets tax the lower back — maintain braced core throughout
execution.range_of_motion_guidance: Full arm extension to elbow above torso.
coaching_cues: Full pause at the top — count it
Row to the hip, not the chest
Think about accumulating quality reps, not just quantity

name: L-Sit
description: The L-sit is an advanced calisthenics isometric hold performed on dip bars, parallel bars, or the floor, in which the athlete supports their entire body on straight arms while holding the legs parallel to the floor, forming an L-shape with the body. It simultaneously demands significant triceps and shoulder pressing strength to depress the scapulae and hold the torso up, while the hip flexors and rectus abdominis maintain the legs in the horizontal position. It is a core gymnastics skill and a prerequisite for more advanced bar movements.

execution.starting_position: Stand between dip bars with hands gripping each bar. Arms are fully extended and the body hangs with feet off the floor.
execution.setup_instructions: Set dip bars at a width that allows comfortable hand placement. Alternatively perform on the floor between two yoga blocks or plates.
steps: Step 1: Grip the dip bars with straight arms and depress the scapulae (push shoulders down away from ears).
Step 2: Raise both legs simultaneously until they are parallel to the floor, keeping them straight and together.
Step 3: Maintain fully extended elbows and a tall torso throughout the hold.
Step 4: Point the toes and squeeze the thighs together.
Step 5: Hold for the prescribed duration, then lower the legs with control.
execution.breathing_instructions: Breathe shallowly during the hold. Avoid deep breaths that break core tension.
common_mistakes: Bending the elbows instead of pressing down into straight arms
Allowing the shoulders to shrug upward instead of actively depressing the scapulae
Bending the knees when hip flexor strength is insufficient
Letting the legs drop below parallel
safety_considerations: Build prerequisite triceps pressing strength (dips) and hip flexor strength (hanging knee raises) before attempting the full L-sit.
Wrist discomfort is common on the floor variation — use parallel bars or push-up handles to reduce wrist extension.
execution.range_of_motion_guidance: Legs must be fully extended and held parallel to the ground. The torso must remain upright throughout.
execution.tempo_recommendations: Hold for 5–30 seconds. Accumulate total time over multiple sets. Progress from tuck L-sit → one leg extended → full L-sit.
coaching_cues: Push the floor or bars away from you
Depress the scapulae — shoulders down, not shrugged
Legs are a shelf — keep them flat

name: L-Sit Press-Up on Parallel Bars
description: An L-sit performed on parallel bars where the athlete attempts to press the body upward into a handstand from the L-sit position. This requires extraordinary compression, shoulder pressing strength, and body control. This is a competition gymnastics transition skill.

execution.starting_position: Set up for L-Sit Press-Up on Parallel Bars in proper position.
execution.setup_instructions: Prepare body and equipment for L-Sit Press-Up on Parallel Bars.
steps: Step 1: Establish L-sit on parallel bars with legs horizontal.
Step 2: Compress hips to bring legs toward chest while pressing bars down.
Step 3: Continue pressing until body passes through straddle or tuck position.
Step 4: Extend to handstand at top of press.
execution.breathing_instructions: Breathe steadily; never hold breath during static holds.
common_mistakes: Insufficient L-sit strength before attempting
Losing bar position
safety_considerations: Build prerequisite strength before attempting advanced variations.
Stop if joint pain occurs.
execution.range_of_motion_guidance: Full range of motion with control at all times.
coaching_cues: Full L-sit mastery required
Compress before pressing

name: L-Sit Progression
description: A calisthenics isometric hold where the body is supported on the hands with the legs extended horizontally, forming an L-shape. The L-sit builds extraordinary hip flexor and core strength, tricep pushing endurance, and shoulder girdle stability simultaneously. Progressions range from tuck holds through full L-sit.

execution.starting_position: Support your body weight on two parallel bars or the floor with arms fully extended beneath you. Legs are extended forward parallel to the floor.
execution.setup_instructions: Use parallettes, the floor, or gymnastics rings. Ensure the support surface is at a height allowing the legs to extend without touching the floor.
steps: Step 1 (Tuck): Support the body on hands with knees pulled to chest. Hold for time.
Step 2 (Single-leg): Extend one leg while tucking the other. Alternate.
Step 3 (Full L-sit): Extend both legs forward parallel to the floor. Hold for maximum time.
Step 4: Lower controlled and rest before the next set.
execution.breathing_instructions: Breathe steadily throughout the hold. Do not hold your breath.
common_mistakes: Allowing the hips to drop below the support — the hips must be at or above handle height
Bending the elbows
safety_considerations: Build wrist and elbow strength before attempting this exercise
Progress through the tuck stages before the full version
execution.range_of_motion_guidance: Legs parallel to the floor. Arms fully extended. Body in an L-shape.
execution.tempo_recommendations: Isometric hold — build to 3 sets of 10-30 seconds
coaching_cues: Push the floor away
Point the toes and squeeze the quads

name: Landmine 180 — Rainbow
description: The landmine 180 (also called the landmine rainbow) is a rotational power exercise in which the barbell end is swung in a large arc from one side of the body to the other, following the path of a rainbow. The movement loads the core in rotation, the shoulders in overhead pressing, and the hips in rotational bracing simultaneously. The continuous arc demands coordinated full-body rotation and is used in rotational power training, sports performance programs, and functional core conditioning.

execution.starting_position: Load a barbell in a landmine anchor (or wedge the bar in a corner). Stand facing the barbell end, feet shoulder-width apart. Grasp the barbell end with both hands (overlapping or interlaced) and hold at approximately chest height.
execution.setup_instructions: Begin with a very light load — the arc is long and the shoulder demand is significant. The landmine anchor must be secure.
steps: Step 1: Begin with the barbell end at the right hip, arms extended to the right side.
Step 2: Swing the barbell end upward and across the body in a smooth arc, rotating the torso to the left.
Step 3: Continue the arc overhead to the left side, controlling the descent as it sweeps down to the left hip.
Step 4: Reverse the arc direction, sweeping the barbell from the left hip upward and over to the right hip. Each full left-to-right-to-left arc equals one repetition.
execution.breathing_instructions: Exhale forcefully as the bar sweeps overhead. Inhale as it descends to the hip.
common_mistakes: Using too much weight — the arc demands shoulder mobility more than strength
Bending the elbows instead of using the full arm extension throughout the arc
Stopping at the top rather than flowing continuously through the arc
safety_considerations: The overhead arc demands full shoulder mobility — do not force range that is not available
Ensure the landmine anchor is completely secure before each set
execution.range_of_motion_guidance: The arc should travel from one hip, overhead, to the opposite hip. Full range is the goal.
execution.tempo_recommendations: Moderate speed — fluid and controlled, not explosive initially. Build speed as technique improves.
coaching_cues: Think of drawing the arc of a rainbow — smooth, continuous, side to side
Keep the arms extended throughout — do not collapse the elbows
Let the torso rotate naturally — do not resist the rotation

name: Landmine Single-Arm Chest Press
description: The landmine single-arm chest press uses one end of a barbell anchored to the floor to create an arcing pressing motion that is gentler on the shoulder joint than a traditional horizontal press. The angled load path recruits the upper and mid pectorals while also engaging the core and serratus anterior for stability.

execution.starting_position: Anchor one end of a barbell in a landmine attachment or a corner. Stand facing the barbell, holding the free end at shoulder height with one hand, feet shoulder-width apart.
execution.setup_instructions: Secure the barbell in the landmine sleeve. Load weight onto the free end only. Grip the end of the bar and position it at chest height with the elbow pointing down and back.
steps: Step 1: Hold the barbell end at upper chest height, elbow below the bar.
Step 2: Brace the core and press the bar forward and slightly upward, extending the arm fully.
Step 3: Hold briefly at the top, then bend the elbow and return the bar in a controlled arc back to the start.
Step 4: Keep the torso stable and avoid rotating to assist the press.
Step 5: Complete all reps on one side before switching.
execution.breathing_instructions: Exhale as you press the barbell forward. Inhale as you lower it back toward the chest.
common_mistakes: Rotating the torso aggressively to get the bar up
Gripping the bar too far from the end, reducing leverage
Letting the elbow flare excessively to the side
safety_considerations: Ensure the barbell anchor is secure before pressing
Start with no added weight to learn the arc of motion
Keep the wrist neutral throughout the press
execution.range_of_motion_guidance: Press until the arm is fully extended and the bar is at face height or above. Return until the hand is at chest level.
coaching_cues: Push the bar in an arc, not straight out
Brace like you're taking a punch
Feel the upper chest engage on each press

name: Dual Landmine Lateral Raise
description: The dual landmine lateral raise uses two landmine setups simultaneously, one on each side, raising both arms laterally at the same time. The bilateral version applies the constant-arc loading of the landmine to both sides simultaneously, training medial deltoids with strict form and removing the possibility of compensating with one side. It is typically performed in front-facing configuration with the bars angled outward.

execution.starting_position: Set up two landmine units with bars angled outward from the floor. Stand between them and hold each bar end in the corresponding hand, arms at sides.
execution.setup_instructions: Ensure both landmine setups are at equal heights and their loaded ends are at the same level. Light loading on each bar.
steps: Step 1: Begin with both arms at sides, bar ends at hip level.
Step 2: Raise both arms simultaneously outward and upward to shoulder height.
Step 3: Hold 1 second at peak.
Step 4: Lower both arms simultaneously under control.
Step 5: Repeat for desired reps.
execution.breathing_instructions: Exhale raising. Inhale lowering.
common_mistakes: One bar going higher than the other — control the symmetry
Shrugging to compensate for heavy load — use lighter bars
safety_considerations: Requires access to two landmine units — plan setup before beginning
Light load on each bar
execution.range_of_motion_guidance: Arms at sides to shoulder height on both sides simultaneously.
coaching_cues: Both arms move in sync
Lead with the elbows — slight bend
Lower slowly — 3 full seconds

name: Landmine Lateral Raise with Pause
description: The landmine lateral raise with pause uses the fixed arc of a landmine barbell to perform a lateral raise with a 2-3 second isometric hold at peak abduction. The pause maximizes time under tension for the medial deltoid at its contracted position and prevents the momentum that often occurs in standard lateral raises, ensuring each repetition delivers genuine deltoid loading through the full range.

execution.starting_position: Stand beside a landmine setup. Hold the bar end with the near hand. Begin with arm at the side, bar end hanging near the hip.
execution.setup_instructions: Position the body so the bar traces a smooth lateral arc when raised. Light load — the fixed arc limits load compared to free-weight lateral raises.
steps: Step 1: Begin with arm at side holding the bar end.
Step 2: Raise the arm laterally to shoulder height, following the arc of the bar.
Step 3: At shoulder height, hold for 2-3 seconds.
Step 4: Lower under full control back to starting position.
Step 5: Complete all reps then switch sides.
execution.breathing_instructions: Exhale raising. Hold breath lightly during pause. Exhale lowering.
common_mistakes: Not actually holding at the top — 2-3 full seconds of contraction
Shrugging the traps to assist the raise
safety_considerations: Very light loads — the pause amplifies the stimulus
Avoid if shoulder impingement is present
execution.range_of_motion_guidance: Arm at side to shoulder height with pause.
coaching_cues: Full pause at the top — count three seconds
No shrug — lead with the elbow
Lower slowly for maximum eccentric benefit

name: Landmine Meadows Rear Delt Flye
description: The landmine Meadows rear delt flye uses the bar end of a landmine setup and a staggered stance to perform a rear delt fly with a fixed arc of motion determined by the pivot of the barbell. Unlike dumbbell reverse flyes, the landmine provides a constant and smoothly changing resistance curve, and the bar's weight progression is more granular, making it excellent for systematically building rear deltoid strength.

execution.starting_position: Secure a barbell in a landmine unit. Stand perpendicular to the bar in a staggered stance, hinge forward at the hips. Grasp the bar end with one hand, arm hanging below the shoulder.
execution.setup_instructions: Hinge to approximately 45-70 degrees forward so the bar end hangs naturally. Use lighter loading than a Meadows row — rear delts are smaller than lats.
steps: Step 1: Begin hinged with bar end hanging in the working hand.
Step 2: Raise the working arm out to the side in a lateral arc, keeping the elbow slightly bent.
Step 3: Continue raising until the arm is at shoulder height.
Step 4: Hold 1 second.
Step 5: Lower under control back to the hanging position.
execution.breathing_instructions: Exhale raising. Inhale lowering.
common_mistakes: Bending the elbow too much — this becomes a row, not a fly
Excessive torso rotation to assist the raise
safety_considerations: Light loads — rear delt is a small muscle group
Maintain stable hinge position throughout
execution.range_of_motion_guidance: Arm hanging to shoulder height lateral position.
coaching_cues: Lead with the elbow — slight bend throughout
Think of pulling the arm upward like opening a wing
Feel the back of the shoulder contract at the top

name: Landmine Meadows Row with Pause
description: The paused Meadows row adds a 2-3 second contraction hold at the peak of each repetition, maximizing lat and teres major activation at their shortest position. The pause eliminates the momentum that can occur in standard Meadows rows while training the ability to generate force from an already-contracted position — a quality associated with improved mind-muscle connection.

execution.starting_position: Barbell end secured in a landmine unit or corner. Staggered stance perpendicular to the bar. Hinge at the hips, grasp the bar end with one hand.
execution.setup_instructions: Reduce load by 20-30% compared to standard Meadows rows to accommodate the pause.
steps: Step 1: Row the bar end explosively to the hip.
Step 2: At the peak position, hold for 2-3 seconds with elbow above torso.
Step 3: During the hold, actively squeeze the lat — think 'armpit to hip'.
Step 4: Lower slowly under full control.
Step 5: Allow full lat stretch at the bottom before initiating the next rep.
execution.breathing_instructions: Exhale on the row. Hold breath lightly during the pause. Exhale through the descent.
common_mistakes: Letting the elbow drop during the pause — maintain height
Using the same load as standard Meadows rows — reduce weight for the pause variation
safety_considerations: Secure the barbell end before loading
Maintain braced core during the full range
execution.range_of_motion_guidance: Full arm extension to elbow above torso with 2-3s hold.
coaching_cues: Squeeze the armpit at the top
Elbow stays high during the entire pause
Full stretch at the bottom before each rep

name: Landmine Press
description: The landmine press is a shoulder pressing exercise where one end of a barbell is anchored to the floor (in a landmine attachment or corner) while the other end is pressed overhead in a natural arc. The angled pressing path is shoulder-friendly compared to vertical overhead pressing, making it an excellent option for lifters with shoulder impingement or limited shoulder mobility while still providing significant anterior deltoid and triceps stimulus.

execution.starting_position: Anchor one end of a barbell in a landmine attachment or wedge it in a corner. Kneel or stand facing the barbell's loaded end, holding it at shoulder height with one hand (or both hands clasped together).
execution.setup_instructions: Insert one end of a barbell into a landmine base or secure it in a corner on a mat. Load the opposite end with appropriate weight. Kneel or stand facing the loaded end.
steps: Step 1: Hold the end of the barbell at shoulder height with the hand of the pressing side. Stagger your stance or kneel for stability.
Step 2: Brace the core firmly. The barbell will arc forward and upward on a fixed path.
Step 3: Exhale and press the barbell end upward and forward in its natural arc until the arm is fully extended.
Step 4: Inhale and lower back down along the same arc to shoulder height. Complete reps, then switch sides.
execution.breathing_instructions: Exhale on the press; inhale on the descent.
common_mistakes: Letting the torso rotate as you press — brace to resist rotation
Pressing straight up rather than allowing the barbell to follow its natural arc
safety_considerations: The angled path is naturally shoulder-friendly, but stop if pain is felt at any point
execution.range_of_motion_guidance: Press to full arm extension along the arc; return to shoulder height.
coaching_cues: Let the bar's natural arc guide your press — don't fight it
Squeeze your core like a vise throughout the movement

name: Landmine Rainbow
description: A landmine exercise where the barbell is swept in a wide arc from one side of the body to the other, tracing a rainbow shape overhead. The anti-rotation demand is significant as the core resists the shifting weight through the arc. This builds rotational stability and power.

execution.starting_position: Set up for Landmine Rainbow in proper position.
execution.setup_instructions: Prepare body and equipment for Landmine Rainbow.
steps: Step 1: Stand with landmine bar held at chest height with both hands.
Step 2: Sweep bar in a large arc from one hip up and over to the other hip.
Step 3: Keep arms relatively straight and move from the core.
Step 4: Reverse the arc to return to starting side.
execution.breathing_instructions: Breathe steadily; never hold breath during static holds.
common_mistakes: Using mostly arms instead of core
Excessive spine bend
safety_considerations: Build prerequisite strength before attempting advanced variations.
Stop if joint pain occurs.
execution.range_of_motion_guidance: Full range of motion with control at all times.
coaching_cues: Drive the arc from hips and core rotation
Smooth continuous arc

name: Landmine Rotational Torso Twist
description: The landmine rotational torso twist uses a barbell anchored in a landmine attachment to train transverse-plane rotation against a fixed arc of resistance, loading the obliques and hip rotators in a standing, sport-specific movement pattern. The arc of the barbell naturally guides the movement through a smooth path that is joint-friendly for the shoulder and spine compared to free-weight rotational exercises. The fixed end-range of the landmine also provides a natural loading curve that increases resistance toward the end of the range.

execution.starting_position: Stand facing the barbell end, feet shoulder-width apart. Cup the end of the barbell with both hands, interlaced, at chest height. Barbell is centered in front of the body.
execution.setup_instructions: Insert one end of the barbell into a landmine attachment or corner of a wall/rack with padding. Load the free end appropriately.
steps: Step 1: Begin with the barbell end at chest center, arms slightly bent.
Step 2: Rotate the trunk and swing the barbell end to one side, keeping the arms relatively straight and pivoting the trailing foot.
Step 3: Allow the barbell to arc to roughly hip height on one side.
Step 4: Return through center and continue to the opposite side in a continuous pendulum motion.
Step 5: Drive the rotation from the hips and trunk — not the arms.
execution.breathing_instructions: Exhale forcefully at each end of the rotation. Inhale at center.
common_mistakes: Using too much arm movement — this is a trunk rotation exercise
Using such heavy load that rotation range is restricted — keep load moderate
safety_considerations: Pivot the rear foot to protect the knee during rotation
execution.range_of_motion_guidance: Full comfortable rotation arc from side to side, maintaining spine length.
coaching_cues: Rotate from the hips, not the arms
Keep the spine tall throughout the arc

name: Landmine Squat
description: The landmine squat is performed by holding the loaded end of a barbell anchored at floor level in a landmine attachment or corner, with the hands clasped at chest height. The angled path of the bar supports a naturally upright squat posture and reduces the need for significant ankle dorsiflexion or shoulder mobility. It is accessible to beginners and is an effective teaching tool for the squat pattern.

execution.starting_position: Anchor one end of a barbell in a corner or landmine attachment. Load the free end with appropriate weight. Hold the free end with both hands clasped together at chest height. Stand with feet shoulder-width apart.
execution.setup_instructions: Place the barbell end in the corner where two walls meet (pad the wall), or use a dedicated landmine attachment. Load weight on the free end. Stand close to the loaded end so the bar is at a moderate angle.
steps: Step 1: Hold the loaded barbell end at chest height with both hands clasped. Stand tall, feet shoulder-width, toes slightly out.
Step 2: Brace your core and initiate the squat by pushing the knees out and sitting the hips down.
Step 3: Descend to at least parallel. The bar will follow the arc naturally — allow this guided path to assist your positioning.
Step 4: Drive through the full foot to return to standing, pressing the bar slightly forward and up along its arc.
Step 5: Exhale at the top.
execution.breathing_instructions: Inhale and brace before descent. Exhale at the top.
common_mistakes: Standing too far from the anchor, creating an excessive bar angle
Not descending to full depth, using the bar as a crutch
Allowing the knees to cave inward
safety_considerations: Ensure the anchor point is secure before loading
Keep hands firmly clasped — do not let the bar slip
execution.range_of_motion_guidance: Aim for parallel. The bar's angle assists depth, making this accessible for those with limited mobility.
coaching_cues: Let the bar guide you — follow its arc
Knees track over toes
Hips and knees extend together on the way up

name: Larsen Press
description: The Larsen Press is a bench press variation performed with the legs extended straight or the feet elevated off the floor, eliminating leg drive from the movement. This strict technique removes the lower body contribution and places the entire pressing demand on the pectorals, anterior deltoids, and triceps, while also increasing core stabilization requirements.

execution.starting_position: Lie on a flat bench under a racked barbell. Grip slightly wider than shoulder-width. Extend the legs straight with heels on the bench edge or raise the feet entirely.
execution.setup_instructions: Set the bench in a power rack. Remove leg drive from the equation by straightening the legs before unracking the bar. Keep the lower back in contact with the bench pad.
steps: Step 1: Unrack the bar and hold it above the chest with arms extended.
Step 2: Lower the bar under control to touch the lower chest, with legs remaining straight throughout.
Step 3: Press the bar back to the starting position through the chest and triceps.
Step 4: Maintain tension in the core throughout to stabilize the torso without leg assistance.
execution.breathing_instructions: Inhale and brace the core before lowering. Exhale at the top of the press.
common_mistakes: Planting the feet mid-set to gain leg drive
Allowing the lower back to arch excessively off the bench
Using the same load as a standard bench press — reduce weight to account for absent leg drive
safety_considerations: Reduce load by 10-20% compared to your regular bench press
Use safety bars in a power rack as the reduced stability makes failing more likely
execution.range_of_motion_guidance: Full touch to the chest at the bottom; full elbow lockout at the top.
coaching_cues: Keep legs long and completely relaxed
Squeeze the bench with your upper back as you press
Breathe into the belly to brace the core without leg assistance

name: Lat Pulldown
description: The lat pulldown is a cable-based vertical pulling exercise that trains the latissimus dorsi and upper back. It is functionally similar to the pull-up but allows precise load adjustment, making it accessible to beginners and useful for high-repetition back training. It is one of the most effective machine-based exercises for developing back width.

execution.starting_position: Sit at the lat pulldown machine with thighs secured under the pads. Grip the bar slightly wider than shoulder width with a pronated grip. Arms extended above, slight backward lean from the hips.
execution.setup_instructions: Adjust the knee pad height to firmly secure the thighs. Select an appropriate weight. A slight rearward torso angle of 10–15 degrees is normal.
steps: Depress the shoulder blades and initiate the pull by driving the elbows down toward the floor.
Pull the bar to the upper chest, squeezing the lats hard at the bottom position.
Control the bar back to the starting position with fully extended arms.
execution.breathing_instructions: Exhale as you pull the bar down. Inhale as you return it.
common_mistakes: Pulling the bar behind the neck, which stresses the cervical spine
Leaning excessively backward, turning it into a rowing movement
Not achieving full arm extension at the top
safety_considerations: Always pull to the front of the body — never behind the neck
execution.range_of_motion_guidance: Full arm extension at the top, bar to upper chest at the bottom.
coaching_cues: Put your shoulder blades in your back pockets as you pull
Think about pulling your elbows to your hips

name: Alternating Lat Pulldown Behind Neck
description: The alternating behind-neck pulldown alternates each rep between pulling to the front (standard) and pulling behind the neck, targeting the lats and trapezius from slightly different angles within a single set. The behind-neck portion challenges the lower traps and upper rhomboids through a downward-angled scapular depression that the front pulldown angle does not fully replicate.

execution.starting_position: Seated at a lat pulldown station with a wide grip bar. Arms extended overhead gripping the bar.
execution.setup_instructions: Use lighter weight than usual — behind-neck pulldowns have a shorter range of motion and require careful neck positioning.
steps: Step 1: Pull rep 1 to the front of the chest (standard pulldown).
Step 2: Return to full extension.
Step 3: Pull rep 2 behind the neck — tilt the head forward slightly to avoid contact.
Step 4: Return to full extension.
Step 5: Alternate front and behind-neck for the duration of the set.
execution.breathing_instructions: Exhale on each pull. Inhale on each return.
common_mistakes: Not tilting the head forward for the behind-neck pull — risks cervical spine impingement
Using heavy weight for the behind-neck portion — this is a moderate-load variation
safety_considerations: The behind-neck pulldown is contraindicated for those with cervical spine issues
Always tilt the head forward — never pull the bar into the neck
execution.range_of_motion_guidance: Full arm extension to full lat contraction on each variation.
coaching_cues: Chin forward on behind-neck reps
Same lat drive regardless of direction
Control the bar path — do not let it pull back up

name: Lat Stretch
description: The lat stretch lengthens the latissimus dorsi by combining shoulder flexion with lateral trunk flexion, placing the broad back muscle on its full stretch. Because the lats originate from the lumbar spine and iliac crest and insert on the humerus, they are most effectively stretched when the arm is raised overhead and the torso bends away. This stretch directly counteracts the lat tightness that often develops from heavy pulling exercises.

execution.starting_position: Stand or kneel. For the kneeling version, place hands on a bench or high surface and sit back.
execution.setup_instructions: No equipment required for the standing version. For a supported version, use a doorway, rack upright, or sturdy surface to grip.
steps: Step 1: Raise one arm overhead and grip a fixed surface (doorway, rack post) or simply raise the arm.
Step 2: Allow the torso to bend away from the raised arm, creating a lateral lean.
Step 3: Breathe into the side of the ribcage on the raised-arm side — this increases the lat stretch.
Step 4: Hold 30–60 seconds until the stretch is felt running from the outer hip up to the armpit.
Step 5: Return to neutral and switch sides.
execution.breathing_instructions: Inhale into the side being stretched — this uses the ribcage expansion to increase tension on the lat.
common_mistakes: Not leaning laterally enough — many people only raise the arm without getting the lateral trunk component
Holding the breath rather than breathing into the stretch
Rotating the torso rather than pure lateral lean
safety_considerations: Avoid if there is shoulder impingement — the overhead position may aggravate it
Support the grip with a stable surface to avoid loading the spine under stretch
execution.range_of_motion_guidance: Lean until a clear stretch is felt running from the hip along the side of the torso to the armpit.
coaching_cues: Breathe into your armpit — expand that side of the ribcage
Think of making yourself as tall as possible on the stretched side
Let the hip slide away from the raised arm

name: Lateral Band Walks
description: Lateral band walks are performed with a resistance band placed above the knees or around the ankles while moving sideways in an athletic stance. This exercise directly targets the gluteus medius and hip abductors responsible for lateral pelvic control and knee tracking stability. It is a staple in lower limb rehabilitation and sports performance warm-ups to prevent injury and improve dynamic hip strength.

execution.starting_position: Place a resistance band just above the knees. Stand with feet shoulder-width apart and lower into a slight squat or athletic stance.
execution.setup_instructions: Choose a band resistance appropriate for the population — lighter for rehabilitation, heavier for performance warm-up.
steps: Step 1: Adopt an athletic stance with knees slightly bent and hips slightly hinged.
Step 2: Take a controlled lateral step with the lead foot, maintaining band tension.
Step 3: Bring the trail foot to restore hip-width stance — keep constant tension throughout.
Step 4: Complete prescribed steps in one direction, then repeat to the other side.
execution.breathing_instructions: Breathe naturally throughout the movement. Do not hold your breath.
common_mistakes: Allowing knees to cave inward (valgus) during lateral steps
Moving too fast and losing control of the step
Letting feet come fully together reducing band tension
safety_considerations: Ensure the band is seated comfortably above the knee — not on the kneecap
Consult a physiotherapist for use in formal rehabilitation programs
execution.range_of_motion_guidance: Steps should be moderate width — enough to maintain tension without causing the torso to tilt laterally.
coaching_cues: Maintain tension on the band throughout — never let it go slack
Keep knees tracking over middle toes
Drive the step from the hip, not the knee

name: Lateral Band Walks — Low Squat Position
description: A lateral band walk performed in a deep squat position (hips at or below knee level), which dramatically increases the gluteus maximus and quadriceps demand compared to the standard quarter-squat lateral walk. The low position also recruits the hip abductors through a longer arc of abduction. This advanced rehabilitation progression is used in late-stage ACL, hip, and knee programs when the patient has developed sufficient strength for high-load lateral movement patterns.

execution.starting_position: Place a mini band loop above the knees. Descend to a deep squat position with hips at or slightly below knee level, feet hip-width apart and toes slightly out.
execution.setup_instructions: Only use this variation once the standard lateral band walk is mastered. Clear a straight path of 10-15 meters for the walk.
steps: Step 1: Descend to a deep squat position with the band above the knees maintaining tension.
Step 2: Maintain the squat depth throughout — hips must not rise during the walk.
Step 3: Take controlled lateral steps in one direction for the prescribed number of steps.
Step 4: Reverse direction without rising. Continue for the full prescribed distance.
execution.breathing_instructions: Breathe continuously. The sustained squat is very demanding — rhythm breathing is essential.
common_mistakes: Rising out of the squat between steps — the hip must remain at the prescribed depth throughout
Taking too large steps that force knee valgus under band resistance
Letting the knees collapse inward — actively push the knees out against the band
safety_considerations: Ensure full ROM squat is pain-free and cleared before attempting loaded lateral movement at this depth
Reduce squat depth if knee pain is present — work at a pain-free depth
execution.range_of_motion_guidance: Hip at or below knee level maintained throughout. Step width keeps band taut without valgus collapse.
execution.tempo_recommendations: 1 step per 1.5-2 seconds. Controlled — no rushing.
coaching_cues: Push the knees out against the band — do not let them cave inward
Stay down — your hips should not rise between steps
Take medium steps — too wide creates valgus; too narrow loses the stimulus

name: Lateral Bound
description: The lateral bound is a unilateral plyometric exercise in which the athlete pushes off one leg to jump laterally, landing on the opposite leg and absorbing the force through a single-leg deceleration. It trains the lateral power production of the gluteus medius and abductors alongside the hip and knee stability required during single-leg landing, closely replicating the lateral change-of-direction mechanics common in court and field sports.

execution.starting_position: Stand on one leg with the opposite leg slightly raised. Slight forward lean at the hip.
execution.setup_instructions: Mark a starting point. Ensure a non-slip surface with adequate lateral space.
steps: Step 1: Balance on one leg with a slight hip hinge.
Step 2: Drive off the supporting leg laterally, extending the hip and pushing forcefully to one side.
Step 3: Land on the opposite foot, absorbing the impact through the hip, knee, and ankle.
Step 4: Pause to stabilize on the landing leg, then immediately bound in the opposite direction.
Step 5: Continue alternating for the prescribed repetitions.
execution.breathing_instructions: Exhale on each bound takeoff. Breathe during the momentary pause between bounds.
common_mistakes: Landing with the knee caving inward (valgus collapse) — the hip must actively control alignment
Not pausing to stabilize on landing before rebounding
Pushing off with both feet — this must be a single-leg drive
safety_considerations: Single-leg landing requires good hip and knee stability — regress to split-stance jumps if unable to control the single-leg landing.
Ankle sprains risk on uneven or slippery surfaces.
execution.range_of_motion_guidance: Maximize lateral distance while maintaining control of the single-leg landing.
execution.tempo_recommendations: Explosive drive. Brief stable pause on landing. 6–10 bounds per set.
coaching_cues: One foot takeoff — drive to the side
Stick the landing — balance before you bound again
Knee stays over the toes on landing

name: Lateral Lunge
description: The lateral lunge steps to the side rather than forward or backward, loading the working leg in the frontal plane and providing a unique training stimulus for the adductors, gluteus medius, and quadriceps simultaneously. The inner thigh of the stationary leg is stretched while the working leg squats. It develops frontal-plane strength and mobility that forward/backward lunges do not address.

execution.starting_position: Stand with feet together, core engaged, hands on hips or holding dumbbells at the sides.
execution.setup_instructions: Wear footwear with good lateral grip. Perform bodyweight first to establish the movement pattern before adding load.
steps: Step 1: Take a large step directly to one side — the foot lands flat and pointed forward or slightly outward.
Step 2: Sit the hip of the stepping leg back and down, bending that knee while keeping the stationary leg straight.
Step 3: Keep the torso relatively upright and reach the hands forward or keep them on the hips for balance.
Step 4: Drive through the working heel to push back to the starting position.
Step 5: Alternate sides each rep or complete all reps on one side.
execution.breathing_instructions: Inhale as you step out and lower. Exhale as you return to standing.
common_mistakes: Taking too small a step, reducing the adductor stretch and hip loading
Letting the working knee cave inward
Excessive forward lean of the torso
safety_considerations: Adequate hip adductor flexibility is necessary — start with a shorter step and increase gradually
If adductor soreness is severe the day after, reduce step width in the next session
execution.range_of_motion_guidance: The working knee bends until the thigh approaches parallel. The stationary leg stays straight with the foot flat.
coaching_cues: Sit back into the hip, not down onto the knee
Keep the stationary leg long and straight
Foot flat on the working leg — don't let the heel rise

name: Lateral Raise
description: The lateral raise is a shoulder isolation exercise that targets the lateral (middle) head of the deltoid through shoulder abduction. It is the most effective direct exercise for building shoulder width and is commonly used as a high-repetition accessory movement in hypertrophy programs.

execution.starting_position: Stand with feet shoulder-width apart holding a dumbbell in each hand at the sides of the thighs. Slight forward lean from the hips and a slight bend in the elbows.
execution.setup_instructions: Use a relatively light weight — the lateral head of the deltoid is a small muscle. Avoid going too heavy, which shifts the movement to the traps.
steps: Raise both dumbbells simultaneously out to the sides in an arc.
Lead with the elbows slightly, with the pinky finger side slightly elevated (internal rotation) to maximize lateral delt activation.
Raise until arms are roughly parallel to the floor.
Lower the dumbbells under control back to the starting position.
execution.breathing_instructions: Exhale on the raise, inhale on the descent.
common_mistakes: Raising too high above parallel, increasing trap involvement
Using momentum from the torso to swing the dumbbells up
Keeping palms fully facing the floor — tilt the pinky side slightly up
safety_considerations: Avoid if experiencing shoulder impingement — the supraspinatus passes through a narrow space during this movement
execution.range_of_motion_guidance: Raise until upper arms are parallel to the floor. Do not raise significantly above horizontal.
coaching_cues: Lead with your elbows, not your hands
Think about pouring a jug of water at the top — tilt the pinky up slightly

name: Leaning Cable Front Raise
description: The leaning cable front raise leans the torso away from a low cable pulley, increasing the range of motion of the anterior deltoid by starting with the working arm pulled behind the hip at a greater angle. The lean increases the stretch placed on the anterior deltoid and upper pec at the bottom while maintaining constant cable tension through the top, making it one of the most complete anterior deltoid loading options available.

execution.starting_position: Stand with one side facing away from a low cable. Grasp the handle with the near hand. Lean the torso away from the cable — 10-20 degrees. The working arm is pulled behind the hip by the cable.
execution.setup_instructions: Set the cable to the lowest position. Lean against a fixed object if balance is challenging initially.
steps: Step 1: Establish the lean with the cable pulling the arm behind the hip.
Step 2: Raise the working arm forward and upward to shoulder height or slightly above.
Step 3: Hold 1 second at peak.
Step 4: Lower under control back to the extended behind-hip position.
Step 5: Complete all reps then switch sides.
execution.breathing_instructions: Exhale raising. Inhale lowering.
common_mistakes: Not leaning enough — the lean is what creates the extended starting position
Torso swinging forward during the raise
safety_considerations: Moderate lean — do not lean so far that balance is compromised
Light loads — anterior deltoid isolation
execution.range_of_motion_guidance: Arm behind hip to shoulder height, using the full extended range created by the lean.
coaching_cues: Lean creates the stretch — maintain it throughout
No torso swing — stay leaned back
Feel the front of the shoulder through the full arc

name: Leaning Cable Lateral Raise
description: A cable lateral raise performed while the lifter leans away from the pulley, anchoring one hand on the cable column for support. The lean creates a longer moment arm at the beginning of the movement (where free-weight lateral raises are easiest) and provides constant tension throughout, making it superior to dumbbell lateral raises for medial deltoid development.

execution.starting_position: Stand sideways to the cable pulley, gripping the upright with the near hand for support. The far hand holds the cable handle.
execution.setup_instructions: Attach a single handle to the low cable pulley. Stand sideways, lean away from the machine, and grip the cable handle with the far hand.
steps: Step 1: Lean away from the cable to create a natural stretch on the medial deltoid.
Step 2: Raise the arm upward and out to the side until it is horizontal or slightly above.
Step 3: Hold briefly at the top, squeezing the medial deltoid.
Step 4: Lower under control back to the starting position.
execution.breathing_instructions: Exhale on the raise. Inhale on the return.
common_mistakes: Using momentum to swing the arm up instead of controlled deltoid abduction
Allowing the torso to rotate during the raise
safety_considerations: The cable provides constant tension even at the bottom — this is the advantage over dumbbells
Keep the support arm straight
execution.range_of_motion_guidance: Arm raised to horizontal or slightly above at the top. Full arm by the side at the bottom.
coaching_cues: Lean into it
Raise with the deltoid, not the trap

name: Leaning Cable Lateral Raise (Foot Forward Stance)
description: The leaning cable lateral raise with foot forward stance uses a split/lunge stance with the same-side foot as the working arm placed forward, stabilizing the lean angle differently than the common same-side foot braced on the cable unit. This stance variation allows a more consistent lean angle throughout the set and provides a stable base from which to isolate the lateral deltoid through a fuller range than the standard leaning version.

execution.starting_position: Stand beside a low cable pulley. Take a split stance — the foot closer to the cable goes forward. Hold the low cable handle with the far hand, leaning slightly away from the cable.
execution.setup_instructions: Foot forward on the working-arm side provides stable counterbalance to the lean. Set the cable to the lowest position.
steps: Step 1: Establish the split-stance lean, working hand holding the cable below hip level.
Step 2: Raise the working arm out and up to shoulder height.
Step 3: Hold 1 second at the top.
Step 4: Lower under full control.
Step 5: Complete all reps then switch sides.
execution.breathing_instructions: Exhale raising. Inhale lowering.
common_mistakes: Shifting the torso during the raise — the lean angle is fixed
Using the non-working hand to assist balance inappropriately
safety_considerations: Light load — isolation exercise for medial deltoid development
Ensure the foot placement gives stable balance before beginning
execution.range_of_motion_guidance: Arm at side to shoulder height.
coaching_cues: Lean is set before you start — don't drift
Raise to shoulder height — stop there
Elbow leads the movement

name: Leaning Dumbbell Lateral Raise
description: The leaning lateral raise is performed by holding a fixed support with one hand and leaning the body away, then raising a dumbbell with the free arm in a lateral arc. The lateral lean places the medial deltoid under a greater stretch at the bottom position and creates a more consistent resistance profile throughout the range of motion compared to a vertical stance. This enhanced stretch at the bottom makes it one of the most effective dumbbell lateral raise variations for medial deltoid hypertrophy.

execution.starting_position: Stand beside an upright support (rack post, cable column). Grip the support with the inside hand. Lean the body away from the support, creating a straight angled line from feet to head. Hold a dumbbell in the outside hand with arm hanging down.
execution.setup_instructions: The lean angle determines the bottom stretch — a greater lean creates a greater stretch. Begin with a moderate lean of 15-20 degrees.
steps: Step 1: Hold the support, lean away, dumbbell at the side.
Step 2: Raise the dumbbell laterally in an arc from the hanging position.
Step 3: Raise until the arm is parallel to the floor.
Step 4: Lower slowly under control, letting the dumbbell hang for a full stretch.
Step 5: Complete all reps, switch sides.
execution.breathing_instructions: Exhale on the raise, inhale on the lowering.
common_mistakes: Not using the full hang at the bottom — the stretch is a key advantage of this variation
Excessive trap shrug at the top
safety_considerations: Ensure the fixed support is stable before leaning
execution.range_of_motion_guidance: Full hang at the bottom (enhanced stretch position), raise to shoulder height.
coaching_cues: Let it hang fully at the bottom
Raise from the elbow, not the wrist
Feel the stretch — that's the point

name: Lying Leg Curl
description: The lying leg curl is an isolation exercise for the hamstrings performed on a machine. It trains knee flexion in a prone position, isolating the hamstrings without meaningful hip involvement. It is one of the few exercises that directly isolates the hamstrings and is commonly used as a finishing movement in leg training.

execution.starting_position: Lie face down on the machine with the ankle pad resting on the lower legs just above the heels. Hips flat on the pad, hands gripping the handles.
execution.setup_instructions: Adjust the ankle pad so it sits comfortably above the Achilles tendon. Align the knee joint with the pivot point of the machine.
steps: Curl the lower legs upward toward the glutes by flexing the knees.
Raise until the lower legs are as vertical as possible.
Lower under control back to full knee extension.
execution.breathing_instructions: Exhale on the curl, inhale on the descent.
common_mistakes: Lifting the hips off the pad to generate momentum
Stopping short of full range at both the top and bottom
safety_considerations: Ensure the pivot point is aligned with your knee to avoid joint stress
execution.range_of_motion_guidance: Full extension at the bottom, maximum comfortable knee flexion at the top.
coaching_cues: Squeeze your hamstrings hard at the top of each rep
Resist the weight on the way down — the eccentric is as important as the concentric

name: Leg Extension
description: The leg extension is a machine-based isolation exercise for the quadriceps, performed by extending the knee against a padded resistance arm. It is the only exercise that directly isolates all four heads of the quadriceps simultaneously and is commonly used as a finishing movement or for rehabilitation of the quadriceps.

execution.starting_position: Sit on the leg extension machine with the back against the pad and the ankle pad resting against the front of the lower legs just above the ankle. Knees are bent at approximately 90 degrees.
execution.setup_instructions: Adjust the seat so the back of the knee aligns with the pivot point. Adjust the ankle pad to a comfortable position on the lower leg.
steps: Extend the knees to lift the pad, straightening the legs.
Raise until the legs are nearly fully extended.
Squeeze the quadriceps at the top, then lower under control.
execution.breathing_instructions: Exhale on extension, inhale on return.
common_mistakes: Jerking the weight up with momentum instead of controlled quad contraction
Not fully extending at the top
safety_considerations: Some individuals with patellar tendon or anterior knee issues may find this movement uncomfortable — reduce range or avoid it
Do not hyper-extend the knees at the top
execution.range_of_motion_guidance: Full extension at the top without joint hyperextension. Full return to 90 degrees at the bottom.
coaching_cues: Squeeze your quads hard and hold for one second at full extension
Control the descent — the eccentric is where muscle damage occurs

name: Leg Press
description: The leg press is a machine-based lower body pushing exercise in which the lifter pushes a weighted platform away from the body with both feet. Because the spine is supported, it allows very heavy loading of the quadriceps with minimal lower back involvement, making it an effective accessory or primary leg exercise.

execution.starting_position: Sit in the leg press machine with the back and head against the pad. Place feet shoulder-width apart on the platform, toes pointing slightly outward. Release the safety handles.
execution.setup_instructions: Adjust the seat so the knees are at approximately 90 degrees with feet on the platform. Do not place the feet so low that heels lift at the bottom.
steps: Release the safety catches and control the platform toward your body by bending the knees.
Lower until knees are at approximately 90 degrees or slightly more.
Press the platform away by extending the knees and hips back to the starting position.
execution.breathing_instructions: Inhale as the platform descends. Exhale on the press.
common_mistakes: Placing feet too low on the platform, causing heels to lift and rounding the lower back
Locking the knees out aggressively at the top
Allowing the knees to collapse inward
safety_considerations: Never remove the safety catches while weight is on the sled
Do not go so deep that the lower back rounds off the pad
execution.range_of_motion_guidance: Approximately 90–100 degrees of knee flexion at the bottom. Full extension (without hyperextension) at the top.
coaching_cues: Push the platform away through your heels and mid-foot, not just the toes
Keep knees tracking over toes throughout the movement

name: Single-Leg High-Foot Leg Press
description: A unilateral leg press with the foot positioned high on the platform, shifting the loading emphasis from the quadriceps to the glutes and hamstrings. By positioning only one foot high on the platform and pressing with that leg alone, the hip-dominant pattern is intensified and bilateral load sharing is eliminated.

execution.starting_position: Position yourself in the leg press machine with one foot high on the platform, near the top edge. The other foot rests off the platform.
execution.setup_instructions: Set the leg press to a comfortable range-of-motion stop. Load conservatively for the unilateral variation.
steps: Step 1: Unrack the sled with both legs, then lift one leg off the platform.
Step 2: Lower the sled slowly by bending the working knee, allowing the high-placed foot to drive the hip into flexion.
Step 3: Descend until the hip is well flexed and the thigh approaches the chest.
Step 4: Drive through the heel to press the sled back to the starting position.
execution.breathing_instructions: Inhale on the descent. Exhale on the press.
common_mistakes: Letting the lower back round off the pad at the bottom
Using too much weight for the unilateral variation
safety_considerations: Ensure the lower back stays in contact with the pad throughout
Start with roughly 50-60% of your bilateral leg press load
execution.range_of_motion_guidance: Full hip flexion at the bottom (thigh approaching chest). Full extension without locking the knee forcefully.
coaching_cues: Drive through the heel
Keep the lower back on the pad

name: Lying Leg Raise
description: The lying leg raise trains the hip flexors and lower abdominals by raising the legs from a flat position to vertical while keeping the lower back in contact with the floor. It is an effective exercise for developing lower abdominal strength and hip flexor endurance.

execution.starting_position: Lie flat on your back with legs extended and hands at the sides or tucked under the lower back for support. Lower back in contact with the floor.
execution.setup_instructions: If the lower back arches off the floor, the core is not strong enough for this exercise — start with bent-knee raises.
steps: With legs straight or slightly bent, raise them from the floor to vertical (90 degrees).
Lower under control back toward the floor.
Stop just before the heels touch the floor to maintain tension.
execution.breathing_instructions: Exhale as legs rise. Inhale as they descend.
common_mistakes: Allowing the lower back to arch off the floor
Dropping the legs quickly without eccentric control
safety_considerations: If the lower back arches significantly, perform bent-knee raises instead
execution.range_of_motion_guidance: Legs from just above floor level to 90 degrees. The lower you go, the more core demand.
coaching_cues: Push the lower back into the floor the entire time
Slow descent — the eccentric is where the work happens

name: Log Bar Overhead Press
description: The log press is a strongman overhead pressing event using a large cylindrical log bar with parallel neutral-grip handles. The neutral grip (palms facing each other) and wide diameter of the implement demand greater pectoral and shoulder activation compared to a standard barbell overhead press, and the cleaning motion required to bring the log to the shoulder before pressing adds a significant full-body power component. The log press is a primary overhead strength test in strongman competition and is an effective developer of pressing strength and stability.

execution.starting_position: The log is on the floor or on a platform at approximately hip height. Stand in front of the log with feet shoulder-width apart. Grip the neutral-grip handles inside the log.
execution.setup_instructions: If cleaning from the floor: position the log at the shins and deadlift to the lap, then roll and clean to the shoulder. If starting from a rack: position the log at chest height on safety pins.
steps: Step 1: Clean the log from the floor or rack to the chest. The log sits against the chest with the elbows pointing forward and downward.
Step 2: Take a full breath and brace the core. Set the feet slightly wider than hip-width for the press.
Step 3: Dip slightly at the knees (a push press dip), then drive upward with the legs and press the log overhead simultaneously.
Step 4: Lock out both arms overhead with the ears between the arms. The log should be over or slightly behind the head.
Step 5: Lower the log to the chest under control, or for maximum reps, use a slight bounce off the chest to initiate the next repetition.
execution.breathing_instructions: Take a full breath and brace before each press. Exhale forcefully at lockout.
common_mistakes: Pressing with the bar in front of the head rather than finishing with it stacked over the spine
Using an excessive layback through the lower back rather than initiating the dip from the knees
Not cleaning the log correctly to the chest, which compromises the starting position for the press
safety_considerations: Have collar pins or spotter arms set at chest height in case the press fails
Build barbell overhead pressing strength before transitioning to the log — a log press requires established overhead pressing ability
execution.range_of_motion_guidance: Full lockout overhead. Arms fully extended with shoulders shrugged at the top. Neutral grip (palms facing each other).
execution.tempo_recommendations: Strength: 1–3 reps × 5–6 sets at 85–95% 1RM. Hypertrophy: 5–8 reps × 4 sets. Competition: maximum reps in 60–75 seconds.
coaching_cues: Drive the log straight up from the chest — no arc forward
Dip with the knees, not the hips
Lock out hard and hold — show the judges

name: Low-Bar Barbell Back Squat
description: The low-bar barbell back squat positions the bar across the rear deltoids and upper traps, lower than the high-bar position. This creates a more forward torso lean during the descent, recruiting the hips and glutes more prominently than a high-bar squat. It is the preferred squat variation in powerlifting due to the mechanical advantage it provides for heavier loads.

execution.starting_position: Stand inside a power rack with the bar resting across your rear deltoids and upper traps, below the spine of the scapula. Grip the bar slightly wider than shoulder width, feet shoulder-width or slightly wider with toes turned out 20-30 degrees.
execution.setup_instructions: Set the bar on the rack at upper-chest height. Duck under the bar and position it across your rear delts. Unrack by straightening the legs, step back two steps, and set your stance.
steps: Step 1: Take a deep breath into your abdomen and brace your core fully (Valsalva maneuver).
Step 2: Initiate the descent by pushing the knees out and sitting the hips back and down simultaneously.
Step 3: Descend until the hip crease is at or below parallel to the knee, maintaining a forward torso lean.
Step 4: Drive through the entire foot, pushing the knees out, and extend the hips and knees together to return to standing.
execution.breathing_instructions: Inhale and brace before each rep. Exhale at the top after completing the repetition.
common_mistakes: Bar sliding up onto the neck instead of staying on the rear delts
Knees caving inward during the ascent
Raising the hips faster than the shoulders out of the hole
Insufficient core bracing leading to lumbar rounding
safety_considerations: Always use a power rack with safety bars set appropriately
Develop adequate hip flexor and ankle mobility before attempting heavy loads
Learn to bail the bar safely to the safeties if needed
execution.range_of_motion_guidance: Hip crease must reach at least parallel with the top of the knee for a full squat. Powerlifting requires breaking parallel.
execution.tempo_recommendations: 3-1-1-0 (3s down, 1s pause at bottom, 1s up, no pause at top)
coaching_cues: Bar on the shelf — rear delts make the shelf
Push the floor away
Knees out, chest up
Drive the hips through at lockout

name: Low Cable Rear Delt Flye — Crossed Cables
alternative_names: Cable Face Pull Rear Delt Crossed
description: A posterior deltoid isolation exercise using two low cable pulleys with the cables crossed — the right hand holds the left pulley's handle and the left hand holds the right pulley's handle. This crossing creates a unique starting position where the arms are crossed in front of the body, allowing a greater stretch on the rear deltoid and infraspinatus before each repetition. The cross-cable setup also changes the resistance angle compared to standard cable rear delt flyes, targeting the posterior deltoid through a different force vector.

execution.starting_position: Stand between two low cable pulleys facing the cables. Reach across to grip the right handle with the left hand and the left handle with the right hand, so the cables cross at your center. Arms are crossed in front at chest height.
execution.setup_instructions: Set both cable stacks to equal weight. The cables are set at the lowest position on both stacks.
steps: Step 1: Grip the crossed cables with arms extended in front of the body, cables crossing at center.
Step 2: Pull both arms outward and back simultaneously in a wide arc, uncrossing the cables and moving the hands out to the sides.
Step 3: Hold the spread position briefly, squeezing the rear deltoids and rhomboids.
Step 4: Slowly return the arms to the crossed starting position. Repeat.
execution.breathing_instructions: Exhale as you pull outward. Inhale as you return to the crossed position.
common_mistakes: Bending the elbows significantly — keep them mostly straight (slight soft bend) throughout
Using upper traps and shrugging to assist the pull
Letting the cables snap back — control the return to the crossed position
safety_considerations: Ensure both pulleys are set to equal weight before starting
If shoulder impingement occurs during the outward arc, reduce range
execution.range_of_motion_guidance: From cables fully crossed in front to arms out to the sides at approximately 90 degrees.
execution.tempo_recommendations: 2s pull outward, 1s hold, 3s slow return to crossed position.
coaching_cues: Think of trying to show the cables to the wall behind you at the top of the movement
The rear deltoid is the primary mover — not the upper back
The crossed starting position gives you a greater stretch — do not rush through it

name: Low Cable Single-Arm Bicep Curl
description: The low cable single-arm curl uses a low cable pulley with a single handle to curl one arm at a time. The cable provides constant tension from the bottom position through the full arc of the curl, maintaining resistance at full elbow flexion where free weights go slack. Training each arm independently allows the lifter to focus on the working side and address strength imbalances between arms.

execution.starting_position: Stand facing the low cable pulley. Grasp a single handle with one hand in a supinated grip. Arm extended toward the pulley.
execution.setup_instructions: Set the low cable pulley with a single handle attachment. Stand one step back from the stack.
steps: Step 1: Begin with the arm extended down toward the pulley, elbow at the side.
Step 2: Curl the forearm upward by flexing the elbow, keeping the upper arm stationary.
Step 3: Curl until maximum elbow flexion is reached.
Step 4: Return slowly to the starting extended position.
execution.breathing_instructions: Exhale on the curl, inhale on the return.
common_mistakes: Elbow drifting forward during the curl
Using body sway to assist
Not supinating the grip at the top
safety_considerations: Keep the shoulder down and relaxed
execution.range_of_motion_guidance: Full extension to maximum elbow flexion.
coaching_cues: Elbow stays glued to the side
Supinate at the top
Squeeze the bicep at peak

name: Low-to-High Cable Fly
description: The low-to-high cable fly is performed with the cable pulleys set at the lowest position. The upward arc of the movement targets the clavicular (upper) portion of the pectoralis major, which is mechanically activated when the arm moves in an upward adduction pattern. This makes it complementary to flat and high-to-low fly variations for complete pectoral development.

execution.starting_position: Set both cable pulleys to the lowest position. Grasp the handles, stand between the stacks, and step forward. Begin with hands at approximately hip height, arms wide with a slight bend at the elbow.
execution.setup_instructions: Set cable pulleys to floor level. Use single-handle attachments. Select a weight that allows smooth control through the full upward arc.
steps: Step 1: Position pulleys at the lowest setting and grasp handles. Step forward and stagger the stance.
Step 2: Start with hands at hip level, arms extended down and to the sides with elbows slightly bent.
Step 3: Exhale and arc both arms upward and inward in a scooping motion, meeting the hands at approximately chest to eye level.
