Step 4: Squeeze the upper chest at the top, then inhale and slowly lower the hands back to hip level.
execution.breathing_instructions: Exhale as you arc the cables upward and in; inhale as you return to the low position.
common_mistakes: Letting the elbows bend excessively, turning this into a curl
Allowing torso rotation instead of moving only at the shoulder joint
safety_considerations: Keep a consistent, slight elbow bend — do not lock out the arms
Control the eccentric to avoid jerking the shoulder at the bottom
execution.range_of_motion_guidance: Full arc from hip height up to eye level, feeling a stretch at the bottom and a contraction at the top.
coaching_cues: Scoop from low to high as if lifting a large ball from your sides to above your head
Feel the upper chest squeeze at the top of the movement

name: Low-to-High Cable Lateral Raise
description: The low-to-high cable lateral raise uses a cable pulley set at the lowest position, pulling upward and outward in a lateral arc. Unlike dumbbells that have minimal tension at the bottom of the movement, the low cable provides meaningful tension at the starting position near the hip and maintains it throughout the raise. This creates a more consistent resistance profile and can be particularly effective for medial deltoid isolation and hypertrophy.

execution.starting_position: Stand beside a cable machine with the pulley at the lowest setting. Grip the handle with the outside hand. The arm hangs at the side, cable pulling slightly toward the machine.
execution.setup_instructions: Stand at a slight distance from the machine to ensure the cable angle is consistent from the start. The handle should cross in front of the body slightly.
steps: Step 1: Stand beside the machine, grip the low-pulley handle with the outside hand.
Step 2: Begin from the hanging position with the cable pulling slightly toward the machine.
Step 3: Raise the arm upward and outward in a lateral arc.
Step 4: Raise until the arm is at shoulder height.
Step 5: Lower under control, maintaining tension throughout. Complete all reps, switch sides.
execution.breathing_instructions: Exhale on the raise, inhale on the descent.
common_mistakes: Standing too close to the cable machine, reducing the tension at the starting position
Raising the arm in front rather than directly to the side
safety_considerations: Adjust your distance from the machine until the cable provides a natural lateral pull
execution.range_of_motion_guidance: Hip level (hanging position) to shoulder height.
coaching_cues: Constant tension from start to top
Pull wide — not forward
Slow on the way down

name: Lu Raises
description: Lu raises are a shoulder conditioning drill popularized by Chinese weightlifting champion Lu Xiaojun. The exercise combines a front raise with a lateral raise in a single continuous motion, moving a plate or light dumbbells from in front of the thighs, out to the sides, and then overhead in one fluid arc, before reversing. The movement targets the anterior, lateral, and posterior deltoids through a comprehensive range of shoulder motion and builds shoulder endurance and coordination.

execution.starting_position: Stand upright holding a weight plate (or light dumbbells) in front of the thighs with arms extended. Use a very light load — this is a conditioning and mobility drill.
execution.setup_instructions: Select a very light plate (5–10 kg maximum for most lifters) or light dumbbells. The movement is primarily for shoulder conditioning, not maximal load.
steps: Step 1: Hold the plate in front of the thighs at arm's length.
Step 2: Raise the plate in a wide arc upward and to the sides (lateral raise pattern) until it reaches overhead.
Step 3: Lower back down by reversing the same arc — out to the sides and back down in front.
Step 4: Alternatively, raise the plate forward (front raise) and then out to the sides and overhead in a continuous sweep.
execution.breathing_instructions: Breathe naturally; exhale on the upward arcs.
common_mistakes: Using too much weight, which limits range of motion and defeats the purpose
Shrugging the traps excessively at the top
safety_considerations: Keep the weight very light — this is a shoulder health and coordination drill
If pain is felt in the shoulder at any angle, reduce load or stop
execution.range_of_motion_guidance: Full arc from thighs to fully overhead in a smooth, controlled sweep.
coaching_cues: Think about painting a wide rainbow arc with the plate
Keep the elbows slightly bent throughout the full movement

name: Lying Cable Chest Press
description: A chest press performed lying on the floor or a flat bench with cable machines positioned at floor level on each side. Unlike dumbbell or barbell pressing, the cable provides constant resistance throughout the full range of motion, including at full extension where free weights would have zero loading. The lying position limits the range (the floor prevents the elbows from dropping below body level) but the cable tension at lockout provides a unique stimulus at the top of the press that free weights cannot replicate.

execution.starting_position: Lie on the floor or a flat bench positioned between two low cable pulleys. Hold the D-handles of the cables with hands at chest level, elbows bent at approximately 90 degrees.
execution.setup_instructions: Position the bench between two cable stacks with the cables at their lowest setting. Adjust so the cables come from low and to the sides, pulling the handles outward and downward at the bottom of the press.
steps: Step 1: Lie with handles at chest level, elbows bent and in contact with the floor (floor press) or just above chest level (bench).
Step 2: Press both handles upward and together, extending the elbows and squeezing the pecs at the top.
Step 3: Hold at full extension with the handles together — the cable tension remains at lockout.
Step 4: Lower under control back to the start. Repeat.
execution.breathing_instructions: Inhale as you lower. Exhale during the press.
common_mistakes: Cables positioned too high, reducing the loading at the bottom
Losing scapular retraction at lockout — maintain shoulder blade position throughout
Pressing one side faster than the other, creating rotation
safety_considerations: Ensure both cable stacks are at the same weight
If using the floor, the elbows cannot go below body level — this limits ROM but reduces shoulder stress
execution.range_of_motion_guidance: Full elbow extension at the top. For floor press: elbows to floor level at the bottom.
coaching_cues: Feel the cable pulling inward at the top — squeeze the chest hard to control it
Keep the shoulder blades retracted on the bench throughout the press
Equal weight on both sides — do not let one arm lead

name: Lying Cable Curl
description: The lying cable curl is performed face-up on a bench placed close to a low cable pulley, with both hands gripping a straight bar or EZ-bar attached to the cable. Because the lifter is horizontal, the cable pull direction creates maximum bicep tension in the stretched (extended arm) position — the opposite of standing curls which are hardest near lockout. This makes it valuable for training the bicep in its lengthened position for hypertrophy.

execution.starting_position: Place a flat bench parallel to and close to a low cable pulley. Lie face-up with the head nearest the pulley. Grasp a straight bar attached to the cable.
execution.setup_instructions: Position the bench so the cable pulls the arms toward the pulley when extended. Ensure the cable travels along the floor to the pulley smoothly.
steps: Step 1: Lie supine, arms extended toward the pulley, bar in supinated grip.
Step 2: Curl the bar toward the face by flexing the elbows.
Step 3: Hold at the peak for one second.
Step 4: Return to the extended position, feeling the stretch in the biceps.
execution.breathing_instructions: Exhale on the curl, inhale on the return.
common_mistakes: Lifting the head off the bench
Upper arms rising off the bench on the curl
Rushing the eccentric
safety_considerations: Keep upper arms pressed to the bench throughout
execution.range_of_motion_guidance: Full extension with stretch at the bottom, full curl at the top.
coaching_cues: Feel the stretch at the bottom
Upper arms stay on the bench
Control the negative

name: Lying Single-Leg Cable Knee Curl
description: The lying single-leg cable knee curl attaches a cuff to the ankle and uses the low cable pulley to provide constant tension throughout the curl, unlike the lying leg curl machine which has variable resistance. Training one leg at a time addresses imbalances. The cable provides resistance from a consistent angle, training the hamstrings in a slightly different tension curve than a machine.

execution.starting_position: Attach an ankle cuff to the low cable pulley. Lie prone on a flat bench placed in front of the cable stack. Attach the cuff to one ankle, leg extended.
execution.setup_instructions: Position the bench a few feet in front of the cable machine so the cable pulls the ankle directly away from the machine at floor level.
steps: Step 1: Lie face-down on the bench, ankle cuff attached.
Step 2: Curl the working leg upward by bending the knee, pulling the cable against resistance.
Step 3: Curl until maximum knee flexion is reached.
Step 4: Lower the leg slowly back to the starting position, maintaining cable tension throughout.
execution.breathing_instructions: Exhale on the curl, inhale on the return.
common_mistakes: Hips rising off the bench to generate momentum
Not controlling the eccentric phase
safety_considerations: Ensure the ankle cuff is securely fastened before beginning
execution.range_of_motion_guidance: Full extension to maximum knee flexion. The cable maintains tension throughout — do not rush.
coaching_cues: Hips pressed into the bench
Lead with the heel toward the glute
Feel the stretch at the bottom

name: Lying Cable Preacher Curl
description: A bicep isolation exercise performed lying face-down on an incline bench with a cable attached below, curling the bar upward. The prone position eliminates the ability to use body swing and keeps the shoulder in a consistent position, targeting the biceps through a unique angle that changes the peak contraction point.

execution.starting_position: Set an incline bench in front of a low cable pulley. Lie face-down on the bench with arms hanging down toward the cable attachment. Grip a curl bar or rope.
execution.setup_instructions: Attach a straight bar or EZ bar to the low pulley. Set an incline bench at 30 to 45 degrees. Lie prone on the bench with arms hanging toward the pulley.
steps: Step 1: Keeping the upper arms stationary hanging straight down, curl the bar upward.
Step 2: Curl to full bicep flexion at the top.
Step 3: Slowly lower back to full arm extension.
Step 4: Repeat without letting the upper arm move.
execution.breathing_instructions: Exhale on the curl up. Inhale on the controlled descent.
common_mistakes: Allowing the upper arms to swing forward during the curl
Using too heavy a load for this strict position
safety_considerations: The prone position is strict — start lighter than expected
execution.range_of_motion_guidance: Full extension at the bottom. Full flexion at the top.
coaching_cues: Upper arms stay still
Squeeze the bicep at the top

name: Lying Dumbbell Leg Curl
description: The lying dumbbell leg curl is performed face-down on a bench or the floor, with a dumbbell clamped between the feet. The lifter curls the dumbbell upward by bending the knees, isolating the hamstrings. It requires no machine and provides a practical home-gym alternative to the lying leg curl machine. Foot stability and control of the dumbbell demand additional concentration.

execution.starting_position: Lie face-down on a flat bench. Hold a dumbbell vertically between the soles of your feet, clamped firmly. Legs extended.
execution.setup_instructions: Choose a dumbbell you can hold securely between your feet. Lie prone on the bench with hips at the edge and legs hanging off.
steps: Step 1: Squeeze the dumbbell securely between both feet.
Step 2: Curl the dumbbell upward by bending the knees, bringing heels toward the glutes.
Step 3: Curl as far as knee flexion allows — ideally past 90 degrees.
Step 4: Lower the dumbbell slowly back to the starting position.
execution.breathing_instructions: Exhale on the curl, inhale on the controlled lowering.
common_mistakes: Dumbbell slipping or rotating — use a secure grip with both feet
Hips rising off the bench during the curl
Using momentum to swing the dumbbell up
safety_considerations: Ensure the dumbbell is firmly secured before each rep
Start light until foot clamping feels natural
execution.range_of_motion_guidance: Curl from full extension to as much flexion as possible.
coaching_cues: Squeeze the dumbbell
Lead with the heels toward the glutes
Hips stay on the bench

name: Lying Dumbbell Tricep Extension
description: The lying dumbbell tricep extension is performed with a dumbbell in each hand while lying on a flat bench. Because each arm works independently, unilateral strength imbalances are addressed and each elbow can travel independently. The dumbbells can be held with the palms facing each other (neutral grip) or supinated, allowing different levels of elbow stress. It is a versatile skull crusher alternative that is gentler on the elbows than the barbell version.

execution.starting_position: Lie on a flat bench, a dumbbell in each hand, arms extended above the chest with a neutral grip (palms facing each other).
execution.setup_instructions: Press the dumbbells into position before lying down, or have a partner hand them. Keep the elbows shoulder-width.
steps: Step 1: Begin with arms extended, dumbbells above the face.
Step 2: Bend the elbows to lower both dumbbells toward the sides of the head.
Step 3: Lower until maximum elbow flexion.
Step 4: Extend the elbows to press back to the starting position.
execution.breathing_instructions: Inhale on descent, exhale on press.
common_mistakes: Flaring the elbows wide
Upper arms moving during the exercise
Letting the dumbbells tap together at the top
safety_considerations: Dumbbells are safer than barbells as each arm can move independently if one side fails
execution.range_of_motion_guidance: Full extension to dumbbells at temple/ear level.
coaching_cues: Elbows stay shoulder-width
Upper arms pinned — just the forearms move
Neutral grip throughout

name: Lying Floor Cable Curl
description: The lying floor cable curl is performed lying face-down on the floor in front of a low cable pulley, gripping a bar or rope attached to the cable. As the elbows flex, the cable direction from the floor creates a tension curve that emphasizes the biceps in a unique way, with the arms braced against the floor to prevent upper arm movement. It is a strict, low-setup bicep isolation technique.

execution.starting_position: Lie face-down on the floor in front of a low cable pulley. Extend arms toward the pulley and grasp the attachment. Upper arms rest on the floor.
execution.setup_instructions: Use a mat for comfort. Set the low cable pulley. A straight bar or EZ attachment works well.
steps: Step 1: Begin with arms extended toward the pulley, upper arms pinned to the floor.
Step 2: Curl the forearms upward by flexing the elbows.
Step 3: Curl as far as possible without the upper arms lifting.
Step 4: Return to the starting extended position.
execution.breathing_instructions: Exhale on the curl, inhale on the return.
common_mistakes: Upper arms lifting off the floor
Using momentum
Insufficient cable tension on the setup
safety_considerations: This is a strict, light-load exercise — do not force heavy loads
execution.range_of_motion_guidance: Full extension to maximum elbow flexion with arms on floor.
coaching_cues: Arms on the floor throughout
Only the forearms move
Squeeze at the top

name: Lying Floor Cable Hamstring Curl
description: A hamstring curl performed lying prone on the floor with a cable ankle attachment from a low pulley. Unlike the lying leg curl machine, this variation uses a cable that provides constant tension through the full range, including the lockout position where the machine lever arm would have minimal mechanical advantage. The floor position and cable angle together create a unique hamstring isolation stimulus that complements machine and dumbbell curl variations.

execution.starting_position: Lie prone on the floor facing away from a low cable pulley. Attach an ankle cuff to one ankle and connect it to the cable. Legs are extended with a slight bend in the working knee.
execution.setup_instructions: Lie far enough from the pulley that the cable is taut at full knee extension. The hip must remain flat against the floor throughout.
steps: Step 1: Begin prone with the ankle cuff attached and the leg extended.
Step 2: Curl the working leg by bending the knee, bringing the heel toward the glute.
Step 3: Hold the fully curled position for 1-2 seconds.
Step 4: Lower the leg slowly back to the extended starting position. Repeat, then switch legs.
execution.breathing_instructions: Exhale during the curl. Inhale during the return.
common_mistakes: Lifting the hip off the floor during the curl — the hip must stay flat
Using a cable tension so high that full range of motion is compromised
Rushing the eccentric — the slow return is where most of the hypertrophy stimulus occurs
safety_considerations: Ensure the ankle cuff is securely attached before starting
If lower back discomfort occurs, place a folded towel under the abdomen to reduce lumbar stress
execution.range_of_motion_guidance: Full extension at the bottom. Maximum knee flexion (heel to glute) at the top.
coaching_cues: Keep the hip flat — do not let it rise during the curl
Feel the hamstring pull the heel toward the glute — not the glute squeezing the heel up
Slow on the way down — the cable fights you all the way back to the start

name: Lying Leg Curl
description: The lying leg curl is performed face-down on a machine, curling the pad from full knee extension to maximum knee flexion against a resistance arm. As an isolation exercise for the hamstrings, it places the hip in extension, which allows the biceps femoris long head to reach a shortened position and trains the hamstrings through the knee flexion function that many compound exercises underemphasize.

execution.starting_position: Lie face down on the leg curl machine. Position the pad just above the heel of the ankle (on the lower calf). Grip the handles and ensure the knees are just at or slightly off the edge of the pad.
execution.setup_instructions: Adjust the machine so the pivot point aligns with the knee joint. The pad should contact just above the heel cord. Set a resistance appropriate for controlled full-range movement.
steps: Step 1: Lie prone, grip the handles, and position the pad on the lower calf near the ankle.
Step 2: Curl the pad upward by flexing the knees as far as the machine allows — ideally to 120–140° of knee flexion.
Step 3: Hold briefly at the top with the hamstrings fully contracted.
Step 4: Lower the weight under control back to full knee extension — do not let the weight stack crash.
Step 5: Repeat for the prescribed number of reps.
execution.breathing_instructions: Exhale as you curl up. Inhale as you lower.
common_mistakes: Using momentum — the hips should not rise off the pad during the curl
Using a range that stops short of full extension, reducing the hamstring stretch
Letting the weight stack crash at the bottom, which loses the eccentric stimulus
safety_considerations: If hip flexors are tight, the hip will flex during the curl — this reduces stimulus and can cause low back discomfort
Avoid this machine if you have posterior knee issues — discuss with a clinician
execution.range_of_motion_guidance: Full extension at the bottom to full available flexion at the top. The hamstrings should be under load through the entire range.
execution.tempo_recommendations: 2-1-3-0 — a slow eccentric (3 seconds) maximizes time under tension
coaching_cues: Don't let the hips leave the pad — keep them pressed down
Control the weight all the way down — no crashing
Squeeze the hamstrings at the top of each rep

name: Lying Single-Arm Cable Extension
description: A unilateral triceps isolation exercise performed lying on a bench with a low cable pulley. One arm extends the cable attachment overhead while the other rests on the torso. This allows independent training of each tricep head.

execution.starting_position: Set up for Lying Single-Arm Cable Extension in the appropriate position.
execution.setup_instructions: Prepare equipment and body position for Lying Single-Arm Cable Extension.
steps: Step 1: Lie on bench with head near low cable pulley. Grasp single handle.
Step 2: Raise arm overhead, upper arm perpendicular to floor.
Step 3: Bend elbow to lower handle behind head, feeling tricep stretch.
Step 4: Extend arm back to starting position.
execution.breathing_instructions: Exhale during the exertion phase, inhale during the return.
common_mistakes: Letting elbow drift outward
Using shoulder to assist the movement
safety_considerations: Keep joints aligned throughout the movement.
Use controlled weight appropriate for skill level.
execution.range_of_motion_guidance: Move through full range of motion without compromising joint integrity.
coaching_cues: Keep upper arm still
Full extension at top

name: Lying Dumbbell Svend Press
description: The Lying Svend Press is performed flat on a bench, extending and returning a weight plate or two pressed-together dumbbells from the chest while maintaining continuous inward squeezing force. The lying position allows slightly greater loads than the standing version and targets the sternal head of the pectoralis major more directly.

execution.starting_position: Lie flat on a bench holding two dumbbells or a weight plate pressed together at chest level, arms slightly bent.
execution.setup_instructions: Use a flat bench. Hold a light plate or two pressed dumbbells above the lower chest. Begin with the weight resting on the sternum.
steps: Step 1: Squeeze the weight firmly together and press upward from the chest to full arm extension.
Step 2: Hold the squeeze and lower slowly back to the chest.
Step 3: Touch the chest and immediately press again without releasing tension.
Step 4: Keep constant adduction force throughout all reps.
execution.breathing_instructions: Exhale as you press up. Inhale as you lower.
common_mistakes: Releasing the squeeze at the chest
Flaring the elbows wide rather than keeping them somewhat tucked
safety_considerations: Light loads only — this is a finishing or isolation exercise
If using round dumbbells, they may slip — hex preferred
execution.range_of_motion_guidance: Full arm extension at top; controlled return to chest.
coaching_cues: Constant squeeze — no relaxation between reps
Feel the inner chest working

name: Seated Machine Abdominal Crunch
description: The seated abdominal crunch machine guides the torso through a fixed arc of spinal flexion against a selectorized or plate-loaded resistance pad, providing a beginner-friendly way to load the rectus abdominis without requiring hip flexor coordination or balance. The fixed movement path isolates the spinal flexion component effectively, and the machine's adjustable resistance allows precise progressive overload. It is a useful tool for individuals learning abdominal training or those rehabilitating from injuries that limit floor-based core work.

execution.starting_position: Sit in the machine with the back against the pad and feet secured under the ankle rollers. Grasp the handles above the shoulders. Position the chest pad so it contacts the upper chest.
execution.setup_instructions: Adjust the seat height so the pivot point of the machine aligns roughly with the hip joint. Select an appropriate weight.
steps: Step 1: Sit tall with a neutral spine. Grip the handles and brace lightly.
Step 2: Flex the spine forward, pulling the chest pad downward and toward the knees. Focus on rounding the lumbar spine rather than simply hinging forward.
Step 3: Pause at the bottom of the movement, fully contracting the abs.
Step 4: Return slowly to the start position, maintaining control against the resistance.
Step 5: Repeat without fully releasing tension at the top.
execution.breathing_instructions: Exhale on the crunch forward. Inhale on the controlled return.
common_mistakes: Using momentum to swing the torso down rather than contracting the abs
Pulling with the arms on the handles rather than initiating from the abdominals
safety_considerations: Avoid very heavy loads that force spinal flexion beyond comfortable range
execution.range_of_motion_guidance: Full arc of motion as guided by the machine — from spine neutral to full flexion.
coaching_cues: Round the lower back — do not just lean forward
Keep the neck neutral — do not crane forward

name: Machine Chest Press
description: The machine chest press is a guided horizontal pressing exercise performed on a dedicated chest press machine. The fixed movement path reduces the stabilization demand compared to free-weight pressing, allowing lifters to focus attention on pectoral contraction or to safely train to or near muscular failure without a spotter. It is an effective tool for hypertrophy, beginners, and individuals returning from injury.

execution.starting_position: Sit in the chest press machine with the back flat against the pad. Adjust the seat height so the handles are at mid-chest level. Grip the handles with an overhand grip, elbows bent and in line with the hands.
execution.setup_instructions: Adjust the seat height so handles align with mid-chest. Set the starting position pin if available so you don't have to reach back awkwardly to initiate. Select weight.
steps: Step 1: Sit with back firmly against the pad, feet flat on the floor. Grip handles at chest level.
Step 2: Brace the core and retract the shoulder blades slightly against the pad.
Step 3: Exhale and press the handles forward until the arms are fully extended but not locked out.
Step 4: Inhale and slowly return the handles to the starting position, feeling a stretch across the chest.
execution.breathing_instructions: Exhale on the press; inhale on the return.
common_mistakes: Allowing the lower back to arch away from the pad during the press
Fully locking out the elbows aggressively at full extension
safety_considerations: Use the machine's start-pin or lever to initiate the rep safely without shoulder strain
Do not adjust seat mid-set
execution.range_of_motion_guidance: Return fully to feel a chest stretch on each rep; press to near full extension without hyperextending.
coaching_cues: Press your back into the seat throughout — don't let it peel away
Think about squeezing the pecs together as you extend

name: Machine Fly
description: The machine fly, commonly called the pec deck, is a seated isolation exercise for the pectoralis major. The user pushes two padded arm rests or handles together in a horizontal arc. The machine's guided path removes the need for shoulder stabilization, allowing near-complete focus on pectoral contraction, making it safe and effective for high-rep isolation work.

execution.starting_position: Sit in the pec deck machine with back flat against the pad. Adjust the seat so the arms or handles are at chest level. Place forearms on the pads or grip the handles with elbows slightly bent.
execution.setup_instructions: Adjust the seat height so the arm pads or handles are at mid-chest level when seated. Set the range limiter if available to protect the shoulder at full extension.
steps: Step 1: Sit with the back against the pad, feet flat on the floor. Position forearms on the pads or hands on the handles.
Step 2: Begin with arms wide, feeling a gentle stretch across the chest.
Step 3: Exhale and squeeze both arms together in front of the chest, holding the peak contraction for a second.
Step 4: Inhale and slowly allow the arms to open back to the start, controlling the eccentric stretch.
execution.breathing_instructions: Exhale as you squeeze inward; inhale as you open back out.
common_mistakes: Opening too wide and creating shoulder impingement at the extreme end range
Rounding the lower back off the seat pad
safety_considerations: Set the starting-width stopper so the arms do not travel behind the plane of the torso
Do not use this machine if shoulder impingement or labrum issues are present
execution.range_of_motion_guidance: Open until a comfortable chest stretch is felt (forearms should not go behind the body); close until the pads nearly touch.
coaching_cues: Lead with your elbows, not your hands, as you squeeze inward
Feel the chest doing the work — not the shoulders or arms

name: Machine Glute Kickback
description: The machine glute kickback is performed on a dedicated kneeling kickback machine that pads the back of the ankle and provides resistance as the leg is extended backward. Because both hands and the supporting knee are braced, the lifter can focus entirely on glute contraction without balance demands. The machine provides a smooth, guided resistance curve that isolates the gluteus maximus effectively.

execution.starting_position: Kneel on the machine's pad with the working leg's ankle behind the resistance pad. Hold the handles and brace the core.
execution.setup_instructions: Adjust the pad to sit at the back of the ankle. Set a moderate weight allowing full glute-driven extension.
steps: Step 1: Begin with the knee bent at 90 degrees, ankle pad behind the foot.
Step 2: Extend the working leg backward by squeezing the glute and driving the foot rearward.
Step 3: Hold at full extension for one second, feeling the glute squeeze.
Step 4: Return the knee to the starting bent position with control.
execution.breathing_instructions: Exhale during the extension, inhale on return.
common_mistakes: Using the lower back to extend rather than the glute
Rushing through reps without a peak contraction
Hips rotating away from center
safety_considerations: Keep the lower back neutral — do not hyperextend the spine
execution.range_of_motion_guidance: Full hip extension without lumbar hyperextension.
coaching_cues: Squeeze the glute — not the back
Think of pushing the heel toward the ceiling
Hips stay square

name: Machine Lateral Raise
description: The machine lateral raise uses a dedicated lateral raise machine that applies resistance through pads positioned against the elbows or wrists, maintaining consistent resistance throughout the full arc of motion. Unlike dumbbells, which lose most tension at the bottom of the movement, the machine provides meaningful resistance at the starting position and maintains it through the full range. This consistent tension profile makes it particularly effective for high-rep medial deltoid hypertrophy work.

execution.starting_position: Adjust the seat height so the pivot of the machine aligns with the shoulder joint. Sit upright and position the arms against the pads (elbows bent to 90 degrees or arms straight depending on machine type).
execution.setup_instructions: Pivot alignment is critical — align the machine's axis of rotation with your shoulder joint before each set.
steps: Step 1: Sit with correct seat height; elbows or wrists positioned against the pads.
Step 2: Starting from a lowered position, raise the arms out to the sides.
Step 3: Raise until the arms reach shoulder height or slightly above.
Step 4: Pause briefly at the top.
Step 5: Lower slowly under control back to the starting position.
execution.breathing_instructions: Exhale on the raise, inhale on the descent.
common_mistakes: Incorrect seat height — misalignment reduces effectiveness and can irritate the shoulder
Using momentum to initiate the movement
Not lowering fully between reps
safety_considerations: Adjust seat for joint alignment before loading the machine
execution.range_of_motion_guidance: Full lowered position to shoulder height.
coaching_cues: Align the pivot point with your shoulder first
Slow and controlled — especially on the way down
No shrugging

name: Machine Preacher Curl
description: The machine preacher curl replicates the preacher bench position using a fixed cam-driven resistance curve. The upper arms rest on a fixed pad and the hands grip a handle attached to the machine, which maintains constant tension throughout the curl. The machine removes the need to stabilize the weight and allows the lifter to focus entirely on the bicep contraction, making it effective for hypertrophy-focused training.

execution.starting_position: Sit at the preacher curl machine with the upper arms resting on the pad. Grasp the handles with a supinated or neutral grip.
execution.setup_instructions: Adjust the seat height so the upper arms rest fully on the pad with shoulders relaxed.
steps: Step 1: Begin with arms extended to the starting angle of the machine.
Step 2: Curl the handles upward by flexing the elbows.
Step 3: Hold at the peak for one second.
Step 4: Lower slowly back to the starting position.
execution.breathing_instructions: Exhale on the curl, inhale on the return.
common_mistakes: Lifting the arms off the pad
Rushing the eccentric
safety_considerations: Machine design varies — check the full ROM on the first rep
execution.range_of_motion_guidance: Full extension to full flexion as allowed by the machine.
coaching_cues: Arms on the pad throughout
Feel the stretch at the bottom
Squeeze at the top

name: Machine Shoulder Press
description: The machine shoulder press is a seated overhead pressing exercise performed on a dedicated shoulder press machine. The guided movement path reduces the stabilization demand compared to free weights, making it accessible for beginners and useful for high-rep training or working through shoulder rehabilitation. The anterior and lateral deltoids are the primary movers.

execution.starting_position: Sit in the shoulder press machine with the back against the pad and feet flat on the floor. Adjust the seat height so the handles are at or just above shoulder level when seated. Grip the handles.
execution.setup_instructions: Adjust seat height so handles begin at approximately ear to shoulder level. Engage the seat pad to your preference for lumbar support.
steps: Step 1: Sit with your back against the pad, feet flat on the floor. Grip the handles at shoulder height.
Step 2: Brace the core and keep the lower back against the seat.
Step 3: Exhale and press both handles upward until the arms are extended overhead.
Step 4: Inhale and lower the handles back to the starting position in a controlled manner.
execution.breathing_instructions: Exhale on the press; inhale on the descent.
common_mistakes: Letting the lower back arch excessively away from the seat
Shrugging the shoulders upward at the top of the press
safety_considerations: If shoulder pain is felt, reduce the range of motion or see a professional before continuing
Do not go behind head with handles — keep press in front plane
execution.range_of_motion_guidance: Press to full arm extension overhead; return handles to ear/shoulder level.
coaching_cues: Keep the rib cage down — don't flare it upward as you press
Press straight up, not forward

name: Machine Tricep Dip
description: The machine tricep dip is performed on a dedicated seated dip machine with pads that the hands push down against. Because the machine guides the movement and provides back support, it eliminates stabilization demands and allows the lifter to focus entirely on tricep loading. The seated position removes body weight from the equation, allowing very precise loading through the full extension movement. It is accessible for beginners and allows easy progression.

execution.starting_position: Sit in the machine with the back against the pad. Grasp the handles and begin with elbows slightly bent.
execution.setup_instructions: Adjust the seat height so the starting position has the elbows at approximately 90 degrees.
steps: Step 1: Begin with elbows at 90 degrees, gripping the handles.
Step 2: Push the handles downward by extending the elbows.
Step 3: Extend to full lockout, squeezing the triceps.
Step 4: Return under control to the starting position.
execution.breathing_instructions: Exhale on the press down, inhale on the return.
common_mistakes: Not reaching full extension at the bottom
Leaning forward off the back pad
safety_considerations: Machine design varies — check the specific ROM before loading
execution.range_of_motion_guidance: 90-degree elbow angle to full extension.
coaching_cues: Full extension at the bottom
Back against the pad
Squeeze the triceps at lockout

name: Maltese Press
description: An extremely advanced rings movement where the arms are held below horizontal in a wide position, lower than a standard iron cross. The body must press up from this compromised position, requiring extraordinary pectoral and anterior deltoid strength. This is competition-level gymnastics.

execution.starting_position: Set up for Maltese Press in proper position.
execution.setup_instructions: Prepare body and equipment for Maltese Press.
steps: Step 1: From an iron cross position, lower arms below shoulder height into Maltese.
Step 2: Maintain body horizontal while arms are at approximately hip level.
Step 3: Press rings back up and inward to transition to another position.
Step 4: Requires exceptional prerequisite strength in iron cross first.
execution.breathing_instructions: Breathe steadily; never hold breath during static holds.
common_mistakes: Attempting without iron cross mastery
Hyperextending elbows
safety_considerations: Build prerequisite strength before attempting advanced variations.
Stop if joint pain occurs.
execution.range_of_motion_guidance: Full range of motion with control at all times.
coaching_cues: Competition-level only
Develop iron cross before approaching this

name: Man Maker
description: The man maker is a multi-movement dumbbell complex in which the athlete performs a push-up, a renegade row on each arm, a squat clean, and an overhead press — all in a single continuous sequence without putting the dumbbells down. It demands upper body pushing and pulling strength, anti-rotation core stability during the row, and total body power during the clean, making it one of the most comprehensive single-exercise conditioning movements available. It is used in advanced circuit training and high-intensity conditioning programs.

execution.starting_position: Stand with dumbbells on the floor, shoulder-width apart. Begin by hinging down to grip the dumbbells in a push-up starting position.
execution.setup_instructions: Use matching fixed dumbbells of moderate weight. Ensure adequate floor space.
steps: Step 1: Begin in a push-up position gripping both dumbbells on the floor.
Step 2: Perform one push-up — lower the chest to the floor and press back up.
Step 3: Perform a renegade row with the right arm — pull the right dumbbell to the hip while balancing on the left.
Step 4: Perform a renegade row with the left arm.
Step 5: Jump or step the feet forward to a squat position, clean the dumbbells to shoulder height, then press them overhead. That is one full rep.
execution.breathing_instructions: Exhale on each push phase (push-up, row pull, press). Inhale between movements.
common_mistakes: Rotating the hips during the renegade row — the hips must remain square to the floor
Using momentum rather than strength during the row phase
Rushing the transitions between movements — control each phase
safety_considerations: Very high demand on the shoulder girdle and core — a prerequisite of proficiency in all component movements.
Wrist neutral grip (dumbbells parallel to the body) reduces wrist stress in the push-up phase.
execution.range_of_motion_guidance: Full push-up range. Full row elbow retraction. Full overhead lockout on the press.
execution.tempo_recommendations: 3–8 reps per set. Full recovery between sets — this is a maximal-effort complex.
coaching_cues: Hips square during the row
Clean up — don't swing
Lock out the press fully overhead

name: Matrix Push-Up
description: The matrix push-up is a dynamic bodyweight variation where the torso moves through a wave-like pattern during the descent and ascent. Rather than a straight vertical path, the chest leads down first, hips follow, then the chest rises as the hips drop. This flowing motion challenges the pectorals and anterior deltoids through an extended range while also mobilizing the spine.

execution.starting_position: Begin in a standard high plank position with hands slightly wider than shoulder width, body in a straight line from head to heels.
execution.setup_instructions: No equipment needed. Ensure adequate floor space and a non-slip surface.
steps: Step 1: Lower the chest forward and down toward the floor first, allowing the hips to remain high momentarily.
Step 2: Continue the wave motion so the chest skims near the floor while the hips descend behind.
Step 3: Reverse the wave: press the chest up first while hips remain lower, creating an arched spinal position briefly.
Step 4: Finish by pressing hips up and returning to the high plank. Each full wave counts as one repetition.
execution.breathing_instructions: Breathe continuously with natural rhythm; exhale during the pressing/rising phase.
common_mistakes: Stopping mid-wave and reverting to a straight push-up
Collapsing the lower back during the cobra-like extension phase
Moving too fast and losing the fluid wave pattern
safety_considerations: Avoid if experiencing lower back pain — the spinal extension component may aggravate lumbar issues
Warm up the spine and shoulders adequately before performing
execution.range_of_motion_guidance: The chest should come close to the floor during the lowest point of the wave. The spine moves through flexion and extension throughout.
execution.tempo_recommendations: Fluid, continuous motion — approximately 3–4 seconds per full wave cycle
coaching_cues: Lead with the chest on the way down, lead with the chest on the way up
Think of a wave rolling through your spine from front to back

name: McGill Curl-Up
description: The McGill curl-up is a modified crunch developed by spine researcher Dr. Stuart McGill to target the rectus abdominis with minimal compressive load on the lumbar discs. The exercise differs from a standard crunch in that the hands are placed under the lumbar curve to preserve its natural lordosis, and only the head, neck, and upper shoulders are lifted off the floor — avoiding the full spinal flexion that increases intradiscal pressure. It is widely recommended as a spine-safe abdominal exercise in rehabilitation and clinical populations.

execution.starting_position: Lie on your back with one leg straight and one knee bent, foot flat on the floor. Place both hands palms-down under the small of the lower back to support its natural curve.
execution.setup_instructions: Use a mat. The hands-under-lumbar position is non-negotiable for the McGill protocol — it preserves spinal lordosis.
steps: Step 1: Lie supine with one knee bent, one leg straight. Hands under the lumbar curve.
Step 2: Brace the entire core — think about creating tension in a corset around your waist.
Step 3: Raise only the head, neck, and upper shoulders off the floor — the elbows remain on the floor.
Step 4: Hold the top position for 7–8 seconds with continuous bracing.
Step 5: Lower with control, rest briefly, and repeat.
execution.breathing_instructions: Exhale during the hold. Breathe shallowly to maintain the brace. Do not hold breath for the entire isometric duration.
common_mistakes: Removing the hands from under the lower back — this defeats the purpose
Flexing the spine significantly as in a standard crunch
Pulling the neck with the hands placed behind the head (the McGill variation keeps hands under the lumbar)
safety_considerations: This exercise is specifically designed for spine health and rehabilitation contexts.
The low ROM and preserved lordosis make it appropriate for those with disc pathology when cleared by a clinician.
execution.range_of_motion_guidance: Only lift the head, neck, and upper shoulders. The lower back remains in contact with the hands throughout. This is not a full sit-up.
execution.tempo_recommendations: Slow initiation (2 seconds), 7–8 second hold, 2–3 second lower. Perform 3–5 repetitions per set.
coaching_cues: Hands under the low back — keep the arch
Lift eyes to the ceiling, not to your knees
Brace like you are about to get punched

name: Meadows Row
description: The Meadows row is a unilateral landmine row variation where one end of a barbell is fixed in a corner or landmine attachment and the lifter rows the loaded end with one hand using a neutral, staggered grip. The unique angled line of pull emphasizes the outer portion of the latissimus dorsi and teres major more than horizontal cable rows, while also loading the upper back through scapular retraction.

execution.starting_position: Wedge one end of a barbell into a corner or landmine attachment. Load the other end with plates. Stand perpendicular to the bar and stagger the feet (lead foot on the same side as the working arm). Hinge at the hips to approximately 45 degrees and grasp the end of the bar with one hand.
execution.setup_instructions: Secure the barbell in a landmine unit or corner. Keep a collar on the loaded end. Stand close enough that the bar end is at approximately knee height when hinged. Use chalk or a towel for grip on the smooth end of the bar if needed.
steps: Step 1: Hinge at the hips and grasp the bar end with the working arm extended toward the floor, allowing the lat to stretch.
Step 2: Drive the elbow up and back, retracting the scapula as you row the bar toward the hip or lower ribcage.
Step 3: At the top, the elbow should be above the level of the torso and the shoulder blade fully retracted.
Step 4: Lower the bar under control back to the starting position, fully extending the arm.
Step 5: Complete all reps on one side before switching.
execution.breathing_instructions: Exhale forcefully as you row the bar up. Inhale as you lower it.
common_mistakes: Allowing the torso to rotate excessively — it should be relatively stable
Pulling toward the chest rather than the hip, losing lat emphasis
Using too much momentum from the lower body to initiate the row
safety_considerations: Ensure the barbell is securely wedged to prevent slipping during the movement
Maintain a braced core and neutral spine throughout — the hip hinge position taxes the lower back
execution.range_of_motion_guidance: Full arm extension at the start to elbow above torso level at the top. Maximize scapular excursion.
coaching_cues: Flare the elbow out slightly compared to a normal row
Drive the elbow toward the ceiling, not behind you
Let the shoulder blade travel away from the spine at the bottom of each rep

name: Meadows Row with Thick Bar Grip
description: The thick-bar Meadows row wraps a fat grip attachment or towel around the barbell end to increase the grip diameter, amplifying forearm and grip strength demands alongside the standard Meadows row benefits. The larger diameter requires greater finger flexor engagement and reduces grip endurance, making it an effective combined lat and forearm training variation.

execution.starting_position: Wrap a fat grip or towel around the barbell end secured in a landmine unit. Stagger the feet with the working-side foot forward. Hinge at the hips and grasp the thick bar end.
execution.setup_instructions: Fat grip adapters (marketed under various brand names) can be slid onto bar sleeves. A folded gym towel is a free alternative that also increases challenge. Load the bar appropriately — the grip will fatigue before the back does.
steps: Step 1: Establish the staggered hinge position and grip the thick bar firmly.
Step 2: Depress the shoulder blade of the working side.
Step 3: Row the bar end to the hip, driving elbow up and out.
Step 4: Hold for 1 second at the top.
Step 5: Lower under control, fully extending the arm and allowing the lat to stretch.
execution.breathing_instructions: Exhale on the row. Inhale lowering.
common_mistakes: Dropping the grip before the back fatigues — increase grip work separately to extend sets
Pulling toward the chest rather than the hip
safety_considerations: Ensure the fat grip is fully seated on the bar and cannot slip
Maintain neutral wrist alignment — do not flex or extend excessively with the thick grip
execution.range_of_motion_guidance: Full arm extension to elbow above torso.
coaching_cues: Squeeze the bar like you're crushing it
Lead with the elbow, not the hand
Full stretch at the bottom of every rep

name: Medicine Ball Chest Pass
description: The medicine ball chest pass is a plyometric upper body exercise in which a medicine ball is explosively thrown forward from the chest against a wall or to a partner, then caught and immediately repeated. It trains the explosive pushing power of the pectoral muscles and triceps through a ballistic press pattern, making it a sport-specific power exercise for athletes requiring rapid upper body force generation in sports such as basketball and wrestling.

execution.starting_position: Stand facing a solid wall at an arm's length plus ball distance, or face a partner. Hold the medicine ball at chest height with both hands.
execution.setup_instructions: Use a solid, reinforced wall or trained partner. Stand 1–2 meters from the wall depending on rebound speed required.
steps: Step 1: Hold the medicine ball at chest height with both hands, elbows bent and pointing outward.
Step 2: Explosively extend the arms and push the ball into the wall or to a partner with maximum force.
Step 3: Catch the rebounding ball with both hands, absorbing slightly, then immediately load and re-throw.
Step 4: Maintain a stable stance throughout. Slight engagement of the legs and trunk on each throw.
execution.breathing_instructions: Exhale sharply on each throw. Inhale as you catch.
common_mistakes: Pausing between catch and throw — the stretch-shortening cycle requires a quick turnaround
Throwing with only the arms — a slight trunk and leg load increases power
Using too heavy a ball — reduces velocity and defeats the plyometric intent
safety_considerations: Use a medicine ball of appropriate weight — heavy enough for resistance, light enough for maximum velocity.
Ensure the wall can withstand repeated impacts.
execution.range_of_motion_guidance: Full arm extension on throw. Catch with slightly bent elbows to absorb.
execution.tempo_recommendations: Rapid fire: 10–20 reps. Focus on minimizing time from catch to next throw.
coaching_cues: Throw hard — catch fast — throw again
Arm extension — not just a push
Minimal pause on catch

name: Medicine Ball Push-Up Switch
description: A dynamic push-up variation where one hand rests on a medicine ball while the other is on the floor. After each repetition, the ball is rolled to the opposite hand, alternating which arm receives the elevated unstable position. This creates a lateral shifting load pattern that trains unilateral pressing strength, shoulder stability, and anti-rotation core control in an alternating fashion.

execution.starting_position: Begin in a high plank with one hand on a medicine ball and the other on the floor, hands roughly shoulder-width apart in total.
execution.setup_instructions: Use a firm, smooth-surfaced medicine ball that rolls easily on the floor surface. A rubberized floor or smooth tile works best for the rolling transition.
steps: Step 1: Begin with right hand on ball, left hand on floor. Perform one controlled push-up.
Step 2: At the top of the push-up, shift weight to the left hand and roll the ball from the right hand to the left hand.
Step 3: Reestablish balance with left hand on ball, right hand on floor. Perform the next push-up.
Step 4: Roll ball back to the right and repeat. Each push-up on each side counts as one rep.
execution.breathing_instructions: Inhale on descent, exhale on press. Breathe normally during the ball transfer.
common_mistakes: Rolling the ball before fully completing the push-up
Losing hip alignment during the lateral weight shift
Using a ball that is too large, making the hand-to-floor height difference too great
safety_considerations: Ensure the ball does not roll away rapidly — keep one hand on it at all times
On slippery floors, place ball against a wall to limit travel
execution.range_of_motion_guidance: Full push-up range on each side. The ball-side hand gets a greater stretch depth due to elevation.
coaching_cues: Control the ball roll — do not let it get away from you
Keep hips square and level during the lateral transfer

name: Medicine Ball Slam
description: The medicine ball slam is a full-body plyometric exercise in which a slam ball or medicine ball is raised overhead and then slammed forcefully into the ground using a whole-body hip hinge. The simultaneous extension and flexion chain, from full overhead reach to rapid hip hinge and forceful arm drive downward, trains the anterior chain's ability to rapidly generate and transfer force. The exercise is used for power development, conditioning, and as an outlet for high-intensity effort.

execution.starting_position: Stand with feet shoulder-width apart, holding the slam ball with both hands at hip height.
execution.setup_instructions: Use a slam ball (non-bouncing) on a hard floor or rubber surface. Ensure adequate overhead and surrounding clearance.
steps: Step 1: Hold the slam ball at hip height with both hands.
Step 2: Raise the ball overhead by extending the hips and reaching the arms fully overhead.
Step 3: Immediately initiate a powerful hip hinge and simultaneous arm drive downward.
Step 4: Slam the ball into the floor as forcefully as possible, hinging deeply at the hips and bending the knees slightly.
Step 5: Pick the ball up (or catch the rebound if using a medicine ball) and repeat.
execution.breathing_instructions: Exhale forcefully as the ball is slammed. Inhale on the way back up.
common_mistakes: Only using the arms — the hip hinge and trunk flexion must generate most of the force
Releasing the ball at the wrong point — release as arms reach the bottom of the arc
Not reaching fully overhead at the top — shortens range and reduces force potential
safety_considerations: Use a slam ball (not a standard rubber medicine ball that may bounce back unpredictably at high force).
Ensure nobody is standing nearby — a ball can bounce sideways.
execution.range_of_motion_guidance: Full overhead extension. Full hip hinge at the bottom.
execution.tempo_recommendations: Maximum effort on each slam. 8–12 reps for conditioning. 5–8 for maximum power.
coaching_cues: Reach high — then slam hard
Hinge at the hip — not just a crunch
Put everything into it

name: Medicine Ball Slam — Kneeling
description: A medicine ball slam performed from the kneeling position (both knees on the floor), which removes the leg drive component and places the full power generation demand on the core and upper body. The overhead-to-ground throw trains explosive hip flexion and spinal flexion with no hip extension assist, creating a unique anti-extension-to-flexion power pattern. Used in core power development, rehabilitation programs where standing is contraindicated, and metabolic conditioning.

execution.starting_position: Kneel on a mat with both knees and shins on the floor. Hold a slam medicine ball with both hands in front of the chest.
execution.setup_instructions: Use a non-bounce slam ball (dead ball). Kneel on a mat for comfort. Begin with a lighter weight (4-6 kg) before increasing.
steps: Step 1: Kneel upright with the ball at chest height.
Step 2: Raise the ball overhead with arms fully extended, rising tall through the torso.
Step 3: Slam the ball to the floor in front of the knees with maximum force, allowing the spine to flex through the motion.
Step 4: Catch or retrieve the ball and return to the overhead position. Repeat.
execution.breathing_instructions: Exhale forcefully during the slam. Inhale as you raise overhead.
common_mistakes: Using a bouncy ball that creates safety hazard — only use slam (dead) balls
Leaning back excessively overhead rather than simply raising the arms
Not following through the slam — the torso should flex fully through the throw
safety_considerations: Use a dead ball only — a rubber bounce ball can rebound dangerously from the floor
Do not perform near low ceilings
Knee comfort requires a thick mat
execution.range_of_motion_guidance: Full overhead extension on the wind-up. Full spinal flexion through the slam.
execution.tempo_recommendations: 1 repetition every 2-3 seconds. Explosive slam, controlled pickup.
coaching_cues: Reach tall overhead before you slam — the full extension before the flexion is key
Slam through the floor — not just to the floor
Drive the ball down with the entire upper body — not just the arms

name: Medicine Ball Wall Ball Shot
description: A powerful throwing movement where a medicine ball is caught from a squat, then thrown against a high wall target on the way up. This integrates lower body power with core transfer and upper body power. It is a staple CrossFit and conditioning movement.

execution.starting_position: Set up for Medicine Ball Wall Ball Shot in proper position.
execution.setup_instructions: Prepare body and equipment for Medicine Ball Wall Ball Shot.
steps: Step 1: Stand facing wall holding medicine ball at chest. Set a target high on wall.
Step 2: Descend into a full squat catching ball to chest.
Step 3: Drive out of squat and throw ball to target using full body extension.
Step 4: Catch returning ball in slight squat and immediately repeat.
execution.breathing_instructions: Breathe steadily; never hold breath during static holds.
common_mistakes: Under-squatting
Throwing with arms only instead of legs
safety_considerations: Build prerequisite strength before attempting advanced variations.
Stop if joint pain occurs.
execution.range_of_motion_guidance: Full range of motion with control at all times.
coaching_cues: Full depth squat before throwing
Drive through heels and extend hips fully

name: Monkey Bar Traverse
description: A continuous traverse across a series of horizontal bars or rungs moving hand over hand. The movement demands grip endurance, shoulder stability, and rhythm. Used in obstacle courses, military fitness tests, and gymnastics, the traverse develops forearm endurance and lat strength.

execution.starting_position: Set up for Monkey Bar Traverse in proper strongman position.
execution.setup_instructions: Prepare all equipment and body position for Monkey Bar Traverse.
steps: Step 1: Hang from first bar with both hands.
Step 2: Swing body forward and reach for next bar with alternating hands.
Step 3: Continue traverse with rhythmic hand-over-hand movement.
Step 4: Traverse full length and dismount safely at the end.
execution.breathing_instructions: Brace core maximally before every lift. Breathe between reps if needed.
common_mistakes: Stopping momentum mid-traverse
Gripping too tightly causing forearm fatigue
safety_considerations: Use collars on all loaded barbells.
Ensure clear path for carries.
Have spotters for overhead movements.
execution.range_of_motion_guidance: Full range of motion specific to the implement being used.
coaching_cues: Maintain rhythm throughout
Loose grip between catches to save forearms

name: Monster Walks with Band Around Ankles
description: Monster walks are a dynamic hip abductor exercise performed by walking laterally with a resistance band looped around the ankles. Maintaining a quarter-squat position throughout keeps constant tension on the hip abductors. This exercise is commonly used in warm-up protocols and rehabilitation to strengthen the gluteus medius, improve lateral hip stability, and address knee valgus patterns during athletic movement.

execution.starting_position: Place a resistance band around both ankles. Stand with feet hip-width apart in a quarter-squat position — knees slightly bent, hips pushed back slightly, chest tall.
execution.setup_instructions: Choose a band that creates meaningful resistance without causing the torso to tip side to side during each step. Clear a path of at least 3-4 meters for lateral movement.
steps: Step 1: Adopt a quarter-squat stance with the band taut between the ankles.
Step 2: Step laterally with the lead foot, widening the stance beyond shoulder width.
Step 3: Follow with the trail foot, returning to shoulder-width — do not let feet come fully together.
Step 4: Continue for the prescribed distance or steps, then repeat in the opposite direction.
execution.breathing_instructions: Breathe rhythmically throughout. Exhale on each step if needed; do not hold your breath.
common_mistakes: Allowing the torso to sway laterally with each step
Letting feet come fully together (releases band tension)
Standing fully upright rather than maintaining the squat position
safety_considerations: If you have knee pain, reduce band resistance and ensure knees track over toes
Stop if you feel hip flexor cramping — reduce range or band resistance
execution.range_of_motion_guidance: Each lateral step should be wide enough to maintain continuous band tension. Avoid shuffling with feet too close together.
execution.tempo_recommendations: Controlled — 1 second per step, maintaining consistent tension throughout
coaching_cues: Stay low throughout — do not bob up and down
Drive through the outer hip to step, not the knee
Keep toes pointing forward — avoid external rotation compensation

name: Monster Walks on Forefeet
description: A monster walk variation performed on the balls of the feet (tiptoe position) while maintaining a mini band resistance above the knees. Rising onto the forefeet during the lateral walk adds a continuous calf and ankle stability demand to the standard gluteus medius activation of monster walks, creating a combined lower limb rehabilitation stimulus. This variation is used in advanced ankle rehabilitation, calf strengthening, and hip-ankle integration programs.

execution.starting_position: Place a mini band loop above the knees. Rise onto the balls of both feet. Assume a quarter-squat position with hips pushed back slightly, feet hip-width apart.
execution.setup_instructions: Ensure adequate space for 10-12 lateral steps in each direction. Begin with a lighter band to master the balance before adding resistance.
steps: Step 1: Rise onto the forefeet with the band above the knees and maintain this elevated position throughout.
Step 2: Take a lateral step to the right, keeping the toes forward and the band taut.
Step 3: Bring the left foot partially in (maintaining some width) to keep band tension.
Step 4: Continue walking laterally for the prescribed steps, then reverse direction. The forefeet stay elevated throughout.
execution.breathing_instructions: Breathe continuously. The sustained tiptoe position is demanding — do not hold the breath.
common_mistakes: Lowering the heels during the walk — the forefoot elevation must be sustained throughout
Letting the feet drift parallel or together, losing band tension
Excessive forward lean — maintain an upright torso
safety_considerations: If ankle stability is compromised, begin with standard monster walks before this elevated variation
Perform near a wall for safety during initial attempts
execution.range_of_motion_guidance: Lateral step width should maintain band tension without forcing knee valgus. Stay on the forefeet throughout.
execution.tempo_recommendations: 1 step per 1-1.5 seconds. Controlled — not rushing.
coaching_cues: Heels never touch the floor — stay on the balls of the feet the whole time
Keep toes pointing forward — not outward
Feel both the outer hip and the calf working simultaneously

name: Narrow-Grip Decline Barbell Bench Press
description: A decline bench press variation using a close, narrow grip that heavily shifts the emphasis from the pectorals to the triceps. The decline angle combined with the narrow grip maximizes triceps long head activation while still providing meaningful lower pectoralis major loading. Favored by powerlifters for triceps development and by bodybuilders targeting the sternal pec fibers with a triceps-intensive pressing movement.

execution.starting_position: Lie on a decline bench (15–30 degrees decline) with feet secured. Grip the barbell with hands roughly shoulder-width apart or slightly narrower. Bar above the lower chest.
execution.setup_instructions: Set the decline bench at 15–30 degrees. Ensure the rack height is appropriate. Secure feet. The grip should be shoulder-width — not so narrow that it stresses the wrists.
steps: Step 1: Unrack the bar and position it above the lower chest, arms extended.
Step 2: Lower the bar to the lower chest keeping elbows relatively tucked (not flared) due to the narrow grip.
Step 3: Touch the lower chest and immediately press back up, extending the elbows forcefully.
Step 4: Fully lock out the elbows at the top. The triceps should be under significant tension at lockout.
execution.breathing_instructions: Inhale before descent, exhale forcefully on the press.
common_mistakes: Grip too narrow — hands closer than shoulder width causes excessive wrist stress
Letting elbows flare wide, reducing triceps contribution
Feet unsecured on the decline bench
safety_considerations: Secure feet firmly on the decline; feet unsecured is a safety risk
Use a spotter for heavier sets
Avoid grips inside shoulder-width — wrist pain is a common result
execution.range_of_motion_guidance: Full range from lower chest to full elbow lockout. The narrow grip actually lengthens the range of motion at the elbow.
coaching_cues: Tuck the elbows to work the triceps — flaring negates the grip advantage
Squeeze hard at lockout — the decline + narrow grip puts peak triceps tension at the top

name: Natural Stone Shoulder
description: A traditional strength feat where an irregularly shaped natural rock is lifted from the ground and placed on one shoulder. The unpredictable shape demands adaptive grip and body position. This develops the same hip drive and upper body power as atlas stone training but with a unique challenge.

execution.starting_position: Set up for Natural Stone Shoulder in proper strongman position.
execution.setup_instructions: Prepare all equipment and body position for Natural Stone Shoulder.
steps: Step 1: Position over natural stone finding best grip on irregular surface.
Step 2: Pull stone up to lap position using deadlift pattern.
Step 3: Continue lifting stone up torso toward shoulder level.
Step 4: Load stone onto shoulder and stand fully upright.
execution.breathing_instructions: Brace core maximally before every lift. Breathe between reps if needed.
common_mistakes: Not adapting to irregular shape
Pulling with arms
safety_considerations: Use collars on all loaded barbells.
Ensure clear path for carries.
Have spotters for overhead movements.
execution.range_of_motion_guidance: Full range of motion specific to the implement being used.
coaching_cues: Find the best grip given the rock's shape
Legs and hips do the heavy work

name: Neck Curl
description: The neck curl is performed lying supine on a bench with the head extending off the edge, using a plate or neck harness to resist cervical flexion. The exercise targets the deep cervical flexors and sternocleidomastoid, building anterior neck strength and stability that supports the cervical spine under load. It is used by combat athletes, football players, and lifters seeking to strengthen the neck musculature for performance and injury prevention.

execution.starting_position: Lie on a flat bench with the head extending off one end. Hold a weight plate against the forehead with both hands, or use a neck harness. Begin with the head in a neutral or slightly extended position.
execution.setup_instructions: Begin with no additional weight (bodyweight) or a very light plate (2.5-5 lbs). The neck musculature is not accustomed to direct loading and must be progressed extremely slowly.
steps: Step 1: Lie supine with the head off the bench edge, holding a plate to the forehead or wearing a neck harness.
Step 2: Begin from the neutral or slightly extended position.
Step 3: Curl the head forward, bringing the chin toward the chest (cervical flexion).
Step 4: Hold briefly at the top.
Step 5: Lower slowly and under full control back to the start.
execution.breathing_instructions: Exhale on the curl, inhale on the descent.
common_mistakes: Using too heavy a weight before the neck is conditioned — build progressively over weeks
Jerking the head — movement must be slow and controlled
Performing this exercise if experiencing any neck pain or disc issues
safety_considerations: This exercise is contraindicated with any cervical disc pathology or acute neck pain
Progress load extremely slowly — the cervical spine is delicate
Always use a spotter or be conservative with plate placement
execution.range_of_motion_guidance: From neutral or slight extension to full cervical flexion (chin to chest).
coaching_cues: Slow and controlled — always
Build weeks of work before adding weight
If it hurts — stop

name: Prone Neck Extension
description: The prone neck extension is performed lying face-down on a bench with the head extending off the edge, using a plate on the back of the head to resist cervical extension. It targets the posterior neck musculature — the cervical erectors and upper trapezius fibers — building strength in the often-neglected extension pattern. Combined with the neck curl, it provides balanced cervical musculature development essential for spine stability and contact-sport performance.

execution.starting_position: Lie face-down (prone) on a flat bench with the head extending off one end. Hold a weight plate against the back of the head with both hands. Begin with the head flexed forward.
execution.setup_instructions: Begin with no weight (bodyweight only). Progress load conservatively over multiple weeks of training before adding any resistance.
steps: Step 1: Lie prone with the head extending off the bench, plate held to the back of the head.
Step 2: Begin from the flexed position (head angled toward the floor).
Step 3: Extend the head upward and backward into full cervical extension.
Step 4: Hold briefly at the top.
Step 5: Lower slowly back to the starting flexed position.
execution.breathing_instructions: Exhale on the extension, inhale on the descent.
common_mistakes: Using excessive range of motion — extend to a comfortable position, not maximum
Adding weight too quickly
Performing with any cervical pathology or acute pain
safety_considerations: Contraindicated with any disc issues, cervical stenosis, or acute neck pain
Progress extremely conservatively
Always use controlled motion — never jerk or bounce
execution.range_of_motion_guidance: From cervical flexion (head down) to comfortable cervical extension (head up and back).
coaching_cues: Slow and controlled always
Don't force the range — work to comfortable extension
Match this volume with neck curl work for balance

name: Neck Harness Extension
description: The neck harness extension uses a specialized head harness with a chain and weight plate, allowing cervical extension against loaded resistance while standing, seated, or in a hip-hinge position. The harness distributes force evenly around the head and skull, enabling heavier loading than plate-on-head variations while maintaining safety. It is a staple neck-strengthening exercise for combat sports athletes, wrestlers, football players, and lifters seeking maximal posterior cervical strength.

execution.starting_position: Fit the neck harness securely on the head. Attach the chain and weight. Stand or sit with the torso bent forward (hip hinge), or lie prone on a bench. Begin with the head in a neutral or slightly flexed position.
execution.setup_instructions: The neck harness is the specialized equipment required. Begin conservatively and add weight only after several weeks of consistent training at bodyweight neck exercises.
steps: Step 1: Don the neck harness with an appropriate weight attached.
Step 2: Take a hip-hinge or seated position, head hanging forward.
Step 3: Extend the neck upward, bringing the head to a neutral or slightly extended position.
Step 4: Hold briefly at the top.
Step 5: Lower slowly back to the starting position with controlled cervical flexion.
execution.breathing_instructions: Exhale on the extension upward, inhale on the descent.
common_mistakes: Using too much weight before the neck musculature is conditioned
Extending too far back — work to a comfortable, not maximum, range
Using jerky movement — controlled motion is essential
safety_considerations: The neck harness must fit properly before loading — a poor fit can create dangerous force distribution
Contraindicated with any cervical pathology
Build very slowly — weeks of unloaded neck work before adding harness resistance
execution.range_of_motion_guidance: Comfortable cervical flexion at the bottom to comfortable extension at the top.
coaching_cues: Fit the harness correctly first
Slow controlled movement always
Don't force range — work to comfortable extension

name: Neutral-Grip Dumbbell Bench Press
description: The Neutral-Grip Dumbbell Bench Press is performed with the palms facing each other (thumbs pointing toward the ceiling) throughout the movement. This grip reduces external rotation demand on the shoulder joint compared to a pronated grip, making it a preferable option for individuals with shoulder impingement, AC joint issues, or rotator cuff concerns while maintaining effective pectoral and triceps training.

execution.starting_position: Lie flat on a bench holding a dumbbell in each hand with palms facing each other. Dumbbells positioned at chest level, elbows bent at approximately 90 degrees.
execution.setup_instructions: No special setup required. The neutral grip is natural with dumbbells — simply orient the grip so thumbs point upward rather than forward.
steps: Step 1: Press the dumbbells upward from the chest, maintaining the neutral grip throughout.
Step 2: Extend the elbows to full lockout.
Step 3: Lower back to the starting position, keeping palms facing each other.
Step 4: Repeat for the prescribed reps.
execution.breathing_instructions: Inhale before lowering. Exhale as you press up.
common_mistakes: Rotating the grip to pronated mid-set, losing the joint-friendly benefit
Allowing the elbows to flare wide
safety_considerations: This is recommended for individuals with anterior shoulder pain — do not force a pronated grip if pain is present
Consult a healthcare provider if shoulder pain persists
execution.range_of_motion_guidance: Full elbow extension at top; elbows descend to 90 degrees or slightly below at bottom.
coaching_cues: Palms face each other — keep them facing each other at all times
Elbows track toward the feet, not flaring to the sides

name: Neutral-Grip Pull-Up
description: The neutral-grip pull-up is performed with palms facing each other, which places the shoulder in a mechanically advantaged and more comfortable position than the pronated (overhand) grip. This variation is typically easier to perform than a standard pull-up and is recommended for those with wrist, elbow, or shoulder discomfort during overhand pulling, while still providing strong lat and biceps stimulus.

execution.starting_position: Grasp parallel handles or a neutral-grip attachment with palms facing each other and arms fully extended. Hang in a dead hang with the core lightly braced.
execution.setup_instructions: Use a pull-up bar with neutral-grip handles, a rack-mounted neutral-grip attachment, or gymnastic rings set parallel. Adjust width to shoulder-width for optimal shoulder mechanics.
steps: Step 1: Begin from a full dead hang, lats on stretch, core braced.
Step 2: Depress the shoulder blades and initiate the pull by driving the elbows down and back.
Step 3: Pull the chest toward the handles until the chin clears or the chest approaches the handles.
Step 4: Pause at the top, squeezing the lats.
Step 5: Lower under control to the full dead hang position.
execution.breathing_instructions: Exhale during the pull. Inhale on the controlled descent.
common_mistakes: Shrugging the shoulders upward rather than depressing the scapulae at the start
Partial reps that do not achieve full arm extension at the bottom
Using kipping momentum rather than strict pulling
safety_considerations: Neutral grip is recommended for those with existing elbow or shoulder issues who struggle with the pronated pull-up
Ensure handles or ring straps are rated for body weight
execution.range_of_motion_guidance: Full dead hang at the bottom. At the top, the chin should clear the handles or the sternum should approach them.
coaching_cues: Depress and retract the shoulder blades before you bend the elbows
Think 'elbows to ribs', not 'hands to shoulders'
Finish the rep completely — full extension at the bottom every time

name: Nordic Hamstring Curl Eccentric
description: The Nordic hamstring curl eccentric is a high-load hamstring exercise in which the exerciser slowly lowers the body forward from a kneeling position while the hamstrings eccentrically resist. It produces the highest eccentric hamstring forces of any bodyweight exercise and is extensively supported by research for reducing hamstring strain injury rates. It is used in both injury prevention programs and hamstring rehabilitation after strain.

execution.starting_position: Kneel on a mat with the ankles secured under a fixed object (a loaded barbell, a partner holding the ankles, or under a GHD pad). The body is upright with hips fully extended.
execution.setup_instructions: Secure the ankles under a barbell, have a partner hold them, or use a GHD machine. Use a mat under the knees. Keep the hips extended throughout — do not allow them to flex.
steps: Step 1: Kneel with ankles secured and body upright in a tall kneeling position.
Step 2: Keeping the hips extended and body in a straight line from knees to head, slowly lower the entire body forward toward the floor.
Step 3: Use the hamstrings eccentrically to resist the fall as long as possible.
Step 4: When the hamstrings can no longer hold the descent, catch yourself with the hands and push back to the start.
Step 5: Use the hands to assist the return to upright — the concentric phase is not the training goal.
execution.breathing_instructions: Exhale during the descent. Inhale at the bottom before pushing back up.
common_mistakes: Hips flexing during the descent — the body must remain in a straight line from knees to head
Descending too fast in early stages — control the tempo
Skipping progression — beginners should start with heavily assisted eccentrics (hands very close to knees) before attempting a full lowering
safety_considerations: Very high hamstring load — this is classified as advanced and should not be performed in the first 2 weeks post-hamstring strain
DOMS (delayed onset muscle soreness) is very common after the first session — start with 2–3 reps only
Progress from 3×5 over several weeks before attempting high volumes
execution.range_of_motion_guidance: Descend as slowly as possible to the floor or as far as the hamstrings can control. Full range is from upright to prone.
execution.tempo_recommendations: Start: 3–5 reps × 2 sets. Progress over 4–6 weeks to 3×10. The descent should take 3–5 seconds.
coaching_cues: Keep your hips locked out — do not let them break backward
Think about fighting gravity for as long as possible
The hands are there to catch you, not to assist the descent
