name: One-Arm Barbell Row
description: A unilateral back exercise using a barbell loaded on one end (the other end is anchored in a landmine or wedged into a corner). The single-arm pulling pattern allows greater range of motion than many cable or dumbbell rows and loads the lat, rhomboid, and rear deltoid through a unique diagonal force vector.

execution.starting_position: Straddle the barbell end with one foot forward. Hinge at the hips and grip the loaded end of the barbell with the outside hand.
execution.setup_instructions: Anchor a barbell in a landmine attachment or corner. Load the free end. Stand beside the weighted end in a staggered stance.
steps: Step 1: Hinge at the hips to approximately 45 degrees with the core braced.
Step 2: Pull the loaded end of the bar up toward the hip, driving the elbow back and out.
Step 3: At the top, rotate the shoulder slightly to increase lat contraction.
Step 4: Lower under control to full arm extension and repeat.
execution.breathing_instructions: Exhale on the pull. Inhale on the return.
common_mistakes: Rotating the torso excessively to assist the pull
Not hinging forward enough
safety_considerations: This row allows the shoulder to pronate at the top for increased range — this is intentional
execution.range_of_motion_guidance: Full arm extension at the bottom. Bar pulled to the hip at the top.
coaching_cues: Drive the elbow back and out
Full stretch at the bottom

name: 1-Board Bench Press
description: The 1-Board Bench Press is a bench press variation where a single wooden board (approximately 2 inches thick) is placed on the chest to shorten the range of motion slightly. This variation allows the lifter to overload the upper portion of the pressing movement, building strength in the mid-to-top range where many lifters experience a sticking point.

execution.starting_position: Lie on a flat bench. A training partner holds a 2-inch board flat against your chest. Grip the bar slightly wider than shoulder-width.
execution.setup_instructions: Have a training partner hold a 2x6 or 2x8 wooden board against the lower chest. The board reduces ROM by approximately 2 inches. Can also be held in place with a shirt or elastic band.
steps: Step 1: Unrack the bar and lower it under control to the board.
Step 2: Touch the board with the bar and pause briefly before pressing.
Step 3: Drive the bar back up to full elbow extension.
Step 4: Repeat for the prescribed reps, keeping the board in contact with the chest throughout.
execution.breathing_instructions: Inhale and brace before lowering. Exhale as you drive the bar up.
common_mistakes: Bouncing off the board rather than pausing
Failing to maintain upper back tension during the reduced ROM
safety_considerations: Requires a training partner to hold the board safely
Can be used with loads slightly above your full ROM max
execution.range_of_motion_guidance: Bar travels to the board surface only. Full lockout at top.
coaching_cues: Touch and go off the board — no bouncing
Stay tight and control the descent as you would a full ROM press

name: Overhead Band Pull-Apart
description: The overhead band pull-apart starts with arms raised overhead holding a resistance band and pulls the band apart behind the head, training the rear deltoids and middle trapezius through an overhead pulling arc. This positioning creates different stress on the shoulder rotators compared to the standard chest-height pull-apart, challenging the external rotators in a more vulnerable and often undertrained overhead position.

execution.starting_position: Hold a resistance band with both hands wider than shoulder width. Raise arms overhead — band taut across the front overhead.
execution.setup_instructions: Use a very light band — the overhead position greatly increases mechanical disadvantage.
steps: Step 1: Begin with arms overhead, band taut.
Step 2: Pull the band apart by moving the hands outward and downward in an arc.
Step 3: Continue until the band reaches behind the head or at least behind the ears.
Step 4: Return to the overhead position.
Step 5: Repeat.
execution.breathing_instructions: Exhale on the pull-apart. Inhale returning.
common_mistakes: Using too strong a band — the overhead position significantly reduces load capacity
Bending the elbows — arms stay straight throughout
safety_considerations: Very light band tension — this is a mobility and shoulder health exercise
Stop if shoulder pain occurs at any point in the arc
execution.range_of_motion_guidance: Band from overhead front to behind the head.
coaching_cues: Light band — quality beats quantity
Lead with the pinkies as you pull apart
Full arc — behind the head, not just beside

name: Overhead Barbell Carry
description: A loaded carry performed with a barbell held overhead at arm's length while walking. This demands extraordinary core stability to prevent spinal extension or lateral flexion under the overhead load. The movement challenges the entire shoulder girdle and core simultaneously.

execution.starting_position: Set up for Overhead Barbell Carry in proper position.
execution.setup_instructions: Prepare body and equipment for Overhead Barbell Carry.
steps: Step 1: Clean and press barbell to overhead lockout position.
Step 2: Walk in controlled steps maintaining barbell directly over center.
Step 3: Keep ribs down and avoid excessive arching at any point.
Step 4: Set barbell down safely at end of walk.
execution.breathing_instructions: Breathe steadily; never hold breath during static holds.
common_mistakes: Excessive lumbar arching
Looking down during carry
safety_considerations: Build prerequisite strength before attempting advanced variations.
Stop if joint pain occurs.
execution.range_of_motion_guidance: Full range of motion with control at all times.
coaching_cues: Keep ribs down and core braced
Eyes forward and slightly up

name: Overhead Cable Rope Tricep Extension
description: The overhead cable rope extension uses a rope attachment on a low cable pulley, with the lifter facing away from the machine and extending the forearms overhead. The overhead position puts the tricep long head in a maximally stretched position before each rep. The cable maintains constant tension even at full extension overhead, providing loading through the entire range of motion that free weight overhead extensions cannot match.

execution.starting_position: Attach a rope to a low cable pulley. Face away from the machine, grab the rope behind the head, elbows bent overhead.
execution.setup_instructions: Set the cable pulley low. Grab the rope with both hands behind the head, elbows pointing upward. Take a step forward to create tension.
steps: Step 1: Begin with elbows bent, rope behind the head, feeling the tricep stretch.
Step 2: Extend the elbows overhead, pressing the rope forward and up.
Step 3: Hold at full extension for one second.
Step 4: Return slowly to the starting position, maintaining the stretch.
execution.breathing_instructions: Exhale on extension, inhale on return.
common_mistakes: Flaring the elbows wide
Leaning excessively forward — maintain an upright torso
Pulling with the front delts instead of the triceps
safety_considerations: Avoid if there is shoulder impingement — the overhead position is demanding
execution.range_of_motion_guidance: Maximum stretch at the bottom to full elbow extension overhead.
coaching_cues: Elbows point up — not out
Feel the long head stretch
Full lockout overhead

name: Overhead Cable Triceps Extension (Straight Bar)
description: An overhead cable extension using a straight bar attached to a low pulley. The straight bar allows a pronated grip position that some lifters find creates better mind-muscle connection with the triceps. This is a classic bodybuilding exercise for the long head.

execution.starting_position: Set up for Overhead Cable Triceps Extension (Straight Bar) in the appropriate position.
execution.setup_instructions: Prepare equipment and body position for Overhead Cable Triceps Extension (Straight Bar).
steps: Step 1: Attach straight bar to low pulley. Face away from cable holding bar overhead.
Step 2: Keep upper arms vertical with elbows by ears.
Step 3: Extend elbows to press bar overhead to full lockout.
Step 4: Lower bar slowly behind head to full stretch position.
execution.breathing_instructions: Exhale during the exertion phase, inhale during the return.
common_mistakes: Dropping elbows forward
Moving upper arms
safety_considerations: Keep joints aligned throughout the movement.
Use controlled weight appropriate for skill level.
execution.range_of_motion_guidance: Move through full range of motion without compromising joint integrity.
coaching_cues: Keep elbows by ears throughout
Full extension and stretch each rep

name: Overhead Cable Tricep Extension
description: A tricep isolation exercise performed with a rope or straight bar attachment at a high cable pulley, extending the arms overhead. The overhead position places the long head of the triceps in a lengthened position, maximizing the stretch and providing greater hypertrophic stimulus compared to pushdown variations.

execution.starting_position: Stand facing away from a high cable pulley holding a rope attachment behind your head, elbows bent and pointing forward.
execution.setup_instructions: Attach a rope to the high cable pulley. Face away from the machine. Grab the rope and position it behind your head.
steps: Step 1: Keep the upper arms stationary and close to the head throughout.
Step 2: Extend the arms forward and downward, straightening the elbows.
Step 3: Fully extend the elbows at the bottom of the movement.
Step 4: Bend the elbows to return the hands behind the head under control.
execution.breathing_instructions: Exhale on the extension. Inhale on the return.
common_mistakes: Allowing the upper arms to drop or flare during the movement
Using momentum by leaning the torso
safety_considerations: Keep the upper arms close to the head and stationary throughout
execution.range_of_motion_guidance: Full extension of the elbows at the front. Full elbow flexion at the back — elbows well above the head.
coaching_cues: Elbows stay up and forward
Full stretch in the long head

name: Overhead Cable V-Bar Extension
description: An overhead triceps extension using a V-bar or angled bar attachment on a low cable pulley. The V-bar allows a neutral-ish grip angle that reduces wrist stress compared to straight bar variations. The overhead cable pull maximizes long head stretch.

execution.starting_position: Set up for Overhead Cable V-Bar Extension in the appropriate position.
execution.setup_instructions: Prepare equipment and body position for Overhead Cable V-Bar Extension.
steps: Step 1: Attach V-bar to low pulley. Face away and hold bar overhead.
Step 2: Bend elbows to lower bar behind head, keeping upper arms by ears.
Step 3: Lower until forearms pass parallel and long head is stretched.
Step 4: Press overhead to full extension.
execution.breathing_instructions: Exhale during the exertion phase, inhale during the return.
common_mistakes: Letting elbows drop outward
Moving torso instead of arms
safety_considerations: Keep joints aligned throughout the movement.
Use controlled weight appropriate for skill level.
execution.range_of_motion_guidance: Move through full range of motion without compromising joint integrity.
coaching_cues: Brace with elbows tight to head
Full extension at top

name: Overhead Dumbbell Extension with Strap Support
description: An overhead dumbbell triceps extension where a strap or pad is used to support the upper arm. The support eliminates upper arm drift under fatigue and ensures pure elbow extension throughout the set. This technique is used by competitive bodybuilders for maximum isolation.

execution.starting_position: Set up for Overhead Dumbbell Extension with Strap Support in the appropriate position.
execution.setup_instructions: Prepare equipment and body position for Overhead Dumbbell Extension with Strap Support.
steps: Step 1: Set up with upper arm resting on pad or against strap at ear level.
Step 2: Hold dumbbell overhead with elbow bent at 90 degrees.
Step 3: Extend elbow to press dumbbell overhead, upper arm against support.
Step 4: Lower slowly behind head maintaining contact with support.
execution.breathing_instructions: Exhale during the exertion phase, inhale during the return.
common_mistakes: Moving upper arm away from support
Using support to bounce
safety_considerations: Keep joints aligned throughout the movement.
Use controlled weight appropriate for skill level.
execution.range_of_motion_guidance: Move through full range of motion without compromising joint integrity.
coaching_cues: Maintain contact with support throughout
Squeeze long head at extension

name: Overhead Dumbbell Lunge
description: A lunge variation with dumbbells locked out overhead. The overhead position dramatically increases core stability demand, shoulder girdle endurance, and thoracic extension requirements while simultaneously training the lower body in a unilateral lunge pattern.

execution.starting_position: Stand tall holding a dumbbell in each hand pressed overhead with elbows fully locked out and arms close to ears.
execution.setup_instructions: Press the dumbbells to lockout overhead before beginning. Confirm shoulder mobility allows a true vertical lockout position.
steps: Step 1: Take a large step forward with one foot and lower into a lunge, keeping dumbbells overhead throughout.
Step 2: Lower the rear knee toward the floor while keeping the torso upright and arms vertical.
Step 3: Drive through the front heel to step forward, bringing the feet together.
Step 4: Repeat on the opposite side, continuing to walk forward.
execution.breathing_instructions: Breathe steadily throughout. Do not hold your breath with heavy overhead loading.
common_mistakes: Allowing the arms to drift forward from vertical overhead
Hyperextending the lower back to compensate for limited shoulder mobility
safety_considerations: Use lighter dumbbells than you would for a standard lunge — the overhead position is very demanding
Lower the weights immediately if shoulder pain occurs
execution.range_of_motion_guidance: Full lunge depth (rear knee near floor, front thigh parallel). Arms remain fully extended overhead.
coaching_cues: Squeeze the armpits to keep arms vertical
Ribs down — do not flare them

name: Overhead Farmer's Walk (Bottoms-Up Kettlebell)
description: The bottoms-up kettlebell overhead carry holds the kettlebell inverted (handle down, bell up) while walking. This grip requires the athlete to squeeze the handle forcefully and maintain precise wrist, elbow, and shoulder alignment to prevent the bell from falling, which dramatically increases rotator cuff activation compared to a standard overhead carry. The instability of the inverted bell creates continuous proprioceptive feedback, making this one of the most effective shoulder stability exercises available.

execution.starting_position: Hold a kettlebell with the bell inverted (bottoms-up) at the shoulder. The handle points down, the bell sits on top of the fist. Squeeze the handle hard.
execution.setup_instructions: Begin with a very light kettlebell — 8 or 12 kg is challenging for most athletes when inverted. Practice the stationary bottoms-up press before walking.
steps: Step 1: Press the inverted kettlebell overhead to lockout while maintaining the inverted position.
Step 2: Walk a designated distance (10-20 metres) while keeping the bell balanced overhead.
Step 3: Squeeze the handle continuously — the squeeze is what stabilizes the bell.
Step 4: Keep the working shoulder packed and the wrist straight.
Step 5: Lower, switch sides, and repeat.
execution.breathing_instructions: Breathe freely. Maintain a braced core throughout.
common_mistakes: Too heavy — the bell will wobble and fall; use a much lighter kettlebell than expected
Releasing the squeeze — the grip intensity is what prevents the bell from tipping
safety_considerations: Have a clear area in case the kettlebell falls
Master the stationary bottoms-up press and hold before walking
execution.range_of_motion_guidance: Maintained overhead lockout for the full walking distance.
coaching_cues: Squeeze the handle like you mean it
Wrist straight — no bend
Shoulder packed, not shrugged

name: Overhead Single-Arm Kettlebell Waiter Carry
description: The single-arm overhead kettlebell waiter carry challenges the entire lateral and anti-rotation core stabilization system by requiring the athlete to walk while holding a kettlebell locked out overhead in one hand. The overhead unilateral load creates a large lateral flexion and rotational demand on the contralateral core musculature, the shoulder girdle stabilizers, and the thoracic spine extensors simultaneously. It is both a core stability and shoulder integrity exercise that is highly transferable to functional strength tasks.

execution.starting_position: Clean and press a kettlebell to full lockout overhead in one hand. Stand tall with the arm straight, elbow locked, bicep beside the ear.
execution.setup_instructions: Begin with a light-to-moderate weight to establish shoulder stability and walking pattern before increasing load.
steps: Step 1: Lock the kettlebell out overhead with the working arm straight and elbow fully extended.
Step 2: Pack the shoulder by depressing the scapula and externally rotating the arm.
Step 3: Walk at a controlled pace for the prescribed distance or time.
Step 4: Keep the torso upright — resist any lateral flexion toward the weighted side.
Step 5: At the end of the distance, carefully lower the kettlebell and switch hands.
execution.breathing_instructions: Breathe normally throughout. Maintain a constant bracing level.
common_mistakes: Allowing the elbow to bend — the arm must remain fully locked out
Laterally flexing the trunk toward the weighted side — the spine should remain perfectly vertical
safety_considerations: Ensure full shoulder external rotation and scapular depression before beginning — a loose overhead position is a safety risk
execution.range_of_motion_guidance: Walk with full arm extension maintained. Distance typically 20–40 metres per set.
coaching_cues: Bicep beside the ear — arm is a pillar
Walk tall — do not lean

name: Seated Overhead Rope Cable Extension
description: A seated variation of the overhead cable triceps extension using a rope attachment. Sitting with cable behind ensures constant tension through the long head of the triceps. The rope allows the hands to separate at peak contraction for enhanced muscle activation.

execution.starting_position: Set up for Seated Overhead Rope Cable Extension in the appropriate position.
execution.setup_instructions: Prepare equipment and body position for Seated Overhead Rope Cable Extension.
steps: Step 1: Set low cable pulley. Sit facing away from cable with rope overhead.
Step 2: Hold rope behind head with elbows bent and upper arms vertical.
Step 3: Extend elbows to press rope overhead, separating handles at top.
Step 4: Lower slowly back behind head maintaining upper arm position.
execution.breathing_instructions: Exhale during the exertion phase, inhale during the return.
common_mistakes: Dropping elbows forward
Shortening range of motion
safety_considerations: Keep joints aligned throughout the movement.
Use controlled weight appropriate for skill level.
execution.range_of_motion_guidance: Move through full range of motion without compromising joint integrity.
coaching_cues: Spread the rope at the top
Keep elbows close to head

name: Overhead Squat
description: The overhead squat is a full squat performed with the barbell held locked out overhead in a wide snatch grip, demanding exceptional shoulder, thoracic, and ankle mobility alongside significant core stability and quadriceps strength. It is used in Olympic weightlifting as the catch position of the snatch, and independently as a mobility assessment tool and accessory exercise. The overhead position creates a large moment arm at the shoulders and spine, making core bracing critical throughout the movement.

execution.starting_position: Bar held overhead in a wide snatch grip with elbows locked out. Feet shoulder-width or slightly wider, toes turned out slightly.
execution.setup_instructions: Press out on the bar actively during the entire movement. Warm up shoulders, thoracic spine, and ankles thoroughly. Begin with a PVC pipe or empty bar.
steps: Step 1: Stand with bar overhead, locked out in a wide grip. Brace the core and press out against the bar.
Step 2: Initiate the squat by pushing the knees out in line with the toes and sitting back and down.
Step 3: Descend to full depth (hip crease below the knee) while maintaining bar position directly over the mid-foot.
Step 4: Keep the torso as upright as possible — the bar should remain over the base of support throughout.
Step 5: Drive through the full foot to stand, maintaining bar lockout throughout.
execution.breathing_instructions: Breathe in and brace before the descent. Exhale as you drive through the top of the squat.
common_mistakes: Bar drifting forward during the descent
Insufficient ankle or thoracic mobility causing the torso to fold forward
Letting the elbows bend under load
Knees caving inward
safety_considerations: This is a highly demanding mobility exercise. Develop prerequisite shoulder, thoracic, and ankle mobility before loading.
If unable to perform with an empty bar, use a PVC pipe to drill the pattern.
Be prepared to drop the bar safely forward.
execution.range_of_motion_guidance: Full depth squat — hip crease below the knee. Bar remains overhead and locked out throughout.
execution.tempo_recommendations: 3-1-1-0: 3 second descent, 1 second pause at bottom, 1 second drive up.
coaching_cues: Press out on the bar — elbows locked
Bar over mid-foot — the whole way down
Knees out, chest up, sit between your legs

name: Overhead Tricep Extension
description: The overhead tricep extension trains the triceps with the arms raised overhead, which places the long head of the triceps under a full stretch. Because the long head crosses the shoulder joint, training it in the overhead position provides a greater range of motion and stretch compared to pushdowns or skull crushers.

execution.starting_position: Sit or stand holding one dumbbell with both hands. Press the dumbbell overhead with arms extended. Grip the inner plate of the dumbbell with both hands, thumbs wrapped around the handle.
execution.setup_instructions: Can also be performed with a cable using a rope attachment set at a low pulley, facing away from the machine.
steps: With upper arms vertical and elbows pointing toward the ceiling, lower the dumbbell behind the head by bending the elbows.
Lower until forearms are approximately parallel to the floor or the stretch becomes significant.
Extend the elbows to press the dumbbell back to full extension overhead.
execution.breathing_instructions: Inhale on the descent, exhale on extension.
common_mistakes: Allowing the elbows to flare out to the sides
Moving the upper arms instead of just hinging at the elbows
safety_considerations: If the dumbbell is heavy, have someone hand it to you overhead
execution.range_of_motion_guidance: Full overhead extension at top, forearms parallel to floor or below at the bottom.
coaching_cues: Keep elbows pointing straight at the ceiling
Feel the long head of the tricep stretching at the bottom of each rep

name: Overhead Tricep Stretch
description: The overhead tricep stretch targets the long head of the triceps brachii, which is the only tricep head that crosses the shoulder joint. By raising the arm overhead and bending the elbow, the long head is placed on maximal stretch as both shoulder flexion and elbow flexion work simultaneously to lengthen it. This stretch is commonly used as part of upper body warm-up and cool-down routines.

execution.starting_position: Stand or sit tall. Raise one arm directly overhead.
execution.setup_instructions: No equipment needed. Can be performed seated or standing.
steps: Step 1: Raise one arm straight overhead.
Step 2: Bend the elbow, allowing the forearm and hand to drop behind the head.
Step 3: Use the opposite hand to gently push down on the elbow of the raised arm, increasing the stretch.
Step 4: Hold until a stretch is felt along the back of the upper arm — 30–60 seconds.
Step 5: Release and switch sides.
execution.breathing_instructions: Breathe slowly and evenly throughout.
common_mistakes: Applying excessive force through the assisting hand, stressing the elbow
Leaning sideways with the torso rather than keeping it upright
Not holding long enough for the stretch to take effect
safety_considerations: Apply gentle pressure only — the elbow joint is sensitive to forcing
If elbow discomfort arises, stop and assess
execution.range_of_motion_guidance: Bring the hand as far down behind the head as the shoulder allows without pain.
coaching_cues: Let the elbow point toward the ceiling
Use the other hand to gently guide, not force
Keep the torso upright and the core lightly engaged

name: Overhead Yoke Carry
description: An extreme strongman variation where the yoke or barbell is pressed and held overhead while walking. This demands elite-level overhead stability and core anti-extension strength under substantial load. Primarily a demonstration of strength and seen in exhibition events.

execution.starting_position: Set up for Overhead Yoke Carry in proper strongman position.
execution.setup_instructions: Prepare all equipment and body position for Overhead Yoke Carry.
steps: Step 1: Clean and press implement to full overhead lockout.
Step 2: Lock elbows fully and brace core maximally.
Step 3: Take controlled steps for target distance with implement overhead.
Step 4: Lower implement safely at the end.
execution.breathing_instructions: Brace core maximally before every lift. Breathe between reps if needed.
common_mistakes: Soft elbows overhead
Excessive lumbar arch
safety_considerations: Use collars on all loaded barbells.
Ensure clear path for carries.
Have spotters for overhead movements.
execution.range_of_motion_guidance: Full range of motion specific to the implement being used.
coaching_cues: Ribs down and core braced
Full elbow lockout before walking

name: Pallof Press
description: The Pallof press is an anti-rotation core stability exercise using a cable or resistance band. The load is set at a fixed angle perpendicular to the body and the lifter presses it out and back while resisting the rotational pull. It trains the core musculature to stabilize the spine against rotation, which is fundamental for athletic performance and spinal health.

execution.starting_position: Stand (or kneel) sideways to a cable machine at mid-torso height. Hold the handle with both hands against the chest. Stand far enough that the cable is taut and pulling the hands toward the machine.
execution.setup_instructions: Set the pulley to chest height. Attach a single handle. The load should be moderate — this is a stability, not strength, exercise.
steps: Press the cable handle straight out in front of the chest, extending the arms fully.
Hold the extended position for 2–3 seconds while resisting the rotational pull of the cable.
Return the handle back to the chest under control.
Complete all reps on one side before switching to the other.
execution.breathing_instructions: Exhale as you press out. Breathe normally while holding.
common_mistakes: Rotating the torso toward the cable — the core must resist this
Using too much weight — the goal is stability, not strength
execution.range_of_motion_guidance: Full arm extension at the press. Hold for the prescribed duration before returning.
coaching_cues: Do not let the cable twist your body — stay square to the wall in front of you
Brace the core before pressing — think about being a stone wall

name: Pallof Press with Overhead Raise
description: The Pallof press with overhead raise extends the standard anti-rotation Pallof press by raising the arms fully overhead after pressing the cable handle out from the chest, dramatically increasing the moment arm and anti-rotation demand on the core. At the overhead position, the torso must resist both rotational and anti-extension forces simultaneously, making this a comprehensive core stability challenge. The movement trains the deep stabilizing musculature of the spine under a large variety of loading directions in a single repetition.

execution.starting_position: Stand side-on to a cable machine with the pulley at chest height. Hold the handle with both hands at the chest, elbows bent. Feet shoulder-width apart, body perpendicular to the cable.
execution.setup_instructions: Set the pulley at chest height. Stand far enough that the cable provides meaningful anti-rotation resistance immediately.
steps: Step 1: Brace the core fully. Press the handle straight out from the chest until the arms are fully extended.
Step 2: Holding the arms straight, raise both arms overhead in a controlled arc until they are fully extended above the head.
Step 3: Pause for 1–2 seconds at the overhead position, resisting the cable pull.
Step 4: Lower the arms back to chest-height horizontal position.
Step 5: Return the handle to the chest. That is one rep. Complete all reps then switch sides.
execution.breathing_instructions: Exhale as pressing out. Hold the breath and brace during overhead phase. Exhale on return.
common_mistakes: Rotating toward the cable during the overhead phase — the spine should remain perfectly perpendicular
Losing the rib-down position as the arms go overhead — indicates insufficient core strength for overhead
safety_considerations: Avoid if shoulder mobility is insufficient for pain-free overhead reach
execution.range_of_motion_guidance: Full extension of the arms horizontally then fully overhead. Spine remains perpendicular to the cable throughout.
execution.tempo_recommendations: 2-2-2-1. Slow and deliberate in every phase.
coaching_cues: Ribs down — do not let the lower back arch as arms go overhead
Resist the pull — your spine does not move

name: Pallof Press
description: The Pallof press is an anti-rotation core stability exercise that challenges the ability to resist rotational forces rather than produce them. Performed with a resistance band or cable anchored to the side, the exerciser extends the arms in front of the chest and holds against the pull — requiring the entire core to contract isometrically to prevent rotation. It is a cornerstone of lumbar rehabilitation, athletic performance, and functional core training.

execution.starting_position: Anchor a resistance band at chest height. Stand perpendicular to the anchor, far enough away to create tension. Hold the band with both hands at the chest.
execution.setup_instructions: Anchor the band at a door frame or rack at chest height. Stand with feet shoulder-width apart, perpendicular to the anchor.
steps: Step 1: Hold the band with both hands pressed against the sternum. The band pulls horizontally toward the anchor point.
Step 2: Brace the core firmly. The feet, hips, and shoulders should all face straight ahead (perpendicular to the anchor).
Step 3: Slowly press the hands straight out in front of the chest, fully extending the arms.
Step 4: Hold for 2–3 seconds at full extension, resisting the pull of the band.
Step 5: Return the hands to the chest with control. Repeat for reps, then switch sides.
execution.breathing_instructions: Exhale and brace as the arms extend. Breathe steadily in the hold position.
common_mistakes: Rotating the torso toward the anchor — the goal is to prevent this rotation entirely
Feet shifting or hips rotating — maintain a stable square stance
Holding the breath excessively — learn to breathe while maintaining the brace
safety_considerations: Use very light resistance initially — the demand on the core is high relative to the apparent load
Safe for most low back pain populations — often one of the earliest core exercises reintroduced in lumbar rehab
execution.range_of_motion_guidance: Full arm extension and return. The range of motion is straightforward — the challenge is in preventing rotation throughout.
execution.tempo_recommendations: 2-second press out, 2–3 second hold, 2-second return. 10–15 reps × 2–3 sets per side.
coaching_cues: Squeeze your core like someone is about to punch you
Your body should look the same at full extension as at the start — no rotation
Press straight out from the sternum

name: Pallof Press with Rotation Step
description: A pallof press variation where after pressing out, the athlete takes a step forward or rotates the leading foot, increasing the lever arm and anti-rotation demand. This dynamic element trains core stability through changing base of support. Sport-specific for rotational athletes.

execution.starting_position: Set up for Pallof Press with Rotation Step in proper position.
execution.setup_instructions: Prepare body and equipment for Pallof Press with Rotation Step.
steps: Step 1: Stand sideways to cable with both hands on handle at chest.
Step 2: Press handle straight out from chest to full arm extension.
Step 3: Take a step or rotate leading foot while holding the press.
Step 4: Return hands to chest then step back to start position.
execution.breathing_instructions: Breathe steadily; never hold breath during static holds.
common_mistakes: Rotating torso while pressing
Using too much weight
safety_considerations: Build prerequisite strength before attempting advanced variations.
Stop if joint pain occurs.
execution.range_of_motion_guidance: Full range of motion with control at all times.
coaching_cues: Resist the cable's pull on the step
Light weight for movement quality

name: Parallel Bar L-Sit Walk
description: An L-sit hold on parallel bars where the athlete walks the bars forward by alternating hand placements while maintaining the L-position. This requires the core to maintain compression while the arms propel the body forward. An advanced gymnastic strength and coordination exercise.

execution.starting_position: Set up for Parallel Bar L-Sit Walk in proper strongman position.
execution.setup_instructions: Prepare all equipment and body position for Parallel Bar L-Sit Walk.
steps: Step 1: Set up in full L-sit on parallel bars with legs horizontal.
Step 2: Maintaining L-sit, shift weight to one hand and move other hand forward.
Step 3: Alternate hand placements to walk forward along bars.
Step 4: Complete distance while holding L-sit position throughout.
execution.breathing_instructions: Brace core maximally before every lift. Breathe between reps if needed.
common_mistakes: Dropping legs during hand transition
Moving too quickly
safety_considerations: Use collars on all loaded barbells.
Ensure clear path for carries.
Have spotters for overhead movements.
execution.range_of_motion_guidance: Full range of motion specific to the implement being used.
coaching_cues: Full L-sit mastery required before this
Slow controlled transitions

name: Passive Hanging — Scapular Decompression
description: Passive hanging involves gripping an overhead bar and allowing the bodyweight to fully decompress the shoulder girdle and spinal column. Unlike active hanging (where the scapulae are actively depressed), passive hanging allows the shoulder blades to elevate fully under the body's weight. This creates traction through the shoulder joint, stretches the latissimus dorsi and teres major, and gently decompresses the intervertebral discs of the thoracic and lumbar spine. Regular passive hanging is used in spinal decompression and shoulder mobility rehabilitation.

execution.starting_position: Grip an overhead pull-up bar or gymnastics rings with both hands shoulder-width apart. Use an overhand or mixed grip. Begin with feet off the floor if possible, or allow a slight bend in the knees if the bar is low.
execution.setup_instructions: Ensure the bar or hanging point is structurally sound and can support the full bodyweight. Use chalk or straps if grip strength is a limiting factor rather than the therapeutic goal.
steps: Step 1: Grip the bar and allow the body to hang freely, letting the shoulder blades rise and the weight fully load through the grip.
Step 2: Breathe deeply throughout the hang, allowing the chest and thoracic spine to expand and release on each exhale.
Step 3: Hold the passive hang for the target duration — beginning at 10-15 seconds and progressively increasing to 60+ seconds.
Step 4: Lower to the floor or step down from the hang under control. Rest and repeat.
execution.breathing_instructions: Deep, slow breathing throughout. Exhale completely to allow the thoracic cage to relax and decompress with each breath.
common_mistakes: Actively depressing the scapulae during what should be a passive hang — allow the shoulder blades to rise naturally
Gripping so tightly that the forearm tension prevents shoulder relaxation
Hanging for too long initially — build duration progressively to avoid elbow flexor soreness
safety_considerations: If you have a diagnosed shoulder subluxation or instability, check with a physiotherapist before passive hanging
Avoid if wrist or elbow pain occurs during the hang
Build hang duration gradually — beginning at 10-15 seconds and working toward 60 seconds over several weeks
execution.range_of_motion_guidance: Full passive elevation of the scapulae is the target. The body should feel fully decompressed and elongated.
execution.tempo_recommendations: Hold for 15-60 seconds per set. Build duration progressively over weeks.
coaching_cues: Let the shoulders rise — this is passive, not a lat pulldown
Breathe into the chest and feel the spine lengthen with each exhale
Relax the hands as much as possible while still maintaining grip

name: Pause Deadlift
description: The pause deadlift involves a deliberate hold at the sticking point — typically mid-shin height — during the ascent phase of the conventional deadlift. The pause eliminates momentum and forces the musculature to generate maximum force from a static position, building strength at the most mechanically challenging portion of the lift. It is a highly effective strength-building variation for powerlifters targeting their weakest point in the pull.

execution.starting_position: Set up identically to a conventional deadlift. Bar over mid-foot, neutral spine, hips below shoulders.
execution.setup_instructions: Use 70-85% of conventional deadlift maximum. Mark the mid-shin position visually before starting.
steps: Step 1: Initiate the deadlift identically to conventional — drive the legs and maintain back angle.
Step 2: When the bar reaches mid-shin height, pause completely for 2-3 seconds.
Step 3: Maintain maximum tightness during the pause — no relaxing.
Step 4: Drive through the pause and complete the lift to lockout.
Step 5: Return the bar to the floor under control and reset before the next rep.
execution.breathing_instructions: Inhale and brace before each rep. Hold the brace through the pause. Exhale at lockout.
common_mistakes: Losing tension during the pause — the hold must be active, not passive
Using too heavy a load, which forces the bar to move through the pause
Pausing at the wrong point — it should be mid-shin, the actual sticking point
safety_considerations: Reduce training load significantly from conventional deadlift maximum
Ensure consistent breath holding and bracing before each rep
execution.range_of_motion_guidance: Floor to lockout. Pause position is at mid-shin, which is the sticking point for most lifters.
execution.tempo_recommendations: 1-0-pause(2-3s)-0 (explosive off floor, hold at mid-shin, then drive through)
coaching_cues: Don't relax at the pause — stay tight
The pause is where you get stronger
Drive through the pause like it's a new rep

name: Pause Squat
description: The pause squat is a barbell back squat variation where the lifter pauses motionless at the bottom of the movement for a prescribed duration, typically two to five seconds, before driving back to the top. The pause eliminates the stretch-shortening reflex that assists normal squatting, forcing the muscles to generate force from a dead stop. This builds positional strength, reinforces technique, and identifies mobility or stability weaknesses.

execution.starting_position: Same setup as a standard barbell back squat: bar on upper traps, feet shoulder-width apart, toes pointed slightly outward.
execution.setup_instructions: Set up identically to a back squat. Use 70–85% of your normal squat working weight for 2-second pauses. Reduce weight further for longer pauses.
steps: Step 1: Unrack the bar and set up as for a back squat. Take a deep breath and brace.
Step 2: Descend under control to full depth — hips at or below parallel.
Step 3: Hold the bottom position completely still for the prescribed time (2–5 seconds). Do not relax. Actively maintain tension throughout: knees out, chest up, core braced.
Step 4: Without any counter-movement, drive explosively through the floor to return to standing.
Step 5: Exhale at the top, reset, and repeat.
execution.breathing_instructions: Inhale and brace before descent. Hold breath through the pause and ascent. Exhale at the top.
common_mistakes: Relaxing the core, knees, or torso position during the pause
Rising onto the toes at the bottom
Using too much weight, which turns the pause into a brief wobble
safety_considerations: Use safety bars — a failed pause squat has less momentum to rescue than a normal squat
Reduce load by 15–25% compared to your regular squat weight
execution.range_of_motion_guidance: Full depth (hips at or below parallel). The pause must be at the deepest position, not above parallel.
coaching_cues: Stay tight during the pause — don't let anything relax
Drive the knees out actively while holding the bottom
Explode up — don't grind up slowly

name: Pec Deck Peak Contraction
description: A pec deck flye variation where each repetition includes a deliberate 2–3 second isometric hold at the fully contracted position (arms together in front). This peak contraction technique maximizes tension on the pectoralis major at its shortest length, where the muscle generates a powerful squeeze. The paused technique is used specifically to develop the mind-muscle connection and improve the ability to feel and contract the chest at peak.

execution.starting_position: Sit in a pec deck machine with the back fully against the pad. Grip the handles or place forearms in the arm pads. Begin with arms open to the sides at shoulder height.
execution.setup_instructions: Adjust the seat height so the arms are at shoulder level when in the starting position. Adjust the starting-width to allow a full range of motion without shoulder discomfort. Select a moderate, controllable weight.
steps: Step 1: Begin with arms open, feeling the chest stretch.
Step 2: Drive the arms together in a sweeping arc.
Step 3: At full contraction — arms as close together as the machine allows — hold the position for 2–3 seconds. Squeeze the chest as hard as possible.
Step 4: Return under control to the starting position, feeling the full stretch. Repeat.
execution.breathing_instructions: Exhale as arms come together, hold breath briefly during the peak isometric, inhale on the return.
common_mistakes: Releasing the squeeze immediately at the top instead of holding the contraction
Using momentum to swing the arms together — slow and deliberate movement is essential
Shoulder blades lifting off the back pad during the squeeze
safety_considerations: Keep the back fully in contact with the seat back throughout
Adjust the starting width if shoulder discomfort occurs at the open position
execution.range_of_motion_guidance: Full range from maximum comfortable stretch to full contraction. The key is the held peak at the top.
execution.tempo_recommendations: 2-3-2-1 (2s sweep in, 3s peak hold, 2s return, 1s stretch)
coaching_cues: Squeeze as hard as you possibly can at the top — try to touch your elbows together
The hold is not a rest — it is the most important part of each rep

name: Pegboard Climb
description: A climbing movement using wooden pegs inserted into a vertical board where the athlete progresses hand over hand upward. This builds extraordinary grip strength, upper body pulling power, and shoulder stability. A staple of gymnastics strength testing and specialty functional fitness.

execution.starting_position: Set up for Pegboard Climb in proper strongman position.
execution.setup_instructions: Prepare all equipment and body position for Pegboard Climb.
steps: Step 1: Grip two pegs at the bottom of the pegboard at shoulder height.
Step 2: Pull body up and insert upper peg into the next hole above.
Step 3: Continue alternating peg placements up the board.
Step 4: Descend with the same alternating pattern under control.
execution.breathing_instructions: Brace core maximally before every lift. Breathe between reps if needed.
common_mistakes: Swinging body for momentum
Not fully locking arm on each reach
safety_considerations: Use collars on all loaded barbells.
Ensure clear path for carries.
Have spotters for overhead movements.
execution.range_of_motion_guidance: Full range of motion specific to the implement being used.
coaching_cues: Smooth deliberate movements
Descent is as important as ascent

name: Pendlay Row
description: The Pendlay row is a strict barbell rowing variation where the bar returns to the floor between every repetition. The dead-stop start eliminates momentum and forces a more explosive concentric contraction of the upper back musculature. With the torso held parallel to the floor, the rhomboids, middle and lower trapezius, and latissimus dorsi are heavily loaded through a full range of motion.

execution.starting_position: Stand over a barbell with feet hip-width apart and the bar over mid-foot. Hinge to grip the bar with an overhand grip slightly wider than shoulder-width. The torso must be parallel or near-parallel to the floor. The bar rests on the floor at the start of every rep.
execution.setup_instructions: Set up exactly as you would for a conventional deadlift but set the torso to horizontal. Use a pronated grip. Bumper plates are helpful so the bar drops safely to the floor each rep.
steps: Step 1: Begin with the bar on the floor, torso parallel to the ground, arms extended.
Step 2: Take a breath and brace the core hard.
Step 3: Explosively row the bar toward the lower chest or upper abdomen by driving the elbows up and back.
Step 4: At the top, squeeze the scapulae together fully.
Step 5: Lower the bar all the way to the floor in a controlled manner and allow it to come to a complete stop before the next rep.
execution.breathing_instructions: Inhale and brace before each rep. Exhale after the bar makes contact with the floor.
common_mistakes: Bouncing the bar off the floor instead of achieving a true dead stop
Raising the torso to assist the row, reducing back stimulus and stressing the lower back
Not reaching full scapular retraction at the top of each rep
safety_considerations: The strict horizontal torso position places significant demand on the erector spinae — do not perform when lower back is fatigued
Use bumper plates if possible to protect the floor and bar
execution.range_of_motion_guidance: Full dead-stop at the bottom to full scapular retraction at the top. No partial reps.
execution.tempo_recommendations: Explosive concentric (as fast as possible under control), controlled 2s eccentric, full stop between reps.
coaching_cues: Torso parallel to the floor the entire set — if it rises, the weight is too heavy
Think of the row as a 'jump' for your upper back
Every rep starts from zero — no rebound

name: Pendulum Quadruped Hip Extension
description: A glute isolation exercise performed on all fours, extending one leg backward and upward with the knee bent at 90 degrees. This movement isolates the gluteus maximus through hip extension while minimizing hamstring involvement due to the bent-knee position.

execution.starting_position: Begin on all fours with hands under shoulders and knees under hips. Working leg has the knee bent at 90 degrees.
execution.setup_instructions: No equipment needed. Position on a padded floor or mat.
steps: Step 1: Keeping the knee bent at 90 degrees, drive the working heel toward the ceiling.
Step 2: Extend the hip fully at the top — sole of the foot faces the ceiling.
Step 3: Squeeze the glute maximally at the top position.
Step 4: Return the knee toward the floor in a controlled manner.
execution.breathing_instructions: Exhale as the leg lifts. Inhale on the return.
common_mistakes: Hyperextending the lower back to gain range instead of using glute strength
Rotating the hip to the side rather than extending straight back
safety_considerations: Keep the lower back neutral — do not let it arch aggressively
execution.range_of_motion_guidance: Full hip extension at the top with the thigh in line with or slightly above parallel to the floor.
coaching_cues: Drive the heel to the ceiling
Squeeze the glute at the top

name: Pendulum Squat Machine
description: The pendulum squat machine places the lifter in an angled standing position on a swinging platform that moves in an arc rather than a straight vertical line. This pendulum arc naturally accommodates the body's mechanics during a squat, allowing a very upright torso and deep knee flexion. The machine is highly effective for quadriceps development with minimal lower back involvement.

execution.starting_position: Step onto the pendulum machine platform, position the shoulder pads over your traps, and stand upright. Feet shoulder-width apart.
execution.setup_instructions: Load the machine and step onto the platform. Lock the shoulder pads in place. Release the safety.
steps: Step 1: Brace and begin bending the knees, allowing the platform to swing in its arc.
Step 2: Descend to full depth — the arc mechanics allow an extremely upright torso.
Step 3: Drive through the feet to extend the knees and return the platform to the starting position.
Step 4: Engage the safety at the end of the set.
execution.breathing_instructions: Inhale before the descent, exhale on the drive.
common_mistakes: Heels rising on the platform
Insufficient depth
safety_considerations: Engage safety handles after each set
Start with light load to understand the arc movement
execution.range_of_motion_guidance: Full depth — the machine accommodates it. Use the full arc.
coaching_cues: Let the machine arc guide you
Full depth every rep
Drive through the entire foot

name: Pigeon Pose
description: Pigeon pose is a yoga-derived hip stretch that places the front leg in external rotation and the rear leg in extension, creating a simultaneous stretch for the hip external rotators and piriformis of the front leg and the hip flexors of the rear leg. It is widely regarded as one of the most effective static stretches for deep hip external rotator tightness and is commonly used by athletes and desk workers alike.

execution.starting_position: Begin in a tabletop position on hands and knees. Slide one knee forward toward the opposite hand and lower the shin to the floor at an angle. The rear leg extends straight back. The front shin may be more or less perpendicular to the torso depending on flexibility.
execution.setup_instructions: Use a mat or padded surface. Those with tight hips may place a folded blanket or yoga block under the hip of the front leg for support.
steps: Step 1: From a tabletop or downward dog position, bring one knee forward and place it behind the same-side wrist.
Step 2: Lower the shin and ankle to the floor, with the foot closer to or further from the groin depending on comfort.
Step 3: Extend the rear leg straight behind you, keeping the hip square to the floor.
Step 4: Lower the torso forward over the front shin, resting on forearms or forehead on the floor.
Step 5: Breathe deeply and hold 60–120 seconds. Gently push back up and switch sides.
execution.breathing_instructions: Breathe slowly and deeply. Allow each exhale to release tension in the hip.
common_mistakes: Letting the hip of the front leg collapse to the floor excessively, reducing the stretch
Front shin perpendicular to the torso when hip flexibility does not allow it — the ankle should be closer to the groin initially
Collapsing the torso to one side rather than squaring the hips
safety_considerations: Avoid if there is knee pain or medial knee discomfort — consider using the figure-four stretch on the back as an alternative
Ensure the knee is not being torqued — the stretch sensation should be in the hip, not the knee
execution.range_of_motion_guidance: The front shin should be at the angle the hip allows — do not force a wider angle. Hold comfortably in the deepest position achievable without knee discomfort.
coaching_cues: Press both hips equally toward the floor
If the front hip is floating, place a prop underneath it
Melt into the floor — do not fight the sensation

name: Pigeon Pose — Loaded (Plate on Hip)
description: A loaded variation of the pigeon pose hip stretch in which a weight plate is placed on the hip of the front leg. The added load deepens the external rotation stretch of the hip joint by applying gentle downward pressure and can help bypass the protective tension reflex that limits passive pigeon pose depth. Used in advanced hip mobility programs and sports-specific flexibility training where passive stretching has reached a plateau.

execution.starting_position: Begin in a standard pigeon pose: front shin angled across the mat, back leg extended straight behind. The front knee is bent and the hip is in external rotation.
execution.setup_instructions: Only add weight after the unloaded pigeon pose is well-tolerated. Begin with a 5 kg plate and progress gradually. Place the plate on the hip of the front (externally rotated) leg.
steps: Step 1: Establish the pigeon pose with the front shin across the mat, back leg extended.
Step 2: Once stable, place a weight plate gently on the hip of the front leg.
Step 3: Hold the loaded position for the prescribed duration, breathing deeply.
Step 4: Remove the plate before transitioning to the other side.
execution.breathing_instructions: Deep breathing throughout the hold. Exhale completely on each breath to allow the hip to relax and deepen.
common_mistakes: Using too heavy a load — the plate deepens the stretch, it does not add resistance in the traditional strength training sense
Placing the plate on the lower back rather than the hip
Using the loaded variation before the bodyweight version is fully tolerated
safety_considerations: If sharp hip or knee pain occurs, remove the plate immediately
Avoid if you have an acute hip labral tear — loading may increase pain
execution.range_of_motion_guidance: The same range as the unloaded pigeon pose, potentially slightly deeper due to the gentle additional load.
coaching_cues: Breathe the hip open — exhale completely and let the hip sink with each breath
Ensure the plate is resting on the outer hip, not the lower back
If the stretch feels like joint pain rather than muscle stretch, reduce the load or return to the unloaded version

name: Pike Push-Up
description: The pike push-up is a bodyweight pressing exercise performed in a pike (inverted V) body position, with hips raised and the torso angled toward vertical. This positions the shoulder joint in a more overhead alignment, making the anterior and lateral deltoids the primary movers rather than the pectorals. It serves as an accessible progression toward handstand push-ups.

execution.starting_position: Start in a push-up position, then walk the hands back toward the feet while raising the hips until the body forms an inverted V shape. Heels may be slightly lifted. Arms and back should be nearly straight.
execution.setup_instructions: No equipment required. The higher the hip position, the more vertical the torso and the greater the shoulder demand.
steps: Step 1: Begin in a push-up position, then walk hands toward feet and raise the hips to form an inverted V.
Step 2: Brace core. Ensure hands are shoulder-width apart with fingers spread.
Step 3: Inhale and bend the elbows to lower the top of the head toward the floor between the hands.
Step 4: When the head nearly touches the floor or reaches the bottom of your range, exhale and press back to the starting inverted-V position.
execution.breathing_instructions: Inhale on the descent; exhale as you press back up.
common_mistakes: Letting the hips drop during the movement, which shifts load to the chest
Flaring the elbows wide rather than allowing them to track naturally
safety_considerations: Develop adequate shoulder strength before progressing to fully vertical handstand push-ups
If you feel neck pain when the head approaches the floor, reduce range of motion
execution.range_of_motion_guidance: Lower until the top of the head is 1–2 cm from the floor, then press back to the pike position.
coaching_cues: Push the floor away as you think about pressing your hips toward the ceiling
Keep shoulders packed away from the ears throughout the movement

name: Pin Press / Anderson Bench Press
description: The Pin Press starts with the barbell resting on the safety pins of a power rack at a predetermined height, eliminating the eccentric phase and any stretch-shortening cycle contribution. Each repetition begins from a dead stop, training maximal concentric pressing force from the most difficult position in the range of motion.

execution.starting_position: Set the safety pins inside a power rack so the bar rests at the desired starting height (chest level, mid-ROM, or near lockout). Lie under the bar and position yourself as for a bench press.
execution.setup_instructions: Set pins at the desired height. Rest the bar on the pins. Lie on the bench under the bar, establish contact with the bar, retract the shoulder blades, brace the core.
steps: Step 1: Position hands on the bar at the chosen grip width while it rests on the pins.
Step 2: Take a full breath, brace, and press the bar off the pins from a dead stop.
Step 3: Drive to full lockout.
Step 4: Lower the bar back to the pins with control. Reset and repeat from a dead stop — do not bounce off the pins.
execution.breathing_instructions: Breathe and brace before each rep. Exhale at lockout. Reset breath between reps.
common_mistakes: Bouncing the bar off the pins rather than pressing from a true dead stop
Setting pins at a height that is too low, reducing the specificity benefit
safety_considerations: The power rack is mandatory — this exercise cannot be performed without one
Start conservatively with load; there is no elastic energy to assist the initial drive
execution.range_of_motion_guidance: Partial ROM from pin height to lockout. Set pin height to match your specific sticking point.
coaching_cues: Treat every rep as a max effort single
Pull the bar apart and try to bend it before you press

name: Pinch Grip Farmer's Walk
description: A grip strength exercise performed by pinching the smooth edge of weight plates between the fingers and thumb and walking for distance or time. The pinch grip isolates the finger flexors and thumb adductors to a greater degree than a standard handle grip and builds crushing and pinching grip strength essential for many athletic and functional tasks.

execution.starting_position: Stand tall holding a weight plate in each hand, pinched between the fingers and thumb, with the smooth surface outward.
execution.setup_instructions: Select a moderate weight plate (25lb or 35lb to start). Grip the smooth outer edge between fingers and thumb on each hand.
steps: Step 1: Stand tall with the plates pinched securely.
Step 2: Walk forward for the prescribed distance or time, maintaining an upright posture.
Step 3: Keep the shoulders level and the core braced throughout.
Step 4: At the end of the distance, carefully set the plates down.
execution.breathing_instructions: Breathe steadily throughout the walk.
common_mistakes: Allowing the torso to lean or the shoulders to drop
Squeezing too hard and fatiguing the grip prematurely
safety_considerations: Set the plates down carefully — do not drop them
Use chalk to improve grip on smooth plates
execution.range_of_motion_guidance: Walk for the prescribed distance (10-30m) or time (20-60 seconds).
coaching_cues: Pinch hard and walk tall
Keep the shoulders level

name: Planche Hold
description: A static gymnastic skill where the body is held parallel to the floor supported only by the hands with straight arms. The body must be perfectly balanced over the hands with the entire core and shoulder girdle engaged. This is one of the most demanding upper body strength feats.

execution.starting_position: Set up for Planche Hold in proper position.
execution.setup_instructions: Prepare body and equipment for Planche Hold.
steps: Step 1: Begin from tuck planche progression. Gradually extend hips and legs.
Step 2: Lean shoulders forward of hands while keeping arms perfectly straight.
Step 3: Protract and depress scapulae to push floor away.
Step 4: Hold rigid horizontal position with body parallel to ground.
execution.breathing_instructions: Breathe steadily; never hold breath during static holds.
common_mistakes: Bending arms
Insufficient lean forward of shoulders
safety_considerations: Build prerequisite strength before attempting advanced variations.
Stop if joint pain occurs.
execution.range_of_motion_guidance: Full range of motion with control at all times.
coaching_cues: Shoulders must be ahead of wrists
Full scapular protraction

name: Planche Lean on Parallettes
description: A foundational planche progression where the body leans forward over parallettes with arms straight, loading the shoulders and core in the planche position without full body elevation. The lean builds the necessary shoulder strength and proprioception for full planche.

execution.starting_position: Set up for Planche Lean on Parallettes in proper position.
execution.setup_instructions: Prepare body and equipment for Planche Lean on Parallettes.
steps: Step 1: Set up parallettes on floor. Grip with straight arms in push-up position.
Step 2: Lean shoulders forward of wrists with protracted, depressed scapulae.
Step 3: Lift heels and shift more weight onto shoulders.
Step 4: Hold lean position working toward legs rising off floor.
execution.breathing_instructions: Breathe steadily; never hold breath during static holds.
common_mistakes: Bending arms
Insufficient scapular protraction
safety_considerations: Build prerequisite strength before attempting advanced variations.
Stop if joint pain occurs.
execution.range_of_motion_guidance: Full range of motion with control at all times.
coaching_cues: Shoulders must pass in front of wrists
Press floor away with straight arms

name: Plank
description: The plank is an isometric core stability exercise in which the body is held in a push-up position with the forearms or hands on the floor. It trains the transverse abdominis, rectus abdominis, and stabilizing muscles of the spine to resist extension, making it fundamental for core stability, lower back health, and athletic performance.

execution.starting_position: Lie face down. Place forearms on the floor with elbows directly below the shoulders. Push up onto the forearms and toes so the body forms a straight line from head to heels.
execution.setup_instructions: No equipment required. Use a mat for forearm comfort. Keep the body in one rigid line — no hip sag or piking.
steps: Squeeze the glutes and brace the core by tightening the abdominals.
Maintain a neutral spine — the head, hips, and heels should form a straight line.
Hold the position for the prescribed duration while breathing normally.
execution.breathing_instructions: Breathe in and out normally throughout the hold — do not hold your breath.
common_mistakes: Hips sagging downward — squeeze the glutes to prevent this
Hips raised too high, piking at the waist
Neck too low or raised — keep a neutral head position
safety_considerations: If lower back pain occurs, reduce duration or perform on knees
execution.range_of_motion_guidance: Isometric hold. No joint movement — maintain the position for the target duration.
execution.tempo_recommendations: Hold for 20–60 seconds per set, progressing duration over time
coaching_cues: Squeeze your glutes hard — this automatically protects the lower back
Think about pulling your elbows toward your feet — this activates the core further

name: Plate Front Raise
description: The plate front raise uses a standard weight plate held with both hands at the edges (like steering a wheel), which places the forearms in a neutral position and distributes the load evenly between both anterior deltoids. The circular shape allows for a natural grip and encourages a consistent hand position throughout the movement. It is an accessible and practical anterior deltoid isolation exercise requiring minimal equipment beyond a single plate.

execution.starting_position: Stand upright. Hold a weight plate at the 3 o'clock and 9 o'clock positions with both hands. The plate hangs at thigh level in front of the body.
execution.setup_instructions: Begin with a 10 or 25 lb plate. The neutral-grip position reduces wrist stress compared to a pronated barbell hold.
steps: Step 1: Hold the plate at the sides, hanging at thigh level.
Step 2: Raise the plate directly in front of the body with arms nearly straight.
Step 3: Raise to shoulder height.
Step 4: Pause at the top.
Step 5: Lower under full control to the starting position.
execution.breathing_instructions: Exhale on the raise, inhale on the descent.
common_mistakes: Using too heavy a plate and swinging the torso
Raising the plate above shoulder height unnecessarily
safety_considerations: Keep a firm grip on the plate at all times
execution.range_of_motion_guidance: Thigh level to shoulder height (90 degrees of shoulder flexion).
coaching_cues: Like turning a steering wheel straight up
Slow on the way down
Controlled arc — no swinging

name: Plate-Loaded Viking Press
description: The plate-loaded Viking press uses a Viking press machine or landmine-based Viking press attachment, which allows the hands to press in a neutral (palms-facing) grip along a fixed arc from shoulder height to full overhead extension. The arcing path of the handles closely approximates the natural pressing pathway of a dumbbell press while allowing barbell-style loading plates, making it a shoulder-friendly alternative to the straight barbell overhead press with the loading capacity of a barbell movement.

execution.starting_position: Grip the Viking press handles with a neutral grip at shoulder height. Feet shoulder-width apart, standing in front of the machine or landmine anchor.
execution.setup_instructions: Load weight plates onto the Viking press arms evenly. Begin with moderate loads as the pressing arc is different from a straight barbell.
steps: Step 1: Begin with the handles at shoulder height, elbows bent.
Step 2: Press both handles upward and slightly forward, following the arc of the machine.
Step 3: Extend to full overhead lockout.
Step 4: Lower under control along the same arc.
Step 5: Repeat.
execution.breathing_instructions: Inhale and brace before pressing. Exhale through the press.
common_mistakes: Fighting the arc — the fixed bar path is an advantage; follow it rather than trying to press straight
Locking the elbows aggressively — control the lockout
safety_considerations: The arcing pressing path is gentler on the shoulder than a straight barbell
Still requires adequate shoulder mobility for overhead pressing
execution.range_of_motion_guidance: Shoulder height to full overhead lockout along the machine's arc.
coaching_cues: Follow the arc — don't fight it
Neutral grip throughout
Full lockout at the top

name: Plate Pinch Hold
description: The plate pinch hold involves gripping one or more weight plates by pinching them between the thumb and fingers, then holding for time. This directly trains pinch grip strength — the grip pattern between thumb and fingertips — which is distinct from crush grip. Strong pinch grip transfers to virtually all pulling movements and is essential for contact sports and manual labor. It is typically performed for time rather than reps.

execution.starting_position: Stand upright. Hold one or two weight plates by pinching the smooth face between the thumb and fingers of one hand.
execution.setup_instructions: Begin with a single 10kg or 25lb plate. Progress by adding plates. Smooth-face plates are more difficult than knurled; pinching with the smooth face out is standard.
steps: Step 1: Pinch the plate(s) securely between the thumb and all four fingers.
Step 2: Lift the plate(s) off the floor or a low platform.
Step 3: Hold for the prescribed duration, keeping the shoulder relaxed.
Step 4: Set the plate down with control.
execution.breathing_instructions: Breathe freely throughout the hold.
common_mistakes: Resting the plate against the thigh (this reduces grip demand)
Not maintaining consistent pinch tension throughout
safety_considerations: Dropping heavy plates is a risk — perform over a rubber mat or low surface
execution.range_of_motion_guidance: Static hold — no movement required.
coaching_cues: Squeeze through the entire hold
Shoulder relaxed — don't shrug
Control the set down

name: Plyometric Push-Up
description: The plyometric push-up is an explosive upper body press variation in which the athlete pushes off with enough force to leave the ground, optionally clapping between repetitions. It trains the stretch-shortening cycle of the pectoral muscles and triceps, developing explosive upper body pushing power. The exercise is a staple of athletic conditioning programs targeting sport-specific upper body force production.

execution.starting_position: Begin in a standard push-up position — hands slightly wider than shoulder-width, body in a straight line from head to heels.
execution.setup_instructions: No equipment required. Ensure adequate floor space and a non-slip surface.
steps: Step 1: Begin in push-up position with the body in a straight plank line.
Step 2: Lower the chest to the floor under control.
Step 3: Press explosively with maximum effort — drive the hands into the floor to generate enough force to lift the hands off the ground.
Step 4: Optionally clap while airborne, then catch the fall by landing with slightly bent elbows.
Step 5: Absorb the landing and immediately lower into the next repetition.
execution.breathing_instructions: Inhale on the descent. Exhale sharply and forcefully at the moment of push-off.
common_mistakes: Letting the hips sag — the body must remain rigid throughout
Insufficient pressing force — the hands must fully leave the ground
Catching with locked elbows — this places severe strain on the elbow joint
safety_considerations: Master standard push-ups before attempting plyometric variations.
Land with soft elbows, never locked out.
execution.range_of_motion_guidance: Full push-up depth — chest to floor or near it. Full extension (hands off ground) at top.
execution.tempo_recommendations: Maximum effort on each rep. 5–10 reps per set for power. Rest fully between sets.
coaching_cues: Push the floor away as hard as possible
Tight core throughout — no hip sag
Catch soft — bend the elbows on landing

name: Poliquin Step-Up / Heel-Elevated Lateral Step-Up
description: The Poliquin step-up is a unilateral exercise developed to specifically target the vastus medialis (VMO). The lifter steps sideways onto a low box or step while keeping the working heel elevated, maximizing knee extension load on the inner quadriceps. The heel-elevated foot position prevents weight shifting to the hip extensors, making this a highly specific VMO strengthening exercise used extensively in knee rehabilitation and sports performance.

execution.starting_position: Stand beside a box or step approximately 4-6 inches high. Place the working foot on the step laterally, with the heel elevated slightly (by the step edge or a plate beneath the heel). The opposite foot remains on the floor.
execution.setup_instructions: Use a low step or box. Place heel on the edge to create slight elevation. Begin with bodyweight.
steps: Step 1: Drive the working heel down into the step, extending the knee from roughly 90 degrees to full extension.
Step 2: At no point does the opposite foot leave the floor or take weight — it is a touch guide only.
Step 3: Lower back down with control, allowing the knee to flex back to about 90 degrees.
Step 4: Repeat all reps on one side before switching.
execution.breathing_instructions: Exhale on extension, inhale on the controlled return.
common_mistakes: Pushing through the floor foot rather than the step foot
Using momentum or body lean
Full knee extension with a lock-out that reduces tension
safety_considerations: Very low-load exercise — appropriate for post-surgery rehabilitation when cleared
Consult a physiotherapist if using for patellar tracking issues
execution.range_of_motion_guidance: Work from approximately 90 degrees of knee flexion to nearly full extension. Keep tension on the VMO throughout.
coaching_cues: Feel the inner quad working
Drive through the heel of the step foot only
No weight on the floor foot

name: Power Clean
description: The power clean is a variation of the Olympic clean in which the bar is received above parallel — in a quarter squat rather than a full front squat — requiring greater bar height and power output from the second pull. It is widely used in sport conditioning programs for developing explosive hip extension power and is more accessible than the full clean due to reduced demands on front rack mobility and squat depth. The power clean is a staple exercise in American football, rugby, and many team sports training programs.

execution.starting_position: Bar over mid-foot, shoulder-width grip, flat back, hips slightly above knees, shoulders over or slightly in front of the bar.
execution.setup_instructions: Use bumper plates. Set the bar on the floor. Establish a neutral spine and proper hip hinge position before each rep.
steps: Step 1: First pull — press the floor away, keeping the back angle constant and bar close to the body.
Step 2: Second pull — explosively extend the hips as the bar passes the knees and hip crease.
Step 3: At full triple extension (ankle, knee, hip), shrug the traps and pull the elbows high and outside.
Step 4: Rotate the elbows under the bar and receive it in the front rack on the shoulders in a quarter squat (above parallel).
Step 5: Stand to full extension, return the bar to the floor with control.
execution.breathing_instructions: Brace before the pull. Hold through the second pull. Exhale after standing from the catch.
common_mistakes: Catching below parallel (this is a full clean — the power clean catch must be above parallel)
Pulling with the arms before hip extension
Letting the bar drift away from the body
safety_considerations: Use bumper plates. Practice the hip drive and high pull before combining into a full power clean.
Wrist pain can occur in the front rack — develop wrist flexibility progressively.
execution.range_of_motion_guidance: Full hip extension before the third pull. Catch above parallel in a stable front rack position.
execution.tempo_recommendations: Explosive pull. Brief pause in front rack. Controlled lower.
coaching_cues: Hips through — extend completely before pulling
High elbows — the bar should land on the shoulders, not the hands
Catch above parallel

name: Power Snatch
description: The power snatch is a variation of the Olympic snatch in which the bar is received above parallel — the athlete catches the bar in a partial squat rather than a full overhead squat. The higher catch position requires greater bar height and more explosive power than the full snatch, making it an effective power development tool and a useful teaching progression. It is widely used in sport conditioning, CrossFit, and as an Olympic lifting warm-up.

execution.starting_position: Same as the full snatch — bar over mid-foot, wide snatch grip, flat back, hips between shoulders and knees.
execution.setup_instructions: Use bumper plates. The power snatch requires the same setup and pulling mechanics as the full snatch — the distinction is in the catch height.
steps: Step 1: Set the starting position with a wide snatch grip.
Step 2: First pull — push the floor away and keep the bar close to the body.
Step 3: Second pull — extend the hips explosively as the bar passes the hip crease, using maximum power.
Step 4: Shrug and pull the elbows high and outside to generate maximal bar elevation.
Step 5: Catch the bar overhead with elbows locked in a squat above parallel (thighs above horizontal), then stand fully.
execution.breathing_instructions: Brace before initiating. Hold through the pull. Exhale after securing the overhead catch.
common_mistakes: Catching too deep (this becomes a full snatch — above parallel is the power snatch standard)
Relaxing the bar path and letting it drift forward
Early arm bend
safety_considerations: Use bumper plates and be prepared to bail the bar safely forward.
Master bar mechanics with lighter loads before increasing weight.
execution.range_of_motion_guidance: Catch must occur above parallel. The overhead catch must have locked elbows and stable shoulder position.
execution.tempo_recommendations: Explosive. Maximum bar speed is the objective. No tempo prescription.
coaching_cues: Pull the bar as high as possible before turning over
Catch above parallel — not in a full squat
Punch the hands up and lock the elbows fast

name: Preacher Curl
description: The preacher curl is a biceps curl variation performed with the upper arms resting on an angled arm pad, which prevents elbow movement and places the biceps under constant tension. The preacher bench position provides a greater stretch on the long head of the biceps at the bottom and prevents cheating with the torso.

execution.starting_position: Sit at the preacher bench with the upper arms resting flat on the angled pad. Hold an EZ-curl bar or dumbbells with a supinated or semi-supinated grip. Arms nearly fully extended.
execution.setup_instructions: Adjust the bench seat height so the upper arms lie flat on the pad with the armpits at the top edge of the pad.
steps: Curl the bar upward by flexing the elbows, keeping the upper arms in contact with the pad.
Raise until full biceps contraction is achieved.
Lower slowly and under control — the eccentric portion is especially important here.
execution.breathing_instructions: Exhale on the curl, inhale on descent.
common_mistakes: Lifting the upper arms off the pad to gain leverage
Not lowering to full extension, missing the stretch
safety_considerations: The preacher position can stress the distal biceps tendon at full extension — control the descent
execution.range_of_motion_guidance: Near-full extension at the bottom (avoid hyperextension), full contraction at the top.
coaching_cues: Keep the upper arms welded to the pad
Control the descent — do not let the bar drop

name: Prone Cobra with Arm Pulses
description: A dynamic variation of the prone cobra exercise in which small rhythmic arm pulses are performed while holding the torso in the cobra extension position. The pulsing arm movement (small lifts from the hip-level position) maintains continuous engagement of the lower trapezius, posterior deltoid, and spinal extensors throughout the hold, increasing time-under-tension beyond what a static hold provides. This exercise is used in thoracic extension rehabilitation and postural correction programs.
