execution.starting_position: Lie face down on the floor with arms by the sides, palms facing upward, and forehead resting on the mat. This is the prone cobra starting position.
execution.setup_instructions: No equipment needed. A thin mat is recommended for comfort.
steps: Step 1: Squeeze the glutes and lift the chest from the floor into the cobra extension. Simultaneously raise the arms slightly from the sides, maintaining the thumb-up orientation.
Step 2: Hold the cobra position and begin performing small rhythmic arm pulses — tiny lifts of the arms toward the ceiling, approximately 2-5 cm per pulse.
Step 3: Perform 10-20 pulses while maintaining the cobra chest elevation.
Step 4: Lower the chest and arms to the floor. Rest and repeat.
execution.breathing_instructions: Exhale as you rise into the cobra. Breathe rhythmically during the pulses — do not hold the breath.
common_mistakes: Losing the cobra chest elevation during the pulses — maintain the thoracic extension throughout
Using large arm swings rather than small controlled pulses
Neck hyperextension — the gaze should be on the floor, not the ceiling
safety_considerations: If acute lower back pain is present, check with a physiotherapist before performing prone extension exercises
Avoid if thoracic or lumbar extension causes sharp, radiating pain
execution.range_of_motion_guidance: Cobra extension is held throughout. The pulse amplitude is small — quality over height.
execution.tempo_recommendations: Hold cobra for 20-30 seconds. Pulses at approximately 1 per second.
coaching_cues: Keep the chest up — do not let it drop during the pulses
Thumbs up with palms facing outward to maximize posterior shoulder activation
Look at the floor — not at the ceiling

name: Prone Cobra Hold
description: The prone cobra is a postural restoration exercise performed face-down on the floor. The exerciser lifts the chest off the ground while simultaneously externally rotating the shoulders and squeezing the scapulae together, holding the position isometrically. This movement counteracts the forward-rounded posture common in sedentary populations and strengthens the posterior chain muscles responsible for upright posture.

execution.starting_position: Lie face-down on the floor with arms at your sides, palms facing down, forehead resting on the floor. Legs are together and relaxed.
execution.setup_instructions: No equipment required. Use a mat for comfort. Ensure there is enough space to extend arms fully.
steps: Step 1: Squeeze the glutes and brace the lower abdominals lightly.
Step 2: Rotate the hands outward so the thumbs point up and palms face outward.
Step 3: Lift the chest and arms off the floor simultaneously, keeping the head in a neutral position aligned with the spine.
Step 4: Hold the elevated position for the prescribed duration, then slowly lower. Repeat.
execution.breathing_instructions: Breathe normally during the hold — do not hold your breath. Exhale as you lift, inhale during the hold.
common_mistakes: Craning the neck backward — the head should stay neutral
Failing to externally rotate the shoulders before lifting
Holding breath rather than breathing through the hold
safety_considerations: Avoid if you have acute lumbar disc herniation — consult a physiotherapist first
Do not force excessive spinal extension — lift only as high as comfortable
execution.range_of_motion_guidance: Lift the chest 3-6 inches off the floor. Focus on quality of contraction, not height of lift.
execution.tempo_recommendations: Hold 5-10 seconds per rep, working up to 30-second holds
coaching_cues: Squeeze the shoulder blades together and down before you lift
Think about making your thumbs point to the ceiling
Keep the neck long — do not crane backward

name: Prone Incline Cobra Raise
description: The prone incline cobra raise is performed lying face-down on a low-incline bench (15-30 degrees), raising the arms overhead while simultaneously extending the thoracic spine and externally rotating the shoulders — forming a 'cobra' posture. It trains the lower trapezius, thoracic extensors, and posterior rotator cuff through a full range of controlled spinal and shoulder movement, commonly used in posture correction and shoulder rehabilitation protocols.

execution.starting_position: Lie prone on a low-incline bench (15-30 degrees). Arms hang down in front of the bench, thumbs facing up.
execution.setup_instructions: No load is needed initially — this is a bodyweight or very light dumbbell movement. Use a bench inclined just enough to allow the arms to hang freely.
steps: Step 1: Begin with arms hanging, thumbs up.
Step 2: Simultaneously raise the arms overhead while extending the thoracic spine.
Step 3: At peak, externally rotate so thumbs point behind — 'cobra' position.
Step 4: Hold 2 seconds.
Step 5: Lower under control, returning to the starting hang.
execution.breathing_instructions: Exhale on the raise and extension. Inhale returning.
common_mistakes: Extending from the lumbar spine rather than the thoracic spine
Not fully externally rotating the shoulders at the top
safety_considerations: Very light loads or bodyweight only — this is a postural and rehabilitative exercise
Avoid if experiencing thoracic or shoulder pain
execution.range_of_motion_guidance: Arms hanging to full overhead position with thoracic extension and external rotation.
coaching_cues: Lead with the chest — extend the thoracic spine, not the lumbar
Thumbs point to the ceiling at the top, then point behind you
Squeeze the shoulder blades together and down

name: Prone Incline Cobra Y-Raise
description: The prone incline cobra Y-raise combines a thoracic extension (cobra) with an overhead Y-arm position, training the lower trapezius and serratus anterior in the overhead range while also loading the thoracic extensors. The Y-arm position (arms raised diagonally overhead at 45 degrees from the spine) targets the lower trapezius more specifically than T or W positions, as the lower trap is primarily responsible for upward scapular rotation and depression when the arms are elevated.

execution.starting_position: Lie prone on an incline bench (15-30 degrees). Arms hang in front. Thumbs pointing up.
execution.setup_instructions: No load or very light dumbbells (1-3 kg). Focus is on motor control, not strength.
steps: Step 1: Begin hanging, thumbs up.
Step 2: Extend the thoracic spine (cobra movement) simultaneously while raising the arms in a Y shape — 45 degrees from the spine.
Step 3: At the top, the arms form a Y overhead, thumbs pointing upward.
Step 4: Hold 2 seconds.
Step 5: Lower both the arms and the thoracic extension simultaneously.
execution.breathing_instructions: Exhale on the raise. Inhale lowering.
common_mistakes: Arms going too wide (T position) or too narrow — the Y angle is 45 degrees
Extending from the lumbar spine — the thoracic spine is what should move
safety_considerations: Bodyweight or very light load only — this is a postural exercise
No pain should occur during this exercise — stop if any shoulder discomfort arises
execution.range_of_motion_guidance: Full hang to Y position with thoracic extension.
coaching_cues: Thumbs point to the ceiling at the top
Y shape — not T, not overhead — 45 degrees
Lead with the chest for the thoracic extension

name: Prone Incline T-Bar Rear Delt Row
description: The prone incline T-bar rear delt row lies the torso on an incline bench with the elbows flared wide to target the rear deltoids and upper trapezius rather than the lats. With the arms abducting laterally and elbows elevated, the movement resembles a horizontal reverse fly performed with the T-bar's fixed line of pull, creating a unique combination of stability and load not achievable with dumbbells.

execution.starting_position: Position an incline bench (30-45 degrees) over the T-bar. Lie prone with chest supported. Grip the bar or handle with both hands, arms extended below.
execution.setup_instructions: Use a wide grip or the bar itself without a handle. The elbows must be able to flare to 90 degrees from the torso.
steps: Step 1: Begin with arms extended, gripping the bar wide.
Step 2: Row by driving elbows out laterally and upward — not back.
Step 3: At peak contraction, upper arms should be approximately horizontal.
Step 4: Hold 1 second.
Step 5: Lower under control to full arm extension.
execution.breathing_instructions: Exhale on the pull. Inhale descending.
common_mistakes: Elbows tracking backward instead of outward — this shifts to lat engagement
Using too much load — the rear delt is a small muscle; use lighter weights
safety_considerations: Light loads only for this variation — rear delts are injury-prone under excessive load
Keep the neck neutral — do not crane upward
execution.range_of_motion_guidance: Full arm extension to arms horizontal with elbows at shoulder height.
coaching_cues: Lead with the elbows — not the hands
Think of opening the elbows like wings
Pinkies up at the top of the movement

name: Prone Neck Bridge
description: The prone neck bridge is a gymnastics and wrestling exercise where the body is supported on the forehead or top of the head with the body arched and feet on the floor, loading the anterior cervical musculature with a significant portion of bodyweight. It develops exceptional cervical and spinal stability through an isometric hold against the entire bodyweight. Used extensively in wrestling, judo, and gymnastics conditioning, it represents the highest intensity isometric load a neck curl progression leads toward.

execution.starting_position: Lie face-down on a mat. Place the top of the forehead on the mat. Feet on the floor behind. Push up with the hands to begin, then lower to a supported position on the forehead only.
execution.setup_instructions: This is an ADVANCED exercise. Prerequisites: several months of neck curl and neck extension training, comfort with isometric neck loading. Begin with hand assistance.
steps: Step 1: Begin in a push-up-like position, forehead on the mat.
Step 2: Slowly walk the feet toward the head, increasing the load through the neck.
Step 3: Use the hands to control how much weight is transferred to the forehead.
Step 4: Hold the bridge position isometrically for the target duration.
Step 5: Use the hands to assist the return to the starting position.
execution.breathing_instructions: Breathe normally throughout the hold.
common_mistakes: Attempting this without progressive neck training over months
Attempting the full bodyweight hold without hand-assisted progressions
Hyperextending the lower back, which is secondary to the neck position
safety_considerations: Contraindicated with any cervical pathology, disc issues, or acute pain
Must be preceded by weeks-to-months of progressive neck training
Always use hand-assisted variations before full bodyweight
Have a spotter when attempting for the first time
execution.range_of_motion_guidance: Isometric hold — no movement through range. The goal is to maintain the bridge position.
coaching_cues: Hands assist as needed — don't be a hero
Progressive — work up over months
Any pain = stop immediately

name: Plank Shoulder Taps
description: Plank shoulder taps are an anti-rotation core stability exercise performed from a high plank position. One hand at a time lifts from the floor to tap the opposite shoulder while the core resists the rotational and lateral shift that the movement creates. This demands simultaneous core bracing, shoulder stability, and hip anti-rotation, making it a highly effective functional rehabilitation drill for the core, hips, and shoulder girdle.

execution.starting_position: Begin in a high plank (push-up starting position) with hands directly under shoulders and feet hip-width apart. The body should form a rigid straight line from heels to head.
execution.setup_instructions: Wider foot stance makes the exercise easier and is a good starting modification. Narrower stance increases the anti-rotation challenge.
steps: Step 1: Establish a rigid plank. Brace the core and squeeze the glutes.
Step 2: Slowly lift the right hand from the floor and tap the left shoulder, then return the right hand to the floor.
Step 3: Immediately lift the left hand and tap the right shoulder, then return.
Step 4: One tap per side equals one repetition. Continue alternating while maintaining a level, non-rotating body.
execution.breathing_instructions: Breathe continuously — do not hold your breath. Exhale as you lift the hand.
common_mistakes: Allowing the hips to rock side to side during the tap — this is the main error to correct
Rushing through the movement — slow taps engage the stabilizers far more effectively
Placing feet too close together, which greatly increases the rotational challenge beyond the user's capacity
safety_considerations: If the lower back sags during the exercise, perform the drill from the knees first to build foundational strength
Avoid if wrist pain is present — use fist plank position as a modification
execution.range_of_motion_guidance: The tap itself is a small movement. The challenge is in keeping everything else completely still.
execution.tempo_recommendations: 2s lift and tap, 1s hold on shoulder, 2s return. Slow and controlled.
coaching_cues: Squeeze the glutes to prevent hip drop during the tap
Move only the arm — nothing else should shift when the hand lifts
Wider feet = easier; narrow feet = harder. Choose based on your current level

name: Prone Scarecrow Press
description: The prone scarecrow press combines an external rotation at 90 degrees of shoulder abduction with a finishing overhead press, performed lying face-down on a bench. The scarecrow portion (elbows at shoulder height, forearms hanging down) isolates the infraspinatus and teres minor through external rotation in the vulnerable abducted position, then the press completes the movement in the overhead plane. This sequence trains rotator cuff function together with deltoid pressing, making it valuable for shoulder health and athletic development.

execution.starting_position: Lie face-down on an incline bench (30-45 degrees). Hold light dumbbells. Upper arms abducted to shoulder height, elbows bent 90 degrees, forearms hanging perpendicular to the floor.
execution.setup_instructions: Very light weight — 2-5 kg. This is a rotator cuff and shoulder health exercise.
steps: Step 1: Begin in the scarecrow position — elbows at shoulder height, forearms hanging down.
Step 2: Externally rotate both shoulders, raising the forearms until they are parallel to the floor (forearms now pointing forward).
Step 3: From this horizontally extended position, press the dumbbells overhead to full arm extension.
Step 4: Reverse the sequence — lower overhead to horizontal, then internally rotate back to the scarecrow hang.
Step 5: Repeat.
execution.breathing_instructions: Exhale through the external rotation and press. Inhale on the return.
common_mistakes: Using too much weight — reduces the external rotation range of motion
Skipping the external rotation — pressing directly from the hang misses the rehabilitation benefit
safety_considerations: Very light loads only
Stop if shoulder impingement symptoms occur during the external rotation phase
execution.range_of_motion_guidance: Full external rotation range before pressing overhead.
coaching_cues: Scarecrow arms first — elbows at shoulder height
Rotate the forearms up before pressing
Reverse it on the way back — press down, then rotate the forearms back down

name: Prone T-Raise
description: The prone T-raise is a posterior shoulder and middle trapezius exercise performed lying face down with arms extended directly to the sides, forming a T shape. This horizontal abduction movement targets the posterior deltoid and middle trapezius and is a staple corrective exercise for improving shoulder blade retraction strength and postural alignment.

execution.starting_position: Lie face down on the floor or an incline bench with arms extended directly to the sides, perpendicular to the torso, forming a T. Thumbs point toward the ceiling.
execution.setup_instructions: No equipment needed for bodyweight. Add light dumbbells (1–3 kg) for increased load. Can be done over an incline bench for greater range of motion.
steps: Step 1: Lie face down with arms extended to the sides in a T shape. Thumbs point up.
Step 2: Depress and retract the shoulder blades.
Step 3: Exhale and raise both arms toward the ceiling, squeezing the middle traps and rear delts.
Step 4: Hold at the top 1–2 seconds, then inhale and lower back to the floor.
execution.breathing_instructions: Exhale on the raise; inhale on the return.
common_mistakes: Letting the shoulder blades wing outward — actively retract them during the raise
Using upper trap shrugging instead of mid-trap retraction
safety_considerations: Very light load only — this is a corrective and endurance exercise
execution.range_of_motion_guidance: Raise arms until middle traps are maximally contracted; they will not go very high.
coaching_cues: Squeeze your shoulder blades together as you raise
Thumbs up keeps the shoulder in a safe external rotation position

name: Prone Y-Raise
description: The prone Y-raise is a shoulder and lower trapezius exercise performed lying face down with arms raised overhead in a Y shape. The lower trapezius is the primary target, as the upward rotation of the scapula is required to raise the arms overhead in this position. It is an important corrective exercise for improving scapular mechanics and counteracting the postural effects of prolonged sitting.

execution.starting_position: Lie face down on the floor or on an incline bench. Arms are extended alongside the head in a Y shape, with thumbs pointing up.
execution.setup_instructions: No equipment required for bodyweight version. Light dumbbells (1–3 kg) can be added. An adjustable bench at a slight incline allows greater range.
steps: Step 1: Lie face down with arms extended forward and slightly out at a 30-45 degree angle from midline, forming a Y shape. Thumbs point toward the ceiling.
Step 2: Keeping the elbows straight, exhale and raise both arms as high as possible while depressing the shoulder blades downward.
Step 3: Hold at the top for 1–2 seconds, feeling the lower traps contracting.
Step 4: Inhale and slowly lower the arms back to the floor.
execution.breathing_instructions: Exhale on the raise; inhale on the return.
common_mistakes: Shrugging the shoulders upward rather than depressing them during the raise
Bending the elbows instead of maintaining straight arms
safety_considerations: Use bodyweight or minimal load — this is a corrective and postural exercise
execution.range_of_motion_guidance: Raise until the arms are as high as possible while actively depressing the shoulder blades.
coaching_cues: Think 'shoulders down and back' as you raise the arms
Thumbs up — this external rotation opens the shoulder impingement zone

name: Prone Y-Raise (Thumbs Up)
description: The prone Y-raise performed with thumbs pointing upward (externally rotated shoulders) on a flat surface trains the lower trapezius through its primary action of upward scapular rotation and depression. The external rotation (thumbs up) is critical — it places the shoulder in its safest overhead position and maximally lengthens the lower trapezius before each repetition, improving the exercise's effectiveness as both a strengthening and postural correction tool.

execution.starting_position: Lie face down on a bench or the floor. Arms extended in a Y position (45 degrees overhead from the spine). Thumbs pointing toward the ceiling.
execution.setup_instructions: Bodyweight or 1-2 kg per hand. The movement is fully achievable without weight for most people.
steps: Step 1: Begin lying prone, arms in Y position, thumbs up.
Step 2: Raise both arms toward the ceiling while maintaining the Y angle and thumbs-up rotation.
Step 3: Squeeze the lower traps — think 'shoulder blades toward the back pockets'.
Step 4: Hold 2 seconds at the top.
Step 5: Lower under control.
execution.breathing_instructions: Exhale raising. Inhale lowering.
common_mistakes: Thumbs rotating down — this internally rotates the shoulder and reduces lower trap activation
Arms going overhead (beyond Y) — the angle must be maintained
safety_considerations: Bodyweight appropriate for all fitness levels
Very light optional load — this is a rehabilitation and activation drill
execution.range_of_motion_guidance: Floor-level to arms raised with scapulae fully depressed and retracted.
coaching_cues: Thumbs point to the ceiling throughout
Y shape — 45 degrees from spine
Shoulder blades pull toward your back pockets

name: Prone YTW
description: The prone YTW is a scapular stability and lower trapezius rehabilitation exercise performed face-down on a bench or floor. Three arm positions — Y (overhead diagonal), T (horizontal), and W (elbows bent at sides) — collectively target the lower, middle, and upper trapezius as well as the rhomboids and posterior deltoid. It is prescribed for scapular dyskinesis, shoulder impingement, and postural correction programs.

execution.starting_position: Lie face-down on a bench or mat with arms hanging relaxed at the sides or slightly off a bench edge.
execution.setup_instructions: No equipment required. Light dumbbells (0.5–2 kg) may be added when bodyweight is mastered.
steps: Step 1 — Y position: Raise both arms overhead in a Y shape (diagonal, thumbs up). Squeeze the shoulder blades down and together. Hold 2 seconds, lower.
Step 2 — T position: Raise both arms out to the sides in a T shape (horizontal, thumbs up). Retract and depress the scapulae. Hold 2 seconds, lower.
Step 3 — W position: Bend the elbows and raise them to shoulder height, pulling the elbows back as if doing a row, hands near the ears forming a W. Hold 2 seconds, lower.
Step 4: Perform 8–12 repetitions of each position in sequence as one set.
execution.breathing_instructions: Exhale on each lift. Inhale when lowering.
common_mistakes: Shrugging the shoulders upward — focus on depressing the shoulder blades, not elevating
Using momentum rather than deliberate scapular retraction and depression
Lifting the head and craning the neck — keep the neck in neutral
safety_considerations: If shoulder pain occurs, reduce the range of motion
This is a low-load exercise — the goal is neuromuscular control, not strength
execution.range_of_motion_guidance: Lift arms only as high as the shoulder blade can maintain depression. Quality of scapular position matters more than height.
execution.tempo_recommendations: 2-second lift, 2-second hold, 2-second lower. 8–12 reps each position, 2–3 sets.
coaching_cues: Pull your shoulder blades into your back pockets
Thumbs point up in all three positions
Think about making the letters with your arms while keeping your shoulders away from your ears

name: Prone YTW-L with Mini Bands on Floor
description: A resistance-band progression of the bodyweight prone YTW-L exercise. With a light resistance band looped around both wrists, each arm position (Y, T, W, L) is performed against additional resistance, increasing the demand on the lower trapezius, middle trapezius, rhomboids, and infraspinatus. The band provides accommodating resistance — meaning the load increases as the arms move outward or upward where the band stretches more. This is an intermediate-level scapular and rotator cuff rehabilitation exercise for shoulder health programs.

execution.starting_position: Lie face down with arms at the sides and forehead resting on the floor. Loop a very light mini resistance band around both wrists.
execution.setup_instructions: Use the lightest available band. The band should provide only mild resistance in the Y and T positions. If the band prevents full range of motion, it is too heavy.
steps: Step 1 (Y): With the band looped around wrists, raise both arms to the Y angle (45 degrees overhead). The band stretches as arms move apart. Hold 2 seconds, lower.
Step 2 (T): Raise arms to the T position (90 degrees from body). The band provides lateral resistance. Hold 2 seconds, lower.
Step 3 (W): With elbows bent to 90 degrees and arms in W position, externally rotate against the band. Hold 2 seconds, lower.
Step 4 (L): Elbows at 90 degrees bent close to the body, externally rotate both arms forward against the band. Hold 2 seconds, lower.
execution.breathing_instructions: Exhale during each lift. Inhale as you lower.
common_mistakes: Using a band that is too heavy — this reduces range and trains compensation patterns
Shrugging during the Y or T positions instead of engaging the lower trapezius
Not completing the hold at each position — the holds are where most of the training stimulus occurs
safety_considerations: If any position causes pain, omit that position and consult a physiotherapist
Start without resistance and add the band only once bodyweight version is tolerated
execution.range_of_motion_guidance: Full range in each position. If the band reduces range, switch to a lighter band.
execution.tempo_recommendations: 2s lift, 2s hold, 2s lower for each of the four positions
coaching_cues: Use a very light band — the range and muscle engagement matter more than the resistance
Feel the lower shoulder blades activating in the Y position
In the W and L positions, the external rotators are the primary target — squeeze them during the hold

name: Prone YTW-L on Floor
description: A prone floor exercise that works through four arm positions — Y, T, W, and L — each targeting a different aspect of scapular and rotator cuff function. The Y position challenges lower trapezius and serratus; T challenges middle trapezius and posterior deltoid; W challenges the external rotators and rhomboids; L challenges the external rotators in a bent-elbow position. Performed as a continuous complex, this exercise is a staple of shoulder rehabilitation and postural correction programs.

execution.starting_position: Lie face down on the floor with arms by the sides and forehead resting on the floor. Lift the chest slightly to establish a neutral spine position.
execution.setup_instructions: No equipment needed. A thin mat is recommended for comfort. Light dumbbells (0.5–2 kg) can be added when bodyweight becomes insufficient.
steps: Step 1 (Y): Raise both arms overhead at a 45-degree angle from the body, thumbs pointing upward. Hold 2 seconds, lower.
Step 2 (T): Raise both arms straight out to the sides at 90 degrees, thumbs pointing upward. Hold 2 seconds, lower.
Step 3 (W): Bend elbows to 90 degrees with upper arms out to sides. Raise the arms by externally rotating at the shoulder. Hold 2 seconds, lower.
Step 4 (L): With elbows at 90 degrees and bent close to the body, externally rotate both arms so the forearms point forward parallel to the floor. Hold 2 seconds, lower.
execution.breathing_instructions: Exhale during each lift. Inhale as you lower. Breathe normally between positions.
common_mistakes: Lifting from the neck or shrugging the shoulders during the Y position
Hyperextending the lower back instead of using the scapular muscles
Using momentum — each position should be held with controlled muscle activation
safety_considerations: If any position causes shoulder pain, omit that portion and consult a physiotherapist
Start without resistance — the positions themselves are challenging enough for most beginners
execution.range_of_motion_guidance: Lift to the point where you feel the target muscles working without compensating with the lower back or neck.
execution.tempo_recommendations: 2s lift, 2s hold, 2s lower for each position. Complete all four before resting.
coaching_cues: Think about pinching the shoulder blades toward the spine for T and W
For Y, reach as long as possible through the fingertips
For L, keep the elbows tucked and close to the torso

name: Prowler Sled Push — High Handles
description: The high-handle prowler push uses the tall vertical posts of the sled, allowing a more upright body position that shifts the primary demand from the quadriceps toward the deltoids and triceps, with the leg drive producing hip extension more than knee extension. The more vertical trunk angle resembles the mid-stride body position of running rather than the acceleration phase, making it an excellent tool for developing sport-specific pushing power and cardiovascular capacity. The high-handle position also makes this variation more accessible for individuals with limited hip flexion or lower back issues.

execution.starting_position: Grip the high handles of the prowler sled. Stand upright or at a moderate forward lean (20–30° from vertical). Arms are approximately straight.
execution.setup_instructions: Load to the desired weight. The more upright position allows greater resistance than the low-handle position for most people. Use the same surface as for low-handle pushing.
steps: Step 1: Grip the high handles and lean slightly forward — not as dramatically as the low-handle position.
Step 2: Drive alternating feet into the ground, pushing the sled forward with each step. Maintain a tall, rigid torso.
Step 3: Push through the arms to maintain handle contact and direction, but the primary power source is leg drive.
Step 4: Maintain consistent pressure on the handles throughout the push distance.
Step 5: Decelerate and release handles at the end of the distance.
execution.breathing_instructions: Exhale forcefully with each push step. Short, rhythmic breathing throughout the effort.
common_mistakes: Fully locking the elbows and pushing off the sled rather than through it — the arms should transmit force, not be the primary mover
Excessive forward lean that collapses to a low-handle body position, losing the intended mechanical advantage of the high handle
safety_considerations: Secure weight plates before pushing
Clear the path for the full distance before beginning
execution.range_of_motion_guidance: Walk 20–60 metres per set. Full leg extension on each push step.
execution.tempo_recommendations: Conditioning: 40m moderate effort × 6–8 sets with 60–90 seconds rest. Strength endurance: 20m heavy × 5–6 sets with 2 minutes rest.
coaching_cues: Drive from the legs, guide with the arms
Stay tall — do not collapse forward
Quick feet, continuous contact

name: Prowler Sled Push — Low Handles
description: The low-handle prowler push requires the athlete to grip the lower posts of the sled (near ground level), producing a more horizontal body position that places greater demand on the quadriceps and hip extensors through deep knee bend angles. This position resembles a sprint start and trains explosive leg drive at angles highly specific to sprinting acceleration mechanics. Because the sled push involves no eccentric loading phase, it produces minimal muscle damage while still creating a significant training stimulus — making it an ideal tool for high-frequency conditioning or active recovery at light loads.

execution.starting_position: Grip the low handles of the prowler sled with both hands. Lean the body forward at approximately 45–60° from vertical. Drive the feet into the floor behind the body in a sprint-start-like position.
execution.setup_instructions: Load the sled to the target weight. Ensure the pushing surface is astroturf, smooth concrete, or appropriate sled surface. Use smooth-soled shoes on turf sleds, training shoes on concrete.
steps: Step 1: Grip the low handles and position the body in a forward-leaning, athletic push position with arms nearly straight.
Step 2: Drive one foot into the ground forcefully and push the sled forward, then immediately drive the other foot. Quick, alternating leg drive is the goal.
Step 3: Maintain a rigid body position from the hands through the core to the pushing leg — do not let the hips drop or rise excessively.
Step 4: Push hard for the prescribed distance, maintaining maximum effort throughout.
Step 5: At the end of the distance, slow the sled and release the handles.
execution.breathing_instructions: Breathe forcefully throughout. Do not hold the breath. Exhale in short, sharp bursts with each push step.
common_mistakes: Letting the hips rise too high, reducing the low-handle advantage and shifting the load from quads to lower back
Taking too long, slow strides — fast, short steps generate more power and speed
Not maintaining a rigid upper body — the core must transmit force from legs to handles without buckling
safety_considerations: Ensure the surface is appropriate for the sled type — wrong surface combinations damage the sled and create uneven resistance
Check that weight plates are secured before pushing at speed
execution.range_of_motion_guidance: Full leg extension on each push step. Distance per set: 20–40 metres for strength, 40–80 metres for conditioning.
execution.tempo_recommendations: Sprint: 20m maximum effort × 6–10 sets. Rest 60–120 seconds. Conditioning: 40m at moderate load × 4–6 sets. Rest 60–90 seconds.
coaching_cues: Hips back, chest forward — stay horizontal
Drive the foot through the floor with every step
Push the earth away — do not lean on the sled

name: Pseudo Planche Push-Up
description: The pseudo planche push-up shifts the body's weight far forward over the hands by rotating the wrists outward and leaning the torso ahead of the arms. This altered geometry dramatically increases the load on the pectorals and anterior deltoids compared to a standard push-up and builds the foundational strength required for a full planche.

execution.starting_position: Begin in a push-up position with hands placed beside the hips rather than the shoulders. Rotate the wrists so fingertips point toward the feet or sideways. Lean the shoulders significantly forward over the hands.
execution.setup_instructions: Hand placement is 6–12 inches behind where you would normally place them in a push-up. The more forward the lean, the harder the exercise.
steps: Step 1: Position hands at hip level with fingers pointing backward or to the sides.
Step 2: Shift the entire body forward so the shoulders are well ahead of the hands.
Step 3: Lower the body by bending the elbows, keeping the body perfectly rigid.
Step 4: Lower until a moderate chest stretch is felt or the nose nears the floor.
Step 5: Press hard through the palms to return to the start, maintaining the forward lean.
execution.breathing_instructions: Inhale as you lower. Exhale as you press back up.
common_mistakes: Not leaning forward enough to shift load from triceps to chest
Allowing the hips to pike upward
Collapsing the wrists inward under load
safety_considerations: This exercise places high stress on the wrists — build wrist flexibility and strength first
Progress from less forward lean to more as strength increases
Stop immediately if you feel wrist pain
execution.range_of_motion_guidance: Lower until the nose or chest nearly touches the floor. The forward lean must be maintained at all points in the movement.
coaching_cues: Push the floor away from you, don't push yourself away from the floor
Keep the lean — that's the whole exercise
Squeeze the glutes to keep the hips from piking

name: Pull-Up
description: The pull-up is a vertical pulling bodyweight exercise performed on a bar using a pronated (overhand) grip. It is one of the most effective exercises for developing latissimus dorsi width and upper back strength. The overhand grip emphasizes the lats and reduces biceps involvement compared to the chin-up.

execution.starting_position: Hang from a pull-up bar with a pronated grip slightly wider than shoulder width. Arms fully extended, body in a hollow position with core lightly engaged. Feet may be crossed behind.
execution.setup_instructions: Choose a bar that can be reached safely. Begin from a full dead hang with shoulders packed and not shrugged.
steps: Depress and retract the shoulder blades slightly to initiate the pull.
Drive the elbows down and back, pulling the chest toward the bar.
Continue until your chin clears the bar or your chest touches it.
Lower with full control back to the dead hang position.
execution.breathing_instructions: Exhale on the pull up, inhale on the controlled descent.
common_mistakes: Kipping or using momentum instead of controlled muscle contraction
Only achieving partial range of motion — not fully extending at the bottom
Shrugging the shoulders rather than depressing them before pulling
safety_considerations: Fully extend the elbows at the bottom of each rep to maintain shoulder health
Warm up the shoulder rotator cuff before pull-up sets
execution.range_of_motion_guidance: Full dead hang at the bottom, chin above bar or chest to bar at the top.
coaching_cues: Pull your elbows into your back pockets
Imagine bending the bar in half as you pull

name: Push Jerk
description: The push jerk is a jerk variation in which the athlete catches the bar in a partial squat with both feet on the same line, as opposed to the split jerk's forward-and-back split stance. The dip-drive mechanics are identical to the split jerk but the catch requires the athlete to drop straight down rather than splitting. It is a useful accessory movement for overhead stability development and is often used as a teaching drill for the split jerk.

execution.starting_position: Bar in front rack position on shoulders. Feet hip-width apart, torso vertical.
execution.setup_instructions: Same starting position as the split jerk. Taken from a clean or the rack.
steps: Step 1: Stand with the bar in the front rack, torso upright.
Step 2: Dip straight down — small controlled knee bend with vertical torso.
Step 3: Drive upward explosively, pressing the bar off the shoulders.
Step 4: Drop the hips straight down to catch the bar overhead in a partial squat, locking the elbows.
Step 5: Stand to full extension while maintaining the locked overhead position.
execution.breathing_instructions: Brace before the dip. Exhale after standing from the catch.
common_mistakes: Pressing the bar with the arms before full hip extension
Letting the torso lean forward during the dip
Catching with bent elbows
safety_considerations: Requires shoulder mobility to achieve a stable overhead position with the bar slightly behind the ears.
Use bumper plates.
execution.range_of_motion_guidance: Full overhead lockout with elbows extended. Catch in a stable partial squat, feet flat.
execution.tempo_recommendations: Explosive drive, fast catch, controlled stand.
coaching_cues: Drive up — then drop straight down
Lock out the elbows fast in the catch
Dip straight — spine stays vertical

name: Push Press
description: The push press is a compound overhead pressing exercise that uses a brief, explosive leg drive (dip and drive) to initiate the press, allowing more weight to be lifted overhead than a strict overhead press. The legs provide initial momentum through the sticking point, after which the shoulders and triceps complete the press to lockout. It is a staple movement in Olympic weightlifting training and functional strength programs.

execution.starting_position: Hold the barbell in a front rack position at the front deltoids, just above the clavicle. Feet are shoulder-width apart, slightly outside hip-width. Elbows are slightly in front of the bar.
execution.setup_instructions: Set the bar in a rack at shoulder height. Clean or take the bar from the rack to the front rack position. Ensure adequate overhead clearance.
steps: Step 1: Hold the bar in the front rack position, elbows slightly forward. Feet shoulder-width apart.
Step 2: Dip slightly at the knees and hips — a shallow, quick bend of approximately 10–15 degrees.
Step 3: Explosively reverse the dip with leg drive, extending hips and knees rapidly to generate upward momentum.
Step 4: Use the momentum to press the bar overhead to full lockout, finishing with ears in front of the arms overhead.
execution.breathing_instructions: Inhale and brace before the dip; exhale at the top of the press.
common_mistakes: Dipping too deep, turning it into a squat and losing the rapid leg drive timing
Pressing forward rather than straight up — the bar should travel vertically
safety_considerations: Learn the strict overhead press first to establish the pressing path before adding leg drive
Use a rack to get the bar into position safely at heavy loads
execution.range_of_motion_guidance: Full lockout overhead with the bar over the mid-foot; full return to the front rack position.
execution.tempo_recommendations: Explosive drive then controlled descent — no tempo count
coaching_cues: Dip straight down, drive straight up — no forward lean
The dip is quick and shallow — a calf raise, not a squat

name: Push-Up
description: The push-up is a foundational bodyweight pushing exercise that trains the chest, anterior deltoids, and triceps simultaneously. It requires no equipment and can be scaled for any fitness level, making it one of the most accessible and widely used exercises for upper body development and functional strength.

execution.starting_position: Begin in a high plank position with hands placed slightly wider than shoulder width, fingers pointing forward. Arms extended, body forms a straight line from head to heels. Core braced.
execution.setup_instructions: No equipment required. Ensure adequate floor space. Use a mat for comfort on the hands and knees if needed.
steps: Brace your core and glutes to keep the body in a rigid plank.
Lower your body by bending the elbows, keeping them at roughly 45–60 degrees from your torso.
Lower until your chest touches or nearly touches the floor.
Push through your hands to return to the starting position, fully extending the arms at the top.
execution.breathing_instructions: Inhale as you lower. Exhale as you push up.
common_mistakes: Sagging the hips downward — maintain a rigid plank throughout
Raising the hips too high into a piked position
Flaring elbows out to 90 degrees, which stresses the shoulder
safety_considerations: If wrist discomfort occurs, use push-up handles or perform on fists
Regress to knee push-ups if unable to maintain spinal alignment
execution.range_of_motion_guidance: Full range: chest touches or nearly touches the floor at the bottom, arms fully extended at the top.
coaching_cues: Your body is a rigid plank from head to heels
Screw your hands into the floor to activate the chest and stabilize the shoulders

name: Standing Quadriceps Stretch
description: The standing quadriceps stretch targets the rectus femoris and other quadriceps muscles through knee flexion while standing on one leg. Because the rectus femoris crosses both the hip and knee, the stretch is enhanced by simultaneously extending the hip of the stretching leg, which is achieved by drawing the foot toward the glute while maintaining an upright posture.

execution.starting_position: Stand on one foot. Bend the other knee and grasp the ankle of the bent leg with the hand on the same side. Stand upright.
execution.setup_instructions: If balance is a challenge, hold onto a wall or sturdy surface with the free hand.
steps: Step 1: Stand on one leg with knees together.
Step 2: Grasp the ankle of the opposite leg and draw the heel toward the glute.
Step 3: Squeeze the glute of the stretching leg to extend the hip slightly, increasing the stretch on the rectus femoris.
Step 4: Keep both knees together and the torso upright — do not let the hip of the raised leg flare outward.
Step 5: Hold 30–60 seconds, then switch legs.
execution.breathing_instructions: Breathe slowly and deeply throughout the hold.
common_mistakes: Letting the knee of the stretching leg flare sideways — keep knees aligned
Leaning forward at the hip, which reduces the stretch on the rectus femoris
Pulling the heel into the glute with excessive force, stressing the knee joint
safety_considerations: Those with knee pain should ensure the stretch is felt in the thigh, not the knee
Do not wrench the ankle — a gentle hold is sufficient
execution.range_of_motion_guidance: Bring the heel toward the glute as far as comfortable without discomfort in the knee.
coaching_cues: Squeeze the glute of the leg you are stretching to increase the stretch
Stand tall — imagine a string pulling you up through the top of your head
Keep the knees touching or close together

name: Quadruped Fire Hydrant with Band
description: The quadruped fire hydrant is a hip abduction and external rotation exercise performed on all fours. With a resistance band looped above the knees, the exerciser lifts one knee out to the side, mimicking the posture of a dog at a fire hydrant. The band adds resistance to the hip abduction movement, increasing gluteus medius and minimus activation. This exercise is frequently used in hip rehabilitation, knee alignment programs, and glute activation protocols.

execution.starting_position: Begin on hands and knees (quadruped position) with wrists directly under shoulders and knees under hips. Place a resistance band loop just above both knees.
execution.setup_instructions: Choose a band resistance that allows the full range without compromising the spine or hip position. Keep the spine neutral — no rotation or lateral lean.
steps: Step 1: Begin in quadruped with the band loop above the knees and spine neutral.
Step 2: While keeping the knee bent at 90 degrees, lift one knee out to the side as high as possible without rotating the hip or tilting the torso.
Step 3: Hold the top position briefly, squeezing the outer glute.
Step 4: Lower the knee back toward its starting position under control. Repeat all reps on one side before switching.
execution.breathing_instructions: Exhale as you lift the knee. Inhale as you lower.
common_mistakes: Rotating the entire torso toward the lifting side — keep the spine square
Tilting the supporting hip outward to gain extra range — the range must come from the hip joint, not the torso
Losing neutral spine by arching or rounding the lower back
safety_considerations: Use a lighter band if the movement causes lower back pain or compensation
Avoid with acute hip labral injuries — consult a physiotherapist
execution.range_of_motion_guidance: Lift to the point where the hip joint reaches its end range without body rotation. Quality of movement over height.
coaching_cues: Imagine your hips are locked between two parallel walls — the torso cannot rotate
Lead with the knee, not the foot — the knee is the highest point of the movement
Squeeze the outer glute at the top of each rep

name: Quadruped Thoracic Windmill
description: A thoracic spine rotation mobility exercise performed from the quadruped position. One hand is placed behind the head, and the elbow rotates downward threading under the body before opening upward toward the ceiling in a windmill motion. This targets segmental thoracic rotation, challenges thoracic extension and rotation simultaneously, and mobilizes the facet joints of the upper and mid back. Used in rehabilitation for thoracic stiffness, shoulder impingement secondary to poor thoracic mobility, and low back pain related to limited thoracic rotation.

execution.starting_position: Begin in a quadruped position with wrists under shoulders and knees under hips. Place one hand behind the head with the elbow pointing out to the side.
execution.setup_instructions: No equipment needed. A mat is recommended for knee comfort.
steps: Step 1: Begin in quadruped with right hand behind head, elbow pointing right.
Step 2: Thread the right elbow downward and under the body, rotating the thoracic spine to the left and reaching the elbow as far left as possible.
Step 3: Reverse the rotation, opening the right elbow upward toward the ceiling, following it with the gaze. Rotate as far as the thoracic spine allows.
Step 4: Return to the neutral position. Each down-then-up rotation equals one repetition. Complete all reps on one side before switching.
execution.breathing_instructions: Exhale as you thread under. Inhale as you open upward and rotate toward the ceiling.
common_mistakes: Rotating through the lumbar spine rather than the thoracic spine — the lower back and hips should remain stable
Rushing through the range without pausing at the end of rotation in each direction
Using the supporting arm to push into rotation rather than allowing the movement to come from the thoracic spine
safety_considerations: If you feel any joint locking or sharp pain in the thoracic spine during rotation, reduce range and consult a physiotherapist
Avoid if you have an acute thoracic disc herniation unless prescribed by a physiotherapist
execution.range_of_motion_guidance: Work at the end-range of comfortable thoracic rotation in each direction. The hips and lower back must not rotate.
execution.tempo_recommendations: 2s thread down, 1s end-range hold, 2s open up, 1s end-range hold
coaching_cues: Imagine your hips are locked in place — only the upper back rotates
Follow the elbow with your eyes — the gaze leads the thoracic rotation
Breathe into the chest as you open upward

name: Quarter Squat
description: The quarter squat limits knee flexion to approximately 25-30 degrees of travel, keeping the torso more upright and the load on the quadriceps near full extension. It is used for sport-specific power training (since most jumping and sprinting occurs in this partial range), for post-surgical rehabilitation where full depth is contraindicated, and for accommodating resistance training with bands or chains where supramaximal loads are used in the strongest portion of the lift.

execution.starting_position: Set up as for a barbell back squat, with the bar on the upper back and feet shoulder-width apart.
execution.setup_instructions: May use safety pins set high in the rack to limit depth, or use a box just above parallel as a guide.
steps: Step 1: Unrack the bar and stand with feet shoulder-width, toes slightly out.
Step 2: Begin the descent by pushing the hips back and bending the knees.
Step 3: Descend only until the knees reach approximately 25-30 degrees of flexion (about a quarter of full depth).
Step 4: Drive upward through the full foot, extending the knees and hips to return to standing.
execution.breathing_instructions: Inhale and brace before descent, exhale on ascent.
common_mistakes: Knees caving inward
Heels rising off the floor
Excessive forward lean of the torso
safety_considerations: The partial range concentrates high loads on the knees — ensure proper alignment
Useful clinically but should not replace full squats for general training
execution.range_of_motion_guidance: Intentionally limited to ~25-30 degrees of knee flexion.
coaching_cues: Knees track over toes
Stay tall — chest up
Drive the floor away

name: Rack Pull
description: The rack pull is a partial-range deadlift variation starting with the bar elevated on safety pins inside a power rack, typically at or just below the knee. The reduced range of motion allows the lifter to overload the upper portion of the deadlift pattern, emphasizing the erector spinae, upper back, and trapezius with loads greater than a full conventional deadlift. It is commonly used to address weaknesses in the lockout portion of the deadlift.

execution.starting_position: Set the safety pins inside a power rack so the bar rests at knee height or just below. Load the barbell heavier than your conventional deadlift working weight. Stand with feet hip-width apart, the bar over mid-foot.
execution.setup_instructions: Set rack pin height to place the bar at or just below knee level. Use a standard barbell and load it heavier than you would for a full deadlift. Use a double overhand or mixed grip.
steps: Step 1: Hinge at the hips and grasp the bar with the chosen grip. Set the back — neutral spine, braced core.
Step 2: Take a large breath into the belly, brace the core hard.
Step 3: Drive through the floor with the legs while pulling the bar up the shins and thighs.
Step 4: Lock out at the top by driving the hips forward and squeezing the glutes.
Step 5: Hinge back to lower the bar to the pins under full control. Reset and repeat.
execution.breathing_instructions: Inhale and brace before each rep. Exhale at the top after lockout.
common_mistakes: Rounding the upper back under the heavy load — prioritize a stiff, braced torso
Hyperextending at lockout rather than achieving a neutral spine with glute contraction
Letting the bar drift away from the body during the pull
safety_considerations: Use a controlled negative — do not drop the bar onto the pins from height unless using bumper plates and appropriate flooring
Rack pulls with very heavy loads demand excellent core bracing — do not perform when fatigued
execution.range_of_motion_guidance: From pin height (knee level) to full lockout. This is intentionally partial range.
execution.tempo_recommendations: Controlled concentric, full lockout hold for 1s, controlled 2–3s eccentric to pins.
coaching_cues: Push the floor away, do not think of it as a pure pull
Keep the bar dragging up the thighs
Squeeze the glutes to lock out — do not lean back

name: Rack Pull Above Knee
description: The above-knee rack pull sets the starting pin height just above the knee, leaving only the final hip-extension lockout portion of the deadlift. This shortened range of motion allows for supramaximal loading and directly trains the lockout mechanics, upper back, and trapezius under heavier loads than a full deadlift allows. It is used by powerlifters to reinforce lockout strength and by athletes to build upper back and grip capacity.

execution.starting_position: Set the safety pins of a power rack just above knee height. Load the bar on the pins. Grip the bar in the same position as a conventional deadlift. The torso will be nearly vertical due to the high starting position.
execution.setup_instructions: Because of the short range of motion, loads can be significantly higher than conventional deadlift — often 110-130%. Lifting straps are commonly used.
steps: Step 1: Position yourself behind the bar with pins set just above knee height.
Step 2: Grip the bar with a double-overhand or mixed grip, brace the core.
Step 3: Drive the hips forward in a hip-extension motion, pulling the bar to lockout.
Step 4: Squeeze the glutes and stand fully erect at the top.
Step 5: Return the bar to the pins under control.
execution.breathing_instructions: Brace before each rep. Exhale at lockout.
common_mistakes: Jerking the bar off the pins — set the tension first, then pull
Not achieving full lockout at the top
Hyperextending the lower back at lockout — the goal is hip extension, not lumbar hyperextension
safety_considerations: High loads place significant demand on the grip and upper back — do not neglect warmup sets
Ensure pins are level and secure before loading
execution.range_of_motion_guidance: Short range — from just above the knee to full lockout only.
coaching_cues: Take up the slack — don't yank off the pins
Drive the hips forward to lock out
Squeeze everything at the top

name: Rack Pull Below Knee
description: The below-knee rack pull sets the safety pins slightly below the knee, training a range of motion that closely mirrors the full deadlift while allowing for a modest load increase and removing the floor-contact phase. It addresses the mid-shin to lockout portion of the pull and is used to build strength through the zone where the bar passes the knee — the first major sticking point for most lifters. The hamstring and glute demand is high throughout.

execution.starting_position: Set the safety pins of a power rack just below the knee. Load the bar on the pins. This setup closely resembles a conventional deadlift starting position, but with less initial knee flexion required.
execution.setup_instructions: Loads are typically 5-15% above conventional deadlift training max. Treat the setup as a deadlift, not a lockout exercise.
steps: Step 1: Set up behind the bar with pins just below knee height.
Step 2: Take a conventional deadlift stance and grip.
Step 3: Brace the core, retract the lats, and create tension without yanking.
Step 4: Drive through the floor and push the hips through to lockout.
Step 5: Return the bar to the pins under control.
execution.breathing_instructions: Full brace before each rep. Exhale at lockout.
common_mistakes: Treating this as a pure hip extension and neglecting initial leg drive
Letting the bar drift forward past the knee
Not resetting the brace between reps
safety_considerations: Although the range is shorter, the demand through the mid-shin zone is high — do not skip lower-back warmup sets
Pin height must be precisely below (not at) the knee for the intended training effect
execution.range_of_motion_guidance: From just below the knee to full lockout — a range similar to the top two-thirds of a conventional deadlift.
coaching_cues: Don't yank off the pins — build tension
Same as a deadlift, just shorter
Full hip extension at lockout

name: Rear Delt Fly
description: The rear delt fly is an isolation exercise for the posterior deltoid performed in a bent-over position. By abducting the arms horizontally with a slight elbow bend, it directly targets the rear delts and recruits the rhomboids and middle trapezius as synergists. It is valuable for shoulder balance and posture correction.

execution.starting_position: Stand with feet shoulder-width apart. Hinge forward at the hips until the torso is roughly parallel to the floor. Hold dumbbells hanging straight down from the shoulders with a neutral or pronated grip and a slight elbow bend.
execution.setup_instructions: Use light weight — the rear delt is a small muscle. Bend the knees slightly to reduce hamstring tension.
steps: With a fixed elbow bend, raise both dumbbells out to the sides in a horizontal arc.
Raise until upper arms are parallel to the floor or slightly above.
Squeeze the rear delts and retract the shoulder blades at the top.
Lower under control back to the starting position.
execution.breathing_instructions: Exhale as arms rise, inhale as they descend.
common_mistakes: Using too much weight, turning it into a row
Extending the elbows too much, losing rear delt isolation
Not hinging far enough forward
safety_considerations: If lower back discomfort occurs, perform seated or lying on an incline bench
execution.range_of_motion_guidance: Raise until upper arms are parallel to the floor.
coaching_cues: Lead with the elbows, not the hands
Feel the pinch between your shoulder blades at the top

name: Renegade Row
description: The renegade row combines a plank position with a unilateral dumbbell row, performed with both hands gripping dumbbells on the floor in a push-up stance. The movement demands simultaneous anti-rotation core stability, pushing muscle endurance in the support arm and pressing muscles, and pulling strength in the rowing arm. It is a highly efficient full-body exercise that trains the back, core, and shoulder stabilizers in a single movement.

execution.starting_position: Place two dumbbells on the floor, shoulder-width apart. Get into a push-up position with hands gripping the dumbbell handles, body forming a straight line from head to heels.
execution.setup_instructions: Use hex dumbbells, which sit flat and provide a stable base. Feet wider than hip-width increases stability and reduces anti-rotation demand.
steps: Step 1: Assume a high plank position with both hands on dumbbell handles.
Step 2: Brace the core and squeeze the glutes to prevent hip rotation.
Step 3: Row one dumbbell to the hip by driving the elbow straight up.
Step 4: Lower the dumbbell to the floor under control.
Step 5: Repeat on the other side. Each side counts as one rep.
execution.breathing_instructions: Exhale as you row, inhale as you return to the floor.
common_mistakes: Rotating the hips as you row — the hips must stay square
Using light dumbbells that allow too wide a foot stance, reducing the core challenge
Rushing the row, losing core position
safety_considerations: Use flat-bottomed hex dumbbells — round dumbbells on a hard floor are unstable and dangerous
Do not perform this exercise with wrist injuries or shoulder instability
execution.range_of_motion_guidance: Dumbbell stays on the floor at the start, pulled to hip level at the top while maintaining rigid plank.
coaching_cues: Hips square — no tilting
Make a T with your body when rowing
If your hips rotate, spread your feet wider

name: Resistance Band Chest Fly
description: The resistance band chest fly is a portable, joint-friendly isolation exercise that trains the pectoral muscles through a wide arc using an elastic band. As the band stretches, resistance increases toward peak contraction, providing an accommodating load curve that complements the natural strength curve of the chest.

execution.starting_position: Anchor a resistance band behind you at chest height or loop it around a stable post. Stand facing away and hold one end of the band in each hand, arms extended out to the sides at shoulder height.
execution.setup_instructions: Secure the band anchor at chest height. Step far enough from the anchor that the band has light tension even at the start position.
steps: Step 1: Stand in a staggered or athletic stance, holding both ends of the band.
Step 2: Begin with arms extended out to the sides, hands at shoulder level.
Step 3: Sweep both arms forward and together in front of your chest, squeezing the pectorals at the meeting point.
Step 4: Slowly open the arms back to the starting position with control, resisting the band's pull.
Step 5: Maintain a fixed, slightly bent elbow throughout the movement.
execution.breathing_instructions: Exhale as you bring the arms together. Inhale as you open them back to the start.
common_mistakes: Anchoring the band too low or too high, altering the exercise angle
Allowing the arms to snap back due to band recoil
Straightening the elbows completely under tension
safety_considerations: Check the band anchor is secure before each set
Inspect bands for tears or wear before use
Start with a lighter band to establish range of motion
execution.range_of_motion_guidance: Open arms until a mild chest stretch is felt. Bring hands together without crossing the midline past the sternum for maximum contraction.
coaching_cues: Control the band on the way back — it's the eccentric that builds
Feel the chest squeeze as hands meet
Keep shoulders away from ears

name: Resistance Band Lateral Raise
description: The resistance band lateral raise provides an accommodating resistance curve that increases tension as the arm approaches the top of the movement, contrasting with dumbbells which lose most tension at the bottom. This increasing resistance toward shoulder height matches the medial deltoid's strength curve more closely, creating a unique training stimulus for the lateral head. It is particularly useful for home training, travel workouts, or as a high-rep finisher after dumbbell lateral raises.

execution.starting_position: Stand on the center of a resistance band. Hold one end in each hand with a neutral grip. Arms at the sides, slight elbow bend.
execution.setup_instructions: Adjust the starting tension by standing on more or less of the band. The resistance increases through the range of motion — this is the key difference from dumbbells.
steps: Step 1: Stand on the band, one end per hand, arms at the sides.
Step 2: Raise both arms out to the sides in a lateral arc.
Step 3: Raise until arms are at or slightly above shoulder height.
Step 4: Pause briefly at the top.
Step 5: Lower under control, resisting the band tension on the way down.
execution.breathing_instructions: Exhale on the raise, inhale on the descent.
common_mistakes: Releasing tension at the bottom — maintain a slight pull at all times
Shrugging the traps as the arms rise
safety_considerations: Ensure the band is secured under the feet before beginning
execution.range_of_motion_guidance: Starting position (arms at sides) to shoulder height.
coaching_cues: Increasing tension is the advantage here — use it
Slow descent
Lead with the elbows

name: Reverse Barbell Curl
description: The reverse barbell curl is performed with a straight bar using an overhand (pronated) grip. It targets the brachioradialis, brachialis, and extensor muscles of the forearm. Because the biceps brachii is in a mechanically disadvantaged position when pronated, the forearm extensors and brachioradialis must work harder. This exercise builds forearm thickness and complements standard underhand curls for complete elbow flexor development.

execution.starting_position: Stand upright holding a barbell with a pronated grip, shoulder-width. Arms extended at the thighs.
execution.setup_instructions: Use lighter weight than underhand curls. The pronated position reduces overall lifting capacity.
steps: Step 1: Curl the barbell upward with the overhand grip, keeping elbows at the sides.
Step 2: Curl to maximum elbow flexion, maintaining pronation throughout.
Step 3: Lower slowly back to the starting position.
execution.breathing_instructions: Exhale on the curl, inhale on the return.
common_mistakes: Wrists breaking into flexion or extension
Using body sway
Grip slipping to neutral
safety_considerations: Straight bar may cause wrist discomfort — use an EZ-bar if needed
execution.range_of_motion_guidance: Full extension to full elbow flexion.
coaching_cues: Overhand grip all the way
Wrists neutral — straight wrists
Slow on the way down

name: Reverse Crunch
description: The reverse crunch is a supine core exercise that targets the lower portion of the rectus abdominis by moving the pelvis toward the chest rather than the chest toward the pelvis. As the knees are drawn toward the face with posterior pelvic tilt, the lower abdominal fibers are trained through spinal flexion initiated from below. It is a spine-friendly alternative to full sit-ups and provides direct lower abdominal engagement without excessive hip flexor recruitment.

execution.starting_position: Lie flat on your back with arms at your sides or holding a stable object overhead. Hips bent to 90 degrees, knees bent to 90 degrees, feet off the floor.
execution.setup_instructions: Use a mat for comfort. Optionally hold a bench or heavy object behind the head for stability.
steps: Step 1: Lie supine with hips and knees both at 90 degrees, feet elevated.
Step 2: Brace the core and exhale as you curl the knees toward the face by posteriorly tilting the pelvis.
Step 3: The lower back and tailbone should lift off the floor at the top — this is what distinguishes it from a simple hip flexor lift.
Step 4: Pause at the top position with maximum abdominal compression.
Step 5: Lower with control back to the starting position.
execution.breathing_instructions: Exhale as the pelvis curls up. Inhale on the descent.
common_mistakes: Lifting the knees without curling the pelvis — this is hip flexion, not a reverse crunch
Using momentum to swing the legs rather than abdominal contraction
Lowering too quickly and losing abdominal tension on the eccentric
safety_considerations: Keep the neck and shoulders relaxed on the floor throughout.
Avoid if experiencing hip flexor tightness that causes lower back arching.
execution.range_of_motion_guidance: The key ROM is the final phase where the lower back and tailbone lift off the floor. Full range = tailbone fully curled toward ceiling.
execution.tempo_recommendations: 2-1-2: 2 seconds concentric, 1 second pause, 2 seconds eccentric.
coaching_cues: Curl your tailbone toward the ceiling
Think about bringing your knees to your nose
The lower back comes off the floor — that is the goal

name: Reverse Crunch on Incline Bench
description: The reverse crunch performed on an incline bench elevates the head end above the hip end, adding gravitational load to the lower abdominal region throughout the movement compared to the flat-bench version. The athlete grasps the bench behind the head, extends the legs below horizontal, and pulls the knees toward the chest by posteriorly tilting the pelvis — a movement almost exclusively controlled by the lower rectus abdominis. The incline increases both the eccentric and concentric challenge.

execution.starting_position: Lie on the incline bench with the head at the high end. Grasp the bench behind the head. Legs are extended, lowered below the hip level.
execution.setup_instructions: Set the bench to 20–30° incline. Ensure the head-end grips are within comfortable reach.
steps: Step 1: Begin with legs extended and lowered below the bench plane (against the gravity).
Step 2: Curl the pelvis backward (posterior tilt) and draw the knees toward the chest simultaneously.
Step 3: At the top, the knees should be at or above the hip level and the lower back is lifted off the bench.
Step 4: Slowly lower the legs back down, resisting the eccentric pull.
Step 5: Return to full extension without letting the legs drop rapidly.
execution.breathing_instructions: Exhale as the knees come toward the chest. Inhale on the controlled descent.
common_mistakes: Using momentum from the legs rather than initiating with posterior pelvic tilt
Not lifting the lower back off the bench at the top — full contraction requires this
safety_considerations: If grip fatigue limits reps before the core does, use wrist straps
execution.range_of_motion_guidance: Legs from full extension below horizontal to knees drawn to chest with lower back lifted.
execution.tempo_recommendations: 2-1-3-0. Slow eccentric is essential on the incline version.
coaching_cues: Pull with the abs, not the hip flexors
Curl the tailbone up — do not just swing the legs

name: Reverse Curl
description: The reverse curl is a curl variation using an overhand (pronated) grip rather than the standard underhand (supinated) grip. This grip change mechanically disadvantages the biceps brachii while placing the brachioradialis and brachialis as the primary movers. It is an important supplementary exercise for building forearm and outer arm thickness and improving wrist and elbow joint resilience.

execution.starting_position: Stand upright holding a barbell (or dumbbells) with an overhand (pronated) grip, hands shoulder-width apart. Arms are fully extended, bar at thigh level.
execution.setup_instructions: Use a straight barbell, EZ-curl bar, or dumbbells. The load will be significantly lower than a standard curl due to the grip change.
steps: Step 1: Hold the bar with a pronated (overhand) grip, hands shoulder-width apart. Stand tall, upper arms at the sides.
Step 2: Brace the core and keep the upper arms stationary.
Step 3: Exhale and curl the bar upward to shoulder level, maintaining the overhand grip throughout.
Step 4: Hold briefly at the top, then inhale and lower the bar back to the starting position.
execution.breathing_instructions: Exhale on the curl; inhale on the return.
common_mistakes: Letting the wrists collapse into flexion during the curl — keep wrists neutral or slightly extended
Using the same weight as a supinated curl — reduce load significantly
safety_considerations: If wrist discomfort occurs, switch to an EZ-curl bar which allows a semi-pronated grip
execution.range_of_motion_guidance: Full arm extension at the bottom; curl to shoulder level at the top.
coaching_cues: Keep wrists flat — do not let them flex toward you during the curl
Lead with the knuckles

name: Reverse EZ-Bar Curl
description: The reverse EZ-bar curl uses an overhand (pronated) grip on an EZ-curl bar to target the brachioradialis and brachialis rather than the biceps brachii, which is in a mechanically disadvantaged position in pronation. The EZ-bar's angle reduces wrist stress compared to a straight bar reverse curl. This exercise builds the forearm and arm thickness from the outside and helps balance pulling strength.

execution.starting_position: Stand upright holding an EZ-bar with a pronated (overhand) grip at the outer grip positions. Arms extended.
execution.setup_instructions: Use the outer grip on the EZ-bar for the most comfortable wrist angle. Use lighter weight than underhand curls.
steps: Step 1: Curl the EZ-bar upward with a pronated grip.
Step 2: Keep the elbows at the sides and curl to maximum elbow flexion.
Step 3: Lower slowly back to the starting position.
execution.breathing_instructions: Exhale on the curl, inhale on the return.
common_mistakes: Rotating to a neutral grip during the curl
Excessive wrist extension at the bottom
Using momentum
safety_considerations: Avoid wrist hyperextension — keep wrists straight throughout
execution.range_of_motion_guidance: Full extension to maximum elbow flexion.
coaching_cues: Pronated grip stays all the way
Wrists straight — don't break them
Elbows at the sides

name: Reverse-Grip Barbell Bench Press
description: The Reverse-Grip Bench Press is performed with a supinated (underhand) grip, meaning the palms face toward the head. This grip changes elbow mechanics, keeping them closer to the body throughout the press and shifting activation toward the upper pectoral fibers (clavicular head) and triceps. It is a useful variation for upper chest development and for lifters with certain shoulder issues.

execution.starting_position: Lie on a flat bench. Grip the bar with palms facing toward your face (supinated). Use a grip slightly inside shoulder-width for comfort. Thumbs wrap around the bar.
execution.setup_instructions: It is strongly recommended to use a power rack. Have a spotter available as the supinated grip is biomechanically weaker and the bar can roll out of control if grip fails. Use a weight below your standard bench max.
steps: Step 1: Unrack bar with a supinated grip. The bar will feel different — elbows naturally tuck closer to the torso.
Step 2: Lower the bar slowly to touch the lower chest, keeping elbows at approximately 45-50 degrees from the torso.
Step 3: Press up and slightly back toward the rack to reach lockout.
Step 4: Control the bar carefully on the return.
execution.breathing_instructions: Inhale and brace before descent. Exhale at lockout.
common_mistakes: Using too wide a grip, creating uncomfortable wrist torque with a supinated grip
Failing to inform the spotter of the grip type before attempting
safety_considerations: The supinated grip is weaker — reduce load by 15-25% from your standard bench
Bar control is different — always use a spotter or power rack safeties
Discontinue if wrist or elbow discomfort occurs
execution.range_of_motion_guidance: Full ROM — bar touches lower chest, elbows extend to lockout.
coaching_cues: Keep elbows tucked — this is the nature of the grip
Think about pressing the bar toward the ceiling, not toward your feet

name: Reverse-Grip Cable Tricep Pushdown
description: The reverse-grip pushdown uses a supinated (underhand) grip on a straight bar or EZ-bar attached to a high cable. The supinated position shifts greater emphasis to the medial head of the tricep compared to the standard pronated pushdown. The underhand grip also involves the forearm flexors more as stabilizers. It is a useful variation for developing the lower and inner tricep for complete three-dimensional arm development.

execution.starting_position: Attach a straight bar to a high cable. Grip with a supinated (underhand) grip at shoulder width. Elbows at the sides.
execution.setup_instructions: Use a straight bar. The supinated grip is the defining feature — maintain it throughout.
steps: Step 1: Begin with elbows at the sides, bar at chest height with supinated grip.
Step 2: Extend the elbows by pushing the bar down.
Step 3: Push to full elbow extension.
Step 4: Return slowly, maintaining the supinated grip.
execution.breathing_instructions: Exhale on the pushdown, inhale on the return.
common_mistakes: Rotating the grip to neutral during the movement
Elbows flaring
Using less weight than the pronated version — this is normal
safety_considerations: The supinated grip can stress the wrist — keep wrists straight and don't use excessive weight
execution.range_of_motion_guidance: Full elbow extension at the bottom.
coaching_cues: Palms face up throughout
Wrists stay neutral — don't break them
Elbows pinned to the sides

name: Reverse Hack Squat Machine
description: The reverse hack squat is performed on a standard hack squat machine with the lifter facing into the pad rather than away from it. This orientation creates a squat pattern similar to a barbell squat but machine-guided, with significantly greater hip hinge component. The chest rests on the shoulder pads and the hips push back during descent, heavily recruiting the glutes and hamstrings in addition to the quadriceps.

execution.starting_position: Face into the hack squat machine with your chest against the shoulder pads and feet on the platform. Feet can be placed lower on the platform to accentuate the hip hinge.
execution.setup_instructions: Load the hack squat machine and face the pads. Position the shoulder pads against your chest and upper torso. Release the safety handles.
steps: Step 1: Brace the core and maintain chest contact with the pad throughout.
Step 2: Bend the knees and push the hips back as you descend, allowing a natural hip hinge.
Step 3: Descend until the thighs are at least parallel to the platform.
Step 4: Drive through the entire foot, extending hips and knees together to return to the top.
execution.breathing_instructions: Inhale and brace before descent. Exhale on the ascent.
common_mistakes: Hips rising faster than the torso on the ascent
Insufficient depth
Letting chest come off the pad
safety_considerations: Engage the safety locks before stepping out of position
The shoulder pads create pressure on the chest — do not load excessively heavy initially
execution.range_of_motion_guidance: Thighs parallel or below. Greater hip flexion than the standard hack squat.
coaching_cues: Hips back as you descend
Drive the hips through at lockout
Chest stays on the pad

name: Reverse Hyperextension
description: The reverse hyperextension is performed face-down on an elevated surface — a reverse hyper machine, a high bench, or a GHD — with the legs hanging free. The legs are swung rearward and upward to full hip extension using gluteus maximus and hamstring strength. Unlike most hip hinge exercises, the spine decompresses during the descent phase, making this exercise popular for simultaneously training the posterior chain and rehabilitating lower back issues.

execution.starting_position: Lie face-down on a hyperextension bench or elevated surface with hips at the edge, legs hanging straight down. Hold the handles or grip the bench edge securely.
execution.setup_instructions: Position the hips at or just past the pad edge so the legs can hang freely. Grip the bench or handles firmly. For added load, hold a dumbbell between the feet.
steps: Step 1: Lie prone on the bench with hips at the edge, legs hanging down. Hold the bench firmly.
Step 2: With control, raise both legs backward and upward by extending the hips — squeeze the glutes.
Step 3: Raise until the legs are parallel to the floor or slightly above — no hyperextension of the lumbar spine.
Step 4: Hold briefly at the top.
Step 5: Lower the legs slowly under control, allowing the spine to gently decompress at the bottom.
execution.breathing_instructions: Exhale as you raise the legs. Inhale as you lower.
common_mistakes: Swinging the legs with momentum — the movement should be controlled, not ballistic
Hyperextending the lumbar spine at the top — stop when the legs are parallel
Not holding the bench firmly — the torso must be anchored
safety_considerations: Avoid excessive lumbar hyperextension at the top
If you have acute lower back pain, consult a professional before performing this exercise
execution.range_of_motion_guidance: Legs hang toward the floor at the bottom. Raise to parallel with the floor at the top — not higher.
coaching_cues: Squeeze the glutes — not the lower back — at the top
Let the legs drop slowly — don't just fall
