Control the movement — no swinging

name: Reverse Hyperextension
description: The reverse hyperextension trains the posterior chain with the opposite movement pattern from a standard back extension — the torso is fixed and the legs swing posteriorly. This arrangement decompresses the lumbar spine on each lowering phase while loading the glutes and hamstrings concentrically on the ascent. It is considered a low-spinal-load alternative for posterior chain development.

execution.starting_position: Lie face down on a hyperextension bench with the hips at the edge of the pad and the torso supported on the bench. Grip the handles or sides of the bench firmly. Let the legs hang down toward the floor.
execution.setup_instructions: Position the hyperextension bench so there is room for the legs to swing below and behind the bench. Grip the handles firmly to stabilize the torso.
steps: Step 1: Begin with legs hanging down, feet near the floor.
Step 2: Swing the legs upward and backward by contracting the glutes and hamstrings, raising them to or slightly above the level of the bench.
Step 3: Hold briefly at the top with glutes squeezed.
Step 4: Lower the legs in a controlled arc back to the starting position.
Step 5: Allow gravity to gently decompress the lower spine at the bottom before the next rep.
execution.breathing_instructions: Exhale as the legs rise. Inhale as they lower.
common_mistakes: Using momentum and swinging the legs rather than muscle contraction
Raising the legs far above horizontal — this compresses the lumbar spine rather than decompressing it
Failing to grip the bench firmly, allowing the torso to slide
safety_considerations: Keep the range of motion controlled — stop when legs are roughly parallel to the floor
This exercise is often cited for its decompressive benefit; however, it should still be performed with control
execution.range_of_motion_guidance: Legs should travel from hanging below the bench up to roughly horizontal or just above. Avoid excessive range.
coaching_cues: Squeeze the glutes to initiate the lift — do not lead with the knees
Think of trying to touch the ceiling with your heels
Let gravity do the work on the way down — stay controlled

name: Reverse Lunge
description: The reverse lunge steps the foot backward rather than forward, reducing shear forces on the anterior knee compared to a forward lunge and improving stability. The front leg performs the primary work of controlled deceleration and propulsion. It is accessible to beginners and those with knee sensitivities, and can be heavily loaded with dumbbells or a barbell for significant lower body hypertrophy and strength development.

execution.starting_position: Stand tall with feet together. If using dumbbells, hold them at the sides. If using a barbell, hold it on the upper traps.
execution.setup_instructions: Choose load based on goal. Bodyweight works for beginners. Dumbbells or barbell can be added progressively.
steps: Step 1: Stand with feet together, core braced, chest tall.
Step 2: Take a controlled step backward with one foot, landing on the ball of that foot.
Step 3: Lower the rear knee toward the floor while keeping the front shin as vertical as practical. The front knee tracks over the toes.
Step 4: When the rear knee is 1–2 cm from the floor, drive through the front foot to return to standing.
Step 5: Alternate legs each rep or complete all reps on one side before switching.
execution.breathing_instructions: Exhale as you return to standing. Inhale as you step back and lower.
common_mistakes: Taking too short a step, causing the front knee to track far over the toe
Letting the torso collapse forward instead of staying upright
Allowing the rear knee to crash into the floor without control
safety_considerations: Keep the front shin vertical or close to it to reduce anterior knee stress
Use a shorter step initially to establish the movement pattern before increasing stride length
execution.range_of_motion_guidance: Rear knee should travel close to the floor (1–2 cm off) for full range. Front thigh reaches approximately parallel.
coaching_cues: Step back far enough to keep the shin vertical
Think: drop straight down, not forward
Drive through the front heel to stand

name: Reverse Lunge to High Knee Lift
description: A dynamic single-leg exercise combining a reverse lunge with an explosive drive to bring the rear knee upward at the end of each rep. The knee drive adds a hip flexor and balance challenge and increases the cardiovascular demand compared to a static reverse lunge.

execution.starting_position: Stand tall with feet together, hands on hips or holding light dumbbells at your sides.
execution.setup_instructions: No equipment needed for bodyweight version. If using dumbbells, select a light to moderate load.
steps: Step 1: Step one foot backward into a reverse lunge, lowering the rear knee toward the floor.
Step 2: At the bottom, pause briefly then explosively drive the rear knee upward and forward toward chest height.
Step 3: Balance on the standing leg momentarily at the top with the knee raised high.
Step 4: Return the foot back to the floor and repeat, or alternate legs.
execution.breathing_instructions: Inhale during the descent. Exhale explosively during the knee drive.
common_mistakes: Using momentum instead of controlled hip flexion for the knee drive
Leaning excessively backward during the knee drive
safety_considerations: Maintain an upright torso throughout to protect the lumbar spine
execution.range_of_motion_guidance: Full lunge descent (front thigh parallel) followed by full hip flexion on the knee drive.
coaching_cues: Lunge down then drive the knee up high
Balance at the top before stepping back down

name: Reverse Nordic Curl
description: The reverse Nordic curl is an eccentric quadriceps exercise in which the knees are on a padded surface, the feet are anchored, and the torso leans backward — the opposite direction of the Nordic hamstring curl. The rectus femoris is loaded eccentrically in its stretched position (hip extended, knee flexed) with the bodyweight acting as the resistance. It is one of the few exercises that trains the rectus femoris under hip-extension load with significant knee flexion, complementing the knee-extension exercises commonly used for quad training.

execution.starting_position: Kneel on a padded surface with feet anchored behind (partner or weighted barbell). Start upright on the knees with hips extended.
execution.setup_instructions: Ankle anchoring is required. Use a partner holding the heels or secure the feet under a barbell. Generous knee padding is essential.
steps: Step 1: Kneel upright with feet secured and hips fully extended. Hold the arms across the chest or overhead for progression.
Step 2: Begin to lean backward by allowing the knees to flex — the body leans away from the anchored feet.
Step 3: The quadriceps eccentrically control the backward lean. Lower as far as quad strength allows.
Step 4: Return to the upright kneeling position using the quadriceps concentrically, or use the hands to push off the floor if needed.
Step 5: Complete the prescribed reps.
execution.breathing_instructions: Exhale as you lean back. Inhale as you return to vertical.
common_mistakes: Hinging at the hip instead of leaning backward as a whole-body unit from the knees
Dropping too fast in early training, causing excessive DOMS or quad strain
Not using knee padding, making the exercise unpleasant and unsustainable
safety_considerations: Severe DOMS is likely after first exposure — start with 2–3 short-range reps
Avoid if experiencing patellar tendinopathy — consult a clinician
If unable to control even a minimal backward lean, build quad strength with leg extensions before attempting
execution.range_of_motion_guidance: Lean as far back as quad strength controls. Begin with minimal range (10–20°) and build progressively.
execution.tempo_recommendations: 5-0-1-0 — the eccentric (leaning back) is the entire stimulus; control it maximally
coaching_cues: Lean back as one unit — don't fold at the hip
Quads on — squeeze them to slow the fall
Catch with hands if needed — that's normal for beginners

name: Reverse Pec Deck
description: The reverse pec deck uses the pec deck or butterfly machine in reverse — facing the pad rather than away from it — to perform a rear deltoid fly motion. The machine provides a guided movement path and consistent resistance throughout the arc, making it an effective and low-skill option for targeting the posterior deltoid and scapular retractors. It is widely used in hypertrophy programs as a finishing or high-rep accessory exercise for rear deltoid development.

execution.starting_position: Face the pec deck machine (reverse of the normal setup). Grip the handles with arms in front of the body at shoulder height. Adjust the seat so the handles are at shoulder height.
execution.setup_instructions: Some pec deck machines have specific attachments or handle adjustments for reverse use. Position the seat so the arms are parallel to the floor at the start.
steps: Step 1: Face the machine, grip the handles with arms extended forward.
Step 2: Begin from the arms-forward position (handles together or close).
Step 3: Pull the handles outward and backward in a horizontal arc.
Step 4: Bring the arms to fully in line with the shoulders (T-position).
Step 5: Squeeze the rear delts and return under control.
execution.breathing_instructions: Exhale on the opening (fly) motion, inhale on the return.
common_mistakes: Letting the shoulder blades slide forward on the return — maintain upper back position
Using too heavy a load, causing the traps to dominate instead of the rear delts
safety_considerations: Keep the neck neutral — do not crane forward toward the machine
execution.range_of_motion_guidance: Arms start forward (closed position) and open to T (arms in line with shoulders).
coaching_cues: Think rear delt squeeze, not elbow drive
Slow and controlled on the return
Shoulder blades stay back

name: Reverse Wrist Curl
description: The reverse wrist curl is an isolation exercise for the wrist extensor muscles performed with the forearms resting on a surface and the palms facing downward. The wrists are extended upward against resistance, targeting the extensor carpi radialis and extensor carpi ulnaris. This muscle group is often undertrained compared to the wrist flexors, and strengthening it is important for balance, elbow joint health, and reducing the risk of lateral epicondylitis.

execution.starting_position: Sit on a bench. Rest forearms on the thighs or bench pad with the wrists hanging off the edge. Palms face downward (pronated). Hold a dumbbell or barbell with an overhand grip.
execution.setup_instructions: Use lighter weight than for wrist curls — the extensors are smaller muscles. Forearms fully supported, only wrists free to move.
steps: Step 1: Forearms resting on a surface, palms facing downward, weight in hands. Allow the wrists to drop into full flexion.
Step 2: Exhale and extend the wrists, lifting the weight upward as far as possible.
Step 3: Hold the peak extension briefly.
Step 4: Inhale and slowly lower the wrists back to full flexion (drop).
execution.breathing_instructions: Exhale on extension; inhale on lowering.
common_mistakes: Using the same weight as for wrist curls — the extensors require significantly less load
Lifting the forearms off the support during the extension
safety_considerations: Keep loads conservative — the wrist extensors are injury-prone under heavy loads
If lateral elbow pain exists (tennis elbow), consult a clinician before loading this exercise
execution.range_of_motion_guidance: Full wrist flexion drop at the bottom; maximum extension at the top.
coaching_cues: Palms down — only the wrists move upward
Light weight, full range — go through the complete drop to extension arc

name: Ring Bodyweight Skullcrusher
description: An advanced skullcrusher variation performed on gymnastic rings at an angle. The rings allow natural wrist movement and require stabilization not present with fixed bars. The lifter's body angle can be adjusted to change difficulty.

execution.starting_position: Set up for Ring Bodyweight Skullcrusher in the appropriate position.
execution.setup_instructions: Prepare equipment and body position for Ring Bodyweight Skullcrusher.
steps: Step 1: Set rings at appropriate height. Grip rings and lean body forward at angle.
Step 2: Bend elbows to lower head between rings, keeping upper arms fixed.
Step 3: Lower until head is level with or below rings.
Step 4: Press through triceps to full extension.
execution.breathing_instructions: Exhale during the exertion phase, inhale during the return.
common_mistakes: Rotating rings randomly
Allowing hips to sag
safety_considerations: Keep joints aligned throughout the movement.
Use controlled weight appropriate for skill level.
execution.range_of_motion_guidance: Move through full range of motion without compromising joint integrity.
coaching_cues: Rotate rings outward on extension
Rigid plank body position

name: Ring Dip
description: A dip exercise performed on gymnastics rings rather than a fixed dipping bar. The unstable nature of the rings requires significant shoulder girdle stability and demands greater pectoralis, triceps, and anterior deltoid activation throughout the movement compared to bar dips, while also training the small stabilizing muscles of the shoulder.

execution.starting_position: Support your body above the rings with arms fully extended, rings turned out slightly, body upright.
execution.setup_instructions: Set the rings at a height that allows full dip depth without touching the floor. Mount by jumping up to ring support position.
steps: Step 1: Lower your body by bending the elbows, allowing a slight forward torso lean.
Step 2: Descend until the upper arms are parallel to the floor or the shoulders are level with the elbows.
Step 3: Turn the rings outward at the bottom for stability and shoulder health.
Step 4: Press through the palms to fully extend the elbows and return to the top position.
execution.breathing_instructions: Inhale on the descent. Exhale on the press up.
common_mistakes: Failing to turn the rings outward at the bottom, increasing shoulder impingement risk
Dipping too fast without controlling the rings
safety_considerations: Ensure you can perform 10 clean parallel bar dips before attempting ring dips
Have a spotter or mat below when learning
execution.range_of_motion_guidance: Descend until upper arms are parallel to the floor. Full elbow extension at the top.
coaching_cues: Turn the rings out at the bottom
Squeeze the rings together as you press up

name: Ring Dip to L-Sit Transition
description: An expert-level gymnastic combination movement that links a full ring dip directly into an L-sit hold at the top. The dip phase heavily loads the pectoralis major, anterior deltoid, and triceps, while the subsequent L-sit isometric demands intense hip flexor and rectus abdominis activation to hold the legs parallel to the ground. This movement develops both upper body pressing strength and core compression simultaneously.

execution.starting_position: Support yourself on gymnastic rings with arms fully extended, rings turned out. Body hangs in a straight line below.
execution.setup_instructions: Set rings high enough that the legs will clear the floor when in the L-sit position. Rings should be approximately head height when standing.
steps: Step 1: Begin with arms extended on rings (top of dip position, rings turned out if possible).
Step 2: Bend the elbows and lower the body until the upper arms are parallel to the ground (full dip depth).
Step 3: Press powerfully back to the top position, fully extending the arms.
Step 4: At the top, immediately compress the hip flexors and abs to lift both legs straight in front of you to hip height, holding the L-sit for 2–3 seconds.
Step 5: Lower legs and descend into the next dip. Repeat.
execution.breathing_instructions: Inhale on the dip descent, exhale on the press upward, hold breath briefly during L-sit contraction.
common_mistakes: Reaching for the L-sit before fully locking out the arms
Allowing rings to wobble during the transition
Bent knees in the L-sit — legs must be straight for full difficulty
safety_considerations: Requires strong ring dips and standalone L-sit ability as prerequisites
Do not attempt if shoulder stability is insufficient for ring dips
Ensure rings are high enough to prevent legs contacting the floor
execution.range_of_motion_guidance: Full dip depth (upper arm parallel to ground) and full L-sit (legs straight, parallel to floor).
coaching_cues: Press the rings apart slightly at the top — this helps initiate the L-sit
Legs stay locked out in the L-sit — squeeze quads, point toes

name: Gymnastic Ring Dips
description: Ring dips are a highly demanding upper-body compound exercise in which the lifter supports themselves on two suspended gymnastics rings and dips down by bending the elbows. The instability of the rings forces the pectorals, triceps, and stabilizers to work far harder than on static parallel bars, making this a premier chest and triceps developer for calisthenics athletes.

execution.starting_position: Hang from the rings at arm's length above the floor, rings at hip height. Begin with arms fully extended, rings turned out so the knuckles face outward and elbows locked.
execution.setup_instructions: Set rings high enough that the legs can hang straight without touching the floor, or bend the knees. Achieve a solid support hold (rings turned out) before attempting dips.
steps: Step 1: Begin in the support position with arms locked, rings turned out.
Step 2: Slowly lower the body by bending the elbows, allowing a slight forward lean for chest emphasis.
Step 3: Lower until shoulders are approximately level with the rings or below.
Step 4: Press powerfully through the rings, extending the elbows to return to the support position.
Step 5: At the top, turn the rings out (externally rotate) for a strong lockout and stabilizer activation.
execution.breathing_instructions: Inhale as you lower. Exhale as you press back up.
common_mistakes: Not achieving the turned-out ring support at the top
Dipping with zero forward lean, targeting only the triceps
Swinging the legs to generate momentum
safety_considerations: Master static ring support and parallel bar dips before ring dips
Do not perform to failure where dropping from rings is risky
Avoid if you have shoulder instability or rotator cuff injury
execution.range_of_motion_guidance: Lower until shoulders drop to ring level. Full lockout with rings turned out at the top.
coaching_cues: Rings out at the top — that is the support position
Lean forward to hit the chest
Control the descent — the rings will want to wobble

name: Ring Flye
description: The ring flye is an advanced chest isolation exercise performed on gymnastic rings. With arms extended to the sides and elbows slightly bent, the athlete drives the hands together in a wide arc, creating intense pectoral stretch and contraction. The unstable nature of the rings demands significantly greater rotator cuff and serratus anterior activation compared to cable or dumbbell flyes.

execution.starting_position: Adjust rings to approximately chest height when standing. Grip one ring in each hand, lean forward, and extend arms out to the sides with a slight bend in the elbows. Body is inclined forward, weight on the balls of the feet.
execution.setup_instructions: Set gymnastic rings at a height where your body angle creates appropriate difficulty — lower rings make the exercise harder. Ensure rings are secured and level.
steps: Step 1: Begin with arms extended out to the sides, elbows slightly bent, body leaning forward at an angle determined by your strength level.
Step 2: Drive both hands together in a wide arc, maintaining the same elbow angle throughout — do not bend the elbows further.
Step 3: Squeeze the pectorals at the peak, hands meeting in front of your chest.
Step 4: Slowly reverse the motion, allowing the arms to open wide and stretch the chest under control.
execution.breathing_instructions: Exhale as you bring the rings together. Inhale during the controlled lowering phase.
common_mistakes: Bending the elbows excessively, turning it into a push-up
Losing body tension and sagging at the hips
Allowing rings to rotate outward at the top position
safety_considerations: This exercise places significant stress on the shoulder joint — ensure adequate rotator cuff strength before attempting
Start with a steeper body angle (more upright) to reduce difficulty and progress gradually
Never lock out elbows under load on rings
execution.range_of_motion_guidance: Open arms as wide as comfortable without shoulder pain, aiming for a full pectoral stretch. Bring hands together at mid-chest level at the top.
coaching_cues: Hug a barrel — maintain the same arm shape throughout
Keep your chest proud and shoulders packed down away from ears

name: Ring Knees to Elbows
description: Knees-to-elbows performed on gymnastic rings instead of a bar. The instability of the rings requires constant adjustments and significantly increases the difficulty. The rings can rotate, adding an element of shoulder and grip stabilization not present on a fixed bar.

execution.starting_position: Set up for Ring Knees to Elbows in proper position.
execution.setup_instructions: Prepare body and equipment for Ring Knees to Elbows.
steps: Step 1: Hang from rings with hands. Engage shoulders actively.
Step 2: Compress hips and raise knees toward elbows.
Step 3: Touch elbows to knees at top of movement.
Step 4: Lower legs slowly back to hanging position.
execution.breathing_instructions: Breathe steadily; never hold breath during static holds.
common_mistakes: Using kip to swing legs up
Rings rotating uncontrolled
safety_considerations: Build prerequisite strength before attempting advanced variations.
Stop if joint pain occurs.
execution.range_of_motion_guidance: Full range of motion with control at all times.
coaching_cues: Stabilize rings with shoulder engagement
Controlled compression motion

name: Ring Muscle-Up with False Grip
description: A muscle-up on gymnastic rings using the false grip technique where the wrist is hooked over the ring. The false grip eliminates the need to regrip at the top of the movement, making the transition smoother. This is the foundational skill for ring gymnastics.

execution.starting_position: Set up for Ring Muscle-Up with False Grip in proper position.
execution.setup_instructions: Prepare body and equipment for Ring Muscle-Up with False Grip.
steps: Step 1: Hang from rings with false grip (wrist over ring, not under).
Step 2: Pull rings explosively toward chest as if doing a row.
Step 3: As rings reach chest, transition by leaning forward over rings.
Step 4: Press to lockout in a dip to complete the muscle-up.
execution.breathing_instructions: Breathe steadily; never hold breath during static holds.
common_mistakes: Losing false grip during transition
Kipping without false grip
safety_considerations: Build prerequisite strength before attempting advanced variations.
Stop if joint pain occurs.
execution.range_of_motion_guidance: Full range of motion with control at all times.
coaching_cues: Maintain false grip throughout
Lean aggressively forward in transition

name: Gymnastic Ring Push-Up
description: The gymnastic ring push-up is a bodyweight pushing exercise performed with the hands gripping suspended rings, adding significant instability that dramatically increases pectoral, serratus anterior, and stabilizer muscle activation compared to floor push-ups. The rings also allow the wrists to rotate naturally, reducing joint stress and enabling a more natural pressing path.

execution.starting_position: Set the rings at a low height above the floor. Grip the rings and assume a push-up position with arms extended, body in a straight line.
execution.setup_instructions: Adjust ring height so the hands are at the same height as a floor push-up starting position. Lower rings = harder. Feet elevated = harder still.
steps: Step 1: Grip the rings and walk out into a plank position, arms straight.
Step 2: Slowly lower the chest toward the rings by bending the elbows, keeping them from flaring wide.
Step 3: At the bottom, press through the rings and extend the arms while actively turning the rings outward (rings turn from neutral to overhand at the top).
Step 4: At full extension, squeeze the chest and externally rotate the rings for a strong peak contraction.
Step 5: Lower smoothly into the next rep.
execution.breathing_instructions: Inhale as you lower. Exhale as you press up and rotate the rings.
common_mistakes: Allowing the rings to drift far out to the sides, losing stability
Not turning the rings outward at the top — this reduces pec activation
Setting the rings too low without adequate strength
safety_considerations: Establish solid floor push-up form before progressing to rings
Adjust ring height to begin — higher rings = less body weight on arms
Ensure ring straps and anchor point can support bodyweight
execution.range_of_motion_guidance: Full depth to 90 degrees elbow flexion or below. Full lockout at the top with external ring rotation.
coaching_cues: Turn the rings out at the top like you're trying to show your thumbs to the ceiling
Control the rings — don't let them control you
Tight body from heels to crown

name: Ring Push-Up with Feet on Swiss Ball
description: An extreme instability push-up variation combining gymnastic rings for the hands and a swiss ball for the feet. Both surfaces are unstable, requiring the entire kinetic chain — from wrist through shoulder, core, hip, and ankle — to continuously stabilize while executing the pressing movement. This creates maximal demand on stabilizer muscles across the full body while still loading the pectoralis major through the pressing range.

execution.starting_position: Set rings low (push-up position height). Place a swiss ball behind the rings. Get into push-up position with hands in the rings and feet resting on the swiss ball. Establish full-body stability before the first rep.
execution.setup_instructions: Set rings at appropriate height for push-ups. Fully inflate the ball. Position ball directly behind rings. Getting into position requires care — have a training partner assist initially.
steps: Step 1: Establish a controlled plank with hands in rings and feet on swiss ball. Take several breaths to find balance.
Step 2: Slowly lower the chest toward the ring level, managing ring rotation and ball roll simultaneously.
Step 3: Descend until chest is at ring level — this is a very challenging position to maintain.
Step 4: Press back to the starting position with full control. Reset between each rep if needed.
execution.breathing_instructions: Inhale before descent, exhale on press. Breathing is controlled and deliberate.
common_mistakes: Attempting without mastering ring push-ups and elevated-feet push-ups separately first
Moving too fast — this exercise requires slow, deliberate movement
Ball positioned too far back — it should be close enough that feet don't have to reach
safety_considerations: Have a training partner present for safety on the first several attempts
Have a clear plan to safely exit the position if stability is lost
Prerequisites: solid ring push-ups AND swiss ball feet-elevated push-ups
execution.range_of_motion_guidance: Full push-up range is the goal, but partial range with full control is acceptable while mastering the exercise.
coaching_cues: Squeeze the rings and the ball simultaneously — pressure in both directions creates stability
Every rep is a new challenge — reset mentally before each descent

name: Ring Push-Up in Weighted Vest
description: A ring push-up performed while wearing a weighted vest, distributing additional load evenly across the torso. Unlike attaching weight to a belt, the vest allows full natural movement of the arms and rings without the load shifting. The rings create an unstable hand surface that maximizes stabilizer demand, while the vest provides simple, clean progressive overload for the pectoralis major and triceps beyond bodyweight capacity.

execution.starting_position: Put on a weighted vest and secure it comfortably. Set rings low enough for push-up position (15–30 cm off the ground). Get into push-up position with hands in the rings.
execution.setup_instructions: Secure the vest before setting up in the ring position. Ensure the vest does not shift during the movement. Set rings at appropriate height. Progress from lighter vest loads, adding 5 kg increments.
steps: Step 1: Establish a stable plank with hands in rings. The vest distributes additional load across the torso.
Step 2: Lower the chest toward the ring level, managing the ring instability.
Step 3: Descend until chest is at ring height.
Step 4: Press powerfully to full arm extension. Turn rings out at the top for shoulder stability.
execution.breathing_instructions: Inhale on descent, exhale on press.
common_mistakes: Vest that shifts or rides up — a poorly fitted vest disrupts balance
Adding too much vest weight before the movement is mastered unweighted
Rings swinging out of control due to inability to stabilize the extra load
safety_considerations: Master bodyweight ring push-ups before adding vest weight
Start with 5–10 kg vest and progress conservatively
Have a training partner observe during the first loaded set
execution.range_of_motion_guidance: Full push-up range, chest to ring level at the bottom, complete lockout at top.
coaching_cues: Turn the rings outward at the top — this external rotation is a key shoulder safety cue
Press the rings apart slightly to engage serratus and stabilize the shoulder

name: Ring Row
description: The ring row is a bodyweight horizontal pulling exercise performed with gymnastic rings suspended at an adjustable height. By walking the feet forward or backward, the difficulty scales dramatically — nearly vertical for beginners, nearly horizontal for advanced trainees. The rings' instability demands significant rotator cuff and scapular stabilizer engagement throughout the pull.

execution.starting_position: Hang rings at approximately waist to chest height. Grasp a ring in each hand and walk feet forward under the rings until the body is at an angle — the more horizontal the body, the harder the exercise. Arms are extended with the body forming a straight line from head to heels.
execution.setup_instructions: Secure rings overhead from a pull-up bar, beam, or dedicated rack. Set height based on difficulty level — higher rings create an easier angle. Keep feet flat on the floor or elevated on a box to increase difficulty.
steps: Step 1: Begin with arms extended, body in a straight plank position, rings at arm's length.
Step 2: Keeping the body rigid, retract the scapulae and row the chest up toward the rings.
Step 3: As you pull, allow the rings to rotate outward naturally and squeeze the chest to the rings.
Step 4: At the top, the rings should be at chest level and the elbows behind the torso.
Step 5: Slowly extend the arms and lower back to the starting position, maintaining body rigidity.
execution.breathing_instructions: Exhale as you row up. Inhale as you lower.
common_mistakes: Letting the hips sag — the entire body must stay rigid as a plank
Pulling the rings to the neck rather than the chest
Not completing full arm extension at the bottom
safety_considerations: Verify ring straps and anchor point are rated for your body weight before beginning
Increase angle gradually — do not attempt a fully horizontal position without sufficient pulling strength
execution.range_of_motion_guidance: Full extension at the bottom to rings touching the chest at the top.
coaching_cues: Your body is a rigid board — nothing bends except the elbows and shoulders
Think 'chest to rings' not 'chin to rings'
Rotate the pinkies up as you pull to maximize rear delt and rhomboid contraction

name: Ring Row (Lat-Dominant)
description: The lat-dominant ring row modifies standard ring rowing by pulling with the elbows flared wide and high, directing the force through the latissimus dorsi more than the rhomboids or middle trapezius. The elbows track outward rather than into the torso, mimicking the lat engagement pattern of a vertical pull within a horizontal plane.

execution.starting_position: Set rings at approximately waist height. Grip rings with palms facing each other. Lean back with arms extended, body in a plank at a moderate angle.
execution.setup_instructions: Lower the rings or walk feet forward to increase difficulty. The more horizontal the body position, the harder the exercise.
steps: Step 1: Begin in the extended arm position, body rigid.
Step 2: Row by driving the elbows out to the sides and upward, rather than straight back.
Step 3: Pull until the hands reach the chest, with elbows elevated wide.
Step 4: Lower under control back to full arm extension.
Step 5: Focus on feeling the lat stretch and contract with each rep.
execution.breathing_instructions: Exhale rowing up. Inhale lowering.
common_mistakes: Driving elbows straight back — this shifts emphasis to the rhomboids
Allowing hips to sag — maintain plank alignment
safety_considerations: Wide elbow rowing increases shoulder impingement risk in those with existing shoulder issues
Start with a steeper body angle (less horizontal) and progress gradually
execution.range_of_motion_guidance: Full arm extension to hands at chest with elbows above torso line.
coaching_cues: Elbows go wide and high, not behind you
Think of pulling the rings apart and up simultaneously
Squeeze the lats at the top — not the shoulder blades together

name: Ring Triceps Extension
description: A bodyweight triceps exercise performed on gymnastic rings. The rings allow natural wrist rotation and require significant stabilization, making this more challenging than bar-based variations. The lifter extends from a tucked position to full arm extension.

execution.starting_position: Set up for Ring Triceps Extension in the appropriate position.
execution.setup_instructions: Prepare equipment and body position for Ring Triceps Extension.
steps: Step 1: Set rings at appropriate height. Grip rings and extend body forward at an angle.
Step 2: Lower by bending elbows forward and down, rings moving toward temples.
Step 3: Lower until upper body is nearly parallel to ground.
Step 4: Push through triceps to return to straight-arm starting position.
execution.breathing_instructions: Exhale during the exertion phase, inhale during the return.
common_mistakes: Letting hips sag
Flaring elbows outward
safety_considerations: Keep joints aligned throughout the movement.
Use controlled weight appropriate for skill level.
execution.range_of_motion_guidance: Move through full range of motion without compromising joint integrity.
coaching_cues: Rotate rings outward at extension
Keep body rigid

name: Ring Triceps Extension with False Grip
description: A ring triceps extension performed with a false grip where the thumb wraps around the same side as the fingers. The false grip on rings creates a different wrist angle and increases the stability challenge. This variant is used in gymnastic strength training progressions.

execution.starting_position: Set up for Ring Triceps Extension with False Grip in the appropriate position.
execution.setup_instructions: Prepare equipment and body position for Ring Triceps Extension with False Grip.
steps: Step 1: Grip rings with false grip, thumb alongside fingers not wrapping.
Step 2: Extend body forward at angle, arms straight.
Step 3: Lower head between rings by bending elbows, maintaining false grip pressure.
Step 4: Press through triceps to full extension.
execution.breathing_instructions: Exhale during the exertion phase, inhale during the return.
common_mistakes: Losing false grip under load
Rotating rings uncontrolled
safety_considerations: Keep joints aligned throughout the movement.
Use controlled weight appropriate for skill level.
execution.range_of_motion_guidance: Move through full range of motion without compromising joint integrity.
coaching_cues: Maintain active wrist contact throughout
False grip requires practice to master

name: Ring Triceps Push-Up (Incline Rings)
description: A push-up on gymnastic rings set to an elevated angle, creating an incline position that reduces body weight load. This is used as a progression step toward full ring push-ups. The unstable rings demand significant stabilizer recruitment even at this reduced intensity.

execution.starting_position: Set up for Ring Triceps Push-Up (Incline Rings) in the appropriate position.
execution.setup_instructions: Prepare equipment and body position for Ring Triceps Push-Up (Incline Rings).
steps: Step 1: Set rings at chest height for incline. Grip rings and lean body at an angle.
Step 2: Maintain body rigidity and lower chest toward rings by bending elbows.
Step 3: Keep elbows tucked, rings allowed to rotate naturally.
Step 4: Press back to full arm extension, rotating rings outward.
execution.breathing_instructions: Exhale during the exertion phase, inhale during the return.
common_mistakes: Letting hips sag
Flaring elbows too wide
safety_considerations: Keep joints aligned throughout the movement.
Use controlled weight appropriate for skill level.
execution.range_of_motion_guidance: Move through full range of motion without compromising joint integrity.
coaching_cues: Turn rings out at the top
Rigid body throughout

name: Legless Rope Climb
description: A rope climb performed with the legs kept straight out in an L-position or simply not wrapping them around the rope. This eliminates leg assistance and places the entire pulling demand on the arms, shoulders, and back. This is significantly harder than standard rope climbing.

execution.starting_position: Set up for Legless Rope Climb in proper strongman position.
execution.setup_instructions: Prepare all equipment and body position for Legless Rope Climb.
steps: Step 1: Grip rope with both hands. Hold legs straight out in front or together below.
Step 2: Pull body up with arms only, hand over hand on the rope.
Step 3: Continue ascending using only upper body pulling strength.
Step 4: Descend carefully and in a controlled manner.
execution.breathing_instructions: Brace core maximally before every lift. Breathe between reps if needed.
common_mistakes: Swinging to generate momentum
Attempting without sufficient pulling strength
safety_considerations: Use collars on all loaded barbells.
Ensure clear path for carries.
Have spotters for overhead movements.
execution.range_of_motion_guidance: Full range of motion specific to the implement being used.
coaching_cues: Strict arm-over-arm pulling
Master standard rope climb first

name: Rowing Machine Intervals — Ergometer
description: Rowing machine intervals on an ergometer produce one of the highest whole-body cardiovascular demands available in a gym setting, engaging approximately 86% of skeletal muscle mass in each stroke. Each rowing stroke follows a sequence of leg drive, body swing, and arm pull, distributing load across the quadriceps, gluteus maximus, latissimus dorsi, rhomboids, and biceps simultaneously. The absence of eccentric ground-reaction forces makes the rower extremely joint-friendly while generating a metabolic demand comparable to running sprints.

execution.starting_position: Sit on the seat with feet strapped securely in the footrests. Grip the handle with an overhand grip, arms extended, shins vertical, and body hinged slightly forward with a neutral spine (the 'catch' position).
execution.setup_instructions: Set the damper (resistance lever) to 4–6 for most training. Higher damper settings feel heavier but are not necessarily better — elite rowers often train at 3–5. Connect the performance monitor and set the target for distance or time.
steps: Step 1: Begin at the catch — shins vertical, arms straight, body leaning slightly forward with a flat back.
Step 2: Drive: push through both legs forcefully, keeping the arms straight until the legs are nearly extended.
Step 3: Swing: once the legs are 90% extended, swing the torso back to 1 o'clock (slightly past vertical) using the hips.
Step 4: Pull: once the body is swung back, draw the handle into the lower sternum by bending the elbows and pulling the shoulder blades together.
Step 5: Recover: extend the arms first, then hinge the torso forward, then bend the knees and slide forward to the catch. Maintain a 2:1 recovery-to-drive ratio in time.
execution.breathing_instructions: Exhale sharply at the beginning of the drive phase. Inhale on the recovery as you slide forward. Maintain a consistent breathing rhythm matched to the stroke rate.
common_mistakes: Pulling with the arms before the legs have driven — the sequence must always be legs, body, arms
Rounding the lower back at the catch, which places the spine under shear load
Jerking the handle rather than maintaining a smooth, connected drive
safety_considerations: Establish proper technique at a moderate intensity before attempting sprint intervals
Avoid excessive layback past 1 o'clock, which compresses the lumbar spine under load
execution.range_of_motion_guidance: Full leg drive from a compressed position to nearly locked-out. Handle should travel from full arm extension to touching the sternum just below the pectoral muscles.
execution.tempo_recommendations: Interval option: 500m hard / 2 minutes easy × 6–8 rounds. Tabata option: 20 seconds maximum effort / 10 seconds rest × 8. Stroke rate during sprint: 28–34 SPM.
coaching_cues: Legs, body, arms — arms, body, legs. That is the entire stroke
Push the foot plate away, do not pull the handle
Hang your body weight off the handle at the catch

name: Russian Twist
description: The Russian twist is a rotational core exercise performed in a seated position with the torso leaned back at an angle. The lifter rotates the torso side to side, training the obliques and transverse abdominis in a rotational pattern. It can be performed with bodyweight, a weight plate, or a medicine ball.

execution.starting_position: Sit on the floor with knees bent and feet flat or slightly elevated. Lean back until the torso is at approximately 45 degrees from the floor. Hold a weight or clasp hands together in front of the chest.
execution.setup_instructions: Feet can be anchored for beginners. Advanced lifters can elevate the feet for greater difficulty.
steps: Rotate the torso to one side, bringing the hands or weight toward the floor beside the hip.
Rotate back through center and to the other side.
One rotation to each side counts as one complete repetition.
execution.breathing_instructions: Exhale on each rotation. Breathe rhythmically.
common_mistakes: Rotating with the arms only — the rotation must come from the torso
Relaxing the core during the movement
safety_considerations: If lower back discomfort occurs, reduce the torso lean angle
execution.range_of_motion_guidance: Rotate as far as the torso allows without losing the leaned-back position.
coaching_cues: Let your ribs lead the rotation — not your arms
Keep the chest up and spine long throughout

name: Safety Bar Squat
description: The safety squat bar (SSB) has padded yokes and forward-angled handles that allow the lifter to hold the bar handles rather than grabbing the barbell behind the neck. This design significantly reduces demands on shoulder and wrist mobility and is an excellent alternative for lifters with upper body limitations. The forward cambered weight naturally creates a more upright torso angle, increasing quad and upper back demands.

execution.starting_position: Position the safety squat bar on the rack at the appropriate height. Step under it and settle the padded yokes onto your traps. Grip the handles in front of you. Stand up to unrack.
execution.setup_instructions: Set the rack height so the bar is at mid-chest level. Adjust safety bars. The SSB tends to pitch the torso forward — actively fight this by pulling the handles down and back.
steps: Step 1: Unrack and step back. Set feet shoulder-width apart with toes out. Brace the core hard.
Step 2: Initiate the squat by pushing the knees outward and sitting the hips back and down simultaneously.
Step 3: Descend to at least parallel. The bar's camber will try to pull you forward — actively fight it by keeping the chest tall and pulling down on the handles.
Step 4: Drive through the full foot explosively to return to standing.
Step 5: Exhale at the top and reset for the next rep.
execution.breathing_instructions: Inhale and brace before descent. Hold through the ascent. Exhale at the top.
common_mistakes: Letting the torso pitch excessively forward due to the bar's camber
Gripping the handles loosely — an active grip helps maintain tension
Not squatting to depth due to unfamiliarity with the bar
safety_considerations: The SSB is heavier than a standard barbell — account for bar weight (typically 60–70 lbs)
Learn to bail safely: the bar can be pushed forward and dropped
execution.range_of_motion_guidance: Aim for parallel or below. The SSB makes the squat harder to maintain position in, so use reduced load compared to back squat.
coaching_cues: Pull the handles down — fight the forward pitch
Chest up, elbows down
Sit between your knees

name: Sandbag Bear Hug Carry
description: A strongman carry where a sandbag is cradled in a bear hug position against the chest and carried for distance or time. The soft and shifting sandbag makes this considerably harder than carrying rigid implements. This builds grip endurance, core bracing, and mental toughness.

execution.starting_position: Set up for Sandbag Bear Hug Carry in proper strongman position.
execution.setup_instructions: Prepare all equipment and body position for Sandbag Bear Hug Carry.
steps: Step 1: Deadlift sandbag up to lap position.
Step 2: Bear hug bag tightly against chest with arms wrapped underneath.
Step 3: Stand upright and walk for target distance or time.
Step 4: Set bag down with control.
execution.breathing_instructions: Brace core maximally before every lift. Breathe between reps if needed.
common_mistakes: Letting bag slip too low
Bent-over carry posture
safety_considerations: Use collars on all loaded barbells.
Ensure clear path for carries.
Have spotters for overhead movements.
execution.range_of_motion_guidance: Full range of motion specific to the implement being used.
coaching_cues: Squeeze bag as hard as possible
Walk tall with upright torso

name: Weighted Sandbag Shoulder Carry
description: The sandbag shoulder carry involves hoisting a heavy sandbag onto one shoulder and walking a prescribed distance, then alternating shoulders. The shifting, unstable load of the sandbag demands continuous core engagement to prevent lateral trunk collapse, making it a highly effective functional strength and conditioning tool that transfers directly to athletic and occupational performance. Unlike rigid implements, the sandbag's shifting contents require constant neuromuscular adjustments that challenge stabilizing muscles far more than a comparable barbell load.

execution.starting_position: The sandbag rests on the ground. Stand beside it in an athletic stance, hips back, chest up.
execution.setup_instructions: Fill the sandbag to the target weight. Filler bags should be sealed. Begin with a sandbag at 25–40% of bodyweight for carry training.
steps: Step 1: Deadlift the sandbag from the floor to lap height, then hug it into the chest.
Step 2: Rotate and load the sandbag onto one shoulder. The bag rests across the shoulder and upper back.
Step 3: Hold the bag in place with the same-side hand and stabilize the torso upright. The opposite hand can be held out for balance.
Step 4: Walk the prescribed distance with an upright posture. Resist lateral trunk lean.
Step 5: At the midpoint or end of the distance, switch the sandbag to the opposite shoulder and return.
execution.breathing_instructions: Breathe short and regularly throughout the carry. Take a full bracing breath before the initial lift from the floor.
common_mistakes: Allowing the torso to collapse laterally toward the loaded shoulder, overloading the QL and lateral trunk
Rounding the back when picking up the bag from the floor
Walking too fast and letting the bag shift uncontrollably
safety_considerations: Drop the bag to the side rather than forward if you lose control — do not fall with it
Start with a lighter sandbag and build tolerance to the awkward loading before adding weight
execution.range_of_motion_guidance: Walk distance: 20–50 metres per set. Shoulder alternation: switch at the midpoint of each length.
execution.tempo_recommendations: 2–4 lengths of 20–25 metres per set, switching shoulders each length. Rest 2–3 minutes. 3–5 sets.
coaching_cues: Resist the lean — stay tall and stack the shoulder over the hip
Keep the core braced throughout — do not relax mid-walk
Look ahead, not at the bag

name: Sandbag Clean
description: The sandbag clean is an explosive hip-extension movement that drives a heavy sandbag from the floor to the shoulder or chest, training the same posterior chain muscles as the barbell power clean but with an awkward, shifting implement that demands superior grip strength and core stability. The unstable load prevents the precise bar path of Olympic lifting, instead requiring the athlete to adapt dynamically throughout each repetition. It is an excellent power development tool for athletes and tactical populations who need to handle irregular loads.

execution.starting_position: The sandbag is on the floor in front of the feet. Hinge at the hips, grab the sandbag handles or hug the bag with both arms, back flat, chest up.
execution.setup_instructions: Choose a sandbag weight that allows an explosive clean without losing postural control — typically 30–50% of bodyweight to start. Use a sandbag with handles for the first attempts.
steps: Step 1: Deadlift the sandbag from the floor to mid-thigh, keeping it close to the body.
Step 2: Extend the hips explosively — the same hip pop as a kettlebell swing. Drive the elbows high as you pull the bag upward.
Step 3: As the bag rises, drop under it slightly and 'catch' it at the shoulder or chest level, rotating the elbows forward.
Step 4: Stand tall in the catch position with the bag at the chest or shoulder, core braced.
Step 5: Lower the bag to the floor with control by hinging at the hips. Repeat.
execution.breathing_instructions: Exhale sharply at the hip extension (the most explosive moment). Inhale on the way back down to the floor.
common_mistakes: Lifting with the back and arms instead of using explosive hip extension as the primary driver
Not pulling the elbows high enough, causing the bag to crash into the chest
Soft catch — always brace the core hard at the moment the bag arrives at the shoulder
safety_considerations: If the bag slips, let it drop — do not catch it awkwardly to protect the lower back
Master the deadlift pattern and kettlebell swing before loading the sandbag clean heavily
execution.range_of_motion_guidance: Full hip extension at the top of the drive. The bag should travel from the floor to shoulder height in one continuous movement.
execution.tempo_recommendations: Power development: 3–5 reps × 4–6 sets. Rest 2–3 minutes. Conditioning: 8–10 reps × 3–4 sets with 90 seconds rest.
coaching_cues: Hips first — do not muscle it up with the arms
Hug the bag tight to your body throughout the pull
Drive the elbows high at the top

name: Sandbag Ground to Overhead
description: A complete power movement where a sandbag is lifted from the ground and pressed or thrown overhead. The shifting weight of the sandbag challenges coordination and grip throughout the lift. This is a staple strongman and functional fitness movement.

execution.starting_position: Set up for Sandbag Ground to Overhead in proper strongman position.
execution.setup_instructions: Prepare all equipment and body position for Sandbag Ground to Overhead.
steps: Step 1: Stand over sandbag with feet wide. Grasp bag and pull to lap.
Step 2: Continue pulling bag up the torso toward shoulder.
Step 3: Transition grip and drive bag overhead using leg drive.
Step 4: Extend fully with bag locked out overhead before lowering.
execution.breathing_instructions: Brace core maximally before every lift. Breathe between reps if needed.
common_mistakes: Not using leg drive to assist overhead
Soft torso during the lift
safety_considerations: Use collars on all loaded barbells.
Ensure clear path for carries.
Have spotters for overhead movements.
execution.range_of_motion_guidance: Full range of motion specific to the implement being used.
coaching_cues: Hips drive the bag up
Catch shifting weight aggressively

name: Sandbag Loading to Platform
description: A strongman event where multiple sandbags of increasing weight are loaded onto a platform or series of boxes. The athlete must move quickly and efficiently through multiple bags under fatigue. Speed, technique, and endurance are all tested in this event.

execution.starting_position: Set up for Sandbag Loading to Platform in proper strongman position.
execution.setup_instructions: Prepare all equipment and body position for Sandbag Loading to Platform.
steps: Step 1: Position first sandbag in front of target platform.
Step 2: Bear hug or deadlift bag to lap then continue up to platform height.
Step 3: Load bag onto platform and immediately move to next bag.
Step 4: Continue loading all bags as quickly as possible.
execution.breathing_instructions: Brace core maximally before every lift. Breathe between reps if needed.
common_mistakes: Resting between bags
Using poor technique as fatigue accumulates
safety_considerations: Use collars on all loaded barbells.
Ensure clear path for carries.
Have spotters for overhead movements.
execution.range_of_motion_guidance: Full range of motion specific to the implement being used.
coaching_cues: Speed is the goal, maintain form throughout
Have next bag positioned before finishing last

name: Scapular Pull-Ups
description: Scapular pull-ups are a foundational shoulder rehabilitation exercise performed from a hanging position on a pull-up bar. Without bending the elbows, the exerciser actively depresses and retracts the shoulder blades, lifting the body slightly through scapular movement alone. This isolates the lower trapezius and serratus anterior with the arms at full extension — a critical position for establishing the shoulder stability needed before progressing to full pull-ups. Used in shoulder impingement rehabilitation, rotator cuff programs, and gymnastics foundations.

execution.starting_position: Hang from a pull-up bar with both hands in an overhand grip, shoulder-width or slightly wider. Arms are fully extended, body hanging passively.
execution.setup_instructions: Begin from a full passive hang (scapulae elevated). Grip firmly. Feet can be slightly bent at the knees if needed to clear the floor.
steps: Step 1: Begin hanging passively with shoulder blades elevated and arms fully extended.
Step 2: Without bending the elbows, actively depress and retract the shoulder blades, drawing them downward and together.
Step 3: This motion will cause the body to rise slightly (a few centimeters). Hold this depressed position briefly.
Step 4: Slowly return to the passive hang, allowing the shoulder blades to fully elevate. Repeat.
execution.breathing_instructions: Exhale as you depress the scapulae. Inhale as you release back to the passive hang.
common_mistakes: Bending the elbows — this converts it into the beginning of a pull-up. Elbows stay locked throughout
Barely activating the scapulae and treating it as a passive exercise — you should feel the lower trapezius working clearly
Rushing — slow controlled depression and return are what build the target muscles
safety_considerations: If you lack grip strength to perform this safely, use lifting straps
Avoid if any shoulder position in the full hang causes sharp pain — stay in a pain-free range
execution.range_of_motion_guidance: The range is small — a few centimeters of body rise from full scapular depression. The arm angle should not change.
coaching_cues: Imagine pulling your shoulder blades into your back pockets
Elbows absolutely straight throughout — this is not a pull-up
Feel the bottom of the shoulder blades activate — that is the lower trapezius

name: Scapular Overhead Press
description: The scapular overhead press begins at the top of a standard overhead press with elbows locked, then adds a final phase of scapular elevation (shrugging the shoulders upward) to fully load the upper trapezius and serratus anterior through the last degrees of overhead range. It is used to train the final phase of overhead reaching and to build the muscles responsible for upward scapular rotation.

execution.starting_position: Hold dumbbells or a barbell at the locked-out overhead position — arms fully extended above the head, shoulders packed.
execution.setup_instructions: Begin from the top of an overhead press. This can be done seated or standing. Moderate weight.
steps: Step 1: Begin with arms fully extended overhead.
Step 2: From the locked position, shrug the shoulders upward toward the ears.
Step 3: At peak elevation, the shoulder blades rotate upward fully.
Step 4: Lower the shoulders back to the packed position.
Step 5: Repeat the shrug without bending the elbows.
execution.breathing_instructions: Exhale shrugging. Inhale returning.
common_mistakes: Bending the elbows — this becomes a standard overhead press movement
Only partial elevation — aim for maximum upward scapular rotation
safety_considerations: Ensure the arms are fully locked before beginning the shrug phase
Avoid if shoulder impingement occurs at full overhead position
execution.range_of_motion_guidance: Packed shoulder position to full upward scapular rotation/elevation.
coaching_cues: Arms stay straight — shrug is the movement
Think 'ears to ceiling'
Feel the traps working at the top

name: Scapular Pull-Up
description: The scapular pull-up is an isolation drill performed at the top of a dead hang, where the shoulder blades are actively depressed and retracted without bending the elbows. It trains the serratus anterior, lower trapezius, and latissimus dorsi to control scapular positioning — a foundational movement for shoulder health and progression to full pull-ups.

execution.starting_position: Hang from a pull-up bar with a shoulder-width overhand grip. Arms fully extended, body relaxed in a dead hang.
execution.setup_instructions: Use a bar at a height that allows full arm extension with feet off the floor. Adjust grip width to shoulder width.
steps: Step 1: Begin in a dead hang with arms fully extended.
Step 2: Without bending the elbows, actively depress and retract the shoulder blades, elevating the body 2-5 cm.
Step 3: Hold the depressed position for 1-2 seconds, feeling the lats engage.
Step 4: Slowly allow the shoulder blades to elevate back to the resting dead-hang position.
Step 5: Repeat for the desired number of repetitions.
execution.breathing_instructions: Exhale as you depress the scapulae. Inhale as you return to the dead hang.
common_mistakes: Bending the elbows — this becomes a partial pull-up rather than a scapular drill
Shrugging the traps upward instead of depressing downward
Moving too quickly — the drill is about motor control, not speed
safety_considerations: Avoid this exercise with active rotator cuff or labral injuries until cleared by a clinician
Warm up wrists and shoulders before hanging
execution.range_of_motion_guidance: Shoulder blades travel from fully elevated dead hang to maximally depressed and retracted — typically 2-5 cm of body elevation.
coaching_cues: Think 'put your shoulder blades in your back pockets'
Squeeze the lats without bending the arms
Chest stays open throughout

name: Scapular Pull-Up on Rings
description: The ring scapular pull-up is performed identically to the bar version — shoulder blades depressed and retracted without elbow flexion — but the unstable ring surface adds a rotational challenge that increases demand on the serratus anterior and rotator cuff stabilizers. It is a superior proprioceptive warm-up and shoulder health drill for ring athletes.

execution.starting_position: Hang from gymnastic rings at shoulder width with arms fully extended. Rings should be turned out slightly.
execution.setup_instructions: Set ring height to allow full dead-hang with feet off the ground. Use a grip with palms facing each other (neutral grip).
steps: Step 1: Begin in a dead hang, body relaxed.
Step 2: Without bending elbows, depress and retract the scapulae, elevating the body slightly.
Step 3: Hold the depressed position 1-2 seconds.
Step 4: Return slowly to the resting dead-hang.
Step 5: Repeat.
execution.breathing_instructions: Exhale as scapulae depress. Inhale returning to dead hang.
common_mistakes: Bending elbows — this defeats the purpose of the drill
Allowing the rings to swing excessively — maintain control
safety_considerations: Inspect ring straps and anchor points before hanging
Build wrist and grip tolerance before full dead hangs
execution.range_of_motion_guidance: Shoulder blades travel from resting elevated position to maximally depressed.
coaching_cues: Shoulder blades into your back pockets
Arms stay straight throughout
Control the rings — do not let them spin

name: Scapular Push-Up on Elevated Box
description: A scapular push-up performed with hands elevated on a box, bench, or step. The incline reduces the percentage of bodyweight being supported, making it easier than the floor version for people who cannot yet perform the floor version with good form. The same protraction-retraction scapular motion is trained without the full bodyweight load. Used in early-stage shoulder rehabilitation to introduce scapular movement under partial load before progressing to the floor version.

execution.starting_position: Place hands on the edge of a bench, box, or step approximately shoulder-width apart. Extend the body into a plank with the arms fully locked. The body angle depends on box height — a higher box means less bodyweight load.
execution.setup_instructions: Choose box height based on current ability. Start at a height that allows 15-20 smooth reps with full scapular motion before progressing lower.
steps: Step 1: Begin in an incline plank on the box, elbows fully locked, body rigid.
Step 2: Allow the shoulder blades to retract (pinch together), letting the chest drop slightly toward the box.
Step 3: Push the box away with both hands to protract the scapulae, rounding the upper back and spreading the shoulder blades wide.
Step 4: Return to retraction. Repeat — elbows remain locked throughout.
execution.breathing_instructions: Exhale during protraction (spread). Inhale during retraction (pinch).
common_mistakes: Bending the elbows — elbows must stay locked. This is not a push-up.
Moving the hips or losing the plank position during the motion
Moving too fast — slow movement ensures scapular isolation
safety_considerations: This is the regressed version of the floor scapular push-up — use it when the floor version is too challenging
Progress to the floor version when 20 controlled reps are achieved at this height
execution.range_of_motion_guidance: Full protraction to full retraction is the goal. The range is small — the chest drops and rises only a few centimeters.
execution.tempo_recommendations: 2s retract, 1s hold, 2s protract, 1s hold at top.
coaching_cues: Arms absolutely straight — if they bend, you are doing a push-up
Spread the shoulder blades as wide as possible at the top
Keep the whole body in a rigid line — only the shoulder blades move

name: Scapular Push-Up on Floor
description: The scapular push-up isolates the serratus anterior by performing the protraction-retraction movement of the scapulae while maintaining a rigid plank position. Unlike a standard push-up, the elbows remain fully locked throughout the movement — only the shoulder blades move. This exercise is a cornerstone of shoulder rehabilitation for winging scapula, rotator cuff issues, and overhead athlete conditioning.

execution.starting_position: Assume a standard push-up position with arms fully extended, hands directly under shoulders. Keep the entire body rigid from head to heels.
execution.setup_instructions: No equipment required. Ensure a non-slip surface. Can be performed from knees for a modified version.
steps: Step 1: Begin in a push-up plank with elbows fully locked. Do not bend the elbows at any point.
Step 2: Allow the chest to drop between the shoulder blades by letting the scapulae retract (pinch together).
Step 3: Push the floor away with both hands to protract the scapulae, making the upper back rounded and scapulae spread wide.
Step 4: Hold the protracted position briefly, then return to retraction. Repeat.
execution.breathing_instructions: Exhale as you protract (spread the shoulder blades). Inhale as you retract (pinch them together).
common_mistakes: Bending the elbows — this converts it into a regular push-up
Losing the rigid plank body position and sagging at the hips
Moving too quickly — slow movement ensures scapular isolation
safety_considerations: Avoid with acute shoulder impingement presenting with protraction pain
Consult a physiotherapist if you have diagnosed scapular winging
execution.range_of_motion_guidance: The range is relatively small — focus on maximum protraction vs. retraction of the shoulder blades, not on raising or lowering the torso.
coaching_cues: Arms stay straight throughout — only the shoulder blades move
Push the floor away as hard as possible at the top
Think about spreading the shoulder blades wide like wings

name: Scapular Push-Up
description: The scapular push-up is a rehabilitation drill that trains serratus anterior strength and scapular protraction control in a push-up position. Unlike a standard push-up, the elbows remain locked throughout and only the shoulder blades move — protracting (spreading apart) and retracting (pinching together). It is prescribed for serratus anterior weakness, scapular winging, and shoulder instability.

execution.starting_position: Begin in a standard push-up position with arms fully extended, hands shoulder-width apart.
execution.setup_instructions: May also be performed from the knees for beginners, or against a wall for very early rehabilitation stages.
steps: Step 1: Assume a push-up position with arms straight and body in a rigid plank.
Step 2: Allow the shoulder blades to pinch together (retract), lowering the chest slightly between the arms without bending the elbows.
Step 3: Push the shoulder blades apart (protract), rounding the upper back slightly and reaching the hands into the floor.
Step 4: At full protraction, the upper back should be slightly rounded and the shoulder blades as far apart as possible.
Step 5: Return to the retracted position with control and repeat.
execution.breathing_instructions: Exhale on protraction (spreading apart). Inhale on retraction.
common_mistakes: Bending the elbows — the elbows stay locked throughout
Moving the hips or lower back rather than isolating the shoulder blades
Not achieving full protraction at the top
safety_considerations: Appropriate for most populations including early post-operative shoulder patients when cleared by a clinician
execution.range_of_motion_guidance: Full retraction to full protraction. The range is typically 2–5 cm of vertical body travel.
execution.tempo_recommendations: 2 seconds retract, 2 seconds protract. 15–20 reps × 2–3 sets.
coaching_cues: Arms stay completely straight — this is all shoulder blade
At the top, push the floor away and round the upper back like a cat
Feel the muscles around the shoulder blades working

name: Scapular Wall Slides
description: Scapular wall slides are performed with the back flat against a wall, sliding the arms overhead while maintaining contact between the arms and wall throughout. They train thoracic extension, scapular upward rotation, and shoulder flexion in a controlled, low-load manner — making them an essential warm-up, postural correction, and shoulder rehabilitation exercise for overhead athletes.

execution.starting_position: Stand with the back flat against a wall. Feet 10-20 cm away from the wall. Arms bent to 90 degrees at shoulder height, pressed against the wall — forearms and elbows maintaining contact.
execution.setup_instructions: Ensure the entire back — lumbar, thoracic, and head — maintain contact with the wall. This is very challenging for those with thoracic kyphosis.
steps: Step 1: Begin with arms at 90-90 position (elbows at shoulder height, bent 90 degrees) against the wall.
Step 2: Slide both arms overhead while maintaining full contact between arms and wall.
Step 3: Try to reach arms overhead to a Y position.
Step 4: Slide back to the 90-90 starting position.
Step 5: Repeat.
execution.breathing_instructions: Exhale sliding up. Inhale sliding down.
common_mistakes: Arms losing contact with the wall during the slide — this defeats the purpose
Lumbar hyperextension — back must stay flat throughout
safety_considerations: Appropriate for all fitness levels as a warm-up or mobility tool
Avoid forcing range of motion — work within comfortable limits
execution.range_of_motion_guidance: 90-90 start position to full overhead Y.
coaching_cues: Back flat on the wall at all times
Arms slide — do not lift off
Feel the shoulder blades rotating as the arms go overhead

name: Scapular Wall Slides with Resistance Band
description: Wall slides performed with a resistance band looped around both wrists, adding external rotation resistance throughout the upward slide. As the arms move overhead, the band pulls the wrists together (into internal rotation), and the exerciser must resist this by maintaining wrist separation and external rotation. This cue amplifies infraspinatus and teres minor activation during the slide while training the full overhead arc, making it an effective combination of shoulder external rotation and scapular upward rotation training.

execution.starting_position: Stand with the back against a flat wall. Loop a light resistance band around both wrists. Begin in the goal-post position with elbows at shoulder height and all contact points on the wall (back, head, elbows, forearms, hands).
execution.setup_instructions: Use the lightest available band. The band should not prevent the wall contact from being maintained. Increase resistance only when full range is achievable with both arms maintaining wall contact.
steps: Step 1: Begin in the wall angel goal-post position with the band between the wrists.
Step 2: Slide both arms upward along the wall, actively resisting the band by keeping the wrists apart (externally rotating at the shoulder against the band's inward pull).
Step 3: Raise as high as wall contact allows while fighting the band.
Step 4: Slide back down to the goal-post position. Repeat.
execution.breathing_instructions: Exhale as you slide up. Inhale as you return.
common_mistakes: Letting the band win — allowing internal rotation as the arms go overhead defeats the purpose
Using a band that is too heavy, preventing overhead range
Losing wall contact with the forearms or lower back during the slide
safety_considerations: If shoulder pain increases with the external rotation demand, remove the band and return to unloaded wall slides
Only add the band after mastering the bodyweight wall angel with full wall contact
execution.range_of_motion_guidance: Full overhead range that allows wall contact to be maintained throughout the arc.
coaching_cues: Fight the band — actively push your wrists apart as you slide up
Maintain all four contact points on the wall throughout the slide
The external rotation demand from the band should feel like work at the mid and upper range

name: Scapular Wall Slides with Foam Roller
description: Wall slides performed with a foam roller held between the forearms and the wall, adding tactile feedback and proprioceptive challenge to the standard wall angel pattern. The foam roller requires the exerciser to maintain even pressure through both forearms simultaneously, detecting asymmetries in scapular movement and motor control. This variation is used in shoulder rehabilitation programs to develop conscious scapular control and bilateral symmetry in overhead movement.

execution.starting_position: Stand facing a wall with a foam roller held vertically between both forearms and the wall surface. Begin with elbows at shoulder height, goal-post position, pressing the roller lightly against the wall.
execution.setup_instructions: Use a half-roller or cylindrical foam roller approximately 30-45 cm long. The roller should be held with both forearms pressing equally against it.
steps: Step 1: Stand with both forearms pressing the foam roller against the wall, elbows at shoulder height.
Step 2: Slowly slide both forearms and the roller upward, keeping even pressure on both sides of the roller.
Step 3: Raise as high as shoulder mobility allows without compensating at the lower back or shrugging.
Step 4: Slide back down to the starting position with the same even pressure. Repeat.
execution.breathing_instructions: Exhale as you slide upward. Inhale as you return.
common_mistakes: Applying more pressure through one forearm than the other — the roller will tilt if asymmetry is present
Losing wall contact with the forearms at the top of the movement
Shrugging the shoulder blades upward rather than rotating them upward
safety_considerations: If the foam roller rolling reveals strong asymmetry, address the weaker side with single-arm work before returning to this bilateral drill
Avoid if shoulder pain increases with overhead movement — stay in pain-free range
execution.range_of_motion_guidance: Slide the roller as high as bilaterally even pressure can be maintained. This is typically less than the range in the unloaded wall angel.
coaching_cues: Keep the roller perfectly vertical — it will tilt if one arm is working more than the other
Light pressure on the roller — this is not a strength exercise; it is a motor control exercise
Think about reaching long through the elbows, not about how high you get

name: Seal Row
description: The seal row is a prone barbell row performed with the chest resting on an elevated flat bench, so the arms hang completely freely and the bar travels from full extension to contact with the underside of the bench on every repetition. This setup eliminates all lower back involvement and momentum, forcing the upper back to do all the work through the full range of motion.

execution.starting_position: Elevate a flat bench on safeties, boxes, or plates so there is enough clearance beneath it for the barbell and loaded plates. Lie prone on the bench with the chest supported. Load the barbell underneath and grasp it with an overhand grip slightly wider than shoulder-width. Arms should be fully extended.
execution.setup_instructions: Place a flat bench on two sturdy boxes or power rack safeties so the underside of the bench is high enough to allow the loaded barbell to pass underneath freely. Load the barbell before mounting the bench.
steps: Step 1: Begin with arms hanging, the barbell at full extension below the bench.
Step 2: Row the barbell up toward the underside of the bench by driving the elbows up and back.
Step 3: Touch or nearly touch the bar to the underside of the bench — this is the range-of-motion marker.
Step 4: Squeeze the shoulder blades together at the top.
Step 5: Lower the barbell fully, allowing the shoulder blades to protract, before the next rep.
execution.breathing_instructions: Exhale as you row the bar up. Inhale as you lower it.
common_mistakes: Not elevating the bench high enough, restricting the range of motion
Failing to lower to full arm extension on each rep
Letting the bar swing forward rather than keeping it in a vertical path
safety_considerations: Ensure the bench supports are extremely stable before lying on the bench
Have a partner load the bar or load it before mounting the bench
execution.range_of_motion_guidance: Full dead hang at the bottom to bar contact with the bench at the top. This is the longest available ROM for a horizontal pull.
coaching_cues: Let the bar hang completely at the bottom — no short reps
Touch the bench every single rep
Imagine pulling the bench down onto the bar, not the bar up to the bench

name: Seated Arnold Press on Incline Bench
description: The incline-bench Arnold press performs the standard Arnold press rotation from supinated-to-pronated while seated on an incline bench (60-70 degrees), which provides a slight forward lean and greater back support than a vertical seated position. The incline alters the starting angle of the press, increasing anterior deltoid pre-stretch at the bottom and making the transition from the supinated starting position slightly more challenging through the mid-range.

execution.starting_position: Sit on a bench inclined to 60-70 degrees. Hold dumbbells in the Arnold press starting position — elbows bent, dumbbells at shoulder level, palms facing the body.
execution.setup_instructions: Set the bench high enough to be nearly vertical but not fully upright — this differentiates from a standard seated Arnold press.
steps: Step 1: Begin with dumbbells at shoulder height, palms facing you, elbows forward.
Step 2: Begin pressing while simultaneously rotating the wrists outward.
Step 3: By the mid-point of the press, palms face forward (pronated).
Step 4: Continue pressing to full overhead extension.
Step 5: Lower while reversing the rotation — returning to the supinated position.
execution.breathing_instructions: Exhale on the press. Inhale on the descent.
common_mistakes: Not completing the full rotation — the supination-to-pronation should be a full 180 degrees
Using too heavy a load — the rotation requires control
safety_considerations: The rotation combined with heavy loads increases wrist stress — moderate weight
Ensure the bench incline is stable and secure before loading
execution.range_of_motion_guidance: Shoulder height supinated to full overhead extension pronated.
coaching_cues: Elbows go from forward to out as you press
Full rotation — 180 degrees of wrist turn
Drive the weight overhead — not just forward

name: Seated Barbell Overhead Triceps Extension
description: A seated overhead barbell extension that isolates the triceps, particularly the long head. Sitting prevents the use of leg drive and momentum, making this an honest isolation movement. Use an EZ bar if the straight bar causes wrist discomfort.

execution.starting_position: Set up for Seated Barbell Overhead Triceps Extension in the appropriate position.
execution.setup_instructions: Prepare equipment and body position for Seated Barbell Overhead Triceps Extension.
steps: Step 1: Sit upright on bench with back support. Hold bar overhead with close grip.
Step 2: Keep upper arms vertical and close to head.
Step 3: Lower bar behind head by bending elbows until forearms are past horizontal.
Step 4: Extend elbows to press bar back overhead.
execution.breathing_instructions: Exhale during the exertion phase, inhale during the return.
common_mistakes: Letting elbows flare sideways
Arching back to compensate
safety_considerations: Keep joints aligned throughout the movement.
Use controlled weight appropriate for skill level.
execution.range_of_motion_guidance: Move through full range of motion without compromising joint integrity.
coaching_cues: Elbows stay by ears throughout
