Sit tall with braced core

name: Seated Barbell Wrist Curl (Overhand / Extension)
description: The seated barbell wrist curl performed overhand (pronated grip) targets the wrist extensor muscles on the back of the forearm. The lifter sits at a bench with the forearms resting on the thighs, bar hanging in a pronated grip, and extends the wrists upward against resistance. This exercise balances the commonly trained wrist flexors and helps prevent wrist extensor weakness-related elbow pain.

execution.starting_position: Sit on a bench. Rest the forearms on the thighs, hands just past the knees, pronated grip on the barbell. Wrists hanging in flexion.
execution.setup_instructions: Use a very light weight — wrist extensors are small muscles. EZ-bar is a comfortable alternative.
steps: Step 1: Begin with wrists in slight flexion, bar hanging in the pronated grip.
Step 2: Extend the wrists upward, raising the back of the hands toward the ceiling.
Step 3: Hold briefly at full extension.
Step 4: Lower the wrists back to the starting position with control.
execution.breathing_instructions: Exhale on extension, inhale on return.
common_mistakes: Using too much weight, causing the arms to lift off the thighs
Wrist deviation rather than pure extension
safety_considerations: Very small range of motion — do not load heavily
execution.range_of_motion_guidance: Wrist neutral to full extension.
coaching_cues: Forearms stay on the thighs
Only the wrists move
Control the descent

name: Seated Barbell Wrist Curl (Underhand / Flexion)
description: The seated barbell wrist curl performed underhand (supinated grip) isolates the wrist flexor muscles on the inner forearm. The forearms rest on the thighs for support, and the wrists flex upward against the barbell's resistance. It is a foundational forearm isolation exercise for building wrist flexor strength and forearm girth, commonly programmed at the end of arm training days.

execution.starting_position: Sit on a bench. Rest forearms on the thighs, hands just past the knees, supinated grip on the barbell. Allow wrists to extend slightly at the bottom.
execution.setup_instructions: Use a light barbell or EZ-bar. Forearms fully supported on the thighs.
steps: Step 1: Begin with wrists extended (bar hanging down in the supinated grip).
Step 2: Flex the wrists upward, curling the bar up with the wrist flexors.
Step 3: Hold briefly at full wrist flexion.
Step 4: Lower the bar back to the starting position.
execution.breathing_instructions: Exhale on the curl, inhale on the return.
common_mistakes: Lifting forearms off the thighs — keep them braced
Using elbow flexion instead of wrist flexion
safety_considerations: Use light weight — excessive loading can strain the wrist flexor tendons
execution.range_of_motion_guidance: Full wrist extension to full wrist flexion.
coaching_cues: Forearms planted on the thighs
Only the wrists flex and extend
Feel the forearm pump

name: Seated Cable High Row to Neck
description: The seated cable high row to neck uses a high cable pulley angled downward and pulls the attachment toward the back of the neck with elbows flared wide. The unique downward-angled pull when combined with the high target position creates intense upper trap, rhomboid, and rear deltoid contraction. It is used in bodybuilding to develop upper back width and rear delt thickness visible from the front.

execution.starting_position: Sit facing a high cable pulley. Attach a wide grip bar or rope. Grasp with an overhand grip, arms extended toward the high pulley.
execution.setup_instructions: Set the cable to the highest available position. Sit close enough that the arms are extended upward at approximately 45 degrees.
steps: Step 1: Begin with arms extended upward toward the high pulley.
Step 2: Pull the attachment toward the back of the neck, driving elbows down and out.
Step 3: At peak, the bar or rope should be at neck level, elbows wide.
Step 4: Hold 1 second.
Step 5: Return under control.
execution.breathing_instructions: Exhale on the pull. Inhale on the return.
common_mistakes: Pulling behind the neck with excessive weight — creates cervical spine risk
Elbows tracking forward rather than out wide
safety_considerations: Moderate loads only — the cervical spine is vulnerable in this position
Do not force the neck into flexion; pull to a comfortable position
execution.range_of_motion_guidance: Arms extended to attachment at neck level with elbows wide.
coaching_cues: Elbows go wide like wings
Pull to the neck, not the face
Upright chest throughout

name: Seated Cable Lat Pulldown — Facing Away from Stack
description: A lat pulldown variation performed while seated facing away from the cable stack with a long bar or rope attached to the high pulley. The reversed orientation changes the angle of pull and places the shoulder in a different position relative to the resistance vector throughout the range, targeting the lower fibers of the latissimus dorsi and creating a unique stretch at the top position compared to a standard forward-facing pulldown. Used as a lat isolation variation to target different fibers and angles.

execution.starting_position: Sit on a bench or the floor facing away from a high cable pulley. Hold the bar or rope overhead with both hands and position the attachment just above and behind the head to create the reversed pull angle.
execution.setup_instructions: Attach a straight bar or rope to the high pulley. Position a bench approximately 1-2 meters from the stack, facing away. The cable will pull from behind and above.
steps: Step 1: Sit facing away from the cable stack, holding the bar above head with arms extended.
Step 2: Depress and retract the shoulder blades, then pull the bar down toward the chest (bar will travel from behind-and-above to in-front-of-chest).
Step 3: Hold the contracted position with the bar at chest level, feeling the lower lat contraction.
Step 4: Slowly return to the starting position. Repeat.
execution.breathing_instructions: Exhale during the pull. Inhale during the return.
common_mistakes: Leaning forward excessively to assist the pull — maintain an upright torso
Using momentum by swinging the torso
Allowing the cable to pull the arms too far back past a comfortable overhead range
safety_considerations: The cable angle creates a different shoulder loading pattern — start with light weight to assess comfort
Avoid if overhead extension causes shoulder impingement symptoms
execution.range_of_motion_guidance: Full extension of the arms overhead at the top to full contraction with the bar at chest level.
execution.tempo_recommendations: 2s pull down, 1s contraction hold, 3s slow return.
coaching_cues: Depress the shoulder blades before you start the pull — do not shrug
Think of pulling the elbows down and forward toward your hip pockets
Feel the lower lats — this variation should produce a different pull sensation than a standard pulldown

name: Seated Cable Lateral Raise (Cable Under Legs)
alternative_names: Seated Lateral Raise Cable Between Legs
description: The seated cable lateral raise with the cable running under the legs is performed seated on a bench beside a cable, with the cable passing beneath the thighs to the working hand. This setup creates a unique loading angle where the cable pulls the working arm downward and inward at the bottom of the range, then shifts to a lateral pull at the top — providing a consistent tension profile that keeps the medial deltoid loaded at the bottom of the movement.

execution.starting_position: Sit on a flat bench beside a low cable pulley. The cable runs underneath the thighs to the working hand. Grip the handle with the far hand, arm resting across the thighs.
execution.setup_instructions: Sit close enough to the cable that the cable can run naturally under the legs. This may require a low bench or the floor.
steps: Step 1: Begin seated with the cable running under the thighs, working arm at side.
Step 2: Raise the working arm out to the side and upward to shoulder height.
Step 3: Hold 1 second at peak.
Step 4: Lower under control — the cable will pull from beneath as you descend.
Step 5: Complete all reps then switch sides.
execution.breathing_instructions: Exhale raising. Inhale lowering.
common_mistakes: Sitting too far from the cable — the cable should run smoothly under the legs
Raising above shoulder height — stop at horizontal for medial delt emphasis
safety_considerations: Ensure the cable path under the legs does not create a tripping hazard
Light loads — isolation exercise
execution.range_of_motion_guidance: Arm across body to shoulder height laterally.
coaching_cues: Lead with the elbow
Feel the tension from the very start of the movement
No torso lean or swing

name: Seated Cable Row
description: The seated cable row is a horizontal pulling exercise using a low-pulley cable machine. It trains the mid and upper back through scapular retraction and arm pulling, while maintaining a constant cable tension throughout the movement. It is particularly effective for developing back thickness and improving posture.

execution.starting_position: Sit on the seated row machine with feet on the foot rests, knees slightly bent. Grasp the cable attachment with both hands. Sit tall with a neutral spine and slight forward lean from the hips.
execution.setup_instructions: Attach a close-grip or straight bar handle. Set a weight that allows full range of motion with controlled form.
steps: Sit upright with a neutral spine, then row the handle toward the lower abdomen.
Drive the elbows behind the torso and squeeze the shoulder blades together firmly at the peak.
Slowly return the handle to the starting position, allowing the shoulder blades to protract fully for a complete stretch.
execution.breathing_instructions: Exhale as you row. Inhale as you return.
common_mistakes: Using excessive forward lean and momentum from the lower back to initiate each rep
Pulling the handle to the chest rather than the abdomen
Not allowing shoulder blades to fully protract at full extension
safety_considerations: Avoid rounding the lower back when leaning forward
Keep the torso upright throughout — only the arms and shoulder blades should move
execution.range_of_motion_guidance: Full protraction at the front, full retraction and row to the lower abdomen at the back.
coaching_cues: Sit tall as if a string is pulling your head to the ceiling
Row with your elbows, not your hands

name: Seated Cable Row High Pull
description: The seated cable row high pull uses a rope attachment at a low or mid cable position and pulls toward the face/neck rather than the abdomen, with elbows flaring wide at shoulder height. It bridges the gap between a standard row and a face pull, training the rear deltoids, upper trapezius, and external rotators through a horizontally-abducted pulling pattern while seated.

execution.starting_position: Sit facing a cable pulley set at low or mid-height. Attach a rope. Grip with both hands, arms extended forward.
execution.setup_instructions: Adjust cable height so the pull angle targets the face/upper chest. Sit far enough from the stack to allow full arm extension.
steps: Step 1: Begin seated with arms extended gripping the rope.
Step 2: Pull the rope toward the face/forehead, driving elbows wide and high.
Step 3: At peak, elbows should be at or above shoulder height, hands beside the ears.
Step 4: Hold 1 second.
Step 5: Return under control to full arm extension.
execution.breathing_instructions: Exhale on the pull. Inhale on the return.
common_mistakes: Pulling to the chest instead of the face — the high pull targets rear delts, not lats
Elbows dropping below shoulder height — keep them elevated
safety_considerations: Light loads recommended — rear delts and external rotators are small muscles
Avoid if experiencing shoulder impingement
execution.range_of_motion_guidance: Full arm extension to hands beside face with elbows at shoulder height.
coaching_cues: Pull to the face, not the belly
Elbows go wide and high
Thumbs point back at the peak

name: Seated Cable Row — Wide Overhand Grip
description: A seated cable row performed with a wide overhand grip using a straight bar. This grip orientation shifts the loading emphasis from the lats to the middle and upper traps, rhomboids, and rear deltoids compared to a close neutral-grip row, targeting the mid-scapular muscles more directly.

execution.starting_position: Sit at a cable row station with feet on the foot rests and knees slightly bent. Hold a wide straight bar with an overhand grip.
execution.setup_instructions: Attach a straight bar to the low cable pulley. Sit down, place feet on the foot rests, and grip the bar wide with an overhand grip.
steps: Step 1: Keep the torso upright and brace the core throughout.
Step 2: Pull the bar toward the upper abdomen, driving the elbows out wide to the sides.
Step 3: Squeeze the shoulder blades together at the peak of the row.
Step 4: Return under control to full arm extension.
execution.breathing_instructions: Exhale on the pull. Inhale on the return.
common_mistakes: Using momentum by swinging the torso
Not squeezing the shoulder blades at the top
safety_considerations: A wider grip means the elbows flare out — this is intentional for mid-trap targeting
execution.range_of_motion_guidance: Full arm extension at the front. Bar pulled to the upper abdomen with shoulder blades retracted at the back.
coaching_cues: Elbows out wide
Squeeze the shoulder blades at the top

name: Seated Calf Raise — Alternating Eccentric
description: A seated calf raise technique that uses both legs for the concentric (rising) phase and one leg for the slow eccentric (lowering) phase, alternating sides each repetition. Rising on two legs reduces the concentric load per limb, while lowering on one leg significantly increases the eccentric stress on the soleus of the working leg. This bilateral-concentric/unilateral-eccentric approach allows the soleus to work at a higher eccentric load than a pure single-leg seated raise, used in Achilles tendinopathy and plantar fasciitis rehabilitation.

execution.starting_position: Sit on a bench with knees at 90 degrees and both feet positioned on the edge of a small block for full range. Rest a dumbbell on each thigh or use a seated calf raise machine.
execution.setup_instructions: Setup as for a standard seated calf raise. Ensure both feet have a secure footing at the start.
steps: Step 1: Press through BOTH feet to rise to the full plantarflexion position.
Step 2: At the top, lift the right foot off the block, leaving only the left foot to lower.
Step 3: Lower slowly on the left foot only, controlling the descent over 3-4 seconds to the full stretch position.
Step 4: Return the right foot to the block. Press through BOTH feet again to rise. At the top, lift the left foot and lower on the right only. Alternate sides each repetition.
execution.breathing_instructions: Exhale as you rise (bilateral). Inhale slowly during the eccentric lower (unilateral).
common_mistakes: Rushing the eccentric — the slow 3-4 second lowering is the most therapeutically valuable component
Not completing the full stretch at the bottom of the eccentric
Using the removed foot to assist the lowering phase
safety_considerations: For insertional Achilles tendinopathy: do not let the heel drop below forefoot level on the eccentric to avoid aggravating the insertion
For mid-portion tendinopathy: full range eccentric is typically indicated
execution.range_of_motion_guidance: Full range: both feet to full plantarflexion on the rise; single foot to full dorsiflexion on the eccentric.
execution.tempo_recommendations: 1s bilateral rise, 1s top hold, 3-4s unilateral eccentric lower.
coaching_cues: Use the second foot only for rising — it does not help on the way down
Think of this as a 'cheat' on the way up and a 'grind' on the way down
Feel the deep calf (soleus) burning during the slow eccentric

name: Seated Calf Raise
description: The seated calf raise targets the soleus muscle specifically because the bent-knee position relaxes the gastrocnemius, removing it from the movement. The soleus is predominantly slow-twitch and responds well to higher repetitions. It is an important complement to standing calf raises for complete calf development.

execution.starting_position: Sit on the seated calf raise machine with the pad resting on the lower thighs just above the knees. Balls of the feet on the platform edge, heels hanging off.
execution.setup_instructions: Adjust the knee pad height to firmly secure the thighs. The 90-degree knee position is what specifically targets the soleus.
steps: Lower the heels as far as possible below the platform.
Raise the heels as high as possible.
Hold the peak contraction for one second, then lower under control.
execution.breathing_instructions: Exhale on the raise, inhale on the descent.
common_mistakes: Not using full range of motion
Using a machine designed for standing raises and incorrectly calling it a seated raise
safety_considerations: Ensure pad is secured before releasing the safety handle
execution.range_of_motion_guidance: Full plantar flexion at top, full dorsiflexion stretch at the bottom.
coaching_cues: Full stretch at the bottom — the soleus responds to the eccentric portion
High reps work well here — the soleus is built for endurance

name: Seated Calf Raise — Toes Angled In
description: A seated calf raise performed with the toes angled inward (pigeon-toed position), which shifts the emphasis toward the outer head of the gastrocnemius and the lateral soleus fibers. The seated position places the knee at 90 degrees of flexion, reducing gastrocnemius contribution and increasing soleus activation relative to a standing variation. This variation is used in calf rehabilitation and strength programs targeting specific fiber imbalances.

execution.starting_position: Sit on a bench or chair with feet flat on the floor or on an edge for greater ROM. Turn the toes inward (internally rotate the feet) approximately 15-30 degrees. Rest a dumbbell or plate on each thigh if adding resistance.
execution.setup_instructions: Use a flat bench with a plate on the thigh for resistance, or a dedicated seated calf raise machine. Position the balls of the feet on the edge of a step if greater stretch is desired.
steps: Step 1: Sit tall with toes turned inward and feet positioned on the edge for full range.
Step 2: Lower the heels as far as comfortable to achieve a full dorsiflexion stretch.
Step 3: Press through the balls of the feet to rise onto the toes, achieving full plantarflexion.
Step 4: Lower back down under control. Repeat.
execution.breathing_instructions: Exhale as you rise onto the toes. Inhale as you lower.
common_mistakes: Using partial range — not achieving full stretch at the bottom
Bouncing at the bottom rather than controlling the eccentric
Rotating the entire lower leg rather than just turning toes in
safety_considerations: If you experience lateral knee discomfort with toes-in position, reduce the angle of inward rotation
Avoid with acute Achilles tendinopathy — consult a physiotherapist
execution.range_of_motion_guidance: Full range: from maximum dorsiflexion (heel at or below forefoot level) to maximum plantarflexion (full toe rise).
execution.tempo_recommendations: 2-1-2-1 (2s lower, 1s stretch, 2s rise, 1s squeeze at top)
coaching_cues: Let the heel drop below the forefoot to get the full stretch
Squeeze the outer calf at the top of each rep
Keep the knee angle constant — do not straighten the leg during the movement

name: Seated Calf Raise — Toes Angled Out
description: A seated calf raise performed with the toes angled outward (duck-footed position), which shifts the emphasis toward the inner gastrocnemius medial head and the medial soleus fibers. Because the seat position keeps the knee bent, the soleus is the primary target regardless of foot angle, but the medial toe-out position creates a slight internal bias in calf muscle fiber recruitment. Used in rehabilitation programs addressing medial calf weakness or asymmetry.

execution.starting_position: Sit on a bench with feet flat, toes turned outward approximately 15-30 degrees. Rest a dumbbell or plate on each thigh or use a seated calf raise machine.
execution.setup_instructions: Position the balls of the feet on the edge of a step or plate for full range of motion. Keep the knee angle at approximately 90 degrees throughout.
steps: Step 1: Sit tall with toes externally rotated and feet positioned for full range.
Step 2: Lower the heels to achieve a full calf stretch at the bottom.
Step 3: Press up through the balls of the feet to full plantarflexion, emphasizing the inner calf.
Step 4: Lower slowly under control. Repeat.
execution.breathing_instructions: Exhale as you rise onto toes. Inhale as you lower.
common_mistakes: Partial range of motion — not achieving full stretch or contraction
Using momentum by bouncing at the bottom
Rotating the entire lower limb rather than just pointing the toes outward
safety_considerations: Avoid if you have medial knee discomfort with toe-out position
Consult a physiotherapist for use in specific Achilles or calf injury rehabilitation
execution.range_of_motion_guidance: Full range from maximal dorsiflexion to full plantarflexion. Quality over speed.
execution.tempo_recommendations: 2-1-2-1 (2s lower, 1s stretch, 2s rise, 1s squeeze at top)
coaching_cues: Feel the inner calf activate at the top of the movement
Control the lowering phase — do not let gravity drop the heel
Maintain the same knee angle throughout

name: Seated Dumbbell Lateral Raise (3-Second Eccentric)
description: The seated lateral raise with a 3-second eccentric phase lowers each repetition over 3 full seconds, dramatically increasing total time under tension for the medial deltoid and potentially enhancing muscle damage (a primary hypertrophy mechanism). The seated position prevents the torso swing that often contaminates standing lateral raises, ensuring the eccentric is performed with strict medial deltoid engagement throughout.

execution.starting_position: Sit on a flat bench. Hold a dumbbell in each hand at the sides. Sit upright.
execution.setup_instructions: Use lighter weight than a standard lateral raise — the slow eccentric is significantly more fatiguing.
steps: Step 1: Raise both arms laterally to shoulder height (1-2 seconds up).
Step 2: At the top, hold 1 second.
Step 3: Lower both arms over exactly 3 seconds — count it.
Step 4: Return to the starting position.
Step 5: Repeat.
execution.breathing_instructions: Exhale raising. Inhale through the 3-second lowering.
common_mistakes: Lowering faster than 3 seconds — time the descent with a count
Using standard lateral raise weight — reduce load by 20-30%
safety_considerations: Light loads — the eccentric focus amplifies the stimulus
Stop if shoulder pain occurs
execution.range_of_motion_guidance: Sides to shoulder height.
coaching_cues: Count one, two, three on the way down
No dropping — keep control the entire descent
Seated means no cheating

name: Seated Dumbbell Lateral Raise (5-Second Eccentric)
description: The 5-second eccentric lateral raise extends the lowering phase to a full 5 seconds, creating even greater time under tension for the medial deltoid than the 3-second version. It is an advanced hypertrophy technique and is typically used by experienced trainees for single set shock protocols or as a technique to maintain medial deltoid stimulus when heavy loads are unavailable or not advisable due to injury constraints.

execution.starting_position: Sit upright on a bench with dumbbells at the sides.
execution.setup_instructions: Use a very light dumbbell — a 5-second eccentric with heavy weight is impossible to control. Many trainees use 2-5 kg.
steps: Step 1: Raise both arms to shoulder height in 1-2 seconds.
Step 2: Hold 1 second at the top.
Step 3: Lower both arms over exactly 5 seconds — one, two, three, four, five.
Step 4: Return to the starting position.
Step 5: Repeat for 8-10 reps.
execution.breathing_instructions: Exhale raising. Inhale controlled through the 5-second descent.
common_mistakes: Cheating the tempo — 5 seconds means 5 seconds
Using too heavy a weight — with 5s eccentric, light weight burns plenty
safety_considerations: Very light loads only — the extended time under tension is the stimulus, not the weight
High fatigue technique — limit to 1-2 sets initially
execution.range_of_motion_guidance: Shoulder height to sides over 5 controlled seconds.
coaching_cues: Count every second of the descent
No shortcuts — the 5-second lower is the entire point
Fight the weight all the way to the bottom

name: Seated Dynamic Hamstring Flossing
description: A dynamic variant of seated hamstring neural flossing where the exerciser performs continuous alternating cycles of knee extension with ankle plantarflexion and knee flexion with ankle dorsiflexion. Unlike the static neural glide, the dynamic flossing version is performed rhythmically and with slightly greater amplitude, progressively working toward full knee extension as neural mobility improves. Used in advanced stages of sciatic nerve mobilization and hamstring neural tension rehabilitation.

execution.starting_position: Sit upright in a chair with both feet flat on the floor. Maintain a neutral or slightly extended lumbar spine. The working leg is the one being flossed.
execution.setup_instructions: No equipment needed. Sit toward the front of a chair so the foot can extend forward freely.
steps: Step 1: Begin with the working knee bent at 90 degrees, foot on the floor.
Step 2: Extend the knee forward while simultaneously pointing the toes (plantarflexion) — this moderately tensions the sciatic nerve.
Step 3: Immediately bend the knee back while pulling the toes toward the shin (dorsiflexion) — this releases tension on the distal nerve while tensioning it proximally.
Step 4: Continue this rhythmic alternating motion for the prescribed repetitions. The cadence should be approximately 1 full cycle per 2 seconds.
execution.breathing_instructions: Breathe continuously throughout. Do not hold the breath.
common_mistakes: Creating sharp, electrical, or radiating pain — stop immediately if this occurs
Extending the knee to end range if it reproduces symptoms — work within a comfortable range initially
Performing the exercise too quickly — moderate pace allows neural tissue to adapt
safety_considerations: CRITICAL: Stop immediately if any sharp, electrical, radiating, or shooting pain occurs down the leg
This is a progression from static neural flossing — ensure static flossing is tolerated before beginning the dynamic version
Not appropriate for active disc herniations without physiotherapy supervision
execution.range_of_motion_guidance: Work within a pain-free range. The range will progressively improve as neural mobility increases.
execution.tempo_recommendations: 1 repetition = 1 full extend-then-flex cycle. Approximately 2 seconds per cycle.
coaching_cues: Keep breathing — do not hold your breath during the leg extension
Work within a range that creates mild tension only — no pain
Gradually increase the knee extension range as your neural mobility improves over sessions

name: Seated Hamstring Neural Flossing with Band
description: Neural flossing (also called neural gliding) is a gentle mobilization technique that moves the sciatic nerve through its neural canal by alternating tension on opposite ends of the nerve. In the seated hamstring version, the exerciser alternately extends the knee (tensioning the sciatic nerve distally) and flexes the ankle into dorsiflexion while the hip remains flexed. This rhythmic 'flossing' improves neural mobility and reduces pain associated with sciatic nerve tension, hamstring injuries, or disc herniations causing radiculopathy.

execution.starting_position: Sit upright in a chair with both feet flat on the floor. Ensure a neutral or slightly extended spine — do not slump. Cross the working ankle over the resting thigh or simply let it hang, depending on the technique variant being used.
execution.setup_instructions: No equipment needed. A chair that allows the foot to hang freely is ideal. The technique must be very gentle — neural flossing is NOT a stretching exercise and should never produce sharp, radiating, or electrical pain.
steps: Step 1: Sit tall in a chair. Extend one knee to straighten the leg as much as comfortable — this tensions the sciatic nerve.
Step 2: Simultaneously point the toes (plantarflex the ankle) to reduce the neural tension slightly.
Step 3: Bend the knee back to roughly 90 degrees while simultaneously dorsiflexing the ankle (pull toes toward shin).
Step 4: Alternate between these two positions rhythmically — extend knee/plantarflex toes, then bend knee/dorsiflex toes. This is the flossing motion.
execution.breathing_instructions: Breathe continuously throughout. The movement should feel like gentle mobilization, not a stretch.
common_mistakes: Forcing range that creates sharp, electrical, or radiating pain — stop immediately if this occurs
Performing the exercise too aggressively — neural flossing should feel like a mild tension, not a hamstring stretch
Holding the extended position rather than keeping the motion fluid and rhythmic
safety_considerations: CRITICAL: If the exercise produces sharp, shooting, or electric pain radiating down the leg, stop immediately and consult a physiotherapist
Neural flossing should produce only mild tension — no pain
Not suitable for anyone with known spinal instability or acute disc herniation without physiotherapy supervision
execution.range_of_motion_guidance: Work only within the range that produces gentle tension and no pain. This range will improve as neural mobility increases.
execution.tempo_recommendations: 1 repetition = 1 full cycle (extend + return). Perform at a steady rhythm — approximately 1 second per position.
coaching_cues: This is a gliding exercise, not a stretch — the movement should be fluid and gentle
Mild tension is correct. Any sharp, electrical, or radiating sensation means you should stop
Consistency over intensity — daily gentle flossing outperforms aggressive weekly sessions

name: Seated Hamstring Stretch
description: The seated hamstring stretch is performed with both legs extended on the floor in a long-sitting position, then hinging the torso forward over the legs. The seated position provides a stable base and allows the lower back to relax, making this variation accessible and suitable for people who struggle to balance during the standing version. The stretch targets the entire hamstring group as well as the calf muscles when the feet are dorsiflexed.

execution.starting_position: Sit on the floor with both legs extended straight in front of you and feet hip-width apart. Sit up tall with spine neutral.
execution.setup_instructions: Sit on a mat for comfort. If the lower back rounds severely in the starting position, sit on a folded blanket to elevate the hips.
steps: Step 1: Sit tall with legs extended and feet flexed (toes pointing toward the ceiling).
Step 2: Take a breath and elongate the spine.
Step 3: Hinge forward from the hips, reaching the hands toward the feet or shins.
Step 4: When a hamstring stretch is felt, stop and hold — do not round the spine aggressively.
Step 5: Hold 30–90 seconds, breathing slowly.
execution.breathing_instructions: Breathe slowly and deeply. Exhale and gently extend further on each breath out.
common_mistakes: Rounding the spine to reach further — this reduces hamstring stretch and loads the lumbar discs
Forcing the legs flat if the hamstrings are very tight — slight knee bend is acceptable for tight individuals
Holding tension in the neck and shoulders
safety_considerations: If a sharp sensation is felt behind the knee or in the lower back, reduce the range of motion
Avoid if experiencing acute hamstring strain
execution.range_of_motion_guidance: Hinge as far forward from the hips as the hamstrings allow while keeping the spine relatively long.
coaching_cues: Lead with the chest, not the hands
Flex the feet — this increases the calf and hamstring stretch
Think of moving your belly button toward your thighs, not your head toward your knees

name: Seated Dumbbell Lateral Raise
description: The seated lateral raise is performed on a flat bench, eliminating any lower body momentum and forcing the medial deltoid to generate force without the assistance of a small body lean or leg drive. By removing these momentum contributors, the seated version isolates the lateral head of the deltoid more effectively than the standing lateral raise for many individuals. The strict position also makes it easier to control tempo and focus on the mind-muscle connection.

execution.starting_position: Sit upright on a flat bench. Hold a dumbbell in each hand at the sides, arms hanging down with a slight bend in the elbows. Palms face the thighs.
execution.setup_instructions: Because momentum is eliminated, use lighter dumbbells than for standing lateral raises initially.
steps: Step 1: Sit tall, dumbbells at sides, slight elbow bend.
Step 2: Raise both dumbbells simultaneously out to the sides in an arc.
Step 3: Raise until arms are parallel to the floor (or slightly above).
Step 4: Pause briefly at the top.
Step 5: Lower slowly under full control to the starting position.
execution.breathing_instructions: Exhale as you raise, inhale as you lower.
common_mistakes: Using momentum — rocking the torso or bouncing the dumbbells
Raising the dumbbells in front rather than directly to the side
Shrugging the traps — keep the neck long
safety_considerations: Keep the neck relaxed to avoid trap compensation
execution.range_of_motion_guidance: Dumbbells start at thigh level, raise to shoulder height.
coaching_cues: Pour from a pitcher at the top
Lead with the elbows, not the hands
No body movement — just arms

name: Seated Leg Curl
description: The seated leg curl trains the hamstrings with the hip in a flexed position, which places the biceps femoris long head — a biarticular muscle — in a greater stretch at the hip while simultaneously training it through knee flexion. This combination of hip flexion and knee flexion produces a unique hamstring stimulus that differs from the prone version and may elicit greater elongation and hypertrophic response in the long head.

execution.starting_position: Sit in the machine with the lower back supported. Position the pad on top of the lower calf near the ankle. Grip the handles. Legs begin at full extension.
execution.setup_instructions: Adjust the seat so the hip is at approximately 90°. Adjust the pad height so it rests on the lower calf, not behind the knee. The pivot point should align with the knee.
steps: Step 1: Seated with back supported and legs extended, grip the handles and brace the core.
Step 2: Flex the knees by pulling the pad downward and backward under the seat as far as the machine allows.
Step 3: Hold the peak contraction briefly with the hamstrings fully shortened.
Step 4: Return to full knee extension under control, resisting the upward pull of the weight stack.
Step 5: Repeat without letting the weight stack rest between reps.
execution.breathing_instructions: Exhale as you curl. Inhale as you return to extension.
common_mistakes: Lifting the hips off the seat to assist at the top
Allowing incomplete extension at the bottom, losing the stretch
Using too much weight, causing the torso to pitch forward
safety_considerations: Avoid if experiencing posterior knee pain
Keep the back flat against the seat — do not lean forward excessively
execution.range_of_motion_guidance: Full extension at the start (full hamstring stretch from the hip-flexed position) to maximum knee flexion.
coaching_cues: Pull down and back — think of driving your heels toward the glutes
Keep hips planted — don't let them rise
Own the eccentric — lower slowly

name: Seated Machine Crunch — Oblique Rotation
description: A variation of the seated machine crunch in which the torso rotates slightly to one side during the crunch, targeting the oblique muscles on the side toward which the rotation occurs. By crunching and rotating simultaneously, the internal and external obliques are recruited in addition to the rectus abdominis. Used in abdominal training programs to develop rotational core strength alongside the standard flexion-dominant crunch.

execution.starting_position: Sit in the crunch machine with the chest pad positioned correctly. Begin in the upright starting position with the spine tall.
execution.setup_instructions: Adjust the machine for your torso length. Set a weight that allows full range with slow, controlled movement.
steps: Step 1: Begin upright in the machine. Initiate the crunch by flexing the spine downward and simultaneously rotating the torso to the right.
Step 2: At the bottom of the crunch, the torso is both flexed and rotated to the right.
Step 3: Return to the upright starting position. On the next repetition, rotate to the left.
Step 4: Alternate sides with each repetition, or perform all reps on one side before switching.
execution.breathing_instructions: Exhale forcefully during the crunch and rotation. Inhale as you return to the start.
common_mistakes: Using the arms and chest pad to push rather than the core to pull
Rotating from the hips rather than the thoracic spine
Rushing through the rotation — the oblique contraction requires a controlled squeeze at the end range
safety_considerations: If the machine does not allow rotational movement, do not force it — this variation may not be possible on all designs
If neck pain occurs during the crunch, reduce the range or change to a supported crunch variation
execution.range_of_motion_guidance: Full flexion with maximum comfortable rotation at the bottom.
execution.tempo_recommendations: 2s crunch and rotate, 1s hold, 3s slow return.
coaching_cues: Bring the right elbow toward the left knee and the left elbow toward the right knee on alternating reps
The rotation comes from the thorax, not the hips
Squeeze the oblique hard at the bottom of each rotated crunch

name: Seated Machine Row
description: The seated machine row uses a selectorized or pin-loaded machine where the user sits facing a chest pad and pulls handles toward the torso. The guided movement path removes the need for spinal stabilization, making it accessible for beginners and useful for high-volume hypertrophy training with reduced injury risk. Available in neutral, pronated, and wide-grip handle configurations targeting slightly different back musculature.

execution.starting_position: Adjust the seat height so the handles are at mid-chest level. Sit with the chest against the pad and grip the handles with arms extended.
execution.setup_instructions: Select the appropriate pin-loaded weight. Ensure the chest pad is set so the torso is upright and comfortable.
steps: Step 1: Sit at the machine with the chest on the pad, arms extended toward the handles.
Step 2: Begin from a position of full scapular protraction.
Step 3: Row the handles toward the lower chest, retracting the scapulae and driving the elbows back.
Step 4: Squeeze the mid-back at peak contraction.
Step 5: Return slowly to the start, allowing the shoulder blades to fully protract.
execution.breathing_instructions: Exhale on the row, inhale on the return.
common_mistakes: Not protracting the scapulae at the start of each rep, missing the full ROM
Pulling with the arms rather than initiating with the scapulae
safety_considerations: Adjust seat and pad before adding heavy weight to ensure proper biomechanical alignment
execution.range_of_motion_guidance: Full scapular protraction at the start, full retraction at the end.
coaching_cues: Let your shoulder blades spread apart at the start
Initiate with the elbows, not the hands
Full retraction at the end of every rep

name: Seated Military Press from Rack Pins
description: The seated military press from rack pins starts from a dead-stop position with the barbell resting on safety pins set at approximately chin height, eliminating the stretch reflex from the eccentric phase. The lifter must generate maximum force from a full dead stop at the bottom of the press, training rate of force development and pure starting strength in the overhead pressing pattern. It is primarily used to overload the sticking point of the standard seated overhead press and to develop explosive pressing force.

execution.starting_position: Sit on a bench inside a power rack. Set the safety pins at chin height. Rest the barbell on the pins. Grip the bar slightly wider than shoulder width. Feet flat on the floor.
execution.setup_instructions: The bar starts on the pins — there is no unracking. Set the spotter arms or pins so the bar rests at the correct height for the sticking point. Load heavier than your standard overhead press since the range is shorter.
steps: Step 1: Sit under the bar resting on the pins. Grip the bar.
Step 2: Take a breath and brace the core hard.
Step 3: Press the bar explosively from dead stop — no dipping under the bar first.
Step 4: Press to full lockout overhead.
Step 5: Lower the bar under control back to the pins. Release the tension. Reset and repeat.
execution.breathing_instructions: Inhale and brace before each rep. Exhale through the press. Full reset between reps.
common_mistakes: Not fully releasing the tension on the pins between reps — the dead-stop is the entire point
Starting with the head in a compromised position — ensure the bar can clear the face on the way up
safety_considerations: Set the spotter pins correctly — the bar must rest securely between reps
Advanced technique — requires established overhead pressing mechanics before using pin press variations
execution.range_of_motion_guidance: Dead stop at chin height to full overhead lockout.
coaching_cues: Dead stop — full reset on the pins between reps
Explosive drive off the pins
Lock out completely overhead

name: Seated Soleus Raise with Pause
description: A seated calf raise performed with a deliberate pause at the top of the movement (maximum plantarflexion), increasing time-under-tension for the soleus muscle. Because the seated position with bent knees isolates the soleus from the gastrocnemius, this exercise is particularly effective for Achilles tendinopathy rehabilitation at the soleus-tendon junction, distal Achilles insertional issues, and plantar fasciitis programs. The pause amplifies the therapeutic loading stimulus at the top.

execution.starting_position: Sit on a bench or chair with knees bent at approximately 90 degrees. Place a dumbbell or weight plate on the thighs just above the knees. Position the balls of the feet on the edge of a small block or plate for full range.
execution.setup_instructions: The key setup requirement is a 90-degree (or greater) knee angle, which disables the gastrocnemius and isolates the soleus. Use a step or block under the forefeet for maximum range.
steps: Step 1: Begin with heels lowered below the forefeet for the full stretch position.
Step 2: Press through the balls of the feet to rise to the full plantarflexed (tiptoe) position.
Step 3: PAUSE at the top for 2-3 seconds, maintaining maximum plantarflexion and squeezing the soleus.
Step 4: Lower slowly (3-4 seconds) back to the full stretch. Repeat.
execution.breathing_instructions: Exhale as you rise. Breathe during the top pause. Inhale slowly as you lower.
common_mistakes: Skipping the pause — the pause is what differentiates this from a standard seated calf raise
Partial range at the top — rise to true maximum plantarflexion
Rushing the eccentric — 3-4 second lowering is prescribed
safety_considerations: For insertional Achilles tendinopathy, do not let the heel drop below the level of the forefoot — this can aggravate the insertion
For mid-portion tendinopathy, full range is typically better tolerated and therapeutically indicated
execution.range_of_motion_guidance: Full dorsiflexion to full plantarflexion. The pause occurs at maximum plantarflexion.
execution.tempo_recommendations: 2s raise, 3s pause at top, 3s slow eccentric lower
coaching_cues: Feel the deep calf (soleus) hold the pause at the top — not the gastrocnemius (which is inactive at 90-degree knee angle)
Squeeze the calf hard during the pause
Let the heel drop for the full stretch — feel the tension through the lower calf and Achilles

name: Seated Tibialis Raise with Band
description: A seated exercise targeting the tibialis anterior through dorsiflexion against resistance from a band. The exerciser sits with one end of a resistance band looped around the forefoot, with the other end anchored forward. By pulling the toes back toward the shin against band resistance, the tibialis anterior — the muscle running along the outer shin — is loaded. This exercise is critical for shin splint prevention, anterior compartment syndrome rehabilitation, and ankle stability programs.

execution.starting_position: Sit on the floor or a chair with the leg extended forward. Loop a resistance band around the forefoot, anchoring the other end to a stable object in front of the foot. Begin with the foot in a neutral or slightly plantarflexed position.
execution.setup_instructions: Anchor the band to something at floor level — a heavy dumbbell, power rack base, or a door anchor near the floor. The band should provide resistance against dorsiflexion (pulling toes up).
steps: Step 1: Sit with the leg extended and the band looped around the top of the foot, anchored in front.
Step 2: Pull the toes and forefoot back toward the shin (dorsiflexion) against the band resistance.
Step 3: Hold the dorsiflexed position briefly, feeling the contraction along the outer shin.
Step 4: Slowly lower the foot back toward the starting position under control. Repeat.
execution.breathing_instructions: Exhale as you dorsiflex (pull toes back). Inhale as you lower.
common_mistakes: Using the entire leg to assist the movement — only the foot should move
Not achieving full dorsiflexion range due to band tension that is too heavy
Allowing the heel to lift from the floor, reducing tibialis anterior isolation
safety_considerations: This exercise should be pain-free in both directions — if pulling back causes sharp shin pain, reduce band tension
For shin splint rehab: start with lighter band and higher reps, progress gradually
execution.range_of_motion_guidance: Full dorsiflexion — toes pull back as far as the ankle allows without the leg lifting from the floor.
execution.tempo_recommendations: 2s dorsiflexion, 1s hold, 3s slow return (the eccentric return is critical for shin splint rehab)
coaching_cues: Feel the muscles along the outer shin working — that is the tibialis anterior
Slow on the way down — the controlled lowering phase builds the most strength for shin splint prevention
Keep the heel grounded throughout the movement

name: Side-Lying Hip Abduction
description: Side-lying hip abduction is performed lying on one side and raising the top leg toward the ceiling with a straight knee, working the hip abductors through a longer lever than the clamshell. The gluteus medius and tensor fasciae latae are the primary movers, and the exercise is a staple of both rehabilitation programs and general glute training. A resistance band above the ankles or a cable at the ankle increases the load.

execution.starting_position: Lie on one side with hips stacked and legs straight. Bottom arm extended under the head. Body in a straight line.
execution.setup_instructions: Use bodyweight or add a mini loop band above the ankles for added resistance.
steps: Step 1: Lie on your side with hips stacked, legs extended, body in a straight line.
Step 2: With the top leg straight and toes pointing slightly downward, raise the leg toward the ceiling by abducting the hip.
Step 3: Raise until 45–60° of abduction or until the pelvis begins to tilt.
Step 4: Hold briefly at the top, then lower under control.
Step 5: Complete all reps on one side then switch.
execution.breathing_instructions: Exhale as you raise the leg. Inhale as you lower.
common_mistakes: Rolling the pelvis forward or back — keep hips stacked vertically
Internally rotating the hip (toes pointing up) — slight external rotation keeps glute medius engaged
Using momentum — the movement should be slow and controlled
safety_considerations: Very low-risk exercise suitable for beginners and rehabilitation
Avoid if the exercise reproduces hip or groin pain
execution.range_of_motion_guidance: Raise the leg to about 45–60°. Stop before the pelvis tilts.
coaching_cues: Toes slightly down — not up
Keep hips stacked — don't roll
Raise with the outer hip, not the lower back

name: Side-Lying Clamshell — Isometric Hold and Pulse
description: A variation of the standard clamshell exercise that combines an isometric hold at the top of the movement with small pulsing contractions. After raising the top knee to its maximum range, the exerciser holds briefly then performs small rhythmic pulses — tiny additional lifts — before fully returning. This technique maximizes time-under-tension for the gluteus medius and deep hip external rotators, making it a highly effective progression for hip rehabilitation programs addressing IT band syndrome, knee valgus, and hip external rotation weakness.

execution.starting_position: Lie on one side with hips stacked and knees bent to approximately 60-90 degrees. The feet remain together throughout. The bottom arm is extended under the head for support.
execution.setup_instructions: No equipment needed. A resistance band above the knees can be added. Keep the hips perpendicular to the floor — do not roll the pelvis backward.
steps: Step 1: Lie on your side with hips stacked and knees bent. Keep the feet together.
Step 2: Raise the top knee as far as the hip external rotation allows without rolling the pelvis backward.
Step 3: Hold the top position for 2-3 seconds.
Step 4: Perform 5-8 small pulses (tiny upward contractions), then lower completely. Each raise-hold-pulse sequence equals one repetition.
execution.breathing_instructions: Exhale during the raise. Breathe during the hold and pulses. Inhale as you lower.
common_mistakes: Rolling the pelvis backward to gain extra range — the hip joint should do all the work
Pulses becoming large movements rather than tiny contractions at the top of the range
Letting the top foot drift away from the bottom foot
safety_considerations: If the hip external rotators are acutely inflamed, begin with standard clamshells before adding the pulse component
If hip pain occurs at the end range, reduce range and consult a physiotherapist
execution.range_of_motion_guidance: Raise to maximum external rotation without pelvic rotation. Pulses are tiny — 1-2 cm above the top position.
coaching_cues: Keep the pelvis stacked — do not roll back for extra range
The pulses should feel like a flicker, not a full movement — stay near the top of your range
Feel the deep burn in the outer hip during the hold and pulse sequence

name: Side-Lying External Rotation
description: Side-lying external rotation is a foundational rotator cuff rehabilitation exercise targeting the infraspinatus and teres minor — the primary external rotators of the glenohumeral joint. Performed with the elbow bent to 90 degrees and resting at the side, it isolates the posterior rotator cuff with minimal deltoid or periscapular compensation. It is a standard component of shoulder impingement, rotator cuff tear, and post-surgical rehabilitation programs.

execution.starting_position: Lie on the non-working side. The working arm is on top with the elbow bent to 90 degrees and upper arm resting against the side of the torso. A small rolled towel may be placed under the upper arm to place the shoulder in neutral.
execution.setup_instructions: No equipment required for bodyweight version. A light dumbbell (0.5–2 kg) or band may be added for progressive resistance.
steps: Step 1: Lie on the non-working side with the working elbow bent to 90 degrees, upper arm against the torso.
Step 2: Starting position has the forearm resting across the abdomen.
Step 3: Rotate the forearm upward toward the ceiling, keeping the elbow pinned to the side.
Step 4: Stop when the forearm is parallel to the floor or slightly above.
Step 5: Slowly return to the starting position with full control.
execution.breathing_instructions: Exhale on the external rotation (forearm rising). Inhale on return.
common_mistakes: Lifting the elbow away from the side — the elbow must stay anchored to the torso
Using too much weight, which causes the shoulder to shrug and involve the deltoid
Moving too fast — this requires slow, deliberate movement to target the small cuff muscles
safety_considerations: If sharp pain occurs in the shoulder, stop immediately
Start with no weight and add resistance only when pain-free movement is established
Consult a clinician before starting if a rotator cuff tear has been diagnosed
execution.range_of_motion_guidance: Rotate until the forearm is parallel to the floor, or to the pain-free range. Do not force end-range if discomfort occurs.
coaching_cues: Keep the elbow pinned to your side throughout
Move slowly — this is about quality, not load
Think about rotating your palm to face the ceiling

name: Side-Lying Leg Raise — Toe Down
description: A side-lying hip abduction exercise performed with the foot internally rotated (toe pointing toward the floor). This internal rotation position preferentially activates the gluteus medius over the tensor fasciae latae (TFL), which is important in rehabilitation programs targeting IT band syndrome or TFL dominance. The exercise isolates the posterior gluteus medius fibers and is a key component of hip abduction rehabilitation.

execution.starting_position: Lie on your side with your body in a straight line, bottom arm extended and head resting on it. Internally rotate the top leg so the toes point toward the floor (not the ceiling).
execution.setup_instructions: No equipment needed. A resistance band above the knees can be added for greater challenge. Ensure the spine stays neutral throughout.
steps: Step 1: Lie on your side with hips stacked and the top foot internally rotated so toes face the floor.
Step 2: Keeping the leg straight and internally rotated, raise the top leg upward to approximately 30-45 degrees.
Step 3: Hold the top position briefly, maintaining the internal rotation throughout.
Step 4: Lower the leg slowly back to the starting position. Complete all reps before switching sides.
execution.breathing_instructions: Exhale as you raise the leg. Inhale as you lower.
common_mistakes: Allowing the foot to rotate outward (externally) during the raise — this recruits TFL instead of posterior glute med
Rotating the entire pelvis backward as the leg rises — the hip must remain stacked
Lifting too high, which causes lumbar spine compensation
safety_considerations: If you have an IT band syndrome diagnosis, ensure this is prescribed by a physiotherapist as part of a structured program
Avoid if internal hip rotation is acutely painful
execution.range_of_motion_guidance: Lift to approximately 30-45 degrees. The foot must stay internally rotated throughout the entire range.
coaching_cues: Imagine the bottom of the foot is facing the ceiling — it should be facing the floor throughout the movement
The small range of motion is correct — do not force height
Feel the outer hip (gluteus medius) contracting, not the front of the hip (TFL)

name: Side Plank
description: The side plank is a unilateral isometric core exercise that challenges the obliques and lateral core musculature to resist lateral flexion of the spine. It is an essential anti-lateral flexion movement for complete core stability and is particularly effective at training the quadratus lumborum and lateral hip stabilizers.

execution.starting_position: Lie on one side with the forearm on the floor directly below the shoulder. Stack the feet on top of each other. Push up so the body forms a straight line from head to feet.
execution.setup_instructions: No equipment needed. Use a mat for elbow comfort. Perform on each side for equal time.
steps: Push the hips upward off the floor, maintaining the straight line.
Top arm can rest on the hip or be extended toward the ceiling.
Hold for the prescribed duration, then switch sides.
execution.breathing_instructions: Breathe normally throughout the hold.
common_mistakes: Allowing the hips to sag toward the floor
Rotating the torso forward or backward
Foot placement — stack feet or stagger for balance
execution.range_of_motion_guidance: Isometric hold. Maintain a rigid lateral plank position.
execution.tempo_recommendations: Hold 20–45 seconds per side, progressing over time
coaching_cues: Push your hips toward the ceiling to maintain the line
Breathe freely — do not hold your breath during the hold

name: Side Plank with Leg Raise
description: A side plank with the top leg raised and held elevated throughout or repeatedly raised and lowered. This adds hip abductor challenge to the core stabilization demands of the standard side plank. The combination builds lateral chain strength from foot to shoulder.

execution.starting_position: Set up for Side Plank with Leg Raise in proper position.
execution.setup_instructions: Prepare body and equipment for Side Plank with Leg Raise.
steps: Step 1: Set up in side plank on forearm with hips elevated.
Step 2: Keep bottom side rigid and raise top leg to 45 degrees.
Step 3: Either hold leg raised or perform slow repetitions up and down.
Step 4: Complete reps then switch sides.
execution.breathing_instructions: Breathe steadily; never hold breath during static holds.
common_mistakes: Dropping hips during leg raise
Using momentum to swing leg
safety_considerations: Build prerequisite strength before attempting advanced variations.
Stop if joint pain occurs.
execution.range_of_motion_guidance: Full range of motion with control at all times.
coaching_cues: Hip stays elevated throughout
Controlled leg movement

name: Side Plank Top Leg Pulse
description: A side plank variation where the top leg performs small pulsing raises rather than full range leg raises. The pulsing motion creates continuous tension in the hip abductors while maintaining lateral core stability. This is excellent for glute medius targeting within a core context.

execution.starting_position: Set up for Side Plank Top Leg Pulse in proper position.
execution.setup_instructions: Prepare body and equipment for Side Plank Top Leg Pulse.
steps: Step 1: Set up side plank on forearm with hips elevated.
Step 2: Raise top leg to hip height.
Step 3: Perform small pulsing raises of 2-4 inches from hip height.
Step 4: Maintain side plank position throughout all pulses.
execution.breathing_instructions: Breathe steadily; never hold breath during static holds.
common_mistakes: Dropping hips during pulses
Large range of motion defeats the purpose
safety_considerations: Build prerequisite strength before attempting advanced variations.
Stop if joint pain occurs.
execution.range_of_motion_guidance: Full range of motion with control at all times.
coaching_cues: Small continuous pulses
Feel the constant abductor tension

name: Single-Arm Cable Biceps Curl — Supine on Bench
description: A biceps curl performed lying supine (face up) on a flat bench with the head near a low cable pulley, gripping a D-handle. This lying position changes the resistance angle — the cable pulls from behind and below the shoulder at the start of the rep, providing a unique lengthened-position loading on the biceps that is not achievable in a standing cable curl. The supine position also eliminates body swing, enforcing strict biceps isolation. Used as an isolation finisher or as a variation to target the stretched portion of the strength curve.

execution.starting_position: Position a flat bench with the head end nearest to a low cable pulley. Lie supine with the head near the pulley, holding a D-handle in one hand with the arm extended back toward the pulley.
execution.setup_instructions: The arm should be extended with the cable pulling toward the pulley (behind and below the head). The upper arm rests along the side of the torso.
steps: Step 1: Lie supine with the working arm extended toward the pulley, palm facing upward.
Step 2: Curl the weight by bending the elbow, bringing the handle toward the shoulder.
Step 3: Hold the fully curled position for 1-2 seconds, squeezing the bicep.
Step 4: Slowly lower the arm back to full extension. Repeat, then switch arms.
execution.breathing_instructions: Exhale during the curl. Inhale during the return to extension.
common_mistakes: Lifting the upper arm from the torso during the curl — the upper arm should stay fixed
Swinging the torso to assist the curl — this cannot occur in the supine position but partial torso rotation should be avoided
Rushing the return — the eccentric with the cable pulling behind you is the unique stimulus
safety_considerations: Ensure the bench is stable and will not slide toward the pulley under load
If the shoulder is uncomfortable in the extended arm position, place the bench slightly further from the pulley
execution.range_of_motion_guidance: Full elbow extension at the bottom (arm extended toward pulley) to full elbow flexion at the top.
execution.tempo_recommendations: 2s curl, 2s hold, 3s slow eccentric to full extension.
coaching_cues: Feel the stretch at the very bottom of the rep — the supine position with cable pulling behind creates a unique loaded stretch
Keep the upper arm fixed on the torso — only the forearm moves
Slow the return — that is where this variation is most different from a standing curl

name: Single-Arm Cable Crossover Punch
description: A single-arm cable movement that mimics a cross-body punching motion, pulling the cable from a high or mid pulley position across the body while rotating the torso. This integrates horizontal adduction of the pectoralis major with rotational core engagement, training the chest in a functional, sport-relevant movement plane.

execution.starting_position: Stand side-on to a cable machine set at shoulder height. Grip the handle with the far hand, arm extended to the side toward the cable stack. Stand with a slight staggered stance.
execution.setup_instructions: Set the cable pulley to shoulder or mid-chest height. Attach a single handle. Stand far enough from the stack that the cable is taut at the start position.
steps: Step 1: Grip the handle with the hand farthest from the machine, arm extended toward the stack. Slight bend in the elbow.
Step 2: Drive the handle across your body in a punching motion — extend the arm forward and across the midline while rotating the torso toward the cable.
Step 3: At full extension, the arm crosses the centerline of the body and the torso has rotated to face the direction of the punch.
Step 4: Return with control to the starting position, resisting the cable's pull back. Repeat all reps on one side, then switch.
execution.breathing_instructions: Exhale forcefully on the punch, inhale on the return.
common_mistakes: Using momentum from the shoulders instead of driving through the chest
Not rotating the torso — the punch should involve the whole core
Standing too close, losing cable tension at the end position
safety_considerations: Keep the shoulder packed — avoid hyperextending the joint at the end of the punch
Control the return — do not let the cable yank the arm back
execution.range_of_motion_guidance: Full extension across the body midline. Torso rotates 30–45 degrees through the movement.
coaching_cues: Punch from the chest — the hand follows, not leads
Rotate the torso at the end — your front shoulder should face forward at full extension

name: Single-Arm Cable Face Pull
description: The single-arm cable face pull uses one hand on the rope or handle to perform the face pull movement unilaterally. The single-arm version allows independent training of each rear delt and external rotator, is more effective at correcting left-right imbalances than bilateral face pulls, and allows slightly greater range of motion as the torso can rotate slightly without losing the training stimulus.

execution.starting_position: Set a cable pulley to upper face level. Attach a single handle. Grasp with one hand, arm extended toward the pulley. Stand facing the cable.
execution.setup_instructions: Set the pulley at approximately eye level. Light load only — rear delts and external rotators are small muscles.
steps: Step 1: Begin with arm extended toward the cable.
Step 2: Pull the handle toward the same-side ear/face, driving the elbow wide.
Step 3: At peak, externally rotate the shoulder — thumb points behind and down.
Step 4: Hold 1 second.
Step 5: Return under control. Complete all reps on one side before switching.
execution.breathing_instructions: Exhale on the pull. Inhale returning.
common_mistakes: Pulling to the chest instead of the face — keep the hand at face level
Omitting external rotation — the ER at peak is essential for shoulder health benefit
safety_considerations: Light loads only — high reps with light weight are more appropriate than heavy low reps
Suitable as a warm-up or shoulder health accessory
execution.range_of_motion_guidance: Full arm extension to hand at face level with full external rotation.
coaching_cues: Pull to the ear, not the chin
Thumb points behind you at the top
Elbow goes wide and high

name: Single-Arm Cable Front Raise (Standing)
description: The single-arm cable front raise performed standing uses a low cable to raise one arm forward to shoulder height, providing constant tension through the anterior deltoid from the bottom of the range (where dumbbell raises are unloaded) through the top. The standing unilateral version also trains core anti-rotation as the cable pulls asymmetrically, adding a secondary stability demand.

execution.starting_position: Stand facing away from a low cable pulley. Hold the handle with one hand behind the hip. Stand upright.
execution.setup_instructions: Set the cable to the lowest position. Use a D-handle attachment. Keep the non-working hand at the side or on the hip.
steps: Step 1: Begin with arm behind the hip, cable running beside the body.
Step 2: Raise the working arm forward and upward to shoulder height.
Step 3: Hold 1 second at peak.
Step 4: Lower under control back to the starting position.
Step 5: Complete all reps before switching arms.
execution.breathing_instructions: Exhale raising. Inhale lowering.
common_mistakes: Torso rotating toward the working arm — maintain square hips and shoulders
Raising above shoulder height — stop at horizontal for anterior delt emphasis
safety_considerations: Light loads — anterior deltoid isolation is a finishing exercise
Avoid torso lean or rotation to assist the raise
execution.range_of_motion_guidance: Arm behind hip to shoulder height.
coaching_cues: Lead with the thumb slightly up
No torso swing or lean
Feel the front of the shoulder contract at the peak

name: Single-Arm Cable High Row — Dual Crossover
description: A single-arm back row performed from a high-pulley dual cable crossover station. With one cable set to the highest position, the exerciser rows downward and inward in a diagonal arc, pulling the handle from an elevated position (above and to the side) toward the hip. This diagonal downward pull engages the latissimus dorsi through its full functional range — from shoulder flexion to extension — with an unusually long range of motion compared to standard lat pulldowns or rows. The unilateral setup allows each side to be trained independently, correcting asymmetries, while the high cable angle specifically targets the lower fibers of the latissimus dorsi.

execution.starting_position: Set one side of a dual cable crossover to the highest pulley position. Stand perpendicular to or slightly angled away from the working cable, with the working arm extended upward and to the side toward the pulley. The arm is in a fully stretched overhead position.
execution.setup_instructions: Use a D-handle or rope attachment. The body position is key: face away at a slight angle so the arm reaches up and across toward the pulley in the starting stretched position.
steps: Step 1: Stand with the working arm extended high toward the pulley, feeling the lat stretch.
Step 2: Row downward and inward, driving the elbow toward the hip on the same side.
Step 3: At the end position, the elbow is at or below hip height and the lat is fully contracted.
Step 4: Slowly return the arm to the overhead stretched position. Complete all reps, then switch sides.
execution.breathing_instructions: Exhale as you row downward. Inhale as you return to the stretched position.
common_mistakes: Using the biceps to pull rather than initiating the movement with the lat
Not fully extending the arm at the top — the stretch position is a key part of the exercise
Leaning the torso excessively to gain range — keep the torso relatively stable
safety_considerations: The overhead starting position should feel like a lat stretch, not a shoulder impingement — adjust body angle if the shoulder is uncomfortable
Avoid excessive weight that causes the torso to collapse toward the cable on the return
execution.range_of_motion_guidance: From full overhead arm extension (lat in a stretched position) to elbow at or below hip (lat fully contracted).
execution.tempo_recommendations: 1s initiation, 2s controlled pull, 2s hold at bottom, 4s slow return to full stretch.
coaching_cues: Feel the lat stretch at the top — this is the unique advantage of the high cable angle
Drive the elbow toward the hip, not the hand
Think of pulling your elbow into your back pocket at the bottom of the rep

name: Single-Arm Cable High Row with Rotation
description: The single-arm cable high row with rotation pulls from a high cable pulley with one hand while adding a torso rotation at peak contraction toward the working side. The rotation engages the obliques and thoracic rotators alongside the standard lat and upper back muscles, training the pulling pattern in a more athletically functional context that mirrors rotational sport movements.

execution.starting_position: Stand side-on to a high cable pulley. Grasp the handle with the near hand, arm extended upward toward the pulley. Feet staggered or parallel at shoulder width.
execution.setup_instructions: Set the cable to the highest available position. Stand far enough from the stack to achieve full arm extension at the starting position.
steps: Step 1: Begin with arm extended toward the high pulley.
Step 2: Pull the cable handle toward the hip or lower ribcage, driving the elbow down.
Step 3: At peak contraction, rotate the torso toward the working side.
Step 4: Hold 1 second at peak rotation.
Step 5: Reverse the motion — unwind the torso then return the arm — to full extension.
execution.breathing_instructions: Exhale on the pull and rotation. Inhale on the return.
common_mistakes: Rotating before the pull completes — the row and rotation should sequence, not co-occur
Using momentum from the rotation to assist the pull — the lat should drive the pull
safety_considerations: Thoracic rotation under load can stress spinal structures — keep loads moderate
Avoid if experiencing thoracic or lumbar spine pain
execution.range_of_motion_guidance: Full arm extension to full torso rotation at peak contraction.
coaching_cues: Pull first, then rotate
Drive the elbow to the hip before the torso turns
Control the reverse sequence on the way back

name: Single-Arm Cable Kickback with Pause
description: A cable kickback variation with a deliberate pause at peak extension to maximize triceps contraction. The cable provides constant tension unlike dumbbells that lose it at the top. The pause increases time under tension for superior muscle growth.

execution.starting_position: Set up for Single-Arm Cable Kickback with Pause in the appropriate position.
execution.setup_instructions: Prepare equipment and body position for Single-Arm Cable Kickback with Pause.
steps: Step 1: Attach single handle to low cable. Hinge forward with back flat.
Step 2: Keep upper arm parallel to floor and extend elbow behind you.
Step 3: Hold the peak contracted position for 2 full seconds.
Step 4: Return arm slowly to bent position and repeat.
execution.breathing_instructions: Exhale during the exertion phase, inhale during the return.
common_mistakes: Swinging the arm
Dropping upper arm during the pause
safety_considerations: Keep joints aligned throughout the movement.
Use controlled weight appropriate for skill level.
execution.range_of_motion_guidance: Move through full range of motion without compromising joint integrity.
coaching_cues: Squeeze hard and count the pause
Upper arm stays parallel throughout

name: Single-Arm Cable Lateral Raise
description: The single-arm cable lateral raise is a unilateral shoulder isolation exercise using a low-pulley cable. With the cable running across the body from the opposite side, constant tension is maintained on the lateral deltoid throughout the entire arc — including at the top where dumbbell lateral raises lose tension. This makes it mechanically superior for lateral deltoid isolation compared to free-weight raises.

execution.starting_position: Stand beside a low-pulley cable machine, holding the handle in the hand furthest from the machine (the cable crosses in front of the body). The working arm begins at the side, slightly in front of the hip.
execution.setup_instructions: Set the cable pulley to the lowest position and attach a single-handle D-ring. Stand perpendicular to the cable stack. Hold the handle in the hand on the opposite side from the machine.
steps: Step 1: Stand beside the cable machine, holding the handle in the far hand. Cable crosses in front of the body.
Step 2: Begin with the arm at the side, slightly in front of the hip. Slight elbow bend.
Step 3: Exhale and raise the arm upward and outward in a lateral arc to shoulder height.
Step 4: Pause briefly at the top, then inhale and lower the arm back to the start. Complete all reps, then switch sides.
execution.breathing_instructions: Exhale as you raise; inhale as you lower.
common_mistakes: Shrugging the traps as the arm rises — consciously depress the shoulder during the raise
Raising too far above shoulder height into impingement range
safety_considerations: Stop the raise at or just above shoulder height unless mobility allows pain-free movement beyond
execution.range_of_motion_guidance: Raise from hip/side to shoulder height; return controlled.
coaching_cues: Lead with the elbow, not the hand — keep the elbow slightly higher than the wrist
Think about pouring water from a jug at the top — slight internal rotation keeps the shoulder safe

name: Single-Arm Cable Row
description: The single-arm cable row is a unilateral horizontal pulling exercise that allows greater range of motion and scapular movement than bilateral rowing variations. Training each side independently corrects strength imbalances and allows the torso to rotate slightly, increasing latissimus dorsi and rhomboid engagement through a fuller range.

execution.starting_position: Stand or sit facing a low-pulley cable machine. Grasp a single handle with one hand. Take a step back (or sit on a bench) and extend the working arm fully forward, feeling the lat on stretch.
execution.setup_instructions: Attach a single-grip D-handle to the low pulley. Stand facing the cable or sit on a bench positioned in front of the cable stack. Set a weight appropriate for single-arm pulling.
steps: Step 1: Begin with the arm fully extended toward the cable, allowing the shoulder to protract and the lat to stretch.
Step 2: Drive the elbow backward, retracting the scapula, and row the handle toward the lower ribcage.
Step 3: At the end of the row, squeeze the lat and rhomboids hard with the elbow behind the torso.
Step 4: Allow slight torso rotation toward the working side to increase the stretch — control this rotation; do not let it become momentum.
Step 5: Slowly extend the arm back to the starting position, fully protracting the scapula.
execution.breathing_instructions: Exhale as you row the handle in. Inhale as you return to the starting position.
common_mistakes: Rotating the torso excessively and using it to swing the weight
Not allowing full scapular protraction at the start, limiting range of motion
Pulling with the biceps by keeping the elbow close to the body from the start rather than driving it back
safety_considerations: Keep the core braced to avoid excessive spinal rotation under load
Do not jerk the weight — control both the concentric and eccentric phases
execution.range_of_motion_guidance: Full extension of the arm at the start to full retraction of the scapula at the end. Allow the shoulder to move freely.
coaching_cues: Think 'elbow to back pocket'
Let your shoulder blade glide forward at the start to get the full stretch
Row to your hip, not your chest

name: Single-Arm Cable Row with Overhead Reach
description: The single-arm cable row with overhead reach adds a full overhead arm extension at the beginning of each rep, allowing the lat to be stretched into an overhead position before initiating the pull. This overhead starting position places the latissimus dorsi and teres major under greater stretch compared to a standard forward reach, potentially increasing their hypertrophy stimulus through lengthened-position loading.

execution.starting_position: Sit or stand at a low cable pulley. Grip the handle with one hand and reach the arm fully overhead, rotating the torso slightly toward the cable.
execution.setup_instructions: Use a single handle attachment. Set the pulley at a low position. Moderate weight — the overhead reach reduces the load you can use.
steps: Step 1: Begin with arm extended overhead, feeling a full lat stretch.
Step 2: Pull the cable down and back toward the hip, driving the elbow down and in.
Step 3: At peak, hold 1 second with elbow behind the torso.
Step 4: Return by allowing the arm to extend overhead again.
Step 5: Complete all reps on one side before switching.
execution.breathing_instructions: Inhale at the overhead stretch position. Exhale on the pull.
common_mistakes: Not actually reaching overhead — a half-reach limits the lat stretch benefit
Using too heavy a load — the overhead range demands reduced weight
safety_considerations: Avoid if shoulder mobility is limited — the overhead reach must be pain-free
Build shoulder flexibility before loading this variation
execution.range_of_motion_guidance: Arm fully overhead in stretch to elbow behind torso at peak.
coaching_cues: Reach all the way overhead — feel the lat pull
Pull the elbow into your pocket
Pause and breathe at the top stretch

name: Single-Arm Cable Row with Rotation
description: The single-arm cable row with rotation adds a deliberate thoracic rotation to the standard seated cable row. As the elbow pulls back, the working side of the torso rotates to follow, increasing the range of lat contraction and recruiting the obliques and spinal rotators. This variation more closely mimics sporting actions such as throwing and rowing and develops rotational power alongside back strength.

execution.starting_position: Attach a single handle to a low cable pulley. Sit sideways or face the cable and grip the handle with one hand. The working arm should be fully extended toward the cable.
execution.setup_instructions: The cable can be performed seated on a bench or standing. The seated variation provides better base stability for learning the movement.
