steps: Step 1: Begin with the arm fully extended and the torso rotated slightly toward the cable.
Step 2: Initiate the row by retracting the scapula and pulling the elbow back.
Step 3: As the elbow passes the torso, allow the working-side shoulder to rotate back naturally.
Step 4: At the end, the elbow is behind the torso and the working shoulder is rotated back fully.
Step 5: Reverse the motion under control, allowing the torso to rotate forward as the arm extends.
execution.breathing_instructions: Exhale as you row and rotate, inhale as you return.
common_mistakes: Rotating the hips instead of the thoracic spine
Using momentum from the rotation rather than muscle contraction
Not allowing enough rotation — treating it as a strict row
safety_considerations: Thoracic rotation is the target — lumbar rotation should be minimal
If lumbar discomfort is felt, reduce the rotation range
execution.range_of_motion_guidance: Full arm extension with torso rotated forward at the start, arm fully rowed with torso rotated back at the finish.
coaching_cues: Let your chest follow your elbow
Rotate through the upper back, not the lower
Full reach at the start, full retraction at the end

name: Single-Arm Cable Tricep Extension
description: A unilateral tricep isolation exercise performed with a single handle attachment at a high cable pulley. Training each arm independently ensures equal development, identifies strength imbalances, and provides a unique range of motion and angle of resistance compared to bilateral cable extensions.

execution.starting_position: Stand facing a high cable pulley, holding a single handle in one hand. Upper arm close to the body.
execution.setup_instructions: Attach a single handle to the high cable pulley. Grasp it with one hand, palm facing down or inward.
steps: Step 1: Keep the upper arm stationary at your side.
Step 2: Push the handle downward by extending the elbow.
Step 3: Fully extend the elbow at the bottom.
Step 4: Return to the starting position by allowing the elbow to flex.
execution.breathing_instructions: Exhale on the extension. Inhale on the return.
common_mistakes: Allowing the upper arm to drift forward or backward during the movement
Using the shoulder to assist
safety_considerations: Keep the upper arm fixed throughout — only the forearm and elbow should move
execution.range_of_motion_guidance: Full extension at the bottom. Full flexion at the top.
coaching_cues: Upper arm stays still
Full extension every rep

name: Single-Arm Cross-Body Cable Extension
description: A cable isolation exercise where one arm reaches across the body to a cable attachment at shoulder height. The cross-body angle creates a unique line of pull that emphasizes the lateral head of the triceps with constant cable tension throughout the movement.

execution.starting_position: Set up for Single-Arm Cross-Body Cable Extension in the appropriate position.
execution.setup_instructions: Prepare equipment and body position for Single-Arm Cross-Body Cable Extension.
steps: Step 1: Stand sideways to cable, reach across body to grasp handle at shoulder height.
Step 2: Keep upper arm fixed and extend elbow pressing hand across body.
Step 3: Extend to lockout feeling the lateral head contract.
Step 4: Return slowly with control, stretching across the body.
execution.breathing_instructions: Exhale during the exertion phase, inhale during the return.
common_mistakes: Rotating torso to assist
Moving upper arm
safety_considerations: Keep joints aligned throughout the movement.
Use controlled weight appropriate for skill level.
execution.range_of_motion_guidance: Move through full range of motion without compromising joint integrity.
coaching_cues: Keep upper arm braced
Feel the cross-body stretch at the bottom

name: Single-Arm Dumbbell Press
description: The single-arm dumbbell press is a unilateral pressing exercise performed lying on a bench with one dumbbell at a time. Because only one side is loaded, the core and obliques must work hard to prevent the torso from rotating, adding a significant anti-rotation stability demand on top of the standard pectoralis and triceps pressing stimulus.

execution.starting_position: Lie on a flat bench holding a single dumbbell in one hand at chest level. The opposite arm can rest on the torso or be held out for balance. Feet are flat on the floor.
execution.setup_instructions: Select a dumbbell lighter than you would use for a bilateral press. Lie on a flat bench and position the dumbbell at chest level before beginning.
steps: Step 1: Lie on a flat bench holding a dumbbell in one hand, elbow bent and arm at chest level.
Step 2: Brace the core firmly to resist the uneven loading.
Step 3: Exhale and press the dumbbell straight up until the arm is extended above the chest.
Step 4: Inhale and lower the dumbbell slowly back to the chest level. Complete all reps, then switch arms.
execution.breathing_instructions: Exhale on the press; inhale on the descent.
common_mistakes: Allowing the torso to rotate toward the working side — resist this with core tension
Using a weight so heavy that the shoulder rolls off the bench
safety_considerations: Keep both shoulder blades in contact with the bench throughout the movement
Start with a conservative weight to gauge the anti-rotation demand
execution.range_of_motion_guidance: Lower to chest level for a full stretch, press to full arm extension.
coaching_cues: Resist the urge to rotate — keep both shoulders pinned to the bench
Brace as if you are about to take a punch to the torso

name: Single-Arm Dumbbell Push-Press
description: The single-arm dumbbell push-press uses a dip-and-drive from the legs to initiate upward momentum, then completes the press overhead with one arm. The unilateral variation requires significant core lateral stabilization to prevent the loaded side from dropping the torso, training anti-lateral-flexion core strength alongside the shoulder and triceps pressing musculature. It is an effective power development tool for overhead athletes.

execution.starting_position: Stand with one dumbbell at shoulder height on the working side. Free hand on the hip or at the side. Feet shoulder-width apart.
execution.setup_instructions: Set up in a neutral stance with the dumbbell resting on the shoulder. Use a weight heavier than you would use for a strict press.
steps: Step 1: Dip the knees 10-15 cm, maintaining an upright torso.
Step 2: Drive upward explosively through the legs.
Step 3: Use the upward momentum to initiate the dumbbell's upward path.
Step 4: Complete the press by extending the arm fully overhead.
Step 5: Lower the dumbbell under control back to the shoulder. Repeat, then switch sides.
execution.breathing_instructions: Inhale and brace before the dip. Exhale explosively through the drive and press.
common_mistakes: Lateral torso lean toward the working side — maintain upright position
Too deep a dip — 10-15 cm is sufficient; excessive depth loses power transfer
safety_considerations: Learn the bilateral push-press first before the unilateral version
High demand on the core — build anti-lateral flexion strength before heavy loading
execution.range_of_motion_guidance: Shoulder height to full overhead lockout.
coaching_cues: Dip straight down — no forward lean
Drive with the legs, finish with the arm
Stay tall — no lean to the side

name: Single-Arm Dumbbell Row with Isometric Hold
description: The isometric-hold dumbbell row adds a 3-5 second contraction pause at the top of each repetition, sustaining peak lat and rhomboid tension through an extended hold. This technique increases time under tension without adding load, making it valuable for building the mind-muscle connection and hypertrophy in the upper back without excessive joint stress.

execution.starting_position: One knee and hand on a bench, other foot on the floor. Dumbbell hanging in working hand, arm extended.
execution.setup_instructions: Use a moderate weight — the isometric hold will make even lighter loads challenging. Focus on quality of contraction, not load.
steps: Step 1: Row the dumbbell to the hip or lower ribcage.
Step 2: At the top position, hold for 3-5 seconds while actively squeezing the lat and rhomboid.
Step 3: Maintain the hold — do not allow the elbow to drop.
Step 4: Lower slowly (3 seconds) under full control.
Step 5: Repeat for all reps on one side before switching.
execution.breathing_instructions: Exhale on the pull. Hold breath lightly during the isometric. Exhale during the lower.
common_mistakes: Releasing tension during the hold — actively squeeze rather than passively hold
Using too heavy a weight — the hold becomes impossible and form breaks
safety_considerations: Moderate loads only — the isometric reduces reliance on heavy weight
Maintain neutral spine throughout
execution.range_of_motion_guidance: Full extension to full contraction, with isometric hold at peak.
coaching_cues: Squeeze as hard as possible during the hold
Think about pulling your elbow to the sky and keeping it there
Own the negative — 3 full seconds

name: Single-Arm Dumbbell Tate Press
description: A unilateral variation of the Tate press targeting the triceps with a single dumbbell. The lifter lies on a bench and lowers one dumbbell in a unique arc to the chest, emphasizing the medial and lateral tricep heads. Greater range is achievable unilaterally.

execution.starting_position: Set up for Single-Arm Dumbbell Tate Press in the appropriate position.
execution.setup_instructions: Prepare equipment and body position for Single-Arm Dumbbell Tate Press.
steps: Step 1: Lie on bench holding one dumbbell with elbow flared to side.
Step 2: Lower dumbbell in arc toward same-side chest keeping elbow wide.
Step 3: Touch dumbbell lightly to chest at bottom of movement.
Step 4: Press back up through tricep extension to lockout.
execution.breathing_instructions: Exhale during the exertion phase, inhale during the return.
common_mistakes: Closing elbow toward body
Bouncing off chest
safety_considerations: Keep joints aligned throughout the movement.
Use controlled weight appropriate for skill level.
execution.range_of_motion_guidance: Move through full range of motion without compromising joint integrity.
coaching_cues: Keep elbow flared wide
Light touch at bottom

name: Single-Arm Floor Dumbbell Glute Bridge Press
alternative_names: Floor Press Glute Bridge Single Arm
description: A floor press variation combining a unilateral dumbbell press with a simultaneous glute bridge hold. The supine position on the floor limits range of motion naturally, protecting the shoulder, while the bridge demand fully activates the glutes and core. The unilateral load creates rotational forces that the core must resist, integrating anti-rotation stability with the pressing stimulus.

execution.starting_position: Lie on the floor with knees bent, feet flat. Perform a glute bridge and hold the hips elevated. Hold one dumbbell in the working hand at chest level, elbow bent. The opposite hand rests on the floor or on the hip.
execution.setup_instructions: No equipment needed beyond one dumbbell. Practice the glute bridge hold first before adding the press.
steps: Step 1: Perform a glute bridge: lift hips so body forms a line from knees to shoulders. Maintain this throughout.
Step 2: With the working arm, press the dumbbell from chest to full arm extension.
Step 3: Lower back to chest level under control, keeping the bridge hold the entire time.
Step 4: Repeat all reps on one side, then lower hips, rest, and switch to the other arm.
execution.breathing_instructions: Exhale on the press, inhale on the return. Continue breathing steadily throughout the bridge hold.
common_mistakes: Hips dropping during the press — the bridge must be maintained throughout all reps
Rotating the torso toward the working arm — stay square
Using too heavy a dumbbell that causes the hip to drop for balance
safety_considerations: If unable to maintain both the bridge and the press form simultaneously, reduce the dumbbell weight
Ensure the floor is comfortable — a mat is recommended
execution.range_of_motion_guidance: Floor contact limits elbow travel naturally. Press from that stop to full arm extension.
coaching_cues: Squeeze the glutes to keep the hips up — they should not move during the press
Press from the chest — the body tries to rotate, resist it

name: Single-Arm Front Lever Negative
description: A front lever regression where only one arm grips the bar while the body is lowered from vertical to horizontal. The negative (eccentric only) allows training the front lever position with one arm at a time. This is an intermediate step toward the one-arm front lever.

execution.starting_position: Set up for Single-Arm Front Lever Negative in proper position.
execution.setup_instructions: Prepare body and equipment for Single-Arm Front Lever Negative.
steps: Step 1: Hang from bar with one hand. Place other hand on wrist for support initially.
Step 2: Engage lat of working arm and slowly lower body to horizontal.
Step 3: Maintain rigid body throughout the negative.
Step 4: Lower fully then reset by using both hands to return to start.
execution.breathing_instructions: Breathe steadily; never hold breath during static holds.
common_mistakes: Rotating body during the negative
Trying without full two-arm front lever
safety_considerations: Build prerequisite strength before attempting advanced variations.
Stop if joint pain occurs.
execution.range_of_motion_guidance: Full range of motion with control at all times.
coaching_cues: Full front lever mastery required first
Control the rotation carefully

name: Single-Arm Incline Dumbbell Flye
description: A unilateral isolation movement performed on an incline bench, targeting the clavicular (upper) fibers of the pectoralis major. Using one arm at a time allows for a greater range of motion, enhanced mind-muscle connection, and identification and correction of left-right strength imbalances. The non-working arm can hold the bench edge for stability.

execution.starting_position: Lie on an incline bench set to 30–45 degrees. Hold one dumbbell in the working hand above the upper chest with a slight bend in the elbow. The opposite hand grips the bench edge for stability.
execution.setup_instructions: Set the incline to 30–45 degrees. Select a dumbbell lighter than you would use for a bilateral flye since there is no counterbalancing load on the other side.
steps: Step 1: Begin with the working arm extended above the upper chest, palm facing inward.
Step 2: Lower the dumbbell out to the side in a wide arc, maintaining the fixed elbow bend. Feel the deep stretch across the upper chest.
Step 3: At full stretch, reverse the arc and bring the dumbbell back above the chest.
Step 4: Squeeze the pectoral at the top. Repeat all reps, then switch sides.
execution.breathing_instructions: Inhale as you lower the dumbbell. Exhale as you bring it back up.
common_mistakes: Letting the elbow bend excessively during the movement, turning it into a press
Rotating the torso toward the working arm — keep hips and shoulders flat on the bench
Using too heavy a dumbbell, compromising shoulder stability
safety_considerations: Use a spotter or place the non-working hand on the bench edge for stability
Control the descent carefully — the shoulder is vulnerable at end-range with single-arm load
execution.range_of_motion_guidance: Open to the furthest comfortable stretch — typically when the upper arm is parallel to the bench surface or slightly below.
coaching_cues: Lead with the elbow, not the hand — keep the arc wide
Think of hugging a barrel with one arm — the motion is a sweep, not a curl

name: Single-Arm Inverted Row
description: The single-arm inverted row is a unilateral horizontal pulling exercise performed with one hand on a bar or ring while the other arm rests at the side or is held in front. It demands significantly greater core anti-rotation strength than the bilateral version and allows for independent loading of each side to identify and address left-right strength imbalances.

execution.starting_position: Grip one side of a bar or ring with one hand. Place the non-working hand across the chest or extended forward. Lean back into the starting position with the working arm extended.
execution.setup_instructions: Set bar/ring height to control difficulty. Begin with a steeper body angle; progress to more horizontal as strength improves.
steps: Step 1: Begin in the angled dead-hang position on the working arm.
Step 2: Row the chest toward the hand, driving the working elbow behind the torso.
Step 3: Maintain strict anti-rotation in the torso — hips and shoulders stay square.
Step 4: Lower under control back to the starting position.
Step 5: Complete all reps on one side before switching.
execution.breathing_instructions: Exhale on the pull. Inhale on the descent.
common_mistakes: Rotating the torso toward the working side — maintain square shoulders
Using the free hand to assist — it must remain off the bar
Allowing the hips to drop
safety_considerations: Regress to bilateral inverted rows until sufficient unilateral strength exists
Progress slowly — single-arm pressing and pulling loads the shoulder asymmetrically
execution.range_of_motion_guidance: Full arm extension to hand at or near the working-side chest.
coaching_cues: Hips stay square — no rotation
Imagine a broom handle through your shoulders — keep it level
Full extension on every rep

name: Single-Arm Kettlebell Swing
description: The single-arm kettlebell swing applies the hip hinge mechanics of the two-handed swing to one arm, which introduces an anti-rotation challenge for the core and demands greater grip strength. The free arm can be used as a counterbalance or held at the side. Training one arm at a time addresses left-right imbalances and builds rotational core stability that bilateral swings cannot replicate.

execution.starting_position: Stand with feet hip-width, kettlebell between feet. Hinge at the hips and grasp the handle with one hand.
execution.setup_instructions: Master two-handed swings before moving to single-arm. Use the same weight or slightly less than your two-handed swing.
steps: Step 1: Hike the kettlebell back between the legs as in a standard swing.
Step 2: Drive the hips forward explosively, swinging the kettlebell to shoulder height.
Step 3: Keep the free arm swinging naturally as a counterbalance — it can swing opposite the kettlebell.
Step 4: Control the bell back between the legs and repeat for reps, then switch sides.
execution.breathing_instructions: Exhale sharply at the hip snap, inhale on the downswing.
common_mistakes: Rotating the torso toward the working arm
Letting the shoulder shrug upward at the top
Leaning to one side
safety_considerations: Keep the spine neutral — resist torso rotation
Build up gradually — the unilateral demand is high
execution.range_of_motion_guidance: Hip hinge to full hip extension with bell at shoulder height.
coaching_cues: Hips drive the bell — not the arm
Stay square to the front
Soft knees on the downswing

name: Single-Arm Landmine Chest Press with Rotation
description: A landmine pressing variation that integrates a rotational torso component with the unilateral press. As the arm extends along the barbell's arc, the torso rotates to follow, loading the pectoralis major, anterior deltoid, and serratus anterior while simultaneously training anti-rotation core strength and shoulder stability through a sport-relevant movement pattern.

execution.starting_position: Anchor a barbell in a landmine attachment or corner. Stand facing the barbell, gripping the sleeve end with one hand at chest level. Stand in a slight stagger stance.
execution.setup_instructions: Load light plates on the barbell or use the bar alone. Position the landmine so the bar end is at chest height when held at the start position.
steps: Step 1: Hold the bar end at chest level, working arm's elbow bent, body centered.
Step 2: Begin the press by extending the arm along the barbell's arc (upward and forward). Simultaneously rotate the torso toward the pressing side.
Step 3: At full arm extension, the torso has rotated and the arm is extended fully along the bar's arc.
Step 4: Rotate back and return the bar to the start position under control. Repeat all reps then switch sides.
execution.breathing_instructions: Exhale during the press and rotation. Inhale on the return.
common_mistakes: Not rotating the torso — the rotation is a deliberate part of the exercise, not a mistake to prevent
Leaning excessively forward — the rotation comes from the torso, not a forward lunge
Pressing too fast and losing control of the bar's arc
safety_considerations: Ensure the landmine anchor is stable before pressing
Use moderate weight — the rotational component creates unfamiliar loading on the shoulder
execution.range_of_motion_guidance: Full arm extension along the bar's arc. Torso rotates approximately 30–45 degrees through the movement.
coaching_cues: Let the torso follow the press — don't restrict the rotation
Press through the chest, not just the shoulder — initiate from the pec

name: Single-Arm Lat Pulldown
description: The single-arm lat pulldown trains each side of the back independently, allowing greater range of motion through freedom of lateral trunk flexion and improved scapular movement. It is particularly useful for identifying and correcting left-to-right strength imbalances in the latissimus dorsi and is an effective finishing exercise after bilateral pulldowns.

execution.starting_position: Attach a single D-handle to a lat pulldown machine or high pulley. Sit or kneel facing the machine and grasp the handle with one hand, arm fully extended overhead.
execution.setup_instructions: Attach a D-handle to the high pulley. Sit at the machine or kneel on the floor. Set an appropriate weight — typically less than half the bilateral pulldown weight.
steps: Step 1: Begin with the working arm fully extended, lat on stretch, allowing a slight lateral lean away from the cable.
Step 2: Depress the shoulder blade of the working side and initiate the pull.
Step 3: Drive the elbow down and toward the hip, pulling the handle to the upper chest or shoulder.
Step 4: Squeeze the lat hard at the bottom and pause briefly.
Step 5: Return under control to full extension, letting the lat fully lengthen.
execution.breathing_instructions: Exhale as you pull down. Inhale as you return to start.
common_mistakes: Rotating the torso excessively rather than isolating the lat
Using the hand and grip rather than the elbow to initiate the pull
Rushing through the eccentric phase
safety_considerations: Keep the core engaged to prevent excessive lateral trunk flexion that shifts load to the spine
execution.range_of_motion_guidance: Full overhead extension to handle at chest/shoulder level. Allow natural lateral trunk movement.
coaching_cues: Imagine trying to put the handle in your front pocket
Let your shoulder reach for the ceiling at the top — full stretch
Drive the elbow, not the hand

name: Single-Arm Machine Chest Press
description: The Single-Arm Machine Chest Press performs a unilateral pressing movement using one arm at a time on a plate-loaded or selectorized chest press machine. This variation corrects strength imbalances between sides, creates an anti-rotation core demand, and allows the working arm's pectoral to be trained through its full active range without the limitation of the weaker arm.

execution.starting_position: Sit in the chest press machine. Grip one handle at chest level. The other arm can hold the frame of the machine for stability.
execution.setup_instructions: If the machine has independent arms, use one arm. Set the seat and handle position as normal. The stationary arm grips the machine frame, not the other handle.
steps: Step 1: Press one arm forward to full extension.
Step 2: Return to starting position under control.
Step 3: Complete all reps on one side, then switch.
Step 4: Resist the rotation created by the unilateral load — keep torso square.
execution.breathing_instructions: Exhale on each press. Inhale on return.
common_mistakes: Rotating the torso toward the pressing arm
Using a machine that does not allow independent arm movement
safety_considerations: Only perform on machines with independent arm mechanisms
Use a significantly lighter load than your bilateral press
execution.range_of_motion_guidance: Full extension; full return to deep stretch on working side.
coaching_cues: Fight the rotation — keep both hips and shoulders square
Feel the working pec from stretch to squeeze

name: Single-Arm Push-Up on Medicine Ball
description: A unilateral push-up progression where one hand rests on a medicine ball while the other is on the floor. The elevated, unstable hand surface increases the range of motion and balance demand on the working side, shifting the loading emphasis to the chest of that side. This variation builds toward the single-arm push-up while developing unilateral pressing strength and core anti-rotation stability.

execution.starting_position: Place one hand on the medicine ball and the other hand flat on the floor, slightly wider than shoulder width apart. Body is in a high plank position with feet together or slightly apart.
execution.setup_instructions: Use a firm, non-bouncy medicine ball of appropriate diameter. A 10–14cm diameter ball provides a good elevation. Place on a non-slip surface.
steps: Step 1: Begin in a high plank, one hand on the ball, one on the floor. Brace the core and squeeze the glutes.
Step 2: Lower your chest toward the floor with control, keeping the body rigid and preventing hip rotation.
Step 3: Descend until chest is near the floor, maintaining even weight distribution between both arms.
Step 4: Press back up powerfully to the starting position. Complete all reps on one side before switching.
execution.breathing_instructions: Inhale on the descent. Exhale during the pressing phase.
common_mistakes: Allowing the hips to rotate or pike up during the movement
Placing the ball-hand too far in or out, reducing stability
Rushing reps and losing core bracing
safety_considerations: Ensure the ball is on a non-slip surface
Master standard and archer push-ups before attempting this variation
execution.range_of_motion_guidance: Lower chest as close to the floor as shoulder mobility allows. The ball-side arm gets a greater stretch due to elevation.
coaching_cues: Hips stay square — resist rotation throughout
Think of pulling the floor apart with both hands

name: Single-Arm Overhead Cable Tricep Extension
description: The single-arm overhead cable extension uses one hand on a rope or handle attached to a low cable, extending one arm overhead at a time. Training each arm independently allows the lifter to identify and correct strength imbalances between the triceps. The overhead position maximally stretches the long head, and the unilateral loading may allow a greater range of motion and more focused mind-muscle connection.

execution.starting_position: Attach a single handle to a low cable. Face away from the machine. Grab the handle with one hand and bring it behind the head with the elbow bent overhead.
execution.setup_instructions: The free hand can grip the working upper arm for stability or hold the cable for balance.
steps: Step 1: Begin with the working elbow bent, hand behind the head.
Step 2: Extend the elbow overhead until the arm is fully straight.
Step 3: Hold at full extension for one second.
Step 4: Return slowly to the starting bent position.
execution.breathing_instructions: Exhale on extension, inhale on return.
common_mistakes: Elbow flaring to the side
Torso rotating to assist
Insufficient range of motion at the bottom
safety_considerations: Ensure the elbow points straight up at the starting position
execution.range_of_motion_guidance: Full elbow flexion with stretch at the bottom to full overhead extension.
coaching_cues: Elbow stays pointing up
Feel the stretch at the bottom
Full lockout overhead

name: Single-Arm Overhead Farmer's Walk (On Toes)
description: The single-arm overhead farmer's walk on toes adds a calf-raise walking component to the standard overhead carry, requiring the athlete to walk on the balls of the feet while maintaining a dumbbell or kettlebell locked out overhead in one hand. The toe-walking increases the postural demand, activates the calf complex, and forces additional core lateral stability, as the reduced base of support increases the demand on the hip abductors and ankle stabilizers on each step.

execution.starting_position: Press a dumbbell or kettlebell overhead with one arm to full lockout. Rise onto the toes of both feet. Free arm held at the side.
execution.setup_instructions: Master the standard single-arm overhead carry before the toe-walking variation. Begin with a light load.
steps: Step 1: Press the dumbbell overhead to full lockout. Pack the shoulder — the working shoulder should be depressed, not shrugged.
Step 2: Rise onto the toes of both feet.
Step 3: Walk a designated distance (10-20 metres) while remaining on the toes.
Step 4: Maintain a vertical torso — no lateral lean toward the loaded side.
Step 5: Return to the start, switch hands and repeat.
execution.breathing_instructions: Breathe freely but maintain a braced core throughout.
common_mistakes: Lateral torso lean — the torso must remain vertical
Shrugged working shoulder — pack the shoulder down
safety_considerations: Learn the standard overhead carry first
Very light load on the first attempt — the balance demand is significant
execution.range_of_motion_guidance: Maintained lockout overhead for the duration of the carry.
execution.tempo_recommendations: Continuous walking at a controlled pace
coaching_cues: Shoulder packed — not shrugged
Walk tall on the toes
No lean to the loaded side

name: Single-Arm Overhead Rope Extension
description: A unilateral overhead cable extension using a single rope attachment that allows one arm to train in isolation. This targets the long head of the triceps with cable tension from below. The single-arm approach helps identify and correct strength imbalances.

execution.starting_position: Set up for Single-Arm Overhead Rope Extension in the appropriate position.
execution.setup_instructions: Prepare equipment and body position for Single-Arm Overhead Rope Extension.
steps: Step 1: Attach rope to low pulley. Stand facing away and hold rope overhead with one hand.
Step 2: Keep upper arm vertical and elbow pointing toward ceiling.
Step 3: Extend elbow to press hand up and slightly forward.
Step 4: Lower slowly behind head feeling the long head stretch.
execution.breathing_instructions: Exhale during the exertion phase, inhale during the return.
common_mistakes: Dropping elbow forward
Swinging torso to assist
safety_considerations: Keep joints aligned throughout the movement.
Use controlled weight appropriate for skill level.
execution.range_of_motion_guidance: Move through full range of motion without compromising joint integrity.
coaching_cues: Brace core for stability
Keep upper arm pressed against head

name: Single-Arm Pec-Deck Flye
description: The single-arm pec-deck flye isolates one side of the chest at a time, allowing you to address muscular imbalances and achieve a deep stretch through the pectorals. By removing bilateral compensation, each side must work independently through the full arc of motion.

execution.starting_position: Sit on the pec-deck machine and grasp one handle with a single hand. Adjust the seat so your elbow is at shoulder height and your upper arm is parallel to the floor.
execution.setup_instructions: Set the machine to a weight you can control with one arm. Position the seat height so the shoulder joint is in line with the machine's pivot point.
steps: Step 1: Sit tall with your back firmly against the pad and feet flat on the floor.
Step 2: Grasp the single handle with one hand, arm slightly bent at the elbow.
Step 3: Drive the handle forward and across your body in a sweeping arc, squeezing the chest at peak contraction.
Step 4: Slowly return the handle to the starting position, allowing a controlled stretch across the chest.
Step 5: Complete all reps on one side before switching to the other.
execution.breathing_instructions: Exhale as you bring the handle forward through the arc. Inhale as you return to the stretched starting position.
common_mistakes: Rotating the torso to assist the movement
Using too much weight, reducing range of motion
Locking the elbow fully, stressing the joint
safety_considerations: Keep a slight bend in the elbow throughout
Do not force the arm behind the body's midline at the stretch
Adjust seat height carefully to protect the shoulder joint
execution.range_of_motion_guidance: Move through the full available arc without torso rotation. Allow a comfortable stretch at the start and a firm squeeze at the end.
coaching_cues: Arc the hand like you're hugging a tree
Keep the shoulder blade anchored to the pad
Squeeze and hold for a beat at peak contraction

name: Single-Arm / Single-Leg Elevated Plank
description: The single-arm or single-leg plank removes one point of contact from the standard high plank, dramatically increasing the anti-rotation demand on the obliques and quadratus lumborum as the core resists the tendency to rotate toward the lifted limb. The contralateral variation — lifting one arm and the opposite leg simultaneously — maximises this anti-rotation challenge while also requiring lumbopelvic control in multiple planes. It is a highly effective progression from the standard plank without adding any external load.

execution.starting_position: Begin in a standard high plank position: hands under shoulders, body in a straight line from head to heel, core braced.
execution.setup_instructions: Master the standard high plank for 60+ seconds before attempting single-limb variations.
steps: Step 1: Begin in a high plank. Brace the core maximally.
Step 2: For single-arm variation: slowly lift one hand off the floor, extending the arm forward or placing it on the lower back.
Step 3: For contralateral variation: simultaneously lift one hand and the opposite foot off the floor.
Step 4: Hold the position without allowing the hips to rotate or drop.
Step 5: Return the limb(s) to the floor and repeat on the other side.
execution.breathing_instructions: Breathe shallowly but continuously. Do not hold the breath during the hold.
common_mistakes: Rotating the hips toward the lifted arm — the hips must remain perfectly square
Widening the support foot to compensate rather than maintaining proper challenge
safety_considerations: Regress immediately if hip rotation cannot be controlled
execution.range_of_motion_guidance: Isometric hold for time — typically 20–40 seconds per side.
execution.tempo_recommendations: Hold for 20–40 seconds each side. Slow, controlled transitions.
coaching_cues: Hips square — a glass of water sits on your lower back and cannot spill
Squeeze the working glute and opposite shoulder

name: Single-Arm Push-Up
description: The single-arm push-up is one of the most demanding bodyweight chest exercises, requiring one side of the chest and triceps to push the full body weight while the core resists significant rotational forces. It builds unilateral pressing strength, anti-rotation core stability, and serves as a benchmark of upper-body bodyweight strength.

execution.starting_position: Begin in a push-up position, then move one hand behind the back or to the side. Place the working hand beneath the center of the chest, feet wider than shoulder-width for stability.
execution.setup_instructions: No equipment required. Begin by practicing archer push-ups and wide-stance negative single-arm push-ups before attempting the full movement.
steps: Step 1: Position the working hand directly under the chest with fingers pointing forward or slightly outward.
Step 2: Extend the non-working arm behind the back or hold it at the side.
Step 3: Lower the body toward the floor under control, keeping the torso square to the floor.
Step 4: At the bottom, press explosively through the working hand, extending the arm fully.
Step 5: Maintain a rigid, non-rotating torso throughout the entire rep.
execution.breathing_instructions: Inhale as you lower. Exhale forcefully as you press back up.
common_mistakes: Letting the torso rotate toward the working side
Placing the hand too far to the side, reducing mechanical advantage
Using momentum or hip twist to assist the press
safety_considerations: Build up through progressions: wall, incline, archer push-ups, negatives
Wide feet stance significantly reduces difficulty and is a valid progression step
Stop immediately if you feel wrist pain
execution.range_of_motion_guidance: Full depth to where the chest nearly touches the floor, full lockout at the top. No torso rotation at any point.
coaching_cues: Keep the hip square — don't twist
Press straight down through the floor
Wider feet = easier; use to build up

name: Single-Arm Tricep Pushdown
description: The single-arm tricep pushdown is a unilateral cable isolation exercise for the triceps. Training one arm at a time allows independent focus on each triceps, eliminates strength imbalances, and enables a greater range of motion with wrist rotation at the bottom for a more complete tricep contraction. The lateral and medial heads are most active, with the long head contributing based on the grip angle used.

execution.starting_position: Attach a single handle to the high pulley of a cable machine. Stand facing the machine, holding the handle in one hand with the elbow bent at 90 degrees and tucked at the side.
execution.setup_instructions: Set cable to high pulley. Attach a D-ring single handle. Stand close enough to the machine so there is tension on the cable with the elbow at 90 degrees.
steps: Step 1: Hold the single handle with one hand, elbow tucked at the side at 90 degrees.
Step 2: Keep the upper arm stationary throughout — only the forearm moves.
Step 3: Exhale and push the handle downward by extending the elbow until the arm is fully straight.
Step 4: Hold the lockout, then inhale and return the forearm to 90 degrees.
execution.breathing_instructions: Exhale on extension; inhale on return.
common_mistakes: Letting the elbow drift forward or away from the side during the push
Rotating the torso toward the working arm
safety_considerations: Keep the wrist in a neutral position — do not flex the wrist at the bottom
execution.range_of_motion_guidance: Full extension at the bottom; return to 90-degree elbow bend at the top.
coaching_cues: Elbow stays glued to your side — it is the pivot point
Straighten all the way — do not stop short of full lockout

name: Single-Leg Balance
description: Single-leg balance is a foundational proprioception and balance rehabilitation exercise. Standing on one leg challenges the ankle stabilizers, peroneals, gluteus medius, and the entire proprioceptive chain from foot to hip. It is a standard initial exercise in ankle sprain rehabilitation, ACL reconstruction recovery, and fall prevention programs. Progressions include eyes closed, unstable surfaces, and reaching tasks.

execution.starting_position: Stand tall near a wall or support for safety. Lift one foot slightly off the ground.
execution.setup_instructions: Perform near a wall for safety. Progress to eyes closed or a folded mat for increased difficulty.
steps: Step 1: Stand tall with feet together, holding a fixed object lightly for safety if needed.
Step 2: Lift one foot off the floor, bending the knee to approximately 90 degrees.
Step 3: Balance on the standing leg, keeping the hip level (do not let the lifted-side hip drop).
Step 4: Hold for 20–60 seconds.
Step 5: Switch sides. Progress to eyes closed when 30+ seconds with eyes open is easy.
execution.breathing_instructions: Breathe normally and steadily throughout.
common_mistakes: The stance hip drops toward the lifted side — the gluteus medius must work to prevent this (Trendelenburg sign)
Grabbing the support heavily rather than using it as a safety touch only
Looking at the feet — fix a point at eye level for best balance
safety_considerations: Always stand near a fixed support — balance challenges can result in falls
In acute ankle sprain rehab, begin on a firm surface with eyes open before progressing
execution.range_of_motion_guidance: Upright stance, standing knee very slightly bent, stance hip level.
coaching_cues: Find a fixed point at eye level and stare at it
Keep the hip of the standing leg level — do not let it drop
Grip the floor with your toes for extra stability

name: Single-Leg Balance — Eyes Closed
description: Single-leg balance performed with the eyes closed removes the visual stabilization system from the balance equation, forcing the proprioceptive and vestibular systems to work in isolation. This is a significant progression from eyes-open balance and reveals the degree to which a person relies on vision for balance rather than sensory input from the ankle and hip. Used as a standard assessment and rehabilitation progression in ankle sprain, ACL, and vestibular rehabilitation programs.

execution.starting_position: Stand on one foot on a firm, flat surface. Have a wall or chair within arm's reach for safety. The eyes-open balance must be steady before attempting eyes-closed.
execution.setup_instructions: Perform near a wall or chair for safety. Never begin with eyes closed on an elevated surface or balance pad. Begin on a firm floor.
steps: Step 1: Stand on one leg with the eyes open and establish a steady balance.
Step 2: Once stable, slowly close the eyes.
Step 3: Maintain the single-leg balance for the prescribed duration with eyes closed.
Step 4: Open the eyes, rest, and repeat or switch sides.
execution.breathing_instructions: Breathe normally throughout. Focus and calm breathing aids balance.
common_mistakes: Closing the eyes before establishing stable eyes-open balance — the foundation must be solid first
Tensing the entire body to compensate for the increased challenge — stay relaxed and allow the ankle to micro-adjust
Performing this without safety nearby — a wall or chair must always be available
safety_considerations: ALWAYS perform near a wall or stable surface when doing eyes-closed balance
If dizziness or significant loss of balance occurs, open the eyes immediately
Not appropriate for patients with severe vestibular dysfunction without specialist supervision
execution.range_of_motion_guidance: Static hold. The goal is duration with controlled micro-adjustments through the ankle and hip.
execution.tempo_recommendations: Hold for 10-30 seconds per attempt. Build to 30 seconds before adding further challenge.
coaching_cues: Close the eyes slowly — do not snap them shut which disrupts balance
Let the ankle work — small wobbles are normal and represent the proprioceptive system working
Stay relaxed — gripping with the toes or bracing the whole body reduces the proprioceptive training benefit

name: Single-Leg Balance on Foam Pad
description: Single-leg balance performed on a foam pad or balance pad adds proprioceptive challenge compared to balancing on a firm surface. The unstable foam surface demands continuous micro-adjustments from the ankle, calf, and hip stabilizers to maintain a steady upright position. This is a progression from firm-surface single-leg balance and is used extensively in ankle sprain rehabilitation, ACL post-surgical protocols, and vestibular rehabilitation programs.

execution.starting_position: Stand on a foam balance pad with one foot centered on the pad. Lift the other foot from the pad. Begin with hands available for safety (near a wall or bar).
execution.setup_instructions: Use a commercially available foam balance pad (Airex or equivalent). Ensure the pad is on a non-slip floor. Stand near a wall or chair for safety during initial attempts.
steps: Step 1: Step onto the foam pad with both feet to establish balance, then lift one foot to stand on one leg.
Step 2: Maintain an upright posture with a slight knee bend in the standing leg.
Step 3: Hold the single-leg balance for the prescribed duration, allowing the ankle to make natural micro-adjustments.
Step 4: Lower the foot and rest before repeating or switching sides.
execution.breathing_instructions: Breathe normally throughout. Focus on balance, not breathing pattern.
common_mistakes: Gripping the floor with the toes — the foot and ankle should work naturally, not grip
Holding onto a wall or bar throughout — use it only for safety, not support
Stiffening the knee completely — a small amount of knee flexion improves balance and reduces joint stress
safety_considerations: Stand near a wall or chair during early progressions
For post-surgical rehabilitation, the foam pad balance duration and progression must follow a clinician-prescribed protocol
execution.range_of_motion_guidance: Static hold — the goal is duration with minimal arm movement and no foot touch-down.
execution.tempo_recommendations: Hold for 20-60 seconds per set. Build to 60 seconds before adding further challenge.
coaching_cues: Let the ankle wobble — that wobbling is the proprioceptive training
Soft knee — not locked out, not deeply bent
Find a fixed visual focus point to aid balance — stare at a point on the wall

name: Standing Single-Leg Balance Reach
description: The single-leg balance reach challenges proprioception and neuromuscular control by requiring the exerciser to stand on one leg and reach the free leg in multiple directions. This exercise rehabilitates ankle and knee instability, improves dynamic balance, and strengthens the hip stabilizers under real-world perturbation. It is widely used in return-to-sport protocols following lower limb injuries.

execution.starting_position: Stand on one foot with the support knee slightly bent. The free leg is held off the floor. Arms can be used for minimal balance assistance at first.
execution.setup_instructions: No equipment required. Use a smooth floor or balance mat. Mark reach targets on the floor if available.
steps: Step 1: Stand on the support leg with a slight knee bend, maintaining a stable pelvis.
Step 2: Reach the free leg forward (anterior direction) as far as possible while maintaining control of the support leg.
Step 3: Lightly touch the floor with the reaching foot, then return to the starting single-leg stance.
Step 4: Repeat the reach in the posteromedial and posterolateral directions. Complete all reps then switch legs.
execution.breathing_instructions: Breathe naturally and controlled throughout. Avoid breath-holding during the reach.
common_mistakes: Allowing the support knee to collapse inward on each reach
Dropping the hip of the reaching side (Trendelenburg sign)
Placing full weight on the reaching foot instead of a light touch
safety_considerations: Begin with a supported version near a wall if balance is compromised
Consult a physiotherapist for use following ACL reconstruction or ankle sprain rehabilitation
execution.range_of_motion_guidance: Reach as far as control allows in each direction without compromising the stability of the support leg.
execution.tempo_recommendations: 2 seconds for each reach, 2 seconds to return — controlled throughout
coaching_cues: Keep the support knee tracking over the second toe
Do not let the hip of the reaching leg drop
Maintain a tall spine — do not round forward to reach further

name: Single-Leg Squat on BOSU Ball
description: A single-leg squat performed on the dome of a BOSU ball (dome side up), combining the balance challenge of the unstable dome surface with the unilateral loading of a single-leg squat. This requires simultaneous control of balance, knee alignment, hip stability, and ankle proprioception on an unstable surface. Used in advanced rehabilitation programs and sport-specific balance training for athletes requiring single-leg stability under load.

execution.starting_position: Step onto the center of the BOSU dome with one foot. Lift the other foot off the dome. Establish balance with the eyes open and a wall or bar within reach.
execution.setup_instructions: Master bilateral BOSU squats and single-leg floor squats before combining them. Have a safety surface or partner nearby at all times.
steps: Step 1: Stand on the BOSU dome on one foot. Find balance.
Step 2: Slowly descend into a single-leg squat, allowing the BOSU to respond to the balance shifts.
Step 3: Descend to 60-70 degrees of knee flexion with the knee tracking over the second toe.
Step 4: Drive through the foot to return to standing. Repeat, then switch sides.
execution.breathing_instructions: Inhale as you descend. Exhale as you drive up.
common_mistakes: Knee caving inward (valgus) during the descent — drive the knee out over the second toe
Not controlling the BOSU wobble — the ankle must actively manage the instability
Using too deep a squat before the balance and strength are adequate
safety_considerations: ALWAYS have a safety surface within reach — a wall, rack, or partner
Do not attempt without first mastering bilateral BOSU squats and single-leg floor squats
If knee pain occurs during the descent, reduce depth
execution.range_of_motion_guidance: 60-70 degrees of knee flexion is the target initially. Full depth only when balance and strength allow.
execution.tempo_recommendations: 3s eccentric, 1s pause at bottom, 2s concentric return.
coaching_cues: Push the knee out over the second toe — no knee cave
Let the ankle respond to the dome — do not stiffen the ankle to prevent wobble
Focus on a fixed point ahead for balance

name: Single-Leg Box Jump
description: A plyometric box jump performed taking off and landing on one leg. This requires significantly greater leg power, hip stability, and landing mechanics than bilateral box jumps. Single-leg jumping develops the unilateral power needed for sprinting, change of direction, and sport performance.

execution.starting_position: Set up for Single-Leg Box Jump in proper strongman position.
execution.setup_instructions: Prepare all equipment and body position for Single-Leg Box Jump.
steps: Step 1: Stand on one foot facing a box of appropriate height.
Step 2: Dip slightly on one leg and drive arms up explosively.
Step 3: Jump from one foot and land softly on the same foot on the box.
Step 4: Step down and reset before each rep.
execution.breathing_instructions: Brace core maximally before every lift. Breathe between reps if needed.
common_mistakes: Landing stiff-legged
Box too high for current ability
safety_considerations: Use collars on all loaded barbells.
Ensure clear path for carries.
Have spotters for overhead movements.
execution.range_of_motion_guidance: Full range of motion specific to the implement being used.
coaching_cues: Soft landing with bent knee
Build from two-leg jumps first

name: Standing Single-Leg Cable Kickback
description: A glute isolation exercise performed standing, using a cable ankle attachment to provide resistance as the leg is extended behind the body. The cable offers continuous resistance throughout the kickback motion, making it superior to bodyweight donkey kicks for progressive overload and glute isolation.

execution.starting_position: Attach an ankle strap to the low pulley and around one ankle. Face the machine and hold the frame for support.
execution.setup_instructions: Attach the ankle cuff to the low cable pulley and around one ankle. Stand facing the machine, feet hip-width apart.
steps: Step 1: Maintain a slight forward lean from the hips for stability.
Step 2: Keeping the working leg straight, extend it backward behind your body.
Step 3: Squeeze the glute maximally at full hip extension.
Step 4: Return the leg forward in a controlled manner and repeat.
execution.breathing_instructions: Exhale as the leg extends back. Inhale on the return.
common_mistakes: Swinging the leg rather than using controlled muscle contraction
Rotating the hip or twisting the torso
safety_considerations: Keep the movement controlled and isolated to the hip joint — do not use momentum
execution.range_of_motion_guidance: Full hip extension at the back — squeeze the glute at peak contraction.
coaching_cues: Squeeze the glute at the back
Keep the torso stable — no twisting

name: Single-Leg Cable Pallof Press
description: A pallof press performed while standing on one leg, dramatically increasing the balance and anti-rotation demands. The unstable single-leg stance forces the core to work in concert with the hip stabilizers. This is an excellent integration exercise for athletes.

execution.starting_position: Set up for Single-Leg Cable Pallof Press in proper position.
execution.setup_instructions: Prepare body and equipment for Single-Leg Cable Pallof Press.
steps: Step 1: Stand sideways to cable on one foot. Hold handle at chest.
Step 2: Press handle directly out from chest with arms extending.
Step 3: Hold pressed position for 2 seconds while balancing on one foot.
Step 4: Return hands to chest with control.
execution.breathing_instructions: Breathe steadily; never hold breath during static holds.
common_mistakes: Rotating toward cable during press
Hopping to maintain balance
safety_considerations: Build prerequisite strength before attempting advanced variations.
Stop if joint pain occurs.
execution.range_of_motion_guidance: Full range of motion with control at all times.
coaching_cues: Resist rotation from core, not foot repositioning
Start with light weight

name: Single-Leg Calf Raise
description: The single-leg calf raise places the entire bodyweight on one calf at a time, dramatically increasing the load relative to the bilateral standing calf raise without requiring additional equipment. The greater per-leg load also facilitates a larger range of motion and addresses left-right strength imbalances. It is an effective and equipment-free progression for gastrocnemius and soleus development.

execution.starting_position: Stand with one foot on the edge of a step, the other leg lifted slightly with knee bent. Hold onto a support with one hand for balance.
execution.setup_instructions: Use a stair, step, or raised plate for a heel drop. Hold a wall or rack lightly for balance. Dumbbell can be held in the same-side hand to increase load.
steps: Step 1: Stand on one foot on the edge of a step. Keep the other foot lifted off the floor.
Step 2: Lower the heel as far below the step as possible — full gastrocnemius stretch.
Step 3: Rise to the highest possible plantarflexion, pressing through the big toe.
Step 4: Hold the peak contraction for one second.
Step 5: Lower under control. Complete all reps then switch sides.
execution.breathing_instructions: Exhale as you rise. Inhale as you lower.
common_mistakes: Rising through the outer edge of the foot rather than through the big toe
Not allowing a full heel drop at the bottom
Moving too fast — the calf responds well to slow, full-range reps
safety_considerations: If balance is challenging, hold the support more firmly initially
Start with bodyweight before progressing to a weighted dumbbell
execution.range_of_motion_guidance: Maximum heel drop at the bottom; maximum plantar-flexion at the top.
coaching_cues: Press through the big toe — not the pinky
Drop the heel all the way
Full contraction at the top — don't cut it short

name: Single-Leg Calf Raise on Step — Full Range
description: A single-leg calf raise performed on the edge of a step, allowing the heel to drop below the step surface for full dorsiflexion at the bottom and full plantarflexion at the top. This full range of motion is essential for Achilles tendon rehabilitation and maximal calf strength development. The eccentric (lowering) phase is of particular therapeutic value — the classic Alfredson protocol for Achilles tendinopathy uses this exact movement pattern with progressive loading.

execution.starting_position: Stand on the edge of a step with the ball of one foot on the edge and the heel suspended in the air. Hold a railing or wall for balance. Keep the other foot off the step or cross it behind the ankle.
execution.setup_instructions: Use a stair step, aerobic step, or dedicated calf raise block. Ensure the step is stable and non-slip. For Achilles tendinopathy rehab, perform BOTH straight-leg (knee extended) and bent-leg (knee slightly bent) variations.
steps: Step 1: Begin with the heel at the level of the step, in a neutral position.
Step 2: Lower the heel as far as the ankle allows, achieving maximum dorsiflexion (a deep stretch in the calf).
Step 3: Press up through the ball of the foot to full plantarflexion (highest toe-rise position).
Step 4: Lower slowly and under control back to the deep stretch position. Repeat.
execution.breathing_instructions: Inhale at the bottom (stretch). Exhale as you rise. Inhale as you lower.
common_mistakes: Partial range of motion — not letting the heel drop to full dorsiflexion
Rushing the eccentric (lowering) phase — the eccentric is the most therapeutic component
Using the hand on the wall to assist with the raising phase — touch for balance only
safety_considerations: For active Achilles tendinopathy: perform eccentric-only (rise with both feet, lower with one) until pain allows full concentric reps
If sharp pain occurs at the tendon during the exercise, reduce range or load and consult a physiotherapist
This exercise must not cause pain above a 3/10 on a pain scale in a clinical rehabilitation context
execution.range_of_motion_guidance: Full range: heel drops as far below the step as the ankle allows; rises as high as full plantarflexion permits.
execution.tempo_recommendations: 1s up, 1s top hold, 3-4s eccentric lowering (slow eccentric is the therapeutic element)
coaching_cues: Slow the lowering — count to 4 on the way down
Full range is what makes this exercise therapeutic — do not shortcut the bottom stretch
Touch the wall for balance only — do not push through it

name: Single-Leg Machine Leg Extension
description: The single-leg machine leg extension trains one quadriceps at a time using the leg extension machine, with the non-working leg hanging free. Training unilaterally ensures equal development of both legs and allows greater focus on the mind-muscle connection. It is particularly useful during rehabilitation after knee injuries when the injured limb requires specific, isolated strengthening.

execution.starting_position: Sit on the leg extension machine. Place one leg under the pad with the knee at approximately 90 degrees. The other leg is free and not on the pad.
execution.setup_instructions: Adjust the seat and pad to fit one leg. Set an appropriate weight — use less than the bilateral version.
steps: Step 1: Grip the handles and brace lightly.
Step 2: Extend the working knee to bring the leg to full extension.
Step 3: Squeeze the quadriceps at the top of the movement.
Step 4: Lower with control back to the starting position.
execution.breathing_instructions: Exhale on extension, inhale on the return.
common_mistakes: Using momentum to swing the weight
Not reaching full extension
Excessive compensatory hip movement
safety_considerations: Very high patellar load — use controlled tempo and appropriate weight
If you have patellar issues, limit range to pain-free only
execution.range_of_motion_guidance: Full extension at the top. Return to 90 degrees of flexion at the bottom.
execution.tempo_recommendations: 2-1-3-0 (slow eccentric is especially valuable for quad development)
coaching_cues: Squeeze the quad at the top
Control the return
No hip rocking

name: Single-Leg Hip Thrust
description: The single-leg hip thrust is a unilateral variation of the barbell hip thrust in which only one foot is on the floor while the other leg is extended forward. Each glute works independently against the entire bodyweight or added load, significantly increasing the per-side stimulus and reducing the ability of the dominant side to compensate. It is an effective exercise for addressing glute asymmetries and developing single-leg hip extension strength.

execution.starting_position: Position the upper back against a bench. Place one foot flat on the floor, the other leg raised and extended forward at approximately 45°.
execution.setup_instructions: Same bench setup as the hip thrust. Begin with bodyweight before adding a dumbbell or plate on the working hip.
steps: Step 1: Upper back on the bench edge, one foot flat on the floor, the other leg extended and raised. Drive through the planted foot.
Step 2: Push the hips upward until full hip extension — the body forms a straight line from shoulder to planted knee.
Step 3: Squeeze the working glute forcefully at the top.
Step 4: Lower the hips under control to just above the floor.
Step 5: Complete all reps on one side before switching.
execution.breathing_instructions: Exhale as hips rise. Inhale as hips lower.
common_mistakes: Letting the hip rotate open toward the raised leg — keep hips level throughout
Using the hands to push off the bench — the working leg does the work
Hyperextending the lower back at the top
safety_considerations: Ensure the bench is stable and will not tip
Start with bodyweight only until the balance is established
execution.range_of_motion_guidance: Full hip extension at top (level hips, straight line from shoulder to knee). Hips to floor level at bottom.
coaching_cues: Drive through the planted heel
Keep the hips level — don't let the free hip drop
Squeeze the glute at the top — think of crushing a walnut

name: Single Leg Hop
description: The single-leg hop is a unilateral plyometric exercise in which the athlete hops continuously on one leg for distance or height, requiring single-leg power production, landing mechanics, and ankle-knee-hip coordination. It develops unilateral lower limb power and is frequently used in return-to-sport testing and rehabilitation as a functional assessment of limb symmetry after lower extremity injury.

execution.starting_position: Stand on one leg with the other leg raised. Slight hip hinge, upper body ready to swing.
execution.setup_instructions: Mark a takeoff line. Use a flat, non-slip surface with adequate forward space.
steps: Step 1: Balance on the working leg with the other leg elevated.
Step 2: Drive off the working leg to hop forward, using the arm on the opposite side to assist.
Step 3: Land on the same foot, absorbing through the ankle, knee, and hip.
Step 4: Immediately rebind forward for continuous hopping or pause for measured distance hopping.
Step 5: Perform equal hops on each leg.
execution.breathing_instructions: Breathe continuously with each hop. Do not hold breath.
common_mistakes: Letting the knee collapse inward on landing
Using excessive forward lean that causes landing on a stiff ankle
Skipping the controlled landing to rush to the next hop
safety_considerations: Not appropriate in early return-to-sport phases after lower extremity surgery without clearance.
Ensure single-leg landing stability before progressing to continuous hopping.
execution.range_of_motion_guidance: Maximize hop distance or height. Full foot landing on a balanced single-leg stance.
execution.tempo_recommendations: For power: maximal distance per hop, 3–5 hops per set. For conditioning: continuous hops for 20–30 meters.
coaching_cues: Drive off a stiff ankle — push the floor away
Land with the hip sitting back — not knee over toe collapse
Equal effort and landing on both legs

name: Single-Leg Leg Press
description: The single-leg leg press uses one foot on the platform of a standard leg press machine, training one leg at a time to identify and correct strength imbalances between limbs. By using half the foot surface area, the single-leg press also increases the demand on balance and hip stability compared to the bilateral version. It is an effective tool for rehabilitation and for addressing limb asymmetries in athletes.

execution.starting_position: Sit in the leg press machine. Place one foot in the center of the platform. Keep the other foot resting on the frame or beside the platform but completely unloaded.
execution.setup_instructions: Use significantly less weight than your bilateral leg press. Load the machine appropriately — expect to use 50-60% of your bilateral load.
steps: Step 1: Brace the core and ensure the working foot is centered on the platform.
Step 2: Release the safety and bend the knee to lower the platform toward you.
Step 3: Descend until the thigh reaches approximately 90 degrees of knee flexion.
Step 4: Press through the entire working foot to extend the leg and return to the starting position.
execution.breathing_instructions: Inhale on descent, exhale on the press.
common_mistakes: Using more weight than appropriate and compensating with hip or back
Knee caving inward during the press
Locking out the knee forcefully at the top
safety_considerations: Do not fully lock out the knee — stop just short of full extension
Ensure the safety handles are within reach
execution.range_of_motion_guidance: Knee to approximately 90 degrees without the lower back rounding off the pad.
coaching_cues: Foot centered
Knee tracks over second toe
Drive through the entire foot

name: Single-Leg Romanian Deadlift
description: The single-leg Romanian deadlift is a unilateral hip-hinge exercise performed standing on one leg while the opposite leg extends behind for counterbalance as the torso hinges forward. It provides all the hamstring and gluteus maximus benefits of the bilateral Romanian deadlift while adding a significant demand for hip and core stability through the single-leg stance. It is excellent for identifying and correcting left-right asymmetries.

execution.starting_position: Stand on one foot. Hold a dumbbell or kettlebell in one or both hands (or no weight for a bodyweight version). The free leg extends slightly behind you.
execution.setup_instructions: Begin with bodyweight to establish the balance and hip hinge pattern. Hold a dumbbell in the opposite hand to the working leg for a 'suitcase' loading style that improves stability, or hold weights in both hands.
steps: Step 1: Stand tall on the working leg with a soft knee. Hold the weight(s) in front of the thigh.
Step 2: Hinge at the hip, pushing the hips backward as the torso leans forward and the free leg extends behind — the body forms a T-shape.
Step 3: Lower the weight(s) toward the floor while keeping the spine neutral and the hips level (avoid rotating open toward the ceiling).
Step 4: Hinge until the hamstring and glute are fully stretched or the torso reaches horizontal — whichever comes first without spinal rounding.
Step 5: Drive through the working heel, contracting the glute and hamstring to return the torso to vertical and the rear leg to standing.
execution.breathing_instructions: Inhale before the descent. Hold or breathe gently during the hinge. Exhale at the top.
common_mistakes: Opening the hip of the rear leg toward the ceiling — indicates insufficient hip stability or hip flexor tightness
Bending the working knee too much, turning it into a squat
Using a weight that challenges balance before the hinge pattern is established
safety_considerations: Have a wall or rack nearby when first learning — touch it lightly for balance without leaning
If hamstring cramping occurs, reduce the range of motion or slow the tempo
execution.range_of_motion_guidance: Hinge until hips are level and spine is neutral — typically until the torso approaches horizontal. Quality over depth.
coaching_cues: Hips level — don't let the free hip open up
Reach the rear leg long — it counterbalances the forward torso
Drive through the heel of the working foot to stand

name: Single-Leg Squat (Pistol Squat)
description: The pistol squat is a unilateral squat performed on one leg while the other leg is extended forward parallel to the floor. It demands exceptional strength, ankle dorsiflexion, hip mobility, and balance. The working leg must squat to full depth and return to standing without the support of the other foot. It is one of the most challenging bodyweight lower body exercises and serves as an excellent test of single-leg strength and control.

execution.starting_position: Stand on one foot with the arms extended forward for counterbalance. Lift the non-working leg off the floor and extend it in front of you.
execution.setup_instructions: No equipment needed. Beginners can hold a TRX strap or doorframe for balance assistance. Use a box or bench for assisted regressions.
steps: Step 1: Stand on the working leg with arms extended forward. Extend the free leg in front at approximately hip height.
Step 2: Brace your core and begin the descent by pushing the hips back and bending the knee over the toes.
Step 3: Descend until the hip is at or below knee height. The free leg stays extended forward throughout. Use the arms for counterbalance.
Step 4: Drive through the entire working foot — heel, midfoot, and ball — to return to full standing extension.
Step 5: Complete all reps on one side, then switch.
execution.breathing_instructions: Inhale before descent. Exhale at the top of each rep.
common_mistakes: Allowing the working knee to cave inward due to insufficient hip strength
Rising onto the toe of the working foot at the bottom
Losing extension of the free leg (bending the knee and placing the foot down)
safety_considerations: Progress through regressions (box squat single-leg, assisted pistol) before attempting a full pistol squat
Ankle dorsiflexion is often the limiting factor — address with mobility work before loading
execution.range_of_motion_guidance: Full depth: hip at or below knee of the working leg. Free leg remains straight and elevated throughout.
execution.tempo_recommendations: 3-0-1-0 — control the descent; a slow eccentric is excellent for building strength
coaching_cues: Reach forward with both arms to counterbalance
Hips back first, then bend the knee
Drive through the heel — don't let the foot roll in

name: Sissy Squat
description: The sissy squat is a unique quadriceps exercise in which the knees travel far forward of the toes while the torso leans backward, creating a long moment arm at the knee and intense quadriceps loading through a full range of motion. Unlike most squat variations, the hip does not flex significantly, making this primarily an open-chain knee extension pattern performed without a machine. It places high eccentric stress on the quadriceps and substantial load on the patellar tendon.

execution.starting_position: Stand with heels slightly elevated (on a small plate or the edge of a step) and hold onto an upright support for balance. Feet are hip-width apart.
execution.setup_instructions: Have a fixed support nearby (rack upright or door frame) to hold during the movement. Heel elevation (1–2 inches) makes the exercise more accessible and reduces ankle mobility demands.
steps: Step 1: Stand tall, holding the support lightly for balance. Begin to lean backward as a unit from the knees — the ankle plantar-flexes and the knee flexes.
Step 2: Continue leaning backward while allowing the knees to travel far forward. The hips remain relatively extended throughout — do not flex at the hip.
Step 3: Descend until the thighs are as close to vertical as possible (nearly parallel to the torso, which is leaning far back).
Step 4: Reverse the motion by contracting the quadriceps powerfully to pull the torso back to vertical.
Step 5: Return to full standing extension.
execution.breathing_instructions: Inhale during the descent. Exhale on the return to standing.
common_mistakes: Hinging at the hip (like a squat) instead of maintaining hip extension throughout
Moving too fast through the eccentric portion — the sissy squat's value is in its slow, controlled range
Attempting without sufficient quad strength — high patellar tendon stress makes unpreparedness risky
safety_considerations: High patellar tendon load — those with patellar tendinopathy should consult a clinician before performing
Avoid the loaded version until bodyweight is controlled comfortably
Heel elevation reduces the ankle dorsiflexion requirement and reduces risk of balance loss
execution.range_of_motion_guidance: Maximize the backward lean while keeping hips extended and feet planted. The more range, the greater the quad stretch.
coaching_cues: Keep the hips long — do not fold at the hip
Lean back as one rigid plank from knee to shoulder
Squeeze the quads to pull yourself back up

name: Skater Squat / Drop Knee Single-Leg Squat
description: The skater squat is a single-leg squat variation where the rear leg drops straight down toward the floor, with the knee approaching but not fully resting on the ground. Unlike the Bulgarian split squat, the rear foot is free and not elevated, requiring greater balance and demanding very high quadriceps and glute force from the working leg. It is significantly more challenging than a standard split squat.

execution.starting_position: Stand on one foot. Extend the arms forward or hold a small counterbalance weight. The rear leg hangs free behind you.
execution.setup_instructions: Master the bodyweight version before adding load. Practice near a wall for balance assistance initially.
steps: Step 1: Shift weight entirely to the working leg, brace the core.
Step 2: Lower the rear knee straight down toward the floor as you squat down on the working leg.
Step 3: Descend until the rear knee nearly touches the floor while the front shin remains relatively vertical.
Step 4: Drive through the working heel to return to the starting position.
execution.breathing_instructions: Inhale on the descent, exhale on the drive up.
common_mistakes: Rear knee tapping the floor and using it as a support
Excessive forward lean of the torso
Working knee caving inward
safety_considerations: Very high demand on knee and ankle stability — progress very gradually
Use bodyweight for many sessions before adding load
execution.range_of_motion_guidance: Rear knee should approach but not touch the floor. Front shin relatively vertical.
coaching_cues: Stand tall on the working leg
Knee traces over the second toe
Drive through the heel

name: SkiErg Double-Pole Pull
description: The SkiErg simulates the double-pole motion of cross-country skiing, pulling two handles downward from an overhead position with a simultaneous hip hinge, engaging the latissimus dorsi, core, triceps, and deltoids under a continuous cardiovascular load. Each stroke begins with the arms raised overhead and ends with a powerful downward pull and hip extension, creating a cyclical full-body pulling pattern. The SkiErg develops both upper-body strength-endurance and cardiovascular conditioning while remaining completely non-impact.

execution.starting_position: Stand facing the SkiErg machine with feet shoulder-width apart. Grasp both handles with arms extended overhead, body tall, slight forward lean at the hips.
execution.setup_instructions: Set the damper (resistance) to 4–6. Plug in the performance monitor and select meters or time for the interval target.
steps: Step 1: Begin with arms extended overhead and a slight hip hinge. This is the catch position.
Step 2: Simultaneously pull both handles downward and hinge the hips forward, bringing the handles past the hips to the finish position.
Step 3: At the finish, the handles are near the hips, body is hinged forward with a flat back, and the core is fully contracted.
Step 4: Recover by allowing the arms to rise overhead as the hips extend back to the start position in a smooth, continuous motion.
Step 5: Maintain a consistent stroke rate — typically 30–40 strokes per minute for intervals.
execution.breathing_instructions: Exhale sharply on the downward pull (the drive phase). Inhale on the recovery as the arms rise back overhead.
common_mistakes: Pulling only with the arms without engaging the hip hinge, which loses the core and hip contribution
Letting the elbows bend excessively rather than keeping a long lever during the pull
Letting go of a smooth rhythm and jerking the handles
safety_considerations: Avoid rounding the lower back at the bottom of the pull — maintain a neutral spine throughout the hip hinge
execution.range_of_motion_guidance: Arms travel from fully overhead to past the hips. The hip hinge should be pronounced — torso moves from tall to roughly 45° forward.
execution.tempo_recommendations: Interval: 500m hard / 2 minutes rest × 5. Time-based: 30 seconds hard / 30 seconds rest × 10. Stroke rate: 30–40 SPM during hard effort.
coaching_cues: Lead with the hip hinge, not just the arms
Think of pulling the handles through the floor
Keep long arms — do not bend the elbows early

name: Skull Crusher
description: The skull crusher is a lying triceps extension exercise performed on a bench with an EZ-curl bar or dumbbells. By lowering the bar toward the forehead or skull from a fully extended arm position, the triceps are trained through a full range of elbow flexion and extension with particular emphasis on the long head.

execution.starting_position: Lie on a flat bench holding an EZ-curl bar with a narrow pronated grip. Press the bar to full extension above the chest with upper arms vertical.
execution.setup_instructions: Keep the upper arms perpendicular to the floor throughout. The bar moves in an arc from above the chest toward the forehead.
steps: With upper arms stationary and vertical, lower the bar by bending the elbows.
Lower toward the forehead or slightly behind the head to maximize long-head stretch.
Extend the elbows to press the bar back to the starting position.
execution.breathing_instructions: Inhale on the descent toward the forehead. Exhale on extension.
common_mistakes: Allowing the elbows to flare outward widely
Moving the upper arms — the elbows should hinge, not the shoulder
safety_considerations: Use a spotter for heavy sets — the bar is directly above the face
Do not bounce or lose control at the bottom
execution.range_of_motion_guidance: Lower until the bar almost touches the forehead or slightly behind it. Full extension at the top.
coaching_cues: Keep your elbows pointing straight at the ceiling throughout
The bar moves like a hinge — upper arms do not move

name: Barbell Skull Crusher
description: The barbell skull crusher is performed lying on a flat bench, lowering a barbell toward the forehead or just above the head by bending only the elbows. It places the triceps under maximum stretch at the bottom position, particularly loading the long head. Because the arms are vertical at the top and angled at the bottom, the triceps work through a large range of motion under significant load. The long eccentric with a heavy bar makes it one of the most effective tricep mass builders.

execution.starting_position: Lie on a flat bench, bar pressed to full arm extension above the chest. Grip the bar slightly inside shoulder width, supinated grip.
execution.setup_instructions: Have a spotter hand the bar off, or take it from a low rack. Use a close grip for maximum tricep isolation.
steps: Step 1: Begin with the bar above the chest at full elbow extension.
Step 2: Keeping the upper arms vertical, bend only the elbows to lower the bar toward the forehead.
Step 3: Lower until the bar is just above the forehead or nose.
Step 4: Extend the elbows to press the bar back to the starting position.
execution.breathing_instructions: Inhale on the descent, exhale on the press.
common_mistakes: Upper arms drifting backward during the descent
Using shoulder movement rather than elbow flexion
Bar path going too far behind the head (increases long head strain)
safety_considerations: Never perform to failure without a spotter — bar failure over the face is dangerous
Use collars to prevent plates sliding
