execution.range_of_motion_guidance: Full elbow extension at top, bar just above forehead at bottom.
coaching_cues: Upper arms vertical and still
Lower to the forehead — not past it
Press straight up

name: EZ-Bar Skull Crusher
description: The EZ-bar skull crusher replaces the straight bar with an EZ-curl bar, reducing wrist and elbow stress while maintaining tricep loading similar to the barbell version. The angled grip positions of the EZ-bar allow a more natural hand angle during the movement. It is the most common skull crusher variation for high-volume training due to its superior comfort and reduced injury risk over straight bar versions.

execution.starting_position: Lie on a flat bench, EZ-bar pressed to full extension above the chest. Grip the inner handles.
execution.setup_instructions: Have a spotter hand the EZ-bar off or unrack from a low rack. Use the inner grips of the EZ-bar.
steps: Step 1: Begin with EZ-bar fully extended above the chest.
Step 2: Keeping upper arms vertical, lower the EZ-bar toward the forehead by bending only the elbows.
Step 3: Lower to just above the forehead.
Step 4: Extend the elbows to return to the starting position.
execution.breathing_instructions: Inhale on the descent, exhale on the press.
common_mistakes: Upper arms drifting forward or backward during the movement
Excessive elbow flare
safety_considerations: EZ-bar still requires careful attention at the bottom — do not go to failure without a spotter
execution.range_of_motion_guidance: Full extension to bar just above the forehead.
coaching_cues: Upper arms pinned — only elbows move
Lower to the forehead
Squeeze the triceps at lockout

name: EZ Bar Skullcrusher to Chin
description: A skullcrusher variation where the bar is lowered to the chin rather than the forehead. This version engages a greater range of elbow flexion and can feel more natural for many lifters. Lowering to the chin changes the angle of tricep loading through the range.

execution.starting_position: Set up for EZ Bar Skullcrusher to Chin in the appropriate position.
execution.setup_instructions: Prepare equipment and body position for EZ Bar Skullcrusher to Chin.
steps: Step 1: Lie on bench with EZ bar held at arm's length above chest.
Step 2: Allow elbows to drift slightly back as you lower the bar.
Step 3: Lower bar to chin level, feeling tricep stretch.
Step 4: Extend elbows to full lockout at starting position.
execution.breathing_instructions: Exhale during the exertion phase, inhale during the return.
common_mistakes: Lowering too far risking chin contact
Excessive elbow drift
safety_considerations: Keep joints aligned throughout the movement.
Use controlled weight appropriate for skill level.
execution.range_of_motion_guidance: Move through full range of motion without compromising joint integrity.
coaching_cues: Control the arc, do not hit chin
Extend to full lockout

name: Sled Pull
description: The sled pull is a functional pulling exercise in which a loaded sled is dragged toward the athlete using a rope or straps in a hand-over-hand pulling motion, or pulled while walking backward. It develops upper body pulling strength, grip endurance, and posterior chain conditioning through sustained, resisted pulling mechanics. The backward walking variation also trains hip extension and hamstring strength in a closed-chain pattern that is distinct from conventional rows.

execution.starting_position: Sit or stand facing the loaded sled at a distance, holding a rope or straps attached to the sled.
execution.setup_instructions: Attach a pulling rope or straps to the sled. The rope-pull variation is performed seated or standing, hand-over-hand.
steps: Step 1: Face the sled at a distance with rope or straps taut.
Step 2: Pull one hand over the other in a continuous hand-over-hand motion, drawing the sled toward you.
Step 3: Keep the torso stable and upright — avoid rotating the spine.
Step 4: When the sled arrives, reload (walk back and restart) or reverse the sled direction.
Step 5: Alternatively, face away from the sled and walk backward, pulling the sled behind via hip harness or handles.
execution.breathing_instructions: Exhale on each pull. Breathe continuously throughout.
common_mistakes: Rounding the back during the pull — maintain a stable, upright torso
Only using the arms — engage the lats by thinking of pulling the elbows down and back
Letting the rope go slack between pulls — keep constant tension on the sled
safety_considerations: Adequate pulling surface — grass or turf is ideal.
Check rope and attachment integrity before loading.
execution.range_of_motion_guidance: Full elbow flexion on each pull cycle. Full rope length for each set.
execution.tempo_recommendations: Performed for distance or time. 20–30 meter rope pulls for conditioning.
coaching_cues: Pull the elbows back — engage the lats
Stay upright — no rounding
Constant tension — no slack

name: Sled Push
description: The sled push is a linear strength and conditioning exercise in which the athlete drives a loaded sled forward across a surface by pushing from handles at the rear, maintaining a forward lean with straight arms. The hip extension and leg drive mechanics closely replicate the acceleration phase of sprinting, making it a highly effective training tool for sport-specific linear power, lower body strength development, and high-intensity metabolic conditioning with minimal eccentric muscle damage.

execution.starting_position: Stand behind the sled, gripping the upright handles. Lean forward at approximately 45 degrees, arms straight.
execution.setup_instructions: Load the sled appropriately — heavier loads develop strength, lighter loads develop speed and conditioning. Use a rubber or turf surface for most sled work.
steps: Step 1: Grip the sled handles and lean forward with the body at roughly 45 degrees and arms straight.
Step 2: Drive off one foot, pushing forcefully into the floor, as the other leg swings through.
Step 3: Maintain short, powerful strides — stay on the balls of the feet, never the heels.
Step 4: Keep the hips down and avoid raising the torso — the lean angle is maintained throughout.
Step 5: Drive the sled forward for the prescribed distance, maintaining consistent force output.
execution.breathing_instructions: Breathe rhythmically throughout. Exhale with each leg drive.
common_mistakes: Letting the arms bend — straight arms transfer force more efficiently to the sled
Pushing with the toes instead of the full foot drive
Standing too upright — reduces horizontal force vector on the sled
safety_considerations: Ensure the surface is appropriate — asphalt can damage sled bases not designed for it.
Adequate lower body warm-up before heavy sled work.
execution.range_of_motion_guidance: Full hip and knee extension on each stride.
execution.tempo_recommendations: Typically performed for distance (20–40 meters). Heavy: slow and powerful. Light: fast and explosive.
coaching_cues: Stay low — maintain the forward lean
Drive the foot into the ground
Arms straight — push through the handles

name: Sledgehammer Lever (Forearm Levering)
description: The sledgehammer lever involves holding a sledgehammer at the very end of its handle with one hand extended and slowly lowering it forward or to the side from a vertical position, then raising it back — using wrist and forearm strength to control the extreme lever arm. The long handle creates significant torque on the forearm even with a lightweight hammer, making it one of the most effective single-tool wrist extensor exercises.

execution.starting_position: Hold a sledgehammer at the very end of the handle with one hand, arm at the side, hammer vertical with head up.
execution.setup_instructions: Begin with a 2-4kg sledgehammer. The lever arm is the challenge, not the head weight. Stand with feet hip-width.
steps: Step 1: Hold the hammer vertical, arm extended slightly forward.
Step 2: Slowly lower the hammer forward (or to the side) by extending the wrist, controlling the lever.
Step 3: Lower as far as wrist control allows without losing the grip.
Step 4: Raise the hammer back to vertical using wrist flexion.
execution.breathing_instructions: Exhale on the raise, inhale on the lower.
common_mistakes: Gripping too close to the head — the grip must be at the very end of the handle
Moving too fast
safety_considerations: Start with a light hammer — the lever arm is deceptively difficult
Perform over a rubber mat in case of drop
execution.range_of_motion_guidance: Vertical to horizontal (or as far as controlled).
coaching_cues: Grip the very end of the handle
Slow and controlled in both directions
Feel the forearm extensors work

name: Sliding Towel / Slider Leg Curl
description: The slider leg curl is performed on a smooth floor using a towel or furniture sliders under the heels. The lifter begins in a supine bridge and slides the heels toward the hips to curl the hamstrings, then slides back to full extension. Because the floor provides no catch, the eccentric phase demands significant hamstring control. It is an effective, equipment-free hamstring exercise that can be progressed to single-leg variations.

execution.starting_position: Lie on your back on a smooth floor. Place a small towel or furniture sliders under both heels. Legs extended, arms at sides.
execution.setup_instructions: Use a smooth floor surface (hardwood or tile). Fold a towel and place it under both heels so they slide easily.
steps: Step 1: Drive the hips up into a bridge, forming a straight line from shoulders to heels.
Step 2: While maintaining the bridge, slide the heels toward your hips by bending the knees.
Step 3: Slide until the heels are close to the glutes.
Step 4: Slide the heels back to the starting extended position with control, maintaining the hip bridge.
execution.breathing_instructions: Exhale on the curl, inhale on the return.
common_mistakes: Hips sagging during the return phase
Sliding too fast — use the hamstrings to control the eccentric
Heels sliding outward
safety_considerations: Ensure the floor surface is smooth and consistent
The eccentric return is high hamstring demand — control it carefully
execution.range_of_motion_guidance: Full extension to maximum knee flexion (heels near glutes).
coaching_cues: Hips stay high — squeeze your glutes
Control the return slide
Heels stay hip-width apart

name: Smith Machine Bench Press
description: The Smith machine bench press is a horizontal pressing exercise performed on a Smith machine, where the barbell is fixed within vertical or slightly angled rails. The constrained bar path reduces the demand on stabilizing muscles and allows safer solo training for pressing, though it alters the natural bar path compared to a free barbell. Useful for beginners, solo training, and specific overloading techniques.

execution.starting_position: Position a flat bench inside the Smith machine. Lie on the bench so the bar is directly above the mid-chest. Grip the bar slightly wider than shoulder-width. Rotate the bar to disengage the hooks.
execution.setup_instructions: Adjust bench position so that the bar tracks over the mid-chest when lowered. Set the safety hooks at a height 1–2 inches above the chest as a fail-safe.
steps: Step 1: Lie on the bench under the Smith machine bar. Grip the bar wider than shoulder-width with an overhand grip.
Step 2: Rotate the bar to release it from the hooks. Extend arms to hold the bar above the chest.
Step 3: Inhale and lower the bar in a controlled manner to touch the mid-chest.
Step 4: Exhale and press the bar back up to the starting position. At the end of your set, rotate the bar back onto the hooks.
execution.breathing_instructions: Inhale as the bar descends; exhale as you press it up.
common_mistakes: Placing the bench too far forward or back, causing the bar to track over the neck or abdomen
Forgetting to re-engage the safety hooks between sets
safety_considerations: Always set safety hooks before beginning to protect against failure
Some Smith machines have an angled track — position accordingly
execution.range_of_motion_guidance: Lower bar to touch the chest, then press to full extension.
coaching_cues: Maintain a natural arch in the lower back — do not flatten excessively
Drive through the mid-foot to maintain leg drive even on the bench

name: Smith Machine Bulgarian Split Squat
alternative_names: Smith Machine Rear-Foot Elevated Split Squat
description: The Smith machine Bulgarian split squat replicates the standard dumbbell or barbell Bulgarian split squat using the guided bar of the Smith machine. The fixed bar path reduces the balance demands and allows the lifter to focus on depth and muscular feel rather than stability. The rear foot is elevated on a bench behind, and the front leg does the primary work.

execution.starting_position: Set the Smith machine bar at shoulder height. Position a bench behind you. Place one foot on the bench (top of foot or heel, depending on comfort). Position the front foot forward so the front shin will be vertical at the bottom.
execution.setup_instructions: Adjust the Smith machine bar to sit across the traps. Place a flat or adjustable bench 2-3 feet behind the machine's path. Set rear foot on bench before unracking.
steps: Step 1: Brace the core and keep an upright torso.
Step 2: Lower the rear knee directly down toward the floor.
Step 3: Descend until the front thigh is at or below parallel. Front shin should remain nearly vertical.
Step 4: Drive through the front heel to extend back to the starting position.
execution.breathing_instructions: Inhale on the descent, exhale on the drive.
common_mistakes: Front foot too close, causing excessive forward shin angle
Rear knee drifting to one side
Leaning the torso too far forward
safety_considerations: The rear foot on the bench creates instability — set up carefully and test before loading
The Smith machine's fixed path may feel unnatural for some — adjust foot position accordingly
execution.range_of_motion_guidance: Front thigh at or below parallel. Rear knee close to floor.
coaching_cues: Front shin stays vertical
Drive the rear knee straight down
Upright chest

name: Smith Machine Decline Bench Press
description: The Smith Machine Decline Bench Press uses a decline angle (feet elevated above head) to target the sternal and lower fibers of the pectoralis major. The fixed bar path of the Smith machine provides stability and allows training without a spotter, making the decline angle more accessible than with a free barbell.

execution.starting_position: Set an adjustable bench to a decline angle (feet 15-30 degrees higher than head). Secure feet under the ankle pads. Position bar at lower chest height in the Smith machine.
execution.setup_instructions: Lock ankle pads before lying back. Adjust the Smith machine bar height so it aligns with the lower sternum when the bench is at the decline angle chosen.
steps: Step 1: Unrack by rotating the bar off the hooks.
Step 2: Lower the bar to the lower chest with controlled speed.
Step 3: Press back to full extension along the fixed bar path.
Step 4: Rerack carefully after the final rep.
execution.breathing_instructions: Inhale before descent. Exhale through lockout.
common_mistakes: Steep decline causing blood to rush to the head — limit to 15-20 degrees for most people
Failing to secure feet before lying back
safety_considerations: Always ensure ankle pads are secured before getting into position
Avoid very steep declines if you have high blood pressure
execution.range_of_motion_guidance: Full touch to lower sternum; full elbow extension.
coaching_cues: Press up and slightly back — do not press straight up
Squeeze the lower pecs at the top

name: Smith Machine Decline Close-Grip Press
description: A close-grip press on a decline bench in the Smith machine combining locked bar path with decline angle for triceps emphasis. The Smith provides safety when training heavy decline presses without a spotter. The fixed path lets full attention go to triceps contraction.

execution.starting_position: Set up for Smith Machine Decline Close-Grip Press in the appropriate position.
execution.setup_instructions: Prepare equipment and body position for Smith Machine Decline Close-Grip Press.
steps: Step 1: Position decline bench under Smith bar. Set close grip on bar.
Step 2: Unhook bar and lower to lower chest with elbows tucked.
Step 3: Keep elbows close to torso throughout descent.
Step 4: Press bar back to lockout fully extending triceps.
execution.breathing_instructions: Exhale during the exertion phase, inhale during the return.
common_mistakes: Gripping too close causing wrist pain
Wide elbow position
safety_considerations: Keep joints aligned throughout the movement.
Use controlled weight appropriate for skill level.
execution.range_of_motion_guidance: Move through full range of motion without compromising joint integrity.
coaching_cues: Track elbows close to ribs
Full lockout at top

name: Smith Machine Floor Press
description: The Smith Machine Floor Press combines the floor press's ROM restriction and triceps emphasis with the Smith machine's fixed bar path and self-spotting capability. The floor eliminates leg drive and limits the eccentric to 90 degrees of elbow flexion, making it an effective triceps and upper chest exercise for home gym setups where a traditional bench may not be available.

execution.starting_position: Lower the Smith machine bar to a few inches above where your elbows touch the floor when lying beneath it. Lie on the floor under the bar and grip it at shoulder-width.
execution.setup_instructions: Adjust Smith machine bar height carefully for the floor position. Place a mat on the floor for comfort. Have the safety catches set appropriately in case of failure.
steps: Step 1: Rotate bar off hooks and hold at arm's length above the chest.
Step 2: Lower bar until upper arms touch the floor (elbows at approximately 90 degrees).
Step 3: Pause on the floor for 1 second.
Step 4: Press back to full lockout and repeat.
execution.breathing_instructions: Inhale before descent. Exhale through lockout.
common_mistakes: Not pausing on the floor, using momentum
Setting the bar height too low, making unracking difficult
safety_considerations: The floor catches the bar if grip fails — this is a self-spotting exercise
Set the bar height precisely before lying down
execution.range_of_motion_guidance: Elbows touch the floor at the bottom; full extension at top. Shorter ROM than bench press.
coaching_cues: Let the floor stop you — don't relax tension when you touch
Pause and press with intent

name: Smith Machine Front Squat
description: The Smith machine front squat positions the bar across the front deltoids and clavicles, guided by the machine's fixed vertical track. The guided bar path removes the balance demands of a free-weight front squat, allowing the lifter to focus entirely on quad depth and torso position. The front rack position promotes an upright torso and maximal quadriceps recruitment.

execution.starting_position: Position the Smith machine bar across the front deltoids (front rack position). Cross the arms over the bar or use a clean grip. Feet shoulder-width, toes turned out slightly, feet positioned slightly forward of the bar.
execution.setup_instructions: Set the Smith machine bar at upper-chest height. Step under and position bar on front delts. Rotate the bar to unlock.
steps: Step 1: Brace the core and keep the elbows high throughout the movement.
Step 2: Bend the knees and squat down, keeping the torso very upright.
Step 3: Descend until thighs are at or below parallel.
Step 4: Drive through the feet to return to the starting position.
execution.breathing_instructions: Inhale and brace before descent. Exhale at the top.
common_mistakes: Elbows dropping, allowing the bar to roll off the delts
Knees caving inward
Insufficient ankle mobility causing heel rise
safety_considerations: Ensure elbow flexibility for the front rack — use a crossed-arm grip if needed
The Smith machine's fixed path can stress the knees if foot position is incorrect
execution.range_of_motion_guidance: Full depth — hip crease below the knee. The upright torso makes this more achievable.
coaching_cues: Elbows stay high
Sit tall between the knees
Drive the floor away

name: Smith Machine Incline Bench Press
description: The Smith Machine Incline Bench Press uses the fixed bar path of a Smith machine to perform an incline pressing movement targeting the clavicular head of the pectoralis major. The guided bar path removes stabilization demands, allowing greater focus on the upper chest and making it accessible for beginners and useful for high-rep isolation work without a spotter.

execution.starting_position: Position an adjustable bench at 30-45 degrees inside the Smith machine. Align the bar to touch the upper chest. Grip slightly wider than shoulder-width.
execution.setup_instructions: Set the Smith machine bar hooks at an appropriate height. Position the bench so that when lying on it, the bar descends naturally to the upper chest without awkward angle. Adjust incline to 30-45 degrees.
steps: Step 1: Unrack by rotating the bar off the hooks.
Step 2: Lower the bar under control to the upper chest.
Step 3: Press up along the fixed bar path to full extension.
Step 4: Rerack by rotating the bar back onto the hooks after the final rep.
execution.breathing_instructions: Inhale before lowering. Exhale at the top.
common_mistakes: Setting the bench at too steep an angle, shifting load from chest to shoulders
Placing the bench too far forward or backward in the Smith machine, creating an unnatural bar path angle
safety_considerations: Ensure the bench is positioned so the natural Smith machine bar path aligns with the upper chest, not the throat
Learn to rerack confidently before training heavy
execution.range_of_motion_guidance: Full touch to upper chest at bottom; full elbow extension at top.
coaching_cues: Position the bench so the bar drops straight down to your upper chest
Drive through the chest — do not lead with shoulders

name: Smith Machine Romanian Deadlift
description: The Smith machine Romanian deadlift uses the guided bar path of the Smith machine to perform the hip hinge pattern. The fixed vertical track removes the need for lateral bar control, allowing the lifter to focus entirely on the hinge mechanics and hamstring stretch. It is a good option for beginners learning the RDL pattern or for those who want to train without a spotter on a hinge movement.

execution.starting_position: Set the Smith machine bar at hip height. Stand with feet hip-width apart, holding the bar with an overhand grip slightly outside hip width.
execution.setup_instructions: Rotate the bar to unlock it. Stand close to the bar with it at your upper thighs.
steps: Step 1: Brace the core, retract the shoulder blades, and push the hips back.
Step 2: Lower the bar along the front of the thighs in a straight path, keeping the bar close.
Step 3: Descend until a strong stretch is felt in the hamstrings, maintaining a neutral spine.
Step 4: Drive the hips forward to return to standing, squeezing the glutes at the top.
execution.breathing_instructions: Inhale and brace before the descent. Exhale as you drive up.
common_mistakes: Lower back rounding to gain additional depth
Bar drifting away from the legs
Knees bending too much, turning it into a deadlift
safety_considerations: The Smith machine's fixed path is vertical — ensure your hinge pattern matches this for natural movement
execution.range_of_motion_guidance: Descend to mid-shin or as far as hamstring flexibility allows without spinal flexion.
coaching_cues: Bar slides down the thighs
Push the hips back, not down
Hamstring stretch guides your depth

name: Smith Machine Reverse-Grip Bench Press
description: The Smith Machine Reverse-Grip Bench Press performs the supinated grip bench press on a Smith machine, which provides a stable bar path for this mechanically weaker grip position. The fixed path makes this upper-chest and triceps emphasis variation considerably safer to attempt alone compared to its free-barbell counterpart.

execution.starting_position: Lie on a flat bench under the Smith machine bar. Take a supinated (underhand) grip with palms facing toward the head. Grip inside shoulder-width for comfort.
execution.setup_instructions: Set the Smith machine bar at the appropriate height. The fixed bar path makes this variation much more manageable than its free-bar version. Reduce load significantly from your standard bench max.
steps: Step 1: Rotate the bar off the hooks with a supinated grip.
Step 2: Lower under control to the lower chest with elbows tracking close to the body.
Step 3: Press up to lockout.
Step 4: Rotate and rerack after the final rep.
execution.breathing_instructions: Inhale and brace before descent. Exhale at lockout.
common_mistakes: Gripping too wide — the supinated grip places wrists under severe stress if too wide
Trying to use the same load as a standard bench press
safety_considerations: The supinated grip is weaker — reduce load by 20% or more
Discontinue if wrist discomfort arises
execution.range_of_motion_guidance: Full touch to lower chest; full elbow extension.
coaching_cues: Elbows track toward your sides, not outward
Feel the upper chest and triceps working, not just the shoulders

name: Smith Machine Sissy Squat
description: A sissy squat variation performed with the Smith machine bar resting across the front of the thighs, with heels elevated on a plate or wedge. The machine guides the movement and reduces balance demand, allowing heavy quad isolation with the knees traveling far forward — a position that maximally stretches and loads the rectus femoris and vastus lateralis.

execution.starting_position: Stand facing away from the Smith machine with the bar set at approximately thigh height. Place heels on a 25lb plate. Bar rests lightly across upper thighs.
execution.setup_instructions: Set the Smith bar at thigh height. Place a 25lb plate flat behind the foot position for heel elevation. Duck under the bar and position it across the upper thighs.
steps: Step 1: Lean back slightly with a rigid torso, engaging the quads.
Step 2: Allow the knees to travel forward over and past the toes while your hips drop toward the floor.
Step 3: Lower until a strong quad stretch is felt, or as far as comfortable knee health allows.
Step 4: Reverse the motion by driving the knees back and straightening to the upright position.
execution.breathing_instructions: Inhale on the descent. Exhale during the return to upright.
common_mistakes: Collapsing the lower back — maintain a rigid torso throughout
Using excessive range before the tendons have adapted
safety_considerations: Avoid if you have patellar tendinopathy or significant knee pain
Progress depth gradually over several weeks
execution.range_of_motion_guidance: Lower until a strong quad stretch is felt. The knees travel well past the toes — this is intentional for this exercise.
coaching_cues: Keep the torso rigid throughout
Let the knees lead forward

name: Snatch Balance
description: The snatch balance is an Olympic weightlifting accessory exercise in which the bar is taken from the back rack position and the athlete uses a dip-and-drive to push themselves under the bar into a full overhead squat. It trains the speed of the third pull (turning the hands over and dropping under the bar) and reinforces the ability to stabilize a heavy snatch catch. The snatch balance is typically performed with higher loads than the actual snatch to overload the catch position.

execution.starting_position: Bar across the back in a high bar squat position, with a wide snatch grip. Feet in squat stance.
execution.setup_instructions: Take the bar from a rack with a wide snatch grip. The dip-and-drop is key — practice with an empty bar first.
steps: Step 1: Hold the bar on the back in a wide snatch grip, feet in squat stance.
Step 2: Dip the knees 10–15 cm with a vertical torso.
Step 3: Drive the bar upward slightly while simultaneously pressing yourself under the bar.
Step 4: Rotate the hands and punch the bar overhead into a locked overhead squat position.
Step 5: Stabilize in the full overhead squat, then stand.
execution.breathing_instructions: Brace before the dip. Exhale after stabilizing overhead.
common_mistakes: Pressing the bar up high before dropping under — the goal is to use minimal upward force and mainly drop
Catching with bent elbows
Insufficient ankle or shoulder mobility causing the squat to collapse
safety_considerations: This exercise requires excellent shoulder and ankle mobility. Use a rack with safeties.
Be prepared to drop the bar safely forward.
execution.range_of_motion_guidance: Full overhead squat depth with locked-out bar position.
execution.tempo_recommendations: Explosive dip-drive. Fast hands. Stable catch before standing.
coaching_cues: Dip straight — drive the bar up slightly, then drop fast
Punch the hands up and lock out
Catch it — stabilize before standing

name: Snatch-Grip Behind-Neck Push-Press
description: The snatch-grip behind-neck push-press uses a wide barbell grip (wider than shoulder width, approximating a snatch grip) with the bar starting behind the head on the traps. The push-press component (leg drive) allows heavier loading than a strict press. The wide grip and behind-neck bar position place the shoulder in maximum external rotation, which trains the posterior capsule and rotator cuff while also loading the lateral and posterior deltoid. This movement is primarily used in Olympic weightlifting and strength sport accessory training, requiring above-average shoulder mobility.

execution.starting_position: Set a barbell on a rack at upper-trap height. Take a wide snatch grip. The bar rests behind the head on the upper traps. Feet shoulder-width apart.
execution.setup_instructions: Requires substantial shoulder external rotation mobility. Screen with a PVC pipe or empty bar before loading. This is an advanced movement for athletes with verified shoulder mobility.
steps: Step 1: Unrack the bar onto the upper traps. Maintain the wide snatch grip.
Step 2: Dip the knees 10-15 cm, maintaining an upright torso.
Step 3: Drive upward explosively through the legs, transferring momentum to the bar.
Step 4: Complete the press by extending the arms overhead.
Step 5: Lower under control back to the traps. Rerack after the set.
execution.breathing_instructions: Inhale and brace. Exhale through the drive and press.
common_mistakes: Attempting this without adequate shoulder mobility — always screen mobility before loading
Narrow grip — the snatch grip width is what distributes the shoulder load
safety_considerations: Requires excellent shoulder external rotation and thoracic extension mobility
Do not perform if any shoulder pain occurs — the behind-neck position is not appropriate for all athletes
Must be learned and practiced with an empty bar before loading
execution.range_of_motion_guidance: Upper trap level to full overhead lockout.
coaching_cues: Wide grip — snatch width
Bar on the traps, not the neck
Dip straight — drive straight — press straight

name: Snatch-Grip Deadlift
description: The snatch-grip deadlift uses the wide grip position typical of the Olympic snatch, requiring the bar to travel a greater distance and demanding superior upper back and trap strength to maintain position. The wide grip drops the hips significantly, increasing quad, upper back, and trap demands relative to conventional deadlift. It is widely used by Olympic weightlifters and strength athletes to develop postural strength and reinforce the snatch starting position.

execution.starting_position: Grip the bar with a snatch-width grip — typically hands outside shoulder width, often indexed off the rings on the bar. The wide grip will lower your hips significantly. Maintain a proud chest and neutral spine.
execution.setup_instructions: Reduce load substantially from conventional deadlift maximum. Wrist straps are recommended due to the wide grip stress on the wrists.
steps: Step 1: Set up with the snatch-width grip. The hips will be lower than in a conventional deadlift due to the wider hand position.
Step 2: Brace the core, retract the scapulae, and set the upper back tight.
Step 3: Drive through the floor as in a conventional deadlift, keeping the bar close to the body throughout.
Step 4: Maintain the upright torso position through the pull — this is more quad-dominant than a conventional deadlift.
Step 5: Lock out hips and knees at the top. Return under full control.
execution.breathing_instructions: Valsalva brace before each rep. Exhale at lockout.
common_mistakes: Letting the bar drift away from the body — it must stay close due to the wide grip
Using too heavy a load, which collapses the upper back
Forgetting the bar travels further — treat it as a training tool at submaximal weights
safety_considerations: Wrist discomfort is common — use lifting straps
Requires significant upper back strength and flexibility — master conventional deadlift first
execution.range_of_motion_guidance: Full hip extension at lockout. The wide grip means the bar hangs lower relative to the hips at the top.
coaching_cues: Bar stays in contact with the thighs
Proud chest throughout
Drive the hips forward at lockout

name: Snatch Pull
description: The snatch pull is the snatch equivalent of the clean pull — the athlete performs the full snatch pulling mechanics with a wide snatch grip but does not turn the bar over into a catch. It trains the specific pulling pattern of the snatch (wider grip, more external hip rotation) with loads exceeding snatch maximum. The snatch pull reinforces bar path, hip drive timing, and upper trap engagement specific to the snatch.

execution.starting_position: Bar over mid-foot, wide snatch grip, flat back, hips between shoulders and knees.
execution.setup_instructions: Same starting position as the snatch. Use straps to focus on pulling mechanics without grip limitation.
steps: Step 1: Set up with the wide snatch grip in the starting position.
Step 2: First pull — drive the floor away, keeping bar close and back angle constant.
Step 3: Second pull — extend hips explosively as the bar reaches the hip crease.
Step 4: Shrug the traps aggressively at full triple extension.
Step 5: Allow bar to rise from shrug momentum, then lower with control.
execution.breathing_instructions: Brace before initiating. Hold through the pull. Exhale as bar descends.
common_mistakes: Early arm bend
Bar path too far from the body
Not achieving full triple extension
safety_considerations: The wider grip lowers the hip starting position compared to the clean pull.
Lower with control. Use straps as needed.
execution.range_of_motion_guidance: Full triple extension (ankle, knee, hip) at the top of the pull.
coaching_cues: Wide grip, bar sweeps close to the body
Full extension before the shrug
Rise on toes at the top

name: Spanish Squat
description: The Spanish squat uses a resistance band looped around a fixed post at knee height, which the lifter presses the shins against during the squat. This creates a vertical shin angle by preventing the knees from traveling forward, shifting nearly all load to the quadriceps while decompressing the patellar tendon. It is widely used in rehabilitation settings for patellar tendinopathy and knee pain.

execution.starting_position: Loop a heavy resistance band around a fixed post at approximately knee height. Step into the band with both shins pressing against it. Stand with feet hip-width apart, shins vertical against the band.
execution.setup_instructions: Secure a resistance band to a stable vertical post. The band should contact the front of the shins at mid-shin level when you are in your squat position.
steps: Step 1: Press the shins into the band and brace your core.
Step 2: Keeping the shins vertical and pressing against the band, squat straight down.
Step 3: Descend to depth while maintaining an upright torso — the band prevents knees from traveling forward.
Step 4: Drive through the heels to return to standing while maintaining shin contact with the band.
execution.breathing_instructions: Inhale at the top, exhale on the ascent.
common_mistakes: Allowing the knees to drift forward past the band, losing the therapeutic effect
Leaning too far back, shifting load away from the quads
Insufficient depth
safety_considerations: This exercise is used therapeutically — progress load conservatively if treating patellar tendinopathy
Consult a physiotherapist if using for knee rehabilitation
execution.range_of_motion_guidance: Descend as deep as comfortable while maintaining vertical shins and upright torso.
execution.tempo_recommendations: 3-2-1-0 (slow descent with pause) for rehabilitation use. Faster for strength.
coaching_cues: Shins stay vertical
Sit straight down, not back
Press into the band throughout

name: Spider Curl
description: The spider curl is performed lying face-down on an incline bench with the arms hanging vertically, so the elbows are in front of the body throughout the range of motion. This position eliminates momentum from body swing and keeps the biceps under tension at both the stretched and contracted positions. With the shoulder in some extension, the long head of the biceps is under greater tension during the curl compared to standard standing variations.

execution.starting_position: Set an adjustable bench to a 45-60 degree incline. Lie face-down on the bench with the chest resting on the pad and the arms hanging straight down, holding dumbbells (or a barbell) with a supinated grip.
execution.setup_instructions: Set the bench to approximately 45 degrees. Lie prone with the chest at the top edge of the pad. Arms hang straight down — the bench supports the chest, not the arms.
steps: Step 1: Lie face-down on the incline bench. Arms hang vertically with dumbbells in a supinated grip.
Step 2: The upper arms remain vertical and stationary — only the forearms move.
Step 3: Exhale and curl the dumbbells upward, bending only at the elbow until the biceps are fully contracted.
Step 4: Inhale and lower the dumbbells in a controlled motion back to full arm extension, feeling the stretch at the bottom.
execution.breathing_instructions: Exhale on the curl; inhale on the controlled lowering.
common_mistakes: Letting the upper arms swing backward during the curl — they must stay vertical
Using momentum by bouncing at the bottom of the range
safety_considerations: Do not hyperextend the elbows at the bottom
If anterior shoulder discomfort occurs, reduce the bench angle slightly
execution.range_of_motion_guidance: Full elbow extension at the bottom; full bicep contraction at the top.
coaching_cues: Let your arms hang straight down like plumb lines — that is the start position
Feel the stretch at the bottom before curling — do not bounce out of it

name: Spiderman Push-Up
description: The Spiderman push-up adds a knee-to-elbow hip flexion movement to each rep of a standard push-up, simultaneously training the chest, triceps, and hip flexors while demanding greater core stability and rotational control. The lateral leg movement also improves hip mobility and increases the cardiovascular demand.

execution.starting_position: Begin in a standard high plank position with hands slightly wider than shoulder-width and body in a straight line.
execution.setup_instructions: No equipment needed. Find a space long enough for a full plank position.
steps: Step 1: Begin in a high plank, bracing the core.
Step 2: As you lower your chest toward the floor, simultaneously bring one knee out to the side and toward the same-side elbow.
Step 3: Touch or bring the knee as close to the elbow as possible at the bottom of the push-up.
Step 4: Press back up and return the leg to the starting position.
Step 5: Alternate legs each rep or complete all reps on one side before switching.
execution.breathing_instructions: Inhale as you lower down and bring the knee out. Exhale as you press up and return the leg.
common_mistakes: Letting the hip drop on the side of the moving leg
Raising the hip rather than keeping the torso level
Rushing the movement without achieving the knee-to-elbow contact
safety_considerations: Establish solid standard push-up form before adding the leg movement
Move the leg laterally, not forward under the body, to protect the lower back
If hip mobility limits the range, work up to it progressively
execution.range_of_motion_guidance: Full push-up range combined with the knee moving as far toward the elbow as mobility allows. The goal is simultaneous floor contact of the chest and knee-to-elbow approximation.
coaching_cues: Touch knee to elbow at the bottom
Keep the hips level — don't let them swing
One smooth movement: down and knee out, up and leg back

name: Split Jerk
description: The split jerk is the most commonly used jerk technique in Olympic weightlifting competition, in which the athlete drives the bar overhead from the front rack position and catches it with one foot forward and one foot back in a lunge-like split stance. The split position allows a lower catch height and a more stable bilateral base, making it the preferred technique for maximum loads. It requires exceptional bar drive from the legs, quick footwork, and stable overhead positioning.

execution.starting_position: Bar in the front rack position on the shoulders, elbows slightly in front of the bar, feet hip-width apart, torso vertical.
execution.setup_instructions: Received from a clean or taken from the rack. Establish a stable front rack before initiating the dip.
steps: Step 1: Stand with bar in front rack, torso vertical.
Step 2: Dip straight down — bend the knees 10–15 cm while keeping the torso perfectly vertical.
Step 3: Drive explosively upward, pressing the bar off the shoulders and pressing overhead.
Step 4: Simultaneously split the feet — step one foot forward into a lunge, one foot back.
Step 5: Lock out the elbows with the bar over the base of the neck. Recover by stepping front foot back, then back foot forward. Stand to full extension.
execution.breathing_instructions: Deep breath and brace before the dip. Exhale after standing from the split.
common_mistakes: Dipping forward (the torso must remain vertical throughout the dip)
Not splitting the feet far enough — inadequate depth of split
Catching with bent elbows — the lockout must be instantaneous
safety_considerations: Practice the dip-drive and split footwork with an empty bar before loading.
The split stance must be wide enough for a stable catch — a narrow split is a common failure point.
execution.range_of_motion_guidance: Full overhead lockout. Front shin vertical. Back knee slightly bent. Recover to full standing before lowering the bar.
execution.tempo_recommendations: Explosive dip and drive. Fast split. Stable catch before recovery.
coaching_cues: Dip straight — not forward
Drive the bar up — not forward
Split wide and lock out fast

name: Split Jump
description: The split jump is a plyometric lunge variation in which the athlete is in a lunge position, jumps explosively, switches the legs in mid-air, and lands in the opposite lunge. It develops unilateral explosive leg drive, hip flexor and extensor power, and airborne leg switching coordination. The exercise is more demanding than a squat jump due to the asymmetric force production and landing requirements, and is commonly used in sport conditioning and circuit training.

execution.starting_position: Begin in a lunge position — right foot forward, left foot back, both knees bent approximately 90 degrees.
execution.setup_instructions: No equipment needed. Ensure adequate space and a non-slip surface.
steps: Step 1: Begin in a lunge position with the right foot forward.
Step 2: Explosively drive off both feet, jumping as high as possible.
Step 3: Switch legs in the air — left foot comes forward, right foot goes back.
Step 4: Land in the opposite lunge (left foot forward) and absorb through the ankle, knee, and hip.
Step 5: Immediately jump again, switching legs back to the starting configuration.
execution.breathing_instructions: Exhale sharply on each jump. Breathe during brief rest if pausing between reps.
common_mistakes: Not fully extending at takeoff before the leg switch
Landing with the front knee excessively forward past the toes
Collapsing the front knee inward on landing
safety_considerations: High knee stress — ensure good knee tracking in the sagittal plane.
Regress to static lunges then alternating reverse lunges before adding the jump.
execution.range_of_motion_guidance: Full lunge depth on landing — front thigh approaching parallel to floor. Full extension at takeoff.
execution.tempo_recommendations: Continuous alternating jumps. 10–20 reps (5–10 per leg) for conditioning; 6–10 for power.
coaching_cues: Drive up — then switch
Land in a controlled lunge
Front knee stays over the toes

name: Split Squat
description: The split squat is a stationary lunge variation where the feet remain fixed in a staggered stance throughout the set. Unlike a walking or reverse lunge, there is no stepping involved — the lifter descends and ascends repeatedly from the same foot position. This makes it an excellent tool for single-leg strength development with greater stability than other lunge variations and a valuable precursor to the Bulgarian split squat.

execution.starting_position: Take a lunge stride and hold it — one foot forward, one foot back. The rear foot rests on its toes. The torso is upright.
execution.setup_instructions: Adjust stride length so the front shin is roughly vertical when the rear knee is near the floor. Hold dumbbells at the sides or use a barbell on the traps for load.
steps: Step 1: Position the feet in a staggered stance with enough stride length that the front shin stays close to vertical at the bottom.
Step 2: Brace the core. Lower the rear knee toward the floor by bending both the front and rear knee simultaneously.
Step 3: Descend until the rear knee is 1–2 cm above the floor.
Step 4: Drive through the front foot — heel and midfoot — to return to the starting position.
Step 5: Complete all reps on one leg before switching.
execution.breathing_instructions: Inhale as you lower. Exhale as you return to standing.
common_mistakes: Stride too short — front knee drifts far over the toe
Leaning forward excessively — keep the torso upright
Pushing off the rear toes instead of emphasizing the front leg
safety_considerations: Establish balance before adding load
If the front knee is painful, check foot position and reduce stride length
execution.range_of_motion_guidance: Rear knee to within 1–2 cm of floor. Full standing extension at the top.
coaching_cues: Drop the rear knee straight down
Front foot drives the work — not the rear
Keep the torso tall throughout

name: Spoto Press
description: The Spoto Press is a bench press variation where the bar is deliberately stopped one to two inches above the chest rather than touching it. This eliminates the elastic rebound from touching the chest, increasing time under tension at the most mechanically demanding point of the lift and building strength at the sticking point.

execution.starting_position: Lie on a flat bench under a racked barbell. Grip the bar slightly wider than shoulder-width. Unrack and hold the bar at arm's length above the chest.
execution.setup_instructions: Set the bench in a power rack. Position the bar above the lower chest. Retract and depress the shoulder blades firmly into the bench before unracking.
steps: Step 1: Lower the barbell under control toward the lower chest.
Step 2: Stop the bar 1-2 inches above the chest without allowing it to rest or touch.
Step 3: Hold the pause for 1-2 seconds while maintaining full tension throughout the chest and arms.
Step 4: Drive the bar back to the starting position by pressing through the chest and triceps until elbows are fully extended.
execution.breathing_instructions: Inhale and brace the core before lowering. Hold the breath through the pause. Exhale as you press the bar back up.
common_mistakes: Letting the bar drift down and briefly rest on the chest, losing the purpose of the variation
Relaxing tension during the pause instead of maintaining active muscle engagement
Using too much weight relative to full ROM bench press
safety_considerations: Use a power rack with safety bars set just below the sticking point
Start lighter than your full ROM bench press max until the movement pattern is established
execution.range_of_motion_guidance: Full elbow extension at the top; stop 1-2 inches off the chest at the bottom. Do not allow the bar to touch or rest on the sternum.
coaching_cues: Pretend the bar has a hot surface you cannot let touch your chest
Stay tight through the pause — do not relax
Drive the floor away with your feet to maintain leg drive and body position

name: Squat Jump
description: The squat jump is a bilateral plyometric exercise in which the athlete descends to a quarter or half squat and then jumps as high as possible, focusing on maximum vertical displacement. Unlike the box jump, the squat jump lands back on the same surface, making it a continuous or repeated power exercise. It directly trains the explosive leg drive mechanics and vertical power output of the quadriceps, glutes, and calves, and is a foundational drill for athletes requiring vertical power.

execution.starting_position: Stand with feet shoulder-width apart. Arms at sides or hands behind the head.
execution.setup_instructions: No equipment required. Adequate overhead clearance needed.
steps: Step 1: Stand feet shoulder-width apart.
Step 2: Quickly descend to a quarter or half squat while swinging the arms back.
Step 3: Explode upward as powerfully as possible, extending fully through the hips, knees, and ankles and driving the arms upward.
Step 4: Land softly by absorbing through the ankles, knees, and hips back into a squat position.
Step 5: Immediately repeat for continuous reps or pause between for maximum effort reps.
execution.breathing_instructions: Exhale sharply at takeoff. Inhale during the squat descent.
common_mistakes: Not fully extending at takeoff — partial extension significantly reduces jump height
Landing with locked legs — the landing must be absorbed through the lower limb chain
Hesitating at the bottom before jumping — the dip-jump should be one fluid motion
safety_considerations: Adequate warm-up of the ankles, knees, and hips before jumping.
Land on the full foot — not just the toes.
execution.range_of_motion_guidance: Full extension at takeoff. Soft, controlled landing back into a squat position.
execution.tempo_recommendations: Maximum effort. For power: 3–6 reps with full rest. For conditioning: 8–15 reps continuous.
coaching_cues: Dip fast, jump hard
Extend everything — ankle, knee, hip at takeoff
Land soft — quiet feet, bent knees

name: Safety Squat Bar Good Morning — Pause on Pins
alternative_names: Cambered Bar Good Morning Pin Pause
description: A good morning variation performed with a safety squat bar (SSB) and a pause against power rack safety pins at the bottom of the range. The SSB's camber places the load in front of the lifter's center of mass, increasing the moment arm on the lower back compared to a straight bar good morning. The pause against the pins at the bottom eliminates the stretch reflex, requiring the posterior chain to initiate the ascent from a dead stop. This is an advanced posterior chain developer used in powerlifting accessory programming.

execution.starting_position: Set up in a power rack with the safety pins at the height where the SSB bar makes contact when the torso is at approximately parallel to the floor. Load the SSB and unrack it. Stand with feet hip-width, slight knee bend.
execution.setup_instructions: Set the safety pins to touch the bar when the torso reaches the target hinge angle (typically parallel or slightly below). Never let the spine round to reach the pins — set them at the appropriate height for your current flexibility.
steps: Step 1: Unrack the SSB and brace the core. Begin with a slight knee bend.
Step 2: Hinge at the hip, keeping the spine rigid and neutral, until the bar makes contact with the safety pins.
Step 3: Fully relax the bar weight onto the pins for 1-2 seconds (this removes the stretch reflex).
Step 4: Rebrace and drive the hips forward to extend back to standing. The concentric begins from a dead stop.
execution.breathing_instructions: Inhale and brace before hinging. Take a secondary brace during the pause. Exhale forcefully during the ascent.
common_mistakes: Rounding the lower back to reach the pins — set the pins higher if this occurs
Using the bounce off the pins rather than pausing fully
Using the SSB's yoke to assist the lift — the arms should remain relaxed on the bar handles
safety_considerations: This is an advanced exercise requiring a thorough understanding of the hip hinge pattern before loading
Start light — the SSB increases the moment arm compared to straight bar good mornings
Never set pins so low that lumbar rounding is required to reach them
execution.range_of_motion_guidance: Hinge until the bar contacts the pins — this is set by pin height, not by flexibility. Work within a pain-free range.
execution.tempo_recommendations: 3s eccentric, 2s full pause on pins, 2s concentric drive
coaching_cues: Hinge like you're trying to push your hips to the wall behind you — not just bow forward
During the pause: fully release the tension and let the bar rest on the pins before rebuilding your brace
Drive the floor away with the feet to initiate the ascent from the dead stop

name: Stability Ball Dumbbell Bench Press
description: A dumbbell bench press performed while lying on a stability ball instead of a bench. The unstable surface requires the core, glutes, and lower body to work significantly harder to maintain a stable pressing position, turning a chest-focused exercise into a full-body stability challenge. The ball also allows greater shoulder range of motion than a standard bench.

execution.starting_position: Sit on a stability ball and walk forward until the ball is under the upper back and shoulders. Feet flat on the floor, hips extended, body forming a table-top position. Hold dumbbells at chest level.
execution.setup_instructions: Use a fully inflated stability ball appropriately sized for your height. Set up near a wall or rack to retrieve dumbbells safely. Keep feet wide for a more stable base.
steps: Step 1: Position with the ball under the upper back and shoulders, hips high, feet flat and wide. Hold dumbbells at chest level.
Step 2: Press the dumbbells upward to full arm extension above the chest.
Step 3: Lower the dumbbells under control back to the chest, maintaining hip height and ball position.
Step 4: Repeat. Focus on keeping the body table-top rigid throughout.
execution.breathing_instructions: Inhale at the bottom, exhale on the press.
common_mistakes: Hips dropping during the press — keep glutes contracted and hips high
Ball positioned too far down the back — it should support the upper back/shoulders
Using too heavy a weight, losing stability and control of the ball
safety_considerations: Have a spotter hand you the dumbbells once in position, or pick them up carefully by walking back along the ball
Ensure the ball is fully inflated — a soft ball compresses unpredictably
Use a non-slip surface under the ball
execution.range_of_motion_guidance: Full range from chest to full lockout. The ball allows the dumbbells to descend slightly past the chest level for a greater stretch.
coaching_cues: Squeeze your glutes to keep the hips up — a sag transfers load away from the chest
Keep feet wide and planted firmly — your base of support keeps the ball stable

name: Stability Ball Hamstring Rollout
description: A hamstring exercise and hip mobility drill performed with the heels on a stability ball. From a supine bridge position with heels on the ball, the exerciser rolls the ball toward the hips by bending the knees (hamstring curl) and then rolls it back out to full extension. The instability of the ball demands continuous core and hip stabilization, while the leg curl motion provides a hamstring strength stimulus through a range that includes hip extension. Used in both rehabilitation and functional training.

execution.starting_position: Lie on your back with both heels on top of a stability ball. Arms are at the sides for balance. Drive the hips up into a bridge position, forming a straight line from heels to shoulders.
execution.setup_instructions: Use a stability ball sized appropriately for your height (55-65 cm is standard). The ball should be stable and fully inflated.
steps: Step 1: Begin in the supine bridge with heels on the ball and hips elevated.
Step 2: Bend both knees and roll the ball toward the hips, curling the hamstrings.
Step 3: Hold briefly with the ball under the bent knees and hips fully extended.
Step 4: Slowly roll the ball back out to the straight-leg bridge position. Repeat.
execution.breathing_instructions: Exhale as you curl the ball in. Inhale as you roll it back out.
common_mistakes: Letting the hips drop during the rollout — the bridge height must be maintained throughout
Rushing the rollout — the eccentric is where most of the hamstring challenge occurs
Using a ball that is too large or too small for the exerciser's leg length
safety_considerations: If hamstring cramping occurs during the curl, reduce range and stretch between sets
If lower back pain occurs, reduce the bridge height or perform from a modified position
execution.range_of_motion_guidance: Full extension of the leg at the rollout and full knee bend at the curl-in. Hips stay elevated throughout.
coaching_cues: Keep the hips high — squeeze the glutes to prevent hip drop during the rollout
Slow the rollout — that is the most challenging and productive phase
Press the heels into the ball throughout — this keeps the hamstrings engaged

name: Stability Ball Pike and Roll-In
description: A stability ball core and hip flexor exercise in which the exerciser begins in a push-up plank position with shins on the ball and then pikes the hips upward while rolling the ball in toward the hands. The pike position demands significant anterior core compression, hip flexor control, and shoulder stability simultaneously. The unstable ball surface amplifies the demand on all stabilizing muscles throughout the movement.

execution.starting_position: Begin in a push-up plank position with both shins resting on a stability ball and hands on the floor directly under the shoulders.
execution.setup_instructions: Use a fully inflated stability ball. Begin with the ball closer to the knees (less leverage) before advancing to the shins-on-ball position.
steps: Step 1: Begin in the plank with shins on the ball, body in a rigid straight line.
Step 2: Drive the hips upward toward the ceiling, rolling the ball in toward the hands. The body forms a pike (inverted V) at the top.
Step 3: Hold the pike position for 1-2 seconds.
Step 4: Slowly lower the hips and roll the ball back to the starting plank. Repeat.
execution.breathing_instructions: Exhale as you pike the hips up. Inhale as you lower back to plank.
common_mistakes: Collapsing the lower back during the plank between repetitions
Rushing the rollout back to plank — control the return
Not achieving a true pike — hips must rise significantly above shoulder level for proper activation
safety_considerations: Requires shoulder stability and core strength — build both before attempting
If lower back pain occurs on the return to plank, brace the core more firmly or reduce range
execution.range_of_motion_guidance: Full pike with hips significantly above shoulder height. Full plank extension on the return.
execution.tempo_recommendations: 2s pike up, 2s hold, 3s slow rollout return.
coaching_cues: Drive the hips to the ceiling — think of an upside-down V
Keep the arms straight throughout — this is not a push-up
Slow on the way back down — control every inch of the rollout

name: Stability Ball Push-Up
description: A push-up variation performed with both hands on a stability ball, creating an unstable surface that substantially increases the activation demand on the serratus anterior, rotator cuff, and core musculature. Because the ball deforms and shifts, the pectorals and stabilizers must work continuously throughout the movement to maintain position and control.

execution.starting_position: Kneel behind a stability ball and place both hands on top of it, shoulder-width apart. Walk the feet back until the body forms a straight plank with arms extended.
execution.setup_instructions: Inflate the stability ball to full firmness. A harder ball is easier to balance on. Use a ball appropriately sized for your height.
steps: Step 1: Establish a stable plank with hands on ball, feet on floor, body straight.
Step 2: Bend the elbows and slowly lower the chest toward the top of the ball, keeping the ball as still as possible.
Step 3: Descend until chest nearly touches the ball.
Step 4: Press back to full arm extension, maintaining body control and ball stability.
execution.breathing_instructions: Inhale on descent, exhale on the press.
common_mistakes: Placing hands too far apart, reducing stability
Allowing the ball to roll forward or backward without correction
Sagging at the hips or piking — the body must stay rigid
safety_considerations: Ensure ball is fully inflated and on a non-slip surface
Master floor push-ups before transitioning to the ball
execution.range_of_motion_guidance: Lower chest as close to the ball surface as control allows. Ball contact is acceptable but do not rest body weight on ball at bottom.
coaching_cues: Squeeze the ball inward with both hands — this activates serratus and improves stability
Think of making the ball stay perfectly still throughout each rep

name: StairMaster / StepMill Climb
description: The StairMaster or StepMill is a continuously rotating staircase machine that simulates stair climbing, maintaining a constant stepping demand that challenges the quadriceps, gluteus maximus, and calves under a sustained aerobic load. Unlike stair steppers that use a simple up-down piston motion, the StepMill requires the user to clear full steps, producing a greater range of hip and knee flexion and significantly higher glute activation. It provides excellent low-impact cardiovascular conditioning and is widely used for lower body muscular endurance and calorie expenditure.

execution.starting_position: Step onto the machine and hold the rails lightly for balance only. Set the speed to a manageable starting pace (level 6–10). Stand upright with a tall posture.
execution.setup_instructions: Set speed before stepping on. Use the rails only for balance — not to support body weight. Many users hang off the rails, which dramatically reduces the training effect.
steps: Step 1: Begin at a comfortable speed. Step onto each rotating step fully, pressing through the whole foot.
Step 2: Maintain an upright torso. Avoid leaning forward heavily onto the console.
Step 3: Push down and through each step from the glutes and quads. Clear each step completely before it rotates under your foot.
Step 4: Keep the core braced and hips level — avoid excessive lateral sway.
Step 5: Continue for the target duration, adjusting speed as needed.
execution.breathing_instructions: Breathe rhythmically. Aim for a sustainable aerobic pace where breathing is elevated but controlled — a conversational pace is appropriate for steady-state sessions.
common_mistakes: Leaning heavily on the handrails, which shifts load away from the legs and spine
Taking very short half-steps that reduce the hip and knee range of motion
Setting speed too high too quickly before the body has adapted to the movement pattern
safety_considerations: Step fully onto each stair — a partial step increases the risk of slipping
Reduce speed before stepping off the machine
execution.range_of_motion_guidance: Each step should bring the knee to roughly 90° of flexion. Full step clearance is essential — do not shuffle.
execution.tempo_recommendations: Steady-state: 20–40 minutes at a moderate level (8–12). Interval option: 2 minutes at high speed / 1 minute at low speed × 10 rounds.
coaching_cues: Let go of the rails
Step through the full step — do not shuffle
Drive from the glute, not just the quad

name: Standing Ab Wheel Rollout
description: The standing ab wheel rollout is an advanced progression of the kneeling rollout that starts with the athlete fully upright, dramatically increasing the moment arm at the shoulder and hip. The exercise demands elite levels of anti-extension core stiffness, shoulder stability, and lat engagement to prevent collapse of the lumbar spine as the wheel rolls forward. It represents one of the highest anti-extension challenges achievable with minimal equipment and should only be attempted after mastering the kneeling variation.

execution.starting_position: Stand upright holding the ab wheel handles with both hands, wheel on the floor just in front of the feet.
execution.setup_instructions: Only attempt after achieving 15+ controlled kneeling rollouts with full range of motion. Use a non-slip surface.
steps: Step 1: Brace the core maximally. Begin to roll the wheel forward while simultaneously hinging at the hips.
Step 2: Lower the torso toward the floor under strict anti-extension control — do not allow the lumbar spine to hyperextend.
Step 3: Extend forward as far as can be controlled — ideally until the body is nearly horizontal.
Step 4: Pull the wheel back toward the feet by engaging the lats and abs simultaneously, returning to upright.
Step 5: Maintain a hollow-body position throughout — ribs down, pelvis neutral.
execution.breathing_instructions: Inhale and brace before rolling out. Exhale sharply on the return.
common_mistakes: Lumbar hyperextension at the bottom — indicates insufficient core strength for this variation
Failing to engage the lats on the return — the pullback is lat-driven, not just abs
safety_considerations: Stop immediately if lower-back pain occurs — regress to kneeling rollout
execution.range_of_motion_guidance: Roll out as far as can be controlled without lumbar collapse. Full return to standing upright.
execution.tempo_recommendations: 3-1-3-0. Each repetition should be fully deliberate and controlled.
coaching_cues: Ribs to hips — hollow position always
Pull the floor toward you on the way back

name: Standing Cable Chest Press
description: The Standing Cable Chest Press is performed upright with cables set at chest height, pressing both handles forward simultaneously. The standing position engages the core and lower body for stability, while the cables provide continuous tension throughout the entire range of motion — unlike barbells or dumbbells that have varying torque curves. This makes it effective for hypertrophy and functional strength.

execution.starting_position: Set both cable pulleys to chest height. Stand in the center of the cable machine facing away from it. Hold one handle in each hand at chest level, stagger the feet for balance.
execution.setup_instructions: Set both cable adjustable arms or dual-pulley machine to shoulder/chest height. Attach single handles. Stand in the center facing away, cables taut before pressing.
steps: Step 1: Hold handles at chest level with elbows slightly bent.
Step 2: Press both hands forward until arms are fully extended, allowing a slight arc inward.
Step 3: Return under control to starting position, feeling chest stretch.
Step 4: Maintain a staggered foot stance for balance throughout.
execution.breathing_instructions: Exhale as you press forward. Inhale as you return.
common_mistakes: Leaning too far forward, turning it into a core exercise
Locking out elbows with a jerk rather than a controlled press
safety_considerations: Ensure cable clips are secure before pressing
Do not load more than you can control in a standing position
execution.range_of_motion_guidance: Full extension with slight internal rotation at peak; full return to chest level.
coaching_cues: Press forward and let the hands come together slightly at the front
Squeeze the chest at peak extension

name: Standing Cable Chest Press with Band
description: A standing cable chest press with an additional resistance band looped around the user's back and held in both hands alongside the cable handles. The cable provides constant tension throughout the range while the band adds accommodating resistance that increases toward full extension. This dual-resistance combination produces an ascending load curve from the start through the lockout, maximizing stimulus across the entire pressing range simultaneously.

execution.starting_position: Face away from a cable machine with both cables at chest height. Loop a resistance band around your mid-back and hold both ends alongside the cable handles. Stand in a split stance for stability.
execution.setup_instructions: Set both cable pulleys to chest height. Loop the band around the mid-back, gripping both ends with the cable handles in the same hands. Begin with a light band to understand the combined resistance.
steps: Step 1: Face away from the machine, holding cable handles plus band ends, hands at chest level.
Step 2: Press forward, extending both arms. Feel the cable's constant tension and the band's increasing resistance.
Step 3: At full lockout, both cable and band are at maximum tension simultaneously.
Step 4: Return under control against the combined resistance. Repeat.
execution.breathing_instructions: Exhale on the press, inhale on the controlled return.
common_mistakes: Band that is too heavy — the cable already provides significant load; the band is an accent, not the primary load
Leaning forward to escape the combined resistance
Cables set at wrong height for the target muscle angle
safety_considerations: Ensure the band is securely positioned around the back before pressing — a slipped band can cause sudden load change
Start with a light band and assess the combined resistance before increasing
execution.range_of_motion_guidance: Full elbow extension at the top. At the bottom, hands are at chest level with elbows behind the torso plane.
coaching_cues: Press hard all the way to lockout — both resistances combine at the top
Control the return — the double resistance on the way back is significant

name: Standing Cable Hip Abduction — Lateral Lean
description: A hip abduction exercise using a low cable pulley in which the exerciser leans laterally away from the working leg to increase the hip abduction arc and change the angle of the resistance relative to the hip joint. The lean position shifts more of the load onto the gluteus medius and reduces tensor fasciae latae contribution compared to the standard upright cable abduction. Used in gluteus medius isolation programming and hip abductor rehabilitation.

execution.starting_position: Attach an ankle cuff to the right ankle and connect to the left low cable pulley. Stand facing the cable stack with the right ankle crossing over or beside the left. Lean the torso slightly to the right (away from the working leg).
execution.setup_instructions: Hold onto the machine frame or a support with the hand on the side of the working leg. The lean should be approximately 10-20 degrees from vertical.
steps: Step 1: Attach the ankle cuff and lean slightly to the working-leg side. The cable crosses in front of the body.
Step 2: Raise the working leg outward in abduction, moving it away from the midline and slightly behind.
Step 3: Hold the top position for 1-2 seconds, squeezing the outer glute.
Step 4: Lower slowly under control. Repeat, then switch sides.
execution.breathing_instructions: Exhale as you raise the leg. Inhale as you lower.
common_mistakes: Using the lean to gain extra range rather than to change the resistance angle — the lean should be modest and stable
Swinging the leg with momentum — controlled lift only
Using too much weight that forces compensation through the lower back
safety_considerations: The lean requires lateral trunk stability — do not lean so far that balance is compromised
If lower back pain occurs during the leaned position, reduce the lean angle or perform the standard upright version
execution.range_of_motion_guidance: Raise to the point where hip abduction ends — approximately 30-45 degrees from midline.
coaching_cues: Feel the outer glute contracting — not the hip flexors or IT band
The lean should feel like it stretches the glute of the working leg
Slow the return — the eccentric loading through the cable is constant all the way down

name: Standing Cable Incline Press
description: A standing chest press performed with cables set at a low position, pressing upward and forward at an incline angle. This replicates the vector of an incline bench press in a standing, free-movement context. The standing position adds core anti-extension demand while the cable maintains constant tension through the full pressing range, particularly at the top where free weights become lighter.

execution.starting_position: Face away from a cable machine with low pulleys set near the floor. Hold both handles with arms bent, hands at lower chest/hip level. Stand in a split stance for stability.
execution.setup_instructions: Set both low pulleys at the lowest position. Attach single D-handles. Stand far enough from the stack to have taut cables at the bottom of the press.
steps: Step 1: Face away from the machine, cables running from low behind you. Hands at hip/lower chest level, elbows bent.
Step 2: Press the handles forward and upward at an incline angle — toward where a high wall meets the ceiling.
Step 3: Fully extend the arms in the incline press direction.
Step 4: Return under control, following the same angled path back to the starting position.
execution.breathing_instructions: Exhale on the press upward, inhale on the controlled return.
common_mistakes: Pressing straight forward instead of upward at the incline angle
Leaning excessively forward, reducing core engagement
Using too much weight, causing the torso to pitch backward
safety_considerations: Keep the core braced to prevent lower back hyperextension
Use a split stance with the same side forward as the dominant pressing arm for stability
execution.range_of_motion_guidance: Full elbow extension at the top. At the bottom, hands are at lower chest level with elbows bent approximately 90 degrees.
coaching_cues: Press up and out — think incline angle, not flat
Keep the chest tall and proud — do not let the torso collapse forward

name: Standing Cable Kickback
description: A triceps kickback performed standing upright with a low cable pulley attachment. The cable provides constant tension throughout the kickback motion unlike dumbbells which lose tension at the extended position. The standing position requires core stability.

execution.starting_position: Set up for Standing Cable Kickback in the appropriate position.
execution.setup_instructions: Prepare equipment and body position for Standing Cable Kickback.
steps: Step 1: Attach single handle to low pulley. Stand facing cable and hinge forward.
Step 2: Keep upper arm parallel to floor, elbow bent at 90 degrees.
Step 3: Extend elbow to kick arm back to full extension behind body.
Step 4: Hold peak position briefly then return to start.
execution.breathing_instructions: Exhale during the exertion phase, inhale during the return.
common_mistakes: Raising upper arm during extension
Swinging to assist
safety_considerations: Keep joints aligned throughout the movement.
Use controlled weight appropriate for skill level.
execution.range_of_motion_guidance: Move through full range of motion without compromising joint integrity.
coaching_cues: Upper arm stays parallel to floor
Full extension at the back

name: Standing Cable Pullover with Rope
description: The standing cable pullover with a rope attachment allows the hands to pronate and spread at the bottom of the movement, creating a more natural wrist path and greater lat contraction than a straight bar pullover. The rope version is performed facing a high cable with the torso bent slightly forward, drawing the rope from overhead to the thighs in a large arc while maintaining straight elbows.

execution.starting_position: Stand facing a high cable pulley. Attach a rope. Grasp the rope and step back, bending forward slightly at the hips. Arms extended overhead toward the pulley.
execution.setup_instructions: Set the cable to the highest position. Bend forward 20-30 degrees at the hips to allow a fuller arc. Moderate weight.
steps: Step 1: Begin with arms extended overhead, lats stretched.
Step 2: Pull the rope down in a broad arc, keeping elbows straight.
Step 3: As the rope reaches hip level, spread the hands apart slightly.
Step 4: At the bottom, squeeze the lats hard for 1 second.
Step 5: Return under control — the stretch at the top is as important as the contraction.
execution.breathing_instructions: Exhale on the pull. Inhale returning overhead.
common_mistakes: Bending the elbows — this becomes a pulldown, not a pullover
Standing too upright — a slight forward lean increases the range and lat emphasis
safety_considerations: Keep the core braced — a bent-over position with heavy loads stresses the lower back
The shoulder must be healthy to load the overhead stretched position
execution.range_of_motion_guidance: Full overhead stretch to thigh contact at the bottom.
coaching_cues: Spread the rope apart at the bottom to maximize lat contraction
Think of pulling your armpits to your hips
Long arms throughout — no elbow bend

name: Standing Calf Raise
description: The standing calf raise is a plantarflexion exercise performed with extended knees, emphasizing the gastrocnemius. It is typically performed on a calf raise machine or on the edge of a step, and is the primary exercise for developing calf size and plantar flexion strength.

execution.starting_position: Stand on the calf raise platform with the balls of the feet on the edge and heels hanging off. Shoulders under the pads. Knees straight but not locked.
execution.setup_instructions: Adjust pad height so there is slight pressure on the shoulders. Keep knees nearly fully extended throughout.
steps: Lower the heels as far as possible below the platform for a maximum calf stretch.
Press up onto the toes as high as possible, fully contracting the calves.
Hold the peak position for one second, then lower under control.
execution.breathing_instructions: Exhale on the raise, inhale on the descent.
common_mistakes: Bouncing at the bottom, missing the eccentric stretch benefit
Using a partial range of motion — go as far down and up as possible
Bending the knees, which shifts emphasis to the soleus
safety_considerations: Achilles tendon tightness is common — warm up well before heavy sets
execution.range_of_motion_guidance: Full plantar flexion at the top, full dorsiflexion stretch at the bottom.
coaching_cues: Full stretch at the bottom — let the heels drop all the way
Drive up onto the big toe side of the foot at the top

name: Standing Calf Raise on Wedge Board
description: A standing calf raise performed with the heels elevated on a wedge board, which pre-loads the ankle into dorsiflexion before the plantarflexion movement begins. The wedge position places the calf under a greater stretch at the bottom of each repetition and is used in Achilles tendinopathy rehabilitation to bias the soleus and reduce the range demands at the ankle compared to a full-range step calf raise. The wedge reduces the risk of tendon overloading while still providing therapeutic loading.
