execution.starting_position: Stand with both heels on the elevated end of a 15-25 degree wedge board, toes on the lower end. This places the ankle in partial dorsiflexion as the starting position. Hold a wall or bar for balance.
execution.setup_instructions: A foam or wooden wedge board angled between 15-25 degrees is ideal. Alternatively, place a folded mat or wedge under the heels. The steeper the wedge, the more dorsiflexion pre-load.
steps: Step 1: Stand on the wedge with heels elevated, feeling the initial calf stretch from the wedge position.
Step 2: Rise onto the balls of the feet to full plantarflexion.
Step 3: Hold the top position briefly.
Step 4: Lower slowly back to the wedge starting position. The wedge provides the dorsiflexion range; do not go below it.
execution.breathing_instructions: Exhale as you rise onto the toes. Inhale as you lower.
common_mistakes: Letting the heels drop off the back of the wedge — stay on the wedge surface at all times
Using partial range at the top — press to full plantarflexion
Rushing the eccentric — the slow lowering is the therapeutic component
safety_considerations: The wedge reduces the risk of Achilles tendon overload compared to step calf raises, but loading should still be progressed gradually under physiotherapy guidance for rehabilitation
Ensure the wedge is stable and cannot slide
execution.range_of_motion_guidance: Full plantarflexion at the top. Bottom position is defined by the wedge surface — do not force below it.
execution.tempo_recommendations: 2s rise, 1s top hold, 3s slow eccentric lower
coaching_cues: Press through the big toe knuckle at the top of each rep
Slow on the way down — 3 seconds minimum for the lowering phase
Keep the knees straight (for gastrocnemius emphasis) or slightly bent (for soleus emphasis)

name: Stationary / Spin Bike Sprint Intervals
description: Stationary bike sprint intervals use a fixed or spin cycle to perform repeated bouts of maximal pedalling resistance and cadence, separated by low-intensity recovery periods. The seated position eliminates ground-reaction forces, making it a joint-friendly alternative to running-based sprints while still imposing high demand on the quadriceps, gluteus maximus, and cardiovascular system. The resistance dial controls the mechanical load, allowing precise scaling from beginner to elite training intensities.

execution.starting_position: Adjust the seat height so there is a slight bend (5–10°) in the knee at the bottom of the pedal stroke. Adjust the handlebar height for comfort. Clip in or place feet in the cages securely.
execution.setup_instructions: Set resistance at a moderate level for the warm-up. Identify the resistance range for sprint intervals (heavy) and recovery (light) before starting.
steps: Step 1: Warm up for 5 minutes at a comfortable pace with light resistance.
Step 2: Increase resistance to a heavy setting and pedal at maximum cadence (100–120 RPM) for 20–30 seconds.
Step 3: Reduce resistance to minimal and slow cadence to 60–70 RPM for 60–90 seconds recovery.
Step 4: Repeat the sprint-recovery cycle 8–12 times.
Step 5: Cool down for 5 minutes with light resistance and easy pedalling.
execution.breathing_instructions: Breathe forcefully and continuously during sprints. During recovery, focus on slowing the breathing rate by exhaling fully through pursed lips.
common_mistakes: Using too little resistance and spinning the legs at an unsustainable cadence with no load — this produces minimal metabolic stress
Rising out of the saddle during sprints without sufficient resistance, which loads the quads in an inefficient pattern
Skipping the seat height adjustment, which causes knee tracking problems
safety_considerations: Ensure the seat post and handlebar bolts are tightened before each session
If using clip-in cycling shoes, practice unclipping before beginning high-intensity intervals
execution.range_of_motion_guidance: The pedal stroke should feel like a full circle — push down through the front, pull through the bottom, and think about pulling up with the rear foot. This distributes load across quads, hamstrings, and glutes.
execution.tempo_recommendations: Sprint 20–30 seconds at maximum effort. Recover 60–90 seconds at easy effort. 8–12 rounds. Total session 20–30 minutes including warm-up and cool-down.
coaching_cues: Push the pedal through the floor, then scrape mud off the bottom of your shoe
Sit tall — do not collapse the chest onto the handlebars during hard efforts
Heavy resistance makes the sprint productive — light resistance just spins the legs

name: Step-Up
description: The step-up is a unilateral lower body exercise in which the lifter steps onto a raised platform with one foot and drives through that leg to bring the body fully upright on top of the box. It trains single-leg strength and hip stability and closely mimics functional movements such as stair climbing. Load can be added with dumbbells, a barbell, or a weighted vest.

execution.starting_position: Stand facing a box or sturdy bench of appropriate height (typically 30–60 cm). Hold dumbbells at the sides if adding load.
execution.setup_instructions: Choose a box height that challenges but allows the working thigh to be near parallel when the foot is placed on top. A higher box increases glute and hip demand.
steps: Step 1: Place one foot fully on the box — the entire foot, not just the toes.
Step 2: Drive through the heel of the working foot to push the body upright and bring the trailing leg up.
Step 3: Stand tall on top of the box with hips extended and working leg straight.
Step 4: Lower the trailing leg back to the floor in a controlled manner by bending the working knee.
Step 5: Complete all reps on one side before switching.
execution.breathing_instructions: Exhale as you step up. Inhale as you lower down.
common_mistakes: Pushing off the trailing leg — the step-up should be powered entirely by the working leg
Only placing toes on the box, reducing stability
Leaning excessively forward on the way up
safety_considerations: Ensure the box or bench is stable and cannot tip
Step fully onto the box before beginning the drive phase
execution.range_of_motion_guidance: Fully extend the hip and knee at the top. Control the entire descent.
coaching_cues: Drive through the heel, not the toe
Don't push off the back foot — make the front leg do the work
Stand tall at the top — full hip extension

name: Sternum Pull-Up / Gironda Pull-Up
description: The sternum pull-up, popularized by Vince Gironda, requires the lifter to pull the chest all the way to the bar rather than stopping when the chin clears it. The torso leans back throughout the movement, shifting emphasis from the lats to the lower lats, rhomboids, and rear deltoids. It demands greater scapular retraction than a standard pull-up and produces a unique contraction in the mid-back musculature.

execution.starting_position: Hang from a pull-up bar with a shoulder-width overhand grip. Allow the body to hang fully with arms extended.
execution.setup_instructions: Use a bar that allows full hang without the feet touching the floor. Lean the torso back slightly at the start.
steps: Step 1: Begin hanging with an overhand grip slightly wider than shoulder width.
Step 2: Initiate the pull by depressing and retracting the scapulae.
Step 3: Lean the torso back as you pull, aiming to bring the sternum — not the chin — to the bar.
Step 4: At peak contraction, the torso is at approximately 30-45 degrees from vertical and the chest touches or nearly touches the bar.
Step 5: Lower under control, maintaining the leaned-back position until arms are nearly extended, then return to full hang.
execution.breathing_instructions: Exhale as you pull up toward the bar. Inhale during the controlled descent.
common_mistakes: Stopping when the chin clears the bar instead of pulling the chest to the bar
Failing to lean the torso back, reducing mid-back activation
Using momentum rather than controlled muscle contraction
safety_considerations: Requires substantial upper body pulling strength — build standard pull-up proficiency first
Do not force the chest to the bar if shoulder mobility is limited
execution.range_of_motion_guidance: Full hang at the bottom to chest contact with the bar at the top. The extended ROM distinguishes this from a standard pull-up.
coaching_cues: Bring your chest to the bar, not your chin
Lean back as you pull
Squeeze the shoulder blades together at the top

name: Stiff-Leg Deadlift
description: The stiff-leg deadlift is a hip-hinge movement performed with the knees kept nearly fully extended throughout. Unlike the Romanian deadlift — which maintains a consistent slight knee bend — the stiff-leg deadlift allows the bar to travel to the floor, requiring greater lumbar flexion and placing an extreme stretch on the hamstrings. It delivers a powerful hamstring and erector spinae stimulus but demands significant flexibility and careful attention to spinal position.

execution.starting_position: Stand with the barbell on the floor in front of you, feet hip-width apart. Grip the bar with both hands just outside the legs.
execution.setup_instructions: Use a double overhand grip or mixed grip. Lifting straps are appropriate for heavier loads as grip will be a limiting factor at extreme hamstring stretch positions.
steps: Step 1: With knees nearly fully extended (a micro-bend only), hinge forward from the hips and grip the bar.
Step 2: Brace the core and maintain a neutral or slightly extended spine as you lift the bar from the floor to standing.
Step 3: To begin the descent: push the hips back and hinge forward, keeping the knees straight, allowing the bar to travel down the legs.
Step 4: Lower the bar toward or to the floor, allowing the lower back to round slightly at the extreme bottom position if flexibility demands it. The key is a controlled, progressive range.
Step 5: Return to standing by driving the hips forward.
execution.breathing_instructions: Inhale and brace before descent. Hold through the stretch. Exhale as you return to standing.
common_mistakes: Fully locking the knees (hyperextending) — a micro-bend protects the posterior joint
Losing control of the lower back rounding too early in the range (should occur only near the floor)
Rounding the upper back significantly, transferring excessive load to the spine
safety_considerations: This exercise is not appropriate for those with insufficient hamstring flexibility — the Romanian deadlift is a safer alternative
Use moderate loads — the extreme stretch position is mechanically disadvantaged and high-risk under heavy load
execution.range_of_motion_guidance: Lower the bar until hamstring flexibility limits further range or the bar touches the floor, whichever comes first while maintaining acceptable spinal position.
execution.tempo_recommendations: 3-1-1-0 — a slow controlled descent to maximize the hamstring stimulus
coaching_cues: Slight knee bend throughout — never lock the knees
Bar stays close to the legs on the way down
Feel the stretch — don't let the low back take over

name: Stir the Pot
description: Stir the pot is a Swiss ball core stability exercise developed by Dr. Stuart McGill in which the athlete maintains a plank position with forearms on the ball and moves the ball in circles, creating a combined anti-extension and anti-rotation core demand. The unstable surface of the ball dramatically increases muscle activation compared to a floor plank, while the circular motion forces the core to resist motion in multiple planes simultaneously. It is a highly effective anti-movement core exercise for athletes and advanced fitness populations.

execution.starting_position: Kneel behind a Swiss ball and place both forearms on the top of the ball, making fists or clasping hands. Walk the feet back until the body is in a straight plank line from head to feet.
execution.setup_instructions: Use a properly inflated Swiss ball sized for your height (55 cm for shorter individuals, 65 cm for average height, 75 cm for taller). Ensure the ball is on a non-slip surface.
steps: Step 1: Set up in the forearm plank position on the Swiss ball.
Step 2: Brace the entire core and ensure the body forms a straight line.
Step 3: Begin slowly rolling the ball in a small clockwise circle using the forearms.
Step 4: Keep the hips level and the lower back from sagging throughout each circle.
Step 5: Complete the prescribed number of circles in one direction, then reverse direction.
execution.breathing_instructions: Breathe continuously throughout. Maintain the core brace without holding the breath.
common_mistakes: Allowing the hips to sag or pike during the circular motion
Making circles that are too large — start small and increase diameter as strength improves
Rotating the torso rather than keeping it rigid throughout
safety_considerations: Ensure the ball is on a non-slip surface to prevent it rolling away.
Regress to a standard forearm plank if unable to maintain spinal neutrality.
execution.range_of_motion_guidance: Start with small circles (20–30 cm diameter) and progress to larger circles as core strength improves.
execution.tempo_recommendations: 2–3 seconds per circle. Perform 5–10 circles per direction per set.
coaching_cues: Hips stay level — no rocking
Rigid from shoulders to heels
Small, controlled circles first

name: Straight-Arm Pulldown
description: The straight-arm pulldown is a cable isolation exercise that targets the latissimus dorsi without recruiting the biceps, as the elbows remain locked throughout the movement. This makes it an effective tool for developing the mind-muscle connection to the lats and for pre-exhausting or finishing the back without fatiguing the elbow flexors.

execution.starting_position: Stand facing a high-pulley cable machine with feet shoulder-width apart. Grasp a straight bar with both hands shoulder-width apart using a pronated grip. Take a step back and lean forward slightly from the hips, extending the arms overhead so the lats are on stretch.
execution.setup_instructions: Attach a straight bar to the high pulley. Set the weight appropriately — this is an isolation exercise and heavier loads commonly break form. Position yourself far enough from the stack to feel lat tension at the start.
steps: Step 1: Begin with arms fully extended overhead, feeling a stretch in the lats and a slight forward lean at the hips.
Step 2: Lock the elbows — they must not bend at any point during the movement.
Step 3: Drive the bar down toward your thighs in a wide arc by contracting the lats and depressing the shoulder blades.
Step 4: Lower the bar to touch the front of the thighs, maximally contracting the lats.
Step 5: Reverse the motion under control, allowing the arms to rise back to the starting position with the lats fully lengthened.
execution.breathing_instructions: Exhale as you pull the bar down. Inhale as you return to the overhead starting position.
common_mistakes: Bending the elbows — this recruits the biceps and reduces lat isolation
Using trunk flexion rather than lat contraction to drive the bar down
Insufficient range of motion by not allowing the arms to fully extend overhead
safety_considerations: Avoid rounding the lower back — maintain a neutral spine throughout
Do not load this exercise heavily; it is intended for isolation work
execution.range_of_motion_guidance: Full extension overhead at the start to the thighs at the bottom. The arc of movement should be smooth and consistent.
coaching_cues: Pretend your elbows are in a cast — they cannot bend
Lead the movement with the shoulder blades, not the hands
Think of crushing something between your lat and your hip

name: Alternating Straight-Arm Pulldown
description: The alternating straight-arm pulldown performs the movement one arm at a time in alternating fashion from a high cable pulley, keeping constant tension on the lats throughout the set. The alternating rhythm ensures that one side is always under load, increasing total time under tension and providing a brief stretch to each lat while the opposite side contracts.

execution.starting_position: Stand facing a high cable with two single handle attachments (or a wide bar you can use one hand at a time). Grasp one handle in each hand. Arms extended overhead.
execution.setup_instructions: If a single rope is used, perform one complete set on one side then switch. For true alternating, two single handles on separate cables are ideal.
steps: Step 1: Begin with both arms extended overhead.
Step 2: Pull the right arm down in a straight-arm arc to the hip while left remains overhead.
Step 3: Return the right arm as the left pulls down.
Step 4: Alternate continuously for the desired rep count.
Step 5: One rep = one pull each side.
execution.breathing_instructions: Breathe continuously with the alternating rhythm.
common_mistakes: Bending elbows during the pull
Losing the stretch on the extended arm — let it reach fully overhead
safety_considerations: Light loads — this is a mind-muscle connection and stretch-focused exercise
Keep the shoulders away from the ears throughout
execution.range_of_motion_guidance: Full overhead extension to hip level on each arm.
coaching_cues: Keep the working arm straight throughout
Let the resting arm reach overhead fully
Feel the lat on each side independently

name: Straight-Arm Cable Pulldown — Straight Bar
description: The straight-arm pulldown with a straight bar is performed identically to the rope version but with both hands fixed to a rigid bar, keeping the hands in a pronated position throughout. The fixed grip limits the ability to externally rotate the hands at the bottom compared to a rope, but allows for heavier loads and a more consistent pulling path. It is a reliable lat isolation finisher.

execution.starting_position: Attach a straight bar to a high-pulley cable. Stand facing the cable, hinge slightly at the hips, and grip the bar with an overhand grip, arms extended toward the cable.
execution.setup_instructions: Position body 2-3 feet from the cable stack. Slight forward lean increases lat engagement at the top.
steps: Step 1: Stand with arms extended toward the cable at approximately head height, overhand grip on bar.
Step 2: Keeping the arms straight (soft elbow), initiate the pull by contracting the lats.
Step 3: Drive the bar in a downward arc, keeping it close to the body.
Step 4: Finish with the bar pressed against the thighs and lats maximally contracted.
Step 5: Slowly return to start against cable resistance.
execution.breathing_instructions: Exhale on pull, inhale on return.
common_mistakes: Bending the elbows and converting to a pulldown
Swinging the torso to generate momentum
Not fully straightening the arms at the top
safety_considerations: Light isolation load only — do not load this movement heavily
Keep soft bend at elbow to protect the joint
execution.range_of_motion_guidance: Arms extended to roughly head height at the start, bar pressed to thighs at the finish.
coaching_cues: Arms stay straight
Think: lats are pulling, not arms
Full extension at the top before every rep

name: Straight-Arm Cable Pulldown — Rope
description: The straight-arm pulldown with a rope attachment is a lat isolation exercise where the arms remain extended throughout the entire movement, eliminating bicep assistance. The rope allows the hands to separate at the bottom, increasing the range of lat contraction and recruiting the posterior deltoid alongside the lats. It is performed standing, hinging forward slightly at the hips.

execution.starting_position: Attach a rope to a high-pulley cable. Stand facing the cable stack approximately 2-3 feet away, hinge at the hips to 15-30 degrees forward lean. Grip both rope ends with arms extended overhead.
execution.setup_instructions: Set cable to shoulder height or above. The slight forward lean increases lat stretch at the top position.
steps: Step 1: Stand with hips slightly hinged, arms extended up toward the cable.
Step 2: With arms kept straight (soft elbow allowed), initiate movement by pulling the hands down and back.
Step 3: Drive the hands downward in an arc, keeping them close to the body as they pass the hips.
Step 4: At the bottom, separate the rope ends and squeeze the lats hard.
Step 5: Return under control to the starting position with arms extended overhead.
execution.breathing_instructions: Exhale as you pull down, inhale as you return.
common_mistakes: Bending the elbows and turning it into a pulldown rather than a straight-arm movement
Using too much weight, forcing elbow flexion
Not hinging at the hips, reducing lat stretch at the top
safety_considerations: Keep a soft bend in the elbow to avoid hyperextension at the elbow joint
Do not use heavy loads — this is an isolation movement
execution.range_of_motion_guidance: Arms extended overhead at start, pulled to hip level with hands separated at the finish.
coaching_cues: Keep arms straight
Think about tucking your elbows to your pockets
Separate the rope at the bottom to maximize lat contraction

name: Strict Muscle-Up
description: The strict muscle-up is an advanced calisthenics movement requiring the lifter to transition from a dead hang to a straight-arm support position above a bar or rings using controlled pulling and pressing strength — without momentum or kipping. It demands exceptional lat, biceps, and triceps strength alongside scapular and core stability.

execution.starting_position: Hang from a pull-up bar with a false grip (wrists slightly over the bar) and a grip slightly narrower than shoulder width. Body in a hollow position.
execution.setup_instructions: A false grip (wrist over the bar) is critical — it allows the transition from pulling to pressing without re-gripping. Practice the false grip on the bar before attempting a full rep.
steps: Step 1: Begin in a dead hang with a false grip and hollow-body tension.
Step 2: Pull explosively and forcefully, bringing the chest high — above the bar if possible.
Step 3: As the chest clears the bar, aggressively lean the torso forward over the bar.
Step 4: Transition by pressing the bar down as the hips hinge over it, shifting to a support position.
Step 5: Lock out the elbows to reach the dip support position at the top.
Step 6: Lower back through the transition phase under control to the hanging start.
execution.breathing_instructions: Inhale before initiating. Exhale through the pull phase. Hold through the transition.
common_mistakes: Attempting without a false grip — the transition will be impossible without it
Not pulling high enough to initiate the transition over the bar
Using kipping momentum rather than pure strength
safety_considerations: Prerequisites: comfortably perform 15+ pull-ups and 15+ dips before attempting
Build toward this movement with negative muscle-ups and weighted pull-ups
execution.range_of_motion_guidance: Dead hang to full lockout in the support position above the bar.
coaching_cues: Pull the bar to your hips, not your chin
Lean aggressively over the bar during the transition
Think of it as a high pull followed by a triceps press-down

name: Suitcase Carry
description: The suitcase carry is a unilateral loaded carry exercise in which the athlete holds a heavy implement in one hand only and walks while actively resisting the lateral lean that the asymmetric load creates. By requiring the obliques and quadratus lumborum on the opposite side to work isometrically against lateral flexion, it develops anti-lateral flexion core strength that transfers directly to real-world carrying tasks and athletic movements. The challenge is significantly greater than a bilateral farmer's carry due to the asymmetric demand.

execution.starting_position: Stand with a dumbbell or kettlebell held in one hand at your side. Spine tall and neutral, shoulders level.
execution.setup_instructions: Pick up the implement with a hip-hinge. Stand and brace the core before initiating the walk.
steps: Step 1: Pick up the implement in one hand and stand tall.
Step 2: Brace the core and actively keep both shoulders level — resist the urge to lean toward the loaded side.
Step 3: Walk forward at a deliberate pace with short, controlled steps.
Step 4: Maintain a vertical torso throughout — the loaded side should not lower toward the ground.
Step 5: At the end of the distance, set down the implement, rest, and switch sides.
execution.breathing_instructions: Breathe continuously with a moderate brace. Exhale every few steps if needed.
common_mistakes: Leaning toward the loaded side — this is exactly what the exercise is meant to prevent
Shrugging the loaded shoulder upward
Taking overly wide steps that promote excessive trunk sway
safety_considerations: Equal sets and distance must be performed on each side.
Pick up and set down with a proper hip hinge.
execution.range_of_motion_guidance: Walk 20–40 meters per side, or for 30–45 seconds per side.
execution.tempo_recommendations: Controlled walking pace. Prioritize upright posture over walking speed.
coaching_cues: Shoulders stay level — imagine a tray balanced across both shoulders
Carry it like a suitcase, not a leaning tower
Squeeze your core like a corset on the opposite side

name: Suitcase Deadlift
description: The suitcase deadlift is a unilateral variation where a single weight (barbell, dumbbell, or kettlebell) is lifted from the floor at the side of the body, mimicking the action of picking up a heavy suitcase. The offset loading creates a significant lateral anti-flexion demand on the core, requiring the obliques and quadratus lumborum to resist lateral bending throughout the lift. It develops functional carrying strength and core stability simultaneously.

execution.starting_position: Stand with a dumbbell or kettlebell on the floor to one side of the body. The weight is positioned beside the hip, not in front. Feet hip-width apart.
execution.setup_instructions: Begin with a moderate weight — the anti-lateral-flexion demand can be deceiving. Perform equal reps on both sides.
steps: Step 1: Stand with the weight to the right side of the body.
Step 2: Hinge at the hip and bend the knee to reach the weight with the right hand.
Step 3: Brace the core hard and resist the pull to lean toward the weight.
Step 4: Drive through the floor and stand tall, keeping the torso perfectly vertical.
Step 5: Lower under control to the floor. Complete all reps, then switch sides.
execution.breathing_instructions: Brace before each rep. Exhale at lockout.
common_mistakes: Leaning toward the loaded side — the torso must remain vertical throughout
Reaching too far to the side, compromising the hip hinge pattern
Using a weight so heavy that lateral flexion cannot be resisted
safety_considerations: If the torso cannot be kept vertical, reduce the load
Perform equal volume on both sides to prevent asymmetry development
execution.range_of_motion_guidance: Full hip extension at the top. Weight returns to the floor between reps.
coaching_cues: Stand tall — don't lean toward the weight
Carry it like you don't want anyone to notice
Shoulder stays level

name: Suitcase Deadlift with Isometric Hold
description: A single-sided deadlift holding a kettlebell or dumbbell at the side, with an added isometric hold at the top position. The lateral load creates anti-lateral-flexion demand throughout the spine. The hold at the top increases time under tension for the quadratus lumborum and lateral core.

execution.starting_position: Set up for Suitcase Deadlift with Isometric Hold in proper position.
execution.setup_instructions: Prepare body and equipment for Suitcase Deadlift with Isometric Hold.
steps: Step 1: Stand with kettlebell at side. Hinge at hips maintaining neutral spine.
Step 2: Grip kettlebell and stand upright without tilting toward the weight.
Step 3: Hold top position for 3-5 seconds actively resisting the lateral pull.
Step 4: Lower kettlebell back down with hinge pattern.
execution.breathing_instructions: Breathe steadily; never hold breath during static holds.
common_mistakes: Tilting toward the weighted side
Rounding lower back
safety_considerations: Build prerequisite strength before attempting advanced variations.
Stop if joint pain occurs.
execution.range_of_motion_guidance: Full range of motion with control at all times.
coaching_cues: Spine stays vertical despite lateral load
Think tall as you hold

name: Suitcase Squat
alternative_names: Goblet Squat with Dumbbells at Sides
description: A squat variation where dumbbells or kettlebells are held at the sides like suitcases, with arms straight and weights hanging beside the hips. This position increases grip and forearm demand, challenges anti-lateral flexion core stability, and shifts the load distribution slightly compared to a barbell back squat.

execution.starting_position: Stand with feet shoulder-width apart holding a dumbbell or kettlebell in each hand at your sides, arms fully extended.
execution.setup_instructions: Pick up two equally weighted dumbbells from the floor using a hip hinge, stand tall, then assume your squat stance.
steps: Step 1: Brace your core and maintain a neutral spine with the weights hanging at your sides.
Step 2: Push your hips back and bend your knees to lower into a squat, keeping your chest up.
Step 3: Descend until your thighs are at least parallel to the floor.
Step 4: Drive through your heels to stand back up, fully extending your hips and knees.
execution.breathing_instructions: Inhale as you descend into the squat. Exhale on the drive upward.
common_mistakes: Allowing the torso to lean excessively forward
Letting the weights pull the shoulders into uneven height (suitcase lean)
safety_considerations: Keep the weights symmetrical to avoid uneven spinal loading
execution.range_of_motion_guidance: Squat to at least parallel. Heels should remain flat on the floor throughout.
coaching_cues: Stand tall between the weights
Knees track over toes

name: Sumo Deadlift
description: The sumo deadlift is a variation of the conventional deadlift performed with a wide stance and toes pointed significantly outward. The grip is placed inside the legs rather than outside. This stance reduces the range of motion and shifts relative emphasis toward the hip adductors, glutes, and quadriceps compared to the conventional deadlift, while also generally requiring less lower back extension.

execution.starting_position: Stand with feet 1.5 to 2 times shoulder width apart, toes pointed out 45–60 degrees. Grip the bar inside the legs with either a double overhand or mixed grip. Hips lower than conventional, shins more vertical.
execution.setup_instructions: Place the barbell over mid-foot as with the conventional deadlift. The wider stance means the bar can be lifted over a shorter distance.
steps: Squeeze the knees outward, bracing the core hard.
Drive the floor apart with your feet (externally rotate) while lifting the bar.
Keep the bar close to the body — drag it up the inner thighs.
Lock out the hips and knees at the top.
execution.breathing_instructions: Full breath and brace before the pull. Exhale at lockout.
common_mistakes: Knees caving inward — actively push them out in line with the toes
Hips rising faster than the shoulders, turning it into a stiff-leg deadlift
Bar drifting forward away from the body
safety_considerations: Hip mobility is a prerequisite — not suitable if hip external rotation is severely limited
Avoid if groin strain is present
execution.range_of_motion_guidance: Full extension at lockout. Bar starts on the floor.
coaching_cues: Push the floor apart — spread the floor with your feet
Lead with your chest as you lift — do not let the hips shoot up first

name: Sumo Deadlift High Pull
description: The sumo deadlift high pull is a combination movement that begins with a wide-stance deadlift and transitions into an upright row as the bar passes the waist, pulling it up to chin height. It trains the posterior chain through the lower phase and the upper back and shoulders through the pull. The wide stance emphasizes the glutes and inner thighs more than a conventional stance, and the explosive transition between phases develops full-body power. It is a staple movement in CrossFit and functional fitness programming.

execution.starting_position: Stand with feet wider than shoulder-width, toes turned out 30–45°. Barbell over mid-foot. Hinge at the hips and grip the bar with a shoulder-width overhand grip inside the legs.
execution.setup_instructions: Set up like a sumo deadlift — wide stance, bar over mid-foot, hips above knees, chest up. Use a barbell or kettlebell.
steps: Step 1: Set up in a sumo deadlift position — wide stance, overhand grip shoulder-width inside the legs, hips high, chest up.
Step 2: Drive through the floor to initiate the lift — extend the hips and knees simultaneously.
Step 3: As the bar passes the knees and hips reach extension, use the momentum to pull the bar upward in a high pull — elbows flare out and rise above the bar.
Step 4: Pull the bar up to chin height with elbows high and wide.
Step 5: Lower the bar under control back to the starting position.
execution.breathing_instructions: Inhale and brace before the pull. Exhale at the top or during the controlled descent.
common_mistakes: Initiating the high pull too early — the hip extension phase must be completed first
Pulling the bar too far from the body — keep it close throughout
Rounding the lower back at the start
safety_considerations: Requires hip hinge and upright row proficiency before combining
Use moderate loads — the explosive transition limits the weight appropriate for this movement
execution.range_of_motion_guidance: Full hip extension at mid-phase. Bar reaches chin height at the top.
coaching_cues: Push the floor away first — then pull
Elbows high and wide at the top
Keep the bar close — it should travel straight up

name: Sumo Romanian Deadlift
description: A Romanian deadlift performed with a wide sumo stance and toes pointed out. This stance shifts loading emphasis to the adductors, inner hamstrings, and glutes compared to a conventional RDL, and allows a more upright torso while still training the hip hinge pattern under load.

execution.starting_position: Stand with feet wider than shoulder-width, toes pointing outward at 30 to 45 degrees. Grip a barbell with a double-overhand grip, hands inside the knees.
execution.setup_instructions: Set a barbell on a rack or start from the floor in a sumo stance. Feet wide, toes flared, bar over mid-foot.
steps: Step 1: Brace the core and hinge at the hips, keeping the knees in line with the toes.
Step 2: Lower the bar along the inner thighs and legs, feeling the inner hamstrings and adductors stretch.
Step 3: Once a strong stretch is felt through the posterior chain, drive the hips forward.
Step 4: Extend the hips fully and squeeze the glutes at the top.
execution.breathing_instructions: Inhale and brace before hinging. Exhale on the drive to standing.
common_mistakes: Allowing the knees to cave inward during the movement
Rounding the lower back at the bottom
safety_considerations: Ensure the knees track in line with the toes throughout the movement
execution.range_of_motion_guidance: Lower until a strong hamstring and inner thigh stretch is felt. Full hip extension at the top.
coaching_cues: Push the knees out in line with the toes
Feel the stretch in the inner hamstrings

name: Sumo Squat
description: The sumo squat uses a significantly wider stance than a conventional squat with the toes pointed outward at approximately 45°. The wide stance shifts the loading emphasis toward the inner thigh adductors and gluteus maximus, while reducing the range of motion required at the ankle. It is accessible to those with limited ankle dorsiflexion and provides a unique adductor stimulus absent from standard squatting variations. It can be performed with a dumbbell, kettlebell, or barbell.

execution.starting_position: Stand with feet much wider than shoulder-width, toes pointed out 30–45°. Hold a dumbbell or kettlebell vertically with both hands between the legs if adding load.
execution.setup_instructions: Foot width depends on hip structure and mobility — start with feet twice shoulder-width and adjust. Toes should point in the same direction as the knees.
steps: Step 1: Stand with wide stance, toes pointed out. Hold weight if applicable. Core braced.
Step 2: Descend by pushing the knees out in line with the toes while sitting the hips directly down.
Step 3: Descend until the thighs are parallel to the floor. The wide stance allows the torso to remain upright.
Step 4: Drive through both feet to return to standing, squeezing the glutes and inner thighs at the top.
Step 5: Exhale at the top.
execution.breathing_instructions: Inhale before descent. Exhale as you return to standing.
common_mistakes: Knees caving inward (valgus) during descent — actively push knees out over the toes
Leaning excessively forward despite the wide stance — the sumo squat should allow a more upright torso
Feet positioned so the toes point further out than the knees
safety_considerations: Ensure hip external rotator flexibility before using a very wide stance
If knees are painful in the wide-stance position, reduce foot width
execution.range_of_motion_guidance: Aim for parallel or below while keeping the spine neutral. The wide stance often allows greater depth without lumbar rounding.
coaching_cues: Knees track over the pinky toe
Drop straight down — don't let the torso pitch forward
Squeeze the glutes and inner thighs to stand

name: Supine Bridge March
description: The supine bridge march builds on the standard glute bridge by adding a single-leg marching component. While maintaining a bridge position with both hips elevated, one foot is lifted from the floor and the knee drawn toward the chest, then returned before alternating sides. This challenges the stance-side glute maximally as a hip stabilizer against rotational and lateral forces, making it a critical rehabilitation exercise for hip, knee, and lower back programs.

execution.starting_position: Lie on your back with knees bent and feet flat on the floor hip-width apart. Drive through both heels to raise the hips into a standard bridge position, with a straight line from knees through hips to shoulders.
execution.setup_instructions: No equipment needed. A mat is recommended for comfort. Ensure a stable surface without slipping.
steps: Step 1: Establish the bridge position with hips fully extended and both feet on the floor.
Step 2: While maintaining the bridge height, slowly lift one foot and draw the knee toward the chest, aiming for 90 degrees of hip flexion.
Step 3: Hold briefly, then lower the foot back to the floor without letting the hips drop.
Step 4: Alternate sides. Each knee lift equals one repetition.
execution.breathing_instructions: Exhale as you lift the knee. Inhale as you return the foot to the floor.
common_mistakes: Letting the hips drop or rotate when one foot leaves the floor — the bridge must stay level
Lifting the foot too fast and losing core bracing
Hyperextending the lower back instead of maintaining neutral spine in the bridge
safety_considerations: If the lower back arches excessively, reduce the bridge height or practice the standard bridge first
Avoid if single-leg hip loading is contraindicated — consult a physiotherapist
execution.range_of_motion_guidance: The marching knee should reach 80-90 degrees of hip flexion. The hips must remain level throughout.
execution.tempo_recommendations: 2s lift, 1s hold, 2s lower. Alternate sides with no rest between.
coaching_cues: Keep the hips level — imagine a glass of water on each hip bone that cannot spill
Press the standing foot into the floor to maximize glute activation on the stance side
Brace the core before you lift the foot — do not let the back arch

name: Supine Neck Bridge
description: The supine neck bridge is performed face-up with the back of the head on the floor, body arched so that the weight is supported through the head and feet, loading the posterior cervical musculature and spinal erectors with significant bodyweight force. It develops exceptional posterior neck strength and spinal flexibility through the held arc position. The supine bridge is a staple conditioning exercise in wrestling, judo, and gymnastics and represents a high-level isometric training stimulus for posterior cervical strength.

execution.starting_position: Lie flat on the back on a mat with knees bent. Place the back of the head flat on the mat. Drive through the feet and the back of the head to push the hips and torso into an arched bridge position.
execution.setup_instructions: This is an ADVANCED exercise. Extensive progressive neck training over months is required before attempting. Begin with hand-assisted holds and progress over time.
steps: Step 1: Lie on the back with knees bent, back of the head flat on the mat.
Step 2: Drive through the feet and push through the head to lift the hips and torso into a bridge.
Step 3: Use the hands to assist and control how much weight transfers through the neck.
Step 4: Hold the bridge position for the target duration with as little hand assistance as the neck allows.
Step 5: Lower under control, using the hands to assist the return.
execution.breathing_instructions: Breathe normally during the held position.
common_mistakes: Attempting without adequate progressive neck training history
Forcing the hold without hand assistance before the neck is ready
Using an overly arched spinal position that strains the lumbar spine
safety_considerations: Contraindicated with any cervical pathology, disc issues, or cervical instability
Must be preceded by consistent progressive neck training over months
Always use significant hand assistance initially
Any pain = immediately return to the floor
execution.range_of_motion_guidance: Isometric bridge hold — no movement through range.
execution.tempo_recommendations: Isometric hold: 10-30 seconds with hand assistance as needed
coaching_cues: Use your hands as much as you need — build the neck first
Hips high — don't sag
Any neck pain = done for the day

name: Standing Dumbbell Svend Press
description: The Svend Press (named after Norwegian strongman Svend Karlsen) involves holding a weight plate or two dumbbells pressed together at chest height and extending the arms straight forward, then returning them back to the chest. The constant inward squeezing force activates the medial pectoral fibers through continuous adduction, making it an effective isolation finisher for the inner chest.

execution.starting_position: Stand upright holding two dumbbells or a weight plate pressed firmly together at chest height with both palms facing each other.
execution.setup_instructions: Use a light weight plate (5-10kg) or two light dumbbells. The load is deceptively light because constant adduction is tiring. Stand with feet shoulder-width apart.
steps: Step 1: Hold the weight pressed together at the chest with both hands, palms facing inward.
Step 2: Squeeze hard and slowly extend the arms forward until fully stretched in front of the chest.
Step 3: Maintain the squeeze and slowly return the weight back to the chest.
Step 4: Repeat without releasing the squeeze.
execution.breathing_instructions: Exhale as arms extend forward. Inhale as they return to the chest.
common_mistakes: Using too heavy a weight, breaking the squeeze
Allowing the elbows to bend rather than pressing straight forward
safety_considerations: Very light loads are appropriate — this is a finishing exercise, not a primary mover
Avoid if shoulder impingement is present
execution.range_of_motion_guidance: Arms extend fully forward to shoulder height; return to light chest contact.
coaching_cues: Squeeze as hard as you can throughout the entire rep
Think 'keep the plate from falling' by pressing inward the entire time

name: Swiss Ball Bench Dips
description: A variation of bench dips with feet elevated on a Swiss ball, adding instability that challenges core engagement and tricep recruitment. The unstable surface of the ball increases the balance demand while maintaining tricep-focused loading.

execution.starting_position: Set up for Swiss Ball Bench Dips in the appropriate position.
execution.setup_instructions: Prepare equipment and body position for Swiss Ball Bench Dips.
steps: Step 1: Place hands on bench edge behind, rest heels on Swiss ball.
Step 2: Slide hips off bench and lower body by bending elbows.
Step 3: Descend until upper arms are parallel to floor.
Step 4: Press through hands to return to starting position.
execution.breathing_instructions: Exhale during the exertion phase, inhale during the return.
common_mistakes: Letting elbows flare
Dropping too quickly
safety_considerations: Keep joints aligned throughout the movement.
Use controlled weight appropriate for skill level.
execution.range_of_motion_guidance: Move through full range of motion without compromising joint integrity.
coaching_cues: Keep hips close to bench
Engage core to stabilize ball

name: Swiss Ball Knees-to-Chest Push-Up
description: A dynamic push-up variation where the feet rest on a swiss ball and each repetition is paired with a knee tuck that rolls the ball toward the chest. The push-up phase loads the pectoralis major and triceps while the knee tuck activates the hip flexors and rectus abdominis in a compound, full-body movement. The alternating push-and-tuck pattern creates a unique time-under-tension pattern and high core demand.

execution.starting_position: Begin in a push-up plank with shins/feet resting on top of a swiss ball, hands on the floor. Body forms a straight line.
execution.setup_instructions: Fully inflate the ball. Place the ball directly behind and position shins on top. Ensure non-slip floor surface. The ball should be directly under the lower legs at the start.
steps: Step 1: Establish the plank position with shins on the ball, hands shoulder-width on floor.
Step 2: Perform a push-up: lower the chest toward the floor.
Step 3: As you press back up, simultaneously tuck the knees toward the chest by rolling the ball forward.
Step 4: At the top of the push-up, knees are tucked and ball is near the hands.
Step 5: Extend the legs back out, rolling the ball to the start. That is one rep.
execution.breathing_instructions: Inhale on the descent, exhale as you press and tuck simultaneously.
common_mistakes: Tucking the knees before completing the push-up — the two movements should be coordinated
Ball rolling sideways due to uneven pressure from the feet
Hips rising too high during the tuck, reducing the push-up challenge
safety_considerations: Master swiss ball plank and standard swiss ball push-ups before adding the tuck
Start with partial knee tucks until coordination is established
Ensure ball is fully inflated and on a non-slip surface
execution.range_of_motion_guidance: Full push-up depth and full knee tuck — knees near the chest at the top of the press.
execution.tempo_recommendations: 2-0-2-1 (2s down, coordinated press and tuck, 1s reset)
coaching_cues: Press and tuck at the same time — they happen together
Roll the ball with control — the hip flexors drive the tuck, the chest drives the press

name: Swiss Ball Leg Curl
description: The Swiss ball leg curl is a bodyweight hamstring exercise performed with the heels resting on a stability ball. The lifter begins in a supine bridge position, then curls the ball toward the hips using knee flexion while maintaining a hip bridge. The instability of the ball increases glute and core activation compared to a lying machine curl. It is an accessible exercise requiring no gym equipment beyond a stability ball.

execution.starting_position: Lie on your back. Place both heels on a Swiss ball with legs extended. Arms by sides or slightly out for stability.
execution.setup_instructions: Inflate the Swiss ball to firm. Place it on a non-slip surface. Lie supine with heels on the ball.
steps: Step 1: Drive the hips up into a bridge position, body forming a straight line from shoulders to heels.
Step 2: While maintaining the hip bridge, curl the ball toward your hips by bending the knees.
Step 3: Pull the ball until the knees are at approximately 90 degrees.
Step 4: Extend the knees to roll the ball back out, maintaining the hip bridge throughout.
execution.breathing_instructions: Exhale on the curl, inhale on the extension.
common_mistakes: Hips dropping during the curl, losing the bridge position
Ball rolling to one side due to uneven foot pressure
Rushing the eccentric extension
safety_considerations: Ensure the ball is on a non-slip surface
Keep the core braced throughout to protect the lumbar spine
execution.range_of_motion_guidance: Full leg extension at the start, curl to 90 degrees or more of knee flexion.
coaching_cues: Hips stay high throughout
Curl the ball with your heels
Control the roll back out

name: Swiss Ball Push-Up with Feet Elevated
description: An advanced push-up variation combining both hands on a swiss ball with feet elevated on a bench or box. The simultaneous unstable hand surface and decline body angle increases upper chest activation and dramatically elevates the demand on rotator cuff and serratus anterior stabilizers. This combination requires high levels of shoulder stability, core rigidity, and proprioceptive control.

execution.starting_position: Place both hands on a fully inflated swiss ball and walk feet back onto a bench, creating a decline position. Arms extended, body in a straight line from feet to shoulders.
execution.setup_instructions: Position the bench behind and the swiss ball in front. The decline angle should be 15–30 degrees. Fully inflate the ball for maximum stability.
steps: Step 1: Establish the starting plank position with hands on ball, feet elevated on bench.
Step 2: Slowly lower the chest toward the ball, keeping the ball as still as possible.
Step 3: Descend until the chest nearly touches the ball top.
Step 4: Press back to full arm extension. Throughout, keep the core braced and ball controlled.
execution.breathing_instructions: Inhale on descent, exhale on press.
common_mistakes: Attempting before mastering flat swiss ball push-ups
Allowing the ball to roll due to uneven hand pressure
Hips rising in a pike — maintain the straight declining line
safety_considerations: Have a stable bench of appropriate height; too high creates excessive shoulder stress
Ensure ball is on a non-slip surface
Master each progression (flat floor push-up → swiss ball push-up → elevated feet) before combining
execution.range_of_motion_guidance: Full depth to near-chest-on-ball, full lockout at top.
coaching_cues: Squeeze the ball inward to stabilize it and activate the serratus
Think of the ball as frozen in place — your job is to keep it there

name: Swiss Ball Push-Up Single-Leg
description: A swiss ball push-up performed with one foot lifted, reducing the base of support and dramatically increasing the demand on the core and hip stabilizers. The combination of the unstable ball surface and the single-leg stance requires sophisticated total-body coordination while still loading the pectoralis major and triceps through the pressing movement.

execution.starting_position: Begin in swiss ball push-up position (both hands on ball, both feet on floor, body in a plank). Lift one foot off the floor before beginning.
execution.setup_instructions: Fully inflate the ball. Place it on a non-slip surface. Master two-leg swiss ball push-ups before attempting this variation.
steps: Step 1: Establish the swiss ball plank with one foot lifted — the lifted leg is held straight and slightly elevated.
Step 2: Lower the chest toward the ball top, maintaining body control.
Step 3: Descend until the chest nearly touches the ball.
Step 4: Press back to the starting position. Maintain the single-leg balance throughout. Complete all reps then switch which leg is raised.
execution.breathing_instructions: Inhale on descent, exhale on press.
common_mistakes: Hips rotating toward the lifted leg — keep them square
Attempting before mastering two-leg swiss ball push-ups
Placing the hands too far apart on the ball — keep them central on the ball top
safety_considerations: Fully inflate the ball — a soft ball deforms unpredictably under single-leg load
Have the ball against a wall as a stop if needed during learning
execution.range_of_motion_guidance: Full push-up range, same as two-leg version.
coaching_cues: The lifted leg is held still — do not let it swing or sway
Squeeze the ball inward with both hands to maximize shoulder stability

name: Multi-Grip / Swiss Bar Bench Press
description: The Swiss Bar (also called a football bar or multi-grip bar) allows the bench press to be performed with a neutral or angled grip rather than a fully pronated grip. This reduces stress on the wrists, elbows, and shoulder joints while maintaining the pectoral and triceps training stimulus, making it a preferred alternative for lifters with joint pain or shoulder impingement issues.

execution.starting_position: Load the Swiss bar onto the rack hooks. Lie on the bench and select the neutral or angled grip handles. Grip width approximately shoulder-width.
execution.setup_instructions: Set the rack hooks at appropriate height for a bench press. The Swiss bar's design places the grip handles facing each other (neutral) or at a slight angle. No adjustments to technique are needed beyond the grip change.
steps: Step 1: Unrack the Swiss bar and hold it above the chest.
Step 2: Lower the bar under control to the chest.
Step 3: Touch the lower chest and press back to the starting position.
Step 4: Maintain a neutral wrist position throughout.
execution.breathing_instructions: Inhale and brace before lowering. Exhale at the top.
common_mistakes: Letting the wrists roll or bend during the press
Using too close a grip handle, which shifts load excessively to the triceps
safety_considerations: Confirm the Swiss bar is compatible with your rack's hook spacing before use
Start lighter than your straight bar bench — the neutral grip changes the leverages slightly
execution.range_of_motion_guidance: Full ROM from chest-touch to lockout.
coaching_cues: Palms face each other — keep them facing each other throughout
Drive the elbows down and in rather than flaring wide

name: Swiss Bar Overhead Press
description: The Swiss bar overhead press uses a multi-grip bar to press overhead with the hands in a neutral (palms facing each other) or semi-pronated grip, reducing the degree of shoulder external rotation required at the bottom position compared to a standard straight barbell. This reduces impingement risk in athletes with limited shoulder mobility or existing rotator cuff irritation while still allowing heavy overhead pressing loads. The neutral grip also shifts some emphasis toward the anterior deltoid and long head of the triceps.

execution.starting_position: Set the Swiss bar in a rack at upper-chest height. Grip the neutral handles. Unrack and hold at shoulder height with elbows slightly forward of the bar.
execution.setup_instructions: Set up like a standard overhead press. The neutral grip handles will be at approximately shoulder width.
steps: Step 1: Begin with the bar at shoulder height, elbows forward.
Step 2: Press the bar straight overhead, extending the arms fully.
Step 3: At lockout, the bar is directly over the base of the skull.
Step 4: Lower under control back to the starting position.
Step 5: Repeat.
execution.breathing_instructions: Inhale and brace before pressing. Exhale at the top or through the press.
common_mistakes: Flaring the elbows wide — with the neutral grip, elbows should stay close to 45 degrees from the torso
Leaning excessively backward under load
safety_considerations: Learn the standard barbell overhead press before switching to the Swiss bar
Use for rehabilitation from shoulder impingement — the neutral grip is gentler on the glenohumeral joint
execution.range_of_motion_guidance: Shoulder height to full overhead lockout.
coaching_cues: Neutral grip — palms face each other
Elbows slightly forward — 45 degrees from the torso
Lock out fully overhead

name: T-Bar Row
description: The T-bar row is a horizontal pulling exercise in which one end of a barbell is anchored and the loaded end is rowed toward the chest in a bent-over position. The angled bar path and neutral or close grip emphasize the mid-back and lats, and the fixed anchor allows for significant loading with relatively lower spinal stress than a free barbell row.

execution.starting_position: Stand astride the barbell with one end anchored. Hinge at the hips to approximately 45 degrees with a neutral spine. Grip the close-grip handle or the bar itself just inside the loaded end.
execution.setup_instructions: Place a landmine anchor (or wedge a barbell into a corner). Attach weight plates to the free end. Use a close-grip attachment or a V-bar over the bar if available.
steps: With a braced core and hinged position, row the barbell toward your chest.
Drive the elbows behind the torso and squeeze the mid-back at the peak.
Lower under control until the arms are fully extended.
execution.breathing_instructions: Exhale on the row, inhale on the descent.
common_mistakes: Standing too upright, reducing back activation
Using momentum by bobbing the torso up and down
safety_considerations: Maintain a neutral spine — do not round the lower back under heavy load
execution.range_of_motion_guidance: Full arm extension at the bottom, plates touch or near-touch the chest at the top.
coaching_cues: Hinge like a hinge door — keep the angle consistent
Squeeze your back like you are cracking a walnut between your shoulder blades

name: Tate Press
description: The Tate press is a dumbbell tricep exercise where the elbows flare outward and the dumbbells are lowered toward the chest with the forearms folding down, then pressed back up. Named after powerlifter Dave Tate, this movement keeps the upper arms stationary with elbows high and wide, creating a unique load angle that targets the medial and lateral tricep heads. The exercise is performed lying on a bench and is used heavily by powerlifters for tricep accessory work.

execution.starting_position: Lie on a flat bench. Hold a dumbbell in each hand with the dumbbells touching above the chest, palms facing away (pronated). Elbows pointing out to the sides.
execution.setup_instructions: Begin with the dumbbells at the top position, touching above the chest. The elbows should be high and pointing outward throughout.
steps: Step 1: Begin with dumbbells above the chest, elbows pointing to the sides.
Step 2: Lower the dumbbells by bending the elbows, letting the forearms fold down toward the chest.
Step 3: The dumbbells lower toward the chest while the elbows stay high and pointed out.
Step 4: Extend the elbows to press the dumbbells back to the starting position.
execution.breathing_instructions: Inhale on descent, exhale on press.
common_mistakes: Elbows dropping toward the body (this becomes a press rather than a Tate press)
Rotating the hands during the movement
safety_considerations: Use moderate weight — the flared elbow position is not suitable for heavy loads
execution.range_of_motion_guidance: Dumbbells lower to chest level, full extension at the top.
coaching_cues: Elbows stay high and wide
Forearms fold down — not the elbows
Squeeze at the top

name: Tate Press Heavy
description: The Tate press performed with heavy dumbbells to build maximum triceps strength. This version prioritizes strength gains over pump, using weights that allow only 3-6 reps with strict form. The flared elbow position and heavy load build dense tricep tissue.

execution.starting_position: Set up for Tate Press Heavy in the appropriate position.
execution.setup_instructions: Prepare equipment and body position for Tate Press Heavy.
steps: Step 1: Select heavy dumbbells. Lie on bench with elbows flared wide.
Step 2: Hold dumbbells at chest height with elbows pointing outward.
Step 3: Press dumbbells straight up by extending elbows fully.
Step 4: Lower slowly back to chest maintaining flared elbows.
execution.breathing_instructions: Exhale during the exertion phase, inhale during the return.
common_mistakes: Closing elbows inward with heavy weight
Partial range of motion
safety_considerations: Keep joints aligned throughout the movement.
Use controlled weight appropriate for skill level.
execution.range_of_motion_guidance: Move through full range of motion without compromising joint integrity.
coaching_cues: Maintain the flare even with heavy weight
Full lockout required

name: Terminal Knee Extension
description: Terminal knee extension (TKE) is a rehabilitation exercise that strengthens the quadriceps specifically in the final degrees of knee extension (from about 30 degrees to full extension). Using a resistance band anchored behind the knee, the exercise targets the VMO (vastus medialis oblique) and the final-range quad strength that is critical for knee stability. It is a standard exercise in ACL rehabilitation, patellar tendinopathy management, and post-surgical knee recovery.

execution.starting_position: Anchor the resistance band loop at knee height behind you. Loop the band around the back of one knee. Stand facing away from the anchor with the band behind the working knee.
execution.setup_instructions: Anchor the band at a rack or door frame at approximately knee height. The band pulls the knee into slight flexion.
steps: Step 1: Face away from the band anchor, loop the band behind the working knee.
Step 2: Stand on the working leg with a slight knee bend (10–30 degrees). The band will pull the knee into further flexion.
Step 3: Straighten the knee fully against the band's resistance, contracting the quadriceps hard at full extension.
Step 4: Hold the fully extended position for 1–2 seconds.
Step 5: Slowly allow the band to flex the knee back to the starting position with control.
execution.breathing_instructions: Exhale as the knee extends. Inhale as it returns.
common_mistakes: Hyperextending the knee forcefully — extend to neutral, not beyond
Using momentum rather than a controlled quad contraction
Letting the hip drop on the non-working side
safety_considerations: Safe for most post-surgical knee populations when cleared by a clinician
Avoid hyperextension if the patient has posterior capsule or PCL involvement
execution.range_of_motion_guidance: From 30 degrees of flexion to full extension. Focus on the terminal range — the last 15–20 degrees.
coaching_cues: Squeeze the quad hard at full lockout
Straighten the knee without snapping it back
Feel the inside of your thigh (VMO) fire at full extension

name: Terminal Knee Extension with Band
description: Terminal knee extension with a resistance band targets the final degrees of knee extension, emphasizing the vastus medialis oblique (VMO). A band is anchored behind the knee, and the exerciser extends the knee against the band's pull from a slightly flexed position. This exercise is widely used in knee rehabilitation protocols following injury or surgery to restore quadriceps activation and patellar tracking.

execution.starting_position: Anchor a resistance band to a fixed point behind you at knee height. Stand facing away and loop the band behind one knee. Begin with that knee slightly flexed, weight on the working leg.
execution.setup_instructions: Secure a resistance band at approximately knee height to a squat rack or door anchor. Stand far enough from the anchor that the band provides tension when the knee is at 15-20 degrees of flexion.
steps: Step 1: Stand facing away from the anchor with the band behind your knee, maintaining a slight forward lean if needed for balance.
Step 2: Begin with the knee bent approximately 20 degrees against band resistance.
Step 3: Contract the quadriceps to fully extend the knee to lockout, squeezing the VMO.
Step 4: Slowly return to the starting flexed position under control. Repeat.
execution.breathing_instructions: Exhale as you extend the knee to lockout. Inhale as you return to the flexed starting position.
common_mistakes: Allowing the knee to drift inward (valgus) during extension
Using momentum rather than controlled muscle contraction
Not fully extending to lockout — partial extension misses the VMO stimulus
safety_considerations: Consult a physiotherapist before using this exercise for post-surgical rehabilitation
Do not perform with acute joint swelling
Keep the movement slow and controlled throughout
execution.range_of_motion_guidance: Work through approximately 20 degrees of flexion to full extension. Focus quality on the last 10-15 degrees where VMO activation peaks.
execution.tempo_recommendations: 2-0-2-1 (2s flex, no pause, 2s extend, 1s squeeze at lockout)
coaching_cues: Feel the inner quad contract at lockout
Drive the heel into the floor as you extend
Do not hyperextend the knee — stop at neutral

name: Thick-Grip Deadlift / Fat Bar Deadlift
description: The thick-grip deadlift is performed with a barbell that has a diameter much larger than a standard bar (typically 50-65mm vs 28mm), or with thick grip sleeves applied to a standard bar. The larger diameter prevents the fingers from wrapping fully around the bar, dramatically increasing grip strength demand. The movement itself is identical to a standard deadlift, but grip becomes the primary limiting factor rather than leg or back strength.

execution.starting_position: Approach the thick-bar deadlift set up at floor height. Stand with feet hip-width, bar over mid-foot. Grip the bar double overhand — no hook grip, no straps.
execution.setup_instructions: Fat bar or axle is preferred. Alternatively use thick grip sleeves on a standard bar. No chalk removal — the thick grip is intentional.
steps: Step 1: Set up as a conventional deadlift — hinge at the hips, flat back, lats tight.
Step 2: Grip the thick bar as hard as possible — it will not feel fully locked.
Step 3: Drive the floor away, maintaining back position, until standing erect.
Step 4: Lower the bar under control back to the floor.
execution.breathing_instructions: Deep breath and brace before the pull, exhale at lockout.
common_mistakes: Using standard bar with straps (negates the grip demand)
Dropping the bar without control
safety_considerations: The thick bar will slip more easily than standard — maintain maximum grip tension throughout
execution.range_of_motion_guidance: Floor to full hip and knee lockout.
coaching_cues: Grip is the point — squeeze everything
Same cues as a standard deadlift
No straps, no hook grip

name: Thoracic Extension over Foam Roller
description: Thoracic extension over a foam roller is a passive mobilization technique for improving thoracic spine extension range of motion. The foam roller is placed horizontally across the mid-back, and the person drapes the thoracic spine over it into extension, targeting stiffness from prolonged sitting, upper crossed syndrome, and thoracic kyphosis. It is used in posture correction programs, shoulder rehabilitation, and as a preparatory drill before overhead pressing.

execution.starting_position: Place the foam roller horizontally on the floor. Sit in front of it and gently recline so the roller sits across the mid-thoracic spine (between the shoulder blades, approximately T4–T8).
execution.setup_instructions: Use a full-length foam roller. Support the head with the hands clasped behind it.
steps: Step 1: Sit on the floor in front of the foam roller with knees bent and feet flat.
Step 2: Recline so the foam roller contacts the mid-thoracic spine between the shoulder blades.
Step 3: Support the head by interlacing the fingers behind it. Keep the elbows wide.
Step 4: Gently drape the upper back over the roller, allowing thoracic extension. Hold 5–10 seconds.
Step 5: Use the feet to shift the roller up or down one vertebral segment and repeat, working from the lower to upper thoracic spine.
execution.breathing_instructions: Take a deep inhale, then exhale fully, relaxing into extension on the exhale.
common_mistakes: Placing the roller on the lumbar spine — keep it on the thoracic spine only (between the shoulder blades)
Pulling the head forward with the hands rather than supporting it
Forcing the extension aggressively — allow gravity to produce the mobilization
safety_considerations: Do not use on the lumbar spine
If sharp pain occurs in the spine, stop immediately — this indicates possible facet joint issue
Osteoporosis patients should consult a clinician before performing spinal extension drills
execution.range_of_motion_guidance: Allow the thoracic spine to extend over the roller as far as the stiffness allows. Do not force end-range.
execution.tempo_recommendations: Hold 5–10 seconds at each segment. Spend 60–90 seconds total on the thoracic spine per session.
coaching_cues: Let gravity do the work — just breathe and relax
Keep the roller between your shoulder blades, not in your lower back
Exhale and let the chest open toward the ceiling

name: Thoracic Foam Roller Extension with Arm Sweeps
description: A dynamic progression of the passive thoracic extension over a foam roller that adds active arm sweeps. While draped over the roller in thoracic extension, the exerciser sweeps both arms overhead and back in a controlled arc, adding active thoracic mobilization and latissimus dorsi stretching to the passive extension component. The arm sweep increases the range demands at each thoracic segment and trains active control of the newly gained mobility.

execution.starting_position: Position the foam roller perpendicular under the mid-thoracic spine. Support the head. Begin with arms crossed over the chest.
execution.setup_instructions: Same setup as standard thoracic roller extension. Ensure the roller is at the target thoracic segment before adding the arm sweep.
steps: Step 1: Position over the roller and allow the thoracic segment to extend over it.
Step 2: Begin the arm sweep by uncrossing the arms and sweeping them overhead in a large arc, reaching as far overhead as shoulder mobility allows.
Step 3: Hold the overhead reach for 2-3 seconds, feeling the combined thoracic extension and lat stretch.
Step 4: Sweep the arms back to the chest. Repeat 5-8 times on each thoracic segment before moving the roller.
execution.breathing_instructions: Exhale as you sweep the arms overhead — this assists thoracic opening. Inhale as you return.
common_mistakes: Moving the roller before the arm sweep — the sweep should deepen the mobilization at each level before moving on
Forcing overhead range that is not available — only reach as far as comfortable
Letting the lower back extend — the lumbar spine should not arch over the roller
safety_considerations: Avoid if shoulder pain increases with overhead movement
Osteoporosis or vertebral fracture history — consult a physiotherapist
execution.range_of_motion_guidance: Arms sweep to whatever overhead range is comfortable. The thoracic extension and arm sweep combine to create a greater total stretch than either alone.
execution.tempo_recommendations: 2s arm sweep overhead, 2s hold, 2s return. 5-8 reps per thoracic level.
coaching_cues: Breathe out as the arms go overhead — the exhale helps the chest open
Reach long through the fingertips on the sweep
Feel the stretch from your hips through your armpits to your fingertips on the overhead position

name: Thoracic Extension over Foam Roller
description: A thoracic spine extension mobilization exercise using a foam roller positioned perpendicular to the spine. The exerciser places the roller under the mid-back and allows gravity to extend the thoracic spine over the roller, progressively working segment-by-segment from the mid-thoracic region toward the upper thoracic. This technique counters the thoracic kyphosis that develops from prolonged sitting and desk work, restoring extension range to the facet joints and improving shoulder overhead mobility.

execution.starting_position: Sit on the floor in front of a foam roller positioned perpendicular to the spine. Lie back so the roller contacts the mid-thoracic spine (approximately bra-line level). Support the head with both hands, elbows pointing upward.
execution.setup_instructions: Use a standard cylindrical foam roller. For a softer initial experience, use a half-roller with the flat side down. Avoid placing the roller directly under the lumbar spine.
steps: Step 1: Position the roller under the mid-thoracic spine. Support the head with both hands.
Step 2: Allow the upper body to extend backward over the roller for 20-30 seconds, using gravity to mobilize that segment.
Step 3: Curl up slightly, then shift the roller one segment higher toward the upper thoracic spine.
Step 4: Extend over the roller again. Work progressively from mid- to upper-thoracic over several positions.
execution.breathing_instructions: Breathe deeply during each extension position. Inhale through the nose, exhale completely — this helps relax the chest and increase extension on each breath.
common_mistakes: Placing the roller under the lower back — the lumbar spine should not be extended over a hard roller
Holding breath during the extension position — continuous breathing is essential for relaxation and progress
Moving too quickly through each position — spend at least 20-30 seconds at each thoracic level
safety_considerations: If sharp pain occurs at any point, stop and do not force the extension
Osteoporosis or vertebral fracture history — consult a physiotherapist before attempting this mobilization
execution.range_of_motion_guidance: Work only within comfortable extension range. The sensation should be one of opening and release, not pain.
execution.tempo_recommendations: 20-30 seconds per thoracic level. 4-6 levels from mid- to upper-thoracic per session.
coaching_cues: Let gravity do the work — do not actively push into the roller
Breathe out completely to sink further into extension with each exhale
Support the head — do not let the neck extend excessively

name: Quadruped Thoracic Rotation Reach
description: A thoracic rotation mobility drill performed on all fours in which one arm reaches under and across the body before reversing and reaching upward toward the ceiling. The quadruped position stabilizes the hips and lumbar spine, isolating the thoracic rotation. The reaching motion — threading the arm under the torso then opening upward — creates a full arc of thoracic rotation and is one of the most accessible and effective thoracic mobility exercises available.

execution.starting_position: Begin in a quadruped position with wrists under shoulders and knees under hips. Spine neutral.
execution.setup_instructions: No equipment needed. A mat is recommended for knee comfort.
steps: Step 1: Begin in quadruped with the right hand on the floor.
Step 2: Slide the left arm under the right arm and across the floor to the right as far as possible, letting the left shoulder rest on the floor. This is the 'thread' phase.
Step 3: Hold the threaded position for 2 seconds, then reverse and open the left arm upward toward the ceiling, rotating the thoracic spine to follow the arm.
Step 4: Hold the open position for 2 seconds, following the hand with the gaze. Return and repeat, then switch sides.
execution.breathing_instructions: Exhale as you thread under. Inhale as you open toward the ceiling.
common_mistakes: Rotating through the lumbar spine rather than the thoracic spine — the hips should not rotate significantly
Moving too quickly through the motion — the value is at the end range in each direction
Using the supporting arm to push into rotation rather than allowing the thoracic spine to do the work
safety_considerations: If sharp thoracic pain occurs during the rotation, reduce range and consult a physiotherapist
Avoid if you have an acute thoracic disc herniation unless prescribed
execution.range_of_motion_guidance: Thread as far as the shoulder allows; open as far as thoracic rotation allows. Lumbar and hip rotation should be minimized.
execution.tempo_recommendations: 2s thread, 2s hold, 2s open, 2s hold — continuous flow for each repetition.
coaching_cues: Follow the hand with the eyes — the gaze leads the thoracic rotation
Let the shoulder touch the floor on the thread phase — the deeper the thread, the greater the rotation
Keep the hips stacked — they should not rotate with the thoracic spine

name: Thoracic Rotation Stretch
description: The thoracic rotation stretch performed in a side-lying position targets thoracic spinal mobility through rotation while the hips remain relatively stable. Opening the top arm upward and over allows the thoracic vertebrae to rotate, improving the mobility segment that is most commonly restricted in office workers and strength athletes with tight anterior structures. Good thoracic rotation is fundamental for healthy shoulder and neck movement.

execution.starting_position: Lie on your side with hips bent to 90 degrees and knees stacked. Both arms are extended in front of the chest, palms together.
execution.setup_instructions: Use a mat for comfort. No equipment needed.
steps: Step 1: Lie on one side with knees and hips bent to 90 degrees, knees stacked.
Step 2: Extend both arms in front of the chest with palms together.
Step 3: Keep the hips and knees stacked and stationary — they should not roll during the movement.
Step 4: Slowly rotate the top arm upward and open it toward the ceiling and floor behind you, following with the eyes and head.
Step 5: Allow the arm to open as far as the thoracic spine allows, then hold 3–5 breaths before returning.
execution.breathing_instructions: Breathe deeply into the chest throughout. Each inhale and exhale can help the rotation progress slightly further.
common_mistakes: Rolling the hips during the stretch — the hip block should remain stationary
Forcing the arm to the floor when the thoracic spine is not yet mobile enough
Moving at the lumbar spine rather than the thoracic segment
safety_considerations: Avoid forcing the arm past the range of comfort
If cervical pain occurs, limit head rotation and focus on arm movement only
execution.range_of_motion_guidance: The top arm should travel as far toward the floor on the opposite side as thoracic rotation allows. For many people initially this will be far short of the floor.
execution.tempo_recommendations: Hold each rotation 3–5 breaths. 5–10 reps per side.
coaching_cues: Let your eyes lead your hand
Keep your knees pinned together on the floor — do not roll the hips
Breathe wide into the chest at the end of range

name: 3-Board Bench Press
description: The 3-Board Bench Press stacks three 2-inch boards on the chest, leaving only the top 5-6 inches of the press range to complete. At this board height the movement is almost entirely triceps-driven, with minimal pectoral stretch-shortening involvement. It is used specifically for lockout strength development and as a heavy overload tool.

execution.starting_position: Lie on a flat bench. Partner holds three stacked boards against the chest. Grip the bar at shoulder-width or slightly narrower to maximize tricep involvement.
execution.setup_instructions: Stack three 2x6 boards or use a padded board block. The bar need only travel 5-6 inches to complete the movement. Load can be significantly above full ROM maximum.
steps: Step 1: Unrack bar and lower to the board stack.
Step 2: Touch and briefly pause.
Step 3: Drive explosively to full lockout.
Step 4: Return under control and repeat.
execution.breathing_instructions: Brace fully before each rep. Exhale at lockout.
common_mistakes: Using an overly wide grip that shifts load back to the chest rather than triceps
Failing to reach full elbow lockout
