safety_considerations: Very heavy loads are possible — trained spotters are mandatory
Do not attempt without reliable partner support
execution.range_of_motion_guidance: Top 5-6 inches of pressing ROM only. Full lockout required.
coaching_cues: Squeeze the triceps hard at lockout
Think 'push the ceiling away' for maximum extension

name: Thruster
description: The thruster is a full-body compound exercise that combines a front squat with an overhead press in one continuous movement. As the lifter rises from the squat, the momentum is used to drive the bar or dumbbells overhead to lockout. It is widely used in CrossFit and conditioning programs for its exceptional metabolic demand and full-body recruitment, training the quadriceps, glutes, shoulders, and triceps simultaneously.

execution.starting_position: Hold the barbell in a front rack position (or dumbbells at shoulder height). Feet are shoulder-width apart. This is also the bottom starting position of the front squat.
execution.setup_instructions: Clean the bar to the front rack position or take from a rack. Ensure adequate ceiling clearance for the overhead lockout. Dumbbells are easier to manage for beginners.
steps: Step 1: Begin with the bar in the front rack position, feet shoulder-width apart, elbows high.
Step 2: Descend into a full front squat — hips below parallel if mobility allows — keeping the torso upright.
Step 3: Drive explosively out of the squat, extending the hips and knees with maximum force.
Step 4: Use the upward momentum to press the bar overhead in one continuous motion, finishing at full lockout.
execution.breathing_instructions: Inhale and brace before the squat; exhale at the overhead lockout.
common_mistakes: Pausing between the squat and press, breaking the momentum transfer
Pressing forward rather than straight up at the top
safety_considerations: Requires front squat mobility — practice front squats and overhead press separately first
Use bumper plates if doing high-rep sets so you can safely drop the bar
execution.range_of_motion_guidance: Full depth squat; full overhead lockout with active shoulders.
execution.tempo_recommendations: Controlled descent; explosive through the top
coaching_cues: Let the squat drive the bar overhead — do not 'squat, pause, then press'
Keep your elbows high in the front rack — if they drop, you'll muscle-press instead of thruster

name: Tibialis Raise
description: The tibialis raise is a dorsiflexion exercise that targets the tibialis anterior — the muscle on the front of the shin — by raising the forefoot against resistance while keeping the heels fixed. It is the antagonist movement to calf raises and is frequently neglected in training programs. Strengthening the tibialis anterior is associated with reduced risk of shin splints and anterior leg pain in runners, walkers, and athletes.

execution.starting_position: Stand with heels against a wall or on a step edge, with the toes hanging free. The heels are the pivot point. Stand upright with back against the wall.
execution.setup_instructions: No equipment required for the bodyweight version. A resistance band looped around a fixed object at shin height can add load. Alternatively, perform seated with the heels on the floor and the toes lifted against gravity.
steps: Step 1: Stand with heels on the floor or step edge, back against a wall, toes pointing forward.
Step 2: Raise the forefoot as high as possible by pulling the toes and forefoot upward (dorsiflexion).
Step 3: Hold the peak dorsiflexion contraction for one second.
Step 4: Lower the forefoot under control back to the floor.
Step 5: Repeat for the prescribed reps.
execution.breathing_instructions: Breathe freely — this is a low-intensity isolation exercise.
common_mistakes: Barely lifting the toes — the tibialis anterior should be fully contracted at the top
Moving too fast — slow, controlled reps with a peak contraction are more effective
safety_considerations: Very low injury risk exercise
If shin pain occurs, reduce volume and check for underlying conditions
execution.range_of_motion_guidance: Maximum dorsiflexion at the top (toes pulled as high as possible) and full plantarflexion or return to neutral at the bottom.
coaching_cues: Pull the toes up as high as you can
Feel the front of the shin working
Don't let the foot drop — control the lowering

name: Tibialis Wall Raise with Isometric Hold
description: A tibialis anterior strengthening exercise performed standing with the back against a wall and heels a short distance from the wall. The exerciser raises the toes and forefoot off the floor (dorsiflexion) and holds the top position for a prescribed duration. The isometric hold component greatly increases time-under-tension for the tibialis anterior compared to repetitive raises, making it effective for shin splint rehabilitation and tibialis anterior endurance development.

execution.starting_position: Stand with the back flat against a wall, feet approximately 30-40 cm from the wall, heels on the floor. The calves rest gently against the wall for proprioceptive feedback.
execution.setup_instructions: No equipment needed. Any wall works. Ensure the floor surface is non-slip.
steps: Step 1: Stand with back against the wall, heels on the floor, feet slightly away from the wall.
Step 2: Raise both forefeet off the floor to maximum dorsiflexion — toes pointing toward the ceiling.
Step 3: Hold the dorsiflexed position for the prescribed duration (5-30 seconds), maintaining maximum height.
Step 4: Lower slowly to the floor. Rest briefly and repeat.
execution.breathing_instructions: Breathe continuously during the hold. Do not hold your breath.
common_mistakes: Partial dorsiflexion — not raising the toes to their full height
Pushing through the toes rather than lifting the forefoot
Leaning forward away from the wall — maintain full back-wall contact
safety_considerations: If acute shin splints are present, begin with very short holds (3-5 seconds) and progress as symptoms allow
Pain during the exercise above 3/10 suggests the load or duration should be reduced
execution.range_of_motion_guidance: Full dorsiflexion — toes as high as possible from the floor.
execution.tempo_recommendations: 2s raise, 5-30s isometric hold, 2s lower. Begin at 5s holds and progress to 30s.
coaching_cues: Lift the toes as high as possible toward the ceiling
Feel the outer shin muscles working — that is the tibialis anterior
Keep breathing during the hold — count seconds to track duration

name: Tiger Bend Push-Up
description: An advanced calisthenics movement that combines a forearm position with a tricep-driven press. Starting from a forearm plank, the lifter uses the triceps to press up to straight arms then lowers back. This builds tremendous tricep strength and shoulder stability.

execution.starting_position: Set up for Tiger Bend Push-Up in the appropriate position.
execution.setup_instructions: Prepare equipment and body position for Tiger Bend Push-Up.
steps: Step 1: Start in forearm plank position, elbows under shoulders.
Step 2: Push through forearms and hands simultaneously to extend elbows.
Step 3: Finish in a standard push-up top position with arms extended.
Step 4: Lower back to forearm position with control.
execution.breathing_instructions: Exhale during the exertion phase, inhale during the return.
common_mistakes: Dropping hips
Using momentum instead of tricep strength
safety_considerations: Keep joints aligned throughout the movement.
Use controlled weight appropriate for skill level.
execution.range_of_motion_guidance: Move through full range of motion without compromising joint integrity.
coaching_cues: Drive hands into floor
Keep body rigid throughout

name: Tire Flip
description: The tire flip involves driving a large tractor or implement tire from the ground to a vertical position and then pushing it over, combining elements of a deadlift, a hip-extension power clean, and an overhead push in a single continuous movement. The initial drive from the floor mirrors a deadlift in posterior chain loading, the mid-section acceleration resembles a clean pull, and the final push-over engages the chest and shoulders. The tire flip is a full-body power and conditioning exercise foundational to strongman training and widely used in athletic strength and conditioning programmes.

execution.starting_position: Stand facing the flat side of the tire. Squat down and position both hands underneath the tire at the base. The feet are slightly wider than hip-width, toes pointed out. The chest and thighs are pressed against the tire.
execution.setup_instructions: Choose a tire weight appropriate for training level. Begin with a tire that can be flipped with consistent, controlled technique — typically 100–200 kg for intermediate trainees. Ensure the tire is on a stable, flat surface.
steps: Step 1: Drive through the legs explosively, extending the hips and knees to begin driving the tire upward from the floor.
Step 2: As the tire rises, step one foot forward (into a lunge position) and re-grip higher on the tire surface.
Step 3: Continue the hip extension drive and begin pushing the tire forward with the arms as it approaches vertical.
Step 4: Once the tire is at or beyond 90°, deliver a final explosive push with both arms to send it over and onto the flat side.
Step 5: Move clear of the falling tire, then reposition for the next repetition.
execution.breathing_instructions: Take a full breath and brace before the initial lift. Exhale explosively at the moment of the hip drive. Breathe again before the push-over.
common_mistakes: Trying to lift the tire like a deadlift with straight legs rather than driving with the chest against the tire and using hip extension explosively
Re-gripping too low when the tire rises, limiting the ability to push it over
Pushing the tire over too early before it is upright enough — this requires far more upper body strength and reduces lower body contribution
safety_considerations: Never allow the tire to fall backward onto you — if the flip fails, step away to the side
Do not place fingers under a falling tire
Build to heavy tire flipping with lighter tires first
Ensure adequate lower back warm-up before tire flipping — it places high load on the erector spinae in a rounded back position
execution.range_of_motion_guidance: The tire travels from flat on the ground to fully overturned — a rotation of approximately 180° around the horizontal axis.
execution.tempo_recommendations: Strength: 3–5 flips × 4–6 sets. Rest 2–3 minutes. Conditioning: 10 flips as fast as possible × 3–5 rounds. Rest 2 minutes.
coaching_cues: Drive the chest into the tire — it should feel like a squat, not a deadlift
Explode the hips — the arms just guide it, the legs lift it
Re-grip high before the push-over

name: Tire Flip Sprint
description: A conditioning complex where a heavy tire is flipped multiple times followed immediately by a sprint. The tire flip builds explosive hip extension and upper body power while the sprint develops speed and anaerobic capacity. This combination is a staple of strongman conditioning.

execution.starting_position: Set up for Tire Flip Sprint in proper strongman position.
execution.setup_instructions: Prepare all equipment and body position for Tire Flip Sprint.
steps: Step 1: Position over tire in deadlift stance with hands under tire.
Step 2: Drive hips and flip tire forward explosively for target distance.
Step 3: After final flip, immediately sprint a set distance.
Step 4: Rest and repeat for target rounds.
execution.breathing_instructions: Brace core maximally before every lift. Breathe between reps if needed.
common_mistakes: Lifting with back instead of legs
Resting too long between flip and sprint
safety_considerations: Use collars on all loaded barbells.
Ensure clear path for carries.
Have spotters for overhead movements.
execution.range_of_motion_guidance: Full range of motion specific to the implement being used.
coaching_cues: Drive through legs, not lower back
Transition immediately to sprint

name: Terminal Knee Extension — Band Hold and Pulse
description: A terminal knee extension variation that adds an isometric hold followed by small pulsing contractions at the point of full knee extension. After extending the knee against band resistance, the exerciser holds the extended position for 2-3 seconds and then performs 5-8 short pulsing contractions before returning. This technique maximizes VMO (vastus medialis oblique) activation time and is used in patellofemoral rehabilitation programs targeting quad insufficiency at terminal extension, common after ACL reconstruction and knee arthroplasty.

execution.starting_position: Stand facing away from a resistance band anchor with the band looped around the back of the knee. Begin with a slight knee bend (20-30 degrees of flexion).
execution.setup_instructions: Anchor the band behind and above knee height. The band should provide noticeable resistance against knee extension.
steps: Step 1: Begin with the knee in slight flexion against the band's pull.
Step 2: Extend the knee to full extension, contracting the quadriceps, particularly the inner quad (VMO).
Step 3: Hold the fully extended position for 2-3 seconds.
Step 4: Perform 5-8 small pulsing contractions (tiny additional squeezes) at full extension, then slowly return the knee to the starting flexion position. That is one repetition.
execution.breathing_instructions: Exhale during the extension. Breathe during the hold and pulses. Inhale as you return.
common_mistakes: Not reaching full knee extension before the hold — partial extension reduces VMO activation
Pulses becoming large movements rather than small squeezes at the end range
Locking the knee so hard that the popliteal fossa compresses painfully
safety_considerations: Avoid if hyperextension of the knee is contraindicated — stop at neutral extension (0 degrees)
For post-surgical use: confirm full extension range is cleared by the treating physiotherapist
execution.range_of_motion_guidance: Full knee extension (0 degrees) must be reached before the hold. The pulses occur at this end range.
execution.tempo_recommendations: 2s extension, 3s hold, 5-8 pulses at ~1s each, 2s slow return.
coaching_cues: Feel the inner quad (teardrop muscle above the kneecap) contracting during the hold
Pulses should feel like extra squeezes, not additional movement
Press the kneecap upward at the top of each extension

name: Terminal Knee Extension — Fast Release
description: A speed-focused variation of the terminal knee extension (TKE) that trains the quadriceps eccentric braking capacity. After performing the standard TKE knee extension against the band, the exerciser releases the hold quickly and allows the band to pull the knee back into flexion faster than the standard controlled return. The quadriceps must react and control this rapid eccentric loading, training the neuromuscular reflex required for activities like landing, deceleration, and cutting. Used in late-stage ACL and knee rehabilitation.

execution.starting_position: Stand facing away from a resistance band anchor with the band looped around the back of the knee. Slight forward lean with a soft knee bend (approximately 20-30 degrees of knee flexion).
execution.setup_instructions: Anchor the band behind the knee at approximately waist height. Use a band resistance that is challenging but allows controlled movement. Stand close enough to the anchor that the band creates meaningful tension at the starting position.
steps: Step 1: Begin with the knee in slight flexion against the band's pull.
Step 2: Extend the knee to full extension (or near full extension), contracting the quadriceps.
Step 3: Hold briefly at full extension.

Step 4: Intentionally release the quadriceps contraction more quickly than normal and allow the band to pull the knee back into flexion. Control the return with eccentric quadriceps activation — allow it, but do not let the knee snap back uncontrolled.
execution.breathing_instructions: Exhale as you extend the knee. Inhale as you control the band-assisted fast return.
common_mistakes: Allowing the knee to snap back completely uncontrolled — the eccentric must still be active
Releasing too fast before adequate rehabilitation readiness — this is a late-stage drill
Losing upright posture during the drill
safety_considerations: Appropriate only in late-stage rehabilitation when pain-free and cleared by a physiotherapist for reactive training
Ensure the band anchor is secure before performing the fast release component
execution.range_of_motion_guidance: Full extension to approximately 30 degrees of flexion on the return. The speed of the return is controlled — faster than a standard TKE but not fully uncontrolled.
execution.tempo_recommendations: 1s extension, 0.5s hold, fast controlled return (0.5-1s band pull back). The return is intentionally reactive.
coaching_cues: Let the band pull back but actively control it — your quadriceps must work eccentrically
Think of this as catching the knee as it snaps back, not bracing against it
This should feel like reactive training, not like a strength exercise

name: Toes to Bar
description: Toes to bar is a hanging core exercise performed from a pull-up bar in which the athlete raises both legs simultaneously until the toes make contact with the bar. The movement demands strong hip flexor force production, full rectus abdominis tension to posteriorly tilt the pelvis, and sufficient lat engagement to stabilize the shoulder girdle against the upward leg drive. It is a staple exercise in CrossFit and gymnastics conditioning programs.

execution.starting_position: Hang from a pull-up bar with an overhand grip at shoulder-width or slightly wider. Arms fully extended, body in a controlled dead hang.
execution.setup_instructions: Use a secure pull-up bar. Chalk improves grip. Begin with hanging knee raises if unable to perform the full movement.
steps: Step 1: Begin in a dead hang with arms fully extended.
Step 2: Engage the lats to stabilize the shoulder position.
Step 3: Drive both legs upward simultaneously, initiating with the hip flexors and reinforcing with abdominal compression.
Step 4: At the top of the movement, the toes should contact the bar between the hands.
Step 5: Lower the legs with control back to the starting dead hang position.
execution.breathing_instructions: Exhale forcefully as the legs rise. Inhale on the descent.
common_mistakes: Using excessive kipping (swinging momentum) which reduces core demand
Bending the knees to reach the bar instead of using straight-leg form
Failing to engage the lats — the shoulders should not shrug to the ears
safety_considerations: Grip failure can cause falls — use chalk and ensure the bar is secure.
Build from hanging knee raises and hanging leg raises progressively.
execution.range_of_motion_guidance: Full range requires the toes to touch the bar. Partial range (legs to 90 degrees) is an acceptable progression.
execution.tempo_recommendations: 1–2 second concentric, 2 second eccentric. Avoid uncontrolled bouncing at the bottom.
coaching_cues: Squeeze the bar hard and pull lats down
Curl the tailbone up — not just the legs
Toes reach for the bar — do not let the bar come down to your toes

name: Towel-Grip Cable Seated Row
description: The towel-grip cable seated row loops a gym towel through the cable attachment and grips both ends, dramatically increasing grip and forearm activation compared to standard handles. The towel's unstable, compressible surface requires constant grip force throughout each rep, adding a significant forearm training stimulus to the standard lat and upper back benefits of the seated cable row.

execution.starting_position: Loop a gym towel through the cable carabiner. Sit at the cable row station, feet on the footplate. Grip both ends of the towel. Lean back slightly, arms extended.
execution.setup_instructions: Use a hand towel or wrist-sized rope for the grip. Ensure the towel is threaded securely through the attachment. Set weight lower than a standard handle row — the grip will fatigue earlier.
steps: Step 1: Sit tall and grip both towel ends firmly.
Step 2: Depress and retract the shoulder blades to initiate.
Step 3: Row the towel ends toward the lower abdomen.
Step 4: At peak contraction, squeeze the grip and the lats.
Step 5: Return under control to full arm extension.
execution.breathing_instructions: Exhale on the row. Inhale returning.
common_mistakes: Grip loosening mid-set — squeeze the towel continuously
Not using the towel's instability as a training stimulus — it should feel different from a standard handle
safety_considerations: Inspect the towel for fraying — a torn towel snapping under load can cause injury
Use a durable gym towel, not a thin household towel
execution.range_of_motion_guidance: Full arm extension to elbows behind torso.
coaching_cues: Squeeze the towel like your life depends on it
Back does the rowing; hands are just hooks
Full stretch at the bottom of every rep

name: Towel Grip Pull-Up
description: The towel grip pull-up drapes one or two towels over a pull-up bar and has the lifter grip the hanging ends rather than the bar itself. The unstable, thick towel grip dramatically increases forearm and grip strength demands compared to standard pull-ups. This variation is used to develop crushing grip strength and is a popular training tool for climbers and grapplers.

execution.starting_position: Drape one or two towels over a pull-up bar. Grip the hanging ends of the towels with both hands. Hang at full arm extension.
execution.setup_instructions: Use gym towels or thick rope draped over a sturdy bar. Ensure the towels are secure and cannot slip off.
steps: Step 1: Grip the hanging ends of the towels with both hands, palms facing each other (neutral grip).
Step 2: Begin hanging with elbows fully extended.
Step 3: Depress and retract the scapulae, then pull the elbows down and back.
Step 4: Continue pulling until the chin clears the bar or the chest approaches the bar.
Step 5: Lower under control to full hang and repeat.
execution.breathing_instructions: Exhale on the pull, inhale on the descent.
common_mistakes: Letting the grip slip by not squeezing the towel tightly enough
Using momentum to compensate for grip fatigue
safety_considerations: Ensure towels are securely draped and will not slip off the bar mid-set
Grip failure can result in a sudden fall — perform over a padded surface
execution.range_of_motion_guidance: Full arm extension at the bottom to chin above the knot level at the top.
coaching_cues: Squeeze the towel as hard as possible throughout
Pull the elbows to your pockets
Control the descent — don't drop

name: Towel Pull-Up Bar Hang
description: The towel hang involves looping a thick towel over a pull-up bar and gripping the towel's fabric with both hands, then hanging from the bar using only the towel grip. The irregular surface of the towel challenges the fingers and hand to grip differently than a standard bar, building crush grip and finger flexor strength. It is a simple but effective tool for combat sports athletes, climbers, and those with standard grip limitations.

execution.starting_position: Loop a thick gym towel over a pull-up bar, with both ends hanging down. Grip one end in each hand.
execution.setup_instructions: Use a heavy-duty gym towel or gi jacket. Ensure the bar and towel can support your bodyweight safely.
steps: Step 1: Grasp the two ends of the towel firmly.
Step 2: Lift the feet off the ground, hanging from the towel.
Step 3: Hold the hang for the prescribed duration with the arms fully extended.
Step 4: Lower the feet and release.
execution.breathing_instructions: Breathe freely throughout the hold.
common_mistakes: Gripping too close to the bar (reduces towel challenge)
Swinging during the hang
safety_considerations: Ensure the towel is securely looped over the bar before hanging
Start with short holds — towel grip is very taxing
execution.range_of_motion_guidance: Static hang — arms straight.
coaching_cues: Squeeze the towel — not the bar
Stay still
Build up hold duration progressively

name: Trap Bar Deadlift
description: The trap bar deadlift is performed inside a hexagonal barbell, gripping handles at the sides with a neutral grip. Standing inside the bar shifts the center of mass closer to the body compared to a conventional deadlift, reducing the moment arm at the hip and lumbar spine while increasing the moment arm at the knee. The result is a more quad-dominant pattern than a conventional deadlift, with less spinal stress — making it an effective compound exercise for general strength and power development.

execution.starting_position: Stand inside the trap bar with feet hip-width apart and the handles beside your hips. Push the hips back and bend the knees to grip the handles.
execution.setup_instructions: Load the bar with appropriate weight. The high handles on most trap bars reduce the range of motion — use the low handles for a full range similar to a conventional deadlift. Neutral grip is automatic with the trap bar.
steps: Step 1: Stand inside the bar, feet hip-width. Push the hips back and bend the knees until the hands reach the handles. Take a neutral grip.
Step 2: Brace the core, take a deep breath, and pull the bar tight against the floor before beginning the lift.
Step 3: Push the floor away — the leg drive is prominent with the trap bar. Drive through the full foot.
Step 4: Extend the hips and knees simultaneously to reach a fully upright position with hips locked out.
Step 5: Return the bar to the floor under control, maintaining spinal position throughout.
execution.breathing_instructions: Inhale and brace before the pull. Hold through the lift. Exhale at the top.
common_mistakes: Letting the hips rise faster than the shoulders — turning it into a stiff-leg pull from the lower back
Rounding the lower back due to setting up with hips too high or too low
Not using the full foot — think of leg-pressing the floor rather than just pulling with the back
safety_considerations: Easier to learn than conventional deadlift — good entry point for beginners
Still requires proper bracing — do not lift with a relaxed core
execution.range_of_motion_guidance: Full extension at the top. Full setup position at the bottom with spine neutral and hips loaded.
coaching_cues: Push the floor away, not pull the bar up
Hips and shoulders rise together
Squeeze the glutes at the top to lock out

name: Trap Bar Deadlift with Band Around Torso
description: A trap bar deadlift variation in which a resistance band is looped around the hips and anchored behind the lifter, creating a horizontal pulling force that challenges anti-flexion stability and hip hinge mechanics simultaneously. The band pulls the hips backward during the lift, forcing the lifter to actively resist the band by driving the hips forward through the top of the movement. This provides instant proprioceptive feedback for hip extension completion and is used in both strength training and deadlift technique correction.

execution.starting_position: Loop a resistance band around the hips and anchor the other end to a fixed point behind the lifter at approximately hip height. Stand inside a trap bar loaded with weight. The band should provide meaningful horizontal tension when standing.
execution.setup_instructions: The band anchor should be at or slightly above hip height. The band must be securely anchored to a power rack or similar fixed point. Use a trap bar for the reduced shoulder demand and more natural stance.
steps: Step 1: Step inside the trap bar and position the band around the hips, holding the tension from behind.
Step 2: Hinge at the hip to reach the trap bar handles. Take a breath and brace.
Step 3: Drive through the floor to lift the bar, simultaneously driving the hips forward against the band's resistance.
Step 4: At lockout, fully extend the hips and push through the band tension. Lower under control.
execution.breathing_instructions: Inhale and brace before the pull. Exhale forcefully at lockout as you drive the hips forward.
common_mistakes: Not fully extending the hips at lockout — the band should be maximally tensioned at the top
Using a band anchor that is too low, creating a downward rather than horizontal pull
Using a band that is too light to provide meaningful resistance at lockout
safety_considerations: Ensure the band anchor is completely secure before lifting
If the band causes balance issues, reduce the bar weight until the movement pattern is stabilized
execution.range_of_motion_guidance: Full deadlift range — floor to full hip extension against the band.
execution.tempo_recommendations: 2s pull, 1s lockout hold against band, 3s eccentric lower
coaching_cues: Drive the hips through the band at the top — it should feel like you are pushing forward against resistance at lockout
Feel the difference in glute activation at lockout compared to a standard trap bar deadlift
The band teaches you to complete the hip extension — do not stop at 90% of the way up

name: Trap Bar Heavy Farmer's Carry
description: The trap bar farmer's carry uses a hexagonal trap bar as the carrying implement, loading very heavy weights while keeping the load centred at the body's midline rather than hanging at the sides. The trap bar's neutral-grip handles and frame allow heavier loads than standard farmer's handles for most athletes, while the centred load distribution reduces spinal lateral flexion demands and allows trainees to overload the grip and trapezius safely. It is a staple in strength and conditioning programmes for developing absolute carry strength and grip endurance.

execution.starting_position: The trap bar is on the floor. Step inside the frame, feet hip-width apart. Grip the high handles. Hinge at the hips to reach the handles, back flat.
execution.setup_instructions: Use the high handles for most carry work — they reduce the range of motion of the initial deadlift and allow heavier loading. Ensure plates are secured with collars before walking.
steps: Step 1: Deadlift the trap bar from the floor: hinge, brace, stand up with hips and knees extending simultaneously.
Step 2: Once standing, adjust posture — tall, shoulders back, core braced firmly.
Step 3: Walk with short, quick steps. Keep the frame of the bar travelling straight — do not let it swing or sway forward.
Step 4: Maintain upright posture throughout the walk. Keep the gaze forward.
Step 5: At the end of the distance, reduce pace and lower the bar by hinging at the hips.
execution.breathing_instructions: Breathe short and regularly throughout the carry. Full brace before the initial lift from the floor.
common_mistakes: Letting the bar drift forward or backward during the walk, causing the trap bar frame to contact the legs
Overstriding, which creates instability and reduces walking speed
safety_considerations: Ensure collars are tight before carrying — a shifting plate inside the trap bar frame is a serious hazard
Walk a clear, unobstructed path
execution.range_of_motion_guidance: Walk 20–40 metres per set at heavy loads. At moderate loads, 40–60 metres.
execution.tempo_recommendations: Strength: 20–30m at 1.5–2× bodyweight × 4–5 sets. Rest 2–3 minutes. Conditioning: 40m at bodyweight × 5–6 sets with 60–90 seconds rest.
coaching_cues: Stand tall inside the frame
Short steps, high turnover
Crush the handles — do not relax the grip

name: Trap Bar Romanian Deadlift
description: A Romanian deadlift performed with a trap bar (hex bar). The trap bars neutral grip and symmetrical loading reduces torque on the lumbar spine compared to a standard barbell RDL, while still training the hip hinge pattern with an emphasis on glute and hamstring development through a large range of eccentric loading.

execution.starting_position: Stand inside the trap bar with feet hip-width apart, gripping the handles. Bar should be loaded on the floor or start from the top position.
execution.setup_instructions: Load the trap bar. Stand inside it, grip the handles, and stand upright with hips fully extended as the starting position.
steps: Step 1: Keeping the knees soft and spine neutral, hinge at the hips and push them back.
Step 2: Lower the bar along the sides of the thighs, feeling a progressive stretch in the hamstrings.
Step 3: Once a strong hamstring stretch is felt (typically mid-shin), drive the hips forward.
Step 4: Extend the hips fully at the top, squeezing the glutes, and return to the starting position.
execution.breathing_instructions: Inhale and brace before hinging. Exhale on the drive to standing.
common_mistakes: Rounding the lower back at the bottom of the movement
Bending the knees excessively, turning it into a deadlift
safety_considerations: Keep the bar close to your body throughout the movement
Do not hyperextend the lower back at the top
execution.range_of_motion_guidance: Lower until a strong hamstring stretch is felt. Full hip extension at the top.
coaching_cues: Push the hips back, not the chest down
Feel the hamstring stretch at the bottom

name: Trap Bar Squat
description: A squat movement performed with a trap bar (hex bar), where the handles are at hip level and the lifter stands inside the frame. The trap bar's geometry allows a more upright torso than a traditional barbell back squat and shifts loading to the quadriceps and glutes, with reduced shear force on the lumbar spine.

execution.starting_position: Stand inside the trap bar with feet shoulder-width apart and the bar centered around your body. Grip the handles.
execution.setup_instructions: Load the trap bar on the floor. Stand inside it, feet shoulder-width, handles at mid-thigh. Hinge to grip the handles.
steps: Step 1: Brace your core hard, chest up, and drive through the floor to stand.
Step 2: Extend the hips and knees simultaneously to rise from the bottom.
Step 3: Lock out fully at the top with hips and knees extended.
Step 4: Lower the bar back to the floor with control, maintaining a neutral spine.
execution.breathing_instructions: Inhale and brace before the pull. Exhale at the top.
common_mistakes: Squatting with excessive forward torso lean (turning it into a deadlift pattern)
Allowing the knees to cave inward
safety_considerations: The trap bar squat is excellent for beginners — the neutral grip is easy to learn
execution.range_of_motion_guidance: Full extension at lockout. Lower under control — do not bounce the plates off the floor.
coaching_cues: Push the floor away
Chest up throughout

name: Treadmill Incline Power Walk
description: Treadmill incline power walking places the treadmill at an elevated grade — typically 10–15% — and maintains a brisk walking pace to maximise cardiovascular demand without the joint impact of running. The steep angle shifts the primary load from the calves and hip flexors toward the gluteus maximus, hamstrings, and soleus while simultaneously elevating heart rate into aerobic training zones. It is a low-impact, sustainable conditioning tool well suited to active recovery sessions, fat-loss protocols, and individuals managing joint pain.

execution.starting_position: Stand on the treadmill belt with feet hip-width apart. Set the incline to 10–15% and the speed to a brisk walking pace (3–4 mph / 5–6.5 km/h). Hold the handles lightly only for balance, not to support body weight.
execution.setup_instructions: Set the treadmill incline first, then gradually increase speed. Do not grip the handles tightly as this reduces caloric expenditure and alters posture.
steps: Step 1: Set incline to 10–15% and speed to 3–4 mph. Step onto the moving belt carefully.
Step 2: Walk with a tall, upright posture — chest open, shoulders back, gaze forward. Avoid leaning forward excessively.
Step 3: Drive each stride from the glutes, pushing through the heel as the foot strikes the belt.
Step 4: Swing the arms naturally at your sides in opposition to the leg movement.
Step 5: Maintain the pace for the target duration, typically 20–45 minutes.
execution.breathing_instructions: Breathe naturally and rhythmically through the nose and mouth. Aim to maintain a pace at which you can still hold a conversation (Zone 2 aerobic).
common_mistakes: Gripping the handrails, which unloads the lower body and reduces caloric output by up to 30%
Leaning excessively forward into the incline, reducing glute activation
Using too high a speed that forces a jogging gait rather than a walking stride
safety_considerations: Step off carefully by straddling the belt if you need to stop suddenly — do not jump off a moving belt
Reduce incline gradually before stopping to avoid lightheadedness from abrupt postural change
execution.range_of_motion_guidance: Full hip extension on each stride is the goal. Focus on pushing through the rear leg rather than pulling with the front leg.
execution.tempo_recommendations: Sustained steady-state: 20–45 minutes at 3–4 mph, 10–15% incline. Interval option: 2 minutes at 15%, 1 minute at 5%, repeated 8–12 times.
coaching_cues: Walk tall — imagine a string pulling the top of your head toward the ceiling
Drive from the glute, not the hip flexor
Let go of the handles

name: Treadmill Sprint Intervals
description: Treadmill sprint intervals alternate short bursts of maximal or near-maximal running speed with active recovery periods at a slow jog or walk. The repeated acceleration and deceleration demands high power output from the quadriceps, hamstrings, and gluteus maximus while imposing strong cardiovascular stress. Sprint intervals are time-efficient for improving both aerobic capacity and anaerobic power, and produce a significant post-exercise calorie burn through excess post-exercise oxygen consumption (EPOC).

execution.starting_position: Begin with a 5-minute warm-up walk at 3–4 mph, gradually increasing to a light jog. Stand on the treadmill with feet straddling the belt, then step on when the belt reaches sprint speed — or accelerate from the jog speed.
execution.setup_instructions: Set the sprint speed before the interval begins. For safety on a treadmill, pre-set the target sprint speed, then straddle the belt and step on when it reaches that speed, rather than accelerating mid-stride. Alternatively, build up from a jog.
steps: Step 1: Warm up for 5 minutes with a walk progressing to an easy jog.
Step 2: Increase belt speed to sprint pace (8–12 mph / 13–19 km/h depending on fitness). Sprint for 20–30 seconds.
Step 3: Reduce speed immediately to walk or slow jog (3–4 mph). Recover for 60–90 seconds.
Step 4: Repeat the sprint-recovery cycle 6–10 times.
Step 5: Cool down with a 5-minute walk, gradually reducing speed.
execution.breathing_instructions: During sprints, breathe as forcefully as needed — do not try to control breathing rhythm. During recovery, focus on deep, controlled exhalations to lower heart rate faster.
common_mistakes: Holding the handrails during the sprint, which completely changes the biomechanics and reduces the training stimulus
Setting the sprint speed too high before building a base, increasing fall risk
Skipping the warm-up, which raises injury risk for hamstrings and hip flexors
safety_considerations: Never jump onto a treadmill moving at sprint speed from a standing start — accelerate progressively
Know how to emergency-stop the machine before beginning sprints
Clip the safety key to your clothing
execution.range_of_motion_guidance: Full hip extension behind the body during the push-off phase is the goal. Knee drive upward should bring the thigh roughly parallel to the ground during the swing phase.
execution.tempo_recommendations: Classic protocol: 20–30 seconds sprint / 90 seconds recovery × 8 rounds. Tabata variation: 20 seconds sprint / 10 seconds walk × 8 rounds.
coaching_cues: Drive the elbows back forcefully — arm drive powers the legs
Stay on the balls of the feet, not the heels
Push the belt away behind you — attack each stride

name: Bench Tricep Dips
description: Bench tricep dips are a bodyweight exercise where the hands are placed on a bench behind the body with the hips off the edge, and the body is lowered by bending the elbows. The triceps are the primary movers during elbow extension, while the anterior deltoid and pectoralis minor assist. Placing the feet flat on the floor makes this easier; elevating the feet increases difficulty.

execution.starting_position: Sit on the edge of a flat bench. Place hands beside the hips on the bench edge, fingers pointing forward. Slide the hips off the edge so the torso is suspended, feet flat on the floor.
execution.setup_instructions: No additional equipment beyond a bench. For increased difficulty, place feet on another bench or box in front.
steps: Step 1: Sit on the bench edge, hands beside hips, fingers forward. Slide hips off the edge. Feet flat on the floor, knees bent.
Step 2: Begin with arms extended, supporting body weight.
Step 3: Inhale and lower the body by bending the elbows, keeping them pointing backward — not flaring to the sides.
Step 4: Lower until elbows are approximately 90 degrees, then exhale and press back to full arm extension.
execution.breathing_instructions: Inhale on the way down; exhale on the press up.
common_mistakes: Letting the hips travel too far from the bench, which creates a shoulder impingement position
Flaring the elbows wide rather than keeping them pointing behind
safety_considerations: Keep hips close to the bench — do not reach too far forward
Stop if shoulder impingement or anterior shoulder pain is felt
execution.range_of_motion_guidance: Lower to 90-degree elbow bend; press to full arm extension.
coaching_cues: Elbows go back — not out to the sides
Stay close to the bench — your hips should brush it on the way down

name: Tricep Kickback
description: The tricep kickback is a dumbbell isolation exercise for the triceps performed in a bent-over position with the upper arm held parallel to the floor. The forearm extends backward past the hip to create elbow extension, with peak contraction occurring at full extension. With the shoulder in a relatively neutral position, the lateral and medial heads of the triceps are the primary movers during this strict isolation movement.

execution.starting_position: Hinge forward at the hip until the torso is nearly parallel to the floor. Place one hand and knee on a bench (or stand with both feet staggered). Hold a dumbbell in the working hand. Raise the working upper arm until it is parallel to the floor, elbow bent at 90 degrees.
execution.setup_instructions: Place one hand and same-side knee on a bench for support, or hinge over with a staggered stance. The upper arm must stay parallel to the floor throughout.
steps: Step 1: Hinge forward, upper arm parallel to the floor, elbow bent at 90 degrees. Hold the dumbbell.
Step 2: Keep the upper arm pinned in place.
Step 3: Exhale and extend the elbow by moving only the forearm backward until the arm is fully extended and parallel to the floor.
Step 4: Hold the peak extension for a moment, then inhale and return the forearm to 90 degrees.
execution.breathing_instructions: Exhale as you extend backward; inhale as you return.
common_mistakes: Dropping the upper arm during the movement — it must stay parallel to the floor
Using too heavy a dumbbell, causing the torso to rotate
safety_considerations: Keep the spine neutral — do not round the lower back when hinging
execution.range_of_motion_guidance: Full elbow extension at the back; return to 90 degrees elbow bend at the front.
coaching_cues: Pin your elbow to your side like you're holding something under your armpit
Full lockout at the back — straighten the arm completely

name: Tricep Pushdown
description: The tricep pushdown is a cable isolation exercise for the triceps performed by pushing a rope or bar attachment downward from a high pulley. It trains all three heads of the triceps with the rope variation providing additional wrist pronation at the bottom that may improve medial and lateral head activation.

execution.starting_position: Stand facing a high cable pulley holding a rope or bar attachment at chest height. Elbows tucked at the sides, upper arms stationary.
execution.setup_instructions: Set the pulley to the highest position. Use a rope for greater range of motion and contraction, or a straight bar for heavier loading.
steps: Push the attachment downward by extending the elbows fully.
With a rope: rotate hands outward at the bottom for maximum tricep contraction.
Return under control to the starting position.
execution.breathing_instructions: Exhale on extension, inhale on the return.
common_mistakes: Allowing the elbows to drift forward and away from the sides
Leaning forward excessively — maintain an upright torso
execution.range_of_motion_guidance: Full elbow extension at the bottom. Return to 90-degree elbow angle or slightly more at the top.
coaching_cues: Keep your elbows glued to your sides — only your forearms move
Spread the rope at the bottom for a full tricep squeeze

name: Tricep Rope Pushdown with Flare
description: A rope pushdown where the hands flare outward at the bottom of the movement to maximize tricep contraction. The flare at lockout adds extra peak tension compared to a standard rope pushdown. This technique is widely used for tricep detail work.

execution.starting_position: Set up for Tricep Rope Pushdown with Flare in the appropriate position.
execution.setup_instructions: Prepare equipment and body position for Tricep Rope Pushdown with Flare.
steps: Step 1: Attach rope to high pulley. Stand with elbows at sides.
Step 2: Push rope down toward thighs extending elbows.
Step 3: At the bottom, actively spread rope ends outward in a flare.
Step 4: Hold the flared position briefly then return with control.
execution.breathing_instructions: Exhale during the exertion phase, inhale during the return.
common_mistakes: Skipping the flare at bottom
Swinging the torso
safety_considerations: Keep joints aligned throughout the movement.
Use controlled weight appropriate for skill level.
execution.range_of_motion_guidance: Move through full range of motion without compromising joint integrity.
coaching_cues: Actively spread the rope
Lock elbows to sides throughout

name: TRX Atomic Push-Up
description: The TRX atomic push-up combines a push-up with a simultaneous knee tuck, performed with both feet in TRX foot cradles. The push-up phase challenges the chest, triceps, and anterior shoulder; the knee tuck phase challenges the hip flexors and anterior core in compression. The TRX suspension element makes both phases harder by creating instability in multiple planes. This is a highly demanding combined push and core exercise.

execution.starting_position: Place both feet in the TRX foot cradles and assume a push-up plank position with hands on the floor. The TRX straps should be at approximately mid-calf height.
execution.setup_instructions: Adjust the TRX to a medium height. Begin with the standard TRX push-up and TRX knee tuck separately before combining them.
steps: Step 1: Begin in the push-up plank with both feet in the TRX cradles.
Step 2: Lower the chest to the floor in a controlled push-up.
Step 3: As you press back up, simultaneously drive both knees toward the chest in a knee tuck.
Step 4: Extend both legs back to the plank position. That is one repetition.
execution.breathing_instructions: Inhale during the push-up descent. Exhale forcefully during the press-up and tuck simultaneously.
common_mistakes: Hips rising during the knee tuck rather than tucking from the core
Doing the push-up and tuck sequentially rather than simultaneously
Losing rigid plank on the return — the body must stay straight as the legs extend back
safety_considerations: This is advanced — master TRX push-up and TRX knee tuck separately before combining
Wrist discomfort may require push-up handles or reduced range
execution.range_of_motion_guidance: Full push-up range combined with a full knee tuck to chest.
execution.tempo_recommendations: 3s eccentric push-up, then explosive simultaneous press-up and tuck, then 2s controlled extension back to plank.
coaching_cues: Press up and tuck at the same time — not one then the other
Squeeze the core hard during the tuck — the knees come to the chest, not toward the hands
Control the return — do not let the legs swing back to the plank position

name: TRX Fallout
description: A TRX-based anti-extension core exercise in which the exerciser holds the TRX handles and falls forward, extending the arms overhead while keeping the core rigid and preventing the hips from dropping. The TRX adds a suspension element that requires the shoulder girdle and core to work together to control the forward fall. This is a suspension-based analogue to the ab wheel rollout and is used in core stability and anti-extension training.

execution.starting_position: Adjust TRX straps to fully shortened position. Hold the handles and face away from the anchor point. Lean forward at an angle, with arms extended forward at chest height. Body is in a rigid plank position.
execution.setup_instructions: More forward lean = harder. Begin with a small lean angle (less than 30 degrees) and progress the lean as strength improves.
steps: Step 1: Hold the TRX handles and lean forward into the starting position, body rigid.
Step 2: Allow the arms to fall forward and overhead while keeping the body in a rigid plank — no hip drop or lumbar arch.
Step 3: Reach the furthest overhead position that you can hold without the hips dropping.
Step 4: Pull the arms back to the starting position by engaging the lats and core. Repeat.
execution.breathing_instructions: Inhale as you fall forward and overhead. Exhale forcefully as you pull back.
common_mistakes: Hips sagging as the arms extend overhead — this is the most common fault and reduces core training
Using the arms to push back rather than the core and lats to pull back
Using a body angle (lean) that is too steep too soon
safety_considerations: Ensure the TRX anchor can support the full bodyweight load in the extended position
If lower back pain occurs during the fallout, reduce the lean angle significantly
execution.range_of_motion_guidance: Extend as far overhead as the core can hold the plank position. The hips must not drop.
execution.tempo_recommendations: 3s fallout to overhead, 1s hold, 2s pull back.
coaching_cues: Squeeze the glutes before you start and keep them squeezed throughout — this prevents the hip drop
Think of the return as a lat pulldown, not an arm pull
The further you lean forward, the harder this becomes — start conservative

name: TRX Fallout — Single Arm
description: A single-arm variation of the TRX fallout that adds an anti-rotation challenge to the anti-extension demand. Using one arm, the exerciser must resist both forward extension and lateral rotation of the torso, dramatically increasing the oblique and contralateral lat demand. This unilateral variation is used in advanced core training and rotation sport preparation.

execution.starting_position: Hold both TRX handles in one hand (or use a single-handle attachment). Face away from the anchor. Lean forward at an angle, one arm extended forward with the TRX.
execution.setup_instructions: Master the bilateral TRX fallout first. Start with a significantly more upright angle than the bilateral version — single-arm demands are substantially higher.
steps: Step 1: Hold the TRX single handle and face away from anchor. Establish a rigid plank with the working arm extended forward.
Step 2: Allow the working arm to fall overhead, resisting both the forward extension and the rotation toward the working side.
Step 3: Reach the end range that the core can hold without rotation or hip drop.
Step 4: Pull back to the starting position. Complete all reps on one side, then switch.
execution.breathing_instructions: Inhale as you extend overhead. Exhale as you pull back.
common_mistakes: Rotating toward the working arm — the core must resist this rotation
Using too steep a lean angle before the movement is mastered
Rushing the movement — slow and controlled is essential
safety_considerations: This is a high-demand exercise — only attempt after mastering bilateral TRX fallout
Shoulder discomfort in the extreme overhead position warrants reducing range
execution.range_of_motion_guidance: Extend as far overhead as the core can hold with no torso rotation and no hip drop.
coaching_cues: Don't rotate — the torso faces the floor throughout the entire movement
Squeeze the opposite glute harder as the arm extends further
Think of the return as pulling the floor toward you with your lat

name: Tuck Jump
description: The tuck jump is a vertical plyometric exercise in which the athlete jumps as high as possible and pulls both knees toward the chest before landing. The knee tuck shortens the moment of inertia during flight and demands greater hip flexor activation at the top of the jump compared to a standard vertical jump. It is used to develop explosive lower body power, hip flexor strength in the air, and landing mechanics, and is a common conditioning exercise in gymnastic and athletic training.

execution.starting_position: Stand with feet shoulder-width apart. Arms relaxed at sides.
execution.setup_instructions: Ensure adequate overhead clearance for the full jump.
steps: Step 1: Stand with feet shoulder-width apart.
Step 2: Dip into a quarter squat, swinging arms back.
Step 3: Explode upward as high as possible.
Step 4: At the peak of the jump, pull both knees toward the chest as high as possible.
Step 5: Extend the legs to land softly with bent hips and knees.
execution.breathing_instructions: Exhale sharply at takeoff. Breathe during rest between reps.
common_mistakes: Pulling the knees without achieving maximum jump height first
Landing with straight legs
Not fully extending at takeoff before the tuck
safety_considerations: Ensure adequate overhead space.
Land softly — knee and hip flexion on landing.
execution.range_of_motion_guidance: Maximum vertical height, then maximum knee tuck. Extend to land.
execution.tempo_recommendations: Maximum effort. 5–10 reps per set for conditioning; 3–5 reps for power focus.
coaching_cues: Jump first — then tuck
Pull the knees to the chest at the peak
Land quietly with bent knees

name: Turkish Get-Up
description: The Turkish get-up is a multi-step functional strength exercise in which the athlete transitions from a supine position to a standing position while holding a weight extended overhead in one arm. The movement passes through a half-kneeling and tall-kneeling phase, demanding shoulder stability, hip mobility, core anti-rotation strength, and total body coordination. It is considered one of the most comprehensive single-exercise assessments of functional movement quality.

execution.starting_position: Lie supine on the floor, kettlebell in the right hand, arm extended toward the ceiling, right knee bent with foot flat on the floor, left arm at 45 degrees to the left.
execution.setup_instructions: Use a light load initially to learn the movement. Clear surrounding space for the full standing phase.
steps: Step 1: From supine, press the kettlebell to full arm lock and roll up to the left elbow, then the left hand.
Step 2: Drive the right hip up into a bridge position, sweeping the left leg back to arrive in a half-kneeling position.
Step 3: From half-kneeling, rise to a tall-kneeling position, then stand up.
Step 4: Reverse the sequence: lunge down, return to half-kneeling, bridge, roll down to lying.
Step 5: Complete all reps on one side then switch.
execution.breathing_instructions: Breathe at each transition point. Do not hold breath during any single phase.
common_mistakes: Bending the locked elbow — the overhead arm must remain fully extended throughout
Watching the floor instead of the kettlebell — eyes on the bell at all times
Rushing transitions — each phase should be controlled and deliberate
safety_considerations: Shoulder instability contraindicates this exercise until corrected.
Learn each phase segment in isolation before combining.
execution.range_of_motion_guidance: Full lying to full standing, reversed to full lying again. Arm locked throughout.
execution.tempo_recommendations: Slow and deliberate. 2–5 reps per side. Quality over speed.
coaching_cues: Eyes on the bell — always
Arm locked — straight elbow throughout
Pause at each transition

name: Turkish Get-Up with Pause
description: The Turkish get-up performed with deliberate pauses at each transition point to increase time under tension and improve positional awareness. The pauses expose weaknesses in each phase and build comprehensive strength throughout the entire movement chain.

execution.starting_position: Set up for Turkish Get-Up with Pause in proper position.
execution.setup_instructions: Prepare body and equipment for Turkish Get-Up with Pause.
steps: Step 1: Begin lying with kettlebell pressed overhead in one hand.
Step 2: Move through each phase of the Turkish get-up.
Step 3: Pause for 3 seconds at each transition point: roll, elbow, hand, kneeling, standing.
Step 4: Reverse all phases with same pauses to return to floor.
execution.breathing_instructions: Breathe steadily; never hold breath during static holds.
common_mistakes: Rushing through transitions
Letting overhead arm collapse
safety_considerations: Build prerequisite strength before attempting advanced variations.
Stop if joint pain occurs.
execution.range_of_motion_guidance: Full range of motion with control at all times.
coaching_cues: Pause reveals every weakness
Kettlebell stays directly overhead at all times

name: Two-Arm Dumbbell Bent-Over Row
description: The two-arm dumbbell bent-over row is performed identically to the barbell bent-over row, but with two dumbbells instead of a barbell. The independent dumbbells allow each arm to move through its natural path, reducing stress on the wrists and elbows compared to a fixed-bar variation. This version allows greater individual limb accountability and can help address left-right strength imbalances.

execution.starting_position: Hold a dumbbell in each hand. Hinge at the hips to 45 degrees of forward lean with a neutral spine. Let both dumbbells hang at arm's length.
execution.setup_instructions: Choose matching dumbbells. The bilateral version requires greater torso stability than the single-arm variation.
steps: Step 1: Hinge at hips to roughly 45 degrees, dumbbells hanging straight down.
Step 2: Retract scapulae and pull both dumbbells simultaneously toward the lower ribcage.
Step 3: Keep elbows close to the body or allow slight flare based on grip position.
Step 4: Squeeze the lats and rhomboids hard at the top.
Step 5: Lower both dumbbells under control to full extension.
execution.breathing_instructions: Inhale and brace before each rep. Exhale on the row.
common_mistakes: Rounding the lower back due to hamstring tightness
Using momentum by rocking the torso
Allowing the elbows to flare too wide, shifting from a lat-focused to rear-delt-focused pull
safety_considerations: Maintain neutral spine throughout — reduce weight if the lower back rounds
Hamstring flexibility determines hip hinge depth; do not force depth beyond neutral spine
execution.range_of_motion_guidance: Dumbbells hang at full arm extension at the bottom, pulled to lower ribcage at the top.
coaching_cues: Hinge and hold — no torso bounce
Pull both elbows back simultaneously
Neutral spine is non-negotiable

name: 2-Board Bench Press
description: The 2-Board Bench Press uses two stacked 2-inch boards on the chest, reducing range of motion by approximately 4 inches. This version shifts the mechanical emphasis further toward the triceps and mid-to-upper pressing range, making it a highly effective overload and sticking-point training tool for powerlifters and advanced bench pressers.

execution.starting_position: Lie on a flat bench. A partner holds two stacked 2-inch boards on the chest. Take a shoulder-width or slightly wider grip on the bar.
execution.setup_instructions: Stack two 2x6 or 2x8 boards. Have a training partner hold them or secure with elastic bands around the torso. Approx 4 inches of reduced ROM.
steps: Step 1: Unrack the bar and control the descent to the board stack.
Step 2: Touch the boards and pause for one second.
Step 3: Press powerfully back to full lockout.
Step 4: Lower under control and repeat.
execution.breathing_instructions: Inhale and brace before the descent. Exhale as the bar passes the sticking point on the way up.
common_mistakes: Relaxing the upper back during the touch at the board
Letting the boards shift position during the set
safety_considerations: Loads used should be greater than full ROM max — ensure spotter awareness
Partner must hold boards securely throughout the set
execution.range_of_motion_guidance: Bar to board surface only. Full elbow lockout at top.
coaching_cues: Treat the board like the floor — press explosively off it
Keep tension in the lats throughout

name: Typewriter Pull-Up
description: The typewriter pull-up is an advanced calisthenics variation where the lifter pulls to the top of a pull-up and then traverses horizontally across the bar — moving from side to side like a typewriter carriage — before descending. This lateral movement under full load targets the lats, biceps, and scapular stabilizers through a unique range of motion and builds exceptional pulling strength and body control.

execution.starting_position: Hang from a pull-up bar with a wide overhand grip, arms fully extended.
execution.setup_instructions: Use a straight pull-up bar wide enough to allow lateral movement. Ensure a solid grip on the bar.
steps: Step 1: Pull up until the chin clears the bar.
Step 2: While maintaining the top position, shift the body laterally toward the right hand by extending the left arm.
Step 3: Move fully to the right side so the chin is near the right hand.
Step 4: Traverse back across to the left side.
Step 5: Once back in the center, lower slowly to full dead hang.
execution.breathing_instructions: Exhale during the initial pull. Breathe steadily while traversing. Inhale on the controlled descent.
common_mistakes: Dropping from the top position before completing the traverse
Lacking the shoulder stability to control the lateral shift safely
Using a bar too narrow to allow meaningful lateral movement
safety_considerations: Ensure grip strength is sufficient — dropping from this position unexpectedly can cause injury
Only attempt after mastering controlled pull-up negatives and archer pull-ups
execution.range_of_motion_guidance: Full range from dead hang through traversal at the top.
coaching_cues: Stay at the top — do not let yourself drop during the traverse
Slide smoothly side to side rather than jerking
Engage the core hard to prevent leg swing

name: Typewriter Pull-Up (Core Focus)
description: A pull-up variation where at the top of the movement, the body traverses laterally from side to side while maintaining the chin-over-bar position. This taxes the core obliques and lateral stabilizers intensely through the lateral movement. High grip endurance is also demanded.

execution.starting_position: Set up for Typewriter Pull-Up (Core Focus) in proper position.
execution.setup_instructions: Prepare body and equipment for Typewriter Pull-Up (Core Focus).
steps: Step 1: Pull up to chin-over-bar position with wide grip.
Step 2: Shift weight to one side, extending the opposite arm.
Step 3: Traverse across to the other side, keeping chin at bar level.
Step 4: Lower after completing one full pass across.
execution.breathing_instructions: Breathe steadily; never hold breath during static holds.
common_mistakes: Dropping below bar during traverse
Pulling with arms instead of using lat
safety_considerations: Build prerequisite strength before attempting advanced variations.
Stop if joint pain occurs.
execution.range_of_motion_guidance: Full range of motion with control at all times.
coaching_cues: Chin stays at or above bar throughout traverse
Use smooth lateral shifting

name: Underhand Barbell Row / Yates Row
description: The underhand barbell row, often called the Yates Row after bodybuilder Dorian Yates, uses a supinated (palms-up) grip and a more upright torso angle than a standard Pendlay or overhand row. The supinated grip increases bicep recruitment and shifts lat activation toward the lower fibers, while the more erect posture reduces lower back stress. The elbows travel closer to the body compared to an overhand row.

execution.starting_position: Stand with feet hip-width apart. Hold a barbell with a supinated (underhand) grip at approximately shoulder width. Hinge at the hips to 45-70 degrees of forward lean — more upright than a Pendlay row.
execution.setup_instructions: Set the barbell on the floor or in a rack at mid-shin height. Maintain a neutral spine with shoulders pulled back.
steps: Step 1: Hold the bar with an underhand grip, torso between 45 and 70 degrees from vertical.
Step 2: Brace the core and retract the scapulae slightly before each rep.
Step 3: Pull the bar toward the lower abdomen or navel, keeping elbows close to the torso.
Step 4: At the top, squeeze the lats and rhomboids hard.
Step 5: Lower the bar under control until arms are extended.
execution.breathing_instructions: Inhale before the pull, exhale during the concentric phase, inhale on the descent.
common_mistakes: Using excessive body swing to initiate the row
Gripping too wide, reducing bicep and lower lat activation
Allowing the torso to drop too parallel, shifting the exercise pattern
safety_considerations: The supinated grip can place wrist stress at heavy loads — use lifting straps if grip becomes limiting
Maintain a neutral spine and avoid rounding the lower back
execution.range_of_motion_guidance: Full arm extension at the bottom to bar touching lower abdomen at the top.
coaching_cues: Palms up, elbows in
Pull to the belly button
More upright than a standard row

name: Underhand Lat Pulldown with Lean Back
description: The underhand lat pulldown with an intentional lean-back combines a supinated grip (mimicking a chin-up) with a slight torso lean of 20-30 degrees, shifting the bar's target from the clavicle to the lower sternum and increasing lower lat activation. The lean also allows slightly more weight to be used than a strict upright supinated pulldown, making it effective for progressive overload on lat thickness.

execution.starting_position: Sit at a lat pulldown machine with a close to shoulder-width underhand (supinated) grip. Set the thigh pad to secure the legs. Lean the torso back 20-30 degrees.
execution.setup_instructions: Maintain the same lean angle throughout the set. The lean is a fixed position, not a dynamic movement.
steps: Step 1: Begin seated with arms extended, leaning back 20-30 degrees, supinated grip.
Step 2: Depress and retract the shoulder blades.
Step 3: Pull the bar to the lower chest/sternum.
Step 4: Hold 1 second at peak contraction.
Step 5: Return under control to full arm extension.
execution.breathing_instructions: Exhale on the pull. Inhale on the return.
common_mistakes: Leaning back too far — 20-30 degrees is sufficient; more becomes a row
Pulling to the chest instead of the sternum — the lean makes the sternum the natural target
safety_considerations: Excessive lean places stress on the lower back — keep it moderate
Ensure the thigh pad is tight to prevent pulling the body up
execution.range_of_motion_guidance: Full arm extension to bar at lower sternum.
coaching_cues: Lean is fixed — the torso does not move during the set
Lead with the chest toward the bar
Squeeze the elbows to the sides

name: Underhand T-Bar Row
description: The underhand T-bar row uses a supinated (palms-up) grip on the T-bar, allowing the elbows to track close to the body and placing the biceps in a mechanically advantageous position. The supinated grip enables a fuller range of motion and facilitates lower lat engagement at the bottom of the pull, making it a popular choice for developing lower lat thickness.

execution.starting_position: Straddle the T-bar machine. Turn the hands supinated (palms up) on the handles or bar. Hinge to 45-60 degrees, arms extended.
execution.setup_instructions: Some T-bar machines do not accommodate a supinated grip — in that case, use a straight bar end on a landmine setup where the hands can grip palm-up.
steps: Step 1: Begin with arms extended, palms facing up.
Step 2: Initiate the row by driving the elbows back alongside the torso.
Step 3: Pull until the elbows pass torso level.
Step 4: Squeeze at the top, feeling the lower lats contract.
Step 5: Lower under control to full arm extension.
execution.breathing_instructions: Exhale on the row. Inhale on the descent.
common_mistakes: Supinating the wrists so far it becomes uncomfortable — find a comfortable angle
Bicep-dominant pulling — think lat stretch and contraction, not curl
safety_considerations: The supinated wrist position can stress the wrist joint — progress load conservatively
Avoid this variation with wrist injuries
execution.range_of_motion_guidance: Full arm extension to full lat contraction.
coaching_cues: Palms face up throughout
Elbows track alongside the ribs
Feel the stretch under the arms at the bottom

name: Upright Row
description: The upright row is a pulling exercise in which a barbell or dumbbells are lifted vertically from the hips to the chin, with elbows leading and rising above the hands. It trains the lateral deltoid and upper trapezius simultaneously and is effective for shoulder and trap development, though grip width significantly affects both efficacy and shoulder comfort.

execution.starting_position: Stand with feet shoulder-width apart holding a barbell at hip level with a pronated grip. Use a grip slightly wider than shoulder width to reduce shoulder impingement risk.
execution.setup_instructions: A wider grip is generally safer for the shoulder than a narrow grip. Avoid narrow-grip upright rows if you have history of shoulder impingement.
steps: Pull the barbell upward along the body, leading with the elbows.
Raise until the bar is at upper chest or chin height with elbows above the bar.
Lower under control back to the starting position.
execution.breathing_instructions: Exhale on the upward pull, inhale on the descent.
common_mistakes: Using a very narrow grip, which internally rotates the shoulder at end range and can cause impingement
Raising the bar above chin height
safety_considerations: Individuals with existing shoulder impingement should avoid this exercise or use a wider grip and limited range of motion
Stop the bar at upper chest height to avoid end-range shoulder impingement
execution.range_of_motion_guidance: Raise bar to upper chest level. Elbows should be level with or slightly above the bar.
coaching_cues: Lead with the elbows — let the bar follow
Keep the bar close to your body throughout the entire movement

name: V-Sit
description: The V-sit is an advanced isometric calisthenics hold in which the athlete balances on the tailbone with both arms and legs raised, forming a V-shape with the torso and legs. It simultaneously demands strong hip flexor strength and rectus abdominis tension to hold the torso upright against the hip-flexion load. The exercise requires significant core compression and spinal control, making it a progression from the hollow hold.

execution.starting_position: Sit on the floor with legs extended and hands lightly on the floor beside the hips.
execution.setup_instructions: Use a mat for comfort. No other equipment is required.
steps: Step 1: Sit tall with legs straight in front of you and hands beside your hips.
Step 2: Lean back slightly while simultaneously lifting both legs off the floor to approximately 45 degrees.
Step 3: Raise your arms forward parallel to the floor so they are pointing toward your feet.
Step 4: Balance on your tailbone and hold the V-shape, keeping the spine as long as possible.
Step 5: Hold for the prescribed duration, then lower with control.
execution.breathing_instructions: Breathe shallowly during the hold. Exhale as you raise into position and inhale to lower.
common_mistakes: Allowing the spine to collapse into a rounded C-shape instead of maintaining length
Bending the knees to make the hold easier when progression should come from time, not technique shortcuts
Letting the legs drop below 45 degrees due to insufficient hip flexor strength
safety_considerations: If hip flexor cramping occurs, lower legs immediately and stretch the hip flexors.
Avoid if experiencing lower back pain that is aggravated by sustained hip flexion.
execution.range_of_motion_guidance: Legs should form a 45-degree angle with the floor. The torso should lean back enough to counterbalance the legs.
execution.tempo_recommendations: Hold for 10–30 seconds. Build duration progressively.
coaching_cues: Sit tall through the crown of your head
Squeeze your thighs together and point your toes
Create a V — not a C

name: V-Squat Machine
description: The V-squat machine guides the lifter along a fixed V-shaped arc, placing the load on shoulder pads while the feet remain on the floor or a low platform in front of the body. The angled path of the machine produces a movement pattern that is deeper than a standard hack squat machine while keeping the spine supported. It is a popular alternative to the squat and leg press for lifters who want significant quad loading with reduced spinal loading.

execution.starting_position: Step into the machine, positioning the shoulder pads on your shoulders. Feet on the platform, hip-width apart. Stand upright with the machine unlatched.
execution.setup_instructions: Adjust shoulder pads to fit comfortably. Set foot position on the platform to target quad emphasis (higher = more glute) or quad (lower feet).
steps: Step 1: Unlatch the machine and control the descent by bending the knees along the guided arc.
Step 2: Descend until the thighs reach at least parallel to the floor or deeper if flexibility allows.
Step 3: Drive through the heels and quads to press upward along the arc to the starting position.
Step 4: Lock out at the top without hyperextending the knees.
execution.breathing_instructions: Inhale on descent, exhale on ascent.
common_mistakes: Knees caving inward
Rising onto the toes
Not reaching sufficient depth
safety_considerations: Engage the safety latches before stepping in or out of the machine
execution.range_of_motion_guidance: Thighs to at least parallel; full depth preferred if mobility allows.
coaching_cues: Knees track over toes
Heels stay flat
Full depth — don't stop at parallel

name: Victorian Cross Hold
description: A front lever variation performed on rings where the body is horizontal facing up, an inversion of the standard front lever. The arms press down on rings alongside the hips while the body is held rigid and horizontal. This demands exceptional compression strength and hip flexor engagement.

execution.starting_position: Set up for Victorian Cross Hold in proper position.
execution.setup_instructions: Prepare body and equipment for Victorian Cross Hold.
steps: Step 1: From an L-sit on rings, lean back and extend body to horizontal.
Step 2: Press rings down alongside hips with straight arms.
Step 3: Maintain body parallel to floor facing up.
Step 4: Hold position with maximum tension then exit safely.
execution.breathing_instructions: Breathe steadily; never hold breath during static holds.
common_mistakes: Bent elbows
Insufficient hip flexor and compression strength
safety_considerations: Build prerequisite strength before attempting advanced variations.
Stop if joint pain occurs.
execution.range_of_motion_guidance: Full range of motion with control at all times.
coaching_cues: Compress hips actively
Straight arms pressing rings down

name: W-Raises
description: W-raises are a prone shoulder rehabilitation and strengthening exercise where the arms form a W shape at the top of the movement. Lying face down or bent over, the lifter externally rotates and raises the arms to replicate the shape of the letter W. This movement specifically targets the posterior deltoid, infraspinatus, and middle trapezius, making it valuable for rotator cuff health and postural correction.

execution.starting_position: Lie prone (face down) on a bench or floor. Arms hang toward the floor or rest alongside the torso. If using light dumbbells, hold them in each hand.
execution.setup_instructions: No equipment needed if using bodyweight. If using light dumbbells, select very light weights (1–5 kg). Can also be performed standing with a hinge.
steps: Step 1: Lie face down on a bench or floor with arms hanging down.
Step 2: Bend the elbows to 90 degrees so the forearms hang perpendicular to the floor.
Step 3: Externally rotate the shoulder by raising the forearms upward so the hands are now at forehead level — the arms now form a W shape.
Step 4: Squeeze the rear delts and middle traps at the top, then lower the arms back to the hanging position.
execution.breathing_instructions: Exhale as you raise into the W position; inhale on the return.
common_mistakes: Raising too fast with momentum instead of using controlled muscle contraction
Shrugging the upper traps — keep the neck long
safety_considerations: Use very light or no additional weight — this is a rotator cuff and postural exercise
execution.range_of_motion_guidance: Raise until the forearms are approximately horizontal, forming a clear W shape. Full external rotation at the top.
coaching_cues: Think 'elbows wide, forearms up' to get the W shape
Keep the neck long and trap-free — this is a mid-trap and rear delt exercise

name: Waiter Curl
description: The waiter curl is performed by holding a weight plate by its rim with both hands underneath, palms facing upward as if carrying a tray. The underhand plate position keeps constant supination tension on the biceps throughout the curl, emphasizing the short head and brachialis. It is a simple, low-setup bicep exercise that also challenges the forearms and wrist stability.

execution.starting_position: Stand upright holding a weight plate by the rim with both hands underneath, palms facing up. Elbows at the sides.
execution.setup_instructions: Choose a plate with a comfortable grip around the rim. A 10-25kg plate works well for most lifters.
steps: Step 1: Begin with arms extended, plate hanging below, palms supinated.
Step 2: Curl the plate upward by flexing the elbows, keeping the palms facing up throughout.
Step 3: Curl until maximum elbow flexion, keeping the plate horizontal.
Step 4: Lower slowly back to the starting position.
execution.breathing_instructions: Exhale on the curl, inhale on the return.
common_mistakes: Letting the plate tilt
Swinging the torso to assist the curl
Elbows drifting forward
safety_considerations: Ensure a firm grip on the plate rim before beginning
execution.range_of_motion_guidance: Full extension to full flexion.
coaching_cues: Palms face the ceiling the whole way
Elbows stay at your sides
Plate stays level

name: Walking Lunge
description: The walking lunge is a unilateral lower body exercise that trains the quadriceps, glutes, and hamstrings in a dynamic stepping pattern. By stepping forward and alternating legs, it trains single-leg strength and balance while requiring the muscles of the hip and knee to work through full range of motion.

execution.starting_position: Stand tall with feet together and core braced. If using dumbbells, hold one in each hand at the sides.
execution.setup_instructions: Ensure adequate floor space to walk several meters. Bodyweight is recommended before adding load.
steps: Step forward with one leg, landing heel first.
