Lower the rear knee toward the floor until the front thigh is roughly parallel to the floor.
Drive through the front heel to bring the rear foot forward and step into the next lunge on the other leg.
Continue alternating legs for the prescribed distance or rep count.
execution.breathing_instructions: Exhale as you push off the front foot. Inhale as you step forward.
common_mistakes: Front knee caving inward — push the knee out in line with the toes
Leaning excessively forward with the torso
Taking too short a stride, forcing the knee too far over the toes
safety_considerations: If knee pain is present, reduce range of motion or switch to a split squat
execution.range_of_motion_guidance: Front thigh parallel to floor or lower. Rear knee just above or touching the floor.
coaching_cues: Long stride — your shin on the front leg should be close to vertical
Tall torso throughout — do not let your upper body collapse forward

name: Wall Angel
description: The wall angel is a postural rehabilitation drill that trains the ability to elevate the arms overhead while maintaining contact between the head, upper back, and arms with a wall. It simultaneously strengthens the lower trapezius and serratus anterior while stretching the pectoral muscles and improving thoracic extension. It is frequently prescribed for forward head posture, rounded shoulders, and thoracic kyphosis correction.

execution.starting_position: Stand with the back flat against a wall, feet approximately 15–30 cm from the base, knees slightly bent. The head, upper back, and both elbows make contact with the wall.
execution.setup_instructions: Stand against a smooth wall with enough room to slide arms overhead. If the low back arches significantly off the wall, bend the knees more.
steps: Step 1: Stand against the wall with head, upper back, and both elbows (bent to 90 degrees) touching the wall.
Step 2: The low back should maintain a natural curve — do not force it flat but do prevent excessive arch.
Step 3: Slowly slide both arms upward along the wall, maintaining contact with the wall with the elbows and forearms.
Step 4: Slide as high as the shoulder mobility and wall contact allow.
Step 5: Slowly slide back down to the starting position with the same wall contact maintained.
execution.breathing_instructions: Exhale as arms slide up. Inhale on the way down.
common_mistakes: Losing elbow or wrist contact with the wall as the arms rise — this is the main challenge
Excessive lower back arch pushing the ribcage forward
Shrugging the shoulders — focus on depression throughout the upward slide
safety_considerations: This drill is safe for most populations
If shoulder impingement symptoms occur, reduce the overhead range before full clearance
execution.range_of_motion_guidance: Slide as high as possible while maintaining elbow and forearm contact with the wall. Many beginners cannot get past shoulder height initially.
execution.tempo_recommendations: 3 seconds up, 2-second hold at top, 3 seconds down. 10–15 reps × 2–3 sets.
coaching_cues: Keep the elbows glued to the wall the entire time
Feel your shoulder blades slide down your back as your arms go up
Breathe out through the effort of maintaining wall contact

name: Wall Angels
description: Wall angels are a scapular mobility and postural correction exercise performed with the back flat against a wall. The exerciser slides their arms upward from shoulder height to overhead while maintaining full contact between the back, head, and arms against the wall. This exercise challenges thoracic extension, scapular upward rotation, and shoulder external rotation — all critical for overhead mobility and shoulder health.

execution.starting_position: Stand with your back against a flat wall. Press the entire back — including the lower back and head — against the wall. Raise arms to a goal-post position (elbows at 90 degrees, upper arms parallel to floor) with forearms and backs of hands touching the wall.
execution.setup_instructions: No equipment needed. Stand against any flat wall. If the lower back cannot contact the wall, slightly bend the knees.
steps: Step 1: Begin in the goal-post position with head, back, elbows, forearms, and hands all in contact with the wall.
Step 2: Slowly slide both arms upward along the wall, keeping the entire arm in contact with the surface.
Step 3: Raise as high as possible while maintaining all contact points — stop if the lower back begins to arch away from the wall.
Step 4: Slowly slide the arms back down to the starting goal-post position. Repeat.
execution.breathing_instructions: Inhale to prepare, exhale as you slide the arms upward. Inhale as you return.
common_mistakes: Allowing the lower back to arch away from the wall during the upward slide
Letting elbows or forearms lose contact with the wall by shrugging
Forcing range that the thoracic spine does not currently allow
safety_considerations: This exercise reveals mobility deficits — work within the range that allows full wall contact
If the head cannot contact the wall, place a small pillow behind the head to close the gap and work toward eliminating it over time
execution.range_of_motion_guidance: Work only as high as wall contact can be maintained. The goal is eventually to reach full overhead extension with all contact points preserved.
execution.tempo_recommendations: 3-2-3-1 (3s slide up, 2s hold, 3s slide down, 1s reset)
coaching_cues: Press the lower back into the wall throughout — do not let it arch
Lead with the elbows as you slide up, not the hands
Breathe out as you reach — relaxing the chest helps overhead mobility

name: Wall Ball
description: Wall ball is a functional conditioning exercise in which the athlete performs a full squat holding a medicine ball and then uses the momentum of the squat ascent to propel the ball upward and throw it against a target on a wall, catching the rebounding ball to begin the next squat. It trains the full lower body squat pattern combined with an explosive upper body press in a continuous, high-intensity movement pattern, making it a staple of functional fitness conditioning workouts.

execution.starting_position: Stand facing a wall at approximately 1 meter distance, holding the medicine ball at chin height with both hands.
execution.setup_instructions: Mark a target on the wall at the prescribed height (typically 3 meters for men, 2.7 meters for women in functional fitness standards). Use a soft medicine ball rated for wall-ball impact.
steps: Step 1: Hold the ball at chest/chin height, stand facing the wall.
Step 2: Descend into a full squat — hip crease below the knee.
Step 3: Drive out of the squat explosively, transferring momentum into the arms.
Step 4: Push the ball upward and release it toward the wall target.
Step 5: Catch the ball as it rebounds and absorb into the next squat immediately.
execution.breathing_instructions: Exhale sharply at the top of the throw. Inhale on the descent.
common_mistakes: Not reaching full squat depth — the hip crease must pass below the knee
Throwing too early — the throw should be powered by the leg drive, not the arms alone
Catching the ball with straight arms — absorb with slightly bent elbows
safety_considerations: Missing the catch can result in the ball dropping on the face or head — stay alert throughout.
Adequate shoulder mobility for the overhead throw position.
execution.range_of_motion_guidance: Full squat depth. Full overhead extension at ball release.
execution.tempo_recommendations: Performed for reps (10–30) or time (60–120 second intervals) in conditioning workouts.
coaching_cues: Squat deep — hip crease below the knee
Drive up — throw at the top
Catch and load — smooth transition

name: Wall Decline Push-Up
description: A bodyweight push-up variation where the feet are braced against a wall at elevation, creating a decline angle. Unlike using a bench, the wall allows for a steeper decline while requiring the feet to actively press into the wall for stability. This targets the lower pectoralis major fibers while also loading the core and shoulder stabilizers differently than a bench-based decline.

execution.starting_position: Begin in a plank position facing away from a wall. Walk the feet up the wall to a comfortable decline angle (30–60 degrees). Hands on the floor, arms extended.
execution.setup_instructions: Use a solid wall with a non-slip floor. Wear shoes for better traction against the wall. Start at a lower decline and progress steeper as strength improves.
steps: Step 1: Position feet on the wall at a comfortable height. Establish a rigid plank position with arms extended.
Step 2: Bend elbows and lower the chest toward the floor in a controlled descent.
Step 3: Descend until chest is 2–3 cm from the floor or as far as shoulder health allows.
Step 4: Press powerfully back to the starting position, maintaining the plank through the entire set.
execution.breathing_instructions: Inhale on descent, exhale on the press.
common_mistakes: Feet slipping down the wall mid-set — push actively into the wall with the feet
Hips sagging or piking — maintain a strict plank
Hands placed too wide, stressing the shoulders
safety_considerations: Wear grippy shoes to prevent foot slippage
Start at a low angle and only increase the wall height when comfortable
Have clear floor space below in case of foot slip
execution.range_of_motion_guidance: Full push-up range, chest to near-floor at the bottom, full arm extension at the top.
coaching_cues: Press your feet into the wall — this keeps you stable and activates the lower body
Squeeze the glutes to keep the plank rigid

name: Wall-Facing Handstand Push-Up
description: The wall-facing handstand push-up positions the chest toward the wall rather than the back, forcing the body into a truly vertical and hollow position. This variation eliminates the arch that commonly occurs in the back-to-wall version and requires more core control. It is used as a bridge to the freestanding HSPU and trains the same deltoid and triceps musculature with more demanding postural requirements.

execution.starting_position: Walk feet up the wall while facing it until the chest is close to the wall. Hands on the floor, chest touching or very close to the wall, body vertical.
execution.setup_instructions: Begin from a push-up position facing the wall. Walk the feet up while walking the hands closer. Find the vertical with the chest against the wall.
steps: Step 1: Establish the chest-to-wall handstand position.
Step 2: Lower the head toward the floor slowly.
Step 3: Descend to full range — head touches the floor.
Step 4: Press back to full arm extension.
Step 5: Maintain chest contact or near-contact with the wall.
execution.breathing_instructions: Inhale descending. Exhale pressing.
common_mistakes: Letting the hips pike away from the wall during the press
Losing the vertical body line and reverting to an arched position
safety_considerations: Have a mat under the head for protection
Prerequisites: comfortable back-to-wall HSPU for multiple reps
execution.range_of_motion_guidance: Full arm extension to head on the floor.
coaching_cues: Chest stays close to the wall
Body vertical — hollow position
Press all the way to lockout

name: Wall Sit
description: The wall sit is an isometric lower body exercise in which the lifter holds a squat position with the back flat against a wall, thighs parallel to the floor, and knees at 90°. Because it requires no movement, it trains muscular endurance and time-under-tension of the quadriceps. It is used for rehabilitation, athletic conditioning, and as a simple test of quad endurance.

execution.starting_position: Stand with your back flat against a smooth wall. Walk your feet forward until they are approximately 60–90 cm from the wall.
execution.setup_instructions: Find a smooth, flat wall. Wear shoes with grip. The feet should be shoulder-width apart and directly below the knees when in position.
steps: Step 1: Slide your back down the wall until your thighs are parallel to the floor and your knees are at 90°.
Step 2: Ensure your knees are directly over your ankles — not in front of them.
Step 3: Keep your back flat against the wall throughout. Do not lean forward.
Step 4: Hold the position for the target duration while breathing steadily.
Step 5: To exit, slide back up the wall to standing or step forward.
execution.breathing_instructions: Breathe steadily throughout the hold. Do not hold the breath for extended durations — this increases blood pressure unnecessarily.
common_mistakes: Knees extending past the toes due to feet placed too close to the wall
Back peeling away from the wall due to core fatigue
Thighs not reaching parallel — reduces quad demand significantly
safety_considerations: Those with knee pain should check that knees track over toes and that feet are positioned appropriately
Avoid performing to failure on a slippery floor
execution.range_of_motion_guidance: Thighs must reach parallel to the floor. Anything shallower significantly reduces the training stimulus.
execution.tempo_recommendations: Isometric hold — measure in seconds or minutes rather than reps
coaching_cues: Thighs parallel — don't cheat with a shallow squat
Back flat to the wall at all times
Breathe steadily — don't hold your breath

name: Wall Walk to Handstand
description: The wall walk to handstand starts in a push-up position with feet against the wall, then progressively walks the feet up the wall while walking the hands toward the wall, until the body is near-vertical in a wall handstand position. It builds the shoulder endurance, scapular stability, and body awareness required for handstand work, and each repetition is a full shoulder press equivalent in terms of muscular loading.

execution.starting_position: Begin in a push-up position with feet flat against the base of a wall.
execution.setup_instructions: Clear the wall area. The floor directly below should be unobstructed to allow hand walking.
steps: Step 1: Begin in push-up position, feet against the wall.
Step 2: Walk feet up the wall — take small steps.
Step 3: Simultaneously walk hands toward the wall to maintain balance.
Step 4: Continue until the body is as vertical as possible (chest close to the wall).
Step 5: Hold 2 seconds at the top, then walk back down under control.
execution.breathing_instructions: Breathe continuously during the walk. Hold at the top.
common_mistakes: Walking too fast — losing control is dangerous
Not walking hands close enough — the body must be close to vertical for maximum benefit
safety_considerations: Have clear bail-out space on both sides
Beginners should practice with a spotter on the first attempts
execution.range_of_motion_guidance: Push-up position to near-vertical handstand against the wall.
execution.tempo_recommendations: Slow controlled walk, 2s hold at top
coaching_cues: Small steps — do not rush the walk
Walk the hands in as the feet go higher
Lock the core — no excessive arch

name: Weight Plate Pinch Press
description: The weight plate pinch press is a unique chest exercise in which two weight plates are pressed together between the palms and pushed overhead or forward. The act of pinching the plates isometrically activates the pectoral muscles throughout the pressing motion, making it an excellent finishing or isolation movement for inner chest development.

execution.starting_position: Hold two smooth-faced weight plates sandwich-style between your palms at chest level. Stand or lie on a flat bench.
execution.setup_instructions: Choose two plates of equal size (10lb plates are common). Smooth faces should be in contact with each other. Grip the outer edges with palms facing inward.
steps: Step 1: Squeeze the plates firmly together and hold them at chest level.
Step 2: Keeping the squeeze constant, press the plates forward (standing) or upward (lying) until the arms are extended.
Step 3: Hold the top position and intensify the squeeze for 1 second.
Step 4: Lower the plates back to the starting position while continuing to press inward.
Step 5: Never release the squeeze between reps.
execution.breathing_instructions: Exhale as you press the plates away. Inhale as you bring them back to the chest.
common_mistakes: Releasing the inward squeeze on the press, allowing plates to slide
Using plates with rough or ridged outer faces that cut into the palms
Going too heavy and losing control of the pinch
safety_considerations: Use smooth-faced steel plates, not bumper plates with raised lips
Do not use this exercise to failure — dropping the plates could cause injury
Start with lighter plates until the pinch coordination feels stable
execution.range_of_motion_guidance: Press to full arm extension, maintaining the inward squeeze the entire time. Lower under control.
coaching_cues: Squeeze the plates like your life depends on it
Feel the sternum compress on the press
Don't let the squeeze go — that IS the exercise

name: Weighted Bench Dips
description: Weighted bench dips are performed the same as bodyweight bench dips but with weight plates placed across the lap to increase the loading. The hands are on a bench behind the body, the feet are on a surface in front, and the hips dip down between. Adding weight plates allows the exercise to progress beyond bodyweight limitations. The exercise primarily works the triceps with significant anterior deltoid involvement.

execution.starting_position: Place hands behind on a flat bench, feet on another elevated surface in front. Place weight plates across the lap. Begin with arms extended.
execution.setup_instructions: Have a training partner place or remove the plates safely. The feet should be elevated to increase the range of motion and tricep demand.
steps: Step 1: Begin with arms extended, weight across the lap.
Step 2: Lower the hips downward by bending the elbows to 90 degrees.
Step 3: Push through the hands to extend the elbows and return to the starting position.
Step 4: Keep the torso close to the bench edge throughout.
execution.breathing_instructions: Inhale on the descent, exhale on the press.
common_mistakes: Letting the hips drift too far from the bench (strains the shoulder)
Insufficient depth
safety_considerations: The anterior shoulder is under significant stress — avoid very heavy loading which can damage the shoulder capsule
Feet elevation should allow 90-degree elbow flexion at the bottom
execution.range_of_motion_guidance: Upper arms to parallel with the floor at the bottom.
coaching_cues: Keep the torso upright and close to the bench
Elbows bend straight back — not flared
Squeeze at the top

name: Weighted Decline Sit-Up
description: The weighted decline sit-up adds external resistance — typically a weight plate held at the chest or extended overhead — to the standard decline sit-up, dramatically increasing the demand on the rectus abdominis and providing a stimulus sufficient for muscular hypertrophy. Holding the load overhead increases the lever arm and further challenges the abs throughout the movement. Progressive overload is straightforward by incrementally increasing plate weight.

execution.starting_position: Lie on the decline bench with feet secured. Hold a weight plate at the chest with both hands, or extend it overhead.
execution.setup_instructions: Begin with a light plate (5–10 kg) held at the chest before progressing to overhead positioning. Secure feet firmly.
steps: Step 1: Lie fully extended on the bench, holding the plate at the chest.
Step 2: Curl the torso upward by contracting the abs, raising the plate as the torso rises.
Step 3: Continue until the torso is fully upright.
Step 4: Lower slowly back to the starting position, controlling the eccentric against the added resistance.
Step 5: For overhead variation, press the plate overhead at the top of the movement.
execution.breathing_instructions: Exhale on the way up. Inhale on the controlled descent.
common_mistakes: Using too heavy a load before mastering unweighted form
Dropping quickly on the descent and losing eccentric tension
safety_considerations: Avoid if lumbar disc issues are present — the combination of flexion and load is contraindicated
execution.range_of_motion_guidance: Full extension at the bottom to fully upright at the top.
execution.tempo_recommendations: 3-1-3-0. Full eccentric control is critical with added load.
coaching_cues: Squeeze the plate to maintain tension
Control the descent — the eccentric is where the gains are

name: Weighted Parallel Bar Dips
description: Weighted parallel bar dips add external load via a dip belt, vest, or dumbbell held between the legs to the standard dip movement, increasing the demand on the lower pectorals, triceps, and anterior deltoids. This is one of the best absolute strength builders for the chest-triceps complex and allows progressive overload far beyond bodyweight limitations.

execution.starting_position: Attach the desired weight to a dip belt or hold a dumbbell between crossed ankles. Mount the parallel bars with arms extended, body upright.
execution.setup_instructions: Ensure the dip bars are stable and wide enough for a comfortable grip. Attach weight securely to the belt before mounting. Begin with modest added weight and progress gradually.
steps: Step 1: Mount the dip bars in the support position with arms locked, slight forward lean.
Step 2: Lower the body by bending the elbows, maintaining a consistent forward torso lean.
Step 3: Descend until shoulders are at or below elbow level for full depth.
Step 4: Drive powerfully upward through the hands, pressing back to the lockout position.
Step 5: Maintain a controlled tempo — do not use the weight as momentum.
execution.breathing_instructions: Inhale as you lower. Exhale as you press up through the lockout.
common_mistakes: Adding too much weight before achieving clean bodyweight dips
Using too upright a torso, shifting all load to the triceps
Locking the elbows aggressively at the top with excessive weight
safety_considerations: Master 15–20 clean bodyweight dips before adding external load
Use a dip belt designed for this purpose — improvised attachment can be dangerous
Avoid if you have anterior shoulder impingement or rotator cuff issues
execution.range_of_motion_guidance: Lower until shoulder is at or below elbow level. Full lockout at the top without hyperextending the elbow joint.
coaching_cues: Lean forward for chest — stay upright for triceps
Full depth every rep
The added weight is a privilege earned with clean bodyweight dips

name: Weighted Ring Dips (Triceps Focus)
description: Ring dips performed with added weight and an upright torso to maximize triceps involvement over chest. The instability of rings adds rotator cuff and stabilizer demands. This is an elite-level triceps and chest developer.

execution.starting_position: Set up for Weighted Ring Dips (Triceps Focus) in the appropriate position.
execution.setup_instructions: Prepare equipment and body position for Weighted Ring Dips (Triceps Focus).
steps: Step 1: Hang weight from belt or use weighted vest. Mount rings at lockout.
Step 2: Keep torso upright and elbows close to body throughout.
Step 3: Lower by bending elbows until upper arms are parallel to floor.
Step 4: Press back to lockout, rotating rings outward at the top.
execution.breathing_instructions: Exhale during the exertion phase, inhale during the return.
common_mistakes: Leaning forward excessively
Flaring elbows outward
safety_considerations: Keep joints aligned throughout the movement.
Use controlled weight appropriate for skill level.
execution.range_of_motion_guidance: Move through full range of motion without compromising joint integrity.
coaching_cues: Turn rings out at lockout
Upright torso for tricep emphasis

name: Weighted Ring Push-Up
description: A ring push-up performed with additional load, typically via a weight vest or a plate suspended from a dip belt. The gymnastic rings create an unstable surface that maximizes stabilizer recruitment, while the added external load increases the progressive overload on the pectoralis major and triceps beyond what bodyweight alone provides. This bridges the gap between bodyweight and barbell pressing.

execution.starting_position: Set rings low enough for push-up position (approximately 15–30 cm off the ground). Don a weight vest or attach a plate to a dip belt. Get into push-up position with hands in the rings, body straight.
execution.setup_instructions: Set rings at appropriate height. Put on weight vest before getting into position. Ensure extra load is secure before beginning.
steps: Step 1: Establish push-up plank on the rings. Keep rings turned out slightly for shoulder health.
Step 2: Lower the chest toward the ring level, controlling the inherent ring rotation.
Step 3: Descend until chest is at ring height.
Step 4: Press powerfully back to full arm extension, maintaining ring control.
execution.breathing_instructions: Inhale on descent, exhale on press.
common_mistakes: Adding weight before mastering unweighted ring push-ups
Rings swinging out uncontrollably on descent
Weight vest riding up during the movement, shifting center of gravity
safety_considerations: Master bodyweight ring push-ups with controlled descent/ascent before adding load
Start with minimal added weight (5–10 kg) and progress conservatively
Ensure ring straps are secure before beginning loaded sets
execution.range_of_motion_guidance: Full push-up range, chest to ring level at the bottom, full lockout at top.
coaching_cues: Turn the rings out at the top for maximum shoulder stability
Keep the rings close to the body — wide rings are harder to control

name: Weighted Side Plank with Hip Lift
description: A side plank with a weight plate placed on the hip, combined with repeated hip lowering and lifting through a full range. The added weight increases lateral core load while the hip lift adds a strength-endurance component. This builds robust lateral chain strength.

execution.starting_position: Set up for Weighted Side Plank with Hip Lift in proper position.
execution.setup_instructions: Prepare body and equipment for Weighted Side Plank with Hip Lift.
steps: Step 1: Set up side plank on forearm with plate balanced on hip.
Step 2: Lower hip until nearly touching floor.
Step 3: Drive hip back up to full plank height.
Step 4: Complete all reps then switch sides.
execution.breathing_instructions: Breathe steadily; never hold breath during static holds.
common_mistakes: Plate sliding off hip
Dropping hip uncontrolled
safety_considerations: Build prerequisite strength before attempting advanced variations.
Stop if joint pain occurs.
execution.range_of_motion_guidance: Full range of motion with control at all times.
coaching_cues: Stabilize plate before beginning
Full range of motion on each rep

name: Seated Cable Row — Wide Lat Bar
description: The seated cable row with a wide lat bar uses a pronated (overhand) wide grip, shifting emphasis from the lower lats and biceps toward the rhomboids, middle trapezius, and rear deltoids compared to a neutral-grip V-bar row. The wider grip requires greater horizontal shoulder abduction and places the shoulder in a position that more directly targets the upper back retractors. It is an effective mid-back mass builder.

execution.starting_position: Attach a wide lat bar to the seated cable row machine. Sit with feet on footrests, knees slightly bent. Grip the bar with an overhand grip wider than shoulder width.
execution.setup_instructions: Adjust the seat so the cable is at chest height when seated. Sit tall with a neutral spine before initiating each rep.
steps: Step 1: Sit with the arms extended toward the cable, gripping the wide bar overhand.
Step 2: Begin from a slight forward lean with the shoulder blades protracted.
Step 3: Row the bar toward the lower sternum by retracting the scapulae and driving the elbows out and back.
Step 4: Squeeze the mid-back hard at peak contraction.
Step 5: Return under control to the starting extended position.
execution.breathing_instructions: Exhale on the row, inhale on the return.
common_mistakes: Rocking the torso back excessively instead of using the back muscles
Not fully protracting the scapulae at the start of each rep
Pulling the bar to the abdomen — target is the lower sternum with this grip width
safety_considerations: The wider grip places the shoulder in greater external rotation — do not force range of motion if discomfort is felt
execution.range_of_motion_guidance: Full scapular protraction at the start, full retraction at the end of each rep.
coaching_cues: Let the shoulder blades spread at the start
Pull elbows back and out
Squeeze the mid-back — not just the lats

name: Wide-Grip Barbell Curl
description: The wide-grip barbell curl uses a grip wider than shoulder width on a straight barbell, which internally rotates the shoulders slightly and shifts greater emphasis to the short head of the biceps. The short head contributes to the width and peak of the bicep when developed well. It contrasts with close-grip curls which emphasize the long head.

execution.starting_position: Stand upright holding a barbell with a supinated grip wider than shoulder width. Arms extended at the thighs.
execution.setup_instructions: Grip wider than shoulder width — approximately 1.5x shoulder width. Keep the elbows slightly forward.
steps: Step 1: Curl the barbell upward by flexing the elbows, keeping the upper arms at the sides.
Step 2: Curl until maximum elbow flexion is achieved.
Step 3: Lower the bar slowly back to the starting position.
execution.breathing_instructions: Exhale on the curl, inhale on the return.
common_mistakes: Swinging the torso
Elbows flaring excessively outward
Using momentum
safety_considerations: Avoid if wide grip causes wrist discomfort — use an EZ-bar instead
execution.range_of_motion_guidance: Full extension to full flexion.
coaching_cues: Wide grip, short head focus
Elbows at the sides
Control the descent

name: Wide-Grip Barbell Bench Press
description: The Wide-Grip Bench Press uses a hand placement significantly wider than shoulder-width, reducing the bar travel distance and shortening the range of motion at the elbow. This grip places greater mechanical advantage on the pectorals and shifts some load away from the triceps, making it a useful variation for chest-dominant pressing development.

execution.starting_position: Lie on a flat bench under the bar. Grip the bar with hands placed 2-4 inches wider than your standard grip on each side, outside the smooth center knurling.
execution.setup_instructions: Position on the bench with shoulder blades retracted and depressed. Grip the bar in a full grip (thumb wrapped). Ensure forearms are vertical when the bar touches the chest.
steps: Step 1: Unrack and hold the bar at arm's length above the chest.
Step 2: Lower the bar under control to touch the lower sternum.
Step 3: Press back to the starting position.
Step 4: Keep the elbows at approximately 70-80 degrees from the torso — wider grip naturally increases elbow flare.
execution.breathing_instructions: Inhale and brace before lowering. Exhale at the top.
common_mistakes: Gripping excessively wide, which places severe strain on the shoulder joint
Allowing the wrists to bend backward under load
safety_considerations: Very wide grip significantly increases shoulder joint stress — do not exceed a grip where forearms are vertical at the bottom
Shoulder pain is a common complaint; reduce grip width immediately if it occurs
execution.range_of_motion_guidance: Full touch to chest at bottom; full elbow extension at top. ROM is slightly shorter than standard due to wider grip.
coaching_cues: Forearms vertical at the bottom — that is the widest safe grip
Squeeze the bar like you are trying to break it in half

name: Wide-Grip Decline Barbell Bench Press
description: A decline barbell bench press using a grip wider than shoulder-width. The wide grip on the decline angle combines maximum lower pectoralis major stretch with reduced range of motion at the elbow, allowing heavy loading of the sternal pec fibers. The wide grip shifts the demand away from the triceps, placing greater emphasis on chest contribution throughout the pressing movement.

execution.starting_position: Lie on a decline bench (15–30 degrees) with feet secured. Take a wide grip on the barbell — pinkies at or near the outer ring marks. Unrack and hold above the lower chest.
execution.setup_instructions: Set the decline to 15–30 degrees. Secure feet. Use collars. The wide grip should be comfortable — do not go beyond the outer grip marks.
steps: Step 1: Unrack with a wide grip. Bar positioned above the lower chest.
Step 2: Lower the bar toward the lower chest. Elbows flare wider than a shoulder-width grip would allow.
Step 3: Touch the lower chest and press back to lockout, following the bar's natural arc.
Step 4: Keep the upper back pinched and feet secured throughout.
execution.breathing_instructions: Inhale before descent, exhale on the press.
common_mistakes: Grip too extreme — beyond the outer rings creates shoulder and wrist injury risk
Feet unsecured on the decline bench
Excessive elbow flare that places the shoulder in a compromised position
safety_considerations: Wide decline pressing stresses the shoulder joint — start lighter than standard decline press
Use a spotter for heavier sets
If wrist discomfort occurs, slightly narrow the grip
execution.range_of_motion_guidance: Full range from lower chest to lockout. The wide grip slightly shortens the elbow's range of motion.
coaching_cues: Lead with the chest, not the elbows — the wide grip already does the shoulder work
Keep the shoulder blades tight to protect the shoulder at the wide position

name: Wide-Grip Incline Barbell Bench Press
description: An incline barbell bench press performed with a grip wider than shoulder-width. The wide grip reduces the range of motion required at the elbow and shifts the shoulder position to greater horizontal abduction, increasing the stretch on the pectoralis major clavicular fibers at the bottom position. This grip is commonly used by powerlifters and bodybuilders to maximize chest contribution in incline pressing.

execution.starting_position: Lie on an incline bench (30–45 degrees) under a racked barbell. Grip the bar with hands outside the standard bench press grip — typically with pinkies near the outer ring marks on most bars.
execution.setup_instructions: Set incline to 30–45 degrees. Rack height should allow unracking with slightly bent arms. Use collars on the barbell.
steps: Step 1: Unrack the bar with a wide grip and position it above the upper chest.
Step 2: Lower the bar to the upper chest, allowing the elbows to flare wider than a standard grip would permit.
Step 3: Touch the clavicular area lightly and press back to full lockout.
Step 4: Keep the upper back pinched against the bench throughout.
execution.breathing_instructions: Inhale before descent, exhale through the press.
common_mistakes: Grip too wide — beyond the outer ring marks places excessive stress on the wrists and shoulders
Excessive elbow flare that strains the shoulder joint
Bar drifting toward the belly during the press — maintain the vertical bar path
safety_considerations: Wide grip incline pressing places greater shoulder stress — start with less weight than standard grip
Use a spotter, particularly when the grip is wider and control may be compromised
Avoid taking the grip to the extreme — 1–2 finger widths outside standard grip is sufficient
execution.range_of_motion_guidance: Full range from chest contact to lockout. The wide grip slightly reduces the range of motion needed at the elbow.
coaching_cues: Lead the bar with the chest, not the elbows
Keep the shoulder blades pulled together — this protects the shoulder in the wide grip position

name: Wide-Grip Pronated T-Bar Row
description: The wide-grip pronated T-bar row uses a wider than shoulder-width overhand grip on a T-bar or landmine setup, shifting emphasis toward the middle trapezius, rear deltoids, and rhomboids compared to the standard close-grip version. The pronated wide grip limits biceps involvement and demands greater scapular retraction strength to complete each repetition.

execution.starting_position: Straddle the T-bar machine or landmine bar. Grip the wide handles (or bar itself) pronated, hands wider than shoulder width. Hinge to 45 degrees.
execution.setup_instructions: If a T-bar machine is used, set the chest pad appropriately. For a landmine, use a straight bar without a handle attachment.
steps: Step 1: Begin hinged with arms extended gripping the bar wide.
Step 2: Initiate by squeezing the shoulder blades together.
Step 3: Row elbows back and wide — not tucked into the torso.
Step 4: At the top, hold 1 second with shoulder blades fully retracted.
Step 5: Lower under control.
execution.breathing_instructions: Exhale on the row. Inhale descending.
common_mistakes: Elbows tracking too close to the body — wide grip requires wide elbows
Excessive torso extension at the top — maintain the hinge
safety_considerations: Wide pronated grip increases wrist stress — ensure wrists are strong and healthy
Do not add excessive spinal extension to assist the row
execution.range_of_motion_guidance: Full arm extension to elbows behind torso level.
coaching_cues: Elbows go wide — think 'flying elbows'
Drive the shoulder blades together, not just back
Lead with the chest

name: Wide-Grip Pull-Up
description: The wide-grip pull-up is performed with the hands significantly wider than shoulder-width in a pronated grip, which shortens the range of motion but increases the mechanical tension on the latissimus dorsi by emphasizing shoulder adduction over elbow flexion. The wider hand position reduces biceps involvement and isolates the outer lats more directly.

execution.starting_position: Grasp the pull-up bar with a pronated grip wider than shoulder-width — roughly 1.5× shoulder width. Hang in a full dead hang.
execution.setup_instructions: Use a straight pull-up bar long enough for a wide grip. Avoid grip positions so wide they compromise shoulder health.
steps: Step 1: Begin in a dead hang with the wide pronated grip.
Step 2: Depress and retract the scapulae slightly before pulling.
Step 3: Pull the body up by driving the elbows down and in toward the hips.
Step 4: Aim to bring the chest to the bar or pull until the chin clears.
Step 5: Lower slowly back to full extension.
execution.breathing_instructions: Exhale as you pull up. Inhale as you lower.
common_mistakes: Gripping excessively wide, which stresses the shoulder joint and reduces ROM
Not achieving full arm extension at the bottom
Pulling only to chin level when chest-to-bar is achievable
safety_considerations: Very wide grips place more stress on the shoulder joint — use a grip no wider than 1.5× shoulder width for most trainees
If shoulder discomfort occurs, reduce grip width
execution.range_of_motion_guidance: Full dead hang to chin above bar. The wider grip reduces total range of motion compared to shoulder-width — this is normal.
coaching_cues: Drive the elbows toward the hip pockets
Think 'lat spread' — visualize spreading the elbows wide as you pull
Keep the chest up and spine long

name: Wide-Grip Push-Up
description: The wide-grip push-up is performed with hands placed wider than in a standard push-up. The wider grip reduces triceps involvement and increases the range of motion for the pectoral muscles, shifting more demand to the chest. It is a good bodyweight variation for those who want to emphasize chest development.

execution.starting_position: High plank position with hands placed 1.5 to 2 times shoulder width apart, fingers angled slightly outward. Body forms a straight line from head to heels.
execution.setup_instructions: No equipment needed. Wider hand placement increases pectoral stretch but also increases shoulder joint stress — avoid excessively wide placement.
steps: Brace the core and maintain a rigid plank position.
Lower the body by bending the elbows outward until the chest is close to or touching the floor.
Push back up to the starting position, extending the arms fully.
execution.breathing_instructions: Inhale on descent, exhale on the push.
common_mistakes: Placing hands so wide that shoulder impingement occurs
Letting hips sag
safety_considerations: If shoulder discomfort occurs at a very wide grip, narrow the hand position
execution.range_of_motion_guidance: Full range, chest nearly to the floor.
coaching_cues: Feel the chest stretch at the bottom of each rep
Press outward into the floor as you push up

name: Windshield Wipers
description: Windshield wipers are an advanced hanging core exercise performed from a pull-up bar in which the athlete raises both legs to horizontal or above, then rotates them side to side like windshield wipers. The exercise heavily loads the obliques as they both decelerate and produce trunk rotation under a large external moment arm. It also demands significant lat and grip strength to remain stable on the bar throughout.

execution.starting_position: Hang from a pull-up bar with an overhand grip, hands shoulder-width or slightly wider apart. Arms fully extended, body hanging straight.
execution.setup_instructions: Use a sturdy pull-up bar capable of supporting dynamic swinging loads. Chalk or straps may be used for grip.
steps: Step 1: Hang from the bar with straight arms in a dead hang position.
Step 2: Raise both legs simultaneously until they are perpendicular to the torso (horizontal or above).
Step 3: Keeping legs together and straight, rotate the legs to one side as far as controllable, ideally toward the bar.
Step 4: Return through center and rotate to the opposite side — one complete repetition.
Step 5: Continue alternating sides for the prescribed reps, controlling the rotation throughout.
execution.breathing_instructions: Exhale as you rotate to each side. Inhale as you return through center.
common_mistakes: Bending the knees to reduce the lever arm — this reduces core demand significantly
Using hip flexor swing momentum rather than oblique-driven rotation
Letting the body swing and rotate as a whole, losing bar stability
safety_considerations: Requires strong hanging and core prerequisites. Train toes-to-bar first.
Grip failure is a risk — use chalk or straps if needed.
execution.range_of_motion_guidance: Legs should ideally reach toward the bar at the top position. Rotation should bring the legs toward the bar on each side.
execution.tempo_recommendations: 2–3 seconds per rotation side. Control is essential — never use swing momentum.
coaching_cues: Legs stay locked together and straight
Drive the rotation from your obliques, not your hips swinging
Return to center before each rotation — no rebounding

name: Windshield Wipers on Rings
description: Windshield wiper movements performed while hanging from gymnastic rings instead of a bar. The instability of the rings adds rotational challenge to the standard windshield wiper. The athlete must control both the core rotation and the ring stabilization simultaneously.

execution.starting_position: Set up for Windshield Wipers on Rings in proper position.
execution.setup_instructions: Prepare body and equipment for Windshield Wipers on Rings.
steps: Step 1: Hang from rings with legs raised to 90 degrees, arms straight.
Step 2: Rotate legs to one side, bringing feet toward the same-side ring.
Step 3: Pass through center and rotate to opposite side.
Step 4: Continue windshield wiper motion with control.
execution.breathing_instructions: Breathe steadily; never hold breath during static holds.
common_mistakes: Swinging rather than rotating
Dropping hips during the rotation
safety_considerations: Build prerequisite strength before attempting advanced variations.
Stop if joint pain occurs.
execution.range_of_motion_guidance: Full range of motion with control at all times.
coaching_cues: Control both rings throughout
Slower rotation means harder exercise

name: Wobble Board Balance
description: Standing balance on a wobble board (a circular board mounted on a rounded base) challenges multi-directional ankle and hip proprioception. Unlike a foam pad (which provides soft, predictable instability), a wobble board creates dynamic tilting in all planes simultaneously, making it a higher-level proprioceptive challenge. Used in ankle sprain rehabilitation (late-stage), ACL protocols, and sport-specific balance training.

execution.starting_position: Step onto the wobble board with both feet centered on the platform. Find your balance with the board flat (edge not touching the ground). Stand near a wall for safety.
execution.setup_instructions: Use a commercially available wobble board. Begin with bilateral (both feet) balance before attempting single-leg. Stand near a stable surface for safety.
steps: Step 1: Step onto the wobble board center. Find a balanced position with the board flat.
Step 2: Allow the board to wobble naturally in all directions, responding with ankle and hip micro-adjustments to prevent the edge from contacting the floor.
Step 3: Maintain balance for the prescribed duration.
Step 4: Step off carefully. Rest and repeat.
execution.breathing_instructions: Breathe normally throughout. Focus and calm breathing aids balance.
common_mistakes: Gripping with the toes — allow the ankle to respond to the board naturally
Locking the knees — a small knee bend improves balance and reduces joint stress
Standing too close to the edge of the board rather than centered
safety_considerations: ALWAYS stand near a wall or stable surface
Use the wall or bar for safety when first learning the wobble board — do not attempt hands-free too quickly
Wet or slippery wobble boards are hazardous — ensure the surface is dry
execution.range_of_motion_guidance: Bilateral balance target: board edge should not touch the floor. Single-leg progression: same target on one foot.
execution.tempo_recommendations: Hold for 30-60 seconds per set. Build to 60 seconds bilateral before progressing to single-leg.
coaching_cues: Soft knees — do not lock out the knees
Allow the board to respond to your weight shifts — do not fight it; dance with it
Keep the gaze on a fixed point — visual focus aids balance

name: World's Greatest Stretch
description: The world's greatest stretch is a dynamic compound mobility sequence that combines a hip flexor stretch, thoracic rotation, and hamstring mobilization in a single flowing movement. Starting in a lunge position, the lifter places the same-side hand on the ground while reaching the opposite hand to the ceiling, rotating through the thoracic spine. It is considered one of the most time-efficient warm-up movements as it targets multiple restrictions simultaneously.

execution.starting_position: Begin standing, then step one foot forward into a lunge with the front foot flat and the back leg extended.
execution.setup_instructions: No equipment needed. Use a mat for comfort on the rear knee if needed.
steps: Step 1: Step the right foot forward into a large lunge. Lower the left knee to the floor if needed.
Step 2: Place the right hand on the ground just inside the right foot.
Step 3: Reach the left arm up and open the chest, rotating the thoracic spine toward the ceiling.
Step 4: Hold the rotation for 2–3 breaths, feeling the stretch across the chest, hip flexor, and thoracic spine.
Step 5: Return the left hand to the floor, then stand up and alternate sides.
execution.breathing_instructions: Inhale into the rotation. Exhale and sink slightly deeper on each breath.
common_mistakes: Rotating from the lower back rather than the thoracic spine
Front knee caving inward — keep it tracking over the second toe
Moving too quickly through the rotation, skipping the breathing component
safety_considerations: If wrist discomfort occurs, make a fist for the supporting hand
Take it slowly — this is a preparatory movement, not a loaded exercise
execution.range_of_motion_guidance: Rotate the upper arm as high as the thoracic spine allows. Hips stay square.
execution.tempo_recommendations: 2–3 breaths per side, 5 reps per side, 1–2 rounds.
coaching_cues: Let your eyes follow your hand to encourage the rotation
Press the front knee outward with the inside of your elbow as you rotate
Think tall — reach for the ceiling, not just open to the side

name: Wrist Curl
description: The wrist curl is an isolation exercise for the wrist flexor muscles of the forearm, performed with the forearms resting on a flat surface and the wrists hanging free beyond the edge. The palms face upward, and the wrists flex to curl the weight toward the forearm. It directly targets the flexor carpi radialis and flexor carpi ulnaris, with contribution from the finger flexors. It is a fundamental forearm-strengthening exercise for grip-dependent sports and activities.

execution.starting_position: Sit on a bench. Rest the forearms on the thighs or on the bench surface with the wrists hanging beyond the edge, palms facing up. Hold a dumbbell (or barbell) in the hands with the fingers curled around it.
execution.setup_instructions: Sit on a flat bench. Place both forearms on the thighs or bench pad so they are fully supported. The wrists hang off the edge. Use a relatively light weight — the forearm flexors fatigue quickly.
steps: Step 1: Forearms resting on a surface, wrists hanging off the edge, palms facing upward, weight in hands.
Step 2: Allow the wrists to relax fully downward into extension before each rep.
Step 3: Exhale and flex the wrists, curling the weight upward as far as possible.
Step 4: Inhale and slowly lower the wrists back to full extension.
execution.breathing_instructions: Exhale on the curl; inhale on the lowering.
common_mistakes: Not allowing the wrists to fully extend at the bottom, reducing the range of motion
Using excessively heavy weight, which forces the forearms off the support surface
safety_considerations: Keep forearms fully supported on the bench or thighs throughout
Stop if sharp pain is felt at the wrist or elbow
execution.range_of_motion_guidance: Full wrist extension (drop) at the bottom; maximum wrist flexion (curl) at the top.
coaching_cues: Let the weight roll to the fingertips at the bottom — full drop
Curl only the wrists — the forearms stay on the bench

name: Wrist Roller
description: The wrist roller uses a short bar with a rope attached to the center, weighted at the rope's end. The lifter holds the bar at arm's length (or at shoulder height) and winds the rope upward by alternately rotating each wrist, then unwinds it. This continuous motion trains both wrist flexors and extensors through their full range repeatedly, producing an intense forearm pump. It is one of the most demanding forearm exercises available.

execution.starting_position: Hold the wrist roller bar with both hands, arms extended forward at shoulder height. The rope and weight hang below.
execution.setup_instructions: Attach the desired weight to the rope. Hold with shoulder-width grip.
steps: Step 1: Begin with arms extended forward at shoulder height, weight hanging.
Step 2: Rotate one wrist forward (overhand roll) to wind the rope upward.
Step 3: Alternate wrists, continuing to roll until the weight reaches the bar.
Step 4: Reverse the direction, slowly unrolling the rope back to the hanging position.
execution.breathing_instructions: Breathe freely throughout — focus on rhythm.
common_mistakes: Dropping the arms during the roll
Using too much weight causing grip failure
Rolling too fast to feel the muscles work
safety_considerations: The rolling motion is demanding on the forearm tendons — start very light
execution.range_of_motion_guidance: Full wind up and full unwind — do not stop partway.
coaching_cues: Arms stay level
Feel the burn in the forearms
Control the unroll

name: Yates Row
description: A barbell bent-over row variation using a supinated (underhand) grip, popularized by bodybuilder Dorian Yates. The reverse grip shifts the loading emphasis from the upper lats toward the lower lats and biceps, and the torso is typically held at a less horizontal angle than a standard bent-over row.

execution.starting_position: Stand holding a barbell with an underhand (supinated) grip, shoulder-width. Hinge forward to approximately 70 degrees from vertical.
execution.setup_instructions: Load a barbell on the floor or use a rack. Grip the bar underhand (palms up). Hinge forward to the working angle.
steps: Step 1: Brace the core hard and hold the torso at approximately 70 degrees from vertical.
Step 2: Pull the bar toward the lower abdomen or navel, keeping the elbows close to the body.
Step 3: Squeeze the lats and biceps at the top of the movement.
Step 4: Lower the bar under control to full arm extension.
execution.breathing_instructions: Exhale on the pull. Inhale on the return.
common_mistakes: Letting the torso excessively rise during the pull — maintain the forward lean
Using too much bicep and not enough lat engagement
safety_considerations: The underhand grip is naturally stronger than overhand — expect to use more weight than a standard row
execution.range_of_motion_guidance: Full arm extension at the bottom. Bar pulled to lower abdomen at the top.
coaching_cues: Pull to the belly button
Elbows stay close to the body

name: Yoke Carry
description: The yoke carry involves hoisting a heavy steel frame (the yoke) across the upper back and trapezius, then walking a prescribed distance as quickly as possible under that extreme load. It is a foundational strongman event and an exceptional developer of total-body strength, postural endurance, and anaerobic conditioning. The yoke imposes unique loading because the implement is wider than a barbell and the load is not secured, requiring constant isometric stabilisation from the trapezius, erector spinae, and core throughout the walk.

execution.starting_position: Set the yoke crossbar to upper-back height (slightly below the bar position for a low-bar squat). Walk under the yoke, position the bar across the upper traps, and brace the core hard before unracking.
execution.setup_instructions: Adjust yoke uprights to the correct height for your build. Load weight plates evenly on both sides. Walk the course before loading to identify the turnaround point.
steps: Step 1: Position yourself under the yoke crossbar with the bar resting on the upper traps. Take a wide, stable stance.
Step 2: Brace the core maximally, take a full breath, and stand the yoke up by extending the hips and knees.
Step 3: Begin walking with short, quick steps. Keep the torso upright — do not lean forward.
Step 4: Maintain a tight grip on the yoke uprights throughout the walk for stability control.
Step 5: At the turnaround or finish, slow the momentum carefully and lower the yoke to the ground by hinging at the hips and bending the knees.
execution.breathing_instructions: Take a full breath and brace the core before unracking. During the walk, take short breaths between steps without fully releasing the core brace.
common_mistakes: Taking long strides, which makes the yoke swing and sway laterally
Not bracing the core before the initial stand, causing the spine to load in flexion
Looking at the ground — keep the gaze forward to maintain spinal alignment
safety_considerations: Have collars on the weight plates — a falling plate at speed is a serious hazard
Use a spotter or judge for the first attempts at heavy loads
Do not attempt a yoke carry without a solid foundation in barbell squats and loaded carries
execution.range_of_motion_guidance: Walk distance is event-specific (typically 10–25 metres). Steps should be short and fast — approximately 50–60% of normal walking stride length.
execution.tempo_recommendations: Event training: maximum speed for set distance. Strength training: 10–20 metres at 60–80% of competition weight × 3–5 sets. Rest 3–5 minutes between sets.
coaching_cues: Short, fast feet — not long lunging strides
Drive the head up and back into the bar
Squeeze everything — abs, glutes, traps — before you pick it up

name: Z-Press
description: The Z-Press is a seated overhead press performed on the floor with the legs extended straight in front of the body, eliminating any leg drive or lower body support. The extended-leg position demands exceptional hip flexor flexibility, core stability, and an upright torso to press overhead, making it one of the most demanding shoulder press variations. It directly reveals and addresses postural weaknesses in the overhead pressing pattern.

execution.starting_position: Sit on the floor with legs extended straight ahead. Hold a barbell at shoulder height in a front-rack or press-width grip. The torso must be completely vertical with no lean.
execution.setup_instructions: Begin with a significantly reduced load. Tight hamstrings or hip flexors will cause the torso to lean back, defeating the purpose of the exercise.
steps: Step 1: Sit tall with legs extended, barbell at shoulder height.
Step 2: Brace the core hard to maintain an upright torso.
Step 3: Press the bar straight overhead, keeping the elbows slightly forward.
Step 4: Lock out the arms completely overhead.
Step 5: Return the bar to the shoulder position under control. Repeat.
execution.breathing_instructions: Exhale as you press, inhale on the descent.
common_mistakes: Leaning backward during the press — the torso must remain vertical throughout
Failing to lock out at the top
Insufficient hip flexor mobility causing the legs to come off the floor
safety_considerations: If unable to sit with an upright torso and legs extended, work on hamstring and hip flexor flexibility before loading this movement
Use a spotter or spotter arms if training heavy
execution.range_of_motion_guidance: Full lockout overhead. Barbell returns to shoulder level on the descent.
coaching_cues: Sit up straight — imagine a wall behind you
No lean back during the press
Legs stay flat on the floor

name: Z-Press with Barbell (Snatch Grip)
description: The snatch-grip Z-press uses an extra-wide overhand grip on the barbell while seated on the floor, requiring the bar to travel overhead with the wide grip that characterizes the snatch lift. This variation trains the deltoids and trapezius through a wide-grip pressing pattern while the floor position eliminates leg drive, making it an effective strength quality exercise for Olympic lifters and overhead athletes seeking to develop overhead stability with snatch-width grip.

execution.starting_position: Sit on the floor with legs extended. Grip the barbell in snatch-width grip (at the outer knurling marks). Hold at shoulder height.
execution.setup_instructions: This requires both shoulder mobility and hip/hamstring flexibility. Assess mobility requirements before loading. Light to moderate weight only.
steps: Step 1: Sit tall with legs extended, barbell at shoulder level in snatch grip.
Step 2: Press the barbell straight overhead.
Step 3: At lockout, the wide grip means the bar is directly above and slightly behind the head.
Step 4: Lower under control to shoulder level.
Step 5: Maintain upright torso — no lean.
execution.breathing_instructions: Exhale pressing. Inhale descending.
common_mistakes: Grip narrower than true snatch width — defeats the purpose
Leaning back — requires core strength and hamstring flexibility to stay upright
safety_considerations: Assess shoulder external rotation range before attempting snatch grip overhead work
Light loads only — the wide grip is mechanically disadvantaged
execution.range_of_motion_guidance: Shoulder height to full snatch-grip overhead lockout.
coaching_cues: Grip at snatch width — hands on the outer knurling
Upright torso — legs stay flat
Elbows fully locked at the top

name: Z-Press with Dumbbells (Neutral Grip)
description: The dumbbell neutral-grip Z-press is performed seated on the floor with legs extended, pressing dumbbells overhead with palms facing each other. The floor-seated position eliminates leg drive and forces upright torso posture via hamstring and hip flexor flexibility demands. The neutral grip is more comfortable for many trainees than the standard pronated Z-press grip, reducing wrist and elbow stress while maintaining the same shoulder loading pattern.

execution.starting_position: Sit on the floor with legs fully extended straight in front. Hold dumbbells at shoulder height with a neutral (hammer) grip. Sit upright — torso perpendicular to the floor.
execution.setup_instructions: If hamstring tightness prevents an upright torso, perform with a slight back support initially. Moderate weight — the floor position eliminates leg drive entirely.
steps: Step 1: Begin seated upright on the floor, dumbbells at shoulder height neutral grip.
Step 2: Press both dumbbells overhead, maintaining neutral wrist position.
Step 3: At full lockout, shrug the traps slightly into the top position.
Step 4: Lower under control back to shoulder level.
Step 5: Maintain upright torso throughout — no leaning back.
execution.breathing_instructions: Exhale pressing. Inhale on the descent.
common_mistakes: Leaning back as the press becomes difficult — the upright position is non-negotiable
Feet rotating or legs lifting — legs stay flat on the floor
safety_considerations: Adequate hamstring flexibility required — do not force a rounded-back position
Build up load slowly — no leg drive means lower absolute loads
execution.range_of_motion_guidance: Shoulder height to full overhead lockout.
coaching_cues: Sit tall — no lean
Legs flat and relaxed
Drive the weights straight overhead

name: Zercher Bulgarian Split Squat
description: A Bulgarian split squat variation where the barbell is cradled in the crooks of the elbows rather than placed across the upper back. The Zercher position forces a more upright torso, increases core bracing demands significantly, and shifts loading stress away from the spine while still providing strong quadriceps and glute stimulus.

execution.starting_position: Stand in a split stance with the rear foot elevated on a bench. Cradle the barbell in the crooks of both elbows, holding your forearms parallel to the floor.
execution.setup_instructions: Set a barbell to roughly waist height in a rack. Cradle it in your elbow crooks, secure the grip, then walk to the bench and position your rear foot on it.
steps: Step 1: Brace your core hard and keep your torso upright throughout the movement.
Step 2: Lower your rear knee toward the floor by bending both knees, maintaining an upright torso.
Step 3: Descend until the front thigh is at or below parallel to the floor.
Step 4: Drive through the front heel to return to the starting position, fully extending the front hip and knee.
execution.breathing_instructions: Inhale and brace before descending. Exhale at the top after completing the rep.
common_mistakes: Letting the torso collapse forward under the Zercher load
Allowing the front knee to cave inward during the ascent
safety_considerations: The Zercher position can stress the forearms and biceps tendons — use padding if needed and avoid very heavy loads initially
execution.range_of_motion_guidance: Lower until the front thigh is parallel to the floor or below. Keep the rear shin roughly vertical.
coaching_cues: Chest up, elbows forward
Drive the floor away with your front heel

name: Zercher Carry
description: A loaded carry performed with the barbell cradled in the elbow crooks in the Zercher position. The Zercher carry uniquely combines anterior core bracing, bicep and forearm endurance, and lower body locomotion, making it a comprehensive full-body conditioning and strength exercise.

execution.starting_position: Cradle a barbell in the elbow crooks with forearms parallel to the floor. Stand tall and walk.
execution.setup_instructions: Set a barbell at waist height in a rack. Cradle it in the elbow crooks, secure the grip, then step back to begin walking.
steps: Step 1: Brace the core hard and stand tall with the bar cradled in the elbows.
Step 2: Walk forward for the prescribed distance with controlled steps.
Step 3: Keep the torso upright — do not allow excessive forward lean.
Step 4: At the end of the distance, carefully return the bar to the rack.
execution.breathing_instructions: Breathe steadily throughout the walk. Use short rhythmic breaths.
common_mistakes: Allowing the torso to fold forward under the weight
Taking overly long strides that destabilize the carry
safety_considerations: The bar will press into the forearms — use padding if skin tenderness is an issue
Return the bar to the rack safely — do not drop it
execution.range_of_motion_guidance: Walk for 10-30 meters or the prescribed distance while maintaining the Zercher position.
coaching_cues: Chest up, elbows forward
Walk tall and breathe

name: Zercher Carry (Strongman)
description: A loaded carry where the barbell is held in the crook of the elbows against the forearms in the Zercher position. This squat-like carry places tremendous demand on the anterior chain, upper back, and biceps. The low center of gravity and awkward position build functional carrying strength.

execution.starting_position: Set up for Zercher Carry in proper strongman position.
execution.setup_instructions: Prepare all equipment and body position for Zercher Carry.
steps: Step 1: Load barbell in rack at hip height. Cradle bar in elbow creases.
Step 2: Lift bar from rack and step back. Set feet at walking width.
Step 3: Walk with controlled steps keeping bar stable in arms.
Step 4: Maintain upright torso throughout the carry distance.
execution.breathing_instructions: Brace core maximally before every lift. Breathe between reps if needed.
common_mistakes: Letting the bar roll out of elbows
Excessive forward lean
safety_considerations: Use collars on all loaded barbells.
Ensure clear path for carries.
Have spotters for overhead movements.
execution.range_of_motion_guidance: Full range of motion specific to the implement being used.
coaching_cues: Brace hard and keep torso tall
Pads on bar if elbow pain occurs

name: Zercher Deadlift
description: A deadlift variation where the barbell is cradled in the elbow crooks rather than held in the hands. The Zercher deadlift shifts loading anteriorly, reduces spinal shear forces compared to a conventional deadlift, and significantly increases core stability demand while still training the entire posterior chain.

execution.starting_position: Squat down and cradle a barbell in the elbow crooks at approximately knee height. Bar is on the floor or set at a low height.
execution.setup_instructions: Set the barbell in a rack at knee height or use it from the floor. Squat down and position the bar in the elbow crooks before lifting.
steps: Step 1: Brace the core and keep the torso as upright as possible.
Step 2: Drive through the floor to stand, extending the hips and knees simultaneously.
Step 3: Lock out at the top with hips and knees fully extended.
Step 4: Lower the bar back to the starting position under control.
execution.breathing_instructions: Inhale and brace before the pull. Exhale at lockout.
common_mistakes: Rounding the lower back due to insufficient core bracing
Allowing the elbows to drop, losing the bar
safety_considerations: The Zercher position puts pressure on the forearms — use padding if needed
This is not a maximum-strength lift — use moderate loads
execution.range_of_motion_guidance: Full hip and knee extension at lockout. Bar controlled to the starting position on the return.
coaching_cues: Drive the elbows up to hold the bar
Stand tall at the top

name: Zercher Deadlift from Floor
description: The Zercher deadlift is a variation in which the barbell is lifted from the floor using the crooks of the elbows (antecubital fossa) rather than the hands. The lifter squats down, positions the elbows under and around the bar, then stands up with the bar cradled in the bent arms. This unusual loading position places the barbell closer to the body's center of mass than a conventional deadlift and dramatically increases core and upper back demands. It is a full-body strength exercise that is particularly useful for athletes who need to train the hip and knee extension pattern with strong anterior core bracing.

execution.starting_position: The barbell is set on the floor. The lifter squats down and positions the arms under the bar so it rests in the crooks of both elbows (antecubital fossa). The hands may clasp together in front.
execution.setup_instructions: Begin with a very light barbell — the elbow contact is uncomfortable with heavy loads. Use straps or padding around the bar to protect the inner elbows initially.
steps: Step 1: Position the barbell in the crooks of both elbows, squatting down to reach it. Clasp the hands together.
Step 2: Take a deep breath, brace the core hard, and begin the pull by driving through the feet.
Step 3: Keep the barbell close to the body as it rises. The elbows pull upward and inward.
Step 4: Stand to full hip and knee extension. Lower the bar back to the floor under control.
execution.breathing_instructions: Inhale and brace before the pull. Exhale at the top or in a controlled manner during the descent.
common_mistakes: Rounding the upper back — the elbows must stay high throughout
Letting the bar swing away from the body
Using too much weight before the elbow contact is tolerated — progress load gradually
safety_considerations: The inner elbow contact can be uncomfortable or cause bruising with heavy loads — use bar padding initially
Avoid if elbow or wrist injuries are present
execution.range_of_motion_guidance: Full deadlift range — floor to full standing extension.
coaching_cues: Keep the elbows high — imagine pulling the elbows toward each other under the bar
Drive the floor away — feel the leg drive as much as the hip hinge
Brace hard — the core demand in a Zercher is significantly higher than a conventional deadlift

name: Zercher Squat
description: The Zercher squat is performed with the barbell cradled in the crooks of the elbows at the front of the torso, requiring a very upright posture and strong isometric bicep and upper back engagement. This unusual loading position keeps the center of mass close to the body, promotes a deep, upright squat, and places significant demand on the core. It is an effective alternative for those with shoulder limitations that prevent front or back rack positions.

execution.starting_position: Set the barbell in a rack at mid-torso height. Squat under the bar and position it in the crooks of your elbows by bending your arms to 90°. Clasp your hands together in front. Stand to unrack, then step back.
execution.setup_instructions: Set the safety bars at a height allowing you to get the bar into your elbow crooks easily. Padding on the bar or wearing long sleeves reduces discomfort on the forearms and inner elbows.
steps: Step 1: Stand with feet shoulder-width apart, toes pointed out, holding the bar in your elbow crooks with arms bent and clasped together.
Step 2: Brace your core hard and keep your chest tall as you initiate the squat by simultaneously pushing the knees out and sitting the hips down.
Step 3: Descend to at least parallel or as deep as mobility allows while keeping the torso upright.
Step 4: Drive through the full foot to return to standing. Keep the elbows elevated throughout to prevent the bar from dropping.
Step 5: Exhale at the top and reset the brace before the next repetition.
execution.breathing_instructions: Inhale and brace before the descent. Hold through the squat. Exhale at the top.
common_mistakes: Allowing the elbows to drop, which causes the torso to pitch forward
Rounding the upper back under the load
Using excessively heavy weight before adapting to the discomfort of the bar on the arms
safety_considerations: The bar can be dropped forward in a failed rep — use bumper plates when training alone
Start with light weight to acclimate to the bar position on the forearms
Elbow padding or a bar pad reduces bruising during adaptation
execution.range_of_motion_guidance: Aim for parallel or below while maintaining an upright torso without lumbar rounding.
coaching_cues: Keep your elbows pointing forward — don't let them drop to your sides
Chest up, sit between your knees
Drive through your heels and midfoot equally

name: Zercher Yoke Walk
description: A yoke walk variation where the bar is held in the Zercher (elbow crease) position rather than on the shoulders. This eliminates neck and shoulder stress while increasing anterior chain, bicep, and core demand. The Zercher grip is preferred by some strongman athletes for comfort.

execution.starting_position: Set up for Zercher Yoke Walk in proper strongman position.
execution.setup_instructions: Prepare all equipment and body position for Zercher Yoke Walk.
steps: Step 1: Position yoke bar in elbow creases at appropriate height.
Step 2: Stand and step clear of rack with controlled movement.
Step 3: Walk briskly with quick, controlled steps for target distance.
Step 4: Set yoke down with control at the end of walk.
execution.breathing_instructions: Brace core maximally before every lift. Breathe between reps if needed.
common_mistakes: Slow shuffling steps
Leaning excessively forward
safety_considerations: Use collars on all loaded barbells.
Ensure clear path for carries.
Have spotters for overhead movements.
execution.range_of_motion_guidance: Full range of motion specific to the implement being used.
coaching_cues: Quick controlled steps win events
Keep the bar tight to body

name: Zercher Yoke Walk with Chains
description: A Zercher yoke walk with chains added to the implement for accommodating resistance. The chains increase weight as the athlete stands taller and decrease weight in the bottom position. This variation trains the entire walk with varied loading and builds lockout strength.

execution.starting_position: Set up for Zercher Yoke Walk with Chains in proper strongman position.
execution.setup_instructions: Prepare all equipment and body position for Zercher Yoke Walk with Chains.
steps: Step 1: Attach chains to Zercher yoke. Cradle yoke in elbow creases.
Step 2: Stand and step clear of rack as chains lift from floor.
Step 3: Walk briskly as chains swing and provide dynamic resistance.
Step 4: Set down at end of walk managing chain pendulum motion.
execution.breathing_instructions: Brace core maximally before every lift. Breathe between reps if needed.
common_mistakes: Walking too fast increasing chain swing
Losing Zercher position
safety_considerations: Use collars on all loaded barbells.
Ensure clear path for carries.
Have spotters for overhead movements.
execution.range_of_motion_guidance: Full range of motion specific to the implement being used.
coaching_cues: Smooth steps reduce chain oscillation
Keep elbows tight to cradle bar

name: Zero-Incline Chest-Supported Row
description: The zero-incline (fully flat/horizontal) chest-supported row places the bench at zero degrees, requiring the lifter to row the dumbbells from a fully horizontal prone position. With the torso fully parallel to the floor, the row produces a more vertical pull than inclined versions, heavily recruiting the lower lats and teres major and minimizing upper trap contribution — an ideal configuration for lower lat development.

execution.starting_position: Elevate a flat bench on two sturdy platforms (boxes, plates, or steps) so that the arms can hang below bench level when lying flat. Lie prone on the bench. Hold a dumbbell in each hand hanging beneath the bench.
execution.setup_instructions: The bench must be elevated enough that full arm extension allows the dumbbells to hang below bench height. Usually 30-50 cm elevation is sufficient depending on arm length and dumbbell size.
steps: Step 1: Begin lying flat, arms hanging down with dumbbells below bench level.
Step 2: Row both dumbbells toward the hips simultaneously, driving elbows back.
Step 3: At peak, hold 1 second.
Step 4: Lower under full control back to full arm extension.
Step 5: Maintain flat body position throughout — no hip extension or arch.
execution.breathing_instructions: Exhale on the row. Inhale on the descent.
common_mistakes: Bench not elevated enough — the dumbbells must clear the floor at full extension
Elbows flaring wide — keep them moderately tucked for lower lat emphasis
safety_considerations: Ensure the elevated bench setup is stable before loading
Head position: neutral — no craning
execution.range_of_motion_guidance: Full arm extension (dumbbells below bench) to elbows behind torso.
coaching_cues: Row to the hips, not the chest
Elbows track alongside the torso
Feel the lower lat at the bottom stretch

name: Zottmann Curl
description: The Zottmann curl is a dumbbell curl variation that uses a supinated (underhand) grip on the way up and pronates to an overhand grip on the way down. This technique effectively trains the biceps brachii during the concentric curl and the brachioradialis and forearm extensors during the controlled pronated eccentric. It is a time-efficient method for developing the full upper arm musculature in a single movement.

execution.starting_position: Stand upright holding dumbbells at the sides with a supinated (underhand) grip. Arms fully extended, feet shoulder-width apart.
execution.setup_instructions: Select moderate dumbbells — lighter than your standard curl weight since you will be controlling the eccentric in a pronated position.
steps: Step 1: Hold dumbbells at the sides with a supinated grip. Stand tall, upper arms at the sides.
Step 2: Exhale and curl the dumbbells upward with a supinated grip (biceps curl) to full contraction at shoulder level.
Step 3: At the top, rotate the wrists 180 degrees into a pronated (overhand) grip.
Step 4: Inhale and slowly lower the dumbbells back to the starting position in the pronated position, then rotate back to supinated for the next rep.
execution.breathing_instructions: Exhale on the curl up; inhale on the pronated lowering.
common_mistakes: Rushing the rotation at the top — perform it deliberately and smoothly
Lowering too quickly in the pronated position — the eccentric is where the forearm work happens
safety_considerations: Avoid excessive wrist pronation if pain is felt in the elbow — use lighter weight
execution.range_of_motion_guidance: Full extension at start; full curl at top; full controlled descent in pronated grip.
coaching_cues: Biceps up, reverse grip down — that is the cue for the two-phase movement
Make the rotation at the top smooth — your forearms rotate, not your whole arm
